Tekken on PC, + great perfomance!

Okay, so Tekken 7 makes its debut on pc. below are my impressions after beeting story mode and one online match:
1 My system specs:  my specs are 8gbram 2400, 8tb hd, i7700k, gtx1080ti. 55' 4k tv.
2. Port Quality:
The game is ported gracefully, I am enjoying 60fps on 4k. never a frame drop,
I did CTD once. aside from this, I really have no complaints about the porting part
3: Content:
There is main story chapters and then individual characters chapters. Vs mode, practice mode, online matches (ranked or not) are all there too, there is a treasure mode which you play to get fight money to customize your characters. customization is also quite satisfactory, as you can customize hair, clothes and accessories (even Akuma!!).
4: The Akuma factor:
I have to say that when I knew they would throw Akuma on this game I was very worried about balancing, and well, they did it just great, you don't feel he is overpowered and even though he has all SF moves,  you will probably lose if you play him the same way you do on SF.
5: Online Matches:
I searched 3 times for online matches, only once I managed to find an opponent, maybe because I choose connection 4 from any to 5 on a quality scale. the match was flawless.
6: I'm not very good at reviews, anyway I wanted to write something to you guys.
Conclusion: It looks beautiful and plays like the old Tekken, so if you enjoy tekken, yes, you need this.
Ps: When you play with Akuma you just wish that SF 5 were made by Namco, can't wait for Tekken Vs Street Fighter!!

Deponia is a point-and-click adventure reminiscent of the infamous Monkey Island series. The game is part of a trilogy (Deponia -> Chaos On Deponia -> Goodbye Deponia). You play Rufus, the archetypical anti-hero whose bad jokes are only matched by his failed attempts to leave his junk covered planet Deponia. While the story unfolds you will be busy searching that single missing item to progress, creating thought provoking item combinations and solving mind boggling puzzles. All-in-all an entertaining game, but certainly not up to par with Monkey Island. Good enough to start playing Chaos On Deponia. :)

It's perfect.
DOOM 3 is truly a masterpiece, the graphics, the atmosphere, the shooting, it's grimy, it's gritty, it's evil and not cartoony at all, the way DOOM should be. Now I'm playing it with the 'Doom 3 Redux mod', which doesn't touch gameplay at all, it simply adds cooler sounds and better textures, nothing wrong upgrading a 2004 game visually, so I definitely recommend adding this mod if you never played the game before, still even without the mod, it's perfect, but I think this mod really modernizes it, better gun sounds (blasting imps and zombies with a shotgun has never been so fun), better graphics, better textures, gameplay unaffected = perfect.
Anyways, what to say about the game. It's truly a real DOOM game, it starts slow like the Knee Deep in Dead episode from DOOM 1993 and slowly picks up the pace. You'll face the same monster traps, hallways, UAC base, Mars, Hell, the same demons, keycard hunting, lockers, maze levels, action you experienced in the original DOOM.
To me it's a real DOOM game, and never understood the haters who say it isn't. It has horror elements yes, but this game is NOT a survival horror game. You don't "survive" scrounging for supplies and setting up camp fires, hiding, surviving, you take that shotgun and blast those demon f.ucks straight to hell! DOOM guy is badass in this game as well, don't let people who don't understand DOOM tell you otherwise. I've always enjoyed it and just recently bought it on steam again because DOOM 3 I bought back in 2004 is still in my hometown.
I enjoy all DOOMs, and DOOM 2016 is a great game as well and a real DOOM game as well don't get me wrong, but don't exclude this masterpiece from the series saying it sucks. I say try it! If you don't like it, you can always refund it.
Also, this game has some crazy mods as well, people were very creative with it so when you finish the game you can play numerous cool mods, there's even a mod where someone remade Quake 1 in this, it owns!

Short: This FPS is FUN.
If you love FPS and previously have you never played Doom 3, you're not going to be disappointed.
After all those years Doom 3 still is impressive.
In 2004 the most anticipated shooters were Doom 3 (August) and Half Life 2 (November).  With a couple of interesting surprises in March with the release of Far Cry and Painkiller in April. All these shooters had their pros and cons and very different game mechanics. Far Cry a kind of open world in the jungle with fun explosions and vehicles, HL2 with the gravity gun and physics and Doom 3 with its dark levels.
From all of them Doom 3 was the most criticized: because scripted enemies, graphics too dark, the flashlight was not mounted with the gun, no vehicles, not elaborated story like HL2 and so on. One year after F.E.A.R. was released in November and was better acclaimed.
However, Doom 3 has aged pretty well (in comparison Far Cry and F.E.A.R. they look boring now) you can find mods for everything: Textures, gameplay, guns, sounds, enemies, sp levels, blood and a long etc.
Graphically you have texture mods to upgrade textures to modern standards: Absolute HD, Redux, SikkMod (my personal favorite is Redux) the levels are well designed, fun, claustrophobic and dark (I recommend playing at night).
Gameplay: Frenetic shooting depending on how fast you advance your guns never will stop shooting
with impeccable gun mechanics and gameplay created an awesome FPS that still nowadays is really fun to play. And once that you finish you keep begging for more.
Audio: 5.1 is a must because Doom 3 has impressive Reverb effects.
It dosen't work as a doom game but as a slow paced shooter with a slight horror theme itäs perfect.

First a word of caution for all those who don't plan on buying a 360 controller:
This game is indeed at parts unplayable without a proper two-stick joypad.
I found in my drawer, an old Mega Drive-fashioned joypad that came with a 3.5" floppy and after installing the x360ce wrapper , mapping as many as keys as possible to it, I started doing thumb, pinky and elbow acrobatics trying to achieve simple things. It was long, repetitive, and challenging. Lots of falling off cliffs why trying to keep all my 12 fingers working but towards the end (and it took me many days to reach that - much more than the 3 hours that steam reports)) I realized that most of the time it's much easier NOT to use a joypad (unless you have a 360 one in which case the game is indeed short). There are 2-3 points where you have to use a pad, but for the most part it's more playble with the keyboard. So key that in mind.
Having said all that, the game was a beauty! Crazy graphics, crazy world. A sad story, but a nice one nonetheless and not too cliche. The game is short (unless you handicap yourself with the abovementioned tricks) but the whole world is so rewarding that you could think it as a beatiful interactive movie (and much longer one). With that in mind, it's worth any price (let's say below 20euro)!

This game is...something else.  I hesitate to call it fun, because Brothers deals with some HEAVY issues.  Questioning suicide, survivor's guilt, responsibility of children to their parents, and familial loyalty, Brothers does not stray away from dark subject matter.  Yet, what makes this game so amazing is that there is no spoken dialogue.  It's all done through pantomime and the made up language of the world.  It's a story told through actions rather than through words and...not gonna lie, it made me cry.
The game focuses on using a controller with dual analogue sticks.  Each stick controls one of the two brothers and they have to work together to make their way through several sections of puzzle.  It's not too hard to figure out, but it can be weird trying to control both at once.
Gameplay aside, there is a haunting score attached to this piece and a gorgeous art style, with a real sense of scale, showing off desolated villages with an invisible monster prowling around, an abandoned castle of giants, a field of fallen soldiers, each the size of a mountain, and that's not the half of it.  The game is a wonder to explore, but it's hard to call it fun.  It is very engaging, but the heavy subject matter make it a very somber affair.
I think every real gamer needs to give this a try...just be read to cry when the moment comes, because Brothers will touch you in a way most games can only try.

Pros:
- Only one person needs to own the game
- Brings pen and paper games to a visual medium
- Easy to play for gamers and non gamers
- Allows for roleplaying your character (by reading the script) from choices you make that are known to your friends or only to yourself
- Personal quests that your group doesn't know about unless you tell them
- The mobile app is a great for unclutering the screen and allows everyone to zone into their character sheet at any time without pausing the game. (you can have your character set to follow)
- Player trading of items and resources
Cons:
- Occasional difficulty spikes with groups of less than 3 players
- Character attributes like agility, shrouding, scholar, etc are not explained as to what they do and makes leveling very confusing
- Text on a mobile device is small. I have a Nexus 5. I would suggest using a tablet if you have one.
- The camera has areas that it gravitates to rather than follow the players at times which can be annoying when trying to check corners for loot.
- No cloud saving
Other:
- A lot of lore in the game pushes its way into the story and player character interactions. Like you are forced into a history lesson that has very little to no impact on what is happening.
- Graphicly meh. There is noticable clipping of models and lack of more fluid object rigging which is a little annoying to see as someone who has a graphics background.
- There are no items in the tradition sense of looting gear like armor and swords. All upgrades to your character are done in the upgrade trees
PSA: This is a not a kids game. It's probably the prettiest game I've ever played and cute and painterly but, I repeat, it's not a kids game.

at first,
i joined my voice to the negative reviews in hope that Ubisoft or Uplay would fix the online issues and present a better online experience.. however, after hours of good matches without any of those issues, i am reluctant to keep my review in the negative category..
UNO is a great card game.. and i purchased this game despite of the amount of Negative Reviews it has receieved..
UNO is my favourite since my early childhood; and a deck of UNO cards is always ready in my living room for almost 2 decades.. but as friends grew apart, i can only play UNO online with people whom i've never met before..
in my initial review,
i gave UNO a 3/5 or a C-..
but after few hours playing this game, i can give it a revised review of 4/5 or a B+..
the BIGGEST complaint about the game, is the online mutliplayer part of the game.. it is where you get most of the connection errors..
some as simple as being kicked out from a match in mid-game, and some as critical as closing the frozen game using the Task Manager (by pressing CTRL ALT and Delete)..
`
during online matches, i had the following:
- 20% of the matches, i was kicked out from a match without an explanation..
- 5% of the matches, i had a 'timed-out error' message..
- 4% of the matches, the game had frozen on me that i had to use CTRL+ALT+DEL to escape the game..
- 1% of the matches, i had "UNO.EXE has stopped working" error message..
so 3 out of 10 online matches, i was rudely interrupted from the game.. but 7 out of 10 matches, the game ran smoothly without any errors..
there are certain hours during the day, when those errors were completely gone.. but there are some hours when all the above occured around the same hour..
`
now let me talk about the positive aspects of the game..
- the game is fun.. i had a big wide smile on my face playing this game.. Rabbids is definitely a great feature in the game that i have never experienced before..
- in the online multiplayer menu, you can join any random match that is already on the way.. or you can create your own match, of which you can choose which of sets of rules to keep in the game.. for example: you can turn-off the 0-7 swap-card feature, and switch on the 'No Bluff' feature..
and then you can decide whether to make the match open for anyone to join in, or keep it private for only-friends to join in..
`
if you have created a open match, with only you and one other player in the game.. you can choose to start the game with bots to fill the other 2 positions.. and within minutes, other people will replace those bots..
people can move-in and out anytime during a match replacing the bots or being replaced by bots.. and this happens smoothly..
`
3 out 10 matches, i had error messages while playing online.. and i can COMPLETELY understand why people are so critical of Ubisoft and Uplay..
when the game freezes on you, and when you are being kicked-out from a very long challenging match, you are within your right to feel offended and outraged..
but then, you'll have those long matches where everything works as it should be.. so you will have the biggest smile on your face playing UNO..
this game could have been 5/5 or an A-, if Ubisoft and Uplay can address the issued in this game.. and of they could find a way to introduce in-game chat-box to chat with other players..
but because of those connection issues.. i give it a 4/5..

Spelunky is a great game if you want to bring out the gamer rage in all of your friends.
Do you like one-hit kills? How about procedural level designs that make some tasks impossible? Do you like enemies killing you in completely unfair ways and often losing as a result of conditions outside of your control? Then you'll love Spelunky.
The redeeming quality about Spelunky is that it's as much skill as it is luck. Yes, there are those rare times where death in unavoidable, or progress is impossible, but most times, player coordination and timing can make or break a run.
My biggest complaint is how often you'll find one-hit kills: Anything explosive (enemy bombs, friendly bombs, orange toads, enemy spaceships, psychic aliens, psychic Anubis, psychic alien queen, and landmines, plasma cannon), man-eating plants, traps DESIGNED to crush you, shopkeeper shotguns, floor spikes, spike traps, lava, teleportation, and anything that can repeatedly attack you while your Spelunker is laying on the ground, recovering.
With how much progress Spelunky demands you make, it makes dying feel incredibly cheap and unwarranted.
Despite all that, Spelunky is still incredibly fun and majorly addictive. Buy it, play it, and scream at it when you lose because you just stepped a little too close to something you shouldn't have, and your glorious run comes to a screeching halt.
Fun but there's no denying there's some artificial difficulty going on here, mkay spelunklords?

Spelunky is a procedurally generated “rogue-lite” platformer With a wide variety of well thought out enemies and powerups that can be used or countered in multiple ways.
It’s unforgiving but rewarding with a depth that takes time to master and a worldwide daily challenge map that gives every player one shot at getting the top score on exactly the same map it keeps you coming back again & again trying to avoid yet another stupid death and delve deeper into the catacombs.

Spelunky has been among my favourite games since the free standalone PC version. This version has some additional bells & whistles (most notably, improved graphics), but remains essentially the same experience. Make no mistake, though - the fun alone makes it worthy of its price.
Spelunky may be not your cup of tea, in that it is a difficult game where you die all the time and things often get out of hand. However, it is not as frustrating as most games of this variety, because there is no hand waving, design shortcuts, or plain old "illusion of agency" here. This game is for real. It is a system. You can learn it. You can take advantage of it. You can develop a strategy. You can turn its (deliberate) quirks into tools. And when you die (yes, you will die), for once you will know exactly why it happened, and how to do better next time.

Verdict (tl;dr): 9/10 The game is awesome. In fact, I think it might just be the best fighting game I have ever played. Not 10 out of 10, because it has some things missing. Do not let the low user review rating decieve you: most of the negative reviews don't review the game, but only its launch.
Gameplay and combat: Gameplay is the most important aspect of a fighting game. And in this field Mortal Kombat X truly shines. The movesets are interesting and fluid, and the fights have a really nice pace. The combat mechanisms are a little bit more complex than in MK9, which in my opinion is a good thing, but then again, kombos are pretty easy to learn, so something for everyone here. As a downside some of the moves allow some very cheesy tactics, but this is common in fighting games in general.
All the characters have three different stances from which you pick one before the fight. The stances change some special moves and the way the character is played. Its impact differs from character to character.
Story: No spoilers here, but the story is good for a fighting game. It's not a novel by G.R.R. Martin, but it kept me interested. I was actually surprised how well some of the characters were written.
Roster: The roster is missing out some characters I would have loved to play (for example Baraka), but it's not a huge issue. The game and story has to move forward, right? All in all the roster is full of interesting characters, and some of the new ones really shine.
Performance: Some people have had big performance issues, but I for one get a solid 60fps and everything has been smooth on high settings after I updated to amd's newest beta CCC (Rig: i5 3570k, HD7950 3gb, 8gb ram). There should be more options, for example more AA options. Now there's only FXAA which some people find bad.
Multiplayer: Sometimes it takes a long, long time to find a ranked match online, which sucks. Other than that the online matches have been good. Local multiplayer feels very limited. Tag teams are missing. I would also want to be able to form a local multiplayer team and fight online against other teams. But no.

Deponia is vaguely amusing. Forget comparisons to Terry Pratchett, Deponia is far more firmly based in the ground of a Piers Anthony novel. It excels in slapstick, crudity and vague jokes in reference to science and technology yet lacks the aplomb and depth that Pratchett conveys.
As a game, it works well... the inventory system is effective, the navigation easy to grasp and the puzzles significantly *puzzling* with hints that are not overly obvious yet definitely helpful for someone paying attention.
Graphically the game is most certainly comical, the character designs and environments well executed in terms of conveying character and atmosphere. However even on a system that exceeds specifications I did occasionally experience a drop in frame rate that threw out the animated voice synchronisation which was slightly offputting.
In terms of sound the games is interesting, each animation and area has it's own unique sound, and the music is again... amusing and in keeping with the satirical elements of the game.
However Deponia amused me, it did not quite captivate me as I hoped it would. I enjoyed the puzzles, and the graphics but the story simply failed to grab me. Perhaps this is slightly due to the characterization of Rufus. As much as he is meant to be an egotistical, narcissist incapable of helping others, it's not exactly an engaging sort of character to play. He ended up annoying me rather than maintaining my interest. As for Goal, the "heroine" she lies docile and helpless most of the time, the old archetype of the damsel in distress, so I couldn't even engage with desire to help her... who wants to save a lifeless body in a white jumpsuit... because that's pretty much Goal's character for most of the game?? (or perhaps that's just the feminist critic speaking)
Plotline and characterization issues aside... Deponia does still manage to be fun to play, mainly because of the excellent level designs and puzzles.
So I still recommend it as a fun game to play.

"S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Clear Sky" - Review
Gameplay:  6/10
This second installment "Clear sky" leaves something to be desired. Some elements were indeed improved upon such as weapons: dynamics, upgrade-ability and inaccuracy. The use of image blurring also added more depth. This certainly made the game much more fun. A slightly larger world (even though some of it is lifted straight out of the first game) was just what it needed.These things worked well.
They've taken the game to an exciting new level by going deeper into the RPG genre (e.g. goods trading etc) which unfortunately has come at the expense of the 'first person shooter' gameplay, and the game suffers for it. It's no-longer balanced; it simply doesn't flow as well as it's predecessor. Going from story to action feels like segments of contrived scenarios of RPG then FPS then RPG then FPS. Even though things happen in-game and around the map without me being there (living world) overall it leaves me feeling more like I'm being taken for a ride rather than being an integral part that sways the flow and outcome.
By half way into the game the shoot outs were predicable and by the end of the game the shooting scenes were frustrating unless you have upgraded armor and guns.
Initially it seems like a lesser game than the first one but it gets better the more you play it. It's not a bad game; if you can forgive it's minor short comings it can still be lots and lots of fun.
Game ambiance: 7/10
Standard S.T.A.L.K.E.R. ambiance which is nice as expected. Leaves, birds, rain, wind and weather.
Reliability/Stability: 4/10
Installation was easy enough (both DVD and Steam versions) but in-game there quite a few bugs. Some around AI, the faction wars and some were graphics related. Stability hugely varies depending on the PC.
Story/Plot: 4/10
There were some new ideas expressed which were a lot of fun. However, once you strip away the faction wars and take a good look at the story there's not much there, the overall plot was weak and lacked depth which added to the games segregated feel.
While there is a bit of a twist (if you can call it a twist... more like an interesting angle) i don't much care for it. All i can say without giving anything away is that I felt like all my work in the first S.T.A.L.K.E.R. game was done for nothing, and then undone.
Concept: 8/10
I get the impression that at the beginning of the "clear sky" project the game developers had a good range of ideas, then somewhere along the line they got lost in what can only be described as a quagmire of loose ends and poorly finished tid-bits.
Concept execution: 6/10
Is should have been a well rounded, a matured concept.
Faction wars extend what could have been a short game into an epic one. The novelty of joining factions was fun initially but when it eventually looses it's luster you realise the only motivation for acquiring money in the first place is for weapons. Which is OK, big guns are cool.
The AI is a little better but buggy; rather than going around you the AI guys push you out of their way and straight into the line of fire.
Textures: 8/10
The textures were a great improvement on the first game. There is a warmer feel, they are more sharp and use some more modern features. Although the settings will have to by played with to get optimum results.
I love that the PC's in the game use Norton Commander.
Modelling: 7/10
There really weren't many new elements (most were from the first game). What it does have looks good though.
Graphics: 8/10
The graphics are a vast improvement; 'Clear sky' does blend each element better than the first game and it certainly added to the overall look and feel. Even though the draw distance could have been greater.
That being said, there could have been much more work done in the way of OOP. As on many systems there is a huge draw of resources for graphics that shouldn't require it.
Sound: 7/10
Sound too was an improvement compared to the first game. Clean, clear, crisp.
Music: 5/10
The dynamics of the music was good even though the style was not my personal preference, but hey, it's art. There were some song elements that were from the first game and other songs that sound like songs from Mech Warrior: Mercenaries that didn't make the final cut.
Adjustable shadow mapping: No
Bonus/Extras:
Special edition comes with - Novel Book (Russian), Zone map, extras DVD, Instruction manual, bandana, zippo lighter, dog tag, poster, Russian calender circa 1985, random faction badge and a ball that lights up with S.T.A.L.K.E.R. on it.

Let me preface this short and light review by saying that this is my first review. I felt it necessary to express my positive thoughts and opinions on this fabulous game.
I've been a long time Diablo 2 fan, I played it when it was in it's prime and I was in my early - mid teens. The thought of a Diablo 3 was amazing to me. Unfortunately, when D3 actually dropped, it felt like a disappointment to me and left me yearning something that could scratch my ARPG itch.
Torchlight II is the scratch for that itch. This game is an incredible, top down action role-playing game. I'll give it to you in a brief PROS/CONS
PROS:
-Procedurally generated, and incredibly varied world
-Easily approachable and highly enjoyable multiplayer
-Item drops that really give a sense of power to the weapon and to the character
-Gorgeous cartoon styled graphics that really add to the light hearted, whimsical world of Torchlight
-Engrossing gameplay from start to end
-Infinitely varied end game possibilities with the Map Nexus
-Steam Community mods and add-ons
CONS:
-No voice acting. I know this isn't a legitimate negative, but I personally feel some extra time spent on voice acting really could have bolstered the experience.
-I really can't think of many cons.
In short, if you are looking for a really enjoyable and fun ARPG to play with your friends, by yourself, or with people online, then this game is certainly one to check out.

The original roguelike platformer, and still the best of the bunch.

Spelunky is a procedurally generated “rogue-lite” platformer With a wide variety of well thought out enemies and powerups that can be used or countered in multiple ways.
It’s unforgiving but rewarding with a depth that takes time to master and a worldwide daily challenge map that gives every player one shot at getting the top score on exactly the same map it keeps you coming back again & again trying to avoid yet another stupid death and delve deeper into the catacombs.

Spelunky has been among my favourite games since the free standalone PC version. This version has some additional bells & whistles (most notably, improved graphics), but remains essentially the same experience. Make no mistake, though - the fun alone makes it worthy of its price.
Spelunky may be not your cup of tea, in that it is a difficult game where you die all the time and things often get out of hand. However, it is not as frustrating as most games of this variety, because there is no hand waving, design shortcuts, or plain old "illusion of agency" here. This game is for real. It is a system. You can learn it. You can take advantage of it. You can develop a strategy. You can turn its (deliberate) quirks into tools. And when you die (yes, you will die), for once you will know exactly why it happened, and how to do better next time.

This game turned my girlfriend, a dungeons and dragons / pen and paper / rpg skeptic, into a fan. Who sat through the whole first episode in one go, and by the end was well into acting out our characters speach, and being a sly wee bint with the 'secret thoughts'.
I could leave it there, but I won't.
This game is a pen and paper RPG come to life. Your phone is your character sheet, and it tracks all the usual statistic you'd expect from a pen and paper rpg, as well as modern role playing games. Each class comes with a set of predetermined skills, abilities, and proficiencies. You use the phone to control your character, and take all your actions so as not to disturn the gameplay of the other players.
Dialogue for your character appears on your phone screen for you to act out, as do the choices you get to make. These are not shown to the other players, and allow you to make choices that you they can't see, and allows for some good crossed motivations and party interactions. As well as the dialogue being on your screen only, some of the npc interact secretly with your character by whispering to them, and these interactions are played out on your screen only and its at your discretion whether you share this with your party or not. The rest of the interactions are fully voice acted, and displayed to everyone on the main screen.
This game is tactically difficult at lower levels, and the random combat arena is fantastic. The different mixes of classes can make for so many strange encounter. There's a lot of synergy between the class abilities and affords good oportunities for teamwork.
The combat in the game is tense. With the relatively high power enemies vs hit point of your party, every encounter feels vested. In the higher levels of the combat arena we found ourselves actually cheering a Pyrrhic victory, much like my pen and paper group would.
The player character design is chunky. Your tank character feels like a tank, with exaggerated bulk  and huge shield. Your sneaky rogues are sleak, with short curt attack animations. The aestetic is perfect for the games style, and I really enjoyed it.
In truth, I can't speak highly enough of this game. As a dungeon master, as a player, as a video game player. They have created a great wee experience that emulates the pen and paper investment, tension and group dynamics that's been missing for games recently.
Here's hoping they can keep up the good work.

If Divinity: Original Sin is the 600-hundred-pound gorilla of the Classic Roleplaying Game revival, then EON ALTAR is a Zoboomafoo – the playful Lemur with the power to introduce the wonderful adventure genre to all kinds of new players.
Eon Altar isn’t about throwing a thousand overt systems at a player: It’s about creating an environment where experienced gamers and beginners can work together to create a meaningful experience. Eon Altar works well It’s impossible to “screw up your character” or “mess up a save.”
Because of the ease of setup and polish on the mobile companion app, I’ve seen this game played and enjoyed by folks decidedly outside the target demographic for dungeons and dragons style video games. It’s so easy for people to feel comfortable with the “controller” in their hand (since it’s their own smartphone.) There are downsides to the ease of access, sure, like a shallow loot system, but I don’t mind and you shouldn’t either – here’s why: Everything in this game serves to facilitate the adventure.
Character sheets and battle planning take place on the phone app, allowing newbies to use a controller they're comfortable holding.
Character sheets and battle planning take place on the phone app, allowing anyone to view their character sheet at any time.
Whereas Divinity gives the player access to oil, fire, and the ability to try and set fire to the first town they come across, Eon Altar’s game making tools are simpler, more subtle, and  capture the social element of pen-and-paper roleplaying games in a way that Divinity or Wasteland 2 couldn’t hope to achieve.
And I know, after reading what I’ve written here so far, all I’ve done so far is describe a “Divinity-lite” sword-and-sorcery RPG. Ha! Forgive me my drama, my misplaced sense of suspense, but it truly is so hard to codify the magic of this game, and it becomes easier when comparing Eon Altar to its well-known brother.
I think a big part of the trouble I have when describing what makes Eon Altar special starts with a recent trend for a role-playing game to mean “any game with quest markers and a level-up bar.” Recently, it’s been decided that limitless character creation is the wave of the future, and games that don’t keep up are considered “shallow.” Crafting a player character has become about equipping the hero with the correct amalgamation of combat and exploration skills so the player can pick every lock, hack every computer, and generally access all aspects of the game.   (Wasteland 2 is brutal for this.)
Battles in Eon Altar are fluid and engaging, and work well with the phone controls.
Battles in Eon Altar are fluid and engaging and work well with the phone controls.
In Eon Altar, “role-playing” is about playing a role – like an actor plays a role in play. Within minutes of the opening bell, Eon Altar will have the player reading character lines from their phone. You’ll be talking to stiff-voiced NPC’s, but you’ll also be talking to each other. In the playthrough I had with my girlfriend, we picked characters with complimenting class roles – I was the paladin and she chose the battlemage. In combat, we worked beautifully together: fireballs and holy fire scorching the bandits that crossed our paths.
Out of combat, we fought like cats and dogs. Her character’s dialog had her preaching about love, truth, and the beauty of nature. My character (through my voice) preached on-and-on about how much he hated witches and loved the church. It was an engaging and humorous experience, and it lent it well to promoting camaraderie through the players.
Gaming Together Eon Altar Flying Helmet COOP RPG Cell phone
Eon Altar’s characters are diverse and mechanically interesting, and the dialog between characters serves as a great jumping off point for real life discussion.
EON ALTAR: THE PIZZA PARTY RPG
I’ve maybe done a disservice to Eon Altar by comparing the game so heavily to Divinity: Original Sin, but I feel like it needed to be done. As a reader, I feel like it’s important to understand the author’s experiences – especially if I’m trying to decide whether to spend my money according to that author’s recommendations. This is why, as an author, I feel it’s so important to tell you that I’ve seen the systems (crafting, combat, physics) that allowed Divinity to scoop up every industry award available. I’ve played the games that “set the bar” for classic role-playing games, and even though Eon Altar doesn’t have the depth or polish as some of these titles it succeeds in areas previously uninhabited by any video game ever.
Picture this: you invite three people over to enjoy you for a night of pizza and gaming. In one scenario, you prepare the groundbreaking RPG Divinity: Original Sin (as well as the 4 player COOP mod, of course.) Five minutes in, everyone is hard at work creating their characters. The experienced players are deciding which forms of magic they should take while the newer players are googling what the hell “dexterity” is. Ten minutes, in, you’re viewing the opening cinematic and someone says, “finally” and stands up to take a pee. Now it’s 30 minutes in, two players are lost and one guy decides it’s time to start over because he found a really cool bow and he wants his character to be an archer.
Or, with Eon Altar: at five minutes you’ve got characters picked, the introduction out of the way, and the dude playing the paladin has already come up with a voice for his character and he’s demanding the rest of the group pay their tithes in pizza. Oh, and speaking of pizza – isn’t is great that everyone is rubbing all that grease on their own electronics for once?

Doom 3 is a science fiction first person horror action game developed by ID Software for the ID Tech 4 engine. It follows a nameless space marine as he battles literally demons unleashed by a shady space organization thing.
I own multiple versions of Doom 3. I have that weird truncated version they released for the original black brick xbox, and I also have the BFG Edition version they released for that weird "white thermometer" xbox 360. I have, collectively over both versions, played the main campaign of Doom 3 countless times. I have not, however, beaten the game on my PC, for which I just bought a steam copy of, hence the review. So I supposed I've never beaten the "vanilla doom 3 experience" considering the Xbox copy is shorter than the PC version and the BFG Edition has some changes. But for all intents and purposes, I consider my opinion of this game to be pretty well informed by playing it a ton.
It's totally sweet you guys.
No I mean it, it's awesome. It's got cool guns, and cool levels, cool ideas, cool monsters, it's totally cool I swear. The lighting is great, the story is okay, the atmosphere is killer, it's legitimately cool. ...It's not as cool as the original two Doom games. That's perhaps the most tragic downfall of any creative project, to me. Real passion was put into this, this is an engaging and well realized product. It is thrilling, playful, spooky, it's great. But it doesn't live up to the legacy it's trying to live up to.
If you're expecting a true sequel to Doom II, you aren't getting one, at least not here. Doom 2016 and even Doom 64 are more "Doom 3" than Doom 3 is. But, as I was first exploring the flickering lights of these newly re-invented UAC halls, as I would check every corner, back up against walls, frantically switch between my flashlight and my gun--the tension is palpable, and beyond that, the action is great and the enemies are totally sweet. And the guns are cool too! And so are the levels, and have I talked about the lighting? These shadows still hold up to this day, they blow some modern games fuzzy pixelated shadows out of the water! And some genuinely great sound design the complements the visuals perfectly. And some of these beats are absolutely great, I love the memorable bits, like the guy in the tram, or girl who becomes a lost soul kinda, or the first mancubus you meet, or the way the soulcube says "use us," or that part where you follow a voice into a dead end and something spooky happens that I wont spoil here. Or what about when you pick up the first shotgun and you drop down a hole into a red flashy pit full of zombies?
I can't be objective here, I just love this game. It's great pulpy action horror, a better B-Movie than the original half-life was and when it commits it actually commits. For every stumble it springs forward two steps, and it's too earnest for me to genuinely dislike, even if it's "Not MY Doom Sequel!"
I recommend it, seriously. But, know what you're getting into, and keep an open mind.
Love it, this should get a remake or a sequel that are in the same horror style!

Point and click adventure game in my opinion stand on three pillars as a genre, narrative, game aesthetics and the puzzle complexity. If any of these pillars suffers it could entirely break the game and make a bland if not a terrible experience. This is what happened in Deponia with its narrative that just utterly failed the game's mostly good puzzle and aesthetic design. I just found that I was never engaged with the protagonist or the overall narrative which lead me to simply turn off the game on multiple occasions because I just got bored of the entire affair. The worst part was that even when I finally did finish the game I was given that utterly vapid void of an ending that brings closure to nothing and essentially demands that I play the next Deponia game to get a better picture of the narrative, which just isn't going to happen when I couldn't give a rats♥♥♥♥♥about anything going on to begin with.  I definitely saw the potential in Deponia and I saw the reasons people like it, but I can't in good conscious bring myself to anything other than warn people not to play this game. This is something that I hate to do to game's since I'm a big adherent to the philosophy that a game can be good regardless of how long it is, but for 19.99 a six hour experience just isn't good value for money for the player and that isn't acceptable in my opinion especially when its a mediocre experience at best.

I wanted to recommend this game. I really did... but I can't. Let me stress South Park: The Fractured But Whole is a great game - even better than Stick of Truth. The combat was expanded upon exponentially - the tactical nature of the grid-based combat requires so much more strategy and planning than the rather basic "been there, done that" nature of the combat in Stick of Truth. The game world was expanded upon and is even more interesting, with plenty more secrets to find than before. Every great thing Stick of Truth did, Fractured But Whole does even better.
However, Fractured But Whole is only a good game when you play the version on consoles. Sadly, it seems like Ubisoft gave this game the "Arkham Knight" treatment for this PC port. Any enjoyment you could be having is ruined by a plethora of bugs, framerate issues, and other various problems.
Let's go over the first, most glaring, and most often brought up problems - the DRM and Uplay. Denuvo is infamous for causing players a various amount of problems during their experience. Enough said about that. As for Uplay, forcing people to download your own specific, barely funcioning service in order to play your game is a scumbag move, even more so when you use it as an exuse to lock much of the content of the game behind microtransactions. Not to mention, in order to make this game work for Uplay, you have to link your Steam and Uplay accounts -  a process that can be rather confusing and unintuitive.
That, however, I might be able to look past in order to enjoy the game, but Ubisoft royally screwed up this port. If it's not the constant framerate issues or the abysmal loading times, it's the bugs. Dear God, the bugs. Often times, cutscenes will play without sound for no reason, characters will load incorrectly when entering a new area and you'll be unable to interact with them, and if you're really unlucky then the game will just crash on you without warning. In fact, there's a very infamous bug that appears right as you start the game - the game won't load and will just display a black screen, and the only way to make the game continue as intended it to make it go into windowed mode.
For the love of God, do not buy this game off Steam. Literally any other version of this game is much better, and much more worth your time.

Torchlight II is absolutely fantastic. I don't even know where to start. The mod community is very active and will add dozens of hours of entertainment to an already deep and content rich game. I love the convenience of being able to send your pet to town to shop and sell your unwanted loot. Unlike most loot games these days that adopt the model of dangling carrot on a stick to preserve player count and rarely give good drops, this game is very generous and will shower you with good loot.
You can loot for hours on end and just send your pet to town for errands. Eventually when you go to town, you will be greeted with a wealth of options to customize and expand your equipment. It's all designed so seamlessly and with love. There are many different enemy varieties and the graphics are colorful and full of care and attention to detail. I have a hard time seeing repeated enemie types so far even a few dozen hours later. There is also a lot variety to the enviornments.
If you are getting it, I recommend playing with the Synergies Mod and the Torchlight II Essentials Mod from the get go. I have also seen the way the devs interact with the community and it is very nice and heart warming. Rather than being greedy and make an endless array of DLCs they allow the community to easily mod their game. Two of the developers even made mods on their "spare time" and added many levels to the core game which you could find by subscribing to the Torchlight II Essentials Mod as I mentioned before.

For the one hour I have played I feel I should give a fair warning to those thinking of grabbing the game. So if you want to support these type of sandbox games then I'd strongly suggest playing and supportting these developers to see more of these games.
Pros:
-Amazing graphics and style
-Very good crafting system for an early access game.
-Building in this game could use some more options but so far so good.
Cons:
-Combat could use some work.
-Crafting lacks some complexity but its expected...
-The map sizes are small.
So overall if you caught any interest in the game it is on the sale still as of the date of this review and would recommend it. Going back to the pros the game offers so much for just entering steam and it has so much mmore potential to become of the top games but this is why. Sandbox. It is a sandbox game and has the opportunities to expand on any aspect of the game. While the freedom of a sandbox game is already there. there are many options missing like a trading system for co op/multiplayer. Also, the lack of a skill tree or rather a more complex combat system pulls the game back a bit. Moreover, it feels more generic as the map sizes tend to all be small so it takes a bit away from the exploration aspect of the game.
Final Verdict:
I'd recommend this game as of now it still offers plenty to satisfy its price value. The crafting, combat, and map size can all be fixed and improved over time. I have faith in this developer and hope to see great updates very soon. Hop into the game now and see it grow into an amazing game!

ehhh... mechanically, it's a gorgeously-artistic, excellent point-and-click. with a few flaws.  some of the puzzles are a bit more obscured than it feels they should be, and these tend to crop up when there are dozens of possibilities.  you spend a LOT of time wandering aimlessly when you encounter this.
writing is amusing.  the egomaniac protagonist gives lots of opportunities for humor, and it's lol-worthy surprisingly often.  that said, I couldn't get past the continuous, degrading treatment of every female in the game.  Goal is brainless so she's ogled and manipulated.  old girlfriend is a tropey pain, so she's drugged and manipulated.  they're both targets of many female-only insults through the entire game (there are basically no male equivalents anywhere).
YES, this is almost totally at the hands of a known-egomaniac-jerk (this is the defense in many reviews I've seen), but *that jerk is the protagonist* and you as a player are forced to act these out.  it even portrays this behavior as the norm, not as an obvious character flaw of Rufus's.
add to that the OVERWHELMINGLY male cast (~ 10x more, nearly all with names and significant roles), and that many of the men are basically good people who are not given any personally-degrading treatment, and I really don't see how else you can interpret this side of things.
tl;dr: it's very pretty, well constructed, but good god does it have heavy-handed sexist overtones.  and it sounds like the sequel(s?) are the same or worse.  can we get some women writers at Daedalic?  or playtesters?  the rest of the talent there shouldn't be wasted like this.

Aliens Versus Predator Classic 2000 was actually released in 1999 for the PC. You can play as one of three different campaigns, Predator, Alien, and the Colonial Marine. The Classic 2000 edition also comes with all the content of the original, as well as additional content added over the years both from the Gold Edition and the Millennium add-on pack.
I spent many nights after work staying up until the wee hours of the morning, as I played through each of the three campaigns. From sniping enemies with the Predator, to crawling on ceilings and through ductwork as an alien, this game is still one of those titles I think about from time to time. I am glad to see it being rereleased to a new generation, whom I hope can appreciate it for the classic it is.

Torchlight II is absolutely fantastic. I don't even know where to start. The mod community is very active and will add dozens of hours of entertainment to an already deep and content rich game. Rather than being greedy and make an endless array of DLCs they allow the community to easily mod their game. Two of the developers even made mods on their "spare time" and added many levels to the core game which you could find by subscribing to the Torchlight II Essentials Mod as I mentioned before.

This is not Minecraft. Beyond the aesthetic, this is a completely different game. Ultimately, for an early acces game, this is great, especially for a younger market that are showing interest in RPG style games. There is room for improvement, but on a whole it feels like more than you normally get from early access with a lot of meat on the bones and I'm looking forward to seeing the updates. For 15 bucks, get around it.
Obviously targetted at a younger market, the combat is a little reptitive and the only real objective is to upgrade your gear through a crafting system which is admittedly quite deep, but the pacing of the game is a little slow. There are a number of different armours and weapons that you can craft and use, regardless of your class, which is great, but farming the materials for these items can be quite laborious, bordering on tedious.
The RPG elements aren't that deep. Character progression is rather linear, with only minor choices at certain levels with a "this or that" perk choice. The creative side of the game seems irrelevant to me, comparing to Minecraft, I see no reason to really put time into building a base in this game as you're jumping worlds so often that you'd never have time to appreciate your work. Chuck the tables and workbenches down, and that's all you'll need.
The combat is very - spam click, dodge roll, spam click - at least for the mage. The dodge mechanic can be very clunky, and the TAB targetting is absolute trash. That being said, there's still something rewarding about going around kicking enemy heads in. The enemy models are really nice, everything in this game is lovely to look at. When the dodge mechanics work properly, the combat isn't very challenging. They encourage you to play with friends, but I honestly can't really see how local multiplayer would work outside of boss battles.

This is a really enjoyable game and for it's first few days in early access it's really showing us what we've got to come. I;m not going to say that this is God's gift because yes, some improvements are needed, but again, not even a week in and it's already been addictive and enjoyable.
A lot of people complain that the maps are too small or that they don't see the point of setting up a base but I disagree. As you move through the game the enemies become stronger and it really calls for upgrading your equipment which can only be done at certain workstations after they have been upgraded. As for the maps, yes, they are small, but this is somethign that the devs can easily resolve, but the current state doesn't hinder the game.
The combat system has a familiar Legend of Zelda feel to it, which is great but definitely needs work.
All in all, the game hasn't been out a week but there is plenty to do and worth picking up with the 20% discount right now, definitely something to enjoy now and also keep an eye on for the future.

NOTE: my experience and playtime with Doom 3 come from the console BFG edition
As a Doom game, Doom 3 is a major shift in change for the series and not a good one. While elements of horror have always been in the series since its roots (heck, it started out as Aliens tie-in), it never was a horror game, it was a testosterone fueled shooter with an emphasis on high speed circle strafing and really REALLY big guns. So checking corridors and manuvering at a slow and methodical pace makes it  very out of place and by default the worst entry in the series. Doom 3 is to Doom how Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel is to Fallout, or PREY to...well...Prey.
However, just because a game is bad respective to its series or genre, doesn't neccesarily make it a bad game.
As a game on its own Doom 3 holds up incredibly, the textures are detailed, and the animations even by today's standards are top notch (play the game in third person to know exactly what I mean). Atmosphere is very well done and the game can be unnerving.
Combat, despite being unable to aim is still solid, even though the game becomes rather easy later on. While there is a decent amount of enemy variety you'll be fighting imps and zombie dudes/shotgun guys for a decent chunk of the game, with the occasional pinky.
Weapon selection is typical to what you'd find in a shooter, starting with more conventional weaponary and you work your way up to eventually getting the BFG.
The final boss is very very underwhelming and the game ends on somewhat of a cliffhanger which is followed up in the expansion.
Overall:
I'd recommend Doom 3 if you're looking for a horror shooter that lasts 8-12 hours but I'd advise playing it if you're looking for a Doom game. Doom 4 should sate that appetite nicely.

The storyline in GTA 5 wasn't nearly as lengthy as previous GTA games, not to mention none of the content Rockstar has been pumping out has been for singleplayer.  There is almost no replayability with the singleplayer, unless you have some mods to flesh out the game.
Multi-player is a bit of a bust as well, as you try to grind or farm up the money in order to buy new weapons(and their attachments), cars(and their modifications), and property.  The last 3 or 4 updates from Rockstar have been more or less the same, where you can buy a piece of property (like a motercycle club for example), which allows you to obtain other properties to make money through missions that're done in freemode.  The amount of money you earn through missions compared to how much you need to spend on certain things, is pretty minimal.  The developers definitely made it a bit grindy in order to promote buying shark cards(you buy in game currency with real money) as a way to shorten the time it takes to buy things.
Recently Take Two( Rockstars parent company) has filed a cease and desist against a group that created a major part of singleplayer modding.  Their excuse, as that's what it is, is that it somehow affected people being able to cheat online(when it was proven that the component actually gets caught by the anti-cheat and/or refuses to connect you to the online portion of the game).  As such, any company that is against people modding their game doesn't value their customers and should be avoided at all costs.
As such, I can't recommend anyone picking up GTA 5.

First, look at how many hours I have in this game. I have spent a lot of time in it with friends. However, there is no way I can recommend this game. I'd like to start off by saying I've been playing since the original lauch on Xbox 360. I had technical issues there with the single player and when I contacted their support about it it somehow became my router's problem that I was getting disconnected from GTA Online. "Fine" I thought "I'll just play single player" that was until the game would crash any time I left the city (which was where my story missions were). After dealing with bitter support agents I finally got it to work and I played on 360 until the pc version came out and I used it to push my newly built pc (980 ti, i7 6700k and 16gb of RAM).
All of that said, the single player is pretty fun for one or two playthroughs but it gets old kinda quick.That's where I thought either multiplayer or mods would help increase the lifespan of this game. Let's start with mutliplayer. At first it seemed rather fun. That was until I tried to steal a car that was deemed "too hot" to add to my garage. Um, it's called Grand Theft Auto, why can't I commit the crime the game is named after just because of the value of the car in question? Then, there's how the game punishes your actions by judging your "mental state" which would be fine if it didn't treat player kills and npc kills as the same. Yes, the game will label you a psycopath if you're gunning down NPCs who are shooting at you or passive NPCs that you're just mowing down and/or if you're killing players letf and right or even if you're just trying to defend youreself from another psycopath! To GTA Online it doesn't matter, which IS a problem. Of course they do offer free dlc every so often and the updates that add new missions are...lackluster at best. They usually involve bad writing and no variety as to how you as a player can approach them (which, considering how much variety there should be in a game like this is laughable). Some missions are built up as taking a "stealth approach" but no matter what you do you get caught, so what's even the point of trying to be stealthy? That is, assuming you're doing this with friends like I did. God help you if you want to try doing this with randoms. They don't just add new missions though, they also offer new vehicles and properties to buy, that is, assuming you're willing to shell out hundreds of real life dollars on their shark cards because let's face it, there's no way that you could earn that much money grinding it through missions and it still be worth it. I've lost more money trying to grind because of the way the game incentivises other players to ruin your multimillion dollar investments just for a few RP points. All in all, the multiplayer is an unbalanced mess that wants players to buy into their microtransations scam.
Great, that's mutliplayer out of the way. Now that we know it's garbage let's try out a few mods...and as I'm sure you've heard by now, Take Two Interactive sent a Cease and Desist to OpenIV (which is a very prevalent modding tool, I've not really seen any mods that DON'T use it to be honest). I'll say that while it's not exactly unexpected that they would do this it was far from a good move on their part. From the start of the pc port they said that they would not support nor condone modding, however they wouldn't do anything to stop it so long as players kept it in single player (think content mods or graphical changes) they would be fine, heck rockstar even said they liked a few of the mods. Jump to recent news and apparently even that is a no-no according to Take Two Interactive because "using mods disracts players from our shark cards, how else are we supposed to gouge players for money if they're not playing our terrible multiplayer?"
Lastly, I'd like to say how bad their support agents are. For instance, I was in a lobby where a player was clearly hacking. After I reported him my game slowed to a crawl and then crashed. When I tried to log back in the game it told me I was banned for hacking. I tried to contact support about having a technical issue (because my game orginally started running very poorly before crashing). Even with my system specs IN HAND the rep asked if my pc could even run the game! Dude, of course I can play the game, at this point I already had like 200+ hours in steam and they make you give them system info in the initial contact. What's the point of giving you my system info if you're going to completely ignore it?! Then after finding out that I was banned by an automated system the rep forwarded me to an automated email reply that simply said I had to wait out the 2 month banning period.
TL;DR This game could've been more fun if the executives were more open to the community and willing to focus more on balance instead of money. Only buy it for the vanilla story mode, NOTHING ELSE.

Deponia! This game is breaks all the rules. Without going into too much detail and spoiling the whole thing, I would just like to say that I found myself enjoying a game that I thought I would hate. The opening sequence (not the tutorial) should have been a key indicator of what was about to go down. The humor plays a huge role in this game. Although not outrageously funny, it provided a few chuckles on occasion. The art style is not my favorite, but I also admit that this particular game would not have been as good without that particular style. The puzzles were a key piece to making the game. I did find a few moments throughout the game where I was unsure what to do next. The game is good at letting you know what needs to be done, but not necessarily how it is to be done. Even so, I found a majority of the puzzles had a good balance. They were neither too hard nor too easy and they always seemed have a unique variety to them. Although on the outside the game might seem like a pile of garbage, the game has so much more to offer. The story (not the greatest, but pretty well thought out), the music (you'll see what I mean), the locations (Kuvaq was one of my favorites), the puzzles (probably the best thing about the game) will all transport you to Deponia and unlike Rufus you won't want to leave!

Amazing port. Well optimized. Good online netcode. Large PC community that at the moment rivals Street Fighter V at its absolute peak. If you think that the PC playerbase wont be large enough you have absolutly nothing to fear. Namco did a great job with this port and it is easily the best version to play T7 on.
For people that are new to the game I suggest watching videos from The Main Man, Avoiding The Puddle, and Level Up Your Game. These youtube channels feature lots of great guides on how to play Tekken properly. The good thing about Tekken is that series are iterative, so even if a movement guide is based on Tekken Tag 2 or 6 it still provides a pretty much 1:1 translation to T7.
Of course this is also the button mashers dream game, so if you wanna do that like I did way back in the T3/T5 days you can do that as well and just see cool stuff happen on the screen. The ranking system is solid and will make sure you're matched up against someone of equal skill(that is once all the competitive players rank up, which should only be a couple days).
Get T7. It's a great game and a great port.

before going in depth I must say that this one even though it is a very old game with a grafic which most people would call ugly, then it is the one game installment who has caught the best atmosphere of the franchies and is the scariest one in the aliens versus predator series(especially playing as marine). And if you overlook the old grafic then you have a old gem right here :) but if you hate old grafic, then you will hate this game even though I would say it isn't that bad considered how old it is and the grafic isn't hurting your eyes which some old games tend to do XD
And before reading more of this review, I haven't played the campaign all the way through so there might be some bits which I can't cover for you :)
Aliens versus predator classic 2000 is a game which takes place in the aliens versus predator franchies, the mix of the best where in the middle humans(the marines) stands between aliens and the predators.
In singleplayer you can choose to play one of either of these races - the alien who tries to kill and stop the invading humans - The predator who is trying to find his spaceship and hunting down the aliens and humans -  the marine who is trying to stop these species rampage on humans.
Lets take the cons first
- The grafic is old, yes noone can deny that. Will it hurt your eyes? no, but for many it would without any doubt be a turnoff.
- The singleplayer game can be unfair, sometimes it doesn't really tell you directly what to do(especially in a few maps being the alien) therefore you sometime end up being frustrating and using a lot of time, but so far only a few maps.
- This is both a con and a pro depended on which type of player you are, when you play a map, you can't save, so if you die, you have to redo the whole map.
- Again this can be a con and a pro, the difficulty especially on director's cut, is hard, you can really sometimes die in a instant.
- con and pro again: The game is really fast! If you look in the comment you will see comments about this game having a fast movement. you can as a marines run as fast backwards, from side to side as forward. This can confuse a lot of people but it create a really intense multiplayergame play XD
- The texture of the maps, the walls, the floor and so on is quite repetitive, there isn't that many details of the texture in the maps themselves.
Then there are the pros :)
- This game is really true to the franchies with still some few "artistic freedoms" like in coop multiplayer as marines, they have created some "red aliens" which are much stronger than the normal black ones. So this is really for everyone who is a big sucker for aliens vs predator franchies:)
- Even though it is old, the game engine for me has absolutely made no trouble for me.
- Then there is the atmosphere. Even though I have played some of the later installments, I would say that they really didn't caught the horror/dark atmosphere which this franchies are, they seemed too "bright", too light. And I must say, it gives me the creeps being marines and walking around in the dark with your little bipping radar when suddenly there is movement on the screen moving closer towards you and the intens bipping :P

Incredibly good start for an early access game, i am having a blast with it. but the game is mainly targeted towards rpg players, do NOT buy this expecting massive generated minecraft ish worlds. this is a game where the worls are small sky islands.

The game is visually stunning, which was an extraordinary, but not unwelcome surprise from a game based on block building. Shadows are rendered magnificently, bloom effects and ambient lighting are done perfectly, though the different levels of Anti-Aliasing appear to have less of a change than one would expect.
Multiplayer through Steam was done well, and provides a nice and easy time connecting with a friend.
The game is fairly graphics heavy, though you can turn off many of the effects that can weigh down some weaker graphics cards.
The game was well designed up until this point, and I have seen absolutely no glitches or bugs occur in game. Perhaps I'm just not far enough, but everything so far appears extremely well designed, as if this was the initial release of a game, rather than an early access beta.
Aside from a few features I would like to see in the game, such as inventory stack manipulation (splitting stacks), this game has met my expectations, and blew them out of the water. But then again, those missing features... isn't that what Early Access is for?
If you like those sandbox building/exploration games like Minecraft, Terraria, TUG, and so many others, this game is certainly one to put on your wishlist. Already, I'm pleased with the game, and believe that it's worth every penny of the $14.99 it costs. Of course, if you're not sure, just give it some time until it reaches its official release.

So, this game is a good game, and I would give it a positive review, but some recent actions by Take-Two have led me to give a more negative review. The gameplay of single-player is good, and the story is quite good. The online is quite fun, though the emphasis on their longing for money is evident in the high prices and advertising of microtransactions. But Take-Two's recent "cease and desist" to OpenIV because it "enables recent malicious mods that...interfere with...GTA Online..." pushes me to write a negative review. OpenIV is not a script mod, which is what most Online hacks are. OpenIV has never had malicious intent, it was a basis for modding to mess around in single-player. Take-Two has just made the wrong decision here. If they had a problem with an Online hack enabled by OpenIV, they could have tried to work with OpenIV to stop the Online hack rather than shut down the entire modding community. This was timed in such a way that one could say it had to do with the work on a port of Liberty City into GTA V, but I feel that there is not a single person who would buy a game just for the map. The experience of Liberty City in GTA V would be completly different from GTA IV with the different physics and lighting and stuff. I would advise you to also leave a negative review on GTA V to get as much attention as possible.
EDIT: Now that OpenIV is back, I give this game a positive review because it's fun, but I advise you to avoid large public online sessions.

The storyline in GTA 5 wasn't nearly as lengthy as previous GTA games, not to mention none of the content Rockstar has been pumping out has been for singleplayer.  There is almost no replayability with the singleplayer, unless you have some mods to flesh out the game.
Multi-player is a bit of a bust as well, as you try to grind or farm up the money in order to buy new weapons(and their attachments), cars(and their modifications), and property.  The last 3 or 4 updates from Rockstar have been more or less the same, where you can buy a piece of property (like a motercycle club for example), which allows you to obtain other properties to make money through missions that're done in freemode.  The amount of money you earn through missions compared to how much you need to spend on certain things, is pretty minimal.  The developers definitely made it a bit grindy in order to promote buying shark cards(you buy in game currency with real money) as a way to shorten the time it takes to buy things.
Recently Take Two( Rockstars parent company) has filed a cease and desist against a group that created a major part of singleplayer modding.  Their excuse, as that's what it is, is that it somehow affected people being able to cheat online(when it was proven that the component actually gets caught by the anti-cheat and/or refuses to connect you to the online portion of the game).  As such, any company that is against people modding their game doesn't value their customers and should be avoided at all costs.
As such, I can't recommend anyone picking up GTA 5.

The game is great - but attacking modders? Misguided, ineffective, offensive, bad for the game as a whole.
Shutting down OpenIV won't solve Online hacking. For one, the tool is already in the wild - there's no way to eliminate it entirely. Hackers will simply use their existing copies to build upon.
Secondly, the tool was simply co-opted into making the process more convenient - the software vulnerabilities that allow malicious actors to alter Online gameplay are intrinsic to the game, not the mod toolkit.
I have been the victim of hacking in GTA Online in the past, and I believe that I will not be any safer after the mod toolkit has been shut down. The game is still broken, hackable, exploitable, all to the detriment of the players.

The core gameplay of the previous games is mostly there. You still fight lots of demons in fast paced combat and you still have to find keycards to unlock doors, but the fighting is MUCH slower and unlocking doors feels like a chore at times.
In terms of graphics, well... I'd sure write a lot more if I could see the game. It's always WAY too dark, so much so that sometimes you have to guess where to aim. When you can see the game, it sure is impressive for 2004. Not as good as the Alpha, unfortunately, but still pretty good.
Almost the entire game takes place in futiristic offices, underground facilities and labs. There's also not much room to move around, since most of the time you're fighting in tight corridors. It's such a shame, because Hell is not only a cool part of the game, it's also kinda the main point of Doom. You know, fighting demons and then going to Hell to really kick their♥♥♥♥♥ The buildup to Hell is so long that by the time you get there, you forget it was a plot point anymore and even then, it's just 3 levels and you're done.
Doom 3 gives you many weapons and they're all useful in different situations, although you'll probably be using the shotgun & machine gun most of the time. Unfortunately, the shotgun has fallen from grace since its Doom1&2 days. It now has almost no range and its damage can be anywhere from negligible to instantly killing the enemy. The enemy placement is sometimes weird too. You've got the usual "enemies spawn from behind" and "enemies spawn as soon as you do X", but in most cases, you can kill them while they spawn. When you fight it's fun, although a few of the enemies can be annoying. The bosses are a huge disappointment, sadly.
Of course one cannot mention Doom 3, without mentioning the mechanics and design choices it popularized. An intro sequence to get you immersed in the game before all hell breaks loose, the story is just a background event, almost all of the exposition comes through the form of hidden collectibles, choices that don't actually matter and worst of all, realism at the expense of fun gameplay. These are where a good chunk of Doom 3's problems come from.
It's not all bad, though. As a horror game it does have a decent atmosphere, all the weapons feel extremely satisfying to shoot with, the sound design is great and there are some awesome levels.
However, in the end, it fails to be Doom and it fails to be a horror game. It's just not scary enough to be a horror game (too many jumpscares, too many weapons, enemies are easily killed etc.) and it has too few elements from Doom1&2 to be a true sequel/reboot (and the elements that are there just aren't implemented well enough).
Play it to see what all the fuss was about back in the day and why this game still offers plenty of topics to talk about. Not a bad game overall, certainly unique for an FPS and actually fun for the most part, but it leaves a lot to be desired.

Deponia is a traditional point–and-click (P&C) adventure game which revolves around the protagonist trying to escape from Deponia and ends up saving a mysterious princess. Boasting a charming setting supported by beautifully drawn backgrounds, solid voice acting  and an interesting soundtrack, at its core it is plagued by one of the most insufferable casts and puzzles seen in an adventure game in years.
If the aim of the game was to represent the most insufferable protagonist, something which is fundamentally a backbone of the genre, then it passed with flying colours. Rufus, the protagonist, is quintessentially the pretentious and brainless (at times) jerk every individual should respectfully hate and gives little reason for any sympathy throughout most of the story, even when his act of saving the princess is noble to an extent. Not only is the protagonist ultimately unlikeable, but almost every single support character faces the same setback: being painfully unmemorable, unfunny or annoying.
The humour in Deponia is by and large hit-and-miss. There are a few genuine moments which spark a giggle such as a robot’s guilty obsession with popping bubble-wraps or a transvestite’s fake womanly voice (the best it can get), but these are overshadowed by the blatant misogynistic remarks and uninspiring jokes by poorly written characters.
The puzzles are not great either. They start off fairly easy but eventually end up suffering from a typical syndrome in this genre -- illogicality. Because of this a guide must be acquired, otherwise too much time will be frustratingly spent figuring out what to do next, and there are a few moments where you will ask yourself how were you supposed to know that or why that particular action was required. The game does not give too many hints when it comes to solving its relatively tiresome puzzles.
All of the things mentioned above slowly turn a potentially decent storyline at best into a dreary one. Even now, personally I am not completely sold on the whole damsel in distress approach the story takes when Rufus meets the princess, who spends mostly the entire game unconscious from a fall caused by no one else but Rufus earlier in the game. Regardless, there is also a sense of not much engagement in the story either, all thanks to poor writing. After a few hours sank into the game, everything starts to be a big fat chore.
From a technical standpoint, it is shocking to realise that after almost two years since launch a particular game-breaking glitch in a puzzle, which was also encountered by others (albeit not all), is still present in the game. This glitch stops a particular cutscene to play, preventing any possibility of continuing the game just when you were so close to the end. After some research, a way to overcome this unforgiveable misfortunate is to get access of a save file from someone else who owns the game and got passed this point. At the time of writing this review, I still do not know how the game actually ends. Moreover, reported by others as well is the awful framerate even for high-end computers which can inexplicably drop to as low as 10FPS even at the lowest settings. Deponia is a game which should not require a lot of resources to run smoothly considering it looks like a 2D game done in Flash, and this implies poor coding and optimization.  Lastly, the animations can be a bit clunky at times but passable.
Conclusively, Deponia is kind of a mess, much like its planet. Poor writing, unlikeable characters, illogical puzzles and unfixed glitches simply make it a chore or potentially unplayable and degrade anything interesting the story has to offer.  Its visual charm might be its only selling point for anyone curious about Deponia (mainly the reason I got it), but its flaws in almost everything that is supposed to make a top-notch adventure P&C sadly suck out any enjoyment Deponia could offer to an avid, yet old-school, adventure fan like myself. I cannot recommend this game to any adventure fanatic expecting an overall quality on par to Monkey Island, Gabriel Knight, Broken Sword and other classics. Instead, Deponia should also take an example from a recent modern game like The Book Of Unwritten Tales.
Lastly, if you can actually ignore all its flaws, then it is passable at best. But I would be in awe by how you could ignore such obvious flaws.

In some sense the game is a fairly easy puzzle game. This aspect of it is fine, but nothing particularly amazing.
Where the game is really quite amazing is the environment and story. It does a great job of conveying the atmosphere of the two brothers going on an adventure,.
Overall, it ends up being a fairly relaxing and enjoyable game to play. It does lean more towards the "watching a movie" type of game so if that's not really your thing then you might not like it as much, but in my opinion it does it quite well, as the story is conveyed all through the gameplay and occasional very short cutscenes, with absolutely no text or dialogue (the characters speak, but not actual english words so it is mostly to convey emotion).
As is typical for this sort of game, don't expect a long playtime. It only takes around 3 hours to get through. This is not a bad thing though as it is an enjoyable 3 hours that doesn't overstay its welcome.
I would thoroughly recommend purchasing this game, especially if it is on sale (I purchased it for $3.74).
