"+ Great storytelling.
+ Its themes evolve as the story progresses in Afterstory.
+ Incredibly emotional.
+ Unique characters that all provide purpose to the story in some way or another.
+ Nagisa, Kotomi, Tomoyo, Ibuki, Kyou, and Sunohara are top tier best girls.
+ Akio and Sanae are the best parents I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing.
+ Exceptional humor.
+ Extremely replayable.
+ One of the most genuine MC's in Visual Novels (Tomoya Okazaki)
+ Unique story where you actually SEE the married life of a couple and the relationship they had prior.
+ Easily the best OST I have ever heard in a game, each one contributing so much to the message each scene is trying to portray. Snowfield is honestly one of my favorite song in videogames, making me cry because of the beauty of the scene it was involved in.
+ Afterstory is my favorite 2nd half in a visual novel alongside Steins;Gate, evolving its themes to a much more family orientated setting as well as providing emotional heartbreak that no other game could ever provide except this one.
+ The ending is amazing and the use of the "orb lights" is one of my favorite plot elements ever, being detailed enough for hardcore analysis on the role it played in the final moments of Clannad.
+ The Illusionary World is absolutely genius.
+ Another aspect I enjoy about the themes of Clannad is that they are family orientated and could honestly help anyone in need of advice on what to do with their life, offering many unique perspectives on certain ideals that are evident in the world we live in.
- Art is charming however it is definitely not for everyone.
- The game is on average 80+ hours, being one of the longest videogame scripts EVER!!!
Overall Clannad was a 10/10 for me. I don't think I have experienced a story as great as this one since the original Steins;Gate and Steins;Gate 0. The way Clannad tells its story in such a simple but unique way, constantly evolving with time progressions is truly a thought provoking and "valuable" experience. I'd recommend this to anyone that wants to involve themselves in the "Visual Novel" medium as it is the best one I have ever played besides Steins;Gate. The game is worth every cent, 50 dollars is honestly not a bad price for one of the best games of the genre, BUY THIS and enjoy it, as it a truly profound and life altering experience!"

DOOM, a name synonymous with first-person shooters in their infancy, the epicenter of the most dedicated modding community unrestrained with their creativity when given the right tools, and the birthplace of online multiplayer with the mode, Death Match. Ever since the pinnacle of DOOM 2, the legacy of DOOM has expanded beyond its name in popularizing the first-perspective in games as well as fan-projects that continue the technical prowess of the former iD designers beyond their dreams.
The games that followed D2, however, have deviated in one shape or another that there is a trilogy of DOOM 3 games with wildly different interpretations of what made the originals so beloved. Whenever people lambaste D3 before and after DOOM (2016), they fail to realize that not everyone played the originals for Nightmare-runs of constant carnage that has become the accepted norm behind DOOM. D3 is a return to the survival-horror elements and the level-design of labyrinth like mazes to atmospherically heighten the memories once instilled through the pixels on the screen that used to instill terror, damnation and the fight against Hell itself.

In order to understand the appeals of each successor, it’s worth considering in what ways each game has changed with the memories of what people loved about the originals.
Before D3, there was the misleading named, DOOM 64 (Absolution on PC), an entirely new game that reworked the classics with the Quake engine. With the moniker of 64 added to the title, players likely expected a console-port of the first two games; what the game became was the perfect blend of fast-paced combat and atmospheric horror D3 exclusively desired. Out of all three successors, D64 is by far my favorite because it manages to tap into the classic level-design and pace while making the atmosphere ooze from the monitor that D3 wishes it could achieve. The result kept the action and the horror from becoming monotonous as the ambience and challenge made you think about what was around the next corner.
After D3, however, DOOM (2016) decided to focus exclusively on the frenetic carnage of the original with no sense of suspense and an outright simplification of the original’s level-design. When I say that the level-design of D16 is simplified, I am not referring to the open-ended areas you explore, rather how the combat arenas have become too samey.  This is because how enemies spawn like Painkiller/Shadow Warrior as well as how every combat encounter ultimately feels like the last one, which is what resulted in the game feeling like it had lost its identity. In these modern takes of DOOM, which doesn’t exclude D3, you cannot have rooms full of boss-enemies and an invincibility orb or enemies fighting one another as a tactic, or even the massive traps of the originals. Without these qualities or the methodical pacing for combat, D16 feels the most departed game of the three.
None of this is to say that D3 got everything correct or that it doesn’t have its own issues. However, at its core of suspense, action and exploring maze-like corridors on a space-station of Mars is the personal identity of DOOM that has resonated with me the most. Conserving resources, exploring thoroughly for supplies and secrets, and fighting/fleeing in terror are the qualities I have always enjoyed the most, and it’s this distinction between D3 and D16 that makes it feel like the last true-to-form DOOM game.
Perhaps what is considered more often criticized than the slower pace of D3 is its usage of horror elements to make up for the lack of enemy numbers and action. These aspects include the game’s usage of ambient lighting and sound design, the “monster closet” trope, and the overall emphasis on scavenging for supplies to stay alive.
This last category feels odd to mention as all DOOM games focus on managing your inventory of a one-man’s-Armageddon arsenal as well as the amount of protection and health you have. D16 is perhaps the only one that makes it skill-based to warrant how frugal D3 can be if you play reckless without consideration of your surroundings. As the player’s speed, aiming penalties when hit and other small touches reward more patient players, this aspect is something that feels intentional. There is nothing to stop a player from charging into encounters except for being aware of where enemies are coming from and how to best avoid taking damage. What will constantly instill the player to stop is not the difficulty but its usage of the ambient sound, atmosphere, and, most infamously, its usage of darkness to create a much larger threat than the game will throw at you.
In a day-and-age of Dark Souls “it’s hard but fair”, it’s strange how many people complained about the lighting that was ruined by the BFG edition when it added a rechargeable flashlight and brighter scenery. Having to decide between the ability to see and to defend yourself is a constant choice the player must handle by judging the distance of the threat from its shadows, finding choke-points to bring the threats to you and having the sound design inform the player when in doubt. These three considerations are the core of D3 by always giving the player the ability to determine the next threat and how to handle the situation, and removing that one decision breaks the tension of its horror.  This is perhaps why people become tedious of D3 without the looming fear of being ambushed in the dark to keep the engagements a threat rather than a minor concern.
None of all this is to say playing D3 with a “duct-tape” mod is playing the game incorrectly as that is also a player choice that has its drawbacks, one of which iD believes it should make the decision for you rather than giving you the alternative.
You probably have noticed as a result of this review for D3 that it’s not recommending the BFG edition, perhaps one of the worst rereleases were it not for GearBox’s rerelease of Duke Nukem 3D. As previously mentioned, modding became one of the most influential aspects of DOOM past its successes, and if D3 and D16 are any indication of modern iD it’s one of disinterest, aversion or trivializing to the modding scene.
D3, while not as open-ended as the classics, allowed users to change codes, scripts, UI features and graphical overhauls on an already technically impressive game. BFG charged for a full rerelease that removed native mod-support without a separate launcher and a split user-base, a minor graphical upgrade, some few new levels and the removal of the flashlight system that gave the player the choice to be able to see with a flashlight or have their gun, or download one of hundreds of “duck-tape” mods on PC, in favor of a regenerating suit light. Even excusing the console versions, the decisions made on PC made it arguably the inferior version in the long-run as well as setting the attitude of D16 with the Snap-Map feature that belittles the modding scene by containing its ability to innovate. These changes are why I find the BFG edition deplorable that I cannot in good conscience recommend it.
Although the end of this review was focused on the bad decisions of its publisher, Zenimax, there are a lot of qualities of D3 that are still worth praising in its original form as well as the merits behind D16’s single-player components when viewed on its own.
However great are these games, the continued arrogance of Zenimax with their business practices for games and for review-embargos all began with the fall of iD. The decline of these once great names will become the monsters Zenimax themselves have created when other companies, modders and titles usurp their place, and they themselves will become afraid of the shadows they once casted which now spell their own DOOM.

Deponia is a beautifully produced point-and-click comedy adventure game, that mangages to tell a very old story (boy saves girl from evil pursuers) in a fun and interesting way. In particular, I felt the standout feature was the antihero protagonist, an uncommon and hard-to-pull off choice.
When I first loaded up Deponia, the thing that first stuck me was the art style, which really reminded me of Lucasarts "The Curse of Monkey Island", which was the first adventure game I ever played. I think the cartoony style really lends itself to adventure games of this sort.
At first, the protagonist Rufus reminded me a lot of Monkey Island's Guybrush Threepwood (even the voice acting is similar), but as you play through the game you realise Rufus isn't a bumbling idiot with a heart of gold, but rather a selfish egotist filled with the desire to leave the trash planet of Deponia at any cost.  The writers did a really good job of creating a repellent character that we nevertheless empathise with and want to help succeed, which is hard to do. Other characters are fun, although I would have liked the damsel in distress, Goal, to find her voice a bit sooner. She really only comes to her senses in the last sequence of the game, after being badly injured in the first sequence.
On a general level, the story is interesting because it very clearly only tells the first arc of a standard story. Because Deponia now has two sequels, this isn't the problem for me that it would have been for those who played it on release. I don't own the sequels, but I can grab them whenever I want to continue the story. For anyone who played it on release, it may have been a bit of a hanging ending. For that reason, even though I didn't, I'd recommend buying all three games at once.
The puzzles would be considered easy by someone who started on the early adventure games in the pre-internet era, but I consider that a wholly good thing - the game loses all flow if you can't solve a puzzle. I only got stuck twice - once was from not thinking/acting like Rufus would and missing an interaction, and once because an item was slightly unclear about exactly what it was. The game also has "highlight interactables" and "skip minigame" functions to make it a bit easier if you want.
As with most point-and-click games, replayability is severely diminished after you've won the game once, as there is only one way to play the game. The developers do kind of cheekily allude to this with the inclusion of droggeljug mode.
All in all, Deponia is a good adventure game for the library.

The artwork is decent and the voice acting fairly tolerable, but these hardly compensate for the rest of the game’s faults.  The intended humor is rather offensive.  The gameplay, puzzles, and dialogue are slow, tedious, unengaging, and ruin any potential the plot may have had.
The main character, Rufus, is unlikable.  He is selfish, negative, and undergoes no discernable character transformation making him an unrelatable “pro”tagonist.
The sexism is rampant and extremely disappointing.  There are only two women in the ENTIRE game (not even one female background character).  The first woman is the ex-girlfriend, Toni, who is portrayed as the stereotypical nagging b*tch for asking Rufus to be less slovenly and treat her with respect.  She is also shown in the shower for no reason.  The second female character remains unconscious throughout the majority of the game.  Even her name, Goal, indicates that she is merely an object to be conquered and attained and she is continuously manipulated by the men.
I do not recommend this game and I will not be playing the rest of the series.

Wow. 15 years, and this thing still has charm and oodles of enjoyment waiting to be discovered.
The multiplayer is still supported, and that impresses and pleases me, and to be quite honest, that's where the real value of the game rests; in the multiplayer. The singleplayer had no real value or hook to it, and the levels are confusing as hell to navigate through. Good if you're one of those gamers that enjoys plenty of puzzles and searching, but a real pain for those who are fans of Aliens vs. Predator, and the high-speed combat that the games offer.
Gameplay wise, this thing does sort of leave a lot to be desired, principally through Marine gameplay. Granted, recent Aliens games have kind of buffed up the Colonial Marines, but in this game, there is one critical feature that is noticably absent: the ability to reload. Couple that with gun jams (which I would actually enjoy a lot if the reload mechanic wasn't a fantasy in this game) and a fairly weakened Marine starting rifle, and you have a species whose only real option is to either spam pulse rifle grenades or power weapons (and there are copious amounts of power weapons in this, going far beyond the film arsenals).
The Aliens and Predators, like the Marines, pretty much surf through the maps at ludicrous speed, which is literally where the high-speed combat statement comes from. The Predator does sort of suffer from Marine damage issues - their main weapons, the wristblades, are as weak as the Alien's light attacks, so as a result you'll probably encounted a lot of players either sprinting around firing spearguns or poising their tails to lash out and instakill you.
If you're a fanatic for fast-paced, hyperactive games that will bring you up on your feet and have you laughing for hours, this is a must. It's fairly affordable, and while it is by no means the best Aliens game, it's where it belongs and will give you tons of enjoyment, laughs and jump-scares.

Boy oh boy, it's Tekken on PC! And may I tell you IT IS GOOOOOD!
Probably the first thing that comes to mind when you think about fighters on PC are shoddy console ports. NOT the case here! It's butter smooth, looks really good (just turn post processing to medium to get rid of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ film grain), soundtrack is nice and SFX is really good. It all just feels well polished. Net code seems to be good as well, thankfully.
But what about the gameplay? Well it's Tekken 7 - it's been out on arcades for years now so they had plenty of time to make the game as polished as possible and they did!
You get your standard offline arcade mode, vs mode, treasure mode (which is just random fights for loot) and of course a robust practice mode. Not inspiring by any means but solid. Then there is the story mode. I find the story rather ridiculous and it forces you to play certain charcters which I am not a fan of. They do lend you a helping hand if you really hate playing that Heihachi/Lars/whatever though so it's not that big a deal :) The journalist narrator is god awful but cutscenes are really good and they make a seamless transitions into gameplay parts of the campaign. Overall I'd say not great but not awful either, I'm not really into the Tekken lore so maybe I'm nitpicking too much.
For online you have ranked games, casual games with ability to create rooms with some custom settings and tournament mode. Again, nothing crazy but just what you would expect from the Tekken game.
Character customization is fairly robust so it's easy to make your character stand out. Though I'd like to have more "cool" customization options like wings and less "stupid" ones like pizza on the back or fish in your hand. But hey, everyone likes different things.
Overall I have no doubts that throwing extra money at Harada for the Deluxe Edition was the right thing to do and I can only hope for more games to come out with that much polish. Enough talking, time to get back to playing my sexy bikini vampiress, excuse me.

Sniper Elite 3 is a very enjoyable 3rd person sniper game in which you play as Karl Fairburne. An American sniper. The game takes place throughout Africa from airfields to bases built into mountains.
Visually, the game is very well presented. I was able to play it maxed out with a constant 60FPS with v-sync off (It would seem that it’s capped). Although, even with my 1060, the frame rate would sometimes drop into the low 40s and high 30s and given this game is over 2 years old, I would put this down to poor optimisation of what is clearly meant for consoles. Not only did I have frame rate issues, but screen tearing was also rife with basic movements tearing the screen like an angry child ripping up a piece of artwork he made a mistake on. However, the game was still playable and very enjoyable throughout with no crashes after just under 10 hours.
Gameplay is also very enjoyable. If you have played any other Sniper Elite game, you understand the ins and outs of it. The sniping is fun and it is always enjoyable to shoot a German or Italian and watch the bullet to travel through the air and shatter their eyeball and penetrate their brain, very satisfying stuff. Missions, of which there are around 4, (wide open maps with optional side missions) are a bit repetitive and you will probably never do the side missions unless you want the 100% complete achievement. Although you will probably expect a sniper game to revolve around sniping, it does get very tiring very quickly and I sometimes found myself getting out my Thompson and gunning down a few Germans just to change it up a bit. The machine guns in this game were obviously meant to be a second thought if you alert the base as you can only carry 2 magazines of ammo unless you carry an MP40 (and even in this case you only get around 2-3 bullets from looting an enemy corpse). If you were to get this game, just keep in mind that you probably won’t be playing it non-stop until you finish as it does get very repetitive and sniping does become boring after gunning down your 50th Nazi. The AI is not too bad, sometimes you can walk right in from of them and they won’t see you, other times they can see you hiding behind a box. A lot more work could’ve been done here that unfortunately wasn’t.
The story is very poor. You basically set out the kill some generic Nazi Commander with your missions being to collect information in order to find out where he is and when he will be there. I didn’t really pay attention to it, I was enjoying sneaking around and shoving knives into a bad guy’s ear (yes that is one of the silent kill animations). But the story in this game is basically non-existent apart from a few lines of dialogue from the main protagonist during loading screens (that’s really the only place you find out what you’re doing and why).
Now for the price. At the time of writing this (05/10/2016) the game is £39.99 which is absolutely ridiculous. This game, brand new on release, is only worth about £20 in my opinion. I purchased this game off Ebay for £8 and for that it was very enjoyable. I think this is just a clear example of one of those games that Steam have just forgotten to lower the price but while the game remains at this price, I would find it elsewhere for much cheaper. If you pay any more than £10, you paid too much for this.
Overall, it is a very enjoyable if a bit short (10 hours on the hardest difficulty until I got to credits) but way too expensive on steam. You will have a good time watching Germans trip over trip mines or walk into anti-personal mines, failing that, you will also enjoy getting a perfect shot and watching your targets testicles pop so long as you don’t pay too much.

The game is great - but attacking modders? Misguided, ineffective, offensive, bad for the game as a whole.
Shutting down OpenIV won't solve Online hacking. For one, the tool is already in the wild - there's no way to eliminate it entirely. Hackers will simply use their existing copies to build upon.
Secondly, the tool was simply co-opted into making the process more convenient - the software vulnerabilities that allow malicious actors to alter Online gameplay are intrinsic to the game, not the mod toolkit.
I have been the victim of hacking in GTA Online in the past, and I believe that I will not be any safer after the mod toolkit has been shut down. The game is still broken, hackable, exploitable, all to the detriment of the players.

I got Train Simulator 2016 as part of the Humble Bundle for only a few $$, but I got the Humble Bundle specifically for this game as I was interested and wanted to see if 2017 would be worth the purchase.
Train Simulator is somehow really captivating. Everything you do in a train has to be planned way in advance as trains need a lot of time to slow down and stop or get going. It's also super interesting to learn all the signs and what theys mean. I thought as trains drive on tracks, it could not be that hard. But when traffic gets denser, all the buttons you have to press and signs you have to really look out for, it's harder than driving a car in my opinion. And more lives depend on it. So in principal I'm enjoying this game. But the technology Train Simulator is built upon is so unexcusably outdated, it sucks out all the air of an otherwise nice game.
Tha graphics feel very outdated. For a game that is Train Simulator 2016, or Train Simulator 2017 and costs $40, this is unexcusable. It looks awful. Passengers and their walking animations look terrible. Every few seconds the game needs to reload assets like trees and houses. And every time an object pops up on the horizon, the game stutters. And objects pop up in great numbers every 30 seconds or so, so every 30 seconds you get a huge stutter party for about 5 seconds until all new objects on the horizon are loaded. This is especially nerve wrecking when you're in a tight situation and need to slow down because of a distant signal, as the game doesn't always accept inputs at that time.
I also disliked the tutorial. It's not been given any love. The tutorial explains what home signals, distant signals are and what they display, but you cannt try it out. The tutorial is over after the explanation text disappears. This I could also read in the manual, no need for a tutorial mission for that that takes a long time to load. And that's it! Tutorials do not show you how the PZB signalling system works, when you need to slow down, to what speed you need to slow down, and how you actually do it. You cannot practice. This is only described in the manual or I had to look some additional YouTube videos, that did a better job.
Then, you're driving. And you come to the first yellow distant light signal, where you're supposed to slow down. You make a tiny mistake as you're not familiar with the buttons you have to press and bang, emergency brake. And the game doesn't tell you what you did wrong. Did I forget to press SIFA? Was I too fast? What would have been the correct speed? Tell me, I don't know! The game just lets you alone with all those questions. Very bad for learning and I found it highly frustrating. So you start the mission from scratch, wait on the loading screen for 30 seconds or more (and I have quite a fast machine) and then you drive for 20 minutes, until you make the same error and need to start over.
So, however interesting and fun I think Train Simulator would be, the technical drawbacks, long loading times, stuttering all the time, old and unappealing graphics, and bad tutorials / help system / explanations make Train Simulator an unsatisfactory and frustrating game.

This is simply the most grindy game I have EVER played. With or without a paid subscription.
I enjoy Heroes & Generals, it has a lot of potential, but there are some things I can't overlook.
I have 175 hours played and I have yet to reach the RTS part of the game that is marketed so heavily. I was intrigued by that aspect but it takes a very, very long time to get there. From what I understand, there's not much content there, either.
The Generals/War portion of the game involves: Buying units (In game respawn tickets) spawning them in a queue that is your ENTIRE faction's queue, meaning you never get to see you assault team on the field before the war even ends because they will be produced after 4853 other people's units do. Then you get that unit and you send it around to a city, and that's basically it. They have some leveling to units, but it's really just moving boxes around a world map. There is no depth. But let's say, "hey, I want to play Generals mode and that's it," You can buy a General at the low low price of 9900 Gold, which is roughly $40 dollars. Not worth it at all.
The "Heroes" portion is the only thing you'll see really, which is hit and miss. Every single thing has a price tag of gold or in game credits. I mean everything. Every bullet costs to fire, every weapon and vehicle you use needs repair at the end of the match. Access to weapons is pretty rough too and the game has serious balancing issues. Starting weapons just are not good enough to compete. Everything is extremely pricey and takes serious time to grind to.
Soldiers earn credits based on their damn rank which is awful. A rank 1 soldier makes 6500 credits every hour of gameplay. A rank 12 makes double that. This means if I want to have multiple soldiers with mulitple load outs, I am making less credits for my time leveling new guys. Which wouldn't be a problem except for the fact that all the weapons you buy are specific to THAT SOLDIER and you cannot transfer them. This is the reason I have only played one faction, and only have one Infantry Soldier and one Tanker. I have never played the recon, paratrooper, or pilot. I have 175 hours. This is a problem.
Now I could have purchased those career options, however I wanted to actually enjoy my time so I bought better weapons instead. Because like I said, the weapons are not balanced. The Americans have an M2 carbine option that is fully automatic, has 30 rounds, and can have a scope. The thing might as well be a damn M16.
Spawns systems need work, the game is unclear for new players. There is no voice in game so I cannot communicate to my team.
Say I'm in a battle that has tanks and infantry. If i'm not in a squad that has an auxiliary seat for the tanker type, I cannot switch to my tanker. And there is no way for me to choose my squad as a solo player, it just puts me in one.
The gunplay can be enjoyable and I have had fun moments defending and assaulting bases, but these issues need to be addressed, and I'm not sure they will be. They have added much content and the recent rework to maps is worlds better, but right now, I think I might say "maybe next year" to this game.

I've finished the tutorial and the first well, and I'd have to say it compares well to MGS V. A somewhat jankier version, but it's there. Its ballistics and sound assets are wonderful, graphical fidelity is there with equally good performance, and for the most part quite mechanically sound, but there's a couple little bugbears I've got with it so far.
I'll start with the bad so I can end on a high note. The weapons that aren't explosive or sniper rifles are rather anemic, and it's an incredibly likely scenario to be carrying around more ammo for your rifle than your smg even if you don't use it, like I did, and the silenced pistol only holds one backup mag and tends to be a tad unreliable, not seeming to be able to decide if it wants to penetrate helmets or not.
And while it looks pretty in screenshots, it's not so great in motion. Animation quality, the way things move, is an often overlooked part of graphics. Vehicles in motion that get destroyed just stop instantly rather than skidding in motion. Walking and vaulting are somewhat stiff. Melee kills tend to alternate between jitteryness and stiffness rather frequently.
There's also a couple mechanical oversights I kind of expect from a stealth game. Being able to drag an enemy straight after a stealth takedown's the only really glaring omission, doing it to an enemy on a ledge is a bit of a dice roll as to whether it'll fall back or forward. The rest are just some inconsistencies. Shot masking, using environmental sounds to hide your shots, can't seem to decide whether it wants to hide the shot completely or just alert enemies but mask your position. The other major inconsistency is that you can always throw an enemy corpse, but you can't consistently set them down.
Now, on to the good. The sniper rifle mechanics are somewhat of a treat, provided you're playing on marksman and above. Now the game provides a little blip as to where your shots will land when holding your breath by default, though I'd reccomend turning it off because it can be a bit buggy. I reccomend going with the default reticle and spending a bit of time on the firing range figuring out what notches roughly correspond to what range. For the M1 Garand, the default rifle, each large notch is 100m, though the carcano rifle with its higher muzzle velocity the first large notch is roughly 200m. Penetration and ricochets are modeled quite well, and then there's the sound mechanics, which are a stroke of genius. Certain environmental soundmakers can mask your shots for you, an artillery piece, a backfiring generator, etc. And even if they hear you, as snipers are somewhat terrifying the first shot they hear will make the troops who hear it go to ground a bit before they check out your position, though successive shots will cause them to go hostile unless you move far enough away and shoot from another position, confusing them further.
There's a couple toys to play around with as well. Dynamite can be set and shot, or set on a timer, the binocular tags enemies through walls and highlights enemy vehicle weak points like engines and fuel tanks. AV landmines and tripwire mines can be used to cover your back or prepare an ambush. and all these little toys can be combined, Lay a trap, snipe, then take out more when they come for your position. The maps are also huge and filled with side objectives and mutliple routes, giving a lot more opportunity for freeform decision making. I also like that they made the maps quite dense as well, which is something I wish more open-world/open-ended games did as they have a habit of turning expansive maps with the potential for unintended, chaotic play into glorified mission-selects.
It's not a terribly engaging game for the brain, but that's quite what I like about it. It's a a hidden gem on a low-rating, low budget channel, a dump month cheesefest of a movie. It's up there with Stalker, EYE or Mount and Blade, well designed games with a lack of polish that's almost endearing.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R: Clear Sky seems to take that measurement system and throw it out the 10th storey window. The game has found a very small pocket within the genre to carve out its own place in game history as a deftly challenging, gritty & unique game. It is proof of truly evolved gaming that was made by gamers who have a great understanding of games & have refined it in a very Russian way. Cold, calculative & ultimately, brilliant.

I got Train Simulator 2016 as part of the Humble Bundle for only a few $$, but I got the Humble Bundle specifically for this game as I was interested and wanted to see if 2017 would be worth the purchase.
Train Simulator is somehow really captivating. Everything you do in a train has to be planned way in advance as trains need a lot of time to slow down and stop or get going. It's also super interesting to learn all the signs and what theys mean. I thought as trains drive on tracks, it could not be that hard. But when traffic gets denser, all the buttons you have to press and signs you have to really look out for, it's harder than driving a car in my opinion. And more lives depend on it. So in principal I'm enjoying this game. But the technology Train Simulator is built upon is so unexcusably outdated, it sucks out all the air of an otherwise nice game.
Tha graphics feel very outdated. For a game that is Train Simulator 2016, or Train Simulator 2017 and costs $40, this is unexcusable. It looks awful. Passengers and their walking animations look terrible. Every few seconds the game needs to reload assets like trees and houses. And every time an object pops up on the horizon, the game stutters. And objects pop up in great numbers every 30 seconds or so, so every 30 seconds you get a huge stutter party for about 5 seconds until all new objects on the horizon are loaded. This is especially nerve wrecking when you're in a tight situation and need to slow down because of a distant signal, as the game doesn't always accept inputs at that time.
I also disliked the tutorial. It's not been given any love. The tutorial explains what home signals, distant signals are and what they display, but you cannt try it out. The tutorial is over after the explanation text disappears. This I could also read in the manual, no need for a tutorial mission for that that takes a long time to load. And that's it! Tutorials do not show you how the PZB signalling system works, when you need to slow down, to what speed you need to slow down, and how you actually do it. You cannot practice. This is only described in the manual or I had to look some additional YouTube videos, that did a better job.
Then, you're driving. And you come to the first yellow distant light signal, where you're supposed to slow down. You make a tiny mistake as you're not familiar with the buttons you have to press and bang, emergency brake. And the game doesn't tell you what you did wrong. Did I forget to press SIFA? Was I too fast? What would have been the correct speed? Tell me, I don't know! The game just lets you alone with all those questions. Very bad for learning and I found it highly frustrating. So you start the mission from scratch, wait on the loading screen for 30 seconds or more (and I have quite a fast machine) and then you drive for 20 minutes, until you make the same error and need to start over.
So, however interesting and fun I think Train Simulator would be, the technical drawbacks, long loading times, stuttering all the time, old and unappealing graphics, and bad tutorials / help system / explanations make Train Simulator an unsatisfactory and frustrating game.

The first and so far, the second most authentic video game tie-in with the Alien and Predator franchises. The as of yet anavailable Aliens Vs. Predator 2 is the first, but AVP classic outclasses the 2010 remake in terms of content. The level designs are still limited by walls and confined settings, but the thrill of hunting humans, as both the alien and Predator, or fighting either of these entities, is excellently paced. The weapons are true to the films and the sound effects are nicely recreated. AVP Classic was one of the first games to allow players to manipulate the timeframe and spawn enemy models into the game at will. The atmopshere is tense and the lighting adds a brooding sense of menace that the aliens and predators make even more startling when they appear. In terms of multiplayer, this game will offer a nice look into what evolved into the modern COD games.
Rebellion did very well by cinema goers and even sixteen years down the line, AVP Classic is a great reminder of how film studios can recreate their works in video games pleasingly.

Due to some flooding and my terrible internet, I ended up playing this game in offline mode. It's an okay game, but a decent entry into the series. This game is a prequel to Shadow of Cernobyl. Clear Sky contains the entirety of Shadow of Chernobyl's map, with two new zones included; however, this makes playing the game seem like more of an expansion than a standalone title. Clear Sky lacks the pacing that was present in the first title. Within 10 minutes you're loaded up with a pistol, assault rifle, ammo, and medkits. Compared to Shadow of Chernobyl, this game is a lot more action oriented. I finished the campaign with about 650 Stalker/Military/Faction kills, and 100 mutant kills. With so many kills, the gameplay began to feel a bit stale. My favorite part about Clear Sky was seeing how my actions affected the future game. I recommend playing Shadow of Chernobyl first, and following up with this game for the backstory. Overall, I would suggest you skip this title unless you are a big fan of the series; although, I highly recommend the first game.

I don't understand why some people hate this game so much...
It is probaby the best game in the DOOM series so far. (I haven't played DOOM yet, though.)
I finished the singleplayer campaign years ago and I absolutely loved it. You can play through it multiple times and never get bored of it.  I have yet to finish this game on nightmare mode!

After hell breaks loose, you start to hear cries, whispers, spirits, haunted machinery, and just very off-putting noises.  And you listen to people die for the first 10 minutes after the invasion begins...
The monsters are much scarier than the original DOOM  ones.
Even though the original Dooms are a classic, I can't even compare them to this one. I wish more were made in this style. I love how this one has a storyline, and shows the player what's going on in the Mars base throughout the whole game.
Overall, this game is awesome and I recommend it to anyone who loves horror survival games/movies.

Is heroes and generals a fun and enjoyable game? Yes when you can actually find a match. No for the rest of the time.
Queues for this game for different classes vary in time, an infantryman which is in every battle is easy to find a game, a tanker however is not as easy with wait times of over 15 minutes. One time i got logged out for inactivity while waiting for a queue and watching netflix at the same time.
The Generals mode in which you command assault teams to attack and defend other armies is somewhat fun at first. Then you realize you are 1000 in queue and it takes multiple days to actually be able to command the troops you requested. Then in the middle of the night when you arent there your troops spawn and are taken out by another army. Start queue again, war ends, repeat. This game used to be really fun way back, but I can't recommend it to anyone now. Sure graphics are nicer and they updated the maps but who cares when you cant find a game or even do anything in generals mode.

Heroes and Generals is now out of early access, so lets take a look!
Excellent foundation, Good technical achievements, incredibly poor design choices and missing management.
That about sums it up. But lets elaborate on that.
The foundation of the game- The battles themselves as infantryman are good. Vehicles are well done and fighting over the objectives tends to be pretty big a deal. The physics and gun system are good, once you get past the poor rifle you get at the start of the game, and it becomes more enjoyable when you can actually use a gun that shoots more than spitballs. But then there are things missing, and the game is not really set up for big encounters like it has the maps for. Prepare for a profound feeling of emptiness as you go through a city that is supposedly under attack but without anyone defending anything except one building that has been marked as the objective, and battles happening almost exclusively on a line from your point to the enemy point.
Flanking works well, you can stay still and let your camo make you near invisible even with the default uniforms, but this is not really used that much. You can use it all, be the ultimate soldier, and you will likely still not do as well as the guy who just camped the attic of the capture point and shot four guys who tried to dislodge him by making him run out of bullets. There is no penalty for dying- Not for you at least, but more on that later, and you don't really get rewarded for anything you do either. You play to play, and you win because you want to win.
Then lets get right to the poor design choices. This game is not just pay to win, but pay to progress. The way it is set up is to encourage you as a new player to quit and find an other game. Do you want to group up with a few friends? If there's more than two, then you have to pay for that or you need to spend some time grinding the 'skill' of having a group. After that, prepare for a lot more grind, as you will need several hours just to get the basics for a soldier. And if you want to do anything other than carry a basic rifle and maybe some grenades, you're going to need to grind hard just to afford your own ammo and gun modifications, because every single bullet shot, grenade thrown, mine placed or vehicle you use will cost you a lot. This leads directly to the playerbase adapting to the mentality;
Life is cheap. Ammo is expensive.
If you shoot someone you should pick up their gun because 9 times out of 10 it will be better than yours, even if you've spend 50+ hours on the game.
Of course there are other issues, mainly around balance and the 'generals' portion of the game. I'll spare you the complaints on balance- It's the usual for pay to win games, but more on that other bit later.
That said, if you don't mind the grind, and are fine using subpar weapons for most of your starting hours(10+) the basic infantry combat is good stuff. Moving along to tanks you will find that they're not amazing, but certainly entertaining and useful. Your view is a bit limited when using them but you can generally work them quite well. Airplanes are a joke and they likely always will be, do not even consider getting a fighter because you will be less useful to your team than if you had nothing but a pistol and the idea that you might surprise the enemy if you drive your car right at them. Controls are awful, planes don't do anything, and you take up a valuable spot on the team that could have been used by someone useful. Prepare for a long time of flying around not seeing anything and not doing anything.
And then on to the big complaint with this game, when you're not accounting for the fact that you may as well just be playing a basic trial of the game unless you pay them lots of money. The generals part.
It may as well not exist.
The game may even be better if it did not exist.
The entire generals section is deeply flawed to the point that it is literally unplayable.
First you need to slowly grind your way up to being allowed to use it. Then you will need to spend 3+ days to wait for a small squad of the absolute lowest tier divisions to spawn so you can use them. They will die in about 5 minutes and they will have gained no experience. Everything except infantry is essentially impossible to afford unless you pay the devs money for it, which will last only a few days at most and then you lose them. The map is incredibly poor and you will never have anything resembling a strategy- Merely people throwing their units around hoping it works. Sometimes it does work too, but this is never because of any skill at command.
It all comes down to the people playing the war battles. And they don't care. People will spawn in expensive tanks so that they can drive up to a building and get it blown up by AT. Because they don't have to pay for those tanks. The guy who got the tank brigade does. Same for airplanes, infantry spawns and vehicles. Why would they care that you've waited 3 days to get your infantry squad filled? They will run into machinegun fire and then respawn to do it again until you lose your squad. They will spawn every single vehicle available when they have 1000 infantry spawns and 300 vehicle spawns and they fight 160 infantry and 10 vehicles. And because these vehicles despawn after use, they are gone and they remain gone. The only thing here for you is frustration and poorly designed mechanics, a map that does not work properly and ideas that died before they were put into the game.
And that is most of what you will find when you manage to progress past being a basic rifleman with stock gun. A game with great ideas, pretty good technical achievements, but a team that does not understand even the most basic of design and doesn't care either. Greed above all else, and a complete lack of awareness.
Long ago when this was an early build I gave them a small bit of cash because they had a great concept, good basic gameplay, and claimed to have plans to make it better. I wanted to support them, since they were a small group that seemed to be making something great.
I regret that.
I could have burned that money and it would have gone to better use. The game isn't better than it was back then. It's worse, and it's showing no signs of ever improving.

I have played all 3 Sniper Elite's in the series and was excited to learn they are working on a 4th. I have also played the Zombie versions of the game (which I didn't like NEAR as much).
Overall, this is my favorite in the series and it seems as each release gets more and more polished than the last. While I play single player 99% of the time, I have dabbled in the co-op multiplayer and it is fun but I do wish it allowed multiple snipers instead of the sniper/spotter setup currently. I realize this is technically more correct, we, as players, want to play as the sniper and when we are playing as spotter it feels we are just playing nice until our turn.
I really only have a few gripes with the game that I can think of right now.
First: (And this is a big one) you can't set your elevation on your scope. Every person that shoots firearms knows you can set your "zero" on your scope so that it is "dead-on" at a certain distance. Then, you can hold over or under depending on whether the target it closer or further.
Second: This whole series has suffered from what I refer to as the "trigger effect" where enemies don't appear, or certain things happen until you hit a certain trigger. Usually the trigger is reaching a certain place on the map, or killing a certain person, or percentage of enemies. While not as pronounced as it was on the 2nd in the series, nothing like carefully scouting your approach, then moving forward and hitting a trigger point, and have enemies all around you. Often, once I figured out where that trigger point was, I moved forward until I triggered it, then ran back to my sniper nest and clear a path.
Third: Enemies in vehicles see WAY to well. If you have ever been in an armored vehicle or tank, you will know that visibility is NOT their strong point. They should have excellent defense and firepower like they do in real life and do in the game but shouldn't be able to see you near as well unless near an enemy patrol.
Fourth: Inconsistant mechanics regarding long range shooting alarming enemies. I have played the game 250+ hours, and still can't determine whether an enemy will hear my shots at a given place or distance except around broken generators and such. Incidentally, it seems logical that if backfiring generators at your location mask your sounds, you should be able to shoot a generator near the enemy and make it back firing then you could shoot towards him even if you are not by a generator any longer. (does that make sense?)
A few more "mentions" of other things about the game I wish were different.
Why can't we jump in the game?
I wish you could turn off the wind, without turning off elevation. It is harder to "feel" the wind in a game.
I had some occasional issues with the game doing a red flicker when SLI was enabled. This was the only game that ever did that. Normally, just changing the resolution and restarting it fixed it. Ironically, I could alternate between two resolutions and they both worked; AFTER the other one messed up.
Every time you reload your side arm, it goes through the "chambering" animation. Just because you drop the magazine, and put in a full one, doesn't mean the chamber will be empty. Yes, there are a FEW firearms that the magazine is loaded from the top, usually with a "stripper clip" where you would potentially cycle it like that, but aside from the M1 Garand rifle and the Mauser C96 (which I don't remember any in the game), nothing should load like that. For a game that obviously desires for accuracy and realism, it seems like an odd oversight.
Snipers don't fall for thrown rocks, no way to get them to move short of killing them.

The main PROs of the game:
==========================
+ stealth mechanics (distracting enemies, line of sights, noises - especially sounds to mask your shots )
+ different enemies and tactis (infantry, counter-sniper, vehicles); enemies even try to revive their mates
+ sniping system (which can be adjusted via difficulty)
+ great level design (playing time, visuals, enemy routes, vehicles that spawn)
+ unlock-system for weapons and their upgrades, items
+ all points above are play- and enjoyable via COOP; the entire campaign, some independent scenarios (where you both can play a sniper OR one player is the spotter) and a survival mode
The main CONs of the game:
==========================
- the AI; like already mentioned in other reviews, sometimes they decide to be psionist and on the other moment they are dumb as S-Word
- AI alarm status: once alarmed it would be more intense to keep this status; it feels some kinda stupid if your opponents act like "huh, someone killed one or several of our crew. Lets keep this in mind for just a few minutes and continue work the standard way"
- ammunition after scavenging enemies - maybe its because of difficulty, but I dont think soldiers had just 1/2 clip for the MPs with them at war
- controls are kinda flawless
NEUTRAL:
========
The game also offers some PvP multiplayer modes. Didn't try them, cuz I don't like online 3rd person shooters connected to a "camping simulation". But that's a matter of taste. Sniper fans will have their fun...

It's a good game and a last hurrah for the Wargame series and maybe even Eugen as a whole (sorry, I'm not getting Steel Division, this is the end here). I've been a long time supporter of Eugen back during R.U.S.E. These series have been my dream game (not related to the nomination) come true: A real-time RTS with a myriad of military units from various nations. In the Wargame series there is depth, there is detail, and most importantly, there is fun in both victory as you steamroll the enemy and play hide-and-seek with the last CV, and there is fun in defeat as you fling insults on the enemy, your teammates, and Eugen for making the game unbalanced/unfinished♥♥♥♥♥♥..etc.
Red Dragon, like the rest of the Wargame series is pretty good. It got all the good and bad points of its two previous games (European Escalation, and Airland Battle). There are two main features of RD:
-Adds various East Asian armies and Australia, as well as Finland, Yugoslavia, Netherlands, and Israel (if you count the DLC) to the Wargame roster. Loads of fun for both PACT and NATO, and a nice break from the European theatre of EE and ALB. The timeframe is also shifted a little bit into the '90s, which may be a little late and too fictional for some Cold War enthusiasts (like me). Somewhat related is that there are "prototype" units for several of the armies in-game, which is a bit too much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t for my tastes. like the Fallschrimjäger '90 back when the game was newly released.
-Naval warfare, which is unfortunately very "basic" and very disappointing. Unlike the introduction of fixed-wing aircraft in ALB, the very feature that RD was made for comes very short of expectations. The scaling and range of the weapons systems are just not ideal in many ways. That being said, ships are still relatively fun to use. There is nothing better than seeing an amphibious assault successfully land on the enemy's side on Wonsan, Gunboat, or D-Day. My favorite combination:
Landing craft INF, recon, AA + Smoke screen + Landing CV + Heli support + Naval support = Capture the enemy's main spawn = Easy win.

Is it ded?
There are enough players if you are looking for a game.
Is it hard?
If you got a knack for RTS games, then this will be a fun game to learn. Otherwise, it will be a bit challenging. It isn't anywhere near CMANO, that's for sure.
In the end, you should be able to identify and generally remember the stats of most of the units ingame. As soon as you see "Unit name", you should be able to know what you are up against, how counter it, and what extras come with it. I don't mean literally memorize, but generally remember so you can make a quick decision instead of hovering over unit, pressing TAB, and reading everything all over again...
(I can't say it's hard myself since I've been playing Eugen RTS games since R.U.S.E. and EE.)
Should I buy the game?
It's entirely up to you. If you have a hard-on for military hardware and troops, get this. If you get a raging boner dreaming about "Cold War gone hot" scenarios, get this (personally I prefer EE or ALB). If you get wet thinking about ♥♥♥♥ing around, spouting memes like an immature♥♥♥♥♥in the menu lobby chat instead of playing the game itself, get this. If you just want a good quality real-time RTS that offers a unique experience, definitely get it.

Don't be fooled by the hype. "A Tale of Two Sons" offers inviting cinematics and promises to deliver a charming story, but it fails to deliver in the areas that matter.
Let's start with gameplay... It's boring. Yep, pretty boring. Once the novelty of the dual joystick control of operating both brothers wears off, you realize that they didn't do anything that creative here, and it feels like a poor rendition of Prince of Persia. Did I say poor rendition, yep, because Prince of Persia was actually fun to play. This is not.
Next, the story... Did anyone tell you the characters speak in their own language? Probably not. There's no "subtitles" either. This seems cute, or even 'profound' and interesting, until you realize something.... Character development is really really hard, almost impossible when the characters can't say anything. Ok, so, the brothers interact with their environment in unique, universally understandable, and charming actions, which you can watch. (This interaction turned out to be the most entertaining part of the game for me.) But an unnerving revalation about the cold truth of this idea's limitations dawns on you as you play more and more... you feel like you're a detached God, watching with some mildly bored amusement as your creations carry about their business. Not only do you feel like you don't really impact the process very much, but you don't know anything about what the brothers are thinking, feeling, hoping, fearing... You can't even understand them. When you hear them speak, it's just jibberish. Bottom line, you don't care what happens to the brothers really, and you're bored.
So, I did take a screenshot. The cinematics really are pretty damn good. But, there are plenty of games that deliver nice graphics. Sure, from a design and art standpoint, this game stood out a bit, but I don't think good cinematics really makes it worth my time.
I'm not sure why this game got such good reviews. It still baffles me a little, because I've never been so totally and completely misled by what seemed to be the general concensus of most of the reviews. (Yeah, there's usually some flamers and some fanboys for everything, but this one seemed solid.) I suppose I will have to start validating Steam reviews with 3rd party sites...

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a nice, if short , little adventure.
It's unique gameplay, where you control two brothers at the same time  using the two analog sticks and left and right trigger buttons, is an excellent game emchanic that offers up some interesting ways to proceed through the game.  There are various things to interact with and in many cases each brother will have a different response to a particular object.  Puzzles/challenges will almost always require the brothers work together to surpass them.  While none of the challenges aren't difficult by any means, they are interesting, sometimes clever or fun, and never out of touch with the game or the narrative.
The story itself has a simple yet heartfelt narrative that will leave it impact on you emotionally.  The music suits the narrative well, and is touching and moving in its own right.  The graphics are simple but very charming with some areas quite breathtaking.  The environments are very creative, quite varied for such a short game which bring me to my only real complaint about this game.
Clocking in just over 3 hours of playtime for me this feels like it's over before it had begun.  Still, it's a satisfying short story that will leave a remarkable impression on you for its story and its charm if not for its challenge or length.

O jogo é lindo (enredo, paisagens, personagens, cutscenes, tudo). É um jogo curto e simples. Você controla dois irmãos, ao mesmo tempo. Sugiro que jogue com uma manete, por favor! A movimentação não exige muita complexidade, somente as direções, dois botões para mover a câmera e dois para as ações - um botão para cada irmão -, que variam de acordo com a situação. Depois de um tempo você se acostuma muito bem e não buga mais a sua mente controlando os dois garotos.
Você vai em busca de um objetivo, e para alcançá-lo você passa por diversas aventuras. Você está no mundo de Esopo, das fábulas. Todas as histórias que você já leu ou ouviu quando criança (tá, nem todas) estão colocadas de modo fantasioso no jogo, e que baita País das Maravilhas, com certeza.
Você passa por situações diversas, desafios e lugares diversos; e isso te deixa bastante envolvido no jogo de modo que o faça zerar em poucas horas. É muito interessante o modo com que você pode interagir com os personagens, criaturas, animais e objetos do jogo, cada irmão interage de uma forma.Talvez o final possa ser surpreendente para alguns jogadores, para outros não.

Doom 3 took a huge step away from the original series' gameplay in favor of trying to make a horror game out of the franchise, and it's actually great despite some of the backlash it received on release.
The claustrophobic layout of the base combined with it's lighting creates for the perfect Sci-fi horror scene for demonic invasion. Although it can seem somewhat linear in map design, there are other areas you can explore if you keep an eye on doors that require certain codes or PDAs.
The PDA system itself rewards exploration by giving you codes and clearance to caches of ammo and health, while filling you in on how disturbing life was inside the UAC without obnoxiously pulling you out of the game. You have the choice of either just moving on or listening to audio logs and reading e-mails from employees and learning more about the UAC.
The monsters are excellent, almost all the classic Doom baddies make a comeback (excluding the Pain Elemental) and fill the same classic roles, but with some new twists. Some examples include Imps being able to crawl around now, and are much faster, making them harder targets, and Zombies with guns will take cover and shoot from around corners and pillars, making firefights more intense. New monsters were also added, and fit right into the new theme and feel ID Software went with for 3.
The guns we know and love also make a return (save the Doom 2 super-shotgun), along with a few new ones, like the machinegun and grenades. They feel great, and function great.
All-in-all, if you are looking for a good horror-themed game, this is the one for you. I highly recommend it for veteran and newcomers to horror games alike.

Pros:
-Excellent, cutting-edge (for 2003, anyway) lighting adds a perfectly dank and spooky atmosphere to each and every room
-weaponry is satisfying to use, although frequent reloading puts you in a difficult spot more than a couple times
-sound design and voice acting are top-notch for the time, although the main villain drips with liquid cheese
-came out during a time when navigation and exploration were still heavily encouraged in FPSes, as the level design retains the labyrinthine, self-guided nature of the classics
-is still a challenge when not played on the highest difficulty
-flashlight mechanic as-is (needing to alternate between seeing and shooting your enemies) is kind of interesting and makes fights more tense
Cons:
-slowed pace and small enemy numbers means fights are sometimes not very exciting
-The Trite enemy is overused so heavily that I swear half the ammunition I waste is on hordes of finger-spiders
-While enemy redesigns are definitely intimidating and scary, many of them share similar body types and shapes so it becomes difficult to distinguish them
-EVERYTHING IS ♥♥♥♥ING GRAY. The walls, floor and ceiling are gray, the weapons are gray, the enemies are gray, even the PEOPLE are gray. Finding an area with any significant amount of color is like finding the Ark of the Covenant
-Game overstays its welcome heavily, partly due to its slow pace and lack of variety in enemy encounters
-game does not have many graphical options (though it was an early - 2000s game, so it gets some slack)
Overall, while it's definitely slower, more methodical and at times less exciting than the games that came before or after it, Doom 3 is still an entertaining action-horror shooter and an excellent demonstration of advanced lighting effects that would shape how horror games were built from then on.

DOOM 3 is a game that had me confused, I didn't know if I hated it or not,
The gameplay in DOOM 3 feels like a stable FPS game, it feels nothing like a DOOM game, the gameplay is slow paced and very boring at times as the game will also use alot of cheap jumpscares. The guns in this game feel weak, the only gun that actually sounds satisfying to shoot is the Plasma Rifle. The game does an OK job at setting up a horror setting in the ruined UAC base on Mars. Speaking of which the level design in this game is really good, especially hell. It's a shame we didn't get much of the Hell levels.
In DOOM 3 your flashlight and your gun are two different tools, meaning you'll have to sacrifice one of them for combat, or sight which sounds good on paper, but it seems poorly executed in the game. Except for some really well done sections but besides that, it just feels like a chore.
The combat in this game feels lackluster, while the demon AI (except for the gun wielding foes) is pretty dumb, even for 2004 standards. There is a good variety of demons, although near the beginning it is mostly zombies and imps. The bosses in this game are laughable some left me asking if that was it or if there was a second phase, the final boss especially is just terrible.
The story in this game is interesting in some parts, although it mostly devolves into Marine do this, Marine do that and gets quite annoying, but we don't really play DOOM for it's story anyways.
The sound design for alot of the demons in the game is very well done, many of the ambient sounds make the game very immersive and atmospheric for the most part. The soundtrack is interesting although you won't really hear much besides the music that plays in the main menu.

Attention to detail in the levels of DOOM 3 is obvious that alot of work was put into the engine the game uses, as many of the levels are very detailed and feel like a real facility! The enemy design in the game is more alien for the most part which is also a bit of let down.

I want to start by admitting that this game has its flaws.
The controls are a bit clunky (I spent the first few hours of the game customizing the controls EXTENSIVELY--an unfortunate side-effect of the MANY different items/tools/movement options/etc. at your fingertips-until I got them just the way I liked them). There's also little to no practical description of what button does what. I had to read the control options a few times before I figured them all out.
The learning curve is pretty steep. I spent a lot of time dying and wondering what I could possibly be doing wrong. (This is probably an unfortunate side effect of playing an incredibly difficult/tactical game like it's Halo).
The environment is unforgiving and tremendously dangerous. You'll killed by just about anything at any time until you get the hang of it.
These cons starting to sound at least a little bit like pros? I personally think they are.
The more I play the game, the more I begin to realize that there is a LOT going on here in terms of gameplay dynamic. It takes some patience and a whole lot of trial-and-error, but it definitely pays off in the long run. This game is not a casual stroll in the FPS park, but an immersive and challenging game with a better-than-bad storyline and some really great ideas that were (mostly) pulled off quite nicely. This makes it incredibly rewarding when you start to fall into a rhythm and only die every twenty minutes instead of two...
The game is unforgiving because it's going for its own kind of realism. You can't take out the well equipped soldiers with a mounted machine gun with your AK-74su (ONLY ten, you say? Stop playing so much COD, you'll shoot yer eye out.) because there's TEN of them and a MOUNTED MACHINE GUN and there's ONE of you and not that many bullets or space in your body for their bullets... Just like real life, eh?
Buy it. Try it out. Be impressed... After you get over the soul crushing defeat of being killed by a pack of dogs while trying to loot a body for precious ammo and bandages that turns out to be empty after you get to it on your third or tenth try (depending on how you go about things).
Oh... and quicksave at least every 2 minutes... Or just don't fight anything. Ever.

The first Swamps level is probably the best thing about Clear Sky -- it really does feel like it is building on Shadow of Chernobyl to greater heights! Unfortunately, it builds the game up to a level it cannot sustain.
It's kind of cool to revist a lot of the same places and see them in a slightly different light. But by the time you are going through the Agroprom and Yantar, the novelty begins to wear off.
Add in the numerous bugs and outright crashes towards the end of the game, even with the Complete mod, and I was seriously getting frustrated towards the end of my 150-hour playthrough. Oh, and the final act feels rushed, just like it did in SoC. And don't even get me STARTED on the final level! Argh!
Still, the nod to the film Stalker in the penultimate level is very nice, though it is a shame the game rushes you through it without too much chance to revel in the environments.
Overall -- definitely weaker and less polished that SoC Complete, but still, I managed to clock up a good amount of hours out of Clear Sky. It never quite manages to surpass its opening, though, which is a shame.

So far Portal Knights has been one of the best game purchases i've made in a while.  As an early access game, it is obviously buggy and in need of content, but it is surprisingly well optimized.  It runs at a stable 60fps on my laptop (i7 with a GTX 660M) at the highest settings with only the shadows turned off.  Overall, the game looks beautiful, the controls are tight, and there is already enough content to keep you hooked for hours at a time.
The only major bug i've run into is with the multiplayer/co-op.  My friend and I were playing it, already a good hour and a half into it, and all of a sudden we were disconnected from each other.  Neither of us had any connection problems, and even after restarting, resetting the routers, etc. we still couldn't reconnect.  This was probably an issue with the game's server, so hopefully this gets resolved soon.
But despite that proble, for an early access game, it is remarkably well fleshed out, and I cannot wait to see how the developers expand it as time goes on.
TL;DR, Get this game now!

If steam had a "meh" recommendation, that's what this game would get.  Bullet point time for pros & cons:
:
- The game is smooth, it runs good, and it has it's good qualities.  Like C&C series without the construction.
-Most of the player chat is some of the dumbest♥♥♥♥♥♥I have ever seen.  Like Barrens chat, but a little more raunchy and very little substance.  This could just as easily be in the cons section if you expect helpful and straight answers if you ask questions, but generally don't ask in chat.  You'll most likely just get some fool trying to talk badass and never actually answer the question.
-Challenging is the basic name of the game.  It has an impressive learning curve.
-Units are well defined and have their key applications in realistic fashion.  I find it is more fun to play with your "Deck" build in skirmish mode than it is to play the campaign.
:
-A logistical nightmare.  You can have a FOB, but it has limited supplies that does not replenish itself.  Fuel, ammo and parts are all pooled into one number, hence the logistiacal nightmare part.  You can toggle what gets delivered, but honestly it doesn't matter because every supply guy knows that it will all be equally needed.  What rubs me the wrong way about it is how the FOB doesn't replenish itself.  I mean, that is the purpose of a FOB (to be the distribution warehouse of the battlefield).  After a while, you're gonna have a bunch of 88Ms with nothing to do and a bunch of vehicles that can't shoot or move trying to hunt down the remenants of the opposition (Grunts FTW, although it takes forever).  I could understand a supplies on hand concept, but not a finite stockpile for the entire match, especially with total destruction as the win parameter if that's your thing like it is mine.
-(For singleplayer) The AI is too predictable, though that doesn't mean it's gonna be easy.  Once you have first contact it is gonna throw anything and everything it has that can fly and shoot at you all at once.  It's gonna be a quick burst of Anti-Aircraft, then it is gonna throw every piece of armor it has at you.  If you can survive the several waves, it will try to flank you with infantry while it pounds you with artillery. Then it's just a matter of going objective to objective that they hold and cleaning up whatever is left. Their recon will usually be and stay hidden at that point and it turns into a seek and destroy mission, if you have the fuel and ammo to keep your vehicles functional...
-Unit orders are pretty limited.  I couldn't figure out how to group different units, like M1A1 Abrams with M11P Abrams.  Or Abrams with Bradleys.  Not a huge deal, but I would rather be able to make preset battle groups with a single click than a click and drag that tends to select more than I want.  if you control click you will select all units of that type in that area, but you can't control click to quickly add another type to that selection, it will be either or.  Shift clicking single troops takes too long for this kind of RTS.
Really, those are the biggest cons I can think of that I experienced.   I'd recommend this game to someone who really likes RTS.  I'm sure with the right groups MP is awesome.  After reading the chat, there's a lot of them I don't wanna play with.  They might be good at the game, but they are better at painting themselves like idiots when they speak and that's not my cup o' tea.

Even though the devs have abandoned the game, the community is absolutely cancerous, cheese tactics rule the battlefield and the in-game chat makes /pol/ look like an innocent kitten, I still love the game itself. It's fun if you can control who you play with (read: get friends to play too).

I had to write this review because some people are having doubts about whether or not to buy this game.
I MOST DEFINITELY RECOMMEND THIS GAME.
It is beautiful - not simply visually, but the telling of the story and its emotional impact.
At the start of my play through the first level I thought: "okay this game looks pretty and even a little too cutesy for my taste but nothing staggeringly amazing so far". Then it got darker, much darker (thankfully, this aint Disney)! The journey these too lads take sometimes puts them in such jaw-droppingly perilous situations that you might find yourself gasping. When you're not gasping at regularly picturesque backgrounds, that is. By the way, if you don't have a fear of heights or deep water, you may develop one after playing.
Some people bemoan the shortness of the game. It is true that this game is short and it'll only take about three hours to complete but judging a game by its length alone can create some very skewed perspectives on quality. Remember that the original Portal was only a few hours long but it still holds a special place in many gamers hearts. Brothers too packs a lot in for its few hours!
In short, this game will transport you into a wonderfully polished storybook world and leave you satisfied. If you don't buy this game especially when heavily discounted on sale then you really are a first-class heel.

THE GOOD:
Starting up was super easy. We only needed one copy of the game so I downloaded it, we all downloaded the app (onto our Galaxy S7 Edges) and connected to my wifi (on 2.4Ghz because my 5Ghz seems to sputter sometimes with everything I try to connect to it), started the game and put in a label, started the app on our phones connected and hit "Start" on the game (on the PC). We waited for only a few brief moments for each player to get their starting dialog and get connected with the other players. It was literally that easy.
The game play was good enough that we never ended up stumbling around like morons wondering what to do next (for very long), there was always a dialog or some action going on that kept us entertained. Reading dialog to each other ended up adding depth to the characters right away, and was sometimes comical. The turn based action was amazingly quick, there was no waiting for some assmunch to move around 40 units or to sort through pages of abilities to do something. We kept on trucking from room to room and enjoyed the dialog.
STUFF:
We started the game thinking 5 hours of game time and we are good to call it a night. We ended up playing for 6 hours until my wife came out of the bedroom and yelled at us for being to loud at around 1:30am. I had to kick the guys out unfortunately and I only got about 5.5hrs of sleep last night and the first thing Im doing this morning is writing this review while the Steam Summer Sale is going on. It's worth the money if it's on sale or not. Check it out and have a blast. I haven't played it solo, but I think I might. We also unhooked my Vive to plug in the 60" 4k TV so we could all sit on the couch and watch it played on the big screen easily. NOTE: I mirrored my center monitor to the TV and we could see it on both screens. Doing this isn't something everyone can do, so if you do go in to this game wanting to play remember it is a PC game, you just use your phone as a controller. The controllers have a VERY LIGHT latency and can make moving seem clunky but you will get the hang of when to use point to point movement and when to use joystick movement.
THE BAD:
Myself and two friends sat down last night and figured that I could afford to skip a trip to McD's and get this game at least to check it out. We started looking at the developer video and I have to say we were NOT impressed looking at their video. It seemed laggy, lacking textures and in dire need of some completion. So we went to youtube wanting to give this a second chance and looked and found another video that was much better but the reviewer was very dry. We assume we only missed a little as we managed to continue the game with only getting lost a little bit.
