This game is about the closest you can get to a video game equivolent to a pen and paper RPG session as you can get. I say that as a person who runs tabletop RPG sessions. It's a 1-4 couch co-op game over the same wi-fi connection.
The game starts off with 5 characters, having their own background, meet up to go into an underground fortress. Each of these characters have their own playstyle, along with their own agenda. This is where actual role playing is involved. Each of your characters dialog is spoken out loud by you for the other players to hear (or in some cases to not hear). Interactions between the spellcaster and the cleric are downright fun.
Control is handled by a phone or tablet each person connects to the game through the same wi-fi connection. Your phone/tablet contains all of your characters information and is your control device. Controls handle very well, you can do either point and move style, or joystick like control by touching the outer section of the control ring. Your device will make a notification sound when your character has something to say or think. Some options are entirely up to you to share with the group or to keep them secret.
Combat in the game is turn based, much alike a tabletop RPG. Your character has a range of movement they can move per turn, followed by an action if they are in range to do so. Communication is key when you are playing with friends, turns can be wasted if someone who could have hit a target further out kills one where a close range couldn't.
This leads to character development. In your options menu is where you can upgrade your character. There's two ways to do so. Abilities give your character new skills such as making items, or bonuses to stats. The other is upgrades, this option inceases your abilities of your weapon and armor. New physical attacks, and defensive capabilities to use in combat are learned here. Both of these upgrade types require resources and are tiered by godstones. You earn them at checkpoint like spots throughout the game. The resources you get are common (found on most humans and some smashable items), Remnant (found on monsters, and in food like barrels), and Precious (money like resource found in chests).
This leads to my only gripe with the game is the resources themselves. The person who picks up resources is the one who gets them. Whereas most games have a shared mechanic this one doesn't. Understandably it's a role-playing game and there is a trading interaction, however upgrades are the same across the board for each character and they don't come cheap either, so if you have a friend who likes to hoard every resource, your game can come to a quick stop.
All in all it's a very great game, one i cannot wait for all 9 episodes to come out.

This game is a classic, it does so much so well but has a few CRAPPO moments too. This was meant to be a retelling of the original Doom but simultaneously redefine its own genre.
Story: Its the 22nd century and the Union Aerospace Corporation has a huge cutting edge facility on Mars where they conduct various weapons and genetic research (including opening portals to hell apparently). One of the lead researchers on the site, Dr. Malcolm Betruger has been making preparations for a Demonic Invasion (without the consent of his fellow humans of course) and return for receiving the power to rule over them. The UAC sensing something is wrong due to the increasing amount of on work casualties sends an ambassador, his bodyguard, and an unrelated Marine transfer (you) to Mars. Shortly after arriving all hell breaks loose and your left alone. Now you must regroup with your fellow survivors and find a way to stop the hell portal.
Overall Score for Story: 7/10
Gameplay: The gunplay in Doom 3 isn't anything unique or special. You get tons of guns, they all have the same crosshair, you can sprint, crouch, jump, all the basics are accounted for. However, the guns stand out from the rest of the series due to their weak performance. In most games, each gun has a standout strength, but in this game, each gun has a standout weakness. For example: the pistol has a really low fire rate, the shotgun has horrendous spread, the chain gun is woefully inaccurate etc. However, these attributes do help make Doom 3 feel more like a survival horror. Also the grenades bounce like silly putty when you throw them. One cool thing however was how the marine interacts with in-game screens, instead of merely pressing a button to activate something, your cursor will appear on any screen when you look at it which makes the world feel much more real.
Overall Score for Gameplay 8/10
Characters: There are only five important characters in Doom 3. None have any real development, they leave the screen in the end pretty much the same way that they came in, some more alive than other though.
Overall Score for Characters: 7/10
Graphics: The visuals are what people think of most when they think of Doom 3 and they do hold up well. The lighting is still pretty good. The textures are ugly when you get close up (just like my wife) but in the heat of action you won't notice.
Overall Score for Graphics: 8/10
Sound: The sound is alright in this game, the gun sounds really fake and weak but I guess that's sort of the point since the game wants you to feel vulnerable. Footsteps are ok, they don't have too much weight on them but they work. Monster screams and growls sound convincing enough.
Overall Score for Sound: 8/10
Soundtrack: The soundtrack is practically nonexistent except for the Title/Credits Theme and some ambient noises/chords throughout the game.
Overall Score for Soundtrack: 6/10

Doom 3 isn't the same game as the first 2.
Doom 3 takes the series in a different direction by having a more story focused Single-Player.
It isn't as brutal and action packed, the game has more of a focus on HORROR.
There still are moments of action, but the pacing of Doom 3 is slower than Doom 1 & 2.
Cutscenes are used a lot in the Campaign. Most of the cutscenes are fun to watch, but can come across as cheesey and out of place sometimes.
The level design of this game takes a lot from the Original Doom Games. Most levels make you explore the environment and look for secret areas that contain Health & Ammo.
However, in Doom 1 there were moment where hundreds of Demons were attacking you. In Doom 3, only a handful of Demons attack you at a time.
Most of the enemy types in this game are just updated versions of the Demons from the first two games.
The weapons from the first two games also return. You have: The pistol, Shotgun, Chaingun, Rocket Launcher, Plasma Gun, Chainsaw and BFG 9000. The new weapons included are: The Machine Gun and Soul Cube.
Doom 3 takes a lot of inspiration from Half-Life. Instead of looking for a Red, Blue or Yellow Keycard you are instead going through the levels and interacting with the world & characters around you. Another part that Doom 3 takes from Half-Life is the 30 minute introduction where you are walking around the facilites and interacting with some of personal in the facility.
Now onto the actual Gameplay, Doom 3 is VERY dated. As much as I like Old-School Shooters, Doom 3's Gameplay feels very clunky. The movement of the Doomguy is awkward. The Soldiers have been coded in a way so that EVERY bullet they fire will hit you. You also can't change to another weapon while you are reloading a gun. This may not sound so bad, but when there are enemies all around you then they will just beat the sh*t outta you until you are dead.
Onto graphics, Doom 3 looks amazing for a game that released in 2004. The shadows and dynamic lighting works really well to create this creepy environment. However, Doom 3 gets repetitive visually. The Mars Facility all looks the same and at times you will feel like you are going in circles when you are actually going the right way. Until you go to Hell..........about 2/3 into the Game you go to Hell. This place is dark, blood filled and spooky. The Demons relly fit in with the visuals of Hell and the fire and lava make Hell the best part of the game. The 'Hell' Chapter feels like classic Doom with Doom 3's mechanics. I kinda wish Doom 3 was more like this chapter. Horror mixed with action. Doom 3 makes feel that if Hell was to exist, this is what Hell would look like.
By the way........me saying "You go to Hell in Doom 3" is as much a spoiler as saying that you play as Master Chief in Halo. It isn't a Spoiler, it's just common knowledge.
OVERALL: I'd recommend Doom 3 for someone who is a fan of Horror and FPS games. Due be aware that Doom 3 is a dated and doesn't hold up as well. But the Single-Player is fun and entertaining. With a lot of polish and attention to detail.
Also, don't buy Doom 3 BFG Edition. It messes around with some of the mechanics of the game and it ruins the atomosphere and Gameplay. Just buy a copy of the Original Doom 3 from 2004 and play that version.

I loved Shadow of Chernobyl. It wasn't exactly as originally promised (the developers removed a handful of features), still, the game had a unique atmosphere that made it memorable. Then, not long after Clear Sky was released and everything I liked about SoC simply vanished.
Clear Sky was an unnecessary sequel. The developer quickly made a sequel to cash in on a successful and famous game. They advertised it as a prequel story as the protagonist here follows the hero from the first game. But shouldn't you introduce new environments or areas in a sequel even if it is intended as a prequel story? You venture through the very same areas - even the map looks the same. At the beginning, you have a swamp-like are which is new, yes, but then you encounter the same places.
The game uses the same engine but with DX10 features included. Still, you have a handful of bugs and the game can be very difficult at times - not only do you encounter respawning enemies but sometimes it is difficult to understand why it takes so many shots to finally eliminate someone.
What happened to the super ending of the original game? Here, the final encounter in the centre of the zone seems rushed and non-creative. What happened to the different endings we had in SoC based on the gameplay-style we followed? Where are the new enemy types / gameplay elements / objects / weapons we expect from a sequel? Make no mistake: introducing new things is not a must but at least I would have expected to have the game rid of all the bugs it had in the original one.
I remember the forest area being different. Instead of following the route next to it we finally ventured into it. It was dark and creepy and provided the necessary atmosphere. But this was the only thing in Clear Sky that I remember as good.

- Very polished. So far I didn't experience bugs, crahses or any other issues. Very untypical for an Early Access title. I wish more developers would take their EA releases that seriously.
CONS:
- Honestly, I couldn't find one yet. :-)
SUGGESTIONS:
- Add Steam Workshop support! That would even increase the potential of the game.
- Add key-binding support.
If you liked Minecraft, Starbound, Zeld or Terraria, go buy this game!

400h gametime and played this game since the start of 2016, I'm here to inform you of the pros and cons of this unique game and hopefully drag you in as I myself am in the opinion that every wannabe Tactician (not strategist, they're a different breed) should play this game.   ... except if the cons looks too bad and overshadows the pros.
Pros:
1) Unique Strategy game "gameplay" = Unlike most RTS Strategy games, Wargame isn't about gathering resources on a certain part in the map and building factories to spend said resources to pump out units. Instead, before you would go into a match, you'd need to create a "Deck" of unit cards... kinda like YuGiOh except with Real life Military units. Once on the battlefield, you are assigned points depending on the game settings of the host and spend those points to deploy your "Units" from the Deck that you've made. Deck making is somewhat complex and won't be mentioned here. So after you deployed your units, you'd maneuvre them around the map and beat up your opponent on the field. Keep in mind that you do earn income to purchase more units overtime and it increases depending on the gamemode, or not at all.
2) Nice Graphics and Unit models = The map designs are clean enough and looks good enough, typical of your average everyday modern Strategy Game... but the real charm lies in the details of the ingame units... for the creators have faithfully stuck with the real designs of units as they are real life, all down to that tiny little hook and hose you see on that tiny tiny tank, indeed it would be there too in real life! and there are about like 500 units in the game so...
3) Diverse units and tactical layer = There are around 500 units in this game, each with their own categories and uses. And the thing is, almost every unit has their uses, from the cheap Militia to the deadly Special Forces; the deadly T-72 with upgrades to the lowly T-55; Don't let the prices fool you, no one will buy the most-expensive thing because they aren't "Cost-efficient", so you'll pretty much see every unit in the game thrown at you or used by you by the time you hit 200h gametime.
4) Well-paced game flow = Wargame Red Dragon is a quick RTS, it ain't slow as there is not wait time to purchase and train units then a lag before it spawns out of the Barracks or some mumbo jumbo. Once you place your units, SCRAM! issue those orders, get them rolling, you want to be the FIRST to the battlefield (If possible) as Sun Tzu once said, but I forgot his full quote... goes something like reaching there by noon and digging in or some ching chong. Anyways, the units aren't slow and sluggish either as the game speeds them up compared to their real life counterpart. The idea is that the battlefield you're in is actually raging on for hours instead of the 40m the game timer is set to.
5) No Microtransactions = Thats a Pros right? folks these days like to make a fuss about em
Cons
1) No good tutorial offered by the game itself = The game offers no decent tutorial so you'd need to learn from either others, guides, videos. Maybe this could be a pros since it forces the person to adapt, get creative and formulate his or her own playstyle along the way after absorbing many lessons as there really isn't a "1 way to win all games" playstyle.
2) An odd community = From my own experience you will encounter lots of people who will either keep silent or cuss at you the minute before the game begins. It get's worse by a cube root in team games and then multiplied by pie once a team starts winning and the other starts losing as they taunt the loser and the loser taunts the "weakest" player in their own team. Rarely is there any chivalry in the community, 1v1s are silent commanders facing each other and team games are "I did well but my teammates squandered my efforts so I abuse them" You rarely make friends here... but, there have been a few exceptions.
3) A community that are frightened easily = In most multiplayer game lobbies, it takes 3x longer than usual to finally start, the issue for this is that people always leave. Why do they always leave? because they checked the stats of their opponents and go "Oh, he's 30 levels higher than me and has an 80% winrate, I'm gonna lose so I'm gonna f**k off." I see this attitude everyday, complaining about "stacked" teams. Sure, they may be stacked but they might be friends and just want to play together, and neither are they stopping you from bringing a stack of friends. And if you're afraid of losing, how do you expect to learn? what will you gain? will you only play "Easy" games with people that are low in level and horrid winrate? This attitude needs to stop and people should just play the game regardless of the statistics of their opponents. So what if you lose? Atleast you learned something, you're marginally better than your previous self before the game started. Be happy and never Stat-check and leave, Commanders in real-life don't check their opponents stats too ya know.
4) Random unit debuffs = I get that in real life, plans never survive contact with the enemy, but can you be blamed when you're launching an assault and for some reason your most-expensive tank or Anti-Air vehicle gets "Detracked" or "Stuck in Mud" ? ... This is a rather bad feature in my opinion and should be removed.
5) A small proffesional army = By this I mean a small playerbase. The game is rather... old, but gold! Nonetheless, this game really does not appeal to many RTS Gamers except oddballs like me I suppose
6) The Navy = As in real life, the Navy cannot win wars by itself. They merely support campaigns. It gets worst for the typical Napoleonic-era Admiral as Battleships really become obsolete compared to the Aircraft Carrier. Now to win Navy, you'd either bring submarines (nonexistent in Wargame) or Aircraft Carriers (Also Nonexistent) and have an Airwar but with Frigates at the bottom shooting. That's pretty much what Naval battles are like. The ships also turn oddly if you were to issue an order to turn 180 degrees. Gunboats do have a part to play too when providing coastal Fire support. If you're looking for large naval clashes, don't bother because they too won't happen in real life.
Neutrals (Can be good or bad depending on the individual)
1) Steep Learning Curve = This game is hard and requires skills, knowledge, and luck. You will lose a lot. So this means if you're a casual gamer, you're gonna eat dirt a lot. This is bad as well, hard game, hard life for you but good in a sense that you'd be facing dedicated players who are in to win and of high quality (somewhat).
2) Cold War Era = This game takes place at the end of the cold war (1990-ish) and a clash of ideologies occur. Either pick Vodka, Champagne or Rum
3) If it is your cup of tea, then I hope you won't mind spending hours of your life on it.
4) Warchat = In the main menu of the game when you first enter, you can chat with players around the globe to the left. This chat is rather hard to describe. It's a mixture of everything imaginable if the North Pole and South Pole were squished and launched into another dimension. There is everything there from Geopolitics, Holocaust Remembrance, Stalinium Production Protocols and How Mao Zedong invented coconuts. But don't worry, if you do ask a serious game-related question, you're going to be given a serious answer (From the answerer's point of view anyways)
5) The Battlefield goes East = In the previous game, it was in Europe. In Red Dragon, it's mostly in Asia. I hope you enjoy generic Asian house designs.
I give this game 9.5/10 and put em at my Top 5 Strategy Games riiiiight next to Supreme Commander. The main character is an unlovable piece of work. I get irritated just launching the game and looking at him, and so I can't find the motivation to finish the game. Perhaps he turns out to be some hero sort, but his current whiny, pompous self makes me feel so annoyed I can't ever see him being one short of being an "accidental hero" (at this point I hate him so much that that thought also annoys me). He is unsympathisable.
In addition, I enjoy point-and-click puzzles when the puzzles are canon to the story and make sense (e.g. find the key, the key is with the guard, find a way to distract the guard). Puzzles in Deponia are more of those logic-puzzle based sort – whole lot of pattern recognition, switch flipping, make all the dots on the board green from red sort, which means sometimes the object you need isn't logically related to the task. It is overwhelmingly repetitive and feels pointless.
If you're looking for a good adventure point-and-click, try Chains of Satinav instead, from the same developers. Superb artwork, top-notch voice acting, enthralling storytelling and most importantly puzzles that are innovative and logical to the storyline.

A sometimes amusing adventure game along the lines of Curse of Monkey Island, Deponia features an often unlikeable "Guybrush" in Rufus, a mainly absent damsel in the aptly named Goal, and many frustratingly dumb puzzles. It's a charming game, in a way; hopefully the sequels are an improvement.

The whole Deponia series comprises some of my favourite point-and-click adventure games. They're fun, hilarious, and for the most part the puzzle solutions made sense but were still challenging. The story itself is fantastic, and full of laughs. The gameplay I never found tedious or boring, and there are no tiny hotspots that you just can't quite click that make some other point-and-click games so frustrating. The voice acting, music, and especially the art are all very well done. I highly recommend all the games in this series, but this first is my favourite of the four, and if you're only ever going to play one Daedalic Entertainment game, this should be it!

Super Crate Box is a nice little free single-player arcade game. That has some stability issues on Windows 8, but that's for later.
It's pretty simple one. You get 3 levels to play at, with unlockable difficulties aside from "normal". You are going to appear in arena of platfroms, with 3 types of enemies appearing above, that keep walking forward to their firey salvation (and your doom) at the bottom of arcadeysh arena. When they get there, they will drop from above again, only they will be angry and two times faster, making it more diffiult to jump away from them, but still manageable. Sure thing you should kill them before they arrive to the bottom, but what actually counts (and scores) are the crates, new one appear at random spot everytime you pick one up. And jolly, each and every single one of them contains a random weapon that you will have to use, whetever it's powerful bazooka or dual pistols for puppy players.
See how it works? Quite nice idea, indeed. So there you have it, running between crates, stopping waves of enemies, choosing one of those two. Even more, by scoring a certain amount of picked crates, you will unlock new difficulties, player (pixelated) skin and even more weapons. Yea, by default you have only half of whole game's arsenal, so there is something to look toward to.
Now, the thing is, this game has a crashing love for Windows 8, so get ready to be careful if you use that system. Things like properly using Flame Thrower and blowing full lead of Shotgun into face of Big Skull will crash the game (and will take Steam a while to realise that you aren't playing this game). There are some random crashes as well. Now, I heard that only Steam version contains this issue and version of game off official website (
) is supposed to have those fixed. I didn't try it yet.
Game complaining about missing dll on main menu also doesn't give much confidience, eh.
The graphics in the game are "pixels-in-your-face". Not the best kind, not exactly themed after 8-bit or 16-bit style, but not terribad kind either, with some fine animations and varied player skin design (despite being tiny and pixelish, so it's not much). And hey, it has skull-mutants as enemies! Win.
Sounds are fine and music fits the game really well. You will actually remember those tunes, not something what I can say about majority of other "pixels-in-your-face" music. But I don't think that it's worth listening to it outside of the game.
I heard that this game was supposed to be a prototype for author's upcoming similiar game, but eh... Seems like it didn't happen.
Anyway, this game will give you some fun and free instant arcade fun, but it will not keep you there for ages. Worth checking out.

A game that's been unfairly maligned (including by me) for being too different from its predecessors, I gave this one another shot (I played it on Xbox years ago and thought it was alright) and I'm very glad I did. Yes, I still prefer DOOM, DOOM II, the new DOOM, and yes, even FINAL DOOM—but this game is a terrific horror/shooter experience if you can get into the game's mindset. The emphasis is on set-piece scares, atmosphere, and tight-quarters manuevering in close combat with the minions of hell. If you can accept this deviation from the rest of the series, you can have a lot of fun getting spooked and enjoying the action. Yes, you also need to accept the fact that you can't use a flashlight and a weapon at the same time... a curious design choice, but using mods to override it compromises some of the atmosphere.
The single player campaign is pretty meaty, but the tech base design gets repetitive. The hell levels are the highlight, but over too quickly. Additionally, some of the weapons feel floaty and inaccurate, especially the shotgun beyond close range. This is a big problem for a shooting game, but not game-breaking. Let yourself get sucked into the game's pacing and adrenaline/dopamine rhythm, and you'll have a great time.

Brother's is something we don't see on the gaming scene that often.  A game that acknowledges the medium it is heavily and finds a way to marry its control scheme and narrative cohesively in a way that you just have to actually play yourself to understand how well it works.
Controlling the Brothers is a unique experience not often done in games.  Each Brother moves and interacts with a thumbstick and a trigger (one half of the controller for each brother) and this takes some getting used to.  But the game trains you naturally to get used to it through the use of its gameplay without any handholding tutorial.  The brothers need each other to progress through the puzzles of the environment and diversifies the characters by giving them different abilities for the puzzle solving (i.e. the larger brother Nayaa can boost the little brother Nayee up to a higher ledge and Nayee can find a way to in turn help Nayaa up also).
The game continually finds new ways to use its unique control scheme of two characters working together and it feels like a coop experience but everything is in sync because its a single person controlling both characters.
The gameplay does an amazing job of reinforcing the story which in turn refuels the gameplay in this much more cohesive symbiosis between the two .  The story itself is set in a fantasy universe which people have compared to ICO and Fable series (which is a fair assessment) but they way you discover and interact with this universe is one of the best parts.  I'll try to avoid spoliers but the Brothers are setting out well beyond the borders of the town they are familiar with so their sense of discovery and wonder at all the worlds curiosities is also your own.  To reinforce this the games decided to not use an actual language but still include the concept of dialogue and its perhaps one of the best things about its story.  The interactions between the characters are so well done that despite not understanding a single word as a player you still know exactly what is being said in every exchange simply through the emotive body language and tone of the characters during the interaction and the context of the gameplay both preceeding and during each scene.  This less familiar method of storytelling makes the game a much more emotional journey that you experience as the characters themselves do.  Their highs and lows are your highs and lows and the story is incredibly moving as a result.  Its probably one of the best examples of player immersion you'll be able to find from any game really.
So yes this game was an experience more than it was just any other game.  Don't spoil it for yourself by watching someone play it and don't let it pass you by.  Grab a gamepad (you really need one for this game I think the keyboard controls would unavoidably hamper the experience.), take an evening off (you'll only need one) and give it a go. This is one of those games that any gamer young or old, novice or veteran will have an incredible time playing through.

Seeing as how it's the free weekend...I'll write a little review on it!
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Torchlight II is Torchlight I reimagined to be more open world and feel less bogged down to a single instance that just continually travels downward. Torchlight I offered merchants in a town, as well as other miscellaneous vendors, and then you would simply venture down into the dungeon and find waypoints and just continue to go down. This was fun, but got extremely repetitive over time. Torchlight II takes the good aspects of Torchlight I and fuses them with elements stolen from Diablo III (Yes, I know everyone uses this comparison, but it's the best way to describe it).
Diablo III offers chapters and then it loops back into harder difficulties. This is eerily similar to what Torchlight II does. Although I have not gotten that far into the game, my understanding is you get New Game and New Game++ (And I think a couple more), which simply increase the difficulty. Since we're on the subject of ARPG comparison, let's compare it to the now popular Path of Exile. I personally couldn't get into Path of Exile, mostly because of a lack of dedication to it. I played it in closed beta and stopped when it went into Open Beta, and from my short playtime, I just couldn't do it. Jumping into the Path of Exile community was really toxic, there was a huge learning curve with tons of acronyms to learn (But, that would hopefully be the case with a skill tree that expansive) and it really dilutes the experience for noobs if they don't have the time to keep up to date on it.
But enough about gripes for other games, Torchlight II doesn't have any of that. You can jump in and just play some singleplayer and listen to music. There isn't any acronyms you need to know, there's no meta-game. Almost any build can succeed for the beginning, so there is absolutely no pressure. The combat is nothing stellar, but it's a hack and slash game, if you're looking for revolutionary combat you're in the wrong category of games. The quests seemed a  bit dull and more "fetchy" than anything, but they still offer great procession through the game. That sounded a little bit harsh to squeeze those last two sentences in, but it's the blunt truth. The game does however keep a metaphorical sense of adventure. If the map displays an exclamation mark for a side quest the instant reaction is "Oh sweet, another dungeon! Let's go check it out" where as
games make a player go "Blah, another side-quest...I don't really need that do I...?". Ultimately Torchlight II offers a great sense of adventure and a relaxing gaming experience that many games fail to tackle. It's a game you can play for thirty minutes or even a few hours and just watch as time flies by.
This may meander off into a personal preference, but I highly suggest listening to Podcasts or listening to music while playing this game. The soundtrack is great, don't get me wrong, but it's a pretty mindless hack and slash game that will get boring very fast if you don't entertain yourself with something else. Not saying this is a necessity, it just helps once you get a feel for the game.
I can't say much for the modding community, as I have barely played the game since they released the Workshop, but I do know there are tons of mods, and maybe some of those mods help dilute my personal issues with the game.
Overall I would say Torchlight II deserves an 8.5/10 for it's addictive gameplay and less over-the-top ARPG style, but it lacks in combat variety and has very little difficulty to it. A definite buy though, because you will definitely get your money's worth!

I'm a big STALKER fan and one of my friends, who is a much larger fan of everything related to the series, told me to stay away from Clear Sky. I figured that even something vaguely Stalkery would be still pretty good because Pripyrat and the original were very enjoyable, but I after playing through Clear Sky I see why people say stay away.
1. Very short
2. Very linear with exploration discouraged
3. Less focus on monsters/mutants and more on killing hundreds of human enemies
4. Ending is terrible
5. You have very few, if any, choices beyond which faction to fight for
6. Faction Wars idea feels like it is barely fleshed out
7. Upgrade system and a few other things tied to the factions are not fun
8. Little sense of what either of the other two Stalkers are all about (weird ♥♥♥♥, exploration, mutants and being a Stalker)
9. Only one ending as far as I can tell
10. Several repetitive sections were you just kill waves after waves of human enemies
Let me explain some of those a little more. The game is a bit short, especially comapred to the other two. My record says 20 hours, but 3-4 hours of that are idle-time when I left it on and the rest was doing absolutely everything I could in terms of side missons/faction wars and trying to explore areas that didn't want to explored. I imagine you could easily run though it (without trying hard) in less than 10 hours.
The entire feeling of world is almost erased from what was created in the original game (and Pripyrat even though that came after this one). You can only find things if they are randomly located by this guy back at the original base that randomly gives you locations of stashes, or if you buy tips from people for stashes. If you happen to find that stash on your own without doing either of those things then nothing will be in it, hence discouraging exploration. A lot of the areas are also pretty closed off or empty besides human enemies, which kind of give tiers of loot depending on where you are in the games story. All of this might be fine if the story was good, it isn't because it goes against the original's story and just kind of sucks all around, or if the Faction War system was actually good.
The Faction War system, which is a big focus of the game and one of the main things going on all the time (also one of the main reasons there is less focus on mutants and exploration) is a really shallow offering. You have no real impact on anything and only if you get a mission to take an area will the A.I. faction you are fighting for actually go and capture it. They give you a lot of good rewards for doing missions and taking over areas, but it is all very temporary and the whole system isn't the slightest bit dynamic. The A.I. rarely does anything on their own, they have no ambition, and even when you do the "big mission" that is supposed to supress an enemy faction the area is only captured for 15 minutes at most. You cannot command any squads, request reinforcements if you take somewhere on your own, or really interact with your faction at all beyond their main bases, which just offer shops. It was very disappointing to experience because it could have been something much more complex, dynamic and enjoyable.
Somewhere in all of this is an actual STALKER game with great environments, horrifying enemies, a great upgrade system and so much more, but I whole heartedly recommend playing Pripyrat instead even if you have already beaten it before and you are just looking for another go at this wonderful world.

Train Simulator 2017 is decently good. It is admittedly the best train simulator out there, and every route is realistic enough.
The Good:
- Realistic locos and routes
- Delivers challenging scenarios each route
- The only decent train simulator on the market
- DLC addons gives a fresh take on the game
- Average to decent graphics
The Bad:
- Included routes may not suit everyone
- Games engine is in need of a major upgrade (lacklustre performance, and graphics)
- Needs to be optimised for lower end machines (despite being highly unlikely)
- Cost of DLC addons
- No diverse range of addons (Australia and more of Asia should be more focused rather than many routes based in Europe)
- Cost of future Train Simulator's may not be affordable (assuming)

Overall, TS17 delivers on a decent simulator, and is the only good train simulator out there. The costly DLC, average graphics, and poorly optimised game engine is the deterring factor into buying TS17. Despite this however, the DLC's aren't bad, and the developers at Dovetail are improving. The new game engine in Train Sim World should give much better graphical prowess, and performance but only on high end machines. The game should really be more affordable especially with Train Sim World.

First off if you are the type of guy on a late weekend night just chilling with your Bros and wanting a game to geek out and play and go hard on then Eon Altar is the game for you. You play the game with your smart phone any will do and then from there you can have your friends place and they will be on the same screen as you. Now lets get into the reveiw:
Pros:
-Great Story: Each character has a reason and a story which in turn gives multiple play throughs and comps as a group a lot of fun.
-Talent tree: All abilities and Crafting is done on a unique tree lane base talent system which causes you to build your character how you like.
-Combat: Tricky and actually requires strats, you can accidently hit your friend in a AOE spell and kill them or have to plan unique ways to run across the field to ressurect your friend in time while avoidng millons of guys. Safe to say polish combat.
-Branching Chats:Fun choices in picking dialog and can cause changes to overall story.
-App works so GOOD: app is really precise and combat and navigation through the app is fine
Cons:
-Lag: Some weaker computers have lag in cutscenes and areas with large events.
-Requires Smartphone: Some phones might be just to slow for that stuff.
-Personal Story takes to long: Most characters personal story takes long time to show and some characters don't get any story included til later and kinda feels like you are left out.
-Phone Movement can be weird: Sometimes movement in areas with alot of objects or tight spaces like burning buildings can be tough and near impossible to walk through unhurt or not bumping into walls.
-Map needed: You will get lost so many times in the game and often lose where you need to go.
Conclusion: Great game for group play, has a tough wall to jump with having to share a screen so a hdmi cable to a tv is highly suggested but all and all the game is great and worth the money trust me its a good purchase even if bought for solo play.
Grade: 8.5/10

So I played through DOOM 3 again after almost 13 years and after having finished the latest Doom (2016) and RE7 - and I had a great time!
I still remember playing Doom 3 back in 2004 on a GF4-TI4200 at a meager resolution of 640x480 pixels, no AA and medium details and my system could still not handle 60fps constantly... now I played through it again, everything maxed at 4K 60/60 and on hard difficulty.
I stayed away from any mods that alter image quality on purpose and played trough vanilla Doom 3 at maxed settings for the "true" experience - and I went with the original instead of the BFG Edition for the same reason (Doom 3 just needs the flashlight / weapon toggle in my opinion).
I was surprised how much of the game I had forgotten (like 4 enemy types I did not remember at all) and how enjoyable the game still was - I think it held up surprisingly well.
At times it might drag a little and the build-up and pacing is slower than what we are used to now but it still works.
Of course there´s probably a big chunk of nostalgia blurring my judgement but I think everyone should have played through Doom 3 at least once (talking about single-player, I never cared for its' multi-player part).
True, some of the textures are offendingly low res and the deaths of your enemies can feel anti-climaxing because they dissolve into nothing just too quickly most of the time but the core gameplay is fun and using hard difficulty also challenging.
The lighting tech still produces some great visuals (wearing your nostalgia glasses) and the atmosphere is still frightening and holds its' own.
There even weren't as many cheap jump scares as I remembered but 2 or 3 got me really good :-)
So if you are asking yourself if you should re-play Doom 3 after all those years or if you should rather hold it in dear memory fearing it might not live up to your memory: play it again!
Beware: You may need some console/autoexec.cfg tweaks to get it running properly without micro-stutters and "ultra looks like low" image quality.
Edit: Doom 3 is dirt cheap right now (once again) so grab it! :-)

Brothers is the perfect example that a great story can be told without any words. Every little thing about this game is a gem: the music, the scenery, the two brothers; all these things entwine to give you a profoundly emotional experience.
The story is liniar and the puzzles aren't there to test your brilliant problem-solving mind, but your muscles and hand-eye coordination. More than that, they're there to help you get to know the characters, understand their dynamics and build your relationship with each of them.
What is absolutely horrible, however, is the way you control what the brothers do (keep in mind that I don't have a controller so I played it the old fashioned way). You have to use a gazillion different keys at a time and know precisely what each of them does and time them right in relation to one another so your characters don't fall to their deaths. This does serve a purpose in the end but it still is immensely frustrating for a while.

The added additions to the game like certain mini cutscenes in battle or camera tricks do not change the gameplay AT ALL.  There is just more visual feedback on certain moves that beat out others which can help newer players learn what moves work against others. I also noticed almost zero delay on button inputs, I remember in previous games if you wanted to do a 10 hit combo you can kinda mash the button a few times to make sure that it registered and that would be perfectly acceptable. In this they seemed to have lessened that to a great degree and if your timing is not exact your character would actually drop the combo.  Also, another thing I noticed is that they extended juggle frames.  Makes it so certain characters have more opportunity than others considering their recovery frames, but I am sure that can be patched.  Overall high recommend.

Take it from me when I say, that "Spelunky is just the platformer you're looking for". Being not only oddly charming and colorful, Spelunky also delivers what it promises, challenge. In my first dozen hours of gameplay, I havent even reached the second level, of the second stage. This may be my inferiority at platformers in gerneral, but I can say with ut-most confidence, Spelunky will challenge and addict even the most seasoned platformer fans. As you go farther into the gameplay, you become more and more engrained. Now, when you die on the first level, it will begin to aggrivate you, and when that bomb you thought would land in a web bounces back and blows you to shreds one block away from your cute little miner man, you want to tear your hair out! And as you should, learning from your mistakes in Spelunky will be key to your future success, in the next level, or life.
Spelunky is a rare gem (no pun intended) in the platformer genre that seems to be under appreciated and played. Chanses are, since you landed here, you are looking for your next rogelike adventure, or a new challenge to dump many hours into. Don't miss your chance, THIS IS what you have been searching for, and trust me, you won't be able to get enough of it. If you have the money, or the timing to find this genuinly fun platformer on sale, I would highly recomend the purchase.

At first I didn't particularly like this game.  I thought it was far too difficult.  But, it was 2D, which meant it was one of the few games I own that I could enjoy with my wife.  We take turns playing the single player game and after a short while, we were both addicted.  It's now a thing we always do together.  We watch a little TV while we eat dinner, then we play Spelunky.  It's just someting that's part of our daily routine.
I absolutely adore this game now, both for the challenge it presents and for the time I get to spend with my favorite person.
As far as gameplay goes, it's frustratingly difficult and you will rage quit often.  However, the controls are tight and ultra precise and very rarely do you feel you lost because the game cheated you.  You can almost always find where you made a mistake and that was what resulted in your untimely death.
For difficulty, it took us around 100 hours to beat the first, normal boss.  For the secret, hidden, true boss it took near 170 hours!  That's a huge amount of bang for your buck!

The artistic style is visualy appealing, and the game itself is stable, but there are a lot of tedious elements to this game that don't quite add up. The puzzles aren't exactly connect the dots, more a combination of complete trial and error and hunt and peck. The story, although there, is brought to an almost complete hult by the puzzle mechanics in the game. Usually, a game like this tries to give you enough input that you still have challenging puzzles to figure out, but keeps things flowing enough that the story progresses in a fluent manner; not so much with Deponia.
The game is bogged down by constant running around, back and forth, through the same areas, over and over again--which can get old rather quickly--and re-talking to the same people, time and time again, in order to get new items and information after every completed step, that it starts to bog down. Often times, the way that puzzles are put together (if you can even call most of them puzzles) gets old. Including how you are supposed to combine inventory items, and the silly things you are supposed to do in the environment to trigger actions.
These elements get in the way of what could be a really great game. I enjoyed parts of Deponia, and detested others. A hate to give this game a 'no' recommendation, because of the clear presentation and easy interface, but unless you are a hardcore fan of point and click gaming that is more hunt and peck than puzzle based, and you have lots of time on your hands, this probably isn't the title for you. Certain puzzles make no logical sense and even seem hindering, especially when other solutions seem more readily available, but are completely unavailable. Puzzle and story should be singlular and lead into one another and Deponia is lacking in this respect. If the developer can improve on these elements in future releases then they will have an outstanding product!

This game was not fun for me. It first started out with the fact that the games resolution cannot be changed to fit the screen in game. You can go to the discussion section for the game and find ways to fix this issue, but I thought it was find the way it was so I did not bother. When gameplay started I was very frustrated with the contrast of the game. It’s really dark. I understand that is like this so you need to use your flashlight but areas that were supposed to be light up were very dim so I increased the brightness to fix this issue and it worked well. I found the use of the flashlight to be very annoying at times. Enemies would spawn but the areas were so dark I would have to swap back and forth from flashlight to gun to fight properly.
The main reason I’m giving this game a negative review is because of the design of the guns and enemy mechanics.
Most of the gun are underpowered or are useless in most situations. The pistol is good for shooting the spiders but otherwise is too underpowered to use anywhere else. The shotgun does good damage up close like it should, but shoots too slow for the quick moving enemies. The spread on the shotgun is also really large and does little damage to enemies at mid-range. The pulse rifle’s shots are really slow moving making it hard to hit the fast moving enemies. The biggest issues come from the grenades and the rocket launcher. The grenades are bouncy balls. They luckily explode on impact with enemies but the close quarter fighting makes them very situational, and not very many opportunities arise to use them. In this game you can shoot projectiles out of the air. This makes using the rocket launder really hard and again, close quarter fighting prevents its use for much of the game. The submachine gun is also underpowered.
The enemies in the game spawn usually is sets of two. One in front and the other somewhere behind you. I thought this was a cheap move. It had me always back tracking as soon as I heard them spawn in. Since many of the guns are underpowered, enemies that should not be bullet sponges end up being just that. All the enemies are also very-very fast. They get to you so quickly that you take unavoidable damage most of the time. AI accuracy is also too good and trying to take cover is somewhat useless.
This game tried to stay true to the original DOOM but it was done very poorly. Enemies are too fast and guns are underpowered.

Doom 3 is an art.  It itself is an art which is difficult to describe.  It is a game that doubles as a throwback to old Doom games, and an attempt at an atmospheric horror game.  It attempted to add a story into the Doom-style mayhem that you might expect, but really it comes down to the gameplay.  You are armed to the teeth, and everything appears from everywhere and tries to kill you.  Even in empty, vacant rooms, I felt outnumbered knowing that at any moment, I could be surprised by Hell's minions.  The gameplay felt very direct, in a Doom-like way.  If it moves, shoot it.  There is no cover-based shooting, no one is here to help you, and gameplay largely revolves around "get from point A to point B, and don't die on the way."  This is what the game is, and it delivers a pure FPS experience.  Everything looks amazing, and all enemies are ghoulish at all times.  Even compared to more modern games, I was impressed by the visuals.  All in all, if you liked the classic Doom games, you can't go wrong here.

You can experiment with different powers and attacks, like stealth attack from the shadows, explosive arrows, poison blades, sweep attack with a legion spear, protect your allies with a juggernaut character, heal your comrades with a potion or a healing strike, summon a rock warden, throw fireballs and strike with lightning. I played this game with a friend yesterday and we had no technical difficulties whatsoever. Everything was incredibly smooth and easy to setup. We just had to be in the same wifi as the host pc and run the control app on our smartphones and we were ready to go. The controls are easy to learn and we had no problems moving our characters. Combat in this game is round based. So you can plan out your action with your smartphone and don't need to hurry.
The smartphone control made us expect that Eon Altar is some gimmicky minigame. We thought we would play it for like an hour or so and then be done with it til our next meeting. We were very surprised when we found out that the game is actually anything but a gimmicky minigame. I was especially impressed with the big skill tree and the upgrade tree which allow for specializing your character further.
The best thing about this game though is the roleplaying aspect. NPCs speak on their own but if a player character says anything the dialog appears only on their control app and they have to act and speak it out loud. This is so much fun and quite often hilarious. An example: At one point you initiate a big fight and the game gives you the opportunity to scream a battleshout. My friend played Shasek the sellsword and he selected "For Fun!". I played Barryson the Paladin and of course I selected "For Truth! For Justice! For Honor!". We were laughing our asses off after that.
Quite often in the game you get to make decisions. Every Character is following a personal agenda in addition to the group objectives. At several points you may make your intentions open to the group or keep them to yourself. Also at times NPCs whisper something in the ear of only one member of the group. And you can then decide what to do with that information.
All in all we had great fun with this game and I can fully recommend it. Props to the developers for trying something new and doing it right.

I heard a lot of hype around this game being the best game around brothers. After playing the game I found that there are still 3 better games about brothers, but this one is still pretty good:
Def Jam: Fight for NY: This game has way more brothers like Snoop Dogg, Redman, Method Man and Ghostface Killah.
Super Mario Bros. 3: The brothers in this game can turn into Tanukis and Hammer Bros., something this game lacks.
Mother 3: This game about brothers actually made me cry. Their dad is also pretty cool and not a generic sick parent.
Brothers does have various advantages over those other games, like the fact that you are always controlling the two brothers, that's pretty cool, also the brothers are always cooperating in the game, unlike that jerk Luigi using all the stars. The game is short, sweet, and barely has any filler. While not incredibly hard, there is a satisfaction completing one of the multiple set pieces. The game looks decent, although the animations, especially for the emotional scenes were pretty bad (The other 3 brothers game all have superior animation quality to be honest).
The music is pretty good, and controls manage the balance between being tricky, and also being really simple. The story is also simple and emotional, although I would like more world building for some of the areas. I think the stages present well enough the state of the world and the scope of the brother’s journey.
In short recommended, although the brothers aspect was lacking compared to those other 3 titles, I just hope someone makes the Citizen Kane of games about brothers one day.

Exploring the nuclear wasteland known as the "Zone" and delving into the heart of the Chernobyl reactor #4 to uncover artifacts and to discover the cause of the frequent radioactive emissions that go off more than ever before, all while battling the horrific mutated creatures caused by the second Chernobyl disaster and the bandits that want nothing but you dead and your stuff in their hands. It sounds like a lot of fun right? That is, until you actually play the game.
The Optimization for this game is horrible, I can't even run it in directX 10 at a playable framerate (I can run BF4 on very high/ultra in a 64 player battle at 60+ FPS, as well as Planetside 2 with 200+ players). The NPCs are much too powerful (even on the easiest difficulty and I'm the type of person that always plays on the hardest difficulties), their grenades always seem to appear at your feet and their bullets always end up in your head. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy a challenge in combat but these enemies seem impossible to beat. The game has many bugs and quite a few random lag spikes that can last for more than 10 seconds.
However, the game is not all bad. The ambience is fantastic and it really sets the dark mood of the Zone. The story is actually well written and gripping. The location also makes this game amazing as it takes place in the Chernobyl disaster zone (which I love), it is the perfect place for a game like this and lastly, the landscape is beautiful (I find that the abandoned buildings that nature has taken back are beautiful, that's just my view).
This game has more cons than pros causing me to not recommend this. Stalker Clear Sky was too advanced for its time and had many issues. I would give this game a 65/100 simply due to the reasons I have stated. If you are looking for a game that takes place in a nuclear wasteland that has mutants and bandits I would recommend the Fallout series.

At first I didn't particularly like this game.  I thought it was far too difficult.  But, it was 2D, which meant it was one of the few games I own that I could enjoy with my wife.  We take turns playing the single player game and after a short while, we were both addicted.  It's now a thing we always do together.  We watch a little TV while we eat dinner, then we play Spelunky.  It's just someting that's part of our daily routine.
I absolutely adore this game now, both for the challenge it presents and for the time I get to spend with my favorite person.
As far as gameplay goes, it's frustratingly difficult and you will rage quit often.  However, the controls are tight and ultra precise and very rarely do you feel you lost because the game cheated you.  You can almost always find where you made a mistake and that was what resulted in your untimely death.
For difficulty, it took us around 100 hours to beat the first, normal boss.  For the secret, hidden, true boss it took near 170 hours!  That's a huge amount of bang for your buck!
I highly recommend this game for anyone looking for a great 2D platformer that doesn't pull any punches.

This is my first review of any game on Steam. Though, I have played many, many games in my lifetime. So, Here is my day 1 review - First 7 hour block of Portal Knights.
The basics
Three classes, Ive only tried the Mage/Wizard class so far. So, I cant speak of the other classes. However, Ive died a few times. Mistakes happen. It takes a minute or two just to get used to the combat camera. Once you get over that little hump the game plays really well. Day and Night cycles are nice. The sun looks great rising. Very animated and pretty.
Character creation is alright, limited but the game is new and under development so No worries there. Monsters are of a low IQ, But fighting 8 or so at a time is still tricky.Some hit pretty hard too. A few trickyones early on.
The game itself concerning the quests and exploration are really nice. Basic tutorial that gives you an idea of how it works. Quick and simple. I liked it.
The islands start really small so far, but they clearly grow larger and larger every island you jump to. Different climates and resources on certain places, very nice touch. Its not a linear path either.You can find advanced materials long before you can use them if you explore. There are hidden caches of exp and useful blocks as well, but they require some cunning to find. I truly appreciate that in this game.
The dungeons you find make you explore, the lighting and setups are very awesome. Great scenery you can borrow from them too. Fought the first boss, not too difficult but you will appreciate the combat system so much more when you fight the boss.
I see some of the other reviews dog on the crafting system. Its perfect. Gamers are extremely lazy these days and I truly appreciate the way this crafting system is. Its not too hard (Think EverQuest 1999) and its not too easy (Minecraft/Terarria). Ive come across some recipies and those are awesome too. Looking forward to finding more.
Basically, The game gets a solid 8/10
The only cons I have are as follows:
Splitting stacks. Cant do it yet.
Rebinding Keys. Cant do it yet.
Graphics adjustments. Nothing to adjust. (NOTE: Its 2016. This game isnt groundbreaking graphically. May not be needed)
I am looking forward to getting further in this game and updating my review. for now its solid. Esp for 12 bucks.

Torchlight 2 now fully supports Steam Workshop. A new launcher synchronizes any mods you have subscribed to, and lets you customize their activation state and loading priority. In addition, when playing Internet games in the lobby, you will be able to filter modded games by mod combination, and with a single button click, subscribe to those mods. Torchlight 2 will then restart, synchronize them, and activate them before returning you to the game.
When playing modded games, you can view your mod history, any previously played mods, and the impact disabling mods may have on your character.
We've tried to make the process as seamless as possible, with a focus on allowing modded multiplayer games with a minimum of fuss.

Deponia aims to be quirky to sets itself apart from many of its kind. It has however fail in many different aspects:
1. Characters: In a story-driven game such as this, the characters are far from memorable. Each one seems to try its upmost effort to sound sarcastic, cynical or downright idiotic to an extent that it fails to deliver an exciting blend of characters. Don’t get me wrong, I love characters that make a fool of themselves (e.g. Rincewind from Discworld) but what Rufus tried to portray feels way too forced. Instead of the light, bite-sized comedy pieces that I was expecting, I witnessed sloppy production and narrations. Granted, there were some funny moments, but it is difficult to give proper credit given the rarity of such occasion.
2. Puzzle: Again, another essential element to a point-and-click game. This is the major flaw of the game. I give huge leeway to such games where logic and questionable detours need to be taken or when pesky puzzle elements are involved that somehow blocks the progress of the game simply to discover that it makes little sense. Deponia is King of this behaviour right here.
3. Artwork: Despite the fact that I am not a fan of this kind of artwork, I must say this is where Deponia shines the most, the artwork of its kind is downright stunning, exuding a very unique feel towards the world of Deponia.
4. Music: Passable music, though there are some memorable ones. This, together with artwork, ensures a great thematic feel of its kind.
Problems: As of 11th May 2013 a bug exists in the middle of the game where you will be stuck and unable to continue. I find this very mind-boggling that such a bug could have existed until now. This needs immediate repair.
Overall, if you're a fan of point and click game, this game might be worth it, otherwise, stay clear away.

This won't be a glowing review. I'll recommend it, but with reservations. If it's on sale for $3.50 or less and you want an interesting, fairly unique story, along with some good adventure game puzzles, then it's a good buy. For any more than that, don't waste your time.
So, I'm not an adventure game kinda guy. I didn't like Myst at all, and never got around to many other point-and-click's. A lot felt like pixel hunting and didn't have very logical puzzle solutions. There's very few of those moments in Deponia. Holding the spacebar will reveal all the available hotspots, and many of the solutions make sense. Naturally some seem a little over-complicated, but given the items you're allowed to use they make more sense.
The story is interesting, and I found it quite unique. It doesn't give you any agency to change outcomes, but the dialogue driving it is, for the most part, witty and funny.
The music is awesome and indeed, the chorus guys rule.
Now the bad.
This game is horribly, horribly unoptimized. I understand that a few players haven't had any issues, but I spent a lot of time reading the forums and I'm certain that I had every issue mentioned by anyone, and at least one that I didn't see mentioned.
The game chugs. I'm not certain why it drops performance so bad, but it does. At first, I thought the animations just had low framerates (The walking animations are fine, as well as the movies by the way. I'm talking about the mouse cursor and inventory screen animations), but at one point there was a sound effect happening in the background at a regular interval. When I pulled up my inventory, or when I pressed spacebar to reveal the hot-spots, the sound effect slowed down by at least half. The game seems to run at around 30fps normally, but was dropping to as low as 5fps during these particular times. I really don't know why a point-and-click should be so resource intensive on a machine that can comfortably run AAA games at high settings.
Also, there are a few bugs with not being able to hit certain hotspots at certain times. Trying to exit the listening post is an example. There are workarounds such as talking to the guy who's up there first, but pressing spacebar reveals the exit arrow as an option, so I see no reason it shouldn't be one immediately.
The minecart minigame with the correct solution would not allow me to progress. Thankfully they allow you to skip it. Still, that seems like an awful cop-out.
One more, that I didn't see anyone ask about, is that the dialogue options would occasionally appear partially above the frame they're enclosed in, thereby obscuring some of the options. Or the options would appear partially below the frame, and therefore partially off-screen thereby rendering some options un-clickable. Cycling through the dialogue options usually fixed the problem. Again, the problem should not exist in the first place.
Don't be fooled by the settings, changing them changed nothing about how the game reacted on my machine. Texture compression, weather effects, anything, they all ran exactly the same.
Don't be fooled by the demo. The demo ran fine on my machine, full framerates and no dialogue, hotspot, or puzzle issues at all. These were definitely not indicative of the state of the full game.
To wrap things up, the game has an interesting story, I like the art style, and it's mostly funny. But, those developers did a terrible job with their QA. Don't buy the game if it's not on sale.

Surprisingly, this actually isn't a bad game. It definitely would be better in its original, portable touchscreen format rather than this port that relies on your mouse skills. At times, it can be pretty difficult because of this. However it's definitely fun in small snippets regardless.
Basically, trees have been responsible for some tragic events in your life and you are out for revenge. How does one claim vengeance from trees? Cut them down. Basically, logs will fly in the air and you have to try to cleanly cut them all within a certain amount of time. There are game challenges centered around this that build up your stockpile of wood, which you can then use in the game's version of a store to buy beards, pictures, and buffs (which will allow you to make mistakes and fix them for you as long as you have them). Throughout your woody murder spree, you will also take in a number of forest critters.
Your first critter is a pun telling beaver. None of the other animals I've saved so far have any dialogue other than cute noises when you poke them.
For all intents and purposes, that's about all there is to this game. This was actually my very first Steamgifts win, so I thought I should finally give it a try. It's fun for what it is and I can recommend trying it out. However, with that said, it's also fair to disclose that I probably won't play it anymore as despite the fun and cute factor, I'm just not good enough with a mouse to soldier through the remaining areas without getting frustrated lol.

-- TL;DR --
I've never had more fun playing a co-op rpg with my friends, let alone in the same room. If only two days ago you had told me that i'd be saying this about a phone-based game, i'd have thought you were crazy. Buy this game even if you don't have anyone to play with immediately, because sooner or later the devs will come to their senses and charge more for it.
-- story time --
Some buddies and I were looking for some living room co-op games to play and kick-back last night and amongst a few other games we bought this like "hell, it's $5.00". After playing the other games and being less than impressed, we finally came to this, installed the app, and started it up.
Now as a little backstory to our group that might reveal a little bias: we play D&D on sundays, enjoy all rpg elements (gear, skills, depth, dialogue, etc.), and mostly play games together just to share a few beers and hang out. This game caters to our play-style perfectly, which i'm assuming is something that most gamers share to some extent.
As soon as it started up and we joined the room (which was a breeze btw), we fell into our typical character roles. We all know a guy who is the paladin type, mage type, assassin type, and so on. This was familiar, but not ground breaking. The game reveals to you immediately that your phone is not just the way you interact with the world and do combat, but it provides your innermost thoughts, secret goals, and your dialogue. Yeah, your dialogue. You have to SPEAK YOUR LINES to your friends! This is hilarious when you're all going for it, because it forces you to play your character and make choices based on how your character relates to the world.
We all got a kick out of playing our character, exploring our skill trees, being snarky in dialogue and showing off in combat. The idea behind combat in this game is perfect, but still has some bugs (which is to be expected as early access). All players share a turn, which means you're not waiting on that one guy who always waits til the last second to read his abilities. You get the strategy of turn based combat, while being able to move, aid, or fight the enemies all on the same turn. This time saving approach gives it a real feel of fluidity that impressed me and it made up for all of the time you spent reading your character abilities and skill trees.
We are currently only four hours in, but have already planned our next night to re-gather and play more. It's a blast and I sincerely recommend this game to anyone who likes a good social rpg and is familiar with it's fundamentals.
-- Pros/Cons --
Pros:
- dialogue is fun and social, never a chore.
- every player feels like it's their story.
- combat is well-oiled.
- depth is enough to satisfy rpg die-hards.
- phone interaction not gimmicky, but perfect in this context.
- loot is competitive, but trading is implemented for easy sharing.
- IT'S ONLY $5, what the hell. buy this on principle.
Cons:
- a bit buggy at the time of writing this.
- could be a lot to take in at first for rpg new-comers
- need 3-4 players
- might need phone charger

I've only played an hour at the time of this review however I will update this as I play more.
Summary:
Eon Altar is an innovative couch co-op title that uses a phone app as a controller and to relay seceret information to players which they can then chose to tell the rest of the group or to keep it a secret.
Pros:
+Truly unique and innovative gameplay
+App is reliable and didn't disconnect once through my session. Latency was also very minimal.
+The akward controls do work very well and I got used to them after only about 5 minutes.
+Price
+Stategic
+Unique stories for each character (however this leads to some cons)
+Good checkpoint and save system (however I would like a way to turn off checkpoints for more difficult gameplay)
+Art style fits the gameplay and the combat animations are good
Cons:
-Secret objectives for heroes aren't randomized at the start. The heroes always have the same secret objective which means that if you've already played through once you already know your friend's secret objectives.
-Because of the above con I believe that this game offers zero replayability (even though I haven't finished it yet).
-Misleading title. Game is titled Eon Altar, not Eon Altar Episode 1. I didn't read into the early access information before buying so I thought I was getting a full game and instead I ended up buying into an episodic series.
-Linear as linear gets. No branching paths at all. No fighting your friends over which way to go.
-Lack of interesting loot.
-App drained my battery faster than my phone could charge. I started playing with about 50% battery life and my phone plugged in. When I was done with my 1hr session I had only 10% battery life. I was using an old phone though (Galaxy SII).
-App unavailble on Windows 10 or Windows 10 mobile.
-While you can play alone, it isn't much fun.
-Game options are lacking
-During combat you will find yourself looking between screens a lot. This could be avoided if the app had a small PiP type window or a background that showed what was going on up on the main screen so the player can see what's going on when they are looking down at their phone.
Verdict: 6/10
Even with all of the flaws I reccomend this game, but only to people who are going to be playing with some friends and only if those friends happen to enjoy turn based video games or RPG's like D&D. If you have no friends then DO NOT buy this game.
The future:
This is the first time to my knowledge that a developer has attempted something unique like this. I see this as a starting point for a whole new genre of game. Maybe in the future we will be able to play something like this, but instead of the controller being the phone maybe It'll just use the phone to relay secret info and manage the inventory while using a physical controller to play, hell, maybe even attach the phone to a physical controller with some accessory. That would open up this type of system to more genres of games other than turn based ones. In the future I want to see a game with this type of innovation but with the gameplay of Diablo. Lets make it happen!

I really want to recommend this game, I really, really do. I was hyped for it since I first heard it's announcement, but in it's current form--well--let's say it needs more work. Obviously, it's an Early Access game so I do not expect polish, but the bugs and poor optimization are just killing me. Running on a system with a 980ti the highest three quality settings will plumment my framerate to between 20-40 FPS. It's only while getting to the lowest settings that the game runs at above 60.
Now to the controls. The smartphone & tablet controller is the selling point that truly differentiates "Eon Altar" from anything else out there. As it stands, however, it seems to be more of a detriment than a plus. The App is constantly disconnecting, controls are difficult and at times frustrating enough to throw your phone through a window when you miss a chest or selecting an enemy for the tenth time in a row. Fortunately, the turn-based system saves this aspect from being a total failure. However, the integrated UI and individual conversation that each character sees is a wonderful concept and with a little bit more polish would be completely phenomenal.
So currently, as the game stands, makes it very difficult to give an enthusiastic recommendation to. It's not exactly the prison cell garbage fire most indie games on steam are, but it's certainly not "Pillars of Eternity" either.  I really, really, truly hope the game can pull itself together by the time for full release as there is so much potential trying to claw it's way out from under the rubbish. All told--it can still make a good party game.

I have been a gamer for over 30 years and rarely can I say that I have thoroughly enjoyed every game entry into the franchise. The Sniper Elite series fits the bill for sure!
Sniper Elite III is a great experience from start to finish with well thought out maps and challenges. The graphics, sounds, and storyline are all great. The maps are pretty big and non-linear based, which is great for a third person expirence.
The weapon upgrades are ok, without getting too tedious. The challenges are fun, especially in coop mode. The coop mode is an excellent idea for games like this.
Some downsides are: shooting over walls can be bit buggy, the AI are way too perceptive to your location after making any noise (It's still a major improvement over SE2, however.) Also, players are too rewarded for close range combat.
Multiplayer is fun and challenging. It's a bit slower paced and methodical than most shooters, but that's the way it should be.
This game is all around one of the best I've played in the genre. Rarely do try to gather as many achievements as possible in a game, but this I just couldn't put down.
Im looking forward to next installment.

A WW2 Multiplayer shoot em' up. Play as either the Americans, Russians or Germans in battles of attrition on multiple maps. It's not the greatest but it's damn good at what it sets out to do.

Personally I enjoy this game and totally ignored the bad reviews of people whining about having to pay a little $$ which isn't really required to enjoy it. This game is quite similar in capture/hold objective gameplay to Battlefield game series. But depending on the situation you may not be able to capture an objective behind enemy lines. Heroes and Generals however doesn't have medic classes.. the medicine to heal is found in the game world at stationary boxes, and as upgrades on player owned vehicles. Teamwork and strategy with your squad is key. You can spot enemies simply by keeping them in your sights for about 3 seconds, but it does not follow their position if they move.
Infantry upgrades like grenades, landmines, even panzershreck/bazookas are obtained fairly easily. There are several types of battles ranging from small scale single objective to full scale war with tanks, planes and various other vehicles.

Well, I jumped back in after some time away and initially was surprised not realizing that it had launched.  First impressions were good.  New, modified maps made it interesting and challenging,  Unfortunately the excitement faded quickly, reminding me of why I stayed away.  First let me say, I have 1000+ hours in the game.  I became a tactical player trying to outwit the players realizing my assets, tanks, were really nothing more then game fodder.  In no time the same failing aspects of the game appeared and the luster was gone.  Tanks, with the exception of the Tiger, are even more so fodder with almost every player carrying some form of AT.  Add to that that in many instances the ground types can run faster then a tank can move making it even more of a worthless tool.
Besides this I was again initially thrilled with the new spawn point alteration.  It did give me the sense that I could control my fate while spawning.  Was I ever wrong.  Even worse, besides the loitering tanks, or vehicles with AT laden campers waiting just outside of the zone, aircraft now loiter overhead even more so then before and do nothing but take advantage of what is another inherent flaw in the games design.
I doubt the devs will pay attention to this and by chance if they do even really consider it worthy of time or consideration.  It's a shame because they do have what is a really exceptional idea that can be enjoyable but in their decision tree you can see where the choices made were those that would leverage the most return on their investment, that being to get players to pay up to advance as soon as they can to try and compete, but unfortunately, you never do get there.
So I wish you all some level of enjoyment but you too will grow weary of the grind and inability to really gain a lot of enjoyment from it as it with wear your soul down.
