I loved STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl. It wasn't perfect, but it was a really exciting game. However, after playing STALKER: Clear Sky for over 25 hours, I am unable to continue. The game is broken. Allow me to explain.
Graphically speaking, Clear Sky is a huge step up from SOC. It uses some of the most advanced shadows I've seen in a game, and the day and night cycle is incredibly immersive. All of the haunting art design and character modeling for the first game is there, but with improved models. However, the game is also so poorly optimized that it cannot run DirectX11 shadows without becoming a slide show, and continues to give me burst of awful (5-10 fps) lag on my rig. And trust me, my rig is not the problem. I've confirmed that this problem is widespread among many gamers, and is not just isolated to me.
The sound in the game is exceptional, of course. Weather, ambient noise, howls, fire crackling, gunshots, etc, all really help to immerse you in the zone. I have no complaint's about the sound design.
If the lag was the only issue, I would probably have finished this game lag and all. I certainly tried to. Of course I saw where it was headed, but the thrill *spoiler* of putting Strelok in the place we find him in SOC drove me onward. *spoiler* However, the combat mechanics, which were really great in the first game, especially the gunplay, are broken in this game.
Yes, the AI is more intelligent than in SOC; it uses cover, flanks you, and throws grenades. However, enemies tend to throw grenades in bursts at your EXACT position, and STALKER is NOT a movement friendly game. It feels incredibly unbalanced as one grenade will hurt you even if you sprint away from it immediately, and you will lose your cover. Multiple grenades almost always mean death.
The ballistics model in this game is a big disappointment in comparison to the first. All types of guns are WILDLY inaccurate at ranges above 50 feet, unless they are absolutely tricked out with accuracy upgrades. With a standard AK 74 or Abakan, you can't hit a damn thing at 100m, and are almost always forced to use assault rifles as if they were SMGs (grenade spamming and charging in headlong). I had to spend a good 15000 rubles on my TRS 301 just to get it to perform like it did un-modded in the original game. The AI, of course has none of these accuracy issues, and can happily hit you at 100m plus with any gun in the game, including the MAKAROV!
While the faction wars system is interesting, it's makes the zone feel too crowded, and not nearly as spooky or desolate as in the first game. In addition, whenever you conquer new territory, it takes the AI forever to send backup, which usually consists of 1-3 men to help you fend off the multiple counterattacks the enemy sends, usually consisting of 10 plus total men. You may have total numerical superiority, but if 300 of your best equipped stalkers are sitting in your base territory, you have a problem. This is supposed to be a war, not a one man take down border skirmish.
In conclusion, I'm not wild about the new weapon upgrade system, but I could see it working in a future title, and i love being able to repair my gear, finally. The new detector and revamped anomaly system is good, and the new graphics and AI are great for the most part. Now fix the balance, lag, gameplay issues, performance, and bring back the spookiness, and cut out the generic side quests, and we'll have a great game.

There are many pros and just a few cons.
Pros:
+Smartphone Controller - amaizing idea for new controle style. We have everything except main action, on our devices. There are dialogues too. It's easy to learn and use.
+4 characters with more "Comming soon" - 4 quite typical classes, yet every can be played as solo.

+Gives a feeling of playing classic RPG game with friends and Dungeon Master. - It's first game that gave me that feeling, even if I've played it just that little and it was solo. It's due to idea of dialogues kept on devices.

-You need smartphone to play. But what if someone doesn't have it? Or just hates it? That player just can't play.

For one, character customization. I'm not talking like huge Black Desert Online customization, but just things like being able to change your character's name or gender and possibly even skill sets. That way you connect a little more with the character. I'd like to start off by saying this game has a really good concept and a neat way of playing.
It requires a smartphone to use as a controller and it really separates itself from most game you'd see.
Pros:
-Multiplayer Local Game, one where you'd be able to couch it out with a couple of friends.
-A new way to play which differentiates itself from other games.
-Four current characters available to use with different backgrounds, skills, and dialogue written. (We could possibly see an extra character)
-Turn based combat
-Phone interface without having to hassle yourself and your friends with items, stats, and etc. (Because your controller also works as your menu)
-Roleplay aspect where you say what your character's dialogue says.
Cons:
-Must have a Smartphone and must be updated to fit the minimum requirements of the App it comes with.
-Controller feels a bit weird and could use a bit of work. Moving around is a bit hard to get used to, though I've gotten a bit used to it. It could to be eased for the user.
-The Roleplay aspect I mentioned could also be a con without voiced dialogue for the character being used. (As neat as it is to actually say the lines, it could get tiresome and some people may have trouble speaking)
I will continue to play and update this review but, for now I could recommend this game for people who want to see a intuitive idea something develope into something great. I haven't had too much trouble with the game and if you want to try something new and are a fan of the turn based RPG genre this would be a great buy.
I would not recommend this to somebody who doesn't have the patience to read a bit to learn how the game works and to somebody who doesn't own a smartphone. This is also an Early Access game so please know what you are getting into before you buy it.

Silly little game that seems like it's home would be on a touch device but honestly works just fine with mouse.
Draw lines and cut logs, its a simple gameplan for Jack Lumber. A childishly goofy theme and story set up a tale of revenge; Lumberjack versus tree. Each level consists of multiple stages where some collection of logs is tossed up on the screen. Upon clicking and holding the left mouse button time slows down. You then must drag your mouse through the tops and bottoms of every log before your slowed time ends. You can chain hits together for combos and go for bronze, silver, gold, or "plaid" rankings on every level. The game keeps things interesting with L and S shaped logs as well as ones that take multiple hits or can only be cut from a certain direction. A few other obstacles await in the final stages as well. There's a small handful powerups and gameplay modifiers to challenge yourself with too. A fun casual couple of hours. Or plenty more if you're an achievement junkie.
The big dividing point of the game seems to be the obvious similarities to a popular tablet/mobile/touchscreen title and whether it belongs on PC. Obviously this game looks like that duck, swims like that duck, and quacks like that duck. So it is probably that duck. But. I found the mouse controls perfectly acceptable, as well as accurate! Which is another complaint I've read. There is most definitely mistakes to be made and "ohhh comeon" moments. But I found the controls fair and tight with the mistakes my own.
Perfect bundle game or dollar game if you got card sales cash lying about. Its not going to win any awards but I had fun. Thumbs up!

For the first Tekken game on PC this one knocks it out of the park!! Buy it, you wont regret it!

I'm normally loathe to pre-purchase a game as it's always a crapshoot, but I gave in to my lifelong love of the Tekken series.
I am not disappointed.
My rig is a paltry i5-7500 3ghz and GTX 1050, but this game glides along at 60fps with everything at ultra settings. I cannot confirm, but I've heard of people playing this on laptops with integrated graphics and 2GB system RAM and still getting between 30-40 fps on low settings (which still look serviceable). Never before have I encountered a game so well optimised for PC right on release.
All of the classic Tekken characters we know and love have returned (Hwoarang, the Mishima clan, Eddie, Nina, Yoshimitsu, etc.), along with some exciting new ones.
If I were pressed to criticise anything, it would be that the voiceover of the main storyline is delivered a little too deadpan. I'm not sure if it was a stylistic "noir" choice or just poor voice acting, but the voice of the narrator makes me want to pass out during each cutscene/storyline interlude. The voice acting from everyone else is on point, though, and all characters communicate in their native tongues (Heihachi speaks Japanese, Claudio speaks Italian, and so on) - with the aid of subtitles, obviously. This is a subjective point, but it improves immersion into the story just a tad.
Another potential issue is some of the character customisation options. Don't get me wrong, I love being able to give Hwoarang his old Tekken 3 TKD uniform again (his default Tekken 7 costume is a fashion disaster), but some of the other options are just stupid. Cowboy hats and frog masks have the potential to make it feel a little like "Tekken: Team Fortress Edition", but to each their own, I suppose. Personally I don't like the more ridiculous customisation options, but I understand that this option offers Namco some in-game purchase options without having to go the pay-to-win route, which I appreciate.
To make a long story short, the criticisms are few, subjective and superficial, and in no way detract from what is a surprisingly great fighter even by Tekken standards. The many online and offline game modes mean that this game will have great longevity, and online tournaments and ranked play suggest that this will take the esports scene by storm.
If you have even a passing interest in fighting games, Tekken 7 is worth a look. If you're a fan of the series, this is an absolute must-buy on PC.
Addendum: Personally I would never even think about playing a fighting game without a controller or arcade stick, but I have heard from others that the keyboard input is surprisingly comfortable and intuitive. YMMV.

I started playing Spelunky HD on XBLA.
At first, it seemed like most "super hard" platformers. Then I started to understand. This game is fair. This game has tight controls. This game is addicting like "hell" (huh)... and finally, this is the best 2D platformer I've played (or at the very least, up there with best 8 and 16-bit games).
For the first 3 months, it took 8 hours a day, 7 days a week out of my life. My playtime started waning a bit after that. Then PC / Steam version came. A perfect game just got 10 times better with the inclusion of Daily Challenge. There is always something new happening thanks to interactions between all elements of levels. They might seem like repetitive trial & error cases at first but thanks to Tunnelman, one can practice each chapter until they're ready to do a full run... After that, it's time to go to Hell (Best secret / final chapter in a long time).
Prior to Spelunky, my experience with modern Rogue-like titles was limited to Dungeons of Dredmor. While I also loved that game, Spelunky was something else. It strips the Rogue formula to its barebones and then it takes it to another level. It uses the essentials to build a truly compelling platformer out ot it. If you like Dredmor or Binding of Isaac, this is a must. If you like those and are a fan of platformers, this is the ONLY game you could ever need.

If you can go through all the above, then yes, I think you will like Deponia.

While it's been some months since i last played it, I had a great time playing Sniper Elite 3.  I played through the campaign 2x fully and replayed certain missions a few times more.  Steam doesn't seem to register most of the time I've played so maybe it doesn't count replays or dlc time...dunno.
It was the first game of it's kind I had played in some time.  (imo most FPS games have been new faces for the same tired gameplay mechanics for years just like MMO's).  I'm glad I decided to give this game a fair shake after reading a few reviews for it in various places - Steam among them and have never regretted that decision.
I found the graphics to be quality enough to see what I needed without things blurring/blending at distances.  I never experienced crashes or client failures that i can recall, so obviously if they did happen, they weren't severe enough to dampen the gameplay experience.
While I can agree with a couple other reviewers that the missions seemed a bit far-fetched, as did the locations (RAT factory as example...how the hell would they have ever gotten it out of that mountainside cave when the road that led to the factory wasn't wide enough?  lol)  the landscapes and mission areas were exceptionally well done imo and it never once claimed to be historically accurate in any way though they did proper detail work on uniforms and vehicles and did a wonderful job on the buildings as well.
I never engaged in the multiplayer as I'm not inclined to compete with people, rather I prefer teamwork if not playing solo.
Seeing that v4 is coming soon, I'm quite excited.   If it's done as well as SE3, It'll be worth every penny on release day.
I bought this game at a discount more than a year after it came out, but it too would have been worth full price had I looked for it earlier.

A highly engaging throwback from the days of Dungeons and Dragons, Digitized and streamlined for a more modern and faster paced generation. While it is in early access and I'm currently unsure of how to save, it offers an enjoyable experience for groups of 2 or more. The single player is as of this moment lack luster, though shines when even one more person is introduced. connecting your phone can be a bit of a challenge as lag happens differently on different phones, however this is not a problem necessacarily of the platform. while other games have attempted dungeons and dragons, it's either been unintuitive and overly complex, or just a skin, this however feels like a simpler yet truer spinoff. ther is however no character customization as the game heavily relies on narrative, so only premade characters are available.
Pro's:
simplified D&D style gameplay
intuitive turn based combat
works well for both long term gamers as well as newcomers to gaming
interesting narrative
well made UI
(if applicable) great for couples or groups of friends
for local co-op, only one person needs to have the game (and app is free though that's expected)
fully voice acted
Con's:
lackluster graphics (not bad, just unrefined)
single player is punishing rather than difficult
virtually no character customization
phone required rather than a option
local co-op only
game time limited to phone battery life, though this can be fine if there are enough outlets to charge near by

Surgeon Simulator 2013 is a massively enjoyable indie game and brings a new meaning to the word 'original'. The never seen before gameplay style is a fantastic novelty and matched up against the hilarious content, visuals and audio brings a new experience to gamers which you will no doubt have fun with. The one thing that this game does lack, however, is content. With just a few hours of purely original content available to the player, there isn't a great deal to do. Luckily for the player, the mechanics and style of the game make it such an enjoyment to replay that you can get hours of fun from repeating operations.
+ The uniqueness and outrageousness of the game adds to the enjoyment you'll be having.
+ The funny, cartoony visuals and audio compliment the tongue-in-cheek style of the game perfectly.
+ An incredibly frustrating yet perfectly human control system will both annoy and amuse you.
+ Funny achievements (inspired by several online celebrities) will have you in stitches *clap for the pun*.

- A few more operations or at least environments would have helped ease the lack of game content.
- Having to repeat tough surgeries over and over to progress gets very tedious and stressful.
- Don't expect to get too many hours out of this game, just enjoy it for what it is - a unique title.
The only thing I found lacking was a tutorial for beginners, but otherwise super great game. I really am pleased with this purchase.

Goddamn it feels SO GOOD to finally have a AAA fighting game brought to PC that works DAY 1! For perspective ive been playing Tekken since Tekken 2 on the PS1 and i got to say we have really come a long way. After struggling with holding myself over with the unfinished disaster that was SFV i have been patiently waiting to play this game since my old Tekken Tag 2 days on Xbox 360/PS3.
First lets start by saying this game is OPTOMIZED!!! Its sad i have to make that such a large point but its very important to point out the game is very well optomized. i have literally not experienced a single dropped frame below 60 which is cruical for a fighting game and genuinely impressive given the stunning effects that can appear during gameplay. the story mode which let me remind you is here DAY 1 and not having to be patched in at a later date. Gone are they days when you have to piece together the Canon story in the arcade mode and now we have a premier mode dedicated to telling the story of the

For the first Tekken game on PC this one knocks it out of the park!! Buy it, you wont regret it!

I'm normally loathe to pre-purchase a game as it's always a crapshoot, but I gave in to my lifelong love of the Tekken series.
I am not disappointed.
My rig is a paltry i5-7500 3ghz and GTX 1050, but this game glides along at 60fps with everything at ultra settings. I cannot confirm, but I've heard of people playing this on laptops with integrated graphics and 2GB system RAM and still getting between 30-40 fps on low settings (which still look serviceable). Never before have I encountered a game so well optimised for PC right on release.
All of the classic Tekken characters we know and love have returned (Hwoarang, the Mishima clan, Eddie, Nina, Yoshimitsu, etc.), along with some exciting new ones.
If I were pressed to criticise anything, it would be that the voiceover of the main storyline is delivered a little too deadpan. I'm not sure if it was a stylistic "noir" choice or just poor voice acting, but the voice of the narrator makes me want to pass out during each cutscene/storyline interlude. The voice acting from everyone else is on point, though, and all characters communicate in their native tongues (Heihachi speaks Japanese, Claudio speaks Italian, and so on) - with the aid of subtitles, obviously. This is a subjective point, but it improves immersion into the story just a tad.
Another potential issue is some of the character customisation options. Don't get me wrong, I love being able to give Hwoarang his old Tekken 3 TKD uniform again (his default Tekken 7 costume is a fashion disaster), but some of the other options are just stupid. Cowboy hats and frog masks have the potential to make it feel a little like "Tekken: Team Fortress Edition", but to each their own, I suppose. Personally I don't like the more ridiculous customisation options, but I understand that this option offers Namco some in-game purchase options without having to go the pay-to-win route, which I appreciate.
To make a long story short, the criticisms are few, subjective and superficial, and in no way detract from what is a surprisingly great fighter even by Tekken standards. The many online and offline game modes mean that this game will have great longevity, and online tournaments and ranked play suggest that this will take the esports scene by storm.
If you have even a passing interest in fighting games, Tekken 7 is worth a look. If you're a fan of the series, this is an absolute must-buy on PC.
Addendum: Personally I would never even think about playing a fighting game without a controller or arcade stick, but I have heard from others that the keyboard input is surprisingly comfortable and intuitive. YMMV.

Spelunky is easily one of my favorite games from the past fifteen years. Infinitely replayable, infinitely addictive, infinitely fun - Spelunky is a game that harkens back to the olden days of classic video gaming. You control a spelunker drawn to the lethal depths of the caves, lured in by the mere chance of fame and fortune. You must make it from the beginning of the procedurally-generated (i.e. randomly designed) level to the end, dodging deadly obstacles and not-so-friendly enemies... and, oh yeah, you have to repeat this process over and over, gradually making your way down further and further into the underground below amassing wild amounts of gold and treasures to take back to your old life on the surface. Did I mention that if you die you have to start from the beginning of the caves again? Yeah, Spelunky is one of "those" games (and I love it). You might find surprises along the way, secrets you could never imagine - most of the time, these secrets will lead to your untimely demise and yes, you will get mad but you'll tell yourself "oh, just one more go and then I'll be done" and then six hours will have slipped you by. Spelunky will become your captor, it will ruin your life. It will backhand you hard enough across the face that it'll bloody your mouth but you'll keep coming back for more because you love it. That is something I guarantee...
NOTE: I see some reviewers complaining (for lack of a better word) about the invincible ghost that appears in the level after two minutes and thirty seconds has passed. While the ghost may be invincible, you can avoid and dodge it and continue to traverse the level... the ghost will even turn regular gems into shimmering diamonds worth vastly more than their original lackluster gem value. It seems the ghost is hated but it's just another element of the game - again, Spelunky is one of "those" games (and, I digress, I love it) and it refuses to hold your hand.

Doom 3 has a special place in my heart. It is the game that doesn't belong, the game no one remembers.
Doom 3 actually managed to come out several months before Half Life 2, it was similar both in graphics and gameplay, yet Half Life 2 was the winner in the long run and Doom 3 seemed to fall by the wayside, despite its fair share of cult popularity. I think the difference was that Half Life 2 didn't fall victim to the 00s pressure to dust off old IPs and jack them up them with so-so writing and bizarre storylines.
Doom 3 succeeds in terms of gameplay, it is a lovable action-horror game that can still give you a jump scare, its story and presentation are shaky sometimes, but that doesn't make it a bad game. I consider it a fine game because its fun to play and doesn't really do anything to offend me despite some of its shortcomings.

I was a big fan of Fruit Ninja when it came out; it was actually one of the very first game apps I'd ever had on Android. It was a fun little puck up and play game with little structure, fair challenge, and a nifty idea. Jack Lumber takes a lot of these ideas and builds upon them with structure reminiscent of other mobile games; a game board, star ratings based on scoring per level, trial and error level design, collectibles that are more than cosmetic, and a smattering of humor that may or may not get a chuckle depending on how generous an audience you are.
Unlike the aforementioned Fruit Ninja, Jack Lumber scores better for players that used some added skill and foresight when playing, which again comes to a lot of memorization as well as trial and error. Instead of simply swiping, or in this case mousing, willy-nilly, logs float, fly twirl, fall, and otherwise come into view from any direction in clusters and must be cut from end to end rather than simply any which way you will. To do this you press down on the mouse button as the logs enter your view and they are reduced to slow motion for a set amount of time indicated by a moving bar at the top of the screen. When the bar reaches zero or you released the mouse button your time to slice that group of blocks is done and a little trail showing where you moved your mouse will appear. The logs you managed to chop are blown apart with corny sounds and visuals akin to the old Batman TV series; POW! SLICE! PLAID!
Power ups make play easier in some cases, for example if you miss a block or group of blocks you can get a second try before moving on to the next cluster.
The graphics are a strange combination of cartoon and style that might work with a better palette. As they are in this game, things had a decidedly pink and orange hue that looked more washed out and drab than stylized. The sounds are also okay, with karate style “HOO!” and “HYA!”, and cutesy high-pitched voice 'noises' for the animals you collect throughout the game.
The biggest issue with this game are the controls. For a game that really doesn't demand much, the least they could have done was sharpen the mouse a bit. As it was, for my time playing it, the mouse felt imprecise and this was frustrating. I could see the trail I'd left behind to slice logs but they would inexplicably show that I missed, and the log would fall away while the timer continued. I realize there are other axes to collect and use, but if this is a feature requiring a better ax to improve upon then it's a terrible feature as it frustrated me to no end. If this is not a feature but a design flaw then it's no less frustrating because, once again, this game's controls are so simple that I'd think honing them would have been the least they could have done.
I can see how this might have been fun on a mobile device or a tablet, but on the PC it's mediocre at its best.

I might consider re-installing this game when it gets a real tutorial.  Currently the only "tutorial" consists of several pages of vague instructions that discuss what various unit types will do.  This does not replace a real tutorial that shows you how to actually move units around, how to give orders, or even how to interpret the map.  As a result, after reading the tutorial, the first mission of the easiest campaign seems logical for the first minute when you're looking at the larger strategic screen.  But then the battle begins and....where the hell are you?  Clearly you are in one of these sectors that you saw on the map.  Where are your units?  Where are the enemy units?  How do you move your units?  Ok, a little bit of button mashing gets this unit to move there, but why does this matter in the larger scheme of the battle?
Clearly this game was intended to be an add-on to the previous games in the series.  It was intended for people who have already played the previous games in this series.  I have played Wargame: European Escalation many years ago, but that did not leave me prepared for this game.
If you have played previous games in this series, and you are already familiar with them, and you understand how to play, then this might be worth getting.  If you have not played previous games in this series, do not get this game.
I can understand that the developers wanted to create a hardcore strategy game that does not hold the player's hand, but in the process they have created a game that is impossible for a new player to begin to enjoy.  This is not a learning curve, this is a learning cliff.  Fortunately I received this as part of a larger Humble Monthly Bundle, so I do not feel that I have wasted any money on it, but be advised that if you buy this, you will likely be asking for a refund.
And believe me, I REALLY REALLY REALLY wanted to like this game.  I was excited to see that it was included in the bundle.  I regret having to give this review, but this is a serious failure by the developers.

One of the best RTS games I've ever played. Let me tell you why. You can't play this game like an idiot. You'll get smoked. But you can't just "build" units, ala Command and Conquer. Before the game, you create a "deck". Each deck has a maximum point limit that can be increased by choosing to limit yourself to a specific nation or type of unit (airborne, mechanized, armor, etc.) The units in this deck are all you have for the battle. So if your deck only contains 2 F/A-18C aircraft, once they're gone, they're gone. You need to be careful with your troops.
There's tactical depth here, as units make use of cover, line of sight, and all have different effective weapon ranges, sensor distance, etc.
An incredibly deep game that I'm still playing years later.

So after reading other reviews of this game I was a little wary about what I might be getting myself in to. However seeing the low price tag on it and really liking the concept behind the game I decided to try it and I am very glad that I did.
Lets start with what Eon Altar is. It is at its core a well thought out way for people to play a game co-operatively in a relaxed setting. The game can be as fast paced or as slow as you need it to be and it is very easy to learn. I sat down with my wife after purchasing the game and we both loaded up a character and dove right in. Now I have been a gamer since I was old enough to hold a controler and tall enough to reach a joystick in an arcade, but my wife not so much. Her gaming resume consists of a little Halo 3 and a little bit of racing. She did have a problem getting the hang of moving her character around but I found it to be no issue at all. The controls were responsive and apart from the occasional phone lock-up (due to low battery) it all felt very smooth and a bit nostalgic.
The game is quite fun as well. They do a decent job of teaching you how to play, and you get little mini "walkthroughs" on your phone as you progress. The flow of the game reminds me very much of the classic Gauntlet style games. You move through maps as a group, there are things to loot, items to find, money to spend on upgrades and skills, and fun conversations to be had.
Pros:
-Easy to jump in and play
-Lovely environemnts
-Turn based combat (this allows you and your friends time to plan and fight)
-Spoken voice conversations!!! (You are fed lines to read out load as your character for conversation purposes, the NPCs will talk to you via the game and then you pick options and you can then read a few lines outloud for your friends to hear. This includes your characters knowledge of of lore in the game.)
-Easy to learn
-Personal and group goals (you can keep the personal ones secret from your buddies)
-D&D style skills and upgrades
Cons:
-Phone program can lock up (fixed by force closing it and reopening it, then rejoining the game)
-Personal goals are marked by a colored circle that corrosponds to your character. It was hard for my wife (and me) to see some of her markers unless we got really close to them. The dark purple was hard to see in the environment.
-Playing a new character can slow the game down as you may need to read through abilities and upgrades available while your friends wait for you.
-very addicting (we did not want to stop playing despite needing to sleep for work tomorrow)
-Lack of early healing items. They are there, but they seem to be just enough to squeek by, however death and respawns in the game are prepared for with "respawn" as you progress.
-It is a bit easy to charge ahead of the group too and aggro enemies while your buddies get stuck a bit off screen.
Overall I would give this an 8/10 as it stands now and for an early access game that is pretty awesome. The price can't be beat either and as more of the game becomes available it will just get better. Can't wait to play it some more.

This game is fantastic. True tabletop RPG feeling.
*NOTE: I played this game on another steam account due to their computer being plugged up to a very large TV, so I dont have the hours logged to my account*
So I have a group of friend that I play pathfinder with, when I saw the devs of this game were trying to re-create the tabletop RPG feeling I was instantly sold on this game and we planned a day where we coudl all get together and play it. This game does not have online multiplayer, and the devs said they arent planning on adding it either currently. Local co-op is the only way to play the game (or singleplayer if you're brave) so let me start this off by saying this. Playing this kind of game in person with other people is VERY important. It adds a lot of enjoyment to the game. Seeing peoples faces when they're trying to hide some thing or make a decision changes the feeling. Plus you'll most likely have alot of laughs together.
Now that that's out of the way, lets get to the gameplay. Combat is turn based, obviously. Everything is based on dice rolls depending on your stats. But one of the interesting parts is each turn is simultaneous. Enemies move in a group, players move in a group. You can step on each others toes. Enemies can block each others movement. Some communication is required if things get hairy. I cleaved into my friends multiple times. I've been rained arrows on. I've been shield bashed on accident. I've also missed my massive energy cost healing strike multiple times because it has a slow animation and I didnt tell anyone I was using it before my target died. So far the game is pretty unforgiving and can be difficult at times. Which is honestly great. The panic or teamwork that comes together when its going downhillis really exciting.
Outside of the combat, you have some interactions between characters depending on their alignment, actions and your personal missions. We didnt get too deep into this ourselves, but during our game we called each other out, chose party actions against someone elses moral alignment and practically stole out loot from each others noses. It might sound like a backstab party, but it's not that sinister. It's all mostly fun and games or hard decisions you have to make to come out of the story alive. Though if somone was really a jerk, you could make someone fall really behind if you never let them get any resources to upgrade their gear. I guess thats up to the players.
Now on another note, the game has a few bugs that hurt it, but I mean this is EA. Its pretty much to be expected of a game that's been out less than a year in EA. A few bugs happened last night and actually even caused us to have to restart the game (luckily only about 10 minutes into the game). Here's a list of all the bugs we came across.
-When trying to trade resources, the mobile app got stuck with an ! on the screen like it was trying to wait for someone to say something, but no one could say anything and we couldnt progress (the bug that made us restart)
- Enemies randomly ran past us and started spazing out once
- I once ran past an enemy I tried to attack and swung at the air, attack didnt even attempt (Didnt say I hit or missed)
-
- Skill menu seems to not cycle through skill trees in order (Paladin skill tree comes up 1/3
- Opening chests and containers sometimes takes multiple tries
- If you accidentally close the app, you wont be able to join back.
Despite all the bugs, the game was loads of fun. Even with an ability/gear update coming, there was plenty we could do. Character customization is pretty good, you wont be able to unlock everything but rather focus your character on what you want to be. There are 3 skill trees for each character that focuses on a specific gameplay style or theme for them (Crusader: Melee physical damage, Paladin: A mixture of physical and magic damage with some healing and debuffs. and Cleric: bufffs and healing). One of my complaints is that I would argue that having a +2 skill check bonus to dungeoneering isnt worth 30 skillpoints, when I could also spend 30 skill points on upgrading my defence buff spell. Dungeoneering is an important skill to have, but it feels a little wasteful to spend it on that when I'm the party's cleric and need to keep people alive. I'm all for passives and skill bonuses but it feels like it should cost less. Like in pathfinder for example, you get skillpoints when you level up on top of other class related upgrades and abilities. Using a whopping 30 skillpoints to be able to open chests and break down barricades feels a little wastefull. Hopefully they address that in the future.
Unless I'm remembering wrong, the game is going to be 9 Episodes. So far Episode 1 is out and it has 3 parts to it. We played from 10 pm to 3 am. That's about as much as a normal Tabletop session went for us.
I would 100% reccomend this game. It's loads of fun to get together and play this with some friends. I'll update this review as episodes come out and I play through it with my friends.

In my opinion, the idea of creating a roleplaying game that stresses the social elements of a game night with friends is a very promising endeavour and some of Eon Altar's more innovative aspects certainly point in the right direction: The game controls through phones and tablets work surprisingly well and the fact that each player is requested to read out the dialogue of their character by themselves and receives individual and sometimes secret information or quests through their personal device adds an interesting and enjoyable social dynamic to the game.
However, how some reviewers got the idea of comparing it to an "actual Dungeons & Dragons" experience or even to just traditional PC roleplaying games is beyond me. I am not suggesting that it is a good idea in the first place to hold the game to high standards like that and I recognize that it wasn't even designed to offer D&D-like experiences, but since a number of people have remarked on this positively, I feel compelled to say, that even though the game offers some light pastime for a short while, many of its aspects are rather disappointing:
The aesthetics are infantile,
the story and the characters are uninspired and simply boring,
dialogue and descriptions are written in a preposterously horrible fashion,
the game mechanics are far too simple for an enjoyable role-playing game experience, yet the game itself is too long to offer just a light and amusing game night pastime for one evening or so.
In the end, the game suffers from the fundamental problem of wanting to be both: An actual roleplaying-game and an easily approachable social game. My hope is, however, that the idea of local-coop rpgs stressing a social dynamic as attempted in Eon Altar, doesn't die with this game, but will be developed in a more sophisticated way in the future.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a quite unique gaming experience. It has some very emotional moments and I did like how the story was told. It is like an adult fairytale and it actually has some very heavy moments. and it does focus more on the storytelling than on the actual gameplay. So, it's actually quite easy to play and it doesn't really have difficult moments to master. While this can be seen as a contra for the game, I guess it's up to oneself to judge. Personally I was a little bit bothered that the characters didn't speak an acutal language, I guess this was a choice by the developers to stress the pictorial metaphors used in the game. Also it is quite a short, I played through it in around 3 hours.
Although it isn't a perfect game, due to some minor flaws, I do recommend this game to everyone, because it's one of those rare and unique games you just don't see very often.

So its like I said a short and simple but gripping story of two brothers that must travel the world to save their dying father by  finding some kind of "world tree". The game is a platformer/puzzle game where most puzzles demand that you use one brother to do one thing and the other to do another thing, the brothers also got different "abilities". The older brother can swim but the younger cant for example.
While the puzzles themselves arent so hard the strange control method makes it somewhat of a struggle now and then. And even if the game can at first can be seen as quite childish I promise that it will touch a few very adult matters.

1 x 670g jar morello cherries
2 tablespoons caster sugar
1 tablespoon cornflour
600ml thickened cream
60ml (1/4 cup) kirsch
2 tablespoons boiling water
2 tablespoons caster sugar, extra
100g dark cooking chocolate, coarsely grated
Method:
Step 1
Prepare and bake the chocolate cake mix following packet directions. Turn onto a wire rack to cool completely. Use a large serrated knife to cut the cake horizontally into 3 even layers.
Step 2
Drain the cherries, reserving 160ml (2/3 cup) of the juice. Reserve 10 cherries to decorate. Place the remaining cherries and the reserved juice in a saucepan with the sugar and cornflour. Stir over medium-low heat until the mixture boils and thickens. Transfer to a large bowl. Cover with plastic wrap and place in the fridge to chill.
Step 3
Use an electric beater to beat cream in a medium bowl until firm peaks form.
Step 4
Place kirsch, water and extra sugar in a jug and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Step 5
Place 1 cake layer on a serving plate and drizzle over half of the kirsch mixture. Spread with half of the cherry mixture and a thin layer of the cream. Repeat with the remaining cake, kirsch mixture, cherry mixture and cream, finishing with a layer of cake.
Step 6
Spread some of the remaining cream over the top and side of the cake. Sprinkle the chocolate over the top and gently press onto the side of the cake.
Step 7
Place the remaining cream in a piping bag fitted with a 1cm fluted nozzle and pipe rosettes around the edge of the cake.
Step 8
Arrange the reserved cherries around the cake between the cream rosettes. Cut the cake into wedges to serve.

Doom 3 is probably one of the more disappointing games I've played and it has nothing to do with with its graphics.  The graphics in Doom 3 still look really good today, so thumbs up to Id's workmanship there.
WEAPONS:
First off, the weapons feel and sound weak in Doom 3.  None of the weapons in Doom 3 sound satisfyhing to fire at all.  They sound almost puny.  For a game that, for the most part, utilizes the other sounds in the game so well, they fall very short on the weapons, except maybe the BFG.
In fact, the weapons are all around just plain weak in this game.  The shotgun is really quite powerful, but only point blank (can 1-shot mid strength monsters).  Since you have to pump the shotty after every shot fired, point blank becomes dangerous and damage drops fast at any range.  You don't really get a powerful weapon until the rocket launcher.  The BFG is only slightly more powerful, which is sad compared to the almighty BFG of past Doom games.  For most of the game the levels are so tightly confined that I didn't even want to use those two unless I was desparate because I could easily kill myself in the process (and did a few times).  The Soul Cube puts the RL and the BFG to shame, but it has firing limitations.  THose limitations border on tedious making the effort it takes working towards the next opportunity to fire it annoying and painful.
What I mean by weak.  There is no discernible difference in damage between the pistol, machine gun, chain gun or plasma rifle.  The later 3 just fire faster than pistol.  Using the spider monster in the game as a test, since they come in hordes and it's easy to use them for testing, it took the same number of shots (3) to kill one with any 4 weapons.  If I heard the spiders coming and had some space, I would just pull out the pistol, which has an annoying pause between shots, and pick them off at medium distance.  I'd reserve the other 3 weapons for close quarters, then I would just spray and pray.  This similarity in damage was apparent when used on all monsters.  The chain gun, a detriment to use due to its spin up time.  I usually took more damage with the chain gun than using cover and short bursts with the machine gun or plasma rifle.
The grenades are strong, but a pain.  Their game physics treats them like they are those "Super Bounce" rubber balls but without the vertical bounce.  They have almost no vertical arc when thrown (trying to throw it onto a platform above you, or over a crate an enemy is using for cover?  Forget it!) and they bounce and ricochet horizontally all over the place.  Unless it directly hits a monster and explodes, the grenade is likely to ricochet back to you and kill you instead even if thrown around a corner.
In the end, it was more effective, in most cases, to learn each monster's melee/fight pattern and just rush in, point blank them with the shotty, then jump out before the mob could recover from it's first missed attack to swing again.  I was even using this tactic on the top 4 of the most powerful monsters in the game outside the 3 bosses.
STORY:
The story was pretty bad.  Experiments release the hordes of Hell.  You kill the hordes of Hell seeking to take down those responsible and kill them.  Kill the creature holding the door open and close the gate and save Earth.  Good idea.  Doom 1 and 2 did this as well. The problem?  Tons of written dialogue in the form of e-mails.  Tons of voice dialog in the form of audio log files.  Video logs in the form of propaganda. A few cinematics.  Other than a couple minor things in the story, iD used all of this to tell the same story that Doom and Doom 2 told, which both managed to infer without any of the stuff I just mentioned.
The only purpose most of that served was to add in probably the dumbest game mechanic ever.  Forcing me to browse every e-mail and audio file just so I can get the combination codes for all the storage compartments holding most of the armor, weapons and ammo.  Initially, it wasn't bad, but it got old quick.  Hello Google!
GAMEPLAY:
Doom 3 did wrong, what everything a slighlty newer game "Dead Space," did right.  I'm not talking about graphics eventhough Dead Space, graphically, was superior because it's newer.  In Dead Space, every monster that came at you came from somwhere and by that I mean somewhere that makes sense.  They crawled out of panels in bulkheads, from under bridges, holes they "created," busted out of corpses in which it was incubating, or tranformed said corpse into something else for it's own use.  You could hear skittering and crawling all ofer the place. It felt like they could come out at any point from anywhere and it always made sense.  They could be anywhere, anytime, but where-ever they crawled out, it made sense.
In Doom 3, many monsters were hidden behind wall panels that were clearly wall panels that, when opened, were just empty closet like rooms where a monster clearly just sat there waiting for it to open.  The "closets" clearly served no purpose other than holding a monster to jack your butt the moment you ran into any small piles are armor/ammo lying around. This caught me off guard the first few times, but then never again.  Many times it was clear a monster just spawned somwhere because you triggered a spot walking through it and "boom" monster smacking you in the back.  No tell-tale sign.  Clearly, the game just popped a monster right behind me.  The only monsters that made sense were the ones that were "summoned" in for lack of a better term and you can hear the teleport sound.  Come on!  This style of monster spawn/use worked for earlier Doom and Quake games, but iD, you guys tried to add a story and go for realism.  Old Doom style monster spawning just doesn't cut it.
Dead Space style monster spawning shouldn't be a limitation at the time of Doom 3 and was entirely possible.  Unfortunately, I think iD were still stuck in their Doom (1,2) and Quake (1.2) thinking and failed to bring something new to the table.  Instead Dead Space comes out and blows my socks off, and now I am here wondering how iD couldn't have pulled off something similar a few years earlier.
Doom 3 is also too long for what it gives.  I've read from others that it kind of over stays it's welcome and I agree.  You spend forever in industrial style levels that didn't change until I was sent to Hell.  Once in Hell, I thought I was about to reach the end.  NOPE!  I finally end up back on Mars and I think it's close to the end.  NOPE!!  A linear FPS the deilvers task after task to accomplish before reaching the goal.  Many of which leave the game with a bloated "wasting my time busy work" feel.  Hell has the only interesting looking levels in the game although its hard to enjoy them because you can barely see in Hell.  Even with Max brightness.  Hell breaking into reality upon return to Mars looks neat, but only happens in maybe 2 spots.
And finally, the most annoying thing about Doom 3.  For much of the game you are pretty ammo starved (even on normal).  This WASN'T a problem.  This was an acceptable thing as it adds some intensity.  The problem was that the moment the game finally ramps up and gives you a plethora of ammo so I can go Bat-Crap crazy, you don't get the chance.  The moment you do, you end up in Hell with no guns or ammo.  You spend most of the Hell regaining it.  Once back to Mars, no guns or ammo.  You spend most of the time rebuilding again.
Most of it adds up to excuses to make the game last a bit longer and feel bloated.

This is a very scary horror FPS game, as advertised. The graphics are fairly chintzy at this point in time, & the Acer Aspire had no issue with them. It also had no issue with any of the ASU schoolwork that it was purchased to be used for, but that's another story.  Doom3 is annoying to play for more than an hour or two at a time, because the "jump scares" are exhausting. That is that thing where a demonic & terrible monster bursts out of a closet or vent to try & 'git' you. That is surprising, yes, but also irritating.
Plot (or lack thereof): They do a good job of making the main character go through a lot of fairly specific work environments & scenarios, but while they are doing that they are killing demons & spellcasters & spiders & flying skulls & all that sci-fi♥♥♥♥♥♥ I picture the band Pantera getting a kick out of this game. The story is much like the plot of the book "Armor" by John Steakley, which is an EXCELLENT read that really gets into your head. It is not tightly scripted in Doom3 but it is linear in terms of how the game advances. The main character, Doomguy, obeys orders from a military commander who strongly resembles Republican president George W. Bush, & he is directed by this general to complete various manual labor tasks - finding keys, opening doors, clearing buildings of aliens, etc. In a pivotal & important plot-advancing scene, the male character meets a female secretary & they passionately kiss during what I can only presume is after the end of the 9-to-5 workday period. It looked like they met in a laboratory as an experiment was being done while they were both inside what seems to be either a university lab or a research facility.
Incidentally, Doom3 is the best "single-player only" FPS of the early 2000's & was very successful, if anyone is curious about the history of video games. It was a big deal when it came out. In my opinion, the "best FPS of that time, period" would have to be Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory, as the multiplayer was just so well-sorted out there that it was fun to play at any skill level
Gamers in my day used to say "Shady is the root of all evil." With that in mind, things sure seem shady, sketchy, foreboding & mysterious in DOOM3. Doomguy fights the devil in one level about halfway through the game's plot. He also fights a balrog demon in a different level. The atmosphere is serious & engrossing so I suppose it is good at creating the feeling that they seem to have been intending to create. This is very much a horror game & the other game that comes to mind as being most similar to this one is the Resident Evil franchise, specifically Resident Evil 6: Biohazard Adventures. I'm thinking here specifically of the scene where the main character & his wife go through the suburban high school graduation banquet that has been destroyed by zombies & you kill a popstar
Other games Doom3 is similar to: I feel like this game is similar to Quake4, but turned up to 11, and to Unreal tournament, but more single-player-centric. In terms of graphics it is better than Wolfenstein 3D. It goes well with a pizza & soda, as i discovered myself just now. For $5 it is somewhat fun & probably worth buying if you are gunning to play something scary for a while. It is fun sometimes to run old games in ULTIMATE MAXED OUT graphics settings.

This games seems like a fun and interesting way to play some couch co-op RPG with friends. However, it is still nearly unplayably buggy. I've had the Android client lock up multiple times and render the rest of the session unplayable, on multiple different phones. This happened so many times during the first session we gave up and let the player that was still in play to the end by themselves in order to just unlock the next session. Also it seems that dying has neglible impact, as you are resurrected at the last checkpoint while all the enemies you can have killled are not. This allows you to just grind down large waves or dangerous situations with multiple death/respawn cycles.
The game itself is a fun rpg-lite that basically uses your smartphones to deliver guided pen-and-paper style RP experience. The concept is neat, and it looks like it could be a fun pick up game, but at this point in time I cannot recommend it as it is so buggy it is barely playable (at least in multiplayer). The prequel of the game STALKER Shadow of Chernobyl.
The user starts as a mercenary named Scar who was found by the Clear Sky faction in The Swamps,unconscious ,after the most powerful emission The Zone ever did, near the bodies of some scientists that he was paid to lead. The character is a mercenary but is not part of the faction "Mercenaries" and he was able to survive 2 emissions that affected his nervous system ( this leads to blurry moments during gameplay).The story takes place in The Zone and your task whether you like it or not is to help the Clear Sky faction find out who is messing with The Zone until The Zone turns every living beeing into ashes.
Clear Sky brings new dangerous areas with new quests, a new anomaly called "Space Anomaly", taxi, improvements to the graphics ( like dx10,sun shafts etc ) and gameplay.The user is now able to repair and modify equipment (guns and suits) with the help of data found on usb sticks ( the mechanics will ask for these for advanced changes) and join factions after helping them defeat their rivals but beware you are neutral to all {except monolith and some mercenaries} and taking part in their wars will set your status "at war" with the faction they're at war. Artefacts aren't spread all over the map like in SoC and since they're produced by anomalies they can be found only in anomalies,invisible to the naked eye but visible with the help of detectors. Almost every settlement has a taxi that can lead you in places ( not everywhere) if you pay him.
The game opens the path for Stalker Shadow Of Chernobyl but doesn't give new info on The Zone.
Personally I recommend playing this as vanilla for a true STALKER experience then you can mod it and enjoy unexplored areas.

For a true STALKER there are no cons.

Holy cow, where do I begin?
I was introduced to this game by my lovely girlfriend, and it re-ignited my long-snuffed love of adventure games.  Deponia originally caught my eye after seeing a Let's Play by mangaminx, and truthfully it was the steam/dieselpunk art style that caught me first, and I finally picked it up from the Daedalic bundle.  Well worth it.
Despite some quality issues I could moan about with the audio and the less than polished cutscenes that reminded me more of early Newgrounds flash animation than a final release, the game had me from the word go.  The writing is witty, the characters vibrant, and the story is executed with a loving finesse that embraces its cliche's so fondly it's hard not to excuse their faults, and then makes up for it with a sharp left-turn into some strikingly emotional scenes that defy the conventional tropes.
As far as the puzzles go, I've certainly faced down more maliciously obscure combinations but I won't say there's no fridge-logic to be had here either.  Expect to need a guide once or twice, if for no other reason than to go "Oh, I have to click on -that- pixel?" or "Well I would never have figured that pattern out on my own."  The game leaves you plenty of clues through the comments made when you try to combine or use items at certain spots, it's the minigame puzzles it throws at you that seem to defy any intuition.  Even these, if you're observant enough, have their answers provided to you nearby.
The first Deponia game has its quirks and oddities, it's own peculiar flaws and triumps that are the marks of any labor of love by a smaller company; but where the polish and sweat really shine through here is the lovingly thought out story, characters and level artwork, which is what any adventure game fan is there for in the first place, and it delivers these with plenty of flourish.

So, this version plays better, several times cheaper and can actually look much better with one simple tweak. Open a notepad, paste following (relevant for 16:9, 1080p resolution):
set r_mode -1
set r_customWidth 1920
set r_customHeight 1080
set image_lodbias "-1.0"
set image_anisotropy 8
set r_multiSamples 0
set r_aspectRatio 1
seta com_videoRam "2048"
seta image_useCache "0"
seta image_roundDown "0"
seta image_usePrecompressedTextures "0"
seta image_useCompression "0"
seta image_useNormalCompression “0”
seta image_downSizeLimit "0"
seta image_ignoreHighQuality "0"
seta image_downSizeBumpLimit "0"
seta image_downSizeSpecularLimit "0"
seta image_downSizeBump "0"
seta image_downSizeSpecular "0"
seta image_downSize "0"
seta image_forceDownSize "0"
seta image_roundDown "0"

"World War II Secret Agent Game"
Let me start off by saying that "Sniper" should not even be in the title of this game. So little of what you do in this game is what a Sniper actually does, really frustrated me. I have yet to even complete the story of the game because to me it just felt so disconnected, boring and just plain BAD at times. What it really should be called is "OSS Files" or something of the sort, something that clues you in to be more of a Secret Agent who HAPPENS to be a really good marksman, not a US Army Sniper. I've been playing this series from the get go and time and time again I've been disappointed by it. Between the simple fact that a lot of the rifles in this game wouldn't have been used as Sniper Rifles, to the downright horrendous AI even on higher difficulties, leads me to finally write a sadly quite bad review for this game. Now. Let's dive into the Pro/Con.
Pros:
-Wide variety of tasty WWII-era, mostly authentic weaponry for your Nazi-killing pleasure.
-Did I mention variety?
-Bullet physics and the like are desperately refeshing in a gaming era dominated by CoD and Battlefield where legitmate ballistics are woefully lacking if existant at all.
-The environment is very immersive and authentic, right down to the vehicles.
Cons:
-Remember that variety I mentioned? Yeah. You have to pay for a lot of it.
-The AI ranges from laughably stupid to mind-numbingly difficult.
-Remember those physics I was talking about? Yeah. They only work sometimes.
-"Remote detonated TNT" that you shoot to set off. (Don't even get me started with the physics of this one)
-The lack of any GENUINE sniping got old after the first two or three hours.
-No seriously. You BARELY snipe anyone in this game. 100-300 meters does not constitute sniping. I regularly make shots inside that distance with my Iron-sighted rifle at the gun range.
-Did I mention stupid AI?
-I could go on. No really. I could.
Bottom line is, the game can be really, really enjoyable. It also can be the bane of your existance and WILL drive you absolutely insane with how bad some of the story can be. Honestly a very fun game, with sadly tons and tons of unrealized potential, that the game reminds me of every single time I boot it up.

This game is an open world singleplayer game and a PvP Arena based multiplayer game.
The singleplayer game is an open world, Pirates! like game that revolves around a dynamic economy, land ownership, faction allegiance, diplomacy, and open warfare. This is a very fun game, however it has massive flaws. The dynamic economy is fairly weak, as land ownership and taxation completely dwarf income based on trade. Land ownership itself includes the ability to build buildings, however the time it takes to complete buildings does not correspond with the bonuses that they provide, resulting in building becoming an almost worthless endeavor. Items for sale are randomized, with not all armor sets available for sale. Weapons and armor can have +Attack or +Defense modifiers, forcing the player to rely on RNGesus to collect the strongest version of their preferred armor set. The faction allegiance system is very weak and causes the player to swear total allegiance to one faction, or create their own faction. Having positive reputation with a faction that the player is not curently under allegiance has near no benefits. As a faction leader, having positive relations with other factions will not stop them from attacking you. Individual relationships are basically only useful between the player and allied faction leaders, or the player and a marriage candidate. Each fortress can give a random quest out of a small pool of quest types, with some side quests being extremely frustrating, such as hunting down an invisible enemy. The warfare aspect of this game is where it truely shines, with an innovative combat environment, however the late game is unfair to the Player Character, with the enemies being able to generate armies faster than the Player can, as well as sieging vastly faster than the Player can: this results in a situation where the enemy can spawn 2 new armies an take 2 towns in the time it takes for the Player to take 1 town. Enemy lords can not be killed and will respawn and generate large armies without regard to land ownership or money, enabling them to attack poorly defended settlements. To achieve complete victory, the Player must take all available lands AND hunt down the remaining lords; This can cause problems as the lords may continuously respawn after being defeated and if the game detects 2 "living" landless factions, it will toss the lords into one faction, and then the other faction causing the lord to respawn with a full army making the game impossible to beat. There is vast room for improvement with this game, however it is a great step into a seldom-explored genre.
This game also has excellent mod support, with the vast majority of mods feeling much more complete than the base game. I highly recommend this game for its mod support, with mods covering time periods and themes that are not covered by ANY other video game before. Popular mods cover the Game of Thrones universe, Star Wars universe, Napoleonic Conquests, Early Roman Empire, Medieval Southeast Asia, Sengoku Japan, Warring States China to name a few.
What makes this game worth it to me is the mod campaigns.
The multiplayer aspect of the game is similar to Chivalry, but worse.

TL:DR version:
Good game. Not as good as the first game Shaodw Of Chernobyl as this one shows all the signs of a rushed game. But with some mods installed it's still very enjoyable.
Long version:
Prequel to the first STALKER game Shadow Of Chernobyl (SOC).

They only made like 2 new maps while reusing all the textures and maps from SOC yet still manage to code it badly so it's full of bugs. Simply a lackluster effort.
IMPORTANT TIP:
DO NOT USE QUICK-SAVE QUICK-LOAD FUNCTION BUILT INTO THE GAME UNLESS YOU WANT TO HAVE CORRUPTED SAVEFILE THAT FORCE YOU TO START THE GAME OVER.
So, in order to enjoy this, you will need community-made "mods", or patches since they fix bugs the developers are too lazy to fix.
Sky Reclamation Project (SRP) (thank you Decane)
This mod is a must as it fixes many game-crashing issues and it changes no gameplay so you can play the game how it's meant to be played.
Clear Sky Complete (CS COMPLETE) (thank you Pavel)
The COMPLETE mods for the STALKER games are nice because they make the game look and sound better and play better. HOWEVER, even though this mod contains SRP, the SRP is an early version and does NOT include many fixes the most current version of SRP has. You WILL encounter game crashes and maybe even CORRUPT savefiles with this so use at your own risk.
Now if you have some modding experience or some general knowledge of how script mods work then you can merge the up-to-date version of SRP with CS COMPLETE.  This is what I did so I can enjoy good graphcis+sound with no crashes.

Cons (but not really cons. These are more like areas of improvement):

I think this game is a lot more polished than most of the other Early Access titles. If you plan on buying the game, you might as well try it out now (and go through the refund policy if it turns out you don't like it). The graphics are well-done, especially for a game of this genre. I was expecting a more fluid framerate from my system (i7-4710HQ, GTX 860M, 8GB RAM --> 40FPS 1080p max) seeing as how it's the laptop equivalent, or even better (in some cases) than the recommended desktop specs. Nevertheless, at 40FPS, it is still perfectly playable. There are no dips on my end. The gameplay is alright. If you like Trove, then this feels a lot like it and I'd recommend it. If, however, you were expecting something more along the lines of Minecraft, then do not purchase this game. It is RPG first, sandbox second. The combat feels simplistic, but reminds me of a Zelda game. You basically choose to either attack or dodge, and this will have some consequences (not really such awful consequences, but consequences nonetheless). Some of the reviews target the exploration aspect of the game, and while they are correct in the fact that the first few levels (5-6 or so) offer hardly any exploration, the seventh level (at least on my game, seeing as how it's procedurally generated) had one of the most well-done dungeons I've ever seen. It was a several story tall dungeon/castle system that had some tough fights, epic loot, and an all-around good feel to it. The quests confused me for the first hour of gameplay. In the tutorial, they were apparent, but immediately following it, they vanished. I was wondering if I had done something wrong. I hope more quests are added soon, as well as a bit more variety to the zones, as seen in the tutorial and I believe the seventh zone. The first boss fight was interesting. I felt it was challenging, partly from the mechanics themselves (after you learn them, it's a cakewalk) and partly because of the combat system. Sometimes I felt it just wasn't responsive enough. I apologize for this wall of text, I'm rather bad at formatting reviews.
TL;DR
I see a lot of potential in this game. As long as the devs continue to support it, I'll continue to recommend it. Buy if you want a fresh, unguided RPG with some exploration aspects. Don't buy if you are looking for a Minecraft clone.

Holy cow, where do I begin?
I was introduced to this game by my lovely girlfriend, and it re-ignited my long-snuffed love of adventure games.  Deponia originally caught my eye after seeing a Let's Play by mangaminx, and truthfully it was the steam/dieselpunk art style that caught me first, and I finally picked it up from the Daedalic bundle.  Well worth it.
Despite some quality issues I could moan about with the audio and the less than polished cutscenes that reminded me more of early Newgrounds flash animation than a final release, the game had me from the word go.  The writing is witty, the characters vibrant, and the story is executed with a loving finesse that embraces its cliche's so fondly it's hard not to excuse their faults, and then makes up for it with a sharp left-turn into some strikingly emotional scenes that defy the conventional tropes.
As far as the puzzles go, I've certainly faced down more maliciously obscure combinations but I won't say there's no fridge-logic to be had here either.  Expect to need a guide once or twice, if for no other reason than to go "Oh, I have to click on -that- pixel?" or "Well I would never have figured that pattern out on my own."  The game leaves you plenty of clues through the comments made when you try to combine or use items at certain spots, it's the minigame puzzles it throws at you that seem to defy any intuition.  Even these, if you're observant enough, have their answers provided to you nearby.
The first Deponia game has its quirks and oddities, it's own peculiar flaws and triumps that are the marks of any labor of love by a smaller company; but where the polish and sweat really shine through here is the lovingly thought out story, characters and level artwork, which is what any adventure game fan is there for in the first place, and it delivers these with plenty of flourish.

I was skeptical at first, but this game turned out to be one of the best game purchases I've made in a while. Why? Well.....
and the characters were all quirky and memorable. Throughout my time playing, I was always thoroughly entertained by the story, and even though the puzzles were fun, I always found myself looking forward to the next scene. If you're someone who enjoys story-driven games, look no further than Deponia.
While requiring some creativivity, I found a good portion of the puzzles/minigames to be relatively intuitive and to generally be pretty ballanced, difficulty-wise. The game does a good job of giving you non-cheaty hints to point you in the right direction, so you aren't stuck somewhere trying to combine a fish with a lightbulb, hoping that something will click so you can progress.
Although this is a bit of an odd category, I'm putting it here anyways because it's dreadfully important in point-and-click games. Good item management keeps puzzles from having too many possible-but-wrong solutions (solutions that make logical sense, but aren't coded into the game), and placing items well makes it much easier for players to FIND the items that they need. The game, I believe, manages to pull both of these off very well.
It's a game I had fun just watching myself play.
Honestly, I can't think of much to go here, except that Rufus' (the character you play as) movement speed is attrocious, but that's bearable once you realize that you can skip his long treks with a double-click on his target location.
Actually, if there was one complaint I had, it would be the lack of explanation given to some of the little nuances like the one explained above. Another one of these 'tricks' is that if you hold down the middle mouse button, it displays all of the available 'action spots' on the screen (eliminating the need to drag your cursor over every inch of the landscape). Perhaps I just need to learn how to read a manual, but it seems like these are important enough to at least deserve some kind of closeable pop-up diologue in-game.
Now that that's out of the way, do I think it's worth purchasing? Yes. Most definitely, yes. And unlike most games that I purchase, I believe this one is worth it at it's full price (10$ at the time of me writing this). And if you know me, you know I'm a stingy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, so that's not something I say often.
Good story, memorable characters, well-designed puzzles, and great art. Remember your double-clicks and middle clicks. Reminded me of when I played Freddie Fish as a kid (only Deponia's a lot cooler, imho).

Doom 3 honestly really disappointed me. It’s pretty technically sound; the graphics hold up well, the lighting is great, and the sound design while nothing really  special gets the job done. Doom 3 fails in the fact that is sticks to one formula that gets stale by around half way through the game. The game pushes itself as horror; nothing wrong with that of course. However Doom 3 tries the same tactics throughout the whole game. It pushes the same scares, the same enemies (which once you figure out there patterns there total pushovers), and the same dark industrial environment that look exactly the same as the rest of the game. All these things stop being scary and start being annoying. This wouldn’t be so much of a problem if the staleness was only related to the scares. Unfortunately it affects the combat as well. Due to the cramped environments you will only ever be fighting a few enemies at time, very rarely having the environments open up that much. This leads the game to never really get that much harder while also making every combat encounter feel samey. The game is entirely to long as well, even if the other reasons weren’t a problem it feels like it skips over its natural concluding point by at least a few hours. Overall Doom 3 is a game that overstays its welcome, it’s unwillingness to mix things up leads to a repetitive and boring experience

As a laconic description by TV Tropes says "Monkey Island: Deisel Punk edition", that could not be further from the truth. Deponia is probably one of the wittiest throwbacks to the Point and Click genre in a while. As Rufus, the man who gives Harry Dresden a run for Biggest Snarker in Fiction, you enter a bleak yet gorgeously drawn landscape of junk, amazing characters, and complete d-bags who plot the very destruction of mankind. As generic as it sounds, Deponia manages to remain a fresh experience in light of what most people would dismiss as an over the top MI rip-off. The puzzles are cleverly planned as hints come in the most subtle of dialogue options. The animations are well suited to the setting, giving a comic feel to the bleak planet of Deponia. All in all, if you like adventure, add this to your library.

After replaying through this game again a few nights ago, I realize that I still haven't written a review for it. Well, better late than never (holy crap, it's already been almost a year?!).
If I were to run into you on the street, and (for God only knows what reason) you wanted my overall thoughts on the game in a single sentence, I'd tell you, "I don't know why you're talking to me and not playing this game."
Honestly, if you're just reading this to see if the game's worth $15, take my word for it.
For those who don't know,
is a short adventure puzzle platformer in which each half of your controller (or keyboard, as I hear does work, but I'd imagine it's a bit wonky) controls a separate character - brothers Naia (older - left half) and Naiee (younger - right half). As far as I'm aware, the game is virtually glitchless, although I did have an instance where Naiee fell through the floor and died while picking up a turtle for a sidequest. Speaking of the quest, it's actually incredibly linear, but not in a bad way. The game's layout could not be better suited for the story. Not EVERY game has to be "like Skyrim with guns" as the saying goes. The gameplay is innovative and even plays a crucial role in the story. SPOILER TAG:
When the creator tried getting companies to publish the game, he said it's a singleplayer experience in the guise of a co-op game. Thank God Starbreeze came along and took interest in the game, else we wouldn't have this masterpiece to talk about. However, personally I played this with a friend sharing a controller the first time through, and I would have to disagree. It's equally as great either way. With a friend, it's easier to manage, having to only focus on one character, and the storyline immerses you into creating almost brotherly bonds. However, it's just as good to play alone, because you can experience the story the way it was intended - by not fearing to shed your manly tears in front of your comrades.
Speaking of which, the story is written by Josef Fares, a Swedish film writer who had a really rough childhood. SPOILER TAG:
For those who haven't played the game and are avoiding the spoiler tag, I apologize for tempting you with the enormous spoiler box. Needless to say, Fares' past experiences had a huge impact on his works, so despite what you may think, it may look cute, but there is a monster hidden within. With several instances of morbid scenes and scenery hardly scattered throughout, this game rightfully deserves its rating of T for Teen.
The graphics are some of the best I have ever seen in any game ever. Screw Battlefield 4, Skyrim, or any other stereotypical games with "realistic" graphics. Despite having a cartoonish feel to it,
has the most atmospheric landscape of any game I have ever played. Water, foliage, shadows and sunlight, everything looks absolutely incredible. But every aspect of this game has something morbid or sad, and the graphics are no exception. Have you ever played an FPS and thought about how unrealistic blood looks? In this game, blood looks disgustingly realistic. I gagged a little bit in the land of the giants. At one point, you have to push a corpse holding an axe to chop an arm off that is blocking your path. It's incredibly morbid, and you should expect nothing less from this game.
And finally the soundtrack. Whether the mood of a scene is sad, happy, epic, or scary, the music is always there to accompany it in perfect harmony (see what I did there?). With its orchestral, cinema quality soundtrack,
uses music to make you feel the emotions that characters would feel as if these scenes had happened to you. In a story driven game like this, a fitting soundtrack is
, because unless you are like Fares, you can't relate to all these dark and depressing events, and an emotional soundtrack can give you a push. Obviously, this feeling is nothing close to how it would be if these things
happened to you, but it's probably as close as we would ever want to be.
TL;DR: The game's graphics, soundtrack, gameplay, and most of all storyline are all phenomenal. Don't be fooled, this game is dark. It's a bit short at around 3 hours, but it's fun to replay and reexperience the overwhelming emotions it will give you.
Overall rating: 10/10
