One big screen playing the Dungeon Master, four phones playing character sheet and interface for a  fantasy RPG/Tabletop hybrid. Bam! Sold! Well, almost...
At it's heart, Eon Altar is an innovative concept and I really hope the devs can push it farther than just being an interesting control design. It's first shot in the arm is that the game is very linear due to 4 players on a single screen. This hurts the overall concept they were striving for. There will have to be some clever writing and mapping to really justify the design choices they have implemented and this first chapter currently fails to do so.
NPCs in-game will sometimes tell your character something through the app, usually surrounding loot. You occasionally get a key to open something that others won't have access to but just being told about an item has no value. Loot is first come, first served so knowing an items location is worthless because you can't sneak away from the party - everyone is restricted to a single screen. Hidden doors or rooms could alleviate that, so long as only the character told could open it. Otherwise the whole idea is just superfluous, there simply to push the role-playing concept.
The onscreen players are also silent with the app showing your dialog. This requires you to speak your lines so everyone in the party knows what your character is saying. The app also contains your characters thoughts in various matters. This is all fantastic for role-playing but can end up just making you feel like a larping dork. You'll want to be sure you're playing with good friends or have plenty of alcohol.
The control through the app is surprisingly good, but not great. Running around using touchscreen feels equally as bad as when you play games on them. The layout is good though, with you being able to directly move your character via virtual thumb stick or select where to move him via an in-game cursor, Baldur's Gate style. The app itself is a little busy and sparse with direct help. Other than a single informational screen for each category during specific sequences in the opening, it will be trial an error. You will definitely want to play around with the interface for a bit before you jump into a game with friends.
The graphics could use some detail, it looks very mobile-quality currently. This may be left over from previous design ideas involving the phone itself or perhaps due to future mobile plans. Either way, the PC version needs some graphical TLC.
Their failed kickstarter video showed a lot more pen and paper elements such as dice rolling which looked great. It also showed gameplay footage that was far more cinematic, almost a multiplayer Telltale/Dragon's Lair hybrid. None of these elements are in the game right now though. Hopefully they plan on more than just a little spit and polish before they start selling new episodes. For one, I want to see some more RPG ideas for the phone app than just loot drops. For another, the game just feels lifeless right now, the cinematic gameplay on display in the kickstarter video was fantastic – lets go that direction.
While the game is in early access, it plays better than some “finished” products I have payed for. This is great for perspective buyers but the design ideas alone make this game worth supporting. I purchased it without even owning a phone to show my support, begging and borrowing one from friends to play with. It currently has a lot of promise but needs to make some serious changes and bring the gameplay up to par with the technological ideas it's based on. If what we get at the end of EA is just a shinier version of what's already here then Eon Altar will go down as being a mediocre RPG with some interesting tech attached.

This is a little like a lightweight Neverwinter/Baldurs Gate with a designed exclusively tailored for local co op play.
Basically, you are all using your smart phones as combination mice and inventory management screens. We saw a fair number of UI glitches in the IOS app,  but nothing more than minor annoyances. Sound and graphics are ok, but the iOS mouse interface is amazingly responsive.
The game itself is about two hours for the first quest. Combat is very Baldurs gate, except that all characters can move an attack simultaneously. Combat goes FAST and doesn't slog.
The shining point here is how much the game feels like a computer aided D&d session. The second screens also pop up with secret quests, individual responses and reactions just for that character. Just like a GM passed you a private note. Player dialogue is not voiced, but pops up ONLY on your screen and you are expected to say it in your best full-on Renn Fair voice. This is totally stupid and totally awesome, especially when the dialogue goes all high fantasy cliche.
loot is also handled by whoever opens the chest getting stuff.  There is a trade option, or you can just keep it. No fair sharing.  Except that the other players can easily reach over and dump a beer on your head if you are too annoying.
Character options are also pretty deep and a little baffling. There are 6 trees for each character, split between skills and equipment upgrades. I cannot see where any of this is documented anywhere.  This also contains a bit of a UI sin in that you really have to scroll around to see all of your upgrade options.  These aren't well described in the game at all, mostly a short blurb and some symbols and numbers. Could really use a manual.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Clear Sky is a direct prequel to Shadow of Chernobyl and it's events shed some more light on what went on before SoC and why stuff happened the way it happened. The Zone is also way less of a hostile place in terms of enviorments. The early areas even seem like a cool place to hang out for any man, and the weather is simply splendid from time to time.
The fact that this game takes place before SoC also means some gameplay-wise changes. For example; the artifacts the Stalkers are after are way less common. This means that you'll actually have to hunt for them now, making you actually feel like you're doing what SoC told you Stalkers do: they *hunt* for artifacts. The artifacts themselves also have been redone in terms of bonuses they provide. I actually found myself selling them for quick cash in SoC all the time, while in Clear Sky they are actually useful to keep on your person for their bonuses. Some absorb radiation, others provide bonuses to healing regeneration over time.
But this is not the only gameplay change, far from it. Due to the massive Zone-Emission at the start of the game, the clans of people in the Zone have gone at war with each other, using the confusion of the Emission as a good reason to take over new territory. Each of these factions are joinable by the player, and come with terrain the faction wishes to defend or capture. For the player this means they can engage (when they want) in capture or defense missions of certain locations, often bringing them rewards, and greater rewards for capturing bases. As they do this, the influence of their faction increases, while that of the enemy faction decreases.
Another change is found in AI behaviour, which is (especially on Master) a lot trickier than in SoC. No more wall hugging enemies that are easy to pick off with a sniper rifle. No more♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that will run into your gun; people are actually clever now. If they try to sneak up on you and you spot them, they'll take off and find cover, to shoot you in formation.
Other than these changes, there's numerous other small tweaks and changes, ranging from stalkers that will take you to specific places in the Zone (for a price of course) to the ability to upgrade and maintain weapons and armor, and then I haven't even mentioned the whole -BLOWOUT SOON FELLOW STALKER- part.
Then there's locations to visit. Clear Sky mostly borrows it's locations from SoC, even letting the player visit them in the same order SoC made them visit them in. However, some new areas have been added, some old areas removed and some areas have been changed slightly, or have been added more locations to than in SoC. Still, it's mostly the same♥♥♥♥♥♥you've been through before. This isn't a bad thing per say! After all, the Zone is the Zone and they try to base it on the real Exclusion-Zone in Ukrain, so they did a good job at how they did it.
The thing mostly changed about locations that were re-used, is by filling them up with bases of the factions. For example, the Duty faction has it's base at the Agroprom Research Institute, while that was an abandoned bunch of offices in SoC. They actually made proper use of such empty locations this time around, and that was fun.
However, the endgame is absolutely horrible. The last hour is filled with bugged AI, terrible game design and is just horrificly stupid. The game decides it's a good idea for you to shoot a running target over a long walkway. This walkway is interrupted by several teleports which teleport you to locations where you have to finish off certain enemies only to progress to the next teleport. Not only is this insanely out of place, it's also badly programmed and build in at the most unlogical time possibe. A massive downside.
Overall I'm giving this one an 8/10

List of positive elements:

-no ping restrictions mean you're more often than not up against players with very high latency
-settings cannot be altered inside the launcher
-graphical settings have very limited input

List of negative elements (subjective):

Torchlight was one of the best hack and slash RPG's to come out between the release of Diablo II and Diablo III. It had us turning our head, if even for a short time, and (if your a fan) rejuvenated our love of the genre with its colorful graphic's, epic loot, and random dungeon generator. While it was fairly generic it hit all the right notes, and except for multiplayer, was the perfect game to play till the release of Diablo III. Then Diablo III released....... Well while some did enjoy it, LOT's of players hated it (not a fan myself) and quickly Torchlight's predecessor was to the rescue.
Now with a full multiplayer mode, modding capability, and overall improvements to the gameplay, Torchlight II is a fantastic sequel to the colorful h&s RPG from a few years ago. However there are some problems. Multiplayer is great to have if you want to play with friends, or have a small group on the net that regularly play. However if you expect the multiplayer to be as fully featured as games like Diablo III, Path of Exile, or hell even Diablo II you may be hard pressed. Its pretty much just a list of people playing and if you want to play with them you can, however most games are locked with a password and the games that do have people playing don't allow you to chat with them or anything before joining to find out what there doing. In fact you can only chat in game which kinda sucks if you want to set up quick runs or do any kind trading. As of late the multiplayer is pretty much dead. Overall I have to say that Torchlight II's multiplayer is not going to be the biggest draw for most fans of the genre. If you play games like Path of Exile or Diablo III for multiplayer Torchlight II may not be for you.
However the overall improvements to the gameplay overshadow some of the multiplayer woes. Simple little improvements and details are what make Torchlight II's gameplay different from other's in the genre. While it will feel familiar to anyone who has played a h&s RPG, things like being able to equip not only a sword but dual wield it with a gun or any other single handed weapon give you the need to experiment with you character. Other things like your pet, make life a little easier for your dungeon crawling hero. Your pet can buy items in town, sell loot you find in dungeons, provide extra storage, and even help you in combat. You can also choose what pet you would like (including a freaking headcrab!).
But the crowing achievement of Torchlight II is its just downright fun gameplay. You will never run out of things to do in Torchlight, Literally. While the games story is fairly generic (pretty much taken straight from Diablo II) the colorful environments epic enemies, fun boss fight, and funny cameos and homages make Torchlight II's story campaign all the more worth it. What most will love however is what you unlock after beating the game. You can just go ahead and do a (New Game +) which allows you to start the game over at your current level and fight tougher enemies throughout. Or you can decide to stay in the Mapworks which is the final hub world. It has all you need with every type of shop and merchant and one particular merchant that gives you random dungeons to buy. You can play these dungeons pretty much forever collecting loot and fighting bosses. This give Torchlight infinite playablity.
Modding is also a big part of Torchlight II. Some people have already created epic mods that act as entire expansions to the game giving you plenty of more hours of gameplay. Modders have also fixed some of the issues with the game like, not being able to re-spec your character at will. While I have not done really any modding I am looking forward to playing some mods later on.
Overall Torchlight II is well worth the 20$ price tag (oh did I forget to mention it's only 20$). Its somewhat lacking multiplayer cant overshadow the excellent hack and slash gameplay. If your like me and mostly play these kind of games for the singleplayer, you owe it to yourself to buy this game. At least give it a chance and get it when its like 5 bucks, trust me its worth it.
Thanks for reading!

More technical difficulties than a state school server room. For the want of a new release after V2 for the same reasons, I can't see how there's been any improvement on the first. While the gameplay sets in after a couple of missions, there's a feel for how the Welrod and rifle pair up, but the last save point becomes the most used feature. The list of issues can be accredited to jittery animations, almost like they know you're watching, and the age old know-it-all AI. Take down an alerted enemy, the only of several who know where you are, and the rest come running to your exact position, never having seen you. There also seems to be a bug in the way concealed gunfire works in conjunction with a canon or dodgy stationary motor. Countless times the AI went on alert after shooting during the covering noise, making it confusing to know the outcome of options. AI enjoyed screwing up multiple attempts by detecting my movement through walls, and I don't mean on account of running, but by their mesh sifting through the wall and somehow seeing me. A WTF moment including being shot by a soldier who was shooting me, as he hung suspended in a wall (see screenshots). Other soldiers fired through the corners of buildings, without head-view of my position. Writing this after beating the game in offline mode.
I found the aesthetics and mechanics of the game to be pretty good. The art and animations are nice, the setting is pretty interesting and the voice acting is decent.
The puzzles can get on the cryptic side, but I was able to get through all but one of them without looking at a hint. Somebody that is new to, or doesn't really like point-and-click games might have some trouble with them though.
Now for the reasons I don't recommend the game.
First of all, the protagonist is pretty unlikeable. At first his behavior seems like it's being played up for laughs, or that it's a set up for future character development. Eventually you'll realize that nope, He's just a terrible person, and it's not funny.
This is a big problem when often the protagonist is the driving force behind the player getting past puzzles and finishing the game. Maybe this will change in the sequels.
Secondly, this game is pretty unpleasant throughout. There is a lot of sexism, mean-spirited jokes and uncomfortable implications throughout the game, all seemingly in an effort to make the player laugh.
Some people might think I'm being oversensitive about this, but I'm absolutely not. It is there and it is blatant. The fact that none of these jokes are even clever or funny makes it that much worse.
Despite the game being decent art/mechanics wise, I really can't recommend this.

EDIT: from comments I've removed some of the more "triggered" similes which were supposed to be tongue in cheek but seems it was too dry and it was being taken literally. My bad on that one. So when reading this keep that in mind. And yes it's early access and issues are expected but the very basics two years in aren't done which made me a new-comer to the game want to turn it off and not invest anything further into it regardless of whether it was free or not. So....
Want an actual sound effect induced headache after 5 minutes?
Want to land on your head with no idea how not to or what the controls are?
Want to know what it feels like riding through treacle?
Want tutorials that are incomplete and contradict the menus?
You do? Then this is it.
For anyone wanting snowboarding fun, intuitive mechanics, buttons that make sense, speed (the trailer is clearly on 3x) or an explanantion as to why the man consistently wants to land on his head, avoid.

Menus looks nice but functionally they don't work. Even moving up and down left and right the order is wrong. Resolution requires you to change a file in the game manually via notepad else 572x368 and everything on low/off is what you get. I don't mind configuring things but you have no idea at this point how taxing it is. Which it isn't - I was "playing" at 4k on a 970 with most set to high/very high so tha'ts a plus and it looks ok.
Each mountain consists of a slight incline with about three ramps (you can't do anything off for reasons that will become apparent), there is usually one run on each and about four events to choose from in total. There's nothing to do (EDIT: there is more to do on a revisit but finding it is not easy) once you've tried each once, you are unlikely to want to retry it. (EDIT: I did though on a revisit to no further avail) I didn't even try the half pipe as by the time i got to that I felt like a masochist to the poor snowbarding man. I'd hurt him too much already.
The tutorials
--------------------
Self explanatory - you'd think. Prepare for handy tips like: "spin with RB and LB and flip with [blank]" It's the same throughout. A tutorial that fails to put the controller icons in for the controls. It's like counting cards. You have to remember what's gone before and try to think what's left on the controller they haven't mentioned yet. Early access or not surely the menu two years in should work and the tutorial be in a state that allows you to have a basic grasp of how to play it? It felt like a grind.
So check the controller settings for "in-air" menu, as it's in early access after all but that contradicts the few icons the turoial does tell you. The menu tells you that Left trigger is roll and right bumper is roll. Some of them tie up with the controller settings (those which you are privileged to have an icon) in the tutorial but some don't.
So I went down a ramp and pressed each in turn to see. It all behaved so irratically it wasn't obvious to me. And trying to just do one ramp per button presstook ages and many restarts just to get one lined up to see.
Once you get going its ok
-----------------------------
Assuming by "get going" you define that as wanting to shove him so he actually gets some speed. I managed to actually get half way down the training run (lining up for rail slides is nigh on impossible, not forgetting you can spin with the handy [blank]), got half way down one mountain just about to hit a ramp I'd already done (and using the snow line from before as it was one I'd actually managed to go off once) at about 7mph, came to a standstill for no reason and got stuck, wouldn't move, horrible screeching noises of varying pitches depending what buttons I pressed, came through my earbuds. But again, the early access thing will be your thought here and yes bugs are expected. But they are still very, very frequent even in the short time I played it.
There is trial an error to landing a trick and learning any game, I get that, but I managed two in half an hour and that was pure luck. Once it seems you are in the air (if you charge the spin for the jump by holding A that seems to scrub off three of the five mph you have managed to build up) he disappointingly plops off the lip, usually sideways, onto his head then ragdolls forward faster than you've even managed to get him to go when he's upright.
In short spinning/rotating  is not intuitive at all. You can JUST spin but even then it doesn't stop when you let go of the controls. He keeps going. I'm not sure why that is but I didn't find it fun.
Once you press the roll (I was just pressing anything by this stage to try and make sense of the madness) instant fall off, penalties at the end then it's no points for you. And getting "bad landing -9" is not exactly encouraging.
So if and when you do get to the bottom after several "rewinds" thinking, well it must be me thats just bad, you apply the "break" and you plough headlong into the barrier and once again fall off for more penalties. Why doens't it (like every other game in the world) know you've finished and just take you to the menu? Because it gives you the option of carrying on. But to where? You're at the bottom. So you have to limp your way to a phone box by tapping X to go back up the hill to come down it a bit, then press and hold Y when you're near it, to watch him slide past and you miss your opportunity to quit.
And the gamplay, here's a small list:
- In game, half the time the board disappears into the ground. Clipping is awful.
- I had no idea how far off the ground you are or when you'll land so timing (assuming you do know the buttons or what the bloke is doing compared to what you're pressing) is hopeless.
- It all feels so slow, like you never get going and you're riding through treacle.
- It doesn't tell you how to even get going so at the beginning of the tutorial you are just stood there like a lemon. You have to tap X I found out. Not hold it like it tells you. Maybe that works for skiing but I didn't get round to trying that.
- You can't rebind the controller buttons and to spin and turn (i assume) and pull a trick resolves in a trigger + bumper and the right stick in a direction. How you are supposed to keep a track of all is beyond me hence landings are always "bad" or not at all.
Conclusion
---------------------
1. Why can't someone remake a game that is just N64 "1080" with slightly better graphics.
2. IMO Not worth the 4gb bandwidth. I didn't expect much at all especially as it was early access, but come on now.....
3. The only effect is wind noise even when turned down to 25 (100 is unbearable) is completely headache inducing with headphones on.
4. I'm using the "new 0.9 version" at Dec 2016.
- I spent more time writing this than playing  (written after initial imperssion after half an hour, edited after giving is a further hour)
- Give it a miss, for now at least. I won't be revisitng espeically now I've found the demo for Infinite Air in which I had more fun in ten minutes on an empty mountain. Perhaps look into that.

About a year ago, I decided to spend my money on Street Fighter V. I was confident that it would deliver in terms of a fighting game and it was one of the few times I thought that I'd actually dedicate time to competative play. But like many, I found the game to be disappointing due to the servers constantly going down for maintenance, lack of basic features such as a story mode at launch, and a weak roster of characters. It made me begin to doubt if we'd ever get an excellent fighting game for PC.
Fortunately, Tekken 7 is a prime example of how to release a fighting game. I have had no issues whatsoever when it comes to performance as the game is able to stay at a consistant 60 fps between matches. It's also rich with content with modes such as Story, arcade, treasure battle, online play, and tournaments making up the package.  Character Cutomization is also back from past tekken games, giving players more incenitives to crank out multiple matches in order to gain desired gear for your favorite fighters. On top of that, the game also features a gallery mode that contains cutscenes and artwork from many of the past tekken titles. It's things like this that show that care was put into this release rather than releasing an unfinished game in order to meet a deadline. Simply put, this is one of the best games to be released in 2017 and arguably one of the best fighting games to be released on PC in recent memory. Highly reccomended.

Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 is an absolutely excellent game.
This game (On normal mode) Is very challenging on all three species to play with. I personally enjoy the Marine missions the most, due to the terrifying atmosphere and fast, tight, and frantic First-Person-Shooter gameplay. This game doesn't rely on simple  jumpscares to be a scary game... it has real atmosphere. The Aliens are so smart and every time I hear one of their famous screeches... (nearby or far from me) I frantically spin around and search all over. (And believe me... when you turn around and unsuspectingly find an Alien behind you... it's a real treat. You'll fire your pulse rifle with such intensity... This game just really draws you in. If you (Like I was at first) are nervous about the game being too scary, just know that it still is a brilliant blend between an Action Packed First-Person-Shooter that even a real scaredy-cat like me can  enjoy this game thoroughly.
The other campaigns are... you guessed it, GREAT.
The Alien missions are all centered on some stealth and puzzle solving, and you will move at near BLINDING speeds, taking out anything that stands between you and the end of the level. I love being able to attack in a variety of ways, including lashing out your tail or slashing at your enemies with a swift scratch from your claws. The multiplayer with Aliens only is incredible. It gets really competitive as you dash toward your enemies... instincts set to kill. It feels awesome to overpower every marine (Or Predator for that matter) with the Xenomorph class.
The third campaign, focused on the Predator is very focused on stealth (Turning invisible, sneaking up behind enemies, etc.) You have many ways to attack your enemies. This campaign is pretty great, you will feel very overpowered as you hack through your enemies. There are many fun to use gadgets to take out your enemies, and you can zoom in and snipe or just go all out close combat with your opponents. This class is really awesome to play with during multiplayer, always silent but deadly as the Predator class.
This game really nails it's atmosphere, despite the somewhat dated graphics (Hey, it's from 1999-2000!) The sound is excellent and the dramatic music comes at just the right time to keep the game tense. This game was great for it's time... and still remains a classic that any fan of Aliens (Or any newcomers to the franchise) MUST pick up. At a very affordable price point of $4.99 this game offers so much, including Campaigns, Multiplayer, Survival Mode, and hours and hours of pure ALIEN FUN! I enthusiastically recommend this game.
Now... I need to get back to work on fighting off hordes of Aliens...

Figured that I might as well write a review since I’m already on my second playthrough of the game. Please take my review with a pinch of salt and minor spoilers ahead!
- Super fun combat system
- Hilarious dialogues and cutscenes
- A story that stays true to South Park
- Fun interactions between allies
- A more polished-looking game
- Nice BGM
- New minigames/ crafting system/ levelling mechanics
- Morgan Freeman is your mentor
---
This game is way less offensive than The Stick of Truth. Other than the plethora of swear words and that one mission in the strip club, the game is remarkably tame and actually can be played in public.
The main storyline hilariously stupid in the best of ways and it really makes you feel like you’re watching a 20-hour long South Park episode. However, do keep in mind that the storyline this time isn’t as outlandish as The Stick of Truth and some people may get disappointed by this.
The ending and final boss battle is not particularly bad, but if I were to compare the final boss battle in TFBW to SoT, Nazi Zombie Princess Kenny’s battle would have won by a landslide.
---
I have encountered a few bugs where NPC characters would remain stuck in position until you exit and re-enter the area. There are also times where you get stuck in battle even though you’ve defeated every enemy (this happened to me after defeating Morgan Freeman and I was infuriated).  There are also players who can’t get past the title screen because all they get is a black screen (this can be fixed by playing the game in borderless fullscreen mode). There are also times where the HUD would disappear during battle.
If you don’t have a stronger graphics card, you won’t be able to run the game smoothly - at least not on a medium/ high graphics quality.

The keyboard support for this game isn’t terrible, but if you’re aiming to get that toilet minigame achievement on the PC version of the game, you’ll very much struggle if you’re using a keyboard.
Let’s finally address the elephant in the room.  Without a doubt, this has to be the most expensive game in my inventory at the moment. The main storyline and side quests can all be completed in about 20-22 hours. Some people might find that too short for a $60 game and extra content will cost you a total of $100.
There’ll be a part in the game where you’re required to choose a weakness and if you choose the ‘Vampires’ option without purchasing the season pass, there won’t be any vampires in the base game to be weak against.
Personally, Uplay hasn’t been a problem for me. I barely even noticed its presence while in-game, but I understand why people are mad at it.
—
So with all things considered, do I recommend the game? Absolutely. Maybe it’s just my personal bias from being a South Park fan for the past decade but I honestly did find this game enjoyable - and if you can manage to look past Ubisoft’s incompetence, perhaps you can enjoy it too. If you’re still unsure about purchasing the game at its current price and state, waiting for the next Steam sale never hurts.

Decent F2P title thats not Pay to Win.  Anyone who tells you otherwise is lying or doesn't understand what Pay to Win actually is.  No pay walls of any kind in this title.  Just really long arduous grinds.  Even spending money on this game doesnt make the grinds that much better.  Yes you can just outright buy weapons or vehicles but they are super expensive.  There is no balancing once you get to top tier so don't expect a fiar fight whether you pay your way to the top or grind there.
Hit detection is shoddy at best.  You can't hit stationary targets at 100 meters but you can pull off 400 meter headshots through 3 trees totally blind.  Lots of lag too on the mostly EU servers means a lot of "cheap deaths" and cries of HACKER!  I've had so many terrible deaths where I was 6 steps into a building and 4 bar ping only to be pulled back out and killed in the courtyard.  The aiming is also so unsatisfying. You can have a guy zeroed in on his head at short range and miss over and over yet I have pulled off so many impossible shots from extreme distances just by blind firing.  It also at times feels like some players can do things you physically cant.  Like shoot through floors and one hit kills etc.  Just a cheap feeling overall.
If you can get past that and the awful grinds the game has its moments of fun.  A lot of polish is needed though and the latest map updates really arent helping.  Far too much waiting and running and too much spawn camping now.

I don't usually write serious reviews however Rockstar and Take Twos attitude toward microtransactions and the general economy of it's online mode is absolutely one of the most greediest and downright scummy ways I've ever seen companies conduct themselves.

For those who don't know, GTA:O a while ago introduced "Shark Cards" which in laymans terms are microtransactions that give the player more in-game cash. To put this in perspective, as of writing this review the most expensive jet in the game, the Lazer (which since release was free and easy to take from the games military base) costs $6.5 mil in game. Most if not all high-end vehicles and properties cost upward of $1 mil, and then you have customizability options which in some cases, especially with the aforementioned properties, can QUADRUPLE the price.
"But RetroMystic, there is nothing stopping you from earning the money yourself, why complain?"
You see price wouldn't be an issue if payouts were reasonable. They're not. Most "contact" missions which are your run-of-the-mill standard GTA missions payout anywhere from $10,000-$25,000 depending on factors such as difficulty, the lobby size and so fourth. The AI is purposefully designed to be extremely unfair, with pinpoint accuracy even when you're in, say a helicopter, and the enemy AI is using a PISTOL. I've died more times to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t AI than I have to actual players. Oh yes, the players. Many lobbies that the game loaded me into have been FULL of modders that grief the hell out of everyone causing explosions, aggresive traffic and a plethora of other issues. Modding has become such a prevelant issue with people going as far to say when they spawn in a lobby, "Are there any modders that can give me some money?".
R* and Take-Two continue to create an unfair economy in which actual purchases with real money award players instead of hard work.
"The DLC is free, so stop complaining".
At what cost?
I doubt you can argue that this is justified when you may as well buy a shark card just to get the items released in the DLC itself. It's sad to see such a reputable company such as R* spread their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s nice and wide for corporate America and ruin what could have been the best multiplayer experience in the world.
With ♥♥♥♥♥♥ anticheat, the incessant shark card shilling and broken economy that requires hours if not days of grinding to aquire a luxury item or property that will help you grind even more money, it's clear R* and Take-Two care more about making a quick dime than making a good game.

Portal Knights is a digging adventure game in the same vein as Terraria or Minecraft.
Mostly you will be hopping from portal to portal, leveling up, crafting new weapons and armor, and...well getting to the next portal. (also building things if you so desire). The game isn't an infinite world like Minecraft. Rather it's a bunch of randomly generated bite sized worlds strung together with portals. When you enter a new world...island.....shattered land...place, you'll have to explore and find the portal gate. The gate starts off empty though, so you'll have to fill it with "portal stones." You get these stones by doing basically anything. Killing enemies, mining things, and finishing dungeons will sometimes land you some portal stone fragments. When you fill the portal with said stones, it opens up to another island. The islands are really small. I've only had one that had any kind of underground network. I think they could do with being a bit bigger.
The game has a very light hearted adventure atmosphere with a "cute" aesthetic. This is no voxel game though. The only thing that's square is the ground (and structures). I feel the ground has enough little details like grass and rocks to make it not stick out like a sore thumb. Worlds range from the usually foresty plains and deserts to toxic mushroom lands and tundras. The biomes are all filled with appropriate enemies and vegetation. The lighting is very nicely done, giving things a warm look in light. Overall it looks pretty nice. Dungeons can be a bit samie though.
This is a huge part of the game, so I'm going to split it down further.
While looking for portal gates, you will be fighting whatever monsters are on the world. Combat is very zelda-esque. When you hit an enemy, the camera locks on automatically. While locked on, the jump button turns into a roll button, which is kind of a pain. What if I want to jump in a fight? Well too bad. You can't fight with the camera unlocked either. You CAN unlock the camera, but as soon as you hit something again it will re-lock. Sometimes the camera will lock onto the wrong enemy if you start by using a ranged attack.
THIS GAME IS TOO EASY. That's the biggest problem with the game.
Most of the fighting so far is just holding the mouse button until things die, with the ocassional roll. If you have a ranged weapon then its all over, you've won. Melee enemies can't jump or find a way up a 2 block height, so you're free to wail on them until they die. Even if you're on even ground, they slowly walk at you while taking hits. Your melee hits push foes backwards, so sometimes you accidentally hit them out of range. This can be annoying if the knockback lets them get another hit in on you.
At the start of the game you can pick between 3 classes. Warrior, Ranger, Mage.
These classes only change the passive spells you get when reaching certain levels. The only semi interesting one is at level 30. Every class can use every weapon, there are no stat requirements for weapons. There are basically 3 ways to make things' hp bar go to zero. Melee Weapons, Ranged Weapons, and Spells.
are everything from Swords, Clubs, Axes, etc. Good luck hitting flying things with melee.
are Bows, Crossbows, Slingshots, Magic Wands, ect.
.....well in the first tier of the game's crafting the only offensive spell you can get is a Lightning Bolt. The other 2 spells you can get are a healing spell, and a battlecry damage buff spell. Spells have mana costs and cooldowns.
Your Armor also plays a part in your damage dealing, giving you passive bonuses such as critical hit chance or bonus melee damage.
Killing all this stuff must give some good loot right? Special Armor, Rings, or Weapons.
NOPE. Killing things gives you crafting materials and XP. Speaking of Crafting Materials...
Crafting is the other big part of the game. You mine ore, kill things, and then make items from it. Craft armor, weapons, spells (yes you have to craft those), and decorations. The only problem I have with crafting is that sometimes you never find some of the things you need. I needed something for a spell that I just never got any of. This could be due to the random nature of the game, but when the one offensive spell that I can use sucks and I can't find the materials to upgrade it, I'm gonna throw off the wizard hat and go run up and hit things. When an item finishes crafting (sometimes it takes a few seconds to craft, sucks if you need to make a lot of that thing) It just sits in the crafting statioin. You have to manually click the finished item for it to go into your inventory.
You can change the land block by block to get it how you want, there's a few decorations and a lot of different plant life to decorate gardens with. Didn't mess with this much, but it's there....
The game is pretty good right now. Here's a quick Pro and Con list because those are fun.

+ Sillyness
+ Lots of easter eggs and fun details.
- Tools being unreachable only due to limitations on how far your hand can move 'up'
- Minor thing: wish you had slight more control over your head/camera posistion sometimes.  Even something simple like a 'tilt' so you can see what you are doing a little better.
I wasn't expecting this.  You know what a baby looks like playing with toys.  They'll take a toy and very stiff-armedly bang away on something trying to replicate what they've seen an adult do while giggling or something.  That is essentially what this feels like.  You are in the shoes of a half mad-doctor, half man-child with little to no fine motor skills.
Trying to perform surgery with controls this limited can certainly be frustrating at times, but at the same time, it's what provides a lot of the humor and ridiculousness to what you are doing.  If you had perfect controls the game would not work the same way.  Flailing around an arm and accidentally dropping a power drill into someones chest cavity while trying to do a heart transplant in the back of a moving ambulance is all part of the charm of the game.
There is plenty of interactive small details to find and play with.  Even in your office.  Like a little playground, all this little stuff adds up to make a fun experience.  Plenty of subtle things like you'd find sprinkled into a Valve or Blizzard game.  It's been a long time since a game made me crack a smile.
Don't be put off by the odd controls, once you get a little practice with them you'll be able to do what you intend to do (relatively speaking).  The awkwardness and sillyness they provide is part of the game.
Recommended if you have a little patience and want to have a good time for a few hours.  And there is plenty more to do if you want to explore and try to get every little thing done.

The whole game was fantastic, with brilliant maps from the Subway mimicing the Predator 2 movie, to the LV-426 complex and the Nostromo from the Alien franchise. This is how horror should be
First of all,  I'm aware that this game is not a horror game in it's entirety, it's a gut wrenching, adrenaline pumping fast action game where standing still gets you killed. Always need to be moving.
I've played this game on the colonial marines campaign, and by god it takes me back to the days of Alien Trilogy for the PSX, very dark environments, eerie soundtrack, dead atmosphere and I have no shame in saying I slowly edge my way around corners like a scared mouse about to run out of his hole. The xenomorphs are by god the scariest and brain frying enemies I've ever faced in a game, the sheer speed and appearance (I'm aware the graphics are dated by hey ho), and the sounds they make as they lunge at you can only take me back to the Alien and Aliens film, specifically the second one when the marines get ambushed.
The game cooks up the perfect flavour, the smart gun, the pulse rifle are instantly given a place in my heart, and the little things like acid spray from aliens and elevators moving up and down that make the motion tracker plip are just downright evil and fantastic. The motion tracker is one of those things you don't want to have but you need it, the eerie plip makes your trigger finger stiff and ready to shoot, then you find that it was just an elevator going up and down, but what was making it do that?
To anyone who loved the Alien franchise, definitely give the colonial marines campaign a go, it's by far one of the scariest you'll ever play, the deathmatches are so fun, who knew the predator was so hard to kill...

What can I say about the venerable Spelunky that hasn't been said already? A game of truly staggering (literal and metaphorical) depth, Spelunky dug its way into the gaming world in the late 2000s, and enthralled all who played it with a perfectly calculated blend of skill-demanding platforming challenge, varied level features and enemies that force adaptation to circumstances, a wide array of meaningful player choices, a boatload of secrets and goals that assure players of all skill levels have something to strive for, and last but not least, excellent procedural level generation that assure a new experience and a blank slate on each playthrough. This HD remake, which came to PC in 2013, is the definitive version, adding local co-op and deathmatch multiplayer, an expanaded suite of in-game hazards and enemies, tighter physics, and new inproved graphics and sound. The steam edition also includes the Daily Challenge feature, allowing all players who check in on a given day to try their hand at the same randomly generated set of levels, and compare their scores. All in all, this game is a must-have, and in my personal opinion, the game of the decade so far. In an age of watered-down challenge, unnecessary sequels, DLC-itis and general industry malaise, Spelunky is the perfect remedy: simply an earnest, boundless joy to play.

I was kinda hyped about this game after reading the positive reviews, however, I didn't like it at all.
I haven't tried the multiplayer aspect of the game so I can't really judge that, I've played only single player.
I do like hard games, but I like it when they're fair to you. Here though, sometimes the way the map is generated or some unexpected events, make advancing any further practically impossible.
For example, monster gets killed by a trap and explodes just by the shopkeepers store. Well, from now on, you have to deal with an angry shopkeeper on every single level that is to come and good luck with that.
Or let's say you're going for the full run to get to the bonus levels and then suddenly, darkness modifier on the next level you enter. Of course, it's not impossible to beat the level, but the chances you will succeed drop drastically.
Or just the sole platform/mob placement makes it that you will fail 9 out of 10 times while trying to complete a stunt.
Or you make a tiny mistake, which concludes in you being dead instead of just losing some hp, because that yeti just kept catching you and trowing back at a wall, while you could do nothing.
I also didn't really like the mechanics of holding one item at a time, which is pretty annoying when digging a tunnel to the temple and on some other occasions. After you finally get a weapon, getting the golden idol or Damsel to the exit becomes just a hassle, because you have to juggle between those items, which involves running back and forth several times, also keeping in mind that the ghost will eventually spawn and get you.
I've managed to get to Olmec many times in the end and then finally beat it, with fairly simple tactics, but I've done it strictly for the sake of beating the game, I had no fun in playing it whatsoever.

Consider this a recommendation for the entire STALKER series so far (latest as of this being Call of Pripyat). The STALKER games are FPS/Survival Horror/RPG hybrids where the emphasis is on the FPS gunplay and the survival elements.
You can get thirsty or hungry or need sleep and have to manage those needs alongside that of the deteriorating conditions of your weapons and armors. Ammunition, food, and drink needed to survive are scarce, but can be traded for with almost anyone if you have the right amount of goods or money to sacrifice for it. The game has large maps you can travel between like a sandbox game, and the gunplay is some of the tightest I've seen with really good gun physics. The games also have a wildlife simulation system similar to the one in place in FarCry 3 in a way; animals and mutants will run around and do their own thing after they spawn and kill each other (and maybe you) for survival or food.
Despite the large amount of freedom these games afford you to carve your own path, they feel very focused and are best approached with a strategic mindset.

To be perfectly honest I see this more as a simulation game of how life would be like for an emotionally underdeveloped, mentally unstable, orphaned canadian living through the trauma of having his guardian (grandma) killed by a falling - sorry, evil - tree.
In short: "ooooooh, granneh!" - the immortal wisdom of Jack Lumber, the lumberjack (I get it!),
Pros:
- Very charming graphics (and audio!).
- Depending on your level of involvement and how much you're interested in putting into the game you can have a very hard time getting plaid sashes or a fairly alright time 'only' working up as many stars as you need just to unlock the final boss battle.
- Smooth gameplay that you can regulate the difficulty of further by putting on different beards.
- The entire game is pretty quirky and odd which again feeds into the charms of the game.
- An appealingly bizzare storyline, although it is only very basic as this is, after all, only a fairly short game.
- No animals are supposed to be harmed in this game (if you do, you fail the level). Only evil, evil plants. As a plant hating vegetarian i approve (Please do imagine me seething and foaming at the mouth as hacking and slashing up the disgusting wood logs while laughing manically). I kid. Of course. No. But seriously. Death to plants!
- Canadian simulator.
- The sassy beaver is sassy.
Cons:
- The intro to the level tends to get annoying over time with the whole cutscene that you just cannot skip no matter how much you bash your keyboard.
- In order to purchase all items in the shops and try all the difficulties with different beards while having the comfort of being able to regulate the game difficulty with different syrups you have to play close to insane amounts of games to earn enough wood (currency),  Loses some appeal to me because of this as you need way too much wood to keep me motivated to earn it.
- The noises of the animals tends to get annoying over time.
- Somewhat replayable, but not really. I played it twice with a year between. Enough to forget the setup of each level. But the log tosses are always the same and if you replay it too shortly after last finishing (or have a photographic memory) you'll have memorized each log toss for each level.. if you're as anal about getting best possible ranking for each level as i am, anyway.
Summary:
A very good, charming game with a very calm demeanor to it. Although others may react differently as the tosses are timed I found it soothing rather than stressful and really rather funny. Keep in mind, though, that my humour is beyond ridiculous.
For me it was well worth the full price of the game and i enjoyed it enough to wish to support the developers enough to buy cards enough to get a full tier badge. Would've gotten more of them if that didn't mean i'd have craptons of cards in my inventory i can't do anything with.

Decent Diablo clone. I haven’t played multiplayer yet, so my review is only from single player perspective. I must say, Torchlight I is better. I have three major problems with this sequel.
Difficulty curve is really broken. First two acts are easy; I can beat them with my mouse only. Suddenly in the middle of third act everything is harder. Well, so far so good. I started using keyboard, drinking health and mana potions. But here is the twist; this is the first hack and slash RPG, where my character simply doesn’t have money (in this particular case gold). I just can’t afford potions. It sucks; I was looting everything, picking every item and selling them. Selling price of common bad♥♥♥♥♥axe is about 43gold. One potion costs about 250gold. Just ridiculous. You can argue that my build sucks. Well maybe, however I was playing on normal and then the first Torchlight was easier (I can beat it on my first try without dying too much.).
Second drawback is no real penalty for dying. Your character can respawn, right where his corpse is, with full health. Neither fame, nor experiences are lost in this process. So, you are just losing gold. When you have none, you lose none. The hero is de facto immortal. I should be glad, because my poor hero can’t die. However it is shame, that nothing motivates you to stay alive in game…
Too much items. You are constantly finding better equipment. I like SOME stats comparing, but this was overwhelming.
No thumbs up this time. I still prefer Torchlight I. Average game; wait for some sale.

What can I say, this game is fun. I haven't played much but when you play this game, how long i have played was enough to see this games full integrity.
The Basics
Snow is a free to play snowboarding game which puts you to either complete challenges solo on a mountain, or play on one of the few servers which put you in a game with up to 12 other players. The only good part of this game is multiplayer. It won't be hard to get people to play this game, considering it is free. It is one of those games like skate 3 where you don't pay attension to points, just seeing how high up you can jump at a time. You can play as either a snowboarder or a skiier. I am ussiming with this game constantly updating they will put in new sports.
Singleplayer
The singleplayer isn't nearly as fun as the multiplayer. All you do is complete challenges. The only bonus is ragdolling, which isn't in multiplayer. I do not recommend singleplayer.
Multiplayer
The core to this game, the fabric of it is multiplayer. It is 100x funner when you are playing with friends. You can spawn on people and snowboard or ski with them down mountains, off cliffsides, and off jumps. You earn points for doing tricks which gives allows you to level up once you reach a safe house to do so. The map is surprisingly big, yet it is uncommon to not see a player.
Graphics
For a free game, the graphics are actually quite beautiful. Sure, some texture poppins occure every once in a while but they are rare and infrequent. The snow goes through the air and you can see individual particles as you go down steep cliffs. There isn't much to say, other than this game looks great.
Points
You earn points in both single and mutliplayer which you can cahs out at safe houses to level up. Leveling up unlocks new 'drop points' (teleport to different mountains and bases) and coins to use to unlock gear and clothes. This is all you can currently do with these as the game is in early access.
Pros
+Great Graphics
+Free-To-Play
+No pay-to-win elements
+Terrific Multiplayer
+Realistic, in a small way
+Snowboarding and skiing, more will be added in an update soon
+Fun to play
+Leveling Up
Cons
-When you die, you immediatly turn into a gravestone. No ragdolling
-Sometimes you will die randomly
-Crashes frequently
-Not enough upgrades for your person

I don't usually write serious reviews however Rockstar and Take Twos attitude toward microtransactions and the general economy of it's online mode is absolutely one of the most greediest and downright scummy ways I've ever seen companies conduct themselves.
Unlike the general consensus I don't believe it's R* themselves that are behind the microtransactions, unfortunately it is just a product of being owned by a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ company who puts profit before their consumer base.  For those who don't know, GTA:O a while ago introduced "Shark Cards" which in laymans terms are microtransactions that give the player more in-game cash. However these Shark Cards are RIDICULOUSLY priced beyond any reasonability. 8 million in game dollars is worth about $100 USD. To put this in perspective, as of writing this review the most expensive jet in the game, the Lazer (which since release was free and easy to take from the games military base) costs $6.5 mil in game. Most if not all high-end vehicles and properties cost upward of $1 mil, and then you have customizability options which in some cases, especially with the aforementioned properties, can QUADRUPLE the price.
"But RetroMystic, there is nothing stopping you from earning the money yourself, why complain?"
You see price wouldn't be an issue if payouts were reasonable. They're not. Most "contact" missions which are your run-of-the-mill standard GTA missions payout anywhere from $10,000-$25,000 depending on factors such as difficulty, the lobby size and so fourth. The AI is purposefully designed to be extremely unfair, with pinpoint accuracy even when you're in, say a helicopter, and the enemy AI is using a PISTOL. This isn't a theory either, players have studied and pulled apart the mechanics and the AI always has a lock on you, the moment you exit cover to even fire your weapon you will probably be hit by a bullet. I've died more times to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t AI than I have to actual players. Oh yes, the players. Many lobbies that the game loaded me into have been FULL of modders that grief the hell out of everyone causing explosions, aggresive traffic and a plethora of other issues. Modding has become such a prevelant issue with people going as far to say when they spawn in a lobby, "Are there any modders that can give me some money?".
R* and Take-Two continue to create an unfair economy in which actual purchases with real money award players instead of hard work.
"The DLC is free, so stop complaining".
At what cost?
I doubt you can argue that this is justified when you may as well buy a shark card just to get the items released in the DLC itself. It's sad to see such a reputable company such as R* spread their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s nice and wide for corporate America and ruin what could have been the best multiplayer experience in the world.
With ♥♥♥♥♥♥ anticheat, the incessant shark card shilling and broken economy that requires hours if not days of grinding to aquire a luxury item or property that will help you grind even more money, it's clear R* and Take-Two care more about making a quick dime than making a good game.
I don't know what the future of GTA is, but if it continues like this GTA is on a dangerous path that may kill it.

Played just under an hour of this game and really can't take much more. I saw the unveil trailer a good while ago and got rather excited about it, looked like it could be a fun game to play with some friends, playing as different classes and exploring, killing, and generally having good times. After a short play, I found I wouldn't be getting these things, as;
1. Combat is bad, really bad, melee isn't fun and the game takes control of the camera during combat, rather than giving you the OPTION to lock on, you either let the game control the camera or don't fight it's annoying. On top of this, range and magic are almost too easy considering the game will automatically target enemies for you, simply stand back, hold fire, and that's it, occassionally you have to dodge, or just step to the side a little.
2. Exploration is shoddy, areas are rather miniscule and uninteresting, and there's no incentive to build a house or settle on any island, because soon enough you're going to build a portal and be on your way. Part of sandbox games is generally the ability to create a house and settle, all you need here is a crafting station and that's it, build your equipment and go.
3. The movement of characters and camera are iffy, in order to be comfortable using the camera some tweaking is required, and the character seems a bit slow, not to mention that when trying to jump while beside a wall, characters just seem to slam right back down to the earth. Possibly more of a bug than anything, but come on, it's not like jumping mechanics are new, this kid of thing should be a big deal to get right!
These points are basically what makes me dislike the game, destroying the 'RPG Sandbox' nature of the game with poor combat, and poor exploration. I hope this game can become something greater as it progresses through Early Access, but for now, I can't say I like it very much.

Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 is an example of how to do First-Person-Shooters right. The fast gameplay requires more skill and focus than most modern First-Person-Shooters. Instead of trying to level up your character to get OP weapons, most weapons have a legitimate purpose, and most of them don't feel too overpowered (except Disc, Pred Pistol, Skeeter, and Sadar. Not to forget Mines). Instead of grinding to get perks to power yourself up, Aliens versus Predator requires skill from the start.
Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 [Which I will be calling 'AvP' through out the rest of this review] allows the player to take control of three species, Aliens, Predators, or the human Marines. Each have their advantages and disadvantages.
The Alien is a melee only species, a hurtful disadvantage, but is patched up by the speed and wallcrawling ability that the Aliens have. Aliens also can smell the scents of other beings, allowing it to see its victims in the dark. The Alien regains health by headbiting Predators and Humans, you can do this on both the living and the dead. Obviously headbiting live beings is harder than dead ones, but gains back more health.
The Predator is a mix of Melee and ranged weapons, the majority of his weapons, Medicomp, and cloak are powered by 'Field Charge'. This will auto-recharge if you are not using anything that uses charge, or you can find field-charge items around the map which will give you full energy. The only weapons that don't use energy are the Wristblades, and Disc (Unless you use the recall ability, that will use a small amount of energy), as well as the Speargun. But this uses ammo, which only replenishes upon death. The Predator can heal using his Medicomp, this will use a large amount of energy, but puts you back to full health everytime (TIP: Secondary fire of Medicomp will put out fires). In some of the bonus levels the Predator gains a new gadget, the grappling hook, which can pull him to higher heights. The Predator also has three vision modes, which can help him spot enemies. The first vision mode can help spot humans, the second aliens, and the third other Predators and field-charges (Of course you have the default normal vision).
The Marine is a ranged only species, guns guns and more guns. The Marine replenishes health with medkits, found about through-out levels. Armor, which can protect against Alien acid and absorbs small amounts of damage. The Marine has a Motion Tracker, if anything moves, a small dot and a beep sound will appear on it. But it isn't always reliable, if ANYTHING moves it will beep. In some of the bonus levels the Marines get a jetpack, allowing them to fly to spaaaaace! In multiplayer Marines can select a specialist sub-class, this will allow them to pick from any of the weapons in the game (unless game host restricted it), and you will always spawn with the selected weapon, but you can only use that weapon (and the pistol).
Each species can unlock bonus missions after you complete the main game, (you will unlock more if you beat it on a higher difficulty) these levels are the levels from other species singleplayer, for example: You can unlock a backwards version of the Predator's first level as Marine if you beat the Marine SP on Director's cut [Hard]. Pretty cool!
Not to forget, you can unlock cheat options in the game by completing certain objectives through-out the levels. These can be things like slow-mo whenever you are near enemies. Or unlimited speargun ammo and more spears per shot as Predator.
The music will change depending on what species you are playing as, Predator will recall images of the jungle, Marines have a very militaristic beat, while Aliens have a slow and creepy tone. The music really sets the tone well, but I wouldn't find myself listening to it outside the game.
The Multiplayer is where this game shines most. Fast gameplay and the different play-styles of each species make for very fun and memorable experience. This is one of the fastest games ever, you will die, fast, and a lot. It is extremly well balanced, and I almost never feel like a player is winning because of the species they are playing as. But, unfortunatly, this game has a small player base, so at times you may not be able to find a game. Because of this the community doesn't play competitively (most of the time), anymore. Servers will also usually have a small amount of players, 8-player games are kinda rare, but when they happen, it is sooooo fun!
Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 is easily one of the fastest games, and one of the best, ever made.
You would be doing yourself a disservice by not playing this game!
Why are you still reading this review, go buy it and play it?!

Heroes  Generals is many things. Some of those things are done very well, others are executed in a mediocore "meh" sort of way. The game doesn't however do anything exceptionally bad, which makes it mostly a very fun and pleasant experience everytime you jump in game.
The Good news
Do you like world of Tanks? Awesome. You can be a tank and just go around doing tank things It does seem that the tanks are considerably more vulneraable to infantry then you would think, the damage done by all anti-infantry weapons seems to scale all the way up to the heavy tank from the lightest of armored tanks, however when used correctly the tank can be an absolute nightmare to anything (including aircraft) on the battlefield. They have done a supurb job of modeling the tanks visually, and getting into the fight of one is relativly easy.  Each faction has distinct and different tanks with armuments and functions that compliment them nicely. (The russian starter can go in water)
Do you like War Thunder? Great! If there's one thing in this game that they have improved exceptionally well it is the air to air and air to ground combat, no other game has satisfyed my lust for simulated aerial combat. Are the pysics perfect? No, but the AP ammo types and explosive rounds  add an interesting decision when arming your air-craft. Coming in for a bombing run and hitting that moving target perfectly is a great feeling, and although at the start doing so repeatedly seems impossible aiming the bombs just takes some time to get used too. A similar feeling is when you line up perfectly on an armored vechical and unleash a barrage of your AP rounds into its sides setting it ablaze as you whizz by to engage an enemy paratrooper plane. The give and take of the dog fights is also very good, the only thing that matches the intense feeling and victourous momentum of downig an enemy aircraft is shooting it's pilot out of the cockpit with a single well placed expsplosive or AP round, then watching the craft with its still propellers make its decent to the ground. Truly a fantastic game for pilots.
Now the bad news
Do you like Battlefield 1942? Do you like World at War? Sorry. The real disappointment of this game is for sure the infantry combat. Now I have many infantry men, and fully kitted sniper in the game, and I have certainly done my fair share as the boots of the army, however the infantry combat and role does't really offer anything exciting, although infantry are essential to the game they seem to be the least rewarding and fun role to play. The weapons and customizability is there, but the earlier weapons seem like a waste of your ingame money and without playing either a tanker or pilot earning the money to upgrade to better arms seems like a long term goal. I had the pleasure of getting in on the game very early and was able to just buy weapons without having to go through the experience system (Which was a positive change) this definetly makes the infantry class and improving feel like a huge grind though, especially since they receive the least amount of points for doing what they are best at, engaging other infantry and capping points. For the all the hours I have played this I have had the least exciting moments as an infantry man. The sniping is done well and the assualt rifles and Sub machine guns are by far the most effective guns in the game at the moment. Not being able to deploy your bipod on the Machine guns seems like a very dissappointing decision, being able to create a machine gun nest or a cross firing position with a buddy in a town or open field seems like one of the most authetic things about a WW2 battle, going back to Saving Private Ryan and Band of Brothers  where I get a lot of my childhood memories of WW2. The infantry vechicals and other equipmet is fine, but that actual execution of combat and fuctionallity leaves me wanting. Not to say it is a bad game for your hardcore FPS players out there, but there are a lot of COD style "bs" moments that may make you want to take a break from time to time.  Overall the infantry combat isn't horrible but not the experience you would hope for.
Other impovments/thoughts
The lack of anti-tank emplacements throughout the map (even though there are AA batteries throughout each map) seems like an oversight and would really add to the experiece of the infantry player, in my opinion.
Artillery either a class or emplacments throughout the map would add secondary objective/targets for Planes and light tanks or infantry before tryinng to take a point.
Bipobs please! Or mounted light machine guns in the already established bunkers.
Different bomb types for air-craft (Many small ones at once, or pellets/fire-bombs)
Different Aircraft (each faction currently only has one, which are all very different from eachother Think Bombers or scout planes that can spot targets manually or automatically)

I've been playing this game off and on for a long time, so I've seen it develop over time. Ultimately, it's a fun game that's definitely worth playing if you like this style of large multiplayer realistic shooters. I have not really played with a group, but as a Planetside 2 player I can see that the game would be a TON of fun if you had an organized outfit to play with.
That being said, the game has a couple of major issues that get really irritating.
1. There really aren't that maps and it can really start to get old after a while. The maps that exist are all very different, which is good. And when you play them, the starting positions of the attackers (and therefore the places where the defenders have to hold) change due to the larger Generals aspect of the game. Still, they do tend to get a little samey
2. There are a couple balance issues that get really annoying. First, it is too easy to be accurate with tanks. Ultimately, you'll find that some guy in a tank across the map where you can't even see it will snipe you with a headshot as soon as you spawn. And tank players know this, so they often just drive up onto the forested hillsides on the side of the map to just snipe the whole game. The second balance issue that bugs me is that bolt-action rifles can, with certain mod set-ups, 1-shot players with a torso shot. While I understand the realism involved here, it's a real balance issue because it means that a lot of players will just run around with BA rifles for use in close combat and will beat players with SMGs, which are designed for close combat, 80% of the time.
Now, my gripes out of the way....as I said, if you like this style of game, Heroes and Generals is definitely worth a shot.

My recommendation of Spelunky comes with a caveat.
If you've never played a "rogue-like" game (like Rogue Legacy or Paranautical Activity), this is a good one to try out and see if you like the genre.  It has nice, clean graphics, tight controls and a fun premise.  Further, it's got a great price-point where if you buy it and don't like it, you probably won't be upset over dropping the coin.
Here's where the caveat comes in.  If you like rogue-like games, I would absolutely recommend it.  If you're like me, however, you will hate it.
I hate rogue-like games.
To me, these games are purposefully designed to be frustrating.  The idea is to incite the player and light the fire of competitive spirit so that they play over and over and over - perhaps getting just a little bit better with each subsequent attempt.  For me, that competivie spirit doesn't ignite.  Instead, I just bemoan my lack of progress.
If you like these rogue-like games, absolutely give it a shot.  I'll look forward to checking out the next game that Mossmouth puts out.  They seem to make a quality product.

I picked Spelunky up last summer durring the steam sale, and played for around 20 minutes. I decided it was too brutal for me, and being semi-new to PC gaming, found the controls awkward. Now, one year later with an xbox controller in hand and a new appreciation for difficult games, I can heartily say that this game is fantasticc.
First off, and honestly the least important part: the game looks and sounds fantastic. Being a 2d sidescroller, I appreciate its lighting effects and the simplicity of its sound.
But, the gameplay is where this game really shines. You are tossed into a dungeon and you know you need to go down and find treasure. You have some bombs and rope to start, and everything wants you dead. Enemies like spiders and snakes will go after you, and dart traps line the randomly generated halls. Spikes may or may not be at the bottom of pits, and giant boulder traps go off when you steal a certain idol. The game is brutal, as I said above- but it's not unfair. You will learn how each item and enemy works through trial and error. After 2 hours of playing the past few days, I have finally finished the first "world" of apparently 4, and I immediately died upon entering world 2. But I don't care, becuase it's rewarding in its own right, and a very fun experience.
Also there's apparently multiplayer, but I've yet to test that out.
Totally pick this game up if you like a challenging game that will last a long time.

I don't mind iOS ports too much, and while I admire the concept Jack Lumber presents (think Fruit Ninja crossed with connect the dots and bullet time), the core gameplay requires a lot of precision and not a lot of room for error, which is a bit of a problem when playing with a mouse. It's easy during the first 3 or 4 levels, but soon after you're required to get through each minichallenge without screwing up, or else your score won't be high enough to advance.
Once the game starts introducing conditions to finish the challenge, such as cutting through misshapen logs or fast spinning ones, the game loses its charm quickly. The time window they give is very brief, and the more that is thrown at you, the less you can keep up. There are options to purchase 1 use items that can give you a slight edge, but none that I have found or unlocked so far gives me anything permanent, nor extend the amount of time I have to cut. If I had this for the systems it was designed for I imagine I would love it. The art style is great, the humor solid, and the nuances an interesting touch. However, it was not meant for the PC, and those who are looking for laidback fun like this game promises will quickly become irritated.
Don't bother, or at the very least, get it on something with a touchscreen.
