***I WROTE THIS REVIEW IN November of 2006... Found it on my HD and reposted it because I felt it still holds up- hope you enjoy it*
To set the record straight, Doom 3 is hardly a sequel in the sense that none of the events of a Mars invaded Hell ever occurred. Think of it as a Doom adaptation. You are a Marine landing on the surface of Mars at a military research base reporting to your officer for orders. When you arrive you find you are to report to a lab to escort a scientist back to the military headquarters. So you grab a weapon and make your way down the dark passages of laboratories where civilian crewmembers are ominously talking about people who have mysteriously disappeared or have heard voices; hinting that something BIG is about to happen. When you finally meet up with the scientist, something goes terribly wrong and the forces of hell are released while demons pass through portals and soldiers are possessed across the red planet.
For the next twenty minutes the game unleashes the best scare tactics and sequences of events I have ever experienced in a horror video game. But not only is game brilliant in scaring the crap out of you, the dark facility level design is absolutely perfect. Lights flicker as your fellow marines are screaming over the radio. Muffled sounds of shouts and gunfire on other side of walls or even demonic arms reaching through the walls all cause you to walk through each corridor cautiously with an itchy trigger finger.
Gameplay:
Upon your arrival on Mars, you are handed your very own PDA which you use throughout the game to acquire passwords to cabinets, open doors, read scientist's e-mail and voicemail and even watch videos that describe different areas of maps. Reading other scientist's e-mail is important throughout the game for they sometimes describe weakness in enemies and even reveal hidden stashes to ammo and health packs.
So you have your PDA, what else do you need? Oh yeah, a flashlight. A flashlight? Yes a flashlight. To make Doom 3 scarier than it already is, the creators equipped our voiceless, nameless marine with a flashlight to check out those dark scary corners. But the catch is you cannot bear any weapons while you hold your flashlight. This means if there is indeed a zombie lurking in the shadows you better switch to your shotty quick!
The weapons in Doom 3 are almost what you would expect from the original game. You start off with a meager handgun, upgrade to the shotgun, which upgrades to an assault gun, the basic 1, 2, 3 step formula in any FPS. What, you think they're gonna start you off with the BFG? As you progress, you eventually have the entire arsenal from the original Doom plus something special the creators added in the later portions.
About half way through the game, the brilliant scripted sequences start to fade away and Doom 3 becomes more of a repetitive brainless shooter. Demons become less scary (even the newer ones) and you will start to predict where doors will open and how to handle the situations that are supposed to be tough. (that occurs when doors close and you are trapped in a room with 37 demons) What happened to the dazzling writing we saw in the game's opening?
There was also one tribute to Doom the creators added that I absolutely love. Do you remember playing the original Doom, and sometimes when an imp fired one of it's fireballs at you and a possessed marine got in the way, the marine would start attacking the imp? Well I used to see how many enemies I could wake up and just run around the map for 10-15 minutes seeing how many enemies would die without me firing a single shot. Well Doom 3 also kept the same demons fighting demons portion, which made me laugh the first time I saw it. Too bad the maps in Doom 3 aren't square and rectangular like they used to be, it's a lot harder to run away from enemies.
Graphics:
I can't begin to express my satisfaction when I double clicked the Doom 3 icon on my desktop and watched the opening cut scene. From that point on the smooth textures and unique dark/bright lighting produces an amazing environment to battle demons. I also loved as you approach a cut scene, the camera pauses as your character continues to walk forward giving you an outer body experience as the cut scene begins. This happens every time a new monster is introduced over the course of the game. The cut scene ends when the camera seamlessly zooms into the back of your characters head, into is current vision. Very well done.
Multiplayer:
I know most people are not buying Doom 3 for the multiplayer experience but this is 2006 and games today pretty much come standard with multiplayer options. How many games today have an incredible single player story AND incredible multiplayer gameplay (or modification)? It is obvious Id concentrated entirely on the single player aspect and at the last minute threw in a small multiplayer option where you can join servers that supports up to 4 players. A tribute to old school Doom multiplayer maybe? Back when you had to dial your friend on your 14.4 kbps modem and run around shooting each other? Even if it is, the enjoyment quickly diminishes over time... exponentially! In fact, I can't find a reason to ever play Doom 3 MP again. The dark maps and quick paced gameplay does not translate well into multiplayer gaming even if there are only four players in a server. .
Pros: Corridor shooter with heavy emphasis on unpredicted scares.
Cons: Weak multiplayer, formulaic advance through game, well thought out scares turn into mundane annoyances.
Bottom Line: A dark and morbid FPS like nothing you've ever seen. Interesting story and impressive real time action shots that will make your jaw drop. The Doom 3 engine however has room for improvement in an environment that only works for this genre of gameplay.

I played this in November of 2016. It took me about 17 hours to do a play through.
I was really pleased with how well this game aged.  Graphically, it could do with some texture packs, and the lighting effects were probably awesome in the day, but they're a little dated. But it's still alright.
The gameplay is good solid pre-Halo FPS. There are probably only about 8 enemy types, plus bosses. They are mostly simpler, and the challenge comes from getting your health widdled down through the level. (Although the easier difficulties are pretty easy).
I remember when the game came out, there were two controversies: The Flashlight, and Monster Closets. Yes, the game used a whole lot of the best lighting effects it had available, and showed them off. Lots of places are poorly lit or completely dark, and you need to use a flashlight, and you can't have the flashlight and a gun at the same time. I get why it bugged people, but I enjoyed it. The enemies are simpler (especially in the flashlight-intensive areas), and it adds some suspsense and challenge. Monster Closets (that is, there are little closets all over the place that just hide enemies so they can jump out at you from behind later). Monster Closets did start to annoy me, but again, that is how pre-Halo FPSs worked. It helped with the immersion, because I was listening for enemies to come up behind me, and then when you get to rooms with loud machines in it, it was a lot more tense.
I recommend the game, it's cheap, and it's fun.

Portal Knights is a cute and interesting RPG sandbox game with good execution and potential for its future. I will add a TL;DR at the end.
Portal Knights has an interesting and good mix and RPG, exploration, and sandbox elements within its gameplay. For me it felt as if the controls were a bit odd especially in combat, especially since you are unable to jump while in combat mode. Its controls definitely feel odd at first and first person I feel is only useful really useful for building as combat in that view can be tedious. The different recipes that can be created and the idea of upgradable workstations is great. The inventory/ backpack however feels a bit incomplete as some items do not automatically stack in it when you find more of them. You also are forced to click, hold, then drag items from your inventory and are also unable to quickly move them like you can in other sandbox games.
There is no pause option in single player/offline mode which is a tad of an annoyance if you quickly have to go do something and then you die since there is no pause. There are three classes to currently choose from and from what I see there are no specializations in weaponry or armour for any class as you can just equip the other classes armour and are able to craft it. It’s good to make classes stand out to really make them specialize and have special items.
From what I have seen the single player gameplay consists of going from island to island advancing through portals and eventually fighting bosses and being able to settle on of the islands. The first island or the tutorial island is interesting in how it gives objectives and little quests for you to do, but that is not seen in other islands. Perhaps even a kill X amount of creatures quest would be fun if you are allowed to manage your active quests/objectives.
Another cool feature is that the universes where the islands are contained and characters are compatible with each other, meaning that you can start your high level character in a new universe or start your new character in your old universe. So far the gameplay is enjoyable and refreshing and the multiple islands is something of interest and uniqueness to associate with Portal Knights along with its RPG and adventure elements.
The graphics in this game are cute, just really cute. It helps to add to a more laid back and relaxing experience but it’s also beautiful when you look upon the land or your own creations. The art has been done well and the music fits with an adventurous spirit.
+ 44 islands to play through
+ Good mix of RPG and Sandbox elements
+ Graphics are cute and helps to give a relaxing nature
+ Easy to pick up and play
+ 4-person multiplayer
+ 5 chracter slots and 3 universes slots (saves/world progress)
**Note since this is an Early Access title Cons and other parts of the review as well are viable to change as the game continues to develop**
- No real class specializations
- Quests are gone after tutorial island
- No real challenge (From what seen so far, just really easy to go to next islands)
- Combat is odd and removes jump ability
- Some items do not auto stack when you already have the item in your inventory creating two stacks of the same item and forced to click, hold, and drag items to move them
- No quick move from inventory to hand or chest
Here are some suggestions I feel would improve the game
- Quests on individual islands not just the first
- Ability to pause in single play/offline mode
- Ability to keep jump when in combat
- Class specialized clothing and weaponry (Only one class can craft/use)
- Pets
- New class Necromancer (Ability to harvest enemy souls and craft specialized weaponry which will allow summoning of one undead or the ability to set an automatic undead guard for a certain area like the house. Can be added as a specialization of the current mage class available after a certain level to unlock more specialized gear and abilities.)
- Quick move (such as Shift+Click) to move items more efficiently from hand to inventory or to a chest
- Adjustable keybindings
Portal Knights is fun and easy to get into, but like any game in early access it has its share of annoyances. I was able to enjoy it so far in my playtime and I hope to beat every single island. I was able to enjoy my time and relax within Portal Knights and I would definitely say it would be a great title to play with friends. The islands however are a thing of taste in my opinion as some people like open world exploration and being limited to islands which you have to teleport to and from is odd. It took me a bit to get used to it, but it’s also a charming feature that allows you to simply go somewhere brand new every time to kill, mine, or build. Overall I enjoyed Portal Knights except for some snippets here and there and I say that the developers have a really good chance to make this a great game.
Portal Knights is an adventurous sandbox RPG title with interesting gameplay. It consists of individual islands you can teleport to rather than a huge open world (from what seen so far). So far it has good gameplay and cute graphics. Overall I would say it’s a fun casual game which can be easily picked up and played solo or with friend. Feel free to check the updates to see what has been added since the time of this review and if it includes your personal tastes.

Looking at this game's apparent "Overwhelmingly Positive" review state, I'm guessing I'm gonna get a lot of hate for this, but the truth must be head.
Finally, TEKKEN on PC. I'm so happy, and with the 7+ years of development and huge focus on story mode, this is going to be the best Tekken game ever.
Right?
But no. There's huge problems with this game.
The laughable excuse at a "Story" Mode which was said to be the main focus of the game is an absolute joke.
"End of the Mishima Saga" my♥♥♥♥♥ I have more questions now more than ever. There's a ridiculous amount of plot holes, and the ending is so anti-climatic and abrupt.
Besides that horrible mode, there's only two other modes to play - Arcade and Treasure Battle.
Arcade mode no longer has the intro cutscene or ending cutscenes like in Tekken 4/5/6. You just pick a fighter, fight 3 randoms, Heihachi, and Kazumi. Then credits. You also do not unlock anything in this mode, so it's useless playing it since it's so repetitive and it gets you nothing.
The third and last mode is the Treasure Battle, which is basically Ghost Battle. But they even screwed up this mode too! There's no "Get Ready for the Next Battle" sequence, just loading screen then suddenly "ROUND 1 - FIGHT". Stages do not change every fight. I've fought on the same stage for like 6 fights in a row.
So, after completing the story and playing arcade like 3 times and being bored with them, you are literally stuck playing ONE game mode forever - Treasure Battle. Unless you play online. Then you're probably good to go.
Customization is so painfully barebones. There's no way you're going to make a character you picture in your head in the game at all. It's basically just basically playing dress up with the current characters.
In the end, it's still TEKKEN. It's got amazing gameplay, and I'm still loving the core mechanics. But I spent $75 for the "full experience" and this is what you get? Sorry but I can't recommend it for that much money.

I played this game years ago and I really loved it. I was a fan of the Alien and Predator movies so I really liked the idea of an Alien vs. Predator game. The game itself is composed out of 3 campaigns for each species - humans, predators and aliens. Personally I would choose the colonial marines campaign as the best one. It is the longest one out of the three. Also it has that claustrophobic tension and fear of what is going to happen when your motion sensor picks up something hurdling itself towards you while you look around looking for the spot where it will burst out of. So while being the closest to the traditional FPS style it still is unique. The other 2 campaigns are excellent as well and play out totally differently. Predators have their gadgets and claw weapons. Aliens can walk on walls and claw/bite their way through everyone. Noteworthy for the alien campaign is that you get to go through the whole cycle - you start as an egg, hatch as a facehugger and continue until you are a full-grown alien. To this day I dare say there is not an Alien and/or Predator game better than this one (when it comes to single-player). The multiplayer was cool as well although nowadays not many people play it and the newer Alien/Predator titles have better MP in general. Overall a fantastic game worth recommending to anyone who likes the genre or movies or just simply horror games.

Practically everything can kill you, and it takes care and skill to navigate each level. It's easy to mess up. But every element in the game follows specific logic. You can spot most anything before it attacks you, and it gives you plenty of time to figure a way around (or through) it.
It seems best played with a controller, and there are some very annoying tendancies for your character to cling to edges that you really didn't want to cling to. But otherwise the game doesn't arbitrarily limit how you move or fight. It's fast, it's fluid, it's rewarding.
It's got local coop, which makes the game more challenging because of friendly fire. But either single or local, it's fun and worth the price - as long as you're alright with its steep learning curve.

Total War and The Elder Scrolls had a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child. His name is Mount&Blade. He's great, just like his parents. But, he often ignored and kept under wraps. You won't find dozens of awards, nor will you find it in the annals of video game history, but it's still a good game and worth your money.
Graphics and music is Mount&Blade's weakest asset. It's ugly, plain and simple. Even on the highest quality available, it looks like an early to mid PlayStation 2 game. Yes, it was made in 2007. And yes, it's not made by a big studio. But, that doesn't excuse it. Look at Tekken 4 or 5. They look fantastic, and are much older than M&B. The men look like apes. The women have an eternal duck face. The scenery is nothing to write home about either. It's just bland.
The music is disappointing. While they do have the medieval atmosphere M&B aims for, it's just boring and uninteresting. It feels like stock music from a royalty-free website, the songs that have no character or soul. It's also very repetitive and wears on you quickly.
Now this is where the game starts to shine. Mount&Blade is a medieval sandbox. There are many ways you can play the game. There is no plot to the game, but there is a setting. This gives you free reign over how you conduct yourself. There is no final goal (outside of achievements), and you can't really lose. That being said, the real challenge is reaching the high point of any career. You may customize your character's face, skill, and history. The histories you choose determine your starting skills and items. Speaking of skills, you have a wide variety of skills, from combat to diplomacy to trading. You can customize every aspect of your character, from race to sex to fine facial features. You can also choose your starting location.
Since I mentioned the setting, let's talk about it. You start off as a nobody in a continent, called Calradia. There used to be a pseudo-Roman empire, but it's long gone. Now, there are six new kingdoms, all fighting to rule the world. You have the Swiss-Italian Rodoks, the French-English-German Swadians, the Mongolian Khergits, the Russian-Novgorod Vaegirs, the Norse Nords, and the Arab-Persian Sarranids. Each faction's military have their own strengths and weaknesses. Each faction also has a set of nobles with various personalities. Each noble has a family, with their own personalities. You may join any faction, and help out any noble or character.
The most obvious path you can take is the path of a warlord/general. About two-thirds of M&B revolve around combat. From warfare to bandit attacks, you will have to fight; most of the skill are, in one way or another, related to combat. To can visit cities and villages and recruit villages and mercenaries. Train them to become better soldiers. However, the better your soldiers, the higher their wages are. You also have to feed them, or else they will desert. You fight, train, fight, recruit, and fight. When you become famous enough, you can dabble in politics and become a noble. Eventually, you can form your own faction and conquer the world.
Or, you can be kingmaker, and support a usurper to the throne. Or you can be a bandit king, and fight off the law to make a profit. Or, you can be a merchant, and form a caravan that transports good from city to city. There are many, many ways you can play M&B, and there is no correct way.
It's Elder Scrolls, but you can raise an army. It's not a lazy cash grab nor a blatant rip-off. It feels like a small studio took their time to create a magnum opus on a tight budget. There is effort made to M&B, but it's not revolutionizing anything anytime soon.
Here is jewel of M&B. The vanilla game itself is okay. It has a great start and virtually infinite replayability, with all the possibilities you can play the game. Definitely worth buying, as it will eat up your precious time, if you are not prepared. However, the novelty fades quickly, and the quests can be bland and repetitive. For a game with lots of ways to play, there is not a lot of variety within each approach. Most factions are the same, with nothing unique, except for the location and military.
Like all jewels, the game can be polished. The fan base really outdid themselves this time. The fact that the game looks like♥♥♥♥♥is a blessing in disguise. This game is very easy to mod. And the fans have made very good mods. That keeps me hooked on playing. If you buy this game, I highly recommend you check out a few mods online and see for yourself.
Mount & Blade is a decent time waster. It's an ugly duckling that can be changed into a beautiful swan, and that's part of the magic of this game. It feels less like a complete game, and more like a skeleton, where independent developers can create their own game. And that is like buying multiple games for the price of one. For that, it's definitely worth a try. Happy fighting, or trading, or negotiating, or usurping.

Deponia is an adventure game that's a bit difficult to describe.  It has great art, decent writing, some very creative characters, and a pretty interesting story.  The writing and voice acting definitely isn't the best I've seen, but it gets the job done.  The game has a very clean interface, letting you access your inventory with the mouse wheel and providing interact and inspect functions on different mouse buttons.  It's also significantly longer than most adventure games I've played as my playthrough clocked in at around 10 hours.
The one off-putting thing about the game is that you play as an idiot who frequently causes havok around town and everybody hates.  It's a really odd position to be in though the character is quite interesting and is responsible for most of the humor in the game.
The puzzles can get overwhelming at points with tons of items piling up in your inventory with little clue about how to use them though the game keeps it mostly reasonable.
I did run into a very frequent bug where the dialog options window was misaligned, sometimes dropping options off the bottom of the screen, but it never impeded the game.  There were also one or two occasions where certain subtitles were displayed in German.
Deponia is definitely a good game and stands by itself, though it is designed as a trilogy and buying all three games can be a bit of an investment for adventure games.  If you want good adventure games though, it's probably worth the price.

Spelunky is a rogue-likish 2D platformer, where the player takes the role of a treasure hunter in seek of riches within an ever-shifting labyrinth. The gameplay is fluid, the visuals are appreciable, and the music has a mysterious, enticing vibe.
Although difficult and often frustrating, Spelunky is a great joy to experience, and will always have you clicking that retry button. The game offers a local Co-Op option, where up to 4 players can work together (or hilariously kill one another). If the main gameplay is becoming stale, there are mini-games available, such as one with the sole goal of killing other competitors.
Everyday, players can compete against others in daily challenges. The Daily Challenge is a game mode where all players explore the same generated map, with the goal of achieving the highest possible score.
It's worth mentioning that, although the PC controls aren't terrible, the game is best played with an Xbox controller. Demanding hours upon hours of gameplay, Spelunky is an absolute must buy for rogue-likish enthusiasts, as well as players looking for an enjoyable experience, all for a reasonable price of $15 at full price.

But.. in a different way.  A more thoughtful way.  I daresay a better way.
But do you like them?  Then this game's probably for you!
Seriously though, unlike those other games I mentioned that either aren't that hard to begin with or bank on extreme difficulty just for the sake of it and usually though unforgivingly pixel-perfect platforming and extreme precision-memorization, the likes of which didn't even exist to nearly to such a degree in the 8-bit-era games they claim to be trying to emulate, Spelunky is simply difficult in that it has an extremely high skill ceiling... and I would say a pretty high skill 'floor'.  You can play the tutorial and mess around in the game as a complete gaming amateur that only understands the very basics of platforming and smacking things with a whip, but to really get anywhere or do anything, there's a LOT you're going to need to get used to, learn, experience and master.  I'd definitely compare it most closely out of what I listed to the 'Castlevania/Ninja Gaiden' and Cave Story/La-Mulana groups, inspired by classic games that required lots of play and development and refinement of skill rather than split-second platforming perfection or mind-numbing memorization.. which is to say, a superior type of 'extreme difficulty' than the likes of Super Meat Boy and its ilk (as much as I do enjoy that game).  I'd also compare it to a sort of 2d Dark Souls/Monster Hunter in a similar way, except replace "very difficult bosses to master" with "very difficult traps and stage setups to master".
Except.. unlike all of those, Spelunky is a roguelike.  Well, kinda; there's not realy any direct RPG elements per se like most Roguelike-subgenre games tend to have, but it has that nature of "procedurally generated content and when you die, you have to start all over".  And considering it's a tough-as-nails sidescroller in which you start with a whopping 3 hp, things even very early on can deal multiple hp worth of damage, there are traps around every corner and even falling a long distance can hurt you... well, you're gonna be starting all over a LOT.  But that's the beauty of it; it's extremely difficult to advance, and you will die hundreds of times in the first area even after you've finally reached the second for example, but every single death brings more lessons learned and more experience gained (experience for YOURSELF as a GAMER rather than your character) as you metaphorically will 'gain levels and stats', to put it one way, in your ability to play the game itself and thus become more and more likely to advance further, collect more treasure, try out more powerups and face more enemies and obstacles with each subsequent attempt.  Needless to say, it's very, very satisfying as you feel your skill raise in this way, no matter how many times you die.
My one real complaint is that, well, quite frankly, that 3 hp health pool does feel a little bit *too* low and ways to recover it are woefully few and far between, and tend to be very weak.  Luckily there is no actual health cap and you can keep gaining more and more hp to use throughout your run, but barring the specific 'blood-collecting' method which requires a good deal of luck anyway, it's gonna be very tough going, especially considering that you have to sacrifice several of the few tickets to more health you have to get said blood-collecting item.  You'll find yourself wishing quite often that the default health was 5 or so and there were more ways to recover it just so you could simply learn more per run, but alas, in a way such a stringent limitation to your life forces you to game even harder, be even more wary of everything and learn even more as you carefully make your way through the maps.
If you're on the fence about this game, I highly recommend checking out the free, original 8bit version and see what you think.  This remake with its smooth graphics and superb soundtrack (easily rivalling the NES-like original which I adored) does deserve your money if you even think you'd enjoy it, though.

Not since The Binding of Isaac and Super Meat Boy have I been so mind crushingly obsessed and horrified simultaneously just by moving around.
Spelunky holds its own as a marvelous tribute to retro-classic twitch demand of motor skills and attention. The variety of quirks this exploration-platformer holds up its sleeve pour an endlessly entertaining menagerie of traps, enemies, treasures, characters, and level variants. The visuals are ominously charming while maintaining shocking brutal death scenarios. Each hand drawn animation looks lovingly cared for and holds the emotion of Saturday morning cartoons. The distinct style pushes Spelunky into the realm of adorably memorable.

Along with imperfect perfection rogue-likes of similar caliber such as The Binding of Isaac and Risk of Rain, Spelunky astounds and develops the potential of the simplistic. Spelunky will last forever.

Finally, TEKKEN on PC. I'm so happy, and with the 7+ years of development and huge focus on story mode, this is going to be the best Tekken game ever.

Arcade mode no longer has the intro cutscene or ending cutscenes like in Tekken 4/5/6. You just pick a fighter, fight 3 randoms, Heihachi, and Kazumi. Then credits. You also do not unlock anything in this mode, so it's useless playing it since it's so repetitive and it gets you nothing.

I can say for sure the combat of Fractured But Whole adds in more 'strategy' although it's still pretty easy even on the max difficulty. But not entirely a breeze without utilizing skills and items apropriate for specific turns and situations. The expanded character roster is a nice move to give more variety and include secondary characters more closely to the main narrative.
The story itself is stretched over the 'civil war' aspect we've been advertised. As I played, I begin to see that it's not as great when it isn't condensed like Stick of Truth (13ish hour experience). Personally, I enjoyed the story of South Park Fractured But Whole. I'm a huge fan. However, it felt lacking because of the huge delay and this was all we got (the 20ish hour experience that didn't feel much better than the 13 hours of Stick of Truth). Combat was improved but the narrative and side quests (for other stories) didn't at all evolve much. It was indeed crazy and fun but for a sequel it didn't do much better than its predecessor.

One of the biggest negatives that I saw carried through from Stick of Truth was the lack of incentives or content to go back to areas we've been through. Once you rolled through it via the story, there is no reason to go back (other than getting friends on Coonstagram but that's all). So I wonder what that near year long delay was for. I would half expect a flourish of content and value to meet the price tag and time to further develop the game. There aren't many interesting side quests that would develop the heroes we can choose as our allies. It would have been cool to have quests to learn of our allies' backstories of their hero instead of just coming across their character sheet. I also have to wonder if the story bit of PC Principal in the trailer was cut. Randy is a much popular character. I felt his inclusion in the game a bit more was a miss opportunity. I believe much for a lot of the adult characters. He is one of the many NPCs that are good only for one run and they have no use anymore.
This section doesn't add or reduce points for the review....yet. Just some thoughts. The season pass content was detailed in the South Park website. But I fear it may not really do much for some of the stuff in the game we can't go into such as The Mall or Canada. The first story content we are getting is Casa Bonita. And the second we haven't been given much other than a new class. I suppose it has something to do with Mint Berry Crunch but it may open up the mall. Though somehow I have a feeling the mall won't be open until for a third game if it comes. Or even if we will be able to pass the Canadian border with the wall in the way.
Overall, I enjoy the game as a fan. It's a good game to me but I cannot bring myself to recommend others to buy the game at its current price.

Regrettably, I have to NOT recommend this game with one exception - those who have laptops with a touchscreen or a Microsoft Surface will likely have a significantly more enjoyable time with this Fruit Ninja clone than those who have to use a mouse.
Being a Fruit Ninja variant, quick, precise swipes are necessary to maximize your score.  As a result, in the more difficult levels a mouse simply will not do. This leads to very frustrating misses and lower-than-expected scores. I can play this to a much better degree on my laptop's touchscreen, but touchscreen laptops are relatively new and not many people have them yet. I've given up playing this on my main PC and will only play it on my touchscreen laptop due to the significant frustration level when (trying to) play this with a mouse.
The game itself is very cute with a cutout-style art design and some of the levels are very challenging even with a touchscreen. The game really is a lot of fun. I don't care if this is an iOS/Android port, and I really wish that people would stop complaining about that like it's a bad thing. (The game as I write this is only $5, for crying out loud!) But unfortunately this is one game where it is better experienced on a touchscreen device.

Gone are the open "mini-arenas" where you fight hordes of enemies; difficult at times, but fair in the sense that you outrun the enemies and can take cover. Doom 3, on the other hand, just throws you into a narrow corridor, spawning enemies infront and behind you with no possibility for mobility and calls that fair?!?.
And so far, the game has not been difficult for any other reason than that you can not see your targets. That is the main killer for me with this game. So many times I've died not because the enemy would be particulary difficult to kill in itself, but when you get 0 vision, you can't aim. And that's where the BFG Edition comes in: It has a modern system with tac-lights strapped onto your gun (or yourself, whichever) and makes the game playable.
So yeah, stay away from the vanilla version and get the proper game. I'm not gonna write a more in-depth review here, since I'm moving over to the BFG edition and will review that instead.

Okay. I get this game came out in 2004 and it doesn't have the best graphics in the world.
But this game gave me the same rush of horror and suspense as Alien: Isolation, which came out 2 years ago.
DOOM 3 is by far one of the scariest games I've ever played. I've played almost all of the FNaF games, and they mainly use jumpscares of things literally jumping out in your face, and I would say it is a cheap way of scaring you. DOOM 3 uses things like suspense and things popping out not in your face, but just popping out of somewhere you didn't expect or couldn't see. For example, something that runs really fast might start running at you out of the darkness, where you can't see them beforehand and it catches you off-guard. One of the scariest enemies in the game is the simple infected human because of the awful groaning they make as they, ever so slowly, make their way to you, and you can't see them in the dark without your flashlight, so you might not know when they will strike, and it's truly horrifying.
Apart from the horror, this game is also a great shooter. There are many weapons that you will use at least once, even the pistol. They all have their advantages and disadvantages, so there is no perfect weapon. There are boss fights, shootouts, demon summonings, hordes, and just plain enemies around the station. Overall, DOOM 3 is the perfect combo of shooter and true horror.
There should have been a horror game category in the Steam Awards, because if there was, this should win it.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons likely contains the most human story to be told in a video game for the entire year of 2013. Dialogue is absent from the game entirely; instead, there is a tasteful reliance on visuals and sound to tell the tale, and boy oh boy (no pun intended), is this EVER a tale to be told.
The gameplay consists of moving two brothers simultaneously through a vivid fairytale. The player must use both brothers for problem solving, whether it is action-related, puzzle-related, or even a boss fight. There is no attack button, so don’t expect a hack and slash.

Train Simulator 2017 is an ultimate representation of the train driving profession, bearing extreme resemblence to the real experience of driving one of these beautiful beasts. Where to begin with this game.
I suppose in the modern age, it is probably best to start a review with the negative aspects, then move on to the positives. So i shall do just that.
TS20xx's biggest problem is that its engine is now coming up to nearly 10 years old, and is running as designed, as a 32bit piece of software. This brings with it the inherrent problem of a memory limit, that even large space aware, still only gives the engine a maximum of 4GB of ram to play with. With the newer routes, this unfortunately severely limits what content creators are able to do with the game.
Bugs - The game has its fair share of bugs. To be fair to DTG they are now slowly working through a long list and starting to fix content, but in all honesty there are a plethora of bugs that should never have made it past QA. I personally can live with the occasional bug popping up as long as it is not game breaking - I leave it up to you the reader whether you can.
The content. - Although the newer content has tended to be top notch, a lot of the older content, espeially the loco's have tended to be very bare bones and disinteresting, feeling bland and boring to drive at times. Given the age of the simulator, that isn't surprising, but I would warn the reader that they might be disapointed with what they recieve.
Now on to the positives.
The editing tools, although hard to grasp, are excellent and intuitive once you understand them and work with them. This allows content creators to create fun and engaging scenarios for the user base to play.
TS2017 comes with four (five with pioneers edition) routes for you to enjoy with many hours of content included. There are also multiple dlc's available for download which only add to the amount of hours of enjoyment available from the sim.
On the note of dlc - Yes there is a lot of it, but the beauty is you don't need all of it. You can pick and choose what you would like based on your personal preferences.
Overall, TSxx is a wonder to jump in and drive but isn't without its flaws - some of which are down to the age of the core engine.

Grand Theft Auto V used to be an extraordinary video game. A buddy of mine got it for me so him and I could play it on single player and mod the game to play LSPD:FR. LSPD:FR stands for, "Los Santos Police Department: First Response," and is a police modification in the game, where any player can partake in the role of any law enforcement official, ranging from federal, state, and local law enforcement jurisdiction.
In GTA V, I used the program, "OpenIV" to modify the game to my liking. I changed the game's police sirens to my local police department's sirens, my vehicle models to my local PD's vehicles and their exact lighting systems, I changed the police, EMS, and fire dept's uniforms to match that to my department's. I am a modder myself, and I specialize in vehicle decaling, and texturing of the like.
I've shown my vehicle decals and uniforms to my old police chief of my police department. I walked up to him one day and I showed him my beautiful creations. Needless to say, he loves them, and he wanted me to email him all of the images I have of them, and to keep him updated with anything new. So, with that being said, I did so.
He retired as police chief one day, and became chief of police of the state's university, and a new police chief stepped in, what used to be the assistant chief. I haven't had the time to show him yet, but I guarantee he'll LOVE them. The police department loves my vehicle and uniforms I've replicated of their department because I do one hell of a job.
To this day, I continue to play GTA V: LSPD:FR and continue to patrol as my city's police department and take good screenshots for my department to see. However, just recently, the program that was the basis of my modding, OpenIV, was legally shut down by Take Two.
This is a significant loss, as the basis of my modding has been legally shut down, for ridiculous reasons. I still have the program, and do not plan to get rid of it myself, no matter what Take Two says, I have lost all of my utmost respect for the developers of GTA V, thanks to Take Two. I no longer have any respect for them, and will continue to play the game how I want to, modded in single player.
A lot of these modifications tell the player not to go online, as they will get banned, and not to go online with any modified file to begin with. Modding in single player has no negative effect on the game in any way, shape, or form, period. It never has, and it never will. There are players who still continue to hack online servers and exploit the system, yet, what are they doing about it? Little to nothing.
Legally shutting down OpenIV does not hinder modders from modding, as we will always find a way to continue to mod the game as we please. It will also never stop hacking and exploiters in GTA V. In fact, shutting OpenIV down doesn't stop any hacker, period. You outdid yourselves this time, Take Two and Rockstar Games. This is by far, the WORST mistake you have ever made in your lifetime, and you will regret this, I assure you. Give it time, and you'll be regretting what you've done.
I know Rockstar is not the one who did the unreasonable action, however, they're the ones who let some crappy company take them over and buy them. Their fault, and their loss. This is the lesson they will learn. Wait until GTA V stops making the revenue it used to make.
-Sincerely,

When I was a kid I played Monkey Island and Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis so when I spotted this game on Steam and saw the fun, easy going attitude I simply couldn't resist it.
You're playing the local celebrity(?) Rufus who's dreaming about reaching Elysium, the city in the sky and, being the genious you are there's nothing that's gonna stop you.

In addition to the normal adventure clicker you also get to test your wits in some mini-puzzle games in order to progress (they're optional though so if you're not into that then there's a skip button although you won't get achievement for it).
The controls were easy since they were just point and click, the mouse-pointer showing you the options available and the scroll-down inventory was a nice touch as well.
As far as difficulty goes I'd say it's a little bit easier than the Monkey Island games while still hard enough to keep it interresting.
Cons: Low replay value (since you already know where to go, what to do etc) and I also felt as if the game was a bit short compared to for example the Monkey Island games.
Having trouble deciding weither to give it a 4 or a 3 due to the low replay value but I'm guessing that, based on the genre, nobody really expects that to be high anyway so... *drum roll*... 4 it is!

Yeeaaaaahhh..... I want to like it. I really do. I love the movies (well, the first ones anyhow), and I got this for free from selling cards, so maybe I shouldn't complain, but I feel like it was a waste even then. Lemme talk it through:
There are three characters to play. Yeah, so far that's the only cool part of this for me. There's the Alien, the Predator, and the human Soldier.
The soldier was the easiest to play. He was the only one that didn't have a bunch of weird and confusing controls and HUD. Not necessarily that he didn't have any work put into him. Actually I think it's good they left him so simple, otherwise he would be just as confusing and/or difficult to play as the others. He's just the basic soldier-y character, and was fun to play for a few minutes.
The Alien is the one you want to immediately jump to playing, naturally. What cooler character to be than an all-powerful alien crawling on ceilings and ripping apart humans. Except he can't. The crawling is hard because of his super-weird, eye-throbbing x-ray but not-x-ray vision. AND, no matter how hard I try, as soon as I'm seen by humans, they start shooting, and I have five seconds to panic, try to fight, and then die. I don't get it. He's more annoying to play than anything.
The Predator. I really, really thought I was going to enjoy being a super-strong, armored alien. But... he's really, really confusing, and hard to play. Now, there's the expected problems, because of the game being a tiny bit older. Jumping can be tricky, and turning and discriminating a black alien from a low-res brown wall can be a pain, but manageable. But then add a weird hieroglyphic power system, a slew of different weird weapons, and did I mention the power system?, all together makes for a mess of a hard-to-play extra-terrestrial.
So yeah, there's the problems with it being a bit old. But it's not that, it's the weird gameplay mechanics, poor design choices, and over-use of things that older games have obvious problems with anyways that really makes this a hard game to enjoy. I think they put more time into making it about three characters than making each character a good one. If it had JUST been the Alien to play, and they put all the effort on the one rather than three different characters, it would've been way better. I actually do kind of like it, but there's just poor choices here.
6/10, 'cause I wanna like it, but still, not Recommended

The music is great, the animations and graphics are great, the mechanics are unique and have more depth than any other fighting game I've played. And I really want to congratulate the devs and everyone involved on the great job they did on this game. Launch was smooth, the porting was done very well with amazing optimization, netcode is great, really polished game and extremely well done. You can really tell a lot of time, hard work, and care was put into the game and the port. Thank you Bandai Namco.

"STALKER: Clear Sky" is a good prequal to the 2007 title "STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl". "Good", not "great". While its strongest point is its plot (i.e., its part in the series), some areas of game felt a bit rushed.
You play as Scar, a mercenary whose exposure to the zone has caused his nervous system to start shutting down. Sorta. Each new emission is a tick on the countdown for him, but in the meantime he's hardened against some of the Zone's ill effects.
It's a good plotline, but the game has a different feel to it compared to the previous game.
Where SoC ("Shadow of Chernobyl") only emphasized factions as a plot device, CS makes them a central issue. At least, it often feels that way. Each map provides an overhead of the sparring factions, your relationship with each faction, and an overview of controlled territories. Your first mission is basically a tutorial on applying this information.
And zone "emissions" -- though not yet as important or troubling as in the third game ("STALKER: Call of Pripyat") -- are suddenly part of the environment, having seemingly been cut from the first game.
No hidden endings this time... because you should already know how it ends. As often happens with sequels, the final mission is action-oriented but feels very contrived. The ending movie provides great continuity with the first game's footage, solidifying "Clear Sky"'s place in the trilogy.
But don't stop now -- the best game is next.

Deponia invokes feelings reminiscent of playing those old adventure games from my youth. I played through the game without object highlighting, because only a defeated man makes use of that particular button of cowardice. Visually, Deponia excels. The characters and environments are consistently good throughout the entire game. While the humor does fall flat at times, the overall tone and presentation of the game harkens back to a time I remember with nostalgia. Rufus, the main protagonist in the game, is a deeply flawed character. He’s not a hero, but he’s persistent, goal orientated (haha), and in a weird way, endearing. And the puzzles. Modern adventure gaming, I feel, has become too streamlined and simplistic. Objects in many of the newer games have obvious purposes and the puzzles are too easy. This is not the case with Deponia, at least initially. The first “act” of the game takes place in a town filled with interesting objects to interact with and puzzles whose solutions are not readily apparent, but still approachable.
However, the quality of the puzzles, and to some degree, the game itself, degrades when you progress to the “second” and “third” acts. Certainly, Deponia gets progressively worse, as the environments become more linear, and the puzzles become more of a chore than an engaging game play element. That’s not to say that the more advanced stages lack puzzles that will give you some pause, they just don’t have very many of them. Without spoiling too much, the story and characters seem to suffer the same depreciation in quality to an extent. Furthermore, there’s a mini-game type puzzle at the end of the second portion of the game where I encountered a glitch that would not let me proceed, even though I had the correct solution. Luckily, I received a steam achievement upon configuring the solution, so I was able to overcome this glitch after several repetitions using the same configuration.
Overall, I would recommend Deponia to any fans of old adventure gaming, because many of its more charming elements have their roots in the old titles. I like the environments, puzzles, the artistic direction, and many of the characters. It is not a perfect game, nor is it the best in the genre, but if you can pick it up for half of its retail price, the game is worth looking into if you like point and click adventures.

Deponia is a adventure game of the type I like the most. Challenging puzzles, cartoony 2D-graphics, no action elemements and a good humorous story.
The best aspect of the game is probably the creative andsometimes quite challenging puzzles. In some adventure games the solution to a puzzle is almost immediately obvious because there are so few possible things to try. In Deponia trial and error is not a quick and easy approach, since there are many objects and lots of things to interact with. In particular in the first part of the game the puzzles require a bit of out of the box thinking without being unfair. Puzzles are also fairly varied and always feel like a natural part of the game rather than tacked on. My only complaint in this department is that the very end of the game is a bit anticlimactic in terms of puzzle difficulty.
The story is humorous and entertaining with unique character. The humour doesn't always work, but there are moments of brilliance, and it worked often enough to keep me entertained throughout. The ending is a bit disappointing but it does leave things at an appropriate starting point for the sequel.
The cartoony graphics are entirely appropriate given the general tone of the game and are high quality and quite distinctive. Characters each have their own unique appearance and do not look generic at all like they do in too many games.
Voice acting is above average but not exceeptional. The music has a unique style that is very appropriate given the particular setting and is quite appealing too.
All in all this is a highly recommended adventure game if you like pure point and click adventures with challenging puzzles and a healthy dose of humour.

Sniper Elite 3 (SE3) is, like it's predecessor, a third person game where you play as a US sniper who goes around and tries to sneakily whack people who are up to no good. Specifically Germans involved in creating "wunderwaffen", or "wonder weapons" such as the V1, V2, Me-262 and other such projects that, while coming too late to make much difference in the war (Germany was ♥♥♥♥ed by then), were nevertheless cutting edge technology for the time and were the first forms of some of the technologies that we still use today (Cruise Missiles, ICBM's/Atmospheric Rockets, and Jet Aircraft respectively). But since these are war efforts being made by the enemy, your job naturally is to mess them up.
Story-wise this game really isn't worth much. The "wonder weapon" showcased in this game is so impractical and absurdly large that it sucked me out of the story and made me think "yeah, this is a crock." And when a player's reaction to the core part of your game's story is that it is nonsense, then you have a real problem. In other words, you don't play this game for the story.
No, what you play it for is shooting people, and this game's rather uncomfortable need to show me in graphic slow-motion detail of how the bullets I shoot tunnel their way into another person's head/chest/etc and messes up their insides. This existed in SE2, but it seems to happen more often this time. And while you can skip it, I suppose the first few times it happens is kind of novel, if only to know where your bullets are headed. Otherwise, the game itself functions just fine. The stealth is better done, there are more toys to play with, and all the other sorts of little improvements you should expect from a game sequel.
But... here I come to a problem. I don't hate this game. I don't really dislike it. But I don't think it's very good either. It's fairly short, lacks in story, and the "killcam" thing messes up the game's pacing a fair bit (unless you skip it). In other words, this would be a "Maybe" on steam if that was an option, but it's not. If I had to give it an arbitrary "score" I'd say it's a 7/10, or "average".
But since we live in a world where so many things are "below average", particularly in the endless tide of nonsense that finds itself on Steam, an average competent semi-stealthy shooter game kinda does deserve a "yes", if only to distinguish it from all the garbage far worse than this game that deserves to be tossed into a bin and set on fire. SE3, for all it's faults, is not a bad game. Just... don't expect me to replay it unless I get a sudden urge to watch bullets tunnel their way into people's heads. :o

Total War and The Elder Scrolls had a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child. His name is Mount&Blade. He's great, just like his parents. But, he often ignored and kept under wraps. You won't find dozens of awards, nor will you find it in the annals of video game history, but it's still a good game and worth your money.
Graphics and music is Mount&Blade's weakest asset. It's ugly, plain and simple. Even on the highest quality available, it looks like an early to mid PlayStation 2 game. Yes, it was made in 2007. And yes, it's not made by a big studio. But, that doesn't excuse it. Look at Tekken 4 or 5. They look fantastic, and are much older than M&B. The men look like apes. The women have an eternal duck face. The scenery is nothing to write home about either. It's just bland.
The music is disappointing. While they do have the medieval atmosphere M&B aims for, it's just boring and uninteresting. It feels like stock music from a royalty-free website, the songs that have no character or soul. It's also very repetitive and wears on you quickly.
Now this is where the game starts to shine. Mount&Blade is a medieval sandbox. There are many ways you can play the game. There is no plot to the game, but there is a setting. This gives you free reign over how you conduct yourself. There is no final goal (outside of achievements), and you can't really lose. That being said, the real challenge is reaching the high point of any career. You may customize your character's face, skill, and history. The histories you choose determine your starting skills and items. Speaking of skills, you have a wide variety of skills, from combat to diplomacy to trading. You can customize every aspect of your character, from race to sex to fine facial features. You can also choose your starting location.
Since I mentioned the setting, let's talk about it. You start off as a nobody in a continent, called Calradia. There used to be a pseudo-Roman empire, but it's long gone. Now, there are six new kingdoms, all fighting to rule the world. You have the Swiss-Italian Rodoks, the French-English-German Swadians, the Mongolian Khergits, the Russian-Novgorod Vaegirs, the Norse Nords, and the Arab-Persian Sarranids. Each faction's military have their own strengths and weaknesses. Each faction also has a set of nobles with various personalities. Each noble has a family, with their own personalities. You may join any faction, and help out any noble or character.
The most obvious path you can take is the path of a warlord/general. About two-thirds of M&B revolve around combat. From warfare to bandit attacks, you will have to fight; most of the skill are, in one way or another, related to combat. To can visit cities and villages and recruit villages and mercenaries. Train them to become better soldiers. However, the better your soldiers, the higher their wages are. You also have to feed them, or else they will desert. You fight, train, fight, recruit, and fight. When you become famous enough, you can dabble in politics and become a noble. Eventually, you can form your own faction and conquer the world.
Or, you can be kingmaker, and support a usurper to the throne. Or you can be a bandit king, and fight off the law to make a profit. Or, you can be a merchant, and form a caravan that transports good from city to city. There are many, many ways you can play M&B, and there is no correct way.
It's Elder Scrolls, but you can raise an army. It's not a lazy cash grab nor a blatant rip-off. It feels like a small studio took their time to create a magnum opus on a tight budget. There is effort made to M&B, but it's not revolutionizing anything anytime soon.
Here is jewel of M&B. The vanilla game itself is okay. It has a great start and virtually infinite replayability, with all the possibilities you can play the game. Definitely worth buying, as it will eat up your precious time, if you are not prepared. However, the novelty fades quickly, and the quests can be bland and repetitive. For a game with lots of ways to play, there is not a lot of variety within each approach. Most factions are the same, with nothing unique, except for the location and military.
Like all jewels, the game can be polished. The fan base really outdid themselves this time. The fact that the game looks like♥♥♥♥♥is a blessing in disguise. This game is very easy to mod. And the fans have made very good mods. That keeps me hooked on playing. If you buy this game, I highly recommend you check out a few mods online and see for yourself.
Mount & Blade is a decent time waster. It's an ugly duckling that can be changed into a beautiful swan, and that's part of the magic of this game. It feels less like a complete game, and more like a skeleton, where independent developers can create their own game. And that is like buying multiple games for the price of one. For that, it's definitely worth a try. Happy fighting, or trading, or negotiating, or usurping.

This game is great when you spend a fortune of money for all the DLC. But come on, this game looks unfinished.
PROS:
Graphics Quality: Stunning, better than other train simulators I came across.
Amount of DLC: There is a lot to complete your collection, but there are gripes with this (see below), but overall there is a variety.
Workshop: The Community pays so much attention into detail in their scenarios, some of them even replicate a real life service.
CONS:
DLC Prices: Seriously, we have to pay £1000+ to get all routes and trains. Well a lot of the routes are good, but it comes to the trains. The recycled sounds, train physics. The DLC contains little effort for such a high price.
DLC Layout: You get less than 1/4 of the DLC when you buy the base game which means you have to spend a fortune for all DLC. All other games I played have their DLC in a bundle (Yes I know some DLC is bundled, I mean like there should be bundles for parts of countries (London and South East England, South West England, Anglia, Midlands etc.)
Settings Control: You can't tune settings whilst in a scenario which means you have to exit the scenario to change settings. Come on, no other game has this.
Bugs: Some of the older routes have bugs that have persisted into present time and have never been fixed.
Optimisation: Even on a high-end PC, you can't avoid crashes when on high graphics. This is my biggest criticism out of everything here since frequent crashes even on good computers isn't what we expect in 2017.
Simulation Accuracy: The train physics aren't very realistic, to slow/fast breaking and slow/fast acceleration, the class 466 included in the Sheerness Branch Extension route is the worst of all. Come on, stop rushing on your DLC and take your time to get the simulation accuracy excellent, in which I have to say, third-party developer Waggonz is the best of all. Also a lot of the trains don't have functioning destination displays (unless you go into Scenario Editor and change the destiination) and fully functioning headlights (You only get Day Head/Marker Lights and Tail Lights) and I know DTG have recently started this.
Train Sounds: A lot of the sounds of the trains are recycled from other trains and don't sound like the real thing. Please take the time to perform a recording session so you can record the exact sounds just like what Armstrong Powerhouse is doing.
OVERALL: A fairly good game, if only DTG wouldn't price so much for literally low-quality DLC and actually make it a proper, realistic simulator rather than do things enough to get a train moving.
Do I recommend it?: Only in a sale of at least 40% off.

Deponia is a adventure game of the type I like the most. Challenging puzzles, cartoony 2D-graphics, no action elemements and a good humorous story.
The best aspect of the game is probably the creative andsometimes quite challenging puzzles. In some adventure games the solution to a puzzle is almost immediately obvious because there are so few possible things to try. In Deponia trial and error is not a quick and easy approach, since there are many objects and lots of things to interact with. In particular in the first part of the game the puzzles require a bit of out of the box thinking without being unfair. Puzzles are also fairly varied and always feel like a natural part of the game rather than tacked on. My only complaint in this department is that the very end of the game is a bit anticlimactic in terms of puzzle difficulty.
The story is humorous and entertaining with unique character. The humour doesn't always work, but there are moments of brilliance, and it worked often enough to keep me entertained throughout. The ending is a bit disappointing but it does leave things at an appropriate starting point for the sequel.
The cartoony graphics are entirely appropriate given the general tone of the game and are high quality and quite distinctive. Characters each have their own unique appearance and do not look generic at all like they do in too many games.
Voice acting is above average but not exceeptional. The music has a unique style that is very appropriate given the particular setting and is quite appealing too.
All in all this is a highly recommended adventure game if you like pure point and click adventures with challenging puzzles and a healthy dose of humour.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R Clear Sky is the follow up to the sleeper hit Shadow of Chernobyl, a game that somehow managed to overcome it's many flaws and limitations and be a great game. Clear Sky brings along many new additions and upgrades, particularly in the graphics department. And while all of this sounds great on paper the only thing it manges to accomplish is driving home the point that there are no good or bad ideas, only good and bad executions.
The core gameplay remains the same, you are a "Stalker", a traveler in the cordoned off wasteland that surrounds Chernobyl. An area filled with radiation, mutated monsters and dangerous anomalies. Not to mention the rather high population of other stalkers and residents of "The Zone" that are also collecting the rare artifacts spawned by the anomalies and the various factions that each try to impose their own ideals on the zone and it's inhabitants.
The faction system is one of the major new features of Clear Sky. They will send off groups of stalkers on their own attempting to secure various points of importance throughout the game world and if you are allied with them you will often be asked to participate in various offensive and defensive actions as mini-missions. This makes the world seem much more alive and as there are not only constant movement around the maps but it's also directed movement, everybody trying to gain the upper hand.
The second big addition is the increased character customization. Your weapons and armor have many options that allow you to increase their potential in various ways. Many of the upgrades are exclusive as well so instead of making a super gun you have to specialize your weapons and armor. The developers have listened to the community as well and another part of this is the increased rarity of artifacts and the increased difficulty in collection them which is a very welcome addition.
The unfortunate truth however is that both these additions come in a heavily flawed state and especially the faction system will lead to many hours of frustration. The game still has that "raw" feeling, despite the improved graphics, and where in Shadow of Chernobyl this was mostly forgivable the increased problems with Clear Sky makes it come out at you much more.
Clear Sky is a unfortunate sequel that hasn't quite grown enough since Shadow of Chernobyl. It still has all of the problems that Shadow of Chernobyl and adds several of it's own which leads to a sequel that is less than it's predecessor.

I dont know whether whimsical thumbstick adventure is a genre or a thing or whatever, but to say that Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is just that would be an injustice towards the title. Its minimalistic yet rich storytelling draws children of all ages in and while it offers little replay value and only lasts for an afternoon, it still qualifies as a gem. Lush, vibrant summits surround the two brothers gone on a quest to heal their father. The puzzles are pretty simplistic and the only initial difficulty will probably be struggling to teach your brain which thumb is which character, but the streamlined journey is less about overcoming challenges and more about watching the plot unfold.
BUY it if you:
- Own a controller
- Value storytelling and polished art direction over all other aspects of a game
- Would like an indie (alternative) structure with a high-end art direction.
DO NOT BUY it if:
- You expect long hours out of every dollar you spend on games.
- You cannot abide a lack of replay value / violence / difficult puzzles
- Your eyes may feel abused and slightly inflamed after exposure to Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons. This may especially be a problem if you wear contact lenses or big horse blinkers. Ask your video game dealer to suggest some less visually demanding entertainment immediately.

Overall, I would highly recommend this game. It plays like an adventure game with puzzle elements (but I wouldn't call it a puzzle game in itself).

Though my play time says I've only played this for fifteen minutes, rest assured, I played and completed this entire game. It took me many years to work my way through Doom 3, on multiple copies of the game.
Doom 3 is a game that wants to be many things. It is good at basically none of them. Many of the things it wants to be contradict each other. It wants to be scary, but it also wants to be macho action. It wants to be Half-Life (and specifically Half-Life), but it also wants to stay Doom.
It is neither scary nor action-packed, its story doesn't make any sense, and its villain doesn't actually state any real intended motive. Demons arrive on Mars with the help of Dr. Betruger and want to use our space ships to travel to earth. Think about that for a moment: demons have to use our ships for their invasion, and the game goes out of its way to imply they're rare enough that they aren't readily available. When the first 15 or 20 demons get to earth, what do they think will happen when they get there? Do they think they'll just order another shipment of demons from Mars until, 20 demons at a time, they've conquered the entire planet, unopposed?
And why does Betruger want to help the demons reach earth? He just does, because that's all the reason anyone needs, apparently. There are dozens of email logs, a bunch of lore about the origin of the demons and why a portal to hell even exists, but the antagonist is evil just because he's evil, like a Saturday Morning Cartoon villain.
The real heart of the problem is the gameplay. Flashlight issues aside, gun play is slow and clumsy. Weapons take forever to reload, and once you start reloading your gun, you can't switch to something else. Often I'd get in to scenarios where I'd empty the clip in one gun, only to have my character start reloading it automatically, locking me in to a long animation. Your only option in that scenario is to watch your character slowly slot each individual shotgun shell in to the barrel, all the while helplessly dancing around incoming enemies. This feels like a horror game mechanic designed to make you panic, but it most frequently happened to me during a part of the game where it's trying to ramp up the action. It creates a very frustrating disconnect, because any logical human would just switch to a different weapon and reload that other gun later.
And then there's the ending, with one of the most limp final bosses I've ever encountered and a crummy cliffhanger to set up the expansion pack, Resurrection of Evil. The last thing I wanted out of this game at the end was a stupid "Gotcha!" moment, but that's exactly what it has.
Doom 3 has a reputation that can't be ignored, but I figured it was at least interesting enough to see through to the end. I was wrong. Curiosity killed the Cacodemon.

It's been more than ten years since I last touched this game and I'm glad to notice it hasn't aged much; in fact, it's still clearly better than Colonial Marines. The game's map design seems bland at times in terms of details but the game relies so much on lighting and ambient sounds that often you don't even notice the blocky design. All three species are well represented: The Marine is a weakling facing overwhelming odds, the Predator a seasoned (but slow) veteran capable of one-hit killing Xenomorphs with his wristblades, and the Xenomorph (Alien) opens up routes beyond the reaches of humans & predators. The game's incredible speed may disorient at first but it really fits and makes the game more intense. One thing I particularly liked is how in those Marine & Predator maps where you face aliens you can never rely on being absolutely safe; waste too much time doing nothing and more aliens will spawn to come and get you. The game has its drawbacks such as its often confusing map layouts, especially in some of the Alien campaign maps, and the lack of a relevant story, but these are rather minor issues. Beaware; the game is harder on normal than the vast majority of games are on hard, and it's only made harder by the limited number of saves (four on normal) you get per level.

Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 is an example of how to do First-Person-Shooters right. The fast gameplay requires more skill and focus than most modern First-Person-Shooters. Instead of trying to level up your character to get OP weapons, most weapons have a legitimate purpose, and most of them don't feel too overpowered (except Disc, Pred Pistol, Skeeter, and Sadar. Not to forget Mines). Instead of grinding to get perks to power yourself up, Aliens versus Predator requires skill from the start.
Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 allows the player to take control of three species, Aliens, Predators, or the human Marines. Each have their advantages and disadvantages.
The Alien is a melee only species, a hurtful disadvantage, but because of their speed and wallcrawling ability the Aliens have, they're a worthy enemy. Aliens also can smell the scents of other beings, allowing it to see its victims in the dark. The Alien regains health by headbiting Predators and Humans, you can do this on both the living and the dead. Obviously headbiting live beings is harder than dead ones, but gains back more health.
The Predator is a mix of Melee and ranged weapons. The majority of his weapons, Medicomp, and cloak are powered by '
'. This will slowly recharge if you are not using anything that uses charge, or you can find field-charge items around the map which will automatically give you full energy. The only weapons that don't use energy are the Wristblades, and Disc (Unless you use the recall ability, this will use a small amount of energy), as well as the Speargun. But this uses ammo, which only replenishes upon death. The Predator can heal using his Medicomp, this will use a large amount of energy, but puts you back to full health everytime (
). In some of the bonus levels the Predator gains a new gadget, the grappling hook, which can pull him to higher heights. The Predator also has three vision modes, which can help him spot enemies. The first vision mode can help spot humans, the second aliens, and the third other Predators and field-charges (Of course you also have the default normal vision).
The Marine is a ranged only species. The marine uses weapons like the pulse rifle, smartgun, minigun, etc. The Marine replenishes health with medkits, found about through-out levels. The marine can use armor, which can protect against Alien acid and absorbs small amounts of damage. In some of the bonus levels the Marines get a jetpack! In multiplayer Marines can select a specialist sub-class, this will allow them to pick from any of the weapons in the game (unless game host restricted it), and you will always spawn with the selected weapon, but you can only use that weapon (and the pistol).
Each species can unlock bonus missions after you complete the main game, (you will unlock more if you beat it on a higher difficulty) these levels are the levels from other species singleplayer, for example: You can unlock a backwards version of the Predator's first level as Marine if you beat the Marine SP on Director's cut [Hard].
Not to forget, you can unlock cheat options in the game by completing certain objectives through-out the levels. These can be things like slow-mo whenever you are near enemies. Or unlimited speargun ammo and more spears per shot as Predator.
The Multiplayer is where this game shines most. Fast gameplay and the different play-styles of each species make for very fun and memorable experience. This is one of the fastest games ever, you will die, fast, and a lot. While Alien and Marine gameplay is fairly balanced, their's no denying that the predator is too overpowered, but the multiplayer is fun, nonetheless. But, unfortunately, this game has a small player base, so at times you may not be able to find a game. Because of this the community doesn't play competitively [most of the time], anymore. Servers will also usually have a small amount of players. 8-player games are kinda rare, but when they happen, it's a lot of fun!
Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 is easily one of the best games ever made.

The jokes are on point, combat is fun, throwbacks to even more early episodes, dialogs are so well written that I spent a lot of time standing still and try things out only to listen to npcs talking. This is South Park.

Overall a big upgrade to the first game, I laughed way too much when playing this game.
Combat is "too easy" even on the hardest difficulty, the grid styled battles are fun, but you are required to choose a skill that can hit enemies on your side since you can't rotate your skills, which is a downside.
Outfits not having any stats is a big upgrade in my opinion, since it allows me to use the outfit that looks the best to me.
DNA "upgrade" function is really neat, but seems like it's lacking something.
Puzzles in this game are easy, so if you're looking for some intriguing puzzles, this may not be the game for you.
Side quests are basically references to the show, and are worth doing for the timefart upgrades, and the laughs, there are however some side quests that feel like they've been rushed or just left unpolished, I'm talking about the Gay Fish quest, and the "flappy bird" minigame, the only moment where I actually cringed while playing this game.
The game runs smoothly at 144fps for me, and I've encountered one bug that required me to load autosave, it was when Coon and Friends battled the Freedom Pals on the playground, Doctor Timothy's turn came up and he ended up doing nothing for approximately 10 minutes, which is when I loaded my last save and succesfully completed the battle.
There have been some minor graphical glitches such as paintings being on top of characters.
Overall I'd say that this game is 9/10.
If you like South Park, and enjoyed Stick of Truth, you will enjoy this game.
