As a hardcore player I have both positive and negative opinions on this title:
- Satisfying combat.
- Plenty of items and gear.
- Friendly to casual players.
- Randomly generated areas.
- Unique and appealing graphics style.
- Great soundtrack and sound effects.
- Good Co-Op gameplay.
- Save your progress anywhere anytime.
- Decent side quests and challenges.
- Character classes not locked to certain weapons or gear.
- Mod supported.
- Plenty of different enemies and areas.
- Only 4 main classes.
- Lackluster skill trees.
- Unappealing, almost non-existing storyline.
- Short completion time (for hardcore players).
- Almost no voice acting.
If you are experienced make sure to set your difficulty to a high one. I played through the game in two evenings with a friend on Normal which was a mistake from our side. If you are new Normal is fine, if you have kids who wants to play, this game is great for that audience. You can disable blood if that is an issue as well. This is not to be confused with TL2 only being a casual kids game.
If you like a good storyline that immerses you further this game does
offer that. Especially when most of the characters doesn't even have voice acting. It was a let down for sure.
If you are looking for a complex skillsystem this game does not offer that either. Surely there are skills and combinations that are more complicated but perhaps not from hardcore player's eyes. Since there are just a few skills to choose from, you won't have much choice early on since you unlock the skills as you level up. The skills themselves however can be leveled up individually to grant them greater powers and enhancements. It doesn't really compensate the simplicity and limitations however.
If you are looking for a more casual Action-RPG with satisfying combat, exploration, loot, gear and unique look, this game is for you. You don't have to just be a casual gamer to play it but I feel it is aimed more towards this audience.
if you don't consider the storyline and don't bother too much with a complex skill system.
I'd still recommend it to hardcore players if you keep the previous in mind. The game has end-game maps/dungeons that you can play for greater rewards at high levels and you can have it set to a hard difficulty for the challenge as well. Other than that I didn't feel that the replay value was that good.
For casual players = 8.5/10
For hardcore players = 7.5/10

This game is like Fruit Ninja with a twist.
You play as Jack Lumber. A lumberjack who at a young age, witnessed his grandmother get killed by a rouge pine tree. He then gets revenge by cutting all of the trees in the world down.
So at the start of each level, Jack grabs his ax and sends an electric shock through the forest. Sending every tree up into the air. As they fall down, you have to draw a line through the logs to slice them in half. It starts off with normal logs, but then L, U, and T shaped logs come into play as well as logs that need to be cut 2 or 3 times.
At the end of each level, an animal appears inthe middle of a formation of logs. If you slice the animal, you fail, but if you dont, after each level, all of the animals you collect appear in your cabin. You can click them and they will bounce around. When my 8 year old sister watches me play this game, watching the animals jump around is her favorite part.
Depending on how well you do, you get a one, teo, or three star rating,which is represented by a gold, silver, or bronze sash on the critter at the end of each level. Later in the game, you unlock different zones by having certain amounts of stars. This reminds me of Angry Birds or something.

Okay, I was sketchy on this game at first, but once I played it, I thought it was actually fun. Now yes, it's a free game (At least I think for now), and it's new, and yes it has bugs. Some people just don't have enough money for Steep, so they'd like something else that was close to it, and yet get it for little to no price. That's what this game is for. Cons:

With all this said, I say this game is fun, especially with friends. If you like long, slow and drawn out turtling matches that resort to nothing but lobbing artillery at each other, Wargame: Red Dragon is for you.

Very realistic in its approach to modern combat, Wargame: Red Dragon has never bored, even after over 400 hours of gameplay.
Unlike other RTS games, Wargame has no base building, instead you call in units from a reserve pool, which is determined by your choices when you build your army or 'Deck'. Deck building is a great part of the game and one seldom seen in any other RTS. There are many different Deck types for each nation, allowing you to specialize in one particular type of unit or warfare with choices all along the way about trading off quality for quantity. This makes deck building a worthwhile task where striking the right balance for your playstyle is a rewarding exprience.
Although I can't speak for singleplayer, the multiplayer of the game is also well thought out. The main mode is destruction, where the principle objective is to desroy a certain amount of enemy units. Some might think this is encouragement to camp, however the game gives an incentive to fight over the strategic territory because control zones dictate point income. The person who simply camps at his base will lose because his opponent will have many times his income and can simply overwhelm him with sheer numbers. This forces players to strike a balance and use units intelligently to gain the upper hand.
The only complaints I have with Red Dragon are some minor graphical glitches, very weak sound design in many areas, and the fact that some of the multiplayer community are not the friendliest to say the least, but this is not the game's fault.
But in conclusion, I think  Red Dragon is a worthy sucessor to Airland Battle. The maps are huge, and the unit and nation slection is unparalled. This mix allows for an insane amount of tactical diversity. One minute you could be ambushing vehicles in a mountain pass, and in another you could be fighting a fleet action. Combining this with well thought out multiplayer modes and great looking graphics and you have a recipe for one of the best RTS games out there. Although the steep learning curve may turn off some not willing to learn the game's intricacies, If you stick with it you will find that Wargame is a rewarding and satisfying experience. I only wish that Eugen will return to it after the failure of Steel Division and continue to add content to this fantastic game.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons goes smoothly and easily. It plays very fluently, without any significant challenges or tough brain-torturing puzzles.. it also lasts only around 2,5-3 hours of pure gameplay (although you may want to play it again and get all the achievements if you don't manage to do so in your first playthrough - because in this particular case, the achievements are clever, little and very touching hidden stories you may or may not trigger during your playthrough.. going for them WILL improve the whole emotional appeal of this game). NEVERTHELESS, you really should give it a shot and don't let yourself be driven away by those facts. This game is not about challenge, nor about platforming and puzzle solving (even though I have to say that some parts of the gameplay are immensely original and you will find yourself smiling and telling yourself "That's a great idea!").. the point is simple. The experience you get to live through. Marvellous graphics (no screenshot will be able to truly give you the same feeling as you yourself running around and witnessing it all in motion), very lovely and fitting music and... the story that WILL leave you deeply touched. These three elements are combined with such ease and beauty that this game can't be very well compared to anything else in current gaming - except maybe the game ICO combined with a bit of Shadow of the Collossus for the PS2 and To The Moon for PC.  Don't take it as a game, don't go to it for action, brain tease or a test of your reflexes. Just buy it, give yourself a free afternoon alone and go through it as if you've read a book. At the end, you will understand why the game is called "A Tale".

One of the most interesting game mechanics I've seen for a while, attached to an enjoyable, if brief game. The path you lead is very restricted, to the point where there is rarely a *choice* in how to proceed, which reduces the challenge, but the controls make playing it enjoyable regardless (they aren't lying about needing a control pad by the way - the game is impossible without it!)
The story is notable too; it starts off innocently enough but as you progress the tone becomes increasingly dark and melancholy. It's worth playing just for the way events are handled at the game's climax - I won't spoil the story, suffice to say the writers know how to pull the rug from under you.
Overall Brothers is interesting. There's a load of potential in the gameplay and the story is effective. It's just too short and I'd really like to see what else can be done with the concept.

WARNING: The game is now entirely broken on Surface Pro 3 and will no longer load at all. After spending hundreds of dollars on DLC and 200+ hours in RailWorks+TS, it suddenly no longer works. WAS: TS has been the best actual simulator of railroads, but has offered numerous frustrations which I've tolerated. But upon hearing the release plans for TS2017+, I am depressed that it is no longer a viable use of my time and I have wasted hundreds of dollars for years for nothing.
I'm extremely disappointed in:
- the yearly releases that don't add or fix anything for existing players, without requiring those players to fork over extra money for new routes
- the astoundingly overpriced DLC which has many bugs
- the extraordinary lag even on new computers with dedicated GPUs (you can disable lighting but that actually ruins nighttime visibility on some routes and actively removes scenery from others, making them as useless as wireframe)
But most of all, I'm disappointed that every bit of content I bought is now worthless in the "World Edition" which we're being asked to buy. How do the developers expect me to keep gigs upon gigs of binaries & content which I can only play in my old version, and get a new edition comprising gigs upon gigs which I can only play separately? New gamers beware: I can't recommend buying 2017 because you'll have to keep it as a separate game and have to install a future edition that won't play any of the routes you received (or ANYTHING else currently available for sale - look it up, it's true).
Existing gamers, which are bread-and-butter for competitor developers like Auran, already know that this team's behavior is pathetic. This is just the nail in the coffin.

I have mixed opinions about this game.
First off, it isn't really a game, but a simulator. Even then the quality of simulation varies from locomotive to locomotive (will talk about this later)
One thing that a lot of people here mention and what has been picked up by some tech "journalists" is that there are a couple of thousand dollars worth of DLC. At first glance, this seems insane, and it is. If you are buying all of the DLC's you are insane.
What I and others believe the intention of the thousands in DLC is for users like you and me to select routes and locomotives that we like. For example, you might want to simulate the North West of England during the early 80's, and it's possible to do that. Others may want to simulate the modern day North East of the united states and it's possible to do that. If all of the DLC's were included in the base game, it would be a $2,000+ game that's over 100 GB and people would say it's too expensive and too bloated. In concept, I believe this system of fine tuning your experience is fine, and works out for everyone.
If you paid attention, I used in concept instead of in practice. I've had Train Simulator since before it was even called Train Simulator and was called Railworks. In that time, it hasn't really changed that much. There have been some improvements here and there, but nothing game changing. With the DLC's though, its a different story. Once a DLC is made, that's it. It's never updated. Ever. I personally don't have them, but there are reviews of some locomotives today from people who've had the DLC since it was relaeased two years ago complaining about bugs that it's had since day 1. Another problem is the consistency of the quality. You'll find that some locomotives are super realistic, with many of the buttons and controls actually doing something like guard buzzers and windows opening, the modelling being super accurate along with the sounds. Then you'll have ones that have throttle, brake, reverser, horn and light control being on, off, or red and that's it. The models will be OK, and the graphics will be photorealistc, in the sense that someone has taken a photo of a gauge cluster in poor light and from far away, and then cut and pasted that photo on to the model.
I think the real kick is that in a year or two, Dovetail will be releasing a new Train Simulator on a new engine and they will be opening up to hopefully increase the variety of DLC's

I’ve never rage-quitted a game more than this, but the magic of Spelunky keeps me going back for more – adventure, the sense of achievement, or just to♥♥♥♥♥♥the shopkeeper off.
There's no turning back once you've bought Spelunky. Even if you're not a fan of platformers, give Spelunky a chance, and you'll never see platformers the same way again. Judging by the lot of wasted hours I've spent on this game, there's only two outcomes you'll get after playing a few (or ten times more) rounds - rage-quitting because you got nibbled by a bat, or celebrating because you've successfully led the shopkeeper into your strategic trap.
Although Spelunky might seem like an easy adventure game, my hours in this game have never got me past Level 3-1 (i.e. Ice Caves). It took me more than a month to discover Level 2-1 (i.e. Jungle) but the sense of achievement made it all worth it. Even though I've been stuck in the Mines for a hell lot of time, I'm still surprised at the wonders it can create. There are so many mysteries to the game that even being in the same location wouldn't make it boring. From trying to sacrifice two damsels within the same location, to getting the key to the chest, or finding the Black Market in the Jungle, the yearn to play Spelunky never ceases.
In my opinion, Spelunky is also a game of speed, skill and strategy. One example would be the many ways to survive the arrow trap, which would cause you a minus two health if shot. Personally, I know three options, though I mostly use two and there may be more out there. You could take the risk and jump, while whipping the arrow with a carefully timed hit. Or, throw an item infront of the trap, be it a bomb, rock, damsel (I'm sorry.) or an arrow from another trap. Get a taste of your own medicine! The last option would be leading a monster close enough to the trap without endangering yourself, such as a spider or bat, but you'll need to be pretty lucky for them to spawn near the trap.
I guarantee you lots of "Oh,♥♥♥♥♥♥" or "What the hell?" moments as you venture through the forever changing walls of Spelunky. Ranging from times when the stupid damsel decides to suicide into the spikes, to times when you did so much to please Kali and she gives you smoke, and smoke only. There will also be times of laughter (not to forget tears of pain and disappointment) when you hopelessly fall into a river of piranhas and somehow manage to survive with one health left.
I would definitely recommend this game if you're a fan of platformers or roguelike games, or if you just have too much times in your hands and are hoping to find a game to waste your time. Even if you aren't, I'll urge you to give it a try!
I may have missed out a point or two, but I hope you get my message! Spelunky is an awfully awesome game, and I believe it definitely has a spell casted on it or something for me to keep wanting to play even though I've died close to 1000 times.

My opinion of this game has improved greatly over time.
After my first play-through, I would have described this as the most overrated game ever.  I thought that the game was too dark, too narrow, and too difficult.  In retrospect, I didn't give Doom 3 a completely fair shake.  On that first play-through, I immediately cranked up the gamma, I clung stubbornly to my two favorite weapons in every combat situation, and I resorted to cheat-codes to get me through large portions of the game.  I also mostly ignored the various computer screens and audio logs and just barreled forward as quickly as possible.
I kept hearing other people rave about the game though, so I gave it a second chance and then a third chance.  And each time I've played it, I've enjoyed it a bit more.  I started taking my time, carefully choosing different weapons for different situations, and savoring the story told through the audio logs and emails.  At this point I feel that some of my initial criticisms were accurate while others were unfair.
One of the controversial decisions the game designers made was to make you switch between your flashlight and weapon.  When I first got the game, on the recommendation of friends, I immediately installed a mod to enable the flashlight at all times.  However, on subsequent play-throughs I decided to play the game as it was intended, and I have to admit it does make many sections of the game a lot scarier.  However I do think the game goes too far in how dark it keeps everything.  It's one thing to include a few pitch-black sections, but even the brightest sections of this game are ridiculously dark; heck, even the first chapter--when the base is fully operational--is pretty dark.  I'm not sure if this was done to try to make the game scarier or to emphasize the strengths of the graphics engine, but either way I think it was a mistake not to include some well-lit areas.
The graphics are, of course, very good.  They didn't make my jaw drop the way I expected (based on the pre-release hype), but it's certainly the best looking game of its time and the graphics engine is rock solid.  The levels are pretty large, load times are surprisingly short, and my frame-rate was always smooth as can be.  The graphics also appear to scale well to both older and newer systems.  There were a few innovative visual effects that I liked, such as when you stood at the edge of a steaming lava pit or looked through a thick window pane.
It's clear that an effort was made to give Doom 3 a more realistic feel than the original Doom, and this is most obvious when comparing the new look of the monsters to what they used to look like.  An unfortunate downside is that the new enemies have less personality and are less distinctive from one another than they used to be.  In particular, I dislike the texture that was used for the skin of almost every monster - is it flesh? hide? carbon-fiber?  I thought it looked a little too shiny and inorganic.  But those minor complaints aside, the new enemy designs are pretty convincing and some of them are downright frightening to see up close.
Where the game disappointed me most was in the level design, especially in the early sections of the game.  What I disliked was how small and confined every area was.  In the first third of the game, every single fight takes place in a narrow hallway or cramped office.  It gets a little better later in the game, but not much better.  Even the boss fights take place in surprisingly small areas, and the brief 'outdoor' sections are a joke.  The facility you are exploring feels like a real-world location, but there isn't much diversity between the various areas of the base, and there are very few sections that wowed me.  Remember how when you first played Half-Life, you experienced a "holy s---!' moment around ever corner?  There are very few of those type of awe inspiring moments in Doom 3.
Another major complaint I have about this game is the way that bullets bounce off of objects, surfaces, and even enemies in a very unconvincing manner.  Almost none of the environment is destructible.  Computer screens appear to be bullet-proof, office knick-knacks all seem to be glued to desks, and windows survive even the largest explosions.  Furthermore, ricocheting bullets sound the same whether you are shooting a window, a metal girder, or a zombie's flesh.  And worst of all, aside from some blood spatters (which it's too dark to see anyway), there isn't much feedback on whether you are damaging the monster you're fighting or not.  In the original Doom, shooting any of the smaller enemies would cause them to groan and stagger backwards; in Doom 3 they shrug it off and keep charging.  This hampers the gameplay significantly and results in all of the guns feeling less powerful than they really are.
Once you get into the rhythm of the game and familiar with the various enemies, the combat is pretty satisfying.  Some people might find it repetitious by the end, but I never got tired of it.  And now that I've played the game a few times on a few different difficulties, I feel comfortable stating that the difficulty is actually very well balanced.  There are nine different weapons available, with different strengths and weaknesses.  A few of the guns are overpowered in my opinion, but none of them are completely useless.  (The chainsaw is back, and is as much fun to use as ever.)
Despite the linear nature of the level design, the pacing of the enemy encounters is well planned.  Instead of putting a monster behind every corner, there are plenty of sections with no enemies which builds up suspense nicely.  There are also a lot of well scripted encounters with waves of enemies teleporting in all around you.  The one mistake the game makes, however, is delivering certain enemies too often and others not often enough.  Some of the more interesting demons barely make an appearance, while the imps show up again and again and again in every stage of the game.
Doom 3 will probably take you around 20 hours to complete.  The story and the way the story is told borrows a lot from both Half-Life and System Shock 2.  The game gives you access to various characters' emails and audio logs through a PDA interface.  Technically, you could play through the entire game without ever opening your PDA, but if you do so you'll miss out, since most of the game's storytelling happens through the email and audio logs you find.  Many of the email messages are typical mundane office chatter that simply give you a sense of what life was like on the base before your arrival, while the audio logs document recent events that led up to the horror you are now experiencing.  Together, they help to give a bit of background and life to the otherwise barren environments.  (And the writing and voice acting are both very good.)
One feature I really liked was how the game lets you interact with computer screens (to open doors, operate machinery, etc.); as you get close to a screen, your crosshair changes to a mouse cursor, while still centered where you are looking.  It's a very simple thing, but I've never seen another game handle 'use' buttons quite this elegantly.
Finally, I was surprised to see that this game limits you to only run in short bursts, and that you need to hold down a key to do so.  This is a feature that would make sense in a tactical shooter, but it seems out of place in the Doom series, where half your time is spent dodging fireballs.
In conclusion: I don't think I've ever had my opinion of a game improve so drastically over the years.  I still think Doom 3 is slightly overrated; it's not in the same league as the games it most resembles - Doom, Half-Life, and System Shock 2.  But it is a solid gaming experience that I would recommend to anyone, especially to hard-core FPS players and fans of horror. (If you are offended by demonic images or excessive gore you should probably stay away.)

Everyone likes a burly Lumber jack right? Well, we certainly do. And he comes in the form of Jack Lumber. Upon first playing Jack Lumber by OwlchemyLabs, we thought it was just a Fruit Ninja clone. But oh were we wrong. Jack Lumber is much more than a fruit ninja clone. Owlchemy Labs has created an interesting and creative world based on over the top puns. Throw in a simple, yet humorous story, and you have a nicely designed game.
Jack Lumber is a lumberjack who has vowed to kill all the evil trees using his time-freezing, lumberjacking skills, for revenge against the evil trees that murdered his sweet granny. Its silly, but its also a simple pick up and play game for any age group. The key concept of the game is to cut the logs that fly up on the screen by tracing a log through them. What’s also nice is that there is no microtransaction system that the developers added. And in our books, that’s a win-win.
For consumers that have a budget, and simply want the most bang for their buck, Jack Lumber certainly delivers. All in all Jack Lumber is a pretty-straight forward game that we recommend you pick up.

This is easily one of my favorite games of all time.
The thing that really surprises me is that I personally have lost a lot of interest in so-called 'sand box' games that aren't open world, they are just a voxel engine where you are expected to make the game fun on your own.
Mount and Blade is open world and sand box in that you aren't really given an objective early on and the game certainly doesn't hold your hand or explain exactly what you need to do, but there's still a very active game world with wars being fought and uneasy peaces made in the face of greater threats, secret back stabbing plots between competing nobles and alliances sealed with marriages.
The battles are also a lot of fun, a very brutal and unforgiving sort of hack and slash combat, though anything can get reptitive given enough time.
But the most amazing part of the game is really the mods out there. Everything from Star Wars to Medieval Europe to WWI to Napoleonic wars. The engine seems to be very versatile.
If the game has any glaring flaws it's that it has a very aging graphical and audio presentation. It was very bare bones even on its release and now it's really poor locking compared with other more modern games. If that's someting you can deal with then perhaps stay away. Otherwise I can't recommend this game enough.

This game is one of the best games out there. It has terrific gameplay, an amazing combat system, an active and diverse modding community, an extraordinary singleplayer and multiplayer.
The Combat.
So the combat is one of the best out there, i'm being serious, you have to move your mouse in the direction you want to swing/stab in OR which direction you wish to block. This combat, especially for a 2008 game, is unique for this type of game. Things start to get intense when you're surrounded by your foes, swinging their blades into your chainmail, and you're trying to back up whilst blocking off their attacks.
The Singleplayer.
I have mainly invested 600+ Hours into this game purely for its singleplayer. The singleplayer is basic, yet so interesting and intruguing. You start off with basically nothing and have to work your way up to claim Calradia as your own. Along the way you will have to fight off the other Kingdoms and Lords, but be hasty, you're a 'foreigner or commoner' to them. You will also find your trusty companions (favourite is marnid c'mon lads) to help you with your quests, maybe to send them to get a peace treaty or maybe send them to spread your claim about ruling Calradia. The thing that really gets me about the Singleplayer is just how it's made, It's kind've like Total War but more in-depth by far.
The Multiplayer.
Another reason to get this game is its Multiplayer. Multiple different mods have been based just on the Multiplayer, for example the mod 'Star Wars: Bear Force II' or 'The Fall of Mordor', Two active multiplayer mods. In Multiplayer, it is just combat, not like singleplayer with a map and a party. Personally, i didn't get the game for multiplayer, i got it for singleplayer.
The Modding Community.
Mount and Blade: Warband's Modding Community is so diverse and filled with so many great mods. The mods can range from the Napaelonic Era to Zombies! I just... Go look at the mods for yourself.
The Graphics.
Sure, the graphics are bad, so what? Graphics aren't what make a game. A Game is itself, its gameplay.
I would rate this game an outstanding 10/10. Stop reading this and GO PLAY IT!

Dystopian future Monkey Island, what more do you want? Some fiendish puzzles mixed in with great characters and killer lines.
The animations can be a little rough around the edges at times, but it only serves to add to the indie-esque charm of Deponia. Unique, charming, hilarious and a brilliantly written main character make this a must buy if you can get it on sale.

Review time for Deponia.
Story- Deponia is a world of trash... literally. The people live in trash on top of mountains of trash making a living from trash. But for a brash, lazy, young Rufus, he wanted more. So in his latest hair-brained scheme to escape to Elesium, he saves a a damsel in distress from a militant group and finds himself mixed in a conspiracy that will affect everyone on Deponia. The story is a good bit of comedy in the vein of Lucas Arts "The Curse of Monkey Island" with memorable characters and involving plot twists. The world in the story is also very imaginative and filled with a lot of potetial for exploration. A+
Graphics- Those who are familiar with "The Curse of Monkey Island" may see a lot of similarities in art style. It does show that many of the developers and artist were fans of Lucas Arts. But dispite similarities, this game is a whole new beast and completely original in character design and world creation and is every well done. The cutscenes are also very well done and is like looking at a cartoon television show. A
Sound- The voice acting in this game is spot on in terms of delivery, though the lip-sync can be terribly off which was a little bit destracting, but not unforgivable. As for the music... I LOVE THE MUSIC! There is a very good mix of ballads, a touch of hip-hop and just fun altogether. A+
Gameplay- Simple, straight forward point and click interface with combining items for more items. If you've played old school adventure games before then it is very familiar territory. There is also a fair amount of challenges and puzzles that will keep you puzzled but if your stuck, there is an option to skip it. B
Overall- A fantasic throw back for fans of old style P.O.C. games with a fantastic story, great characters and music that should not be missed. Highly recomended. A

Out of those train simulators i have. Trainz 2010, Trainz 2012 and Railworks 2017
Over all, for those who want realism and a proper simulation with graphics railworks do the work even if its a big DLC simulator, it do physics well and has far better graphics than Trainz ( depending on asset ). Gameplay wise... well, if you cross a red signal, thats it! you have to restart compared to Trainz where it simply either cuts or just let you continue on.
Trainz and Railworks is very diffrent kind of simulators except they are practically copies of eachother. Trainz being a arcade game and Railworks being a real hardcore simulator. Trainz being easy to use and very user friendly except it do realism very bad as i sometimes laughted at what exsited in Trainz 2010 and how they mixed trains, wagons from diffrent countries, loco from Hungary and wagons from the US in what would be a harbor industrial area in Austrialia, Meanwhile in railworks its what you expect, US vehicles in the US and UK vehicles in the UK and actually take accuracy ( as i know )
The editors in the game is wroth mentioning as i found my self spending most of my time in it in Trainz and... sadly the editor is hopeless in railworks!   i cant figure out how it works meanwhile Trainz is point and click.      Trainz dont do gradual limits wich means you can make bends that should be impossible for any vehicle to go on while Railworks limit you to its own bends. So if you are the kind of person who loves to make ur own maps and basicly have ur own virtual model railroad, Trainz is the game to go for, especially 2010 as alot where cutout and made pay mods in 2012. Railworks no. just dont go for it as the editor is garbage but it has alot of missions wich is even score based, even if the system is 0 out of 0 score is 100% well done and where going under 0 is overspeeding and doing stuff wrong. You will feel a bit limited in railworks as its all pre made, sure you can go for a freeroam just like in trainz, except in trainz, you can just go of in the other direction during a mission. Trainz also have working factories you can go for so you can see ur wagons drop its content and go pick up and also see how much you have loaded while Railworks is just a haul from A to B, only load you will do is passangers.
As a final score, Trainz surely gives the best over all feel as it has missions you can do and also have a editor you can spend hours in and will probably end up with doing most while railworks is a proper simulation, so if you wanna drive trains and see it in full detail, railworks is what to go for but if you like doing other stuff and dont care in grapghics and have the ability to make ur own routes, go for trainz.

Proto Raider is an auto-runner game with a unique art style.  I love anything that brings back the old retro feel.  The music in this game is also nice and relaxing.  Overall, the whole game's style fits together nicely.
The goal here is to guide your proto man to the exit of each level.  Think that is easy?  You'll have to pick up the key, and, optionally, 3 green chests first.  The only items that keep you on the screen are yellow arrow "walls" that bounce you back in the opposite direction.  You will need to think about your overall path to be able to pick up all the items and reach the end of the level successfully.  One mistake and you'll have to start the level over.  Not as bad as it sounds, really - the levels are not that complicated and when you fail, you don't feel like you just spent too much time to give it another go.
Once you think you've gotten the hang of the game, it throws in a new mechanic such as a scuba suit or wing suit, or some type of dynamic environment that you'll need to overcome.  With 63 actual levels of play, I was able to get through the game in about 3.5 hours total, and I enjoyed the game immensely.  There are some random enemy (or falling object) spawnings on a few levels that can become frustrating, but that's the worst of the frustation in my opinion.
Most of the game is simply relaxing and requires timing of jumps.  You can adjust the speed of the game, as well as tweak the font / color options as well in the options.
If the Steam preview video and screen shots make you wonder if you should get this, I'd say, yes, definitely go for it, you won't be disappointed!
Additional Notes:
In the credits you'll see that it says more levels are coming soon, but to my knowledge, the game has not been updated since August 24th 2016, and never actually updated with additional levels, so I wouldn't expect any new ones any time soon, if ever.  Though, for the price, you still are getting a good solid and unique experience.
If you enjoy the background music and want the OST, you can use/play the included MP3s in the Game's Data\Sounds directory - bonus!

I played the game up to the part where you pick your class and decided to put in for a refund. I just finished the Stick of Truth yesterday and I was really looking forward to this sequel; I even watched the Franchise Prequel episode while the game was installing.
Boy, was I instantly disappointed.
I know a lot of people will argue that I didn't give it a chance, but hear me out. I tried all 3 classes and did the basic combat "tutorials" leading up to the class choice segment and I was just totally disappointed in how they changed the combat system.
The original combat system from Stick of Truth was super simple and fun. Why try to fix something that isn't broken?
Seems like they also changed the looting system to where you basically open a lootable object (fridge/drawer/etc.) and automatically take whatever is contained in it. The items you recieve are shown briefly in a small square popup on the right hand side of the screen. This upset me because there were so many funny/clever weapons and junk items in the first game, I actually enjoyed being forced to manually select loot from specific areas (sex toys & drugs in the nightstand in Cartman's mom's room, etc.)
Also, big thumbs down for being forced to install the uplay launcher to run this game. It's not a huge deal, but I just want to be able to run a game from steam and get right into it.
To be fair, I did have a couple of chuckles in the short time I played this game, but I don't think the storyline (no matter how good it may be) could make up for the combat system.
For right now, I'll just watch Twitch streams or wait a week and watch a playthrough on Youtube to enjoy the story. Maybe I'll buy it again in a year or 2 when it's under $20.

First, I'd like to say I bought this game three times. Once for PS3 on release, then PS4, and again here on Steam when I finally decided to build a gaming PC. This should be a testament to the overall quality of this game's single player alone as I have no real interest in the multiplayer component due to Rockstar's and Take Two's business model and their priorities. However, that said, I have had this game's Social Club render itself defunct for no reason multiple times every week. No matter how many times I reinstall the game and the Social Club, it eventually re-breaks for no reason within the week. While this doesn't impact the quality of the game itself when it works, it very clearly shows how inept Rockstar is at making sure this sort of issue doesn't happen (150 AAA games installed on my PC and one has this issue: GTA5).
The music is on-point and fits the game and the story very well and each of the three main characters are all well-written. The story, while good, feels a bit all over the place at first but I genuinely feel it is due to how much the story seems to just rush. What I mean by that is that it seems like things just keep escalating and escalating for the main characters, rushing from one crazy event to another to another. While it was enjoyable the entire way through, that pacing of the story made it feel a little disjointed for me at times despite making perfect sense. The ending was also a bit lackluster and felt rushed in a bad way to me. An arbitrary A, B, and C choice with one being a very obvious "right choice". Two choices lead to less satisfying endings and the other leads to an ending that is very clearly a "tie up loose ends" mission both literally and narratively. You kill all of the antagonists you run into in the game in a mission that simply screams "we had to wrap it up somehow". That said, it should be noted I've beaten the main story four times. While it has some very glaring flaws narratively, it's still a fun time.
Now on to the multiplayer... The reason I'm not into it is actually not due to me being primarily a single-player-focused gamer but also because of how the entire thing is set up. I played Red Dead Redemptions Free Roam multiplayer for hours upon hours and enjoyed it despite it being fairly empty. GTA Online? It's even emptier than Red Dead Redemption. In order to have any fun whatsoever, you need to make in-game money. You do this by playing deathmatches, heists, races, and various other game modes. The problem is that the payouts are so incredibly low that you will need to grind for countless hundreds of hours to get enough money to keep up with the updates (and this game, while fun, is nowhere near good enough to warrant that type of dedication). The reason for this is so they can get you to spend literally hundreds of dollars on microtransactions. In fact, when GTAO launched, the payouts were actually reasonable and balanced only to be nerfed to insane degrees just to make their Shark Card sales not only more enticing but make it damn near the only way to legitimately have fun in this game.
This turns people to script mods that give them hundreds of millions of in-game money to circumvent this unethical business model. Many modders, however, go further by making themselves invincible, invisible, can insta-kill anyone, and do anything you can think of to ruin your fun. In response, Take Two put an end to OpenIV, which is literally only used for single-player mods (like graphics mods that don't even work on multiplayer). Eventually, Take Two reversed that decision and began allowing OpenIV to be used again for Single Player modding.
However, just a couple short months later has Take 2 and R* stripping a very large number of players of their in-game currency. They started up an event where warehouse missions, which are the best way to make money in the game (despite still being abysmally lower than they should be) yielded twice as much money. People grinded those things from the event's start to finish. When the Smugglers Run DLC hits? A large number of them see ALL of their money whiped. Everyone who contacts R* about this then just gets sent automated, cookie-cutter responses from their automated system and then ignored. Seriously, and then people wonder why this game has such a severe problem with modders online. Maybe it's because R* actively goes out of its way to screw EVERYONE and, as a result, gives everyone a valid reason to say "♥♥♥♥ your microtransactions, I'm going to pay a modder $15 for $100M rather than pay R* $1,250 for $100M". Then there's the fact that the only bug fixes R* does are GTAO money glitches (there are still many bugs left over from the PS3/360 release) and how R* never began work on the three expansions they claimed GTA5's single player was going to get because GTAO padding their wallets was more important.
It's very easy for me to say that I can recommend GTA5's single player, but I cannot in good concience recommend GTAO. If I rated the two parts seperately, the single player is a solid 8/10 with the multiplayer being a 4/10 (6/10 when with friends) at the very most even when you ignore the ethics behind R* and Take Two's decisions.
Basically adding my discust for Take Two's recent actions against the modding comunity for GTA.

Love this game. I like the story, the humor, the voice acting, and the artistic style they've used for the graphics. The puzzles aren't too easy. Most of them are not too challenging to the point you just start grinding your teeth. The puzzles aren't bad. I've not come across anything like that horrid rain dance in the Book of Unwritten Tales yet, which is less a puzzle than it is an exercise in frustration. That required you to tap the keys given in a list that scrolls down the screeen. The list speeds up as you go along so if you're terrible at things that require precise timing or have painful arthritis problems in your hands that stiffen your fingers like I do, a puzzle like that can quickly render a game unplayable. Thankfully, there's nothing like that here in Deponia.
Some of the puzzle solutions are obvious so if you like a constant challenge you may be disappointed. What I definitely find aggravating though is that some of the solutions bear no resemblance to logic at all and I found myself seeking hints. There were a couple points where I resorted to walkthroughs because the solutions made no sense whatsoever and I'd have never figured it out in a million years. I've also been tripped up by the related problem of some of the puzzles not using the logical and, to me, obvious answer and like I've mentioned before, using instead an alternate solution that makes no sense. It would be nice if I could use an alternate solution I see instead of being locked into the one the developers thought of.
Still, those are the only drawbacks and while they are occasionally frustrating they haven't ruined the experience for me. I got enough enjoyment out of the game that I still consider this a good purchase and I have no regrets. I enjoyed the story and can't wait to play the other two games in the series.

This game has a steep learning curve and is fond of punishing your mistakes. I played this game before it went HDR and I do like it better now. That being said, there are still too many little random things that cause what feel like cheap deaths. Need to skillfully roll your bomb down a hole? Too bad you upgraded it with Paste so you could destroy midsections of walls - now it's impossible to angle a bomb down certain holes since Paste is impossible to toggle. Still in the Mines and got one of the randomized dark rooms? Have fun using a Torch that won't let you see any of the off-screen ceiling spiders. Got hit by an enemy? Have fun as they stunlock you and deal 200-500% of the damage you were expecting. Wanted to grab a Gold Idol and make a run for it before exploring the entire map (so as to not waste ropes getting back up)? Too bad the boulder just aggro'd the Shopkeeper and the rest of your playthrough is going to be full of Shopkeepers guarding exit doors with their stupid anti-physics movement, strength, shotgun, and health. Spelunky is by no means a bad game but once you get very good at this game, the next hurdle is to just accept that the majority of your deaths are going to start to feel like they were entirely out of your control. This is quite unfortunate if you like gathering all the loot, because an undeserved death just makes it feel like a waste of time.

As I'm typing this, I have nearly 600 hours on this game and I'm finally almost sort of good at it.
Wargame is my first real RTS (Read: Not a 2D flash game) and in retrospect that may have been a terrible mistake, because this game will flat out annihilate you if you don't know what you're doing, which you probably won't because there's a LOT to know. In other words, if you're new to Wargame, expect to lose a few times.
The trailer was not joking when it said there were over oople-bajillion units in the game. Admittedly, a lot of them are similar or are reskins, but most of them have vastly different stats. For example, there's a cheap, baseline T-72 which is basically a hunk of garbage with tracks and a gun on it, that bursts into flames if the tank commander sneezes. Then there's the highly modernized T-72s that will rip other tanks apart from 2000 meters and shrug off rockets as it roars across the battlefield, powered by diesel, the screams of the innocent, and human souls. Now, you can easily check the stats of a unit in-game by pressing "i", but memorizing them to some extent is helpful. But that's not the point. The point is, if you don't know what you're up against, there's a good chance you're going to get absolutely destroyed.
Once you have a vague understanding of what each unit does sort of, you have to learn how to counter each type. It's kind of like rock paper scissors, except nothing completely beats anything and there's several ways to lose. For example, tank beats infantry unless the infantry are at short range or have an ATGM. Infantry beats anything at short range. Infantry that are good at killing other infantry, beat infantry. Artillery also beats infantry. Plane also beats infantry but not infantry with MANPADs. SAM beats plane, unless the SAM is radar and the plane is SEAD.  Plane beats SAM if the SAM is garbage but only if the plane is ground attack, in certain situations, maybe. Everything on the battlefield plays a different role and you have to find a way to make that role work for you in the grand scheme of things. Learning how to do that can be difficult.
Not only do you have to know what kills what and when and how, but you also need to know the gameplay mechanics too. For example, you need to understand how combat stress affects your units, and how to use that to your advantage by making your enemies scream and cry and soil themselves before you start actually seriously trying to kill them. You need to know how reconnaisance works so you can find your enemy in the first place so that you can actually kill them. You need to figure out how to resupply your units so they don't turn into 60 tonne paperweights, and how to keep your supply units safe so they don't turn into an expensive and tactically ineffective fireball.
Those are just basic gameplay mechanics too. That doesn't even scratch the surface of using tactics and mindgames to actually defeat your enemy.
Wargame will throw you for a loop. This is the only RTS I've really gotten into and my friends who I've suckered into playing it all agree that this is something else. It will take some time to get past the learning curve. No matter how many hours you sink into it, your tactics will keep changing, you'll keep trying different things, but you will never perfect your strategy because a perfect strategy does not exist. This game will challenge you to learn. It will challenge you to think. It will challenge you to adapt, and it will challenge you a lot. But once you start to overcome these challenges, it becomes extremely satisfying to finally win. To lay crushing defeat on your enemies. To know you came from knowing nothing to feeling like a master of warfare.

First, I'd like to say I bought this game three times. Once for PS3 on release, then PS4, and again here on Steam when I finally decided to build a gaming PC. This should be a testament to the overall quality of this game's single player alone as I have no real interest in the multiplayer component due to Rockstar's and Take Two's business model and their priorities. However, that said, I have had this game's Social Club render itself defunct for no reason multiple times every week. No matter how many times I reinstall the game and the Social Club, it eventually re-breaks for no reason within the week. While this doesn't impact the quality of the game itself when it works, it very clearly shows how inept Rockstar is at making sure this sort of issue doesn't happen (150 AAA games installed on my PC and one has this issue: GTA5).
The music is on-point and fits the game and the story very well and each of the three main characters are all well-written. The story, while good, feels a bit all over the place at first but I genuinely feel it is due to how much the story seems to just rush. What I mean by that is that it seems like things just keep escalating and escalating for the main characters, rushing from one crazy event to another to another. While it was enjoyable the entire way through, that pacing of the story made it feel a little disjointed for me at times despite making perfect sense. The ending was also a bit lackluster and felt rushed in a bad way to me. An arbitrary A, B, and C choice with one being a very obvious "right choice". Two choices lead to less satisfying endings and the other leads to an ending that is very clearly a "tie up loose ends" mission both literally and narratively. You kill all of the antagonists you run into in the game in a mission that simply screams "we had to wrap it up somehow". That said, it should be noted I've beaten the main story four times. While it has some very glaring flaws narratively, it's still a fun time.
Now on to the multiplayer... The reason I'm not into it is actually not due to me being primarily a single-player-focused gamer but also because of how the entire thing is set up. I played Red Dead Redemptions Free Roam multiplayer for hours upon hours and enjoyed it despite it being fairly empty. GTA Online? It's even emptier than Red Dead Redemption. In order to have any fun whatsoever, you need to make in-game money. You do this by playing deathmatches, heists, races, and various other game modes. The problem is that the payouts are so incredibly low that you will need to grind for countless hundreds of hours to get enough money to keep up with the updates (and this game, while fun, is nowhere near good enough to warrant that type of dedication). The reason for this is so they can get you to spend literally hundreds of dollars on microtransactions. In fact, when GTAO launched, the payouts were actually reasonable and balanced only to be nerfed to insane degrees just to make their Shark Card sales not only more enticing but make it damn near the only way to legitimately have fun in this game.
This turns people to script mods that give them hundreds of millions of in-game money to circumvent this unethical business model. Many modders, however, go further by making themselves invincible, invisible, can insta-kill anyone, and do anything you can think of to ruin your fun. In response, Take Two put an end to OpenIV, which is literally only used for single-player mods (like graphics mods that don't even work on multiplayer). Eventually, Take Two reversed that decision and began allowing OpenIV to be used again for Single Player modding.
However, just a couple short months later has Take 2 and R* stripping a very large number of players of their in-game currency. They started up an event where warehouse missions, which are the best way to make money in the game (despite still being abysmally lower than they should be) yielded twice as much money. People grinded those things from the event's start to finish. When the Smugglers Run DLC hits? A large number of them see ALL of their money whiped. Everyone who contacts R* about this then just gets sent automated, cookie-cutter responses from their automated system and then ignored. Seriously, and then people wonder why this game has such a severe problem with modders online. Maybe it's because R* actively goes out of its way to screw EVERYONE and, as a result, gives everyone a valid reason to say "♥♥♥♥ your microtransactions, I'm going to pay a modder $15 for $100M rather than pay R* $1,250 for $100M". Then there's the fact that the only bug fixes R* does are GTAO money glitches (there are still many bugs left over from the PS3/360 release) and how R* never began work on the three expansions they claimed GTA5's single player was going to get because GTAO padding their wallets was more important.
It's very easy for me to say that I can recommend GTA5's single player, but I cannot in good concience recommend GTAO. If I rated the two parts seperately, the single player is a solid 8/10 with the multiplayer being a 4/10 (6/10 when with friends) at the very most even when you ignore the ethics behind R* and Take Two's decisions.

Returning to DOOM 3 after twelve (!) years of other first person shooters is simultaneously refreshing and frustrating.
Pacing is generally fantastic, and the game is still oh so atmospheric. Audio logs are fantastically voiced, the environmental storytelling is great, generally speaking it does a fantastic job at creating the impression of a real working facility full of scared and frustrated workers. The dark industrial sci-fi theme is well realised and consistent, everything fits together nicely and the demon designs are my favourite of the series. Though I will admit they look more alienish than demonic, I still think they fit well for this particular game.
DOOM 3 is from a time before mission markers, so if you're not careful you can easily get lost. I found I adjusted fairly quickly to this, and became better at overcoming obstacles without guidance after a few hours. It can be frustrating, but the lack of any assistance does enhance the feeling of isolation and claustraphobia, and gives the game a nice survival horror esq aftertaste. Exploration feels more natural because of the lack of hand-holding, in my opinion. It's not nearly as bad as DOOM II, which had me searching for hours on some levels for that last bloody switch.
Some of DOOM 3 hasn't aged well, though, in my opinion. There's a distinct lack of agility in the player character, you'll rarely be able to dodge enemy attacks up close even by dashing backwards or to the sides. This can leave combat feeling like attrition, more a numbers game than a test of skill. Especially when you factor in DOOM 3's love of monster closets and spawning enemies behind you. The oppressive darkness doesn't help, it's literally pitch black in places which makes picking out targets an utter ballache. You can switch to the flashlight, but most of the time you'll be shooting one enemy whilst another approaches in total darkness from his flank.
Overall, though, I think DOOM 3 still does more right than wrong. It feels a little conflicted at times, like it's unsure whether it wants to be a horror game or an action game, but I think it does both well enough to be consistently enteraining.
It's like a time capsule, the embodiment of design sentiments from a time before Halo and Call of Duty really changed the scene.

Being a long-time fan of ARPGs such as Blizzard's Diablo series or THQ's Titan Quest, having fits of giddy excitement over this game were all but unexpected. Having made large improvements over its predecessor, Torchlight II successfully combines elements from other ARPGs in a fluid synergy that sets the bar higher. Having staff that was involved in the development of games like FATE and Diablo has helped to create a game that is now topping my list for this genre. Gripes of the previous game being to easy to win/ too hard to die need not apply here as Torchlight II's difficulty settings are appropriate. (Casual has you clicking happily without remorse, whereas Elite mode will have you quaffing more potions than an alcoholic.)
In addition to excellent gameplay, we have the seamless Steam Workshop integration which allows for hundreds of mods to be easily installed an kept up-to-date. I really don't think I can overstate how wonderful this is as it makes the game so much more versatile.
Multiplayer supports 6 player co-op over LAN or Internet out of the box, but there is a 8 player mod that works perfectly. I have had the most fun in this game while using the multiplayer mode. In multiplayer, each player has their own individual loot that no other player can steal from the ground. (This goes the same for gold.) This means no more killing the boss and having your epic drops stolen by that jerk rogue with some ridiculous movement speed. Items that you do recieve are immediately trade-able to other players and act as normal once picked up.
To put it simply, Torchlight II is a fantastic game with an excellent value. I am continually amazed at how this game has been designed so articulately and to such a high standard.
If you have ever in your life enjoyed Diablo, Fate, Titan Quest or other ARPGs, BUY THIS GAME. You will not be disappointed.
Recommended Mods: Synergies Mod, 8 Player Mod, Enhanced Retex Mod

There's also a stage that, while not difficult, puts the player into a moving field and randomly rotates him, leaving you with a task of waiting until you're happen to get into the position you need to be in to jump and finish the level.
Despite the few levels with these problems, most are trial-and-error, timing and practice-makes-perfect puzzles that are charming and fun and run with a low system footprint.
So yes, i recommend it, but be prepared to be frustrated by a few nearly impossible levels.

This one was interesting. The visuals were vastly different from basically any game on Steam and I generally liked the look. It was a “one-button platformer” sort. Most of the levels were fun and I was able to get through them without much difficulty, but then there were others that relied solely on luck to get through. Those were awful. It was enjoyable overall, but the end felt like it came out of nowhere (and probably should've come soon).

Proto Raider's title screen proclaims it a "Hardcore Arcade Quest," but it's far more like an "Action Puzzle Platformer." You'll need decent reflexes to clear some of the monster-fighting levels, yes. For 90% of the game, though, it's more about figuring out and executing the optimal path through each one-screen level to collect all the treasure and escape.
The peculiar rules of the game's physics take some getting used to. You can't control how high or far you jump except by timing it so you collide with an obstacle. The jumps themselves use a strange arc that loses all momentum at its peak, dropping you straight down. And though the game's animation moves pixel by pixel, jumps only launch when your character is lined up on a column of the ASCII-styled text grid, leading to a delay in response to your button presses. It's not unfair, exactly, but it requires unlearning old assumptions.
The closing credits promise more levels in later updates, but what we have here is already an optimal length. My recorded time is what it took to 100% the game, collecting all but red-herring chests. It's perfect for its style, giving you time to learn and master the mechanics while retaining a sense of discovery with the surprises each new level introduces. A worthy purchase at full price or otherwise!

I have very mixed feelings about this game. There were some parts of the game that were genuinely funny, which was the goal of the developer of this comedy-based adventure game. There were some puzzles that were really fun and challenging. Unfortunately, there are some major problems in this game that made me consider abandoning it at several points. Some of the puzzles try to be cute and absurd rather than logical, which make them hard to solve other than trial and error. There are some puzzles where the cue to the player is not obvious enough. There are also parts of the game where it is not clear what you are supposed to do next. For example, in many adventure games if you talk to characters in the game, they will tend to point you toward your next task. The characters in Deponia will tell you tons of jokes and wierd stories (I clicked through a lot of it), but 90% of the dialog has nothing to do with helping you finish the game. There are some out-and-out bugs, including a minigame that was flat broken. I used a walk-through more for this game than any other I have ever played (that includes Myst, Riven, Siberia I/II, Machinarium, The Longest Journey, etc). The hero of the story was a little too detestable to be funny. The artwork, style, and creativity were all there for this to be an excellent game, but somehow the developers did not learn from other great games of this genre. The result is a disappointment.

While some of the humor was pretty cheesy in this point and click adventure, it still had enough charm in it to keep me hooked. It helped that the artwork was fantastic, and the puzzles were in the sweet spot between difficult and easy (mostly leaning towards the latter). By the end I was really engaged in the story, which was surprising.
On a side note, there is one achievement for this game that is down right sadistic. But some people are into that, not that there's anything wrong with that.

From the makers of ''The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav''. ''Deponia'' is a game developed and pubished by Daedalic Entertainment.
Preface!
Due to this game being ''story driven'', I am not going to go into mush detail or spoil anything major of the Story.
The story centers around Rufus: a young, sarcastic, bold, lying, selfish man who wants to leave the junk town of Kovaq - a town Rufus has known for so long - and look for his, not-so known, father. Rufus believes his father abandoned him for the floating city of Elysium when Rufus was very young.
And so, Rufus makes it his ultimate destiny to go to Elysium; to prove his own father that Rufus can go to Elysium.
During Rufus Journey, he ends up meeting people and they end up helping him on his travel.
The tone of the story is comedy mixed with seriousness. About 95% of the game is comedy while the small 5% is seriousness. I can't say in which part the game gets serious.
The ending of the game, in a way, touched my heart. I can't say  in detail of what happened in the ending, but it got to do with all Rufus had done during his Jouney.
I like Deponias' animation. The animation is hand drawn. The animation suits well with the comedic tone of the game.
Deponia is a hard point-and-click game and is a lot more harder than ''The Dark Eye: Chains of Satinav''.
Items do not ''highlight'' when you hover over them with something else.
There is no quest log... so... you are probably going to wander aimlessly around in the game and be like ''uhmm... what am I suppose do again?''.
I recommend this game to people who wants a challengine Point-and-click game.
Deponia gets an 8/10.

Starbreeze Studios AB produces a puzzle that is sad and wonderful at the same time. Brothers – A Tale of Two Sons Is a fantastic puzzle game that offers beautiful environments and amazing story bundled into one.
Brothers – A Tale of Two Sons starts off with the story of a young boy and the death of his beloved mother. As she drowns in the ocean the boy learns that his father is on deaths bed. It is up to two brothers to save their father by going to the tree of life, but they have no idea how to get there. The journey takes them across the world as they experience an adventure that none would have ever imagined.
The campaign is broken up into seven parts: a prologue and six chapters. Each level is incredibly beautiful and twists upon itself allowing you to see previous or future parts of the level by simply looking over a cliff or up a mountain. As you play the game the levels become more beautiful, mystical, and terrifying. The campaign combines puzzles, adventure, and action into one brilliant game. As you push through the game you will fight bosses, solve riddles, complete puzzles, and see the most spectacular sites you will ever imagine. The campaign is relatively short and can be easily completed in a couple hours; if you decide to view the scenery, complete the achievements, and interact with as much as you can you could make the game last a few hours.
This game is unique in many ways compared to your traditional action/adventure. You control two characters by using a single controller with each brother being controlled by a different joystick. You essentially move and interact with objects although jumping is done automatically. If you do not have a controller you cannot play this game, and in all honesty it would be ridiculously difficult to play if you could use a keyboard and mouse. There are two brothers: a younger and older. Each one has their benefits for example the younger one can sneak through small places while older one can lift heavier objects.
Brothers – A Tale of Two Sons is a beautiful game with a brilliant story. The game combines wonderful music, amazing ambience, and beautiful scenery. The combination of puzzle solving and adventure offers an amazing game that is a blast to play. By allowing you to control two brothers at once the game offers a unique twist on typical gameplay. I completely recommend this game, but you will need a controller. If you are frugal like me I would recommend getting this game on sale as the campaign is very short and its cost is relatively high.
Pros:
+Beautiful scenery.
+Fantastic music.
+Brilliant ambience.
+Amazing gameplay that offers action, puzzle, and adventure into one amazing experience.
+Unique gameplay experience that allows you to control multiple individuals at once.
+Absolutely fantastic story.
+Fun little boss fights.
+Loads of puzzles.
+Fun achievements.
Cons:
-The dialogue is not in a comprehensible language (For some people this is fine, but this game could be so much more if they provided dialogue that matched the beauty of the story).
-At some points it can be very difficult to control two characters at once.
-They could have made this co-op, which would have been really awesome.

This game is definetely one of the very best I've ever played in any genre. The scenery is jaw dropping, the musical score is excellent and the story is very compelling, even though not a complete sentence of dialogue occurs anywhere in the game.

I don't want to spoil the storyline, but the way emotions are evoked without saying a word is amazing.

This is the first Tekken game I've ever seen on PC, and boy is it a strong showing!
Pros;
1) Good Optimization: This game runs at maxxed out 1080P settings on my GTX 1060 and i5 6500. A quick look on the forums shows that it generally performs well on all systems, but you may need to lower settings on a laptop.
2) Good Netcode: After the iffy netcodes in Street Fighter V and Mortal Kombat, this game impresses right away with great connections and stable gameplay.
3) Robust Settings/Features: Lots of graphics settings for tweaking on the performance side. Tons of customizeable features from your ingame UI (designs around character profiles and health bars) to actual cosmetics for your character. All free, with no microtransactions to be had. Just earn in-game currency by playing the game and unlock cool and absurd stuff. Also some cool hard to unlock options for players who really master the game.
4) Lots of modes: Does Street Fighter 5 have you yearning for the days when fighting games didn't exclude interesting single player content like an arcade mode? This game has one of those. It also has a cinematic story mode, character stories, an endless battle style Treasure Battle mode as well as easily customizable single fights vs AI Opponents. Throw in the standard practice mode, couch versus mode and online mode to round out the package. It even comes with a tournament mode to instantly optimize the game with standard tournament settings and display norms.
Cons;
Look this game does so much right it is hard to criticize it, but I'll try.
1) Some screens and prerendered videos play at 30 fps (even then, most are at 60 fps)
2) Story mode has a few boss fights that do not feel fair to a noob like myself. One boss has a ten hit off the ground combo into a grab, and slowly regains its own health the entire fight. This same boss has a phase where it gains infinite hyper armor until activating a one hit kill super which must be triggered and then dodged or blocked before the fight can continue.
3) The Post Processing setting automatically enables an ugly film grain filter at high settings. This can likely be removed using a .ini file, but currently the fix doesn't quite work. link to a thread on that here;
TL;DR: Buy this game! It is a well made, well optimized port that doesn't leave its player base behind. Devs that release such high quality PC Ports should be rewarded with sales in my opinion.

While looking over the reviews before purchasing this game, I couldn't understand how the opinions of Super Hipster Lumberjack could be so polar, but after playing the game first-hand I completely understand.
On the surface, this  game has pretty much everything I want in an Indie platformer. Uncommon visuals with a steady curb of difficulty without being disproportionately hard at times. That's really all I ask for from this game, pretty simple, but the issue I have is that its not really a "game" at all.
I'm thrown into a world without context or meaning. No story to drive me, and no reason why I should leave the 90's 2D paradise that is my room. I would be perfectly content there honestly, but I suppose that would make for an even more lack-luster game. Even a single speech bubble would be nice, or a booming voice telling me to go right would do this game a lot of good. But no dice.
The mechanics are pretty solid, and even though this "game" doesn't quit bring anything new to the table, its worth the low price tag for some cheap (good) rage, and entertaining visuals. Overall, I recommend this as long as you have the right expectations going into it.

I loved this game, but however I believe the original was way better than this. Despite the first game's short gameplay time and medicore controls, it felt more unique and balanced. Here, they just made it a bit more 'consuming', allowing you to have fair turns. However, I found this pathletic since it was very dull and time consuming, compared to Stick of Truth where it is fairly quick to pick an action and then wait for the enemy's turn.
The story is expected, since it's ♥♥♥♥ing South Park. Unpredictable yet funny at the same time. The added dark humor is a bonus. However, while Fractured does have its few 'Did you just do that?!' moments (for instance, fighting Jared), I felt that Fractured didn't take many risks to create a really strong theme to push the limitations of the censorship system, like what they did to Stick of Truth, for example, the abortion scenes. That was a BIG no-no, and got censored. Since saying that, Fractured doesn't have the 'risky' moments compared to Stick of Truth.
The controls are alright. Feels the same as the original, however the controls for the minigames and companion powers... really irritating.
Gameplay is so-so. It's great at some parts, but 'grindy' at some parts. But since there is a lot happening, you probably won't notice them.
Overall, Fractured But Whole is a great turn-based RPG game, and is 100% a very good sequel to the original. However, the original is better than Fractured at some points.

This is easily one of my favorite games of all time.
The thing that really surprises me is that I personally have lost a lot of interest in so-called 'sand box' games that aren't open world, they are just a voxel engine where you are expected to make the game fun on your own.
Mount and Blade is open world and sand box in that you aren't really given an objective early on and the game certainly doesn't hold your hand or explain exactly what you need to do, but there's still a very active game world with wars being fought and uneasy peaces made in the face of greater threats, secret back stabbing plots between competing nobles and alliances sealed with marriages.
The battles are also a lot of fun, a very brutal and unforgiving sort of hack and slash combat, though anything can get reptitive given enough time.
But the most amazing part of the game is really the mods out there. Everything from Star Wars to Medieval Europe to WWI to Napoleonic wars. The engine seems to be very versatile.
If the game has any glaring flaws it's that it has a very aging graphical and audio presentation. It was very bare bones even on its release and now it's really poor locking compared with other more modern games. If that's someting you can deal with then perhaps stay away. Otherwise I can't recommend this game enough.

Spelunky is a game for someone who wants to play something challenging and always changing.  Its randomly generated levels provide a near infinite amount of variety in your experience while playing through the game.  Sometimes you'll find yourself in a level where all the odds are against you, but there's always a way through it if you know what to do and have the courage to take it on.  Other times, you'll find everything stacked in your favor.  No matter how the levels generate, nothing beats the feeling of defeating what the game deals you.  While playing Spelunky, I have had some of the most frightening, heartbreaking, and funniest experiences throughout my years of gaming.  If you like to go on adventures, be challenged, and experience something that's truly uniquely fun, then you should try out Spelunky.  (The original PC version is available on the creator's website for free if you want to try out a comparable experience before you buy this version.  But if you like it, definitely try out the new one; it really steps up and gives players a new experience!)
So much fun to kill time in.  Easy to pick up.  Easy to die. Easy to start again!

Deponia features the mechanics of a classic point-and-click with a beautiful hand drawn graphics and an interesting (if a little short) soundtrack. In typical P&C fashion you explorer various environments, interacting with set pieces and collecting items to be used later, completing various tasks that range from the mundane to the ludicrous. The first act dragged on a little and had some real out-of-the-box puzzle solutions but the last two acts really pickup and are paced a little better.
The artwork really is gorgeous and does an excellent job of bringing a world full of junk and debris to life. The soundtrack is pretty good but isn't what you would call easy listening so after hearing the same few songs over and over again in each act it can be a little grating. The writing was typically funny and the voice acting is top notch although at times the main character is a little overbearing.
Overall Deponia is good fun (although maybe a little overpriced for the length when not on sale) and if you're a point and click fan it will be right up your alley. Be warned, if you're following the plot at all you're going want the rest of the series, cliffhanger city central.

The keys to having a good experience in my opinion are:
1. Try to play with people you have played with before. Teamwork is important especially recognizing where a push is happening and where a push needs to be made.

3. Play conquest where arty spam is not rewarded nearly as much and playing offensively is rewarded more.
4. Medium income! This to me is the perfect balance of being able to purchase enough units without becoming too spammy.
5. If your new you will most likely suck, but here is what you can do to avoid being flamed.
Don't buy a bunch of arty unless your team has control of enough zones and ask what is needed where first.
Don't buy arty at the start of the game.
Don't buy a bunch of planes at the start.
Let you team know your new and ask where you should go and what units you should buy.
Always buy at least 2 units of ADA.
Recon infantry is your friend.
