Proto Raider is 'one click' inspired Indie title that sounds so basic yet offers so much fun
Proto Raider is basically a puzzle inspired game, that takes away most of the complication of many other games just giving you one input to instruct your game character to jump.
The basic premise on each level is to collect as many chests as possible, pick up the key and exit the level. The game will automatically make your character run in a specified direction and you must use your mind to read the task ahead and decide when is the best time to instruct the character to jump. It sounds rather basic explained in this sense but it is a lot more in-depth experience than that.
The graphics are classic ASCII 8 bit inspired lines and dots, to me personally, I find this rather appealing and applaud any game that uses this style. There was plenty of options available in the options screen to ensure you can have as much ASCII graphical pleasure as your inner retro monster desires.
The music is nice and has a sort of chillout classic 8bit sound to it, I found from replaying levels and listening to it for a few times it never really grated on me.
Pros
+ Graphics are very retro ASCII style.
+ It has the most simple premise of any game but is still so challenging.
+ A lot of levels keeping you busy for some time.
Cons
- Some puzzles can be over frustrating.
- Certain boss fights can appear impossible first time round
I personally received Proto Raider in a bundle and was unsure what to really expect. I was very happy when I played the game to discover it was a rather simple yet satisfying puzzle game and I was surprised how the developed the game to offer so much on a simple premise.
If this is in the sale definitely give this one a shot, it's a good casual time waster if nothing else.

The original overrated monster closet game.
Doom 3 has been widely hailed as one of the scariest games ever made, presumably by the sort of people who think all it takes to file a movie under the horror genre is the presence of a monster and maybe turning a few lights off. Doom 3 is little more than Baby's First Dead Space, and while that's a little bit unfair as it obviously came well before its most obvious imitator, it isn't even remotely scary and is barely passable as a shooter.
Let me start by approaching the horror half the of the equation: the primary emotion that horror feeds on is fear. Fear stems from vulnerability. Now, how can one possibly feel vulnerable while packing more firepower than a Texan wedding, up to and including two different instant-kill weapons? By far the most reliably lethal thing in the game was the bloody level design, between its clumsy platforming and occasionally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t set design (Oh, you shot this fragile glass fuel pipe in the midst of a close-quarters firefight? Enjoy instant vaporization, sucker). Meanwhile, the atmosphere the game attempted to set up was about as scary as Halloween decorations, so if you have a phobia of red color filters and balding middle-aged men laughing at you over the intercom, I suppose you might get a few frights out of it.
As for the shooting... it's just not Doom. Every Doom game before or since has been high-octane shooty-bang action characterized by constant movement and overwhelming firepower on both sides. What it is NOT, is clomping down tight corridors with all the lights off fighting half a dozen enemies at a time - tops - while the lackluster sound design robs you of any situational awareness so the game can 'scare' you with some zombie twatbasket smacking you on the back of your head because somehow a trained marine can't pick up on an obese corpse shambling up behind him on noisy grate floors.
I haven't played the Resurrection of Evil expansion yet, but I'll review that seperately when I do. As for Doom 3 itself, I'd rather just play Dead Space again. Or that System Shock remake, when that comes out.

The game is a well made game. It's very pretty, battles can get very intense, and there are tactics you need to learn in order to survive in the game. The maps are well designed and the campaigns have believable stories behind them. The community also isn't as bad as communities in other games. There's a good deal of military and political talk in chat, but mostly it remains civil. All in all, it's a good game that has more good than bad, so I can recommend it. However, there are several things lacking...
- The economy for unit summoning is out of whack for the stated goal of ultra realism (Abrams, I'm looking at you). American and Soviet units cost the most to deploy on the battlefield, an attempt by the developers to not have the game dominated by those two armies. However, the time period WAS dominated by those two armies, and they had the capability to deploy their best units (M1A1 and A2 Abrams tanks, T90's, F-15's and 16's, MiG 29's) in vast quantities. This simply is not represented well in the game's battles. You can do better as North Korea than you can as the Soviet Union because of this. That being said, I've had some AWESOME battles where it's, say, Israel and France against China and North Korea.
- The AI is not programmed well. In fact, it's programmed like AI were programmed back in the early 2000's. It knows exactly where your units are down to the last soldier. As soon as you fire upon it, all your forces are immediately 'visible' to the AI, even if they wouldn't be to a player, and attacked overwhelmingly. The AI acts like a player using hacks to see all your units and give itself infinite resources. Harder difficulty levels don't mean more advanced algorithms are used. No, harder difficulty levels mean more buffs for resources and unit stats for the AI.
- There's no taking into account some of the superior technological strengths of either side. Units are balanced for a more arcadey feel. For example, NATO tanks have thermal optics that allowed them to see through smokescreens at the time represented in this game. However, because the Soviets did not have this tech, the tech is not represented in game.
- Aircraft performance is still completely idiotic. For example, the aircraft do not naturally try to evade a missile on their own when fired upon, as a real piloted aircraft would regardless of what orders you give. And ground attack fighters armed with specialized anti-tank weapons will abandon the battlefield too early (A-10, I'm looking at you). THey'll expend their missiles then break off and RTB without using their anti-tank gatling guns. And, going into anti-air, you will NOT see any dogfights. The jets do not go to engage each other and enter into spectacular dogfights. No, they fire their long range missiles, and once those are dry, they strafe at each other. Think ye olde knights in a jousting tournament.
Despite these flaws, it is a fun game, especially when you play it with friends, once you figure out how to actually succeed.
Please add submarines, battleships aircraft carriers etc, increase unit capacity from present 60 add cruise missiles these are some things which will make this game really shine.

Okay. After 500+ hours of wargaming i've decide to write my opinion. Bear in mind Wargame Red Dragon isn't like classic RTS games we've known so far. It is more like Blitzkrieg style but with more immersion, freedom of pace, and visuals.
Here are my in-depth gameplay review.
There is no Fog Of War. Use recon.
Planning your assault requires planning especially when recon unit is vulnerable to everything else. However, you your troops cannot survive an assault and ambush without recon. You use recon to detect hidden tanks, incoming aircraft, or to find enemy's artilerry. There are several type of recon. Each type has it's purpose realistically.
Tanks rolling enemy infantry in forest? No and don't do it.
Just like real modern battle scenario, tanks usually used in open field. Never ever a commander stupid enough to send tank into forest and urban areas thinking their tanks is some sort of god. Except the terrifying veteran superheavy when it wasn't flanked. Still can be killed. Use your ATGM plane.
Air support. No longer save from ground unit.
Unlike any other classic RTS. Wargame Red Dragon offered a lot of killing opportunity when using airstrike on your target. And unlike any other classic RTS also, aircraft and helo isn't a magic which keep spawning after every cooldown. A helicopter however are useful only in certain situation. You can helorush the infantry and tanks but not a bunch of anti-air support. Also, a single helo shouldn't do a flyby over a forest and urban in happy manners.
Naval.
To me and several other players. Naval is actually a mistake made by Eugen. There aren't alot of tactical option in naval battle. Which make Total War series naval battle superior. Naval unit's pathing are also the most terrible i've seen.
Artillery and infantry.
These two units always have close relationship even in RTS like Company Of Heroes. Which is why you shouldn't exposed your infantry in the open field and to enemy recon. Or else they'll get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ However, artillery smoke is my choice when commencing an assault to urban areas using infantry.
Multiplayer.
Here is a few tips. If you looking for large scale unfair batlle, try a server with 50000 points destruction and high income. If you are looking a realistic tactical gameplay, then a server with [Tact] title is for you. I've felt  overpopulated maps are less in entertaining and unproductive compared to low income and scarce in point maps. Be aware that some of player like to leave their keyboard after deployment.
But in online multiplayer, whether in game or not, community are very cheerful and revolutionary. Warchat sometimes defeat the purpose of the game.
Pros
-Realistic rock-paper-scissor battle system compared to any other RTS.
-Excellent graphic and framerate.
-Lot of unit choices suited for several playstyles.
-Immersive sound.
-Decent background musics.
-Joyful (and hateful) online community.
Cons
-Naval battles are the terrible one.
-Too powerful artilery.
-Uninteresting single player campaign.
-AI were using mongols running towards player.
-Naval units are too powerful to be taken down by anti-naval ground missiles.
-No electronic warfare. Which make modern battles felt less creative.

With a narrative that will make your heart ache, moments that have you on the edge of your seat, and a dash of laughter at some poignent moments, Brothers is a game that will pull you in from the opening scene. It's sweeping vistas will enthrall you, and its music will haunt you long after you've stopped playing.
Brothers is part adventure game and part puzzle platformer. You spend a lot of time figuring out how to progress, though the game itself has a very linear path. None of the puzzles are so arduous that you'll find yourself searching for answers, and there are plenty of embellishments that add to the atmosphere and world of the game.
While it warns you at the outset that it was designed fopr a controller, I found it to work quite well with a keyboard. If possible, try to play it on a home theater. Its Dolby Digital score and effects help immerse you in the unnamed fantasy world. I played through it in about six hours.

Proto Raider is for the most part a puzzle game, where your only input is the ability to jump. Your character that I'll name Bob for this review, will never stop running and will recklessly run into any of the numerous hazards you will encounter without a second thought. You can't tell him to slow down or change directions either, so what looks like a simple task for any platformer will be a massive undertaking here. Your goals for each level will be to collect the key and exit through the locked door. It is never as simple as that though as they will quickly start introducing elements like quick sand, fire and poison to name a few of the deadly things you will be encountering. As you might imagine things quickly get complex, but Proto Raider is forgiving in a way since there is no timer to speak of and there   is no life system, allowing you to try as many times as you desire without consequence.
Before starting the game you should head into the options menu where you can change how fast the gameplay is, invert colors or change it into monochrome. You can chose to have the ASCII art to be either pixelated, bold or normal. There are a surprising amount of options for a game of this type and all that is really missing is the option to rebind the keys. Yes, you only press one button to play this game but the restart level button will also be used plenty. Getting back into the game itself, there are three treasure chests scattered across the level that may appear optional but are pretty important as you will soon run across a dead end until you collect a certain amount. Getting these makes the game a lot more challenging since getting the key and heading toward the exit is usually a simple task, but you are likely going to have to replay the mission again to collect those chests anyways.
The amount of variety between levels is pretty huge. Seems like every other level has a new feature introduced like a pickaxe to mine, scuba gear to swim or a pick-up that reverses gravity. There is a lot of thinking here and it does get frustrating at times as you see Bob run the wrong direction, straight to his doom, but I never felt it was the anythings fault other than my own. It does have a few annoying bits like having to mine 100% of an area to progress, miss even one pixel and you will have to restart. There are two levels like this in the overall 64 levels this game has to offer, so it is not a major issue. These levels are separated into three themed areas, them being water, dessert and jungle. At the end of each area you will face a boss that you must defeat with a weapon like a sword or a crossbow. Bosses usually die in about 5 hits but careful as their bodies may be hazardous  after death. The blood effects are also quite cool to look at as it splatters all over the objects and drips down. It doesn't look violent since it's just the letter “p” in red floating down but it may be something that interests you if you are purchasing for a child.
Bosses go in a set pattern and don't react at all since they have no AI. They seem to attack randomly though so some reflexes are required. Other than bosses there are no other creatures you will be able to kill, the game is mostly based on avoiding obstacles and figuring out the optimal route for escape. In case you were wondering if there is a story, well kind of. You start off looking for treasure and then find the love of your life in some deep, unexplored jungle and must impress her by collecting tons of wedding rings around the stage, leading me to believe that she may in fact be Sonic the Hedgehog in disguise. Anyways, this is a gameplay above all else type of game and it's story offers very little. Graphics are purely ASCII art and there will never be a background. The artstyle works very well, is easy to run and stays at a smooth frame rate of 100fps. Music has a pretty soothing tone to it and fits the game rather well. There are not many tracks but the soundtrack never became a nuisance. Hanging around the main menu without pressing anything will trigger the credits screen, which seems fine but you can not exit the screen without forcing the game to shut down. Whether that is a glitch or intentional it is a pretty big problem.
It is quite amazing how much they managed to do with the game considering all you do is jump. From sailing across a breeze of wind, to throwing axes at monsters and even mining with one button press works pretty well. The amount of ideas they have from start to end ensure that the game doesn't get stale with it's very simple concept and control scheme. And to top it off the devs plan to add even more levels later on. Proto Raider most likely won't appeal to anyone but puzzle fans. This game does require some precise platforming at times but it most likely won't appeal to platformer fans due to lack of any control besides jumping. Having said that, Proto Raider is a really good puzzle game that requires both brains and reflexes. Looking at the screenshots of the game you may think it is a simple fan project with little content, but you'd be mistaken. This is a fully fledged game with plenty of bang for the buck. Highly recommended to those looking for a forgiving yet difficult  puzzle game.

The thing I love about this game is that it sets the tone of a survival horror type game quite well. It's not scary like amnesia but scary in the sense that you're out of ammo, low on health trying to get around the aliens in the level. The level design is colorful but still manages to be dark and creepy. There are a few different aliens in the game but when you meet the Praetorians or the Predaliens, you'll be running or fighting for your life. The Alien Queen level has probably been the most fun/scary part of the game.
I haven't finished the Alien campaign but I managed to beat Marine and Predator campaigns on the hardest difficulties. The predator campaign throws you up against endless amounts of aliens while leaving you with limited power and ammo. Aliens will mostly best Predators in a melee and if you want to one shot them you need to charge your plasma bolt which takes a lot of power. Gameplay is fast, fun, and adds a small element of horror combined with an excellent level design. The only other game I've played that had this kind of level design was F.E.A.R. which wasn't too different. There are upgrades, ammo, armor, etc. and in order to get special upgrades was to search or explore the level.
As for multiplayer, I kind of ♥♥♥♥♥ about it time to time. The Marines from what I've seen are probably the best, since you can corner camp and gun down countless adversaries with your minigun. It's not fun, just watching two marines sit in a corner and kill you instantly. Not only that, when you're cloaked as a predator they can still see you (if they're veteran) and Aliens don't seem to have too many advantages, sure they have speed, but it means nothing against a guy with perfect aim. The only way I've been able to beat these marines was to use the disc (considered op) and the spear gun (I prefer the spear gun because you have one disc). There's not much element of stealth or strategy in the game, imo, just twitch shooting and melee is quite strange.
If you want to pick up a well designed game with a somewhat decent multiplayer, then sure! Go ahead.

So I picked this game up durring the steam summer sale, thinking it would be a nice expierence.
It was... but not for the hefty real price tag.
The game itself barely has any content right from the start. From missions to guns, there was very little. It seemed to be buy dlc to use this gun type of game. It seemed that the game was aimed for multiplayer.
Second issue, clipping. Usually you think you can fire over cover? Wrong. Most cover was broken in the way that the hitbox was larger than your crouch profile; which ended up fluffing your shots. In this game firing alerts enemys to your position so It is frustrating seeing your shot magicaly not happen and you pressing down the trigger agian thinking it just "missed".
Third issue, "Sniper Elite". You'd think this game was about sniping, from doing cool trick shots or raining death from afar. You are wrong. Most of the game play is geared towards "stealth". Which means you rarely get to fire your sniper. Firing your gun, ANYWHERE, even if there are no enemies around alerts everyone on the map. Utilizing the system of sound masking, gives you an average of 1 shot per minute, unless you find a generator in a good position which is not common. If you break stealth, depening on the difficulty, all the enemies will come alive and chase you down.
Fourth Issue, movement. Sprinting in this game is completly redudant. Normal walking is basicly sprinting without holding shift. Because of this enemies will notice you from afar if you just stand up. This leads to the ENTIRE game of playing CROUCH MAN. Which is completly irratating due to the fact it is slower than a slug. There is no sprint crouch like in MGSV.
In the end I rate this game a 6/10. It has a decent engine, mechanics but lacking in content and riddled with bugs and poor in-game player optimization.

TL:DR A great Game, even if it's a complete 180 from all the other games in the series.
Full Review: Firstly, I would like to say, this game is completely different from every other game in the Series, so don't go in expecting a fast-paced, non-linear FPS game. Instead, this is a slower, more linear, and more atmospheric horror game. With that being said, not only do these changes help to give the game deeper claws to keep its grasp on you, but the first half of the game
for those curious) is pure horror, all the way. For those worried though, The game returns towards (but not all the way to) the classic formula in the 2nd half of the game, while still mixing in some horror elements.
Graphically, it looks fantastic for the time, and still looks good today, even if the polygon count reveals the game's true age (that last part may be due to the fact that I'm transitioning to PC gaming from Consoles...). The action is still DOOM at its core, although you'll need to pay more attention your ammo, as reloading is a thing in this game. One annoying issue, however, is that the game is very dark (again, especially in the first half of the game), which, while adding to the scare quotient, means that you can have issues when firing at demons in the darker rooms. You can easily switch between gun and flashlight using "F", but ideally, the game (probably) is expecting you to use your memory with the flashlight, and your hearing to attack the demons when you can't see it (I say this because the reticule turns red when you sucessfully deal damage to an enemy).
If that does sound too annoying, you have 3 options:
1. Install the "Duct Tape" mod (Google it, Adds a flashlight to the shotgun and the machine gun).
2. Skip this version of the game, and get the BFG edition (Adds a temporary flashlight to use while holding any weapon).
3. Train your memory and hearing, to get used to it (For best results with the scare quotient).
Personally, I went with 1 at first, before switching to 3 later on
. If I had the money, I'd probably get the BFG edition, which also includes the previous two games as well!
Regardless of what edition you pick up, and whether or not you decide to use the Duct Tape mod, You'll be pleasently surprised on how far id goes from the Traditional DOOM formula and still deliver a great, if somewhat flawed, experience.

I just got done playing "Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" and I gotta say, the ending sucks. Not in a bad way, I mean the game is fun and addictive all the way through, but because...well for now let's just say it's pretty personal. The game is well worth the money, especially if you're like me and got it on sale, so pick it up if you have a sibling or a single very best friend whom you love a great deal.
"Brothers" is a fantasy adventure platformer. It starts off like a story book and eventually wastes no time becoming a dark tale rife with death and despair. The selling point with the game is that it's a cognitive challenge, as most of you probably already know, because you control the Big Brother and Little Brother with the left stick and bumper and the right stick and bumper, respectively. It gets pretty confusing to control the two if you get distracted, which you will since the locales in this game are all gorgeous.
The story is all about the actions and the tone in the characters' voices since they all speak professional gibberish. You couldn't understand dang if you weren't invested in it. Speaking of which, it's a pretty simple story: the Brothers' dad get's sick and the village doctor instructs them to find the cure. Forget the cure, getting there is where it's at. There's all sorts of friendly faces and deadly situations you'll come across from wolves to invisible snow giants. There's also tons of interaction with these characters and the environment, even if it does nothing to further your progression, but damn it does wonders for immersion.
There may be a few puzzles or boss fights that may have you stuck for a little while, but nothing too difficult or game breaking. There are only two negatives I can think of. The game is too forgiving. If you fall off a platform to your death or got within 2 millimeters of an enemy (all of the enemies melee by the way, no projectiles), you start over on the platform just before you die. There are no lengthy platforming sequence that fairly tests your skills like the one on the top of the Tula Tree in "Guacamelee." This brings me to my next point: everything is really easy. The clues to the puzzles, the knobs you have to turn, the paths you have to take (this can be good or bad depending on who you are) and the ledges you have to grab are all very apparent. This voids the challenge aside from, of course, your capability to control the brothers. If I weren't such a completionist I would have no reason to replay this game.
It's about the journey, not the destination, and it was one hell of a journey. 9/10. Also, don't be a dumb♥♥♥♥♥and use the keyboard. They control like a wet sponge that way. Get a game pad

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is an adventure/puzzle game with a unique control scheme, and an outstanding story that is one of the best around. This game is set in a somewhat fantasy world, boasting stunning vistas the brothers adventure forth in. The fantasy nature isn't as heavy as in games that make it a huge focus, since this game is more realistic in its graphical approach with well designed nature scenes. The fantasy elements pop up with some of the things the brothers interact with. Each of the characters are stylized with a less realistic style, but do stand out from the beautiful landscapes. As for the music, there are some instrumental and vocal tracks, but they are sparsely played throughout the game. They do put the mood when a song starts playing, and they do help emphasize some key parts of the story very well.
What makes Brothers one of the most well recieved games is its story. This is one of the games you want to have no spoilers before playing. Two brothers, an older and younger brother, must recieve a special healing liquid from the Tree of Life to save their ill father. The story is driven in the game mainly by gestures and actions, as the people in Brothers speak in a fictional language.
The other reason that Brothers is a great game is its unique gameplay. Players control both brothers at the same time in a kind of single player co-op game. Each brother can move around in all directions and have a context specific action button, making this game best played with an Xbox 360 controller or equivalent. The brothers mainly explore around and climb things. For some parts, both brothers have to work together in tandem or do specific tasks with each brother. The older brother is stronger and can pull levers and give a boost, while the younger brother can move between bars. The puzzle aspects of this game by using each brother in specific uses is great, along with the general idea of using two characters at once.
This game is pretty short though, so expect the game to last about 3-4 hours. The difficulty isn't too hard as most puzzles can be self-explanitory, save for some parts that may be unclear as to what to do. The achievements take some exploring and thinking to complete, but they are optional side quests and not part of the main story.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons has its strong story along with a unique control scheme. Well recieved by many to recieve various awards, this game will certainlly enthrall players with a good emotional story and an interesting adventure with puzzles controlling two brothers at once.

Not really sure how I feel about this game. It's good, but there are some issues with it (which may or may not have been fixed, I haven't played for a while TBH).
Pros:
-In depth strategy game which rewards good teamwork and mirco/macro skills.
-LOTS of units.
-Large scale battles.
-About as good as a Wargame simulator can get, and offers a huge amount of different ways to win and have fun.
Cons:
-Teams; players giving up the moment their good unit is killed, putting more pressure onto their teammates, which in turn causes them to get salty as their stuff gets murdered, often leading to them leaving which worsens things for everyone else. It can feel like a 50/50 chance of getting a toxic team or an alright team, which can mean that you can go literally days without seeing a team that doesn't arty your units for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles.
-A lot of hard counters. This is kinda a good and a bad thing, but it's in my con list mainly due to death stacks being impossible to counter if your losing (due to points decreasing as territories get taken off your team which decreases your options in terms of units). Get 2-3 players who know what their doing on the enemy team and you'll be stuck, often on your own as everyone 'conveniently' moves their stuff to the other side of the map, facing down endless waves of bombers, tanks and artillery as your units get utterly flattened.
-The global chat. This is more a personal gripe than a problem with the game itself, but some of the stuff that got posted there during the time I played regularly was actually disgusting, and I had never seen those levels of hate in any game I had played up to that point.
I am going to redownload it sometime soon to see if anythings changed about it for the better, in which case I'll delete this review but my hopes are not particulary high.
Hope this review helped, and as always be somewhat critical of what a random internet gamer has to say. Look it up and decide for yourselves if it is worth it.

Aliens vs Predator Classic 2000 is a first person shooter with a unique gimmick. There are 3 campaigns starring drastically different characters. You can play as a Marine, Predator, or Alien. Each has their own playstyle  and weaponry.
The game is from 2000, so the graphics are quite dated. People, enemies and environments all look very blocky. Thankfully, the devs have increased the resolution for the rerelease, so everything appears a bit sharper than I imagine it did in the original. Still, the graphics are rough and that's something you will have to deal with if you want to enjoy this game.
Each species has a unique control style, and luckily in this update gamepad support was added. That's my preferred method, although I found the aiming to be quite difficult, and probably much easier to handle with a mouse. There are some areas with generally frustrating platforming which you will have to navigate. You are also just thrown into the campaign without a tutorial, so prepare to learn the controls yourself through trial and error. Most games these days at least let you know quickly how to get around the controls, so this game shows its age in that way.
The sound and general atmosphere is pretty well done. There is voice acting, and as a marine you will get your orders from the recording of a live actor. There are some general scary moments, especially playing as a marine in the dark while Xenomorphs are hunting you.
Overall, while I feel this may have been an enjoyable game in its time, that time has passed. Many of the FPS and 3D games from that era feel dated, and it really shows here. From the controls, to the graphics, to the general gameplay, the genre has improved leaps and bounds since 2000. While there's some enjoyment to be had for big time Alien fans or those that played this in the past and are feeling nostalgic, I'd recommend most people to stay away.

There is something about Spelunky that has kept me playing it religiously for about an hour every day – I like to call it ‘Spelunky Fever’. Every day I get home from school, turn on my PC and boot up Spelunky play for as long as possible and consider it time well spent. Whether it be grinding though a stage to unlock the next shortcut, or trying to beat my friend’s scores, I always make a point of playing it.
Mossmouth really have mastered the ‘one more go’ aspect of their game. Simply accepting that I died in the first ten seconds, due to a stone I threw landing on my head, is never an option. I always have to get 100 more gold. I need get to the next level. I must perfect my technique of mercilessly stealing from and slaughtering shopkeepers. Wait, what?
Yes. I did say slaughtering shopkeepers.
This randomly generated platfomer sees you play as an Indiana Jones style adventurer (along with many others, once you have unlocked them) spelunking your way through various levels of a mine, ranging from the sublime to the ridiculous; you will have to make your way through both jungles and ice caves, Egyptian temples and the stomach of a giant worm to reach the final boss.
However, you might not be seeing the final boss for a very long time. This game is hard! A few bites from a spider, or misjudging an already precarious jump over some fatal spikes kills you in one fell swoop, to have you respawn right at the start to begin a new adventure. That is of course, unless you have visited the tunnel man and received your shortcuts to different stages.
These shortcuts allow you to jump back into the action at the start of your chosen level, easing off the difficulty a little. However, in my opinion, these shortcuts could have been taken out. On the contrary, they do no harm if you choose not to use them. They’re more like a stepladder of help instead of a full on escalator to success.
Another part of Spelunky’s charm is how much there is to learn about it, and there’s so much to learn that just watching a YouTube video won’t do. The best way to become familiar with the ins and outs of Spelunky is by playing it. Naturally it’s not everyone’s cup of tea; In fact, my favourite review of Spelunky on Steam is an, ‘I don’t like this game’, review where the author simply states how stupid it is that the tutorial doesn’t tell him about the ghost that spawns after spending too long on a stage.
However I do have some qualms with the game; I hate the controls. At least the ones for keyboard and mouse. I know using Z, X, A, S, and the arrow keys may seem like a logical idea, but in practise it simply isn’t up to par. Too many times have I fallen foul of otherwise easily beaten enemies by not being able to jump away quick enough or by not being able to lob a bomb into the right direction. However, I do find that the gamepad controls are very likeable and did not need re-mapping at all, so in that regard Spelunky redeems itself; the 360 controls are very ergonomic, as one would expect since it was released on XBLA first.
Before being released on Xbox, it was a simple java game – and a free one at that. The HD version then is much prettier, moving from the retro graphics many indie developers love, to have a cartoonier and more stylised feel, which is a step in the right direction. What’s more, I find that the more you play Spelunky the more you respect the detail that has been put into every part of the graphics, not just the character models but the backgrounds and animations and so on.
It isn’t just the aesthetics that’s had a lot of love either. The music is very catchy and enjoyable to listen to. A variety of chip-tune/electronic style tracks provide fitting background music for the game. Although there isn’t the widest variety of music, it never seems to become old at monotonous, instead you learn to use the music as another tool to help you sense what is ahead and get one step closer to beating the game.
Mossmouth have provided a lot of reasons for you to replay the game over and over again. First of all, there are many unlockable skins – with lots of variety. My personal pick is a Viking, but my friend loves to play as a Super Meat Boy cameo he unlocked. Also completing the game and seeing all there is to see in Spelunky is a big draw.
However the biggest reason for my constant return is the Daily Challenge. Every day, a seed is sent out to every player, the same for each individual, which means you, can compete with your friends for high scores and even try to become the very best in the world via the online rankings. I think I got 6387th once! It’s a simple concept, but well implemented and has kept me playing the game for ages.
There is also your standard adventure mode, which is what this review has primarily been about, but there’s also a death match mode too. I dabbled in it a little, but if I’m honest it’s not the most fun I’ve ever had. I’m sure it would be a hoot with 3 other friends, as would the standard adventure mode be, but if your alone or playing with inexperienced players it’s just not fun.
To finish, I think Spelunky is a marvellous game and a great addition to your game library, especially if you have a controller and a lot of time to practice. It’s easy to learn but hard to master, but once you have got the hang of it, you’ll never let go of it!

I bought Train Simulator just over a year ago, and barely a day has gone by without me either driving a train, creating a scenario or watching others play it.  I was a complete novice when I bought it, knew nothing about the controls or signals, and didn't know a Class 66 from a Class 395 Javelin. It was not too difficult to learn how to drive a train in this game...I recommend you do the Training tutorials to begin with and then progress onto Quick Drives, which are a bit more forgiving than jumping right into career scenarios.  Don't be afraid - nobody dies if you crash or SPAD (go through a red signal) and you can always start again...its a simulator!  Watching YouTube videos is another great way to learn how to drive.
Some things you should be made aware of.  Don't buy this game with the expectation of only ever going to own the routes which come with it.  Sure, there are scenarios in the workshop, they say, but a lot of the scenarios use stock from other routes or DLC.  You see, to have more realism, you need a variety of trains, and they don't always come together in the same route/DLC.  So after you've played the routes which came with TS, you'll be hanging out for the steam sales to get more locos and routes, and after awhile you would have amassed quite a collection which will keep you entertained forever more.  The truth is though, you never come to the point of saying 'that's enough, no more!"  There's always another loco, another route...another sale to tempt you.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing...it gives the game longevity.  There's been people playing it a lot longer than I have.  You start to recognise them around the Sales after awhile....some admiring the EMU on sale for half price, others kicking the bogies of a classic diesel locomotive to see if they think its what they are after.  Ok, I got a bit off track there (pardon the pun).  The point is, you will end up playing this game for years as well, especially after all the money you invest in it.
Something else which you should consider is that beyond DTG, there are third party companies who make routes, locomotives and enhancements for Train Sim.  The enhancements/sounds are usually well worth getting, as they can really improve some of the older locomotives.
I won't waffle much longer but to say I do recommend this game.  But be prepared to start selling stuff (furniture, the dog, your brother/sister...) in order to keep buying DLC.

I have been playing this game for 2 years now.
I joined back in the beginning of Open Beta, when the menu still displayed the rank chart across the bottom of the screen (very old layout).
Since then the game has only gone downhill. I have played on every faction in most of the wars, and been part of many privately owned battle groups.
HACKING - Hacking is a major problem in this game, and because Heroes & Generals is a "indie" game their is no Valve server authenticator, there are all sorts of hackers and each one ruins the gameplay just a little bit more
MULTIPLAYER - As this is the only gamemode in the game you would expect it to be the best, but its not. Multiplayer is very laggy, bugged, and takes forever to put you into a game, just to give you a respawn que.
LEVELING - Leveling up in this game used to be very hard and not something for the light of heart, but now in the more recent upates, I was able to go from level 4 to 6 in a matter of 4 hours, something that 2 years ago would be near impossible
CURRENCY - This game has two types of currency, one that you earn through playing multiplayer "Heroes" and the other you earn from playing multiplayer "Generals". The currency used in "Heroes" has been made too easy to achieve as even one year ago gaining 10,000 currency took hours, now it takes you the total of one game. The currency in "Generals" has been made the same way unfortunaetly.
Pay To Win - In Heroes & Generals you can also buy pre-leveled charecters, weapons, vehicles, badges, boosts, money, and war bonds. Pre-leveled charecters are always more powerful than charecters you level up yourself, and just about everyone on the apposing team has them, so if you just want to play for fun, and not spend money, your screwed.
Trolling - Many younger users play this game as well, while I am not opposed to younger users playing video games, in this game they often just buy vehicles and do donuts in fields, or buy explosives/rocket launchers and blow you and your team mates up.
Realisticness - I have noticed that while playing this game has become much like CSGO, were the game was made to be played like a simulator, but is being played based on the now normal FPS "movements".
(NEW) Quick-scoping - While I know this has happened in every FPS since Call of Duty, its a little annoying to have every single Russian enemy one-shot kill you without much thought every time you encounter them.

Like any good horror movie, you might be tempted to look, point and subsequently laugh at Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 whilst guffawing "get a load of those rubbish special effects, who'd be scared of that?". Well, if you do that, you are an ignorant fool. Notwithstanding this game introduced us to the first accurate representation of the Aliens genre, that being an experience that focused more on isolation, tension and near-blind encounters conducted at blinding speed, it was a step forward for games in general.
Harken back to the year 2000, if you can. If you're 14 or under, this whole paragraph is probably pointless. Polygonal shooters are ugly and cartoonish, with true dynamic lighting rare. You've obviously (and rightfully) seen underage screenings of both the Aliens and Predator movies and you excitedly boot up a demo disc containing a sliver of gameplay from the much-anticipated Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 (back then it was just called Aliens versus Predator).
You begin in a pitch-dark APC, the same one seen in the seminal 1986 movie, and instantly you feel a giddy sense of anticipation. You clutch the USCM's weapon of choice, an M41A Pulse Rifle. You scream to yourself, or aloud if feeling bold or just have no consideration for those in the next room, "I am the ULTIMATE badass!". It's dark outside the APC but you don't care. You stride out, eager to pump your enemy full of white lead (not a euphemism) and then it begins. Your motion sensor bleeps. You grin at the sound - it's just like in the movie!
Then an alien shows up and you die.
Now, bear in mind at this point realism in games was restricted to Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six - which your childish mind was not prepared for in 1998 and the disc was subsequently left to reside somewhere under the bed - and you can understand the terror this Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 (Aliens versus Predator back then) demo generated. Aliens and Predators, unless played on the Training difficulty, are fast and deadly. Light is scarcer and arguably more valuable than ammo. Your armour may stop a few bullets but against razor-sharp claws and shoulder cannons? Might as well wear Kleenex, mate.
The single-player campaign features six missions in three distinct flavours. The marine, despite having access to meaty weapons and a sharp haircut, is undoubtedly the most vulnerable of the three. Your xenomorph enemies move swiftly and often you've only got a couple of seconds to react - usually to a telltale hiss, scratch or bite to the head - before you become their food. Add to this the facehuggers, whose surprise one-hit kills have induced fear-comas in the stoutest gents, and you can see the developer's statement of intent. In this game, humans are the prey.
As a Predator, you have access to deliciously effective weapons and equipment. Injured? No sweat. Just whip out your pointy healy-sticks and one agonised scream later, you're ready to go. Naturally, your human opponents are just flimsy, sweaty meatbags in the face of your cloaking-device enhanced magnificence. Properly ambushed, you can exploded them with your shoulder cannon, impale them with your spear gun or give them a good old Carl Weathers-style send off with your wrist blades. Xenomorphs prove a slightly tougher challenge but with your enhanced vision modes (which, like the Mass Effect 3 ending, come in red, green and blue flavours), superior endurance and aforementioned healy-sticks, your chances are a sight better than as a marine. Facehuggers are still cheap, insta-killing little ♥♥♥♥♥, though.
The true beauty of the game, however comes in the shape of the late H.R Giger's chillingly graceful alien killing machines. Or rather, taking control of one. My personal favourite game mode and a real change to the pace of the campaign, the Alien can dismember humans with the flick of a wrist, walk on any surface and providing it's sitting in darkness, can become near-invisible to enemies. While this is disorienting at first, there's a true pleasure in carving up everyone you come across before they can so much as react, or stalking that particularly annoying marine from the ceiling before dropping on him unawares.
Being from the year 2000 (the flashback to that year ended a few paragraphs ago), the game does look its age. Polygons are smooth but the textures are a little muddy, but the Steam version runs well on Windows 7 and at resolutions we'd never thought possible 14 years ago. There are even an additional 5 or 6 missions for each character to be unlocked after finishing the game on each difficulty. The sounds are all accurate and pertaining to their franchises, though for atmospheric purposes I'd recommend turning the music off altogether for the marine missions.
The only truly inexcusable issue relates to the truly awful in-game cinematics. While the original release had a modestly-budgeted yet competently acted cut-scenes of a marine who was black yelling at you (or about you, in the case of the ETs), at some point they re-released the game with vids of fully costumed men who are white, with possibly the worst American accents this side of Gerard Butler. Yes, they look prettier but...well, just don't exit to desktop the first time you hear 'Lissen up Prahvat".
In summary, for anyone who knew and loved this game back in the days before bloom lighting and other graphical terms I can't be bothered to Google, pick it up and see for yourself how easy and forgiving modern games are. For everyone else, just pick it up and receive a masterclass in how an Aliens game should be done, i.e. with darkness, quick deaths and loud, piercing yelps of fear and shock.

Couldn't find a way up to peaks and what not without teleporting there. But you have to ride locations to unlock the teleport to them...and none of this covered. Perhaps you can't get up the mountains without buying the snowmobile in the store?
Either way, would not recommend. Gameplay did not feel smooth at any point. It was just a clunky, sluggish mess.

Questions You Might Be Looking For Before You Buy.
-Can I run it?
Let me tell you, this game is well optimized. Even though I have a good PC, I was still able to run it on my brother's (i5 6600k, RX 480, 16 gb ram), on Ultra Settings in 60 FPS, Fullscreen constantly. Don't worry AMD graphics card users, this game isn't like Nier: Automata where the game just breaks down before you can finish that annoying beginning mission.
-Do I need to know the Tekken Lore?
Yes and no. There are some parts and characters who might confuse you (Kuma, Panda, Feng Wei <--- who even plays him?) but besides that this game does an excellent way to tell the story from beginning to end.
-Do I need to use a controller or fightstick?
Depends, I use a fightstick but controller works just as fine, but the keyboard is a bit confusing and has a bit of a learning curve.
-Should I get Deluxe Edition?
Honestly, yea! It's not overpriced and you get season pass, but that's for cross over characters, the DLC for classic characters of this franchise will be free!
-How are the characters?
Tekken offers over 30 characters to choose from, each with there own type of playstyle based on actual martial arts. Each character has a story-rich background that both the Tekken veterans love and new comers love to research about. Except Feng Wei, screw him. Also more are coming!
-How is the fighting?
You know how Mortal Kombat and Streetfighter has that tedious, stiff, non-fluid combat? In those games it's all about landing combo's off of combo list and the character animations are so stiff and ugly! In this game, combat is so fluid and beautiful, even you MK and SF veterans must admit, you can even create your own combos no need to follow the combo list, but it is recommend for new players. The maps as always in every Tekken amazing, bright, and vibrant. Also you can interact with them by kicking Feng Wei off the balcony or through the second floor to the first. LET ME TELL YOU there's this feature where if both player are low health and they attack at the SAME TIME it goes into slow-motion and it's the best thing in any fighting game, you have to see it!!!!! Also they now have Rage Art and Rage Drive which are special moves in which each characters can use, pretty cool, I was not expecting this in this game. Also if you main Feng Wei, I'm coming for you.
-Customization?
Do you not understand what game you're looking at, this is TEKKEN baby the "King of all Customizables" in the fighting genre. You can customize from each character to your life bar. I made a character as Buddha. Don't believe me? Well you can in Tekken 7!
-Music?
You have no idea how "lit" the soundtracks are, I'm sorry for using that word, but there's no other way to explain how amazing the soundtrack is in this game
-I don't have any friends, should I get it?
So? I'll be your friend (Pomoji), you don't really need a friend to play this game, it's more of a luxury not a necessity and online is good and it works great!

If you take most of the popular trends in Indie Gaming over the last few years and combine them into a well polished and fun package, you get Spelunky.
A 2D Platformer, it has:
- Rogue-like difficulty and permadeath
- Rudimentary character progression
- Procedural level generation
- Tight controls
- Moddability
Passing a level will only take you about 2 minutes if you're a completionist, with about 5 levels per stage and 4 or 5 stages, so you can theoretically finish this game in under an hour. But the chance of that happening is slim to none. This is because you will drop a bomb under your own feet and die. Then you will respawn, jump off your platform onto spikes, and die. You'll respawn again, get through a few levels, but then get hit by an arrow trap and die. A few deaths later and you'll finally manage to survive long enough to make it to the second stage. Things are looking up, until you♥♥♥♥♥♥off a bunch of hornets and they kill you. This goes on for the entire game.
And that's just the normal campaign -- there are daily challenges and multiplayer as well. For such a small package, this game has a ton of content to keep you busy.
All in all, it is one of the best games I've ever played. It is difficult - you will find yourself screaming at your computer while playing it, but you'll be having a good time even still. I can't recommend it enough.

GSC Game World had an unexpected hit with S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl and they keep the momentum going by developing a prequel and pushing it out the door in about a year and a half after Shadow's release.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky had some tough shoes to fill. Expectations were very high and whlist it can't match the first for gameplay, it manages to deliver on the atmosphere and adds some new gameplay elements which can be considered either frustrating or brilliant.
You play as Zone guide and veteran S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Scar who, after amazingly surviving a deadly emission, is rescued by an unknown faction known as Clear Sky. Located in the Swamps, you must work with them secretly to find out why the zone is getting worse.
The game is a 50/50 mix of areas seen in Shadow of Chernobyl and brand new areas. The old areas have some pretty big changes to them and areas that were safe in the first game might be a complete nightmare this time around and vice versa.
The game focuses a lot of its first half on the war between the various factions located in the Zone. You are free, once outside the Swamps, to join any faction you want (Freedom, Duty, Stalkers, even the Bandits) and have the privliges that faction offers, all whilst still secretly working for the Clear Sky faction that saved your life.
The game has had some of its more interesting elements removed; your character no longer needs to eat and drink to stay alive, the systems for detecting how visible you are and how much noise you are making have also been removed.
Finding artifacts is now a bit more challenging then before; in Shadow of Chernobyl they would be bobbing up and down in random places around the Zone and you could just run up to them and pick them up maybe whilst avoiding some anomolies. In Clear Sky, artifacts are now invisible but you have a detector that can guide you to them, you just have to work your way through the deadly anomalies, get close to it and it appears for you to collect. This risk/reward mechanism enhances the values of artifacts greatly.
The story sadly isn't as interesting as the first game and instead of most of the spoken dialogue being in Ukranian like in the first game, it has been translated into very rough English that sounds forced and out of place. This can take away from some of the atmosphere of being a foreigner in a completely strange environment.
The game also has a nasty habit of making enemies invincible unless you are close enough. No more picking off people from a distance which can be incredibly frustrating at times.
It isn't as good as Shadow of Chernobyl story-wise and mechanicly but the atmosphere and general improvements make up for it. A worthy addition to the series and worth playing!
P.S. You can grab the "CLEAR SKY COMPLETE" modification to fix crash to desktop bugs and translation problems.
Still a really fun game, especially in Multiplayer.
Recommended for zombie killers

Without a doubt in my mind the best Doom game ever released. Doom 3 elevated the formula established by the original games and added punchier combat, the ability to look up and, of course, all out intensity. It's horror elements are, granted, fairly rudimentary, resorting to a (quite large) abundance of jump scares and spawning multiple enemies in tight spaces so that you aren't always prepared to attack. These actually get quite tedious after a while and you also start to expect them more as you move through the game.
Doom 3 handles intensity, however, like a professional and delivers a masterclass of suspense-filled FPS action. Importantly, it creates a sense of vulnerability in the player, despite arming them with all the original games' weapon arsenal; you often fight in the dark, against multiple adversaries and, without your flashlight, you'll often fire blindly at walls as the targets scurry off into the shadows. The flashlight taking up a weapon slot was honestly a great idea. I have no idea why people wanted to change this, as it was a fundamental part of what made Doom 3 such an uneasy and suspenseful experience.
For all it's gameplay strengths, the Doom 3 story is still worth mentioning. It's not amazing, and has a particularly gaping plothole revolving around a certain principal character, but is functional and enjoyable enough to provide enough impetus to slug through the dark demon-infested space complex. As with most FPSs, the boss battles are relatively weak affairs but even after 12 years, their designs have the power to creep you out.
I loved Doom 3 due to it's impact in making players view the Doom franchise differently. It built upon the original games' love of trapping you in a room full of weaponry and armour but spawning half a hundred demons, made it darker and spookier (and also more claustrophobic) but kept the running+gunning gameplay and weapon variety intact so that the essence of the originals wasn't totally lost. This new direction for Doom I welcomed and hoped the new 2016 game would follow, though unfortunately that is not the case.
This is a game that is certainly worth picking up and adding to your collection; although it's relatively old, it achieves both encumbering atmosphere and suspense, while retaining the staple 'balls to the wall' combat of the originals. It is different in enough ways that evolves the formula of the original games, yet familiar enough so as not to harm the series' character and established gameplay elements. Highly recommended.

While it might not be as frentic as the originals or this year's title, Doom 3 is a great game. Ranging from animations to lighting, atmosphere and sound this game has aged well were it not for the low-poly models. But hey, back then you had to compensate !
The models look average for the most part (because of the lighting aspect put to good use) and there are only some specific moments where you get to see their true ugly-ness. Textures are blurry even on the highest setting and this is the only thing I feel could be improved on, but otherwise they look good from a distance or at a quick view.
The weapons are so-and-so. Some of them feel just perfect (like the chaingun, plasmagun and rocket launcher) while some are either too weak or too quiet (the pistol and machinegun). Either way they are adequate to use and the combat doesn't feel clunky if you can get on with the slow, methodical aproach Doom 3 wants to take.
Overall I think Doom 3 is a great game but at the same time an acquired taste. If you loved the originals to death I recommend you try this somewhere else before buying just for reassurance. Otherwise you could go blind but would have to be very open-minded.
Make sure to set the sound settings to "Surround" instead of "Stereo" because this is a very important step in immersion. I found myself using some phone headphones (not even real headphones, lol) while playing and wondered why the sound wasn't as great as it used to be.
If there's one thing as to why I would recommend Doom 3 over the BFG Edition is because of mods. Not only you can make it look unimaginably better, but there are also numerous singleplayer maps which can increase your play-time.

Two brothers face the adventure of their lives when their father is struck by a mortal disease and the village's healer sends them on a quest to find the only medicine that can heal him. Brothers is a tale about wonder, companionship and grief, yet it tells its story masterfully without using a single (actual) word.
The gameplay itself is nothing to write home about. It does have an interesting mechanic which lets you control each brother with a different analog stick. While the game does have keyboard support, I haven't tested it, although I think the game is meant to be played with a controller and a keyboard just wouldn't feel right. Despite being interesting at first, the novelty factor wears out quickly, and if you have played adventure games before, the game won't present you with any challenge whatsoever.
While the gameplay will probably fail to get you interested, the game does have other attributes. As mentioned before, it is masterfully told adventure. The premise itself isn't anything particularly exciting, but as some people say, it's the journey that matters, not the destination itself, and it is especially valid in this game. I feel telling anything about the journey would spoil the experience, since part of the game's sense of wonder comes from taking you to all sorts of unexpected places. The exotic soundtrack complements the sense of wonder very well and is a good fit for the game (kind of a personal note, I thought it was a little similar to Mark Knight's soundtrack for Populous 3...).
Brothers is a relatively short (took me 4 hours to complete it with all achievements), albeit powerful experience, and I would recommend it to anyone who's looking for a good adventure.

Doom 3 (published 2004) is an awesome hellish corridor shooter with a great (albeit simple) campaign story, if you please ignore that demons from Hell should be unimpressed by earthly firepower.
It's a very immersive ride that I have taken from A to Z at least 4 times. If you want to forget the world and live through a demonic science fiction story, Doom 3 is the way to go.
The sounds require a bit of getting used to because they are equalized / dynamic compressed too extremely (though not as insanely as in Bioshock Infinite), but after a while this will feel alright.
People say that Doom 3 is visually too dark, but what they are missing is that this is a game for
gamers who want to go on an immersive ride instead of just having fun in the living room with friends. So, turn off the lights, use a big screen, tweak the FOV (The console allows to set anything you want.), and get lost for 12-18 hours in a dark science fiction tale that, while kind of routine once you know how to handle your weapons, will keep you on the edge throughout.
Some people don't like that it takes a while before the action starts. Those, too, are not
gamers. Drink up the mood! Role-play! Explore this science fiction reality while you're not yet under pressure and while things are still well lit.
Doom 3 uses real-time lighting throughout, and I believe it was even the first 3D 1st person campaign shooter that did this. While this has visual downsides (especially since the engine is old, so there is no hint of Global Illumination) compared to baked light-maps, it contributes immensely to the experience, and they show it off in quite a few places. Try to imagine what it's like to see this for the first time. Oooh! Aaah! Who wants to touch me.

I am sure many people have had problems with this game, Heroes And Generals, and to a fair extent, yes, there are bugs, glitchs, and hackers in this game, but isnt that to be expected with a game that has just enterd steam? It is getting way more players than that of what normally played before voted onto steam by Steam Greenlight. The bugs, in my experince of this game, are not glitchs that will break your game. Yes, sometimes you will have to wait five minutes plus to get into a game but that is only because of the way the game works, there are three matchmaking levels, bronze, silver, and the best, gold. In bronze you will most likley instantly get into a match, same as silver, but in gold it is much harder as fewer players are in this matchmaking session.
I think heroes and generals is a masterpeice of a game, that still, like a baby, needs to be nurted my its parents, to polish the game. When you forget the glitchs, this game is great, it combines four great sections of  WW2 together, it combines Planes, Tanks, Infrantry, and the men behind the tactics, Generals, together to create a epic battle situation. Now onto the game istelf.
There are five different charcters at the time of this review, Fighter Pilot, Tank Crew, Recon, Paratrooper, Infrantry, and Generals. Fighter Pilot needs to be polished as i find it extremley hard to fly a plane without a joystick, and currently they do not have the software to support a joy stick. Tank Crew is quite a fun character, you can drive around in your tank, sniping from the hills with a tank destoryer, or rushing into battle with a light tank mowing down infrantry as you go, there are many ways to play with Tank Crew, but it can get redundant if you keep playing with tank crew and dont swich to another class of character. There is Paratrooper, now paratrooper does exactly what it did historically, it is dropped from a plane above the enemey and can land behind enemey linds undetecded. Recon is perfect for the calmer/quick reaction playing style. Recon is used as a sniper class (Even though you can use any of the infrantry class charcters as sniper, recon comes with a scoped Karjack rifle which saves you saving up credits and grinding for a sniper rifle in another class). Infrantry is the basic class of troop, it can be used with pretty much any weapon you want, be it a Light Machine Gun, A Machine Pistol, A pistol, A knife, A Rifle, A Bazooka and more! General i have not experinced so i can not comment on that.
My final opinon is Heroes And Generals is a great game, but in its early stage, quite limited, as you can only play on the European Theater. If you dont like to grind then Heroes And Generals might not be for you. I think that if you are someone who is extremley inrested in WW2, than Heroes And Generals Will be a great game.

I just got to the Roflstomp rank 7 part!!!
Here's my take on it:
If you care about your KDR then either get really good by playing lots or give up!
Up to rank 7, you are basically infantry only with a few jeeps & bicycles, recon & paratroop classes are introduced between rank 1 & 7 can't remember where, you are also going up against similar experienced players, so a good time to learn some of the maps, & the mechanics of the game.
After rank 7 you are in gold match making which basically pits you against people who have been playing months & years, with various tanks , planes & weapons, it is much more difficult & more realistic WW2 gameplay, which by the way you have to get much better at.
Like basic things like using cover (there is no active spotting, although there is some passive spotting) & not running either in the open or on your own, waiting for support, hiding from tanks & anything you can't damage or kill.
You do get a salary (in game currency) per hour (which increases as you rank up) as well as game achievement bonus to pay for repairs & ammo replenishment, & save it up to get an upgrade on your weapon (which costs more to maintain) or buy a new one. It will be a while before you can damage tanks (it's all the more enjoyable preventing a cap by a piece of armour by hiding) although you do get AT mines quite early on but unless the map has choke points like bridges or you sneak up to one (did this lastnight, very rewarding) then they are pretty useless as you only get 2 before you run out & have to rearm & they slow you down quite a bit (the length of time you can sprint with goes down the larger the object you are trying to take.
You can however unlock any vehicles that are abandoned on the battlefield, I managed to pick the lock of a Sherman firefly lastnight, took about 30-40 seconds of holding down E, so you really don't want to be doing it too close to combat!
There are many other game mechanics like badges & ribbons that can make your soldier a more specialised class, but I'll leave that for you to find out!
All in all I really like this game, it has it's flaws but what game doesn't?
If you want a WW2 game that is challenging, where you have to get better & learn then this is for you, if you want a run & gun KDR fest then this is probably not for you, although using a Grease gun to clear a building is a lot of fun!

is a fantastic WW2 stealth shooter, where you play as OSS officer Karl Fairburne (known from the previous
games) set on a special mission to hunt down the German general Vahlen. The game takes place on the North African front. You fight both Italian and German armed forces. As you progress trough eight missions, you gradually reveal Vahlen's plans to build a superweapon and, of course, face himself at the end of the game.
is also a tactical shooter, which means that, first, you explore your surroundings, and then you plan your attack. You can play stealthy or just rush through the maps. Stealthy gameplay is recommended. Not only it's safer, but it's where this game shines the most.
You can sneak behind enemies and take down them with a knife, you can set traps, you can distract and isolate enemies to kill them in a quiet spot, you can blow a vehicle or explosives near the enemies, you can set up a chain reaction, you can snipe them both with and without sound masking, you can shoot them with a silenced pistol - the options are, indeed, many and all of them are fun.
As to the weapons, it's almost all WW2 arsenal (American, Brittish, Soviet, Polish, Japanese. German, Italian), including Panzerfaust, a special rocket launcher in the DLC mission "Belly of the Beast", dynamites, trip-mines, s-mines, hand grenades and land-mines. Not all weapons are available in the base version of the game, though. And, you'll need to unlock some weapons and weapon parts, as you progress through the campaign and ranks. The equipement consists of a sniper rifle, an assault rifle/shotgun/panzerfaust, a pistol and 5 items (explosives/anti-armor ammo or medkits).
Each mission is unique, each level is unique, it's really fun to explore the surrounding, not knowing what's behind the corner, when you play for the first time. The level design is one of the greatest that I have seen. I don't know who is the senior level designer, but, apparently,
has the right team for the job, because the level design is always excellent in the
games.
The graphics are beautiful, as well. I did find the colours a bit too saturated, but, nevertheless, graphic quality is high and you do need a pretty solid system to run this game on highest settings. Also, the fact that North Africa is not that common setting in videogames makes
to stand out. It adds a bit of extra fun.
Finally, this game has a CoOp mode and it's a "real" CoOp, you can play all campaign missions with your friends.
The other modes are survival challenges (solo or MP) and PvP. I did not try PvP, but I tried 10 waves in the Survival mode. I found it boring. Luckily, with the campaign and DLCs missions, there is enough content, so that you don't feel like you've wasted money on nothing.
The DLC packs
and
are highly recommended. As to the weapon packs, see for yourself, how much money you want to spend. The default M1 Garand + Welrod are pretty much the only weapons you need. I also used: Lee Enfield, T99 (Axis Weapon Pack) and Springfield rifles (Patriot Weapon Pack). But, if you play stealthy and aim for the head, there is not much difference, which sniper rifle you use. I got all the DLC packs with the
. From secondary weapons, I also recommend: Panzerfaust and Semi-Auto HDM. MP40 comes handy, if you don't choose to play stealthy, as MP40 magazines are always available behind the enemy lines.

I started playing the Sniper Elite games with V2 and I really enjoy them.  I had initially purchased this game on PS4 and I have been waiting for a Steam Sale to purchase it again on PC.  I'll list a few pros and cons for the game and hopefully that helps
Sniper Elite 3 is set in Africa during WW2.  While I miss the bombed out and burned buildings of WW2 Europe from Sniper Elite V2 the Africa setting is done well and allows for more open levels.
This game is designed to be played at a slower pace than most shooters so if you are looking for Call of Duty style shooter you may as well move on to another game.  If you are looking for a realistic sniping simulation or a hard core survival shooter this isnt the game for you.
Pros
-graphics look great
-xray kill cam (it never gets old)
-open levels with multiple pathways to each objective
-coop campaign and coop modes.  The entire game can be played with another player which is cool.  The only downside is when you are playing in coop the xray kill cam is disabled except for certain situations.
-coop overwatch mode.  One player acts as a sniper while the other (spotter) moves around the level to complete objectives.
-sounds great
-can customize your weapons and loadout
Cons
-can be repetetive (most games are these days)
-AI isnt very bright
-too much close quarters fighting for a sniper game at times.
Obviously this game isnt going to be for everyone. Great cooperative games are hard to find these days and the coop in this game is awesome.
Right now the game is $10 USD on sale.  You really cant go wrong at that price point.
