This has got to be one of the best value games on steam.  I'll make no bones about it, it hasn't aged well.  At all.  I mean it really feels like it's from 2000.  I played it when it first came out back in the day and loved it then.  I still love it now.  The campaign is where the aging is most noticable.  Instead of clear objectives given to you by actual NPCs and an over-arching story line, this is very much a series of "levels" where you have to "get to the finish", and objectives are, at best, given to you via some bloke on a wall-monitor (more typically just some text at the top of the screen).  For £3.00 though, multiplayer is where this game really shines.  Many different game modes provide lots of variation and the three-class system has been thoroughly explored.  While more hectic than AVP2, with a pace reminiscent of the original Unreal Tournament, there are moments of unbelievable atmoshpere which just come out of the woodwork.  For example ending up back to back with another marine at the bottom of a cave, neither of you speaks the other's language, yet you both play the most cooperative tactics you can dig out, because if you don't, you're ♥♥♥♥ing dead.  Or stalking another player as the alien, spotting them from across the map and closing in using cover, waiting 'til they're distracted by someone else and then "boom!" headbite.  It's a lot of fun and if you don't believe me, the price is low enough to not break the bank in finding out for yourself.

A vastly underrated game in its time, Aliens versus Predator succeeded in doing what two sequels would attempt and fail at: creating the feeling of being three different creatures in this rather dangerous universe.  The Alien gameplay was fast and savage, with a fragile player who had to use stealth and speed to tack down vastly superior targets.  The Predator was a superpowered murder god of technology.  The Marine was a slow, underpowered, well armed, tasty treat who ran like hell.
While it is closest to the traditional FPS, the Marine gameplay is my favorite, as each level was a struggle to survive against an enemy that came at you.  No trigger, no prespawned xenos, just a spawn point and the hunt.  That was the first revelation that actually made me pause when playing, that I wasn't in a war, or pursuing a target, but I was the one being hunted.
Grab a rifle, throw a flare, and run.

You can customize your car, modifying tuning and performance. When you visit the garage, you will find out that you can do virtually anything with your car! DOOM 3 is a FPS that isn't quite the same as its predecessors, but it's good in its on unique way. DOOM 3 employs more darker levels, horror and fear tactics (enemies popping out from hidden walls or teleporting around you) which works very well. The graphics and attention to detail all look great and the level designs are a lot tighter and have the player traversing through a lot of hallways and corridors. The campaign is ~8-10 hours long so it's a lot longer than most campaigns. During the middle it becomes a little repetitive as you constantly have to find PDAs or some item before you can open a door but then near the end the game really kicks into another gear and ends on a high note. DOOM 3 is a solid FPS shooter that also may have the player jump out of the seat once or twice!

Rating: 9/10
What is it?
Action/Adventure game where you control two brothers with each joystick on the controller solving puzzles as you progress through the story/enivroments.
The Good:
+What really stands out for me is the gorgeous graphics,atmoshpere, and beautiful vistas. Its a game where you just want to stop and look at everything.
+Varied environments throughout the game make the world feel more real and alive and provide a nice change of scenery
+The game feels like a grand adventure in the span of only 3 hours. It does such a good job of the pacing and the puzzles that it feels like you just completed an epic quest.
+Controller both brothers at the same time can be frustrating however it adds an extra element to the gameplay, and provides some interesting scenarios and puzzles.
+Simple and yet effective story conveyed with no dialogue
The Bad
-The game is very easy, the puzzles are not to challenging at all.
- All achievements are optional and very missable requiring a guide to get them. If you don't care about achievements than this shouldn't be a problem
- Although not required, you really need to play this with a controller.
Conclusion
An excellent adventure/puzzle game. The game is more about the journey and the adventure rather than the puzzles. Although short it really was a great experience.

Stealth, long range precision distance kills and deadly melee takedowns. A major improvement from the 1st and 2nd iterations of the series. This truly defines what a stealth sniping game is all about.
Outstanding by any means. The level of detail is something to behold, I have not seen this much level in detail in a game for so long. This one looks absolutely gorgeous even at low-medium settings. There are also a lot of graphics options to choose from to suit your needs and to maximise your experience.
You have to stop Germany from building a Super Tank that could potentially be used to change the tide of war. Other than that, that is the only ‘story’ you will get from this game as it isn’t really a story heavy game and it wasn’t made to be one. You’re buying this for the sniping experience, not much for the story.
They nailed it. The sound of the rifle, the enemies around you and even your own footsteps can be heard in great detail. Nothing more can be said of how this game sounds. You hear what you’re supposed to hear, nothing else.
This goes without saying but, you can snipe your enemies with skill and precision from a distance or get up close and personal and perform melee takedowns. Setting up traps and distractions can also be very fun if carefully planned and laid out. Oh, and I almost forgot...there are “sounds” in the game which can mask rifle shots which makes for quiet long distance shots; pretty impressive if you ask me. The overall game performed nice and smooth with no significant frame drops to report.
Priced at £39.99 for the base game, it is a little too much for the amount of gameplay hours you’re probably going to have. So, I suggest waiting until it goes on sale to pick it up.

Tekken 7, completes the holy trinity of Tekken Games 3,5 and now 7, that refined unhealthy mechanics from their even-numbered predecessors Tekken (1,)2, 4 and 6/Tag 2. 'Bound' has been removed and replaced by 'Tailspin', a mechanic that makes attacks such as Jins neutral right kick push enemies so far away that the amount of combo continuation options are heavily reduced, as opposed to the character bouncing up from the ground right in your face, which was the case in T6 and Tag 2. It also increases the amount of space that you can gain in a single combo which is a great thing to encourage longer combos despite every consecutive attack in a combo dealing less damage. Rage Arts and Rage Drives are surprisingly non-exploitable, as well as armor moves, but they expand the game meaningfully, and make it a blast to play. Both casually, and competitively.
Not everything is gold though. The story is extremely short, its ending is an abrupt and unsatisfying cliffhanger (HL2 EP2 levels) and the battles are not very well-balanced. Either they're too easy, or they're way, WAY too hard. It is a colossal disappointment for a game that claims to be "the end of the mishima saga", which basically means that it's supposed to end the story surrounding the primary group of protagonists. Spoiler: It doesn't do that. Not at all.
Get it for the gameplay though because that's still awesome. Also support BNamco for finally bringing Tekken to PC <3

Before Halo, Call of Duty, and other new-school shooters that currently saturate the FPS market, there was the old school. I’m talking about games that kept the same spirit as Wolfenstein 3D, like the Doom series, Duke Nukem 3D, Half-Life, the Quake series, and Unreal. If you lived through this time, you know what I’m talking about. These games are representative of a peak in shooters in that their challenge, length, and fun depended on gameplay alone—no cutscenes that pad the game time, no predictable plot elements, and no exploitative glitches that most new school gamers use in games today. Controls were fluid and customizable, combat was fast and furious, and the games were almost exclusively for PC. It took skill to play and if you were killed, you had only yourself to blame. This was when multiplayer was on the rise, before mods and cheating took hold to as great an extent as it does now, and before cheap tactics like quick-scoping were often the deciding factor in encounters.
Aliens vs. Predator Classic 2000, as it’s currently known, in some ways represents one of the last examples of this FPS golden age. It was released in 1999 in the wake of the game-changing Quake (1996) and Half-Life (1998). Its main selling point, of course, is that you can play as each of the three different species, the Marine, Predator, and Alien. There are three different campaigns for each, and beating each on successively harder difficulties unlocks up to five bonus levels for each, which also bestow additional equipment to the predator and marine. Additionally, if you complete certain challenges, you can also unlock new options that may classify as “cheats” in single player. You won’t really see much of a storyline progression between levels because there isn’t really a story. As with most developers of old school shooters, Rebellion focused on gameplay more than anything and the result is excellent.
Being a game now available on Steam, you’re probably thinking about multiplayer, and yes, that is one of the best reasons for this game’s existence. In fact, it seems almost designed as a tournament fighter, given the vast differences between species. If you were to never play the story missions at all, you would still have endless amounts of fun. Of course, I’m referring more to this game in its prime (early 2000’s) rather than now, because as you might expect, not many people still play this game. But when you find a game, you will see that the multiplayer is still very good and holds up today, even if it’s under-populated.
The perfect word to describe this game is balanced. Each species has its own advantages and disadvantages such that you never really feel like one is significantly over- or under-powered. The alien is the fastest, can jump the farthest, and walk on walls, but it’s the weakest physically and only has close-range weapons. The marine is slow and relatively weak, but can resupply through medpacks and armor and has access to the motion tracker and the game’s strongest weapons. The predator is the physically toughest, has strong weapons and cloaking device, but is kind of clunky with its limited energy, limited speargun ammo, and species-specific vision modes.
Now for the gameplay. This game is fast, incredibly fast. Like other old-school shooters, you have to react quickly and precisely or you’ll end up dead. Start spamming your weapons and you’ll just leave yourself open to attack and die. This game can feel relentless but never unfair. As stated above, it’s the product of a more refined and merciless age, before button-mashing, quick-scoping, and button-combinations became as prevalent as they are now. Like the alien itself, this game goes back to the roots of what makes a great shooter by stripping away all the hand-holding.
Need I say more? If you’re a product of the nineties, then you were probably into either the Aliens or Predator series at one point or another. Even if you’re not, this is a great game solely for the gameplay value. And for $4.99 you can’t really go wrong. In my opinion it’s the best AvP game ever released (better than AVP2 and 2010). And honestly, I don’t have any gripes or complaints about it, which is pretty rare for me.
For those of you interested in the more technical aspects, the Steam version is the 2000 update by Rebellion that allows for saving (yes, the original did not allow saves) and has two new weapons, the Skeeter missile launcher and the dual-wielding pistols, both for the marine. You can get graphical updates through what’s called the Redux mod, which you can get at
. You can also pick up extra multiplayer maps and other refinements for this game there as well. Happy hunting.

This review applies to Doom 3 and RoE,
not the other doom games inside this package.
First, you get that nice peaceful playable intro
without action that almost every game have today.
Such intros always gives you a nice entrypoint
(where you come from and why) while it "starts up"
the story in a proper way, and also gives a exploration
opportunity to learn more about the
in-game world without being disturbed by enemies.
Then, you get pretty much thinking.
You must read PDA's, Emails, listen to audio logs,
figure out codes to proceed. Sometimes you need
to read Emails or listen to logs to figure out what to
do next, for example where specific mission-critical
objects are stored.
And you get no help, you need to figure out platforming
for yourself when that becomes applicable.
That makes it extra fun.
Another nice thing is that many ingame objects not
necessary for progressing, is also interactive,
so sometimes the object is just for fun/enjoyment,
sometimes the object is just a red herring to fool
you into thinking this is the next step to take, when
it turns out its not
(For example, a door that never can be unlocked,
eg requires a PDA or keycard not in game).
This interactivity also adds to realism and it
makes the game more fun to play.
Also, the really nice thing is that you sometimes
return to a central "hub" (so theres multiple "hubs")
that is specific for the chapter you played, after
having collected some keycard/PDA or done
some objective, which makes it extra fun as

Video Review:
Text Review Below-
Wargame Red Dragon is the third iteration of the Wargame franchise. To preface this review I just want to say I loved the last two games, the original more than it’s sequel. Does Red Dragon take a step up in the right direction or does it take a step down like Airland Battle did? Let’s find out.
So right off the bat the graphics of this game are gorgeous and they give you plenty of ways to optimize it to your hardware. This is probably one of the heaviest strategy games on a graphics card I have ever seen, in fact. The sound effects are all very fitting and immersive when you zoom in close to watch the fighting. Almost makes you wish you could have a more direct role than giving orders from the sky.
The gameplay of Red Dragon like any Wargame is quite obviously its selling point. It’s phenomenal RTS-esque gameplay focused around controlling a pre-built army rather than building and controlling a base. It’s VERY tactical with line of sight, different terrain types that hide units, serve as cover, or even serve as a no man’s land of death. Aircraft have been brought over from Airland Battle and help to keep you on your guard in multiple ways, as if you march into a charge with zero anti air you’ll find a couple well placed strikes enough to destroy your entire attack force. Red Dragon adds in ships which help spice up the dynamic even more. Assaulting coastal cities from land has never been more dangerous as capital ships threaten to destroy everything you throw at it. Inland attacks don’t go as smoothly either as gunboats with anti tank weaponry, machine guns, and even artillery guns can be placed strategically in straits and rivers and the like to catch you off guard. The relationship between all the different types of units makes for a very attention-consuming experience this time around. From the interaction between the armored main battle tanks of NATO that can out-charge any Warsaw tanks to the tanks of the Soviets whose missile systems can potentially destroy any tank charge before it ever reaches them. Red Dragon retains the in-depth deck building mechanics with all these different types of units that allows you to decide your army pool before heading into battle. You’ll find you spend hours on this screen alone. My only real complaint in the gameplay department is that the AI, whether on easy or very hard difficulty use the same exact strategy. They charge at you in the beginning of the match with anti-air launchers meaning if you stick with aggressive land-based charges in the beginning? The AI can never beat you on any difficulty setting.
The multiplayer is where the real fun of the game is at though. From as little as an intense 1v1 duel of skill to a cooperative 4v4 where someone always quits and ♥♥♥♥s over their team, and all the way to a massive 10v10 which can easily be played very tactically with each player having a small army size or excessively with each player having their entire deck at their command. Red Dragon is unfortunately plagued by the same exact problem in multiplayer that its predecessors were. A problem so massive yet that I haven’t ever mentioned til now. You can see the win/loss ratio and and other stats of every single person in a lobby. This leads to all the good players jumbling onto one team, usually NATO because everyone wants to play NATO, and everyone else just leaving because they either saw that they’re probably going to lose, or they just wanted to play NATO. This makes 10v10s extremely had to start, but still also has you waiting quite a while just to get a 4v4 started which in my opinion has been the most fun and challenging way to play mutliplayer since European Escalation. If they just turned the stats off from public visibility or created a matchmaking system so no one could even get a chance to look at the stats the experience would be a lot better. As it stands right now? Trying to get into a multiplayer game that isn’t some kind of ranked 1v1 is an extremely tedious and frustrating process. The selling point of your game is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to even attempt. That’s bad. With the AI being so predictable, the state of mutliplayer here NEEDS to be fixed in future games.
Of course some might say they prefer singleplayer anyway so what about me? What if I just want to play the campaign? Well let me spell it out quite plainly, and you’ll know what I’m about to say if you read my Airland battle review. The singleplayer in this game is GARBAGE. It’s HORRIBLE. In European Escalation the campaign was an actual story-driven fun experience that got you invested and challenged you. In Airland battle they changed it to a story-absent chess game where you move armies of pre-built decks of which you have no say in building around a map and fighting a battle every time two chess pieces collide. An extremely boring, unfulfilling, and LAZY premise that no one played anyway. But at least that had a coop mode so you could bring a friend along to try to make it fun. Red Dragon? Red Dragon is a copy and paste of that exact campaign mode, but with some snippets of flavor story thrown in that in no way really even affects your singleplayer experience except in the first campaign which is serving to teach you about the game so it’s a LITTLE more guided than the rest. Looking for a satisfying story? Looking for a game mode that can really challenge you and add more of a strategic element to the game? Stop looking. It’s not here. They haven’t put it in a wargame since European Escalation and aren’t likely to ever put such a thing in ever again. But at least you can bring a friend in to make the horribly predictable and EASY AI even on very hard mode somewhat fun, right? Actually,  NO. Cause they removed the cooperative mode from the campaign too. So the one thing that could have made it fun? GONE. Now all you have is a polished pile of garbage that offers dozens of hours of gameplay that you’ll get tired of within three because some idiot thinks that this is what the consumer wants.
So, is Red Dragon worth your money? Honestly? No. I have recommended every Wargame to date and this is the first one I simply cannot recommend. I just can’t do it. The vs AI isn’t fun because they made it too predictable and unchallenging unlike in the last two games. The multiplayer is more screwed up than it’s ever been and finding a non-ranked match that starts in within ten minutes of entering the lobby is like trying to find a pot of gold in a rainbow. And lastly, Eugen insists on giving its consumers the worst possible singleplayer experience I have ever seen in a strategy game in my entire life. I cannot recommend this game, and it pisses me off that I can’t, because this is one of my favorite strategy series of all time. Wargame Red Dragon gets a 6/10. The lowest score I’ve ever given a Wargame. It’s fun, don’t get me wrong. I have plenty of fun when i actually manage to get into a multiplayer game or when I boot up vs AI with some friends who haven’t learned the AI’s repetitive strategy like I have. But this is easily the worst game in the franchise. In comparison, European Escalation got a 9/10 from me and Airland battle got an 8/10. Eugen Systems? Don’t pull this♥♥♥♥♥♥again with your new Normandy game. FIX THIS and give us a fun singleplayer experience, fix the state of your multiplayer, and fix your AI.

It began simple, but after a while you would have no idea what to do with the 10 different items you have. You need to combine 4 items to proceed to the next chapter, it feels long but it's actually quite short, My first play through took about 3-4 hours but from then on (if you are an achievment hunter like me) You will spend the next 8 play throughs tring to get every single achviement with no help or hints what so ever.
Both the art and the story are pretty much the best that I have seen since I Played 'The Walking Dead'. There are plots holes in the Deponia Story line but there no need to pick at them.
There's no need for a meta crittic score here, so I won't give it a score. It's playable but can get rather confusing.

I'll fully admit I bought this for the art style. In that regard, Deponia is exactly what it advertises. The chunky, eccentric designs of characters and backgrounds really brings this game to life.
And that's where the praise ends.
The big issue here is the writing, and it commits what is, to me, the greatest sin. It's trying to be funny. The jokes come at you on a regular basis. But I did not laugh once in my entire playthrough. Perhaps it's because of the mean nature of much of the humor, or it's a style that just doesn't carry over in translation, but most of the time the characters just seemed unlikable and mean-spirited.
My thought is that if you don't get laughs, stop it. Just stop it. Tell a story, be earnest in your delivery, drop all the affected attempts at hilarity. Maybe then they could have spent more time on the puzzles, which range from arbitrary to insulting.
There's a puzzle where you literally have to make an association between the house a person lives in and what their hat is, because three people all have headgear that looks like their occupation. It's that sort of backwards engineered idiot puzzle that makes people give up on adventure games. It has to be logical, sensible but not obvious, or the player will just give up.
This is the sort of series I'd rather view through one of those "Let's Play" Youtube series, but preferrably with the sound off.

Aliens versus predator classic 2000 is a great game for anyone who is a fan of the alien and predator franchise. You get to play 3 campaign modes: The Alien, the predator and the colonial marine. The campaign mode has a somewhat hard difficulty so prepare to be mercilessly slaughtered over and over again. The game fails to provide the player with any checkpoints throughout the levels in the campaigns resulting in you having to replay levels from the start if you die
Apart from the campaign mode there is also a skirmish gamemode in which you can fight off infinite  hordes of aliens playing as either a Colonial marine or a predator in iconic maps such as Hadley's hope and the derelict ship.Unlike Aliens vs predator 3 there are no brightness issues with this game and when you do come across a dark corridor or room you have an unlimited amount of flares at your disposal as well as night vision.
There are a some bugs present such as the water spazzing out but considering this game game out in 2000 the graphics hold up for the time and you won't be disappointed (hopefully!)
There is also a multiplayer mode however  there are very few servers up and running but when there is a server with a substantial number of people playing it can be a very fun and intense experience. In the game you can find a good variety of weapons including the iconic Pulse rifle, Smart gun and flamethrower as well as duel wield pistols and rocket launchers.
Being a big fan of the Alien and Predator franchise I enjoyed this game and recommend it to other fans of the films

Do you like real-time strategy? Do you like the close-combat series? Do you like massive and near-scale battlefields? A game that can handle 1v1 as well as 10v10? Reasonably historically accurate cold war era units, from logistics trucks to mechanized infantry to artillery, self-propelled anti-aircraft artillery, to heavy tanks, to air superiority fighters and bombers? Do you like constructing customized battalion forces from nations and coalitions as your "race" in the game?
If you answered yes to any of these questions, you should check our Wargame: Red Dragon. It's a medium-paced, epic realistic RTS game that has unique battlefields, gameplay, and has large customization of starting armies. Highly recommended.

Fantastic RTS.
There is quite a learning curve with these Wargames but once you get an understanding of them, they are great games. I've played RTS games all my life and this one was probably one of the hardest to learn just based on how they use their mechanics and the sheer amount of stats for each unit as well as the unit diversity. It's just a lot of info to process before you can really dive in, but once you do, its hard to put down.
When you enter a match (non campaign), you use a unit deck, kind of a deck building process. You have access to every unit in the game to add to your deck, and each deck is generally the same size. You can modify the size of the deck with modifiers such as only using units made prior to 1980, which will allow you to take a few extra units. Or you can choose to only use Sweedish units which will give you bonuses to using those units. Overall its a very nice way to let players customize their armies.
The actual gameplay is fun too. After the initial learning curve, the gameplay is pretty straightforward as RTS goes. Move recon ahead, locate enemies, and blow them up. Units in this game are fairly vulnerable at all times and it only takes one mistake and a few seconds to lose 4 main battle tanks sometimes so patience in this game is a must. Graphics are on point as well. Adding in the naval aspect to this game was great too.
Overall this is a fantastic RTS series that you can solo or play with friends for hours and hours. My friends and I have each made about 4 to 5 different army decks to play with to keep things fresh. Buy with confidence.

Unfortunately I went into this with something totally different in mind.  I can definitely see the appeal for anyone who likes to kill time (no pun intended) doing infuriatingly difficult -- though somewhat entertaining -- tasks.  Was I expecting an *actual* surgical simulation? No, not really; and to be honest the sound and blood effects are pretty entertaining on their own.  I guess ultimately my disappointment arises from the fact that the sole purpose of the game really seems to be simply the fact that the surgeon's hand is incredibly imprecise and difficult to control.  Yes, I can see to some degree the comedic value of accidentally knocking a jar into the patient's chest cavity or stabbing them in the heart when you meant to cut their esophagus, but at some point I had to ask myself, "Am I playing this because I like fighting the game's insistence on not doing what I'm trying to control the hand to do, or because I like figuring out how best to perform the surgery and manage blood loss?" I will tell you that the game overwhelmingly shifts toward the former, and I realized that the vast majority of the time wasn't spent figuring out how to do the surgery and keep the patient alive, but simply and almost solely trying to control the surgeon himself.  I got about halfway through before I decided I was tired of fighting the game itself rather than actually playing it.  I guess I don't understand why the devs decided to put all the effort into developing decent graphics, sound effects, music, interface, etc., then phone it in on the controls.
If the point is the lack and difficulty of control, then I guess that wasn't something I understood going into it.  So if a game based on fighting with the controls to manipulate an extremely difficult to maniuplate broken robotic quasi surgeon hand, then this game is for you.  If that sounds like it would be a bit frustrating and unfulfilling, you'll want to pass on this game.  I can assure you, the comedic value quickly gets replaced with frustration, annoyance, and regret at having spent the money.

Deponia is a beautiful designed Point & Click Adventure Game with a lot of humor. You play Rufus, a clumsy and egocentric guy , living on a planet full of trash called Deponia. His biggest wish is to escape from this awful planet and travelling to Elysium, a planet full of harmony.
Rufus experiences a funny adventure in a wonderful designed game, which is only the beginning of a Game Triology. The story continues in the two games Chaos on Deponia and Goodbye Deponia.
I had a lot of fun playing it, so i just can recommend it for you. :)

This is a very hesitant recommendation. For adventure game fans, Deponia has a lot to like: it's a beautiful game, for one. The artwork, animation and overall style is incredibly well done. The interface is also intuitive, utilizing the mouse wheel to quickly show and hide the inventory, and keeping interaction choices to either a left or right click (as opposed to early SCUMM games that would give you a load of often pointless ways with which to interact with objects).
The puzzles are decent, although they'll occasionally have you doing things that don't make complete sense (you'll sometimes feel like you're not trying to solve a particular puzzle as much as just trying to figure out a hazy order of operations). To be fair though, the sometimes ambiguous nature of the puzzles may have been in part due to my not listening to all the dialogue options, which brings me to my main criticism of the game: the writing.
Most of the characters are either irritating or generally unlikable, with a few who're downright obnoxious. The main character, Rufus, being the chief offender. I get that he's supposed to be an anti-hero who (presumably) finds his way over the course of the trilogy. However, after spending a few hours with him in the first game, I'm unsure I want to put myself through having to listen to his irritating whining and dopey commentary in the remaining two. It got to a point near the end of the game where I wanted to skip through every line of dialogue because I couldn't be bothered to listen to his idiotic responses. I sincerely hope he becomes more likable in the remaining two games.
In conclusion, if you're a huge fan of adventure games, I'd say give Deponia a shot. If you're just mildly curious about the genre, give it a pass.

This game provides insane value for money. Well, every free game gives infinite value for money I guess, but here for the price of zero you get a fast and furious twitchy platformer/shooter. Oh, it's also *hard*, but doesn't really feel unfair.
Don't let the simple art style fool you, there's a surprising amount of depth coming from the different weapons you can get, each with their pros and some very distinct cons, going from standard variations such as high damage but limited reach, to trickier fare such as bouncing ammo that's also dangerous to yourself.
So what's keeping you from getting and sticking with your favorite weapon ? One simple thing: picking up the weapon crates is the only way to score points.And this is a game purely played for high scores. So, to get anywhere, you'll rush from weapon crate to weapon crate, getting a random weapon each time you get a point.
While I wouldn't call this a rogue-like, that simple design tweak gives the game the same type of addiction to randomness that good rogue-likes have. You don't get to avoid bad choices here; whatever happens you just have to deal with it.
Would've been nice to have more than 3 levels, but as it is it's a well-rounded package all the same.

I have seen a lot of negative reviews about this game/sim - mostly regarding the price of DLC. It is, without a doubt, the single most expensive game I have ever played or owned.
I started playing Train Sim due to my renewed interest in model railroading - which I haven't been into since I was a teen (many, many years ago). I thought a garden railroad would be something I'd like to do. While researching that, I came across this sim.
As good as model railroading equipment has become, Train Sim allows you to do more for a lot less money. You can "be" the engineer in the cab or watch from many different viewing locations in and around the train itself, or from the surrounding countryside. You can play it as a serious sim or as a relaxing game. The wide variety of content allows you to drive trains from all over the world, from different eras, and with different engines.
The Steam Workshop has many free routes and scenarios that increase the playability of the game as well. You can even create your own. But this brings us back to the DLC issue again.
Many scenarios require more than one DLC package, depending on what the author has in his/her library and the type of scenario they are creating. Steam makes it very easy to get this DLC, but until you have the required ones, these workshop scenarios aren't really free.
One note worth mentioning is that DLC is available from the different iterations of the game. This is good for long time owners of the franchise as their older DLC still works with the latest version (2016) of the game. But be aware that graphic quality may differ from the early DLC to the latest.
This is how I look at the sim and it's cost:
Train Sim is much less expensive than creating an entire model railroad - and I could never build one as varied as what I can play in Train Sim. I can play as soon as the download finishes whereas it would take me quite a long time to build a model railroad. Yes, many people enjoy building as much as (if not more than) operating the trains. I am not one of those people. Train Sim lets you build as well - just using different tools.
Bottom Line:
So what all this comes down to is whether or not you get enough enjoyment from what you are paying for. Enter into it with open eyes and knowing what to expect and I hope your answer will be the same as mine: YES.

Aliens versus Predator...the one that started it all.  Aliens...Predators...Colonial Marines, oh my.
The Good:  Albeit an old, "Classic" game, it's got good, solid controls.  The storyline is decently thought out for the 3 types of campaigns (one for each race), although sadly, they're a bit on the short side.  Where this game shines, though, is the multiplayer.  Aliens are quick and fragile (although they can heal themselves), but are primarily melee fighters.  Predators are big, hulking brutes (that go invisible...actually more of a drawback, though) with a few big guns.  Colonial Marines...they're...well...Humans...but man do they have a LOT of guns.
The Bad:  The campaigns are short, as previously mentioned.  Graphics, if that matters to you, are...well, dated.  And the Aliens' vision...what, at the time, was called Fishbowl Vision, can be...disconcerting (120 view, versus the normal 90 view).  And finally, and sadly, although multiplayer is where the game shines, it's sorely lacking in maps...and since it's such an old game, there's little to no chance of any fan-made content for it.
The Ugly:  The user interface is...weird.  Although you can use a mouse to look around...there is no actual mouse use on the menues.  That's really it...and even then, that's more of a personal inconvenience instead of a really bad feature.
Overall...I think this game rates a 4.5 out of 5.  A great game, a great multiplayer experience.

Well I've been playing this game since over a month ago. Why has it taken me this long to play through it? Probably two things, distractions from other games and the repetition that Doom 3 has.
Doom 3 was made by id Software back in 2004 and it's sort of like a reboot to the original in a way since it doesn't follow the past two games. Just think of it like The Legend of Zelda as you can jump into any game at any time. No need to know any important storyline, not like there is much of a story. Doom 3 is about a scientist in Mars who has gone mad and opens a portal to hell killing nearly everbody thus you're the last marine who must stop the demons invading using the only skill you have. Starting a genicide on anything that the Pope does not approve of. There are some basic characters, cutscenes, even audiologs and emails to read which a lot of the time it's not all that interesting and the only reason to read and listen to said audiologs and emails is to get codes for supply caches.
Weapons are good but not great. You have a decent variety of weapons like the shotgun, SMG and rocket launcher. I enjoyed using the Plasma Gun and the BFG was fun the three times I ever got to use it. Enemies are diverse but are hit or miss. I hate the spider ones because who enjoys shooting a bunch of #!$@ing spiders in every game ever? Also some enemies leap at you as soon as you enter a room which is both unfair and gets annoying real quick. I also found it really weird how sometimes I can shoot an Imp with the shotgun in point blank range and it'll die but the same thing happens again and it takes two hits. I could be wrong but there is something very off about it, possible poor hit detection.
Level design is okay at first, it's really creepy and some noises of screams and creaks tend to unsettle me but sooner or later it's just a matter of entering a room, demons spawning and you gotta shoot them all. It becomes dull, predictable and annoying and some areas are really cramped so dodging an Imp fireball can be at times impossible which makes it again unfair. I found that after I entered and left Hell I got real sick of it and I consider the rest of the game (2-4 hours) to just be padding it out. It really angered me when all I just wanted to do was move forward but a door says I don't have clearence and I need to find a keycard for it. It's not that the environment changes much either. For 80% of the game you'll be in a dark corridor of some kind of science facility and it leaves me wanting a bit more variation.
I think this game has a lot of smaller problems rather than a couple of really big problems. It only shows the longer you play it. You can tell that Doom 3 was influenced by Half Life which is ironic considering Half Life was initially inspired by Doom. I don't think it's a bad game by any means, it's actually an alright game to play through but this wouldn't really be a top recommendation of mine. I'd go with something like Half Life or Bioshock first but that's just my personal tastes. If you're interested then it's worth a go and it goes on sale for very low often. I give it a 6/10.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game. The art style was absolutely breathtaking. There are several benches spread out across the game, and I always took a screenshot at them with the brothers sitting down. I was so blown away with the background and I could go on about that for a while.
The controls are very simple, but they're a little difficult to get used to. I use an Xbox 360 wired controller and one control stick controls the older brother, while the other controls the younger brother. The triggers have the brothers perform an action. I found myself getting the sticks missed up or trying to turn the camera with the right one. However, it was a challenge and fun to master.
The story line was so emotional. As you explore the land (it's a strictly linear exploration) you find a lot of darkness. THere is too much death and sadness to fit in here, and much of it would be a spoiler. The two brothers set out to find a tree to collect its sap to cure their dying father, and you find a lot of evil in the land. But there is nothing you can really do.
I have one complain out of all of this. The game is too short. I completed it in three hours. The ending was very emotional and if the game was extended by at least another hour or two, it would have been even better. I really do recommend this game, but wait for it to go on sale. $15 is a bit much for such a short game.

HIGHLY RECOMMENDED: Ratings 9/10 (Mods, Excellent DLCs, 3rd Party Scenarios)
"The Quest" is an excellent old school turn based RPG that I enjoyed very much and have spend more than 200+ hours on it. I played the base game, the DLC (Islands of Fire and Ice), and 4 other 3rd party scenarios which I bought for $2.99 each (Thor's Hammer, Celtic  Rift, Hero of Lukomorye 1 and 2x).
This game also provide steam workshop, which allows various users to create and share mods. I would highly recommend getting the free, "Islands of Heroes" workshop mod which provide you with an player home at the start of the game. When you get the spells Mark and Recall, you can teleport back to your home for healing, refresh mana, and store your items on any maps that allow teleporting. This is a great convenience especially at early game when your mana is highly limited.
The steam achievements are also very well made, and some of them can be obtained across multiple scenarios (like shooting 2000 arrows). There are also achievements that need you to play the game differently, like being maximum good or maximum evil. The DLCs and 3rd party scenarios are also highly enjoyable.
The only deficiency in the current game is that it is single player. However, "The Quest 2" is currently being tested and will be release sometime in early 2018 which will allow the user to create a party instead. I am really looking forward to the new release.

A Review of the Deponia Trilogy as a whole:
More info on BrokenCartridge:

Score: 4.5/5
I will not be covering the story in complete detail because there is a lot you should experience on your own while playing through the game. The story in a brief few sentences is that you play as Rufus, an egocentric self-centered slob whose only goal is to leave his trash heap of a planet to go to the city in the sky.  The world that he lives on is called Deponia, a planet littered with trash. All of the rich folk moved up into the city in the sky, Elysium some time ago. During one of your endeavors you knock an Elysium girl off of an Organon cruiser. Throughout the first game you try to use her to find your way onto Elysium, only to end up finding out that the Elysians plan on blowing up Deponia! The second and third games are mainly spent trying to stop the Organon from doing this devilish deed while figuring out their motives along the way.
The story is a very big part of the game, which is why I only covered the basics. The series itself does not like to stray too far off of what is expected from a point-and-click game. As great as that is, if you are looking for an innovation in the genre, you might not find that here. Here, you will find a wacky and hilarious adventure that is dependent on the silly world and narrative. If you already enjoy point-and-clicks, you are in for an incredible treat. Besides the awesome narrative and dialogue, we have a lot of things that set the Deponia trilogy above the rest. The game universe in general is surreal and charming; nothing really comes close to its style in my opinion. You will be surprised how much a planet covered in trash can mesmerize you with its environments.
The trilogy gets better as it goes on. While the first game is great, everything just seems to improve with each one. The story makes unexpected yet oh so juicy turns and twists, increased amounts of detailed environments, an increasing diverse cast, and becomes one of my favorite game soundtracks of all time. The amount of information to tie up the trilogy in the third game alone will leave you with your jaw dropped to the floor. Then include that the second and third both have their own unique mechanics that make them much more puzzling, but so much cooler. One of the best things is seeing Rufus evolve as a character. It is incredibly rewarding to see everything come together.
My only sense of bitterness goes towards the ending. Before I go more into it, I am not saying the ending is bad. If anything it is awesome and leaves a lot for you to speculate and imagine. However, in this particular story, it wasn’t what I was hoping for.  There is so much I wanted to see and experience that was sort of thrown up into the air and left for you to speculate. It is not fair to spoil it, so I won’t. It just left me eager to know more, yet knowing the sad information that this is intended to only be a trilogy. Of course the possibility of a fourth game is always possible, but it isn’t intended. With that being said, I am personally dissatisfied with the ending. Not for the ending itself, but for the thing it did not answer. Good thing Daedalic (the developers) have made many more amazing games to sink my teeth into while getting over it.
That is all you need to know about Deponia before poking your head in. This is a must own for any people interested in adventure games. Daedlic is truly becoming today’s Lucas Arts, and now is a better time than ever to find out why by trying out this trilogy.
The main character is pretty unlikeable but the game has a unique setting, decent story, and interesting quirks that made it enjoyable straight to the end.

This was recommended to me by, let's be honest, essentially a total stranger. I decided to check it out, because they seemed to have really enjoyed playing it. SPOILER: I ended up loving this game.
At first, I found a lot of things to criticise. The pause menu is incredibly lackluster (only one option), and pressing escape while the pause menu is open just... Opens the pause menu again.
It took me a while to figure out that you aren't actually supposed to leave your chair, and the instructions weren't exactly placed in what I thought was the most intuitive way.
You only start with one pot, and that pot can only house one flower. When I was just starting, I had a LOT of mediocre plants. Succulents, for the most part. I thought "This is the whole game?" not even bothering to catalogue the plants I'd discovered.
This is important, because the cataloguing of plants is one of the best parts of the game. Every time you discover a plant, it's up to YOU to fill out a card detailing information about that plant. That card is displayed when you pick up seeds in the future, so you know just what you're about to plant, and you can re-order plants when viewing their card in your collection.
Giving each and every plant a unique description is extremely therapeutic, and I found it to actually be kind of fun. You find your way into a cycle:
1. Order new seeds
2. Plant the seeds; see what grows
3. Catalogue the seeds
4. Repeat
and found myself so enamoured by this cycle that I almost forgot to pay attention to the other main feature of the game— Requests, wherein people post what kinds of plants they want on the internet, you send them a picture of a plant you've grown (or arrangement of plants), and they respond with whether or not they want it, the next day.
It's through these requests that you accrue reputation points, which are how you rank up. As you get reputation points, you can buy different pots with pot vouchers. Different pots can house different numbers of plants.
But it's really in that cycle that this game shines. It's more of a relaxing experience, and it's easy to lose yourself to it. Monotonous, but in a way that doesn't quickly get dull or boring.
I'd fully recommend this game, but know what you're getting into. It's more of an experience than an objective-driven game.

A fairly decent, laid-back puzzle game with one real flaw: the developers didn't play to the game's strengths. If this game were almost entirely logic puzzles with the odd bit of combat it would be better than what it is. It gets bogged down with a bit too much combat and some "agility" sections that don't really fit. One level required me to jump and free-fall onto the end level marker far below but aiming the camera straight down doesn't work so you're fighting the spastic camera more than you are aiming skillfully toward the mark. As for the combat, half the enemies are these target dummy bunnies that don't even fight back which could just as well have been switches but instead the pace of the game is killed when you suddenly have to kill 6 or so of them to progress.
Aside from those points, though, the puzzle design is pretty good and the combat with bosses, while sometimes not perfect, is enjoyable. All of the labyrinths rely on the gravity mechanic where you rotate the level by jumping onto walls with a checkerboard pattern. Each labyrinth also has it's own theme which ties into the puzzles like the Pisces labyrinth having a lot of water tiles that push you in a certain direction, for example. The puzzles are the real strength of the game, as I said, and while they're not very difficult, it's still fun in a laid-back sort of way.
On the technical side of things, this game does have all the shortcomings of your average Japanese indie game: it has a pitiful set of options that are only accessible from the launcher, it defaults to a low-res window and max res isn't very high (1400x1050 or something odd like that), the audio is absurdly loud and needs to be lower via the volume mixer instead of in-game, the controls are not rebindable, etc. This is all pretty common for Japanese indie games but it would still be nice if they could step up the settings a bit.
Ultimately, I wouldn't advise against getting this game but I can't give it a strong recommendation, either. Pick it up if it really piques your interest but only if that. I would say it's around a 6/10, maybe lower if I wanted to be harsh about the lack of proper settings.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons was developed by the company Starbreeze Studios, who were responsible for games like The Chronicles of Riddick games, The Darkness and Payday 2 and directed by famous Swedish film director Josef Fares.
The two Brothers, Naiee (the younger brother) and Naia (the older brother) become united as one not only by the plot but with the help of the game’s mechanics and narration. Thrust out their village and into a gorgeous and almost realistic storybook, the Brother’s only weapons are their minds and their only resource is each other.
The brothers then embark on their epic journey through the beautiful landscape of villages, hills, mountains, caves and even the valley of dead giants and trolls that went to war with each other on a very bloody battlefield. At the same time the Brothers also faced challenges like the local bully, a farmer's aggressive dog, and deadly wolves.  Along with these challenges the Brothers also undertake a journey of self-discovery as they learn to work together to overcome each challenge. They even learn and work out how to help out the various characters they meet during their adventure - like reuniting a friendly pair of trolls, saving a man attempting suicide, aiding an inventor, freeing a badly injured griffin that help them before succumbing to its injures and even a girl from being scarified by a blood cult.
The dialogue throughout the game is in an artificial language and there are no signs to really provide any type of information to the player in regards to where you must go. You just follow the path, trusting that the brothers are heading the right way. And this parallels the relationship between the brothers: although you can’t understand what they say to one another, you know they love and look out for one another.
The game’s visuals are gorgeous to look at and the game rarely lets a few minutes pass without offering some sort of staggeringly gorgeous landscape to ogle. There are even benches scattered throughout the game for the Brothers to sit on. The player is given permission to stop and enjoy the vistas; which are not only beautiful but ram home how vast a world Naia and Naiee have to traverse and, by extension, how vital their relationship is to their own survival. The game makes it so clear that the characters themselves are impressed by what they see. The soundtrack was equally as gorgeous. The Swedish vocals added that extra charm when it came to cut scenes and often provided the atmosphere and told the player what they should feel at that precise moment.
The player controls both brothers simultaneously, each mapped to an analogue stick, as that makes button mashing impossible when it comes to puzzle solving. Every action from "grab the ledge above" to "play the harp" is performed with the triggers. When I first played this game I did find it quite hard to control both the brothers the same time. Usually one would end up running into a wall. Ultimately the control scheme acts as a defining piece of storytelling. The control scheme is actually very simple, though. You control both brothers independently; the older brother’s actions are enacted with the left analogue stick and the younger brother with the right analogue stick. Each brother also has one interactive button that is context sensitive to the area or person it is being used on. There is a very brief introduction to the controls, which becomes a very strong narrative choice because it allows the player to naturally grow with the brothers on their journey and experiment a little more, revealing layers of their characters. Coming back to the point I mentioned about the Brother’s communication is almost psychic, we eventually learn that due to the control scheme of this game that the brothers are sharing a brain; which is in fact the player’s brain. But a curious thing happens as you help the siblings solve puzzles and work in concert to skirt danger. You learn. You get better at controlling these two disparate entities and, in turn, they appear to work together more seamlessly.
So after the brothers save the girl from the blood cult’s ritual they decide to ally with her. They reach a point in their journey where the girl urges the Brothers to enter a cave which they presume is the direction that they must head in order to reach the Tree of Life.
Before Naia enters the claustrophobic tunnel, Naiee become hesitant, pulling Naia’s hand and tries to convince him that this is not a good idea, foreboding that something bad is about to happen. Naia insists that nothing is going to happen and since Naiee is too weak to go on by himself he follows both Naia and the girl into the tunnel. As the brothers shuffle forward, you start to notice what appear to be victims mummified in web. Something doesn’t seem right.
In an instant, the girl exposes her true, evil arachnid form and imprisons the brothers in a web and slowly pulls them upwards to feast on.  As Naiee awakes, the brothers devise a plan to escape. To defeat this she-spider Naiee must ram into her while Naia tears off each of her limbs. The fight is pretty easy and feels quite satisfying. As Naia rips off the last leg he is pierced by the spider’s venomous pincher and loses colour of his skin simultaneously. Now Naiee must carry Naia for the remaining way to the Tree of Life, where Naiee must now collect the Water of Life to save not only their father, but Naia’s life too.
As you’re controlling Naiee throughout the Tree of Life using only the right side of your controller, you start to feel alone and awkward. Normally the right analogue stick is used to look around in a game; not to move about. It’s weird, unnatural and disjointed. The control scheme is now missing something and you as the player are not use to using the right side of the controller to move around. What you are feeling is exactly how Naiee is feeling in the story but for different metaphorical reasons. The use of only the right side of the controller is symbolic for the emptiness inside of Naiee. And to top it all off, even after Naiee retrieves the Water of Life you find out it’s too late to save Naia and ends up dying in Naiee arms in the most heart wrecking scene I have ever witness. And it doesn’t end there!
The emotional knife digs in as you control Naiee, again only with the right side of your controller, to bury Naia, a character that even you as the player, have become emotional attached to. And despite never understanding the dialogue in this game you cannot help but empathise with Naiee.  And even after that, Naiee rushes home to deliver the Water of Life to his father. However Naiee must cross the shoreline before doing so. He is faced with his greatest fear! The flashback to his mother’s death at the beginning of the game explains this phobia, and without Naia there to carry him across like he has been throughout the entire game. Using the right trigger only makes Naiee steps back from the water. But as you realise that the ghost of Naia is with Naiee you also realise that he is also in your controller; and by pressing the left trigger Naiee gathers the strength and determination to swim across the shore, climb up the mountain, use the machinery to reach his father. Even though Naia was not physically there to help Naiee or for you to control with the left analogue stick, it didn’t matter at all. He was still there to use in the left trigger button; which then become symbolic for the brother’s true strength. As for what happens after Naiee reaches his father, I’m not going to say. All I will say is it’s better to experience the ending on your own.

After playing 700+ games (on a different Steam account), I must say though that it suffers from a horribly fatal flaw -- you can see the statistics of other players in the lobbies.  Why is this a problem?  Team stacking.  It's horrendous -- I might have played one game in ten that was balanced.  With all the others, the "smart" players (myself included), click around to see which team is better, then go to that team.  And the cycle repeats until you get a team of noobs against a team with 5000+ games of experience between them.  This leads to other problems.  It can sometimes take 30+ minutes to fill a lobby, as skilled players join the team destined to lose, realize it, and quit.  Or they linger hoping a spot on the to-win team opens up, then quit en masse right before the game starts.  Or anonymous lobby hosts will kick newer players and people they aren't buddies with off of the stacked team.
If Eugen simply removed this option -- the ability to see the win ratios and game counts of other players -- this game would be very near perfect.

Oh how the might have fallen.
The GTA Series has long been a champion for digital outlaws. A game, nay community of people who had a game in which they could practically do anything they wanted to do, including the ability to manipulate it however they saw fit through mods. Rockstar themselves have been incredibly supportive of their communities trends over the years but lately due to corporate endeavours have been pushed to do the unthinkable.
Removing a major player in the modding scene (OpenIV) ushers in a change many fear. As PC players, having the freedom to manipulate games as they see fit (Provided its not at the expense of other players enjoyment) is an incredibly important form of expressing our love for games.
Mods bring more players to a game and this obviously makes the developers and publishers more money, but now I fear that they will want to take mods and monetise them for EXTRA personal gain.
I long for the days of games made for the love and enjoyment of them.
I can't in good conscience recommend GTA V to anyone, anymore. Yes the microtransactions bring free content, but at what cost?
Grand Theft Auto is changing, and this change is not for the end users good.

The Quest is more enjoyable than Skyrim or any Elder Scrolls game.  The writing is funny, the graphics are retro cool, the spells are fascinating, the combat is tactical brilliance, and its mechanics feel great to play.  The things that Elder scrolls lost to corporate overhaul are treasured in The Quest.  The indy devs love this craft and have been dedicated to this for quite some time.  This is my 2nd copy, having it on my phone.  It is good enough to replay infinitely.  The options and choices make for a true open world with many expanisions to come.  The HD looks smooth and plays fast.  It was a pleasant suprise after playing the SD version for so long to have updated graphics as well.  I love alchemy and spend a lot of my time looking at flowers and mushrooms;  They have new breath!  The spirit of the Old games is here in spades.  It has the treachery of Wizardy, the dark humor of Ultima, the system play of Elder Scrolls, & with The Quest's modern controls I find myself playing it more than the old favorites.  The Quest deserves rightful place in history's Golden Age of Video Games.

I can not recommend this simulator unless you can afford some/all the DLC addons released weekly. Depending your interest`s mainly US, UK, Germany. They are now interesting addons just largly under detailed, poor headlight setups, poor cab layouts and wrong sounds on the US equipment most especially. Here are more cons Locomotive packs $19.99 USD (Features 1 locomotive and maybe 2-3 cars/wagons) , route addons $39.99 (1-2 locomotives player runnable, 5-10 cars, New trick from these guys is narrowing the locomotives down to one player and one only ai controlled). If you do want to try it I recommend the double deal packs. The very best time recommended is steam sales only! So if your into detailed locomotives and routes this is by far not your simulator. It simulates passenger ops very good. But lack`s a lot to be desired in US freight ops especially. The UK and German freight ops might be lot more accurate. Never really ran those. So cannot comment there. Yes the physics and graphics engine despite dated is somewhat decent. The locomotives and rolling stock and track is rather poorly made. Compared with other simulators such as Jointed Rail`s locomotives and freight cars in Trainz 12. I would have to recommend Trainz 12 or MSTS/OR over this for more accurate and detailed US freight operations. This does have a few decent routes I recommend if you give in and do have to pick it up. All the German and UK addons look particularly nice and run decent. Pacific Surfliner, Stevens Pass, Marias Pass, New York- New Haven. If you can get good performance out of the NJ Transit route it look`s really nice. Anything passenger oriented is best suited in this simulator. Otherwise you will definitely be looking for a lot more out of it and very disappointed.

This game is delightful.  The writing is punchy and wry: easily the highlight.  The colorfully-crafted world breathes life.  Perhaps most importantly, though, the puzzles are expertly crafted--they're not only solveable, but wonderfully absurd.  Deponia oozes charm.  It's an absolute winner.

A great point-n-click adventure with nicely drawn graphics and no pixel hunting or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzles. If you're a fan of the genre, this is greatly recommended but be warned it is the first of a trilogy and it's ending does not provide much closure.

While Telltale have, to much acclaim, been moving the adventure genre in a new, more serious, direction, Daedalic have been working away at old school point and click games, focusing on visual style, witty writing and great characterisation. Deponia places you in the shoes of Rufus, a rather arrogant, unlikable and hilariously callous protagonist, as he attempts to escape his dull life on the titular garbage planet. Along the way players will take blood from a mechanical bull, gas a parrot, contend with cross dressing receptionists and participate in the ancient and arcane ritual of espresso-making. Deponia is clearly a game in the tradition of Monkey Island series, with a manic and  oddball approach to its world building. It's also a worthy sucessor to those games, and well worth a look.

Daedalic is no LucasArts, not being backed by some insanely popular moneymaking franchises that rhyme with Mar Bars or Diana Clones. But the LucasArts we knew isn’t coming back, so I suspect it’s a good try it if you’ve got a hankering for that style of gameplay (with a similar amount of difficulty).
In contrast to its clear inspirations found in series such as Monkey Island, it suffers from production iffiness issues such as variable voice acting and animation quality (in the English version, there are some nasty translation-isms throughout, and multiple lines of that sort where they clearly stressed a word in a sentence that wasn’t the one that should have been stressed), as well as an indecisiveness as to what constitutes an appropriate style of fourth-wall breaking.
Much to the game’s credit, however, the setting is a unique junkyard world and the protagonist Rufus (at least at the start) is more the sort of guy you might expect a point-and-click adventure game kleptomaniac vandal to be: a near-irredeemable jerk. Unfortunately, people are all too willing to point this out to his face, which sometimes works in the story’s favor and sometimes doesn’t. Moreover, there are a lot of artistic details in the world that you simply can’t click on and have Rufus snark about, which is something of a must to get a real feel for an adventure game world’s presence.
One thing that is much nicer than typical old-school examples is that you don’t have to do the pixel-hunting if you don’t want to (hold space to see the interactive spots), and most of the time, you don’t have to watch a slow walk animation just to explore the map (double-click to fast forward through navigational arrows).
Finally, the game is kind of crashy in a few spots (at least the Mac version is), so you may want to do some saving on top of the auto-saving. Some achievements are skippable, but at least one achievement guide in the Steam community is relatively spoiler free.
For all its flaws, the game is usually about as funny as it thinks it is, so at least I can say I enjoyed it. Nonetheless, this game has some mature humor, so don’t get too fooled by the cutesy noseless art; it’s not really for kids.
Droggeljug.

Where to start?
With a lot of point and click adventure games, getting stuck is just part of the process and peeking at a walkthrough is fairly standard. The person making it is trying to be witty, creative, yet logical at the same time with the item combinations and just miss by a long shot.
I’m fairly sure any point and click adventure fan has had this from time to time. There is always a moment or two you ask yourself… “Well, how was I seriously supposed to figure out that you had to put the chicken in the blender to get egg yolk, use that yolk with a daisy to make a cake, eat the cake and fart out the key to why I’m stuck.”
My point being, the solutions aren’t always as obvious as they might think. I was very glad to find that Deponia isn’t like that. It’s consistently logically throughout the whole game.
Admittedly, I did get stuck a few times, but it was more of a “how DIDN’T I get that?” rather than a “how did they think that made sense?”
The Art style in Deponia is beautiful. A planet consisting of junk has never looked so good.
The animation, music, voice acting and humour are all great to. There is a real charm about the characters and the little witty things that they say, that makes this game all that much more enjoyable. Which, talking of voice acting, reminds me…
Droggeljug mode!
I finished this game, looked back on the achievements I had left to get and I thought…
…This is going to be interesting.
Well, I never knew that Droggeljug mode would be as painful as it was. Finishing the game unlocks a new mode, where everything and anything that anyone says ever, comes out: “Droggeljug!”
Now this is amusing all of a 10 second period, but after that it is quite painful. They say it in the same tone of voice every time. You may get the odd “Droggeljug?”, but apart from that it is fairly robotic. That being said it was still a funny little thing that they added which I thought was quite unique.
I can imagine that this mode would make it a lot more challenging to play through if I didn’t literally just finish the game and still have everything fresh in my mind. Due to parts in the story where you need to note where the chat options are to get what you want off of them. (E.g. a character quiz’s you before they’ll give you a key, and all you have is a list of Droggeljugs for answers)
It’s a challenging achievement, but a fun one. Despite that a lot of people probably muted it because the noise drove them crazy, I left it on low. Just to keep reminding me how ridiculous what I was doing really was.
All in all, I love this game, it’s great. I can’t wait to start the next part in the story.
TL;DR : Logical item combinations, engaging story, great humour, wonderful art and definitely a must have for any point and click adventure game lover.

Very little changed from the first game so I'll copy my review (the only reason I bought this version is because the multiplayer had a higher population):
Fun tactical game of modern warfare, with just enough realism to be enjoyable while still being more of a game than a simulator.
One option of score keeping makes your soldiers's lives valuable so that zerg rushes lead to defeat, not victory. You have to attack the enemy where he is weak and without suiciding your units, like in civilized countries in real life.
I applied lessons learned from modern war veterans to great success. Noobs get steam rolled, veterans are dueled in the realm of psychology (feints, bait and trapping, counter-attacking).
Unfortunately the interface is trash, memorized key commands a necessity and air defense requires micro-management, so it's not the perfect game, but still fun occasionally.
Turn off ambient noise or whatever it's called, otherwise it will drive you crazy and you'll still hear it hours after shutting off the game.

When your character gains enough influence, they can join one of these nations and fight as a lord or mercenary. Gaining more prestige and having all the castles and towns you conquer get handed over to lords who didn't do anything while your fat king eats more butter.
The game itself plays rather interestingly. You have two modes, the overworld and actual battles.
In the overworld you do most of your management stuff. You take quests, recruit new units for your army, travel from place to place, start a trade empire, light bags of poo on fire and leave it on people's front door, etc. The game is surprisingly open in what you can do as a character.
You CAN join a nation, sure. Or you could build a trade empire across all of Calradia and do a little bit of war profiteering. Or you could become a bandit king and pillage across the lands, taking advantage of war stricken people. Or you can even say screw it and build an empire yourself, a difficult but rewarding option as you take Calradia for yourself.
But how do you go about doing this when you actually have to fight?
In Mountain Blade, you don't control an army RTS style, you control a commander who controls an army. You play from a third or first person perspective and have to do some fighting yourself. Or you can sit back and let your elite archers do all the work, what do I  care? I'm not your dad, I don't have to tell you how to play.
You have three options in a fight. An attack which direction is based on where your mouse is pointing or what directional key your holding. A block that is either a directional based parry or just all around with the use of a shield. And a kick to break enemy guards and kick them off ladders like the stinky invaders they are.
You can also use projectile weapons such as throwing rocks, javelins, bows, crossbows, etc. This works like a TPS or FPS game where you have to aim manually and hopefully hit them in the head. You can hit them in other places sure, but whats the fun in that?
It would be a rather simple system if every battle wasn't a complete cluster ♥♥♥♥. You bring your armies into battle with you and battles can get rather chaotic, especially if you modded the game and increased the maximum units in battle at once. This leads to a hectic and brutal experience that a lot of games fail to capture. You're in the thick of it, another soldier on the battlefield. Screams of battle, arrows flying overhead, corpses piling up, you and others get covered in blood. You actually feel like you're part of a battle instead of just this overwhelming force like in Dynasty Warriors or similar games.
Oh yeah, the mods, oh man the mods. Mountie's Blade has an amazingly active modding community. You know those guys that go "When are (insert developers here) going to make a (Insert war here) game?", well the Mount and Blade modders don't ask that, they just make them themselves.
So far the mods I've played between both Warband and the original include: Roman Empire, The Greek-Persian War, American Frontier in 1886, Star Wars, Lord of the Rings, Warhammer, Sengoku Jidai Japan, Medieval England, Medieval Europe, homebrew fantasy settings, and even Napoleanic Wars. Just to name a few.
I have a lot of respect for the modding community for these games. The amount of extra content they produce means you have hundreds of more hours between those and the base game. Sure some of them suck, but the good ones usually outnumber the bad in massive volumes.
But should you play Mounts the Blade: Battleguys?
Yeah.
Well okay, uh.
I've actually been following the development of Mount and Blade since the original was still in it's early alpha state and only Swadia and Vaegirs existed. It's an interesting little game turned power house with the help of some passionate devs and dedicated modders.  Warbands is basically the definitive edition of the game, but you've already bought and played it since it's been out for years and I just kind of wanted to review it.
But if you somehow haven't played this game, then you probably should. Calradia is a strangely fascinating world and each playthrough can be completely different. Not to mention all the work the modders do.

Doom 3. What can be said about Doom 3? It's the third game in a long line of games that helped revolutionize the FPS genre. It's also the game that came out around the same time as Half-Life 2, as well as deviating from the run and gun playstyle from the first two, instead opting for a more horror survival gameplay and making lighting a central theme around it as well, has it aged well?
I'd say yes. I think the initial disappointment from a lot of fans came as a result of this game not being the same as the first two, and honestly, in my opinion, I don't think that's a bad thing at all. It's a slower paced game than its predecessors that's for sure, fleshing out its story and narrative through ingame cutscenes and chracter's PDA's, similar to what modern games nowadays are doing... think like BioShock. A lot of people also had complaints with the flashlight system, which is (imo) what lends to the tension you feel throughout the whole game. If you have issues with that however, there's mods, as well the BFG edition which remedies this (which also brightens up some textures from my understanding), but in my opinion that takes away from the atmosphere they were going for in this game. They consciously made the design choice of making you choose between having your gun out, or your flashlight out to scout the darkness, the light giving you a sense of comfort while also leaving you completely defenseless while doing so. Granted, there are some moments when certain enemies will cheaply spawn behind you, or in complete darkness.
The game is also a lot longer than I remember it being, its single player campaign clocking in at around 10-15 hours, depending on how you approach things, although to be fair, I think the game starts off kind of slow, easing the player into the narrative before all hell breaks loose. The latter half of the game being very action packed moreso than the beginning.  I think this game was ahead of its time, and I feel it's not as fondly remembered as HL2, but I still think it's a great experience, and one of the last Doom games to be developed by the original id team, before the license was shipped over to Bethesda, definitely an end of an era.
Closing out, I have to say I played through it with a graphics mod, to bring the graphics up to date a bit, there's several of them out there but the one I installed was Doom 3 Redux, you can find it among others over on the moddb site.
I highly recommend to fans of survival horrors, and first person shooters. One of the better titles that came out during that era. Would definitely suggest playing it with an HD texture pack as well, the game holds up suprisingly well when using them.

So I rebought Doom 3. Why? I could'nt remember why I didnt finish it back in the day. Now I've played it I remember the horror. Not the demon related kind, but the kind derived from poor game design choices.
The core "combat"  experience is just a series of sucker punches as enemies spring in your face as you open a door followed by enemies spawning behind you, this doesnt create a sense of dread rather extreme irratation as it happens over and over and over. The gun play is woeful, with none of the guns sounding or behaving like powerful weapons. Couple this with your cross hair flying off as you are hit, it's like they confused annoying and challenging.
The lighting is cool and the music is fitting but Doom 3 will be more remembered for its technical innovations rather than it's gameplay. And saying that these are all fairly standard now that leaves me no reason to recommend Doom 3 anymore.
