Despite its somewhat underwhelming reputation I couldn't love this game more.
Its true the game has more than its fair share of dark spots, but, well... I call myself a cat I guess darkness is kinda my thing. :P  I actually really like the infamous flashlight mechanic, it adds tension and fear to environments that wouldn't be particularly scary -- and in the BFG edition where that mechanic is removed, they aren't.
The combat is fun and fast-paced, if a bit repetitive, but the variety with certain monsters like Arch-Viles takes some of the repetitiveness out of it once you get deep into the campaign.  The boss fights are really fun with unique mechanics except, somewhat, for the last one -- and they strike a good balance when it comes to difficulty: you'll finish them without much health left but you probably won't die so much it gets frustrating.  Hard mode is very fun as it's not about hiding or taking cover -- the way the monsters spawn you have to be pretty ferocious in order to survive.
Map design is actually not too linear, which is a good thing to see in a game even as old as 2004... levels are maze-like without being confusing, and there's a decent variation in texture and structure schemes especially toward the end of the game -- although that part could still be improved somewhat.  Coming to this as I did about 8 years after it was released this type of level design was like a breath of fresh air.
Graphics are still beautiful even 12 years later, the monsters and especially boss designs are grotesque and disturbing, they really feel like they could be demons out of some hell.
There are a few minor quibbles I have -- just a few straighforward ones, and one or two weird ones...
In a 27-level campaign, a lot of the monsters only appear for three or four levels or stop appearing altogether just after the mid-point.  This seems to especially happen to the most interesting designs like a literal baby insect, the (somewhat) classic lost soul, and the... Mancubus... thing...  Even the ubiquitous Pinky Demon from the original games kinda disappears after the fifteenth map or so.  There are plenty of other monsters that appear later on but it would have been nice to see some demons from the earlier maps stick around especially when enemy variety is one of the game's strong points.
The weapons tend to be kinda same-ish although there's still enough variety to go around and enough situations where you do want to switch from one to the other.  You do have a bloody chainsaw if you get bored and it works well on even some of the high-level monsters like Arch-Viles, but the weapons are still a weak point.  I find myself mostly using the shotgun even when another weapon would work just as well -- it seems even limiting the amount of shotgun ammo you can find or carry (there doesn't seem to be any maximum, or if there is it's so high I've never reached it) would have gone a long way towards resolving this.  Its ammo does get more scarce towards the end of the game but so does the ammo for everything else, leaving you in the same situation.
Finally -- and this is the weird one -- some of the monster sounds are distorted samples taken from tiger calls.  I spend a decent amount of time around tigers and these calls are, quite clearly, "chuffs" (a kind of purr) and mating calls.  I guess Pinky's a succubus now? :P  It can get pretty hard to take a hellish monster seriously when it's literally purring at you.
Interestingly enough, the gameplay isn't the only place you can find big cat sounds in this game...
All in all this is a great game, with a lot of custom content as well that I haven't gone into here just 'cuz I've already been talking long enough.  An underrated classic, I highly recommend giving it a look if all you've heard is its reputation for dark spaces and a weird flashlight.

First, so far, I have a little over 120 hours played on Train Sim 2016.  I purchased it during Steams July Sale (a lot of great deals at that time) and since that time, I put enough hours into it to give a review.
The Pros - The amount of Locos and Routes here is incredible. The Senarios in most of the Routes are numorous and very enjoyable. The Sim Play is very easy unless you start using Real Stream Locomotives or some of the "Cold Start Locos". Then the difuculty gets turned up a few notches, but still ejoyable. Finally, the scenery in most of the Routes are simply spectacular!
The Cons - You need a FAST and POWRFUL Computer to play Train Simulator 2016. Why? Because it is not using the Unreal Engine. Therefore, Train Sim 2016 is not utilizing your Graphics Card or Cards to their full potential. This Sim is very heavy on CPU Power.
For an Example: I am using a home built 2009 Gaming Rig with an Intel Core2 Extreme QX9650 Self Overclocked to 4.0GHz, Two NVIDIA GTX680 Graphics Cards in SLI Self Overclocked, 8GB of SLI DDR2 RAM Self Overclocked, and a 10,000RPM WesternDigital HD using Windows Vista 64bit. The System is Liquid Cooled. I am getting Frame rates of 14-44 max using the High setting on Graphics in the Sim. If I use the Highest setting in the Sim, the frame rates are so bad it is unplayable for me.
Bottomline, If you have a newer and faster computer then I do, you will thoroughly enjoy what this Sim has to offer OR if this Sim went to the Unreal Engine, the frame rates would rise to playable levels using the Sims Highest Graphics Setting even with a computer like the one I have. Endless hours of Train Simulation Enjoyment! Happy Driving!

This is the tekken I hoped for.
To get this out of the way first, performance wise it seems to be a constant 60 fps with my gtx 1060 and my i5 3570k at 1440p with ultra settings. I did manage to achieve 45 fps at the most demanding map I could find on ultra settings at 4k resolution. I couldn't find any problems online in my first few hours of play. However, the options menu is somewhat slacking. It provides not many options as one would wish from modern titles but the important bits are there. It does have a upscaling slider too and borderless window mode works perfect for me. I personally prefer playing with keyboard and I found it to work absolutely flawlessly. Controllers like the xbox one controller seem to work perfect as well.
As for the gamemodes, you got your typical story mode with lots of cutscenes. An arcade mode, online, versus and treasure mode in which you can unlock cosmetics for your character. Unfortunately, nothing outstanding. The training mode is very extensive and offers lots of options as well as some sample combos to give one a rough idea about how the combo system works but it is obvious that new players should start with the story mode as this should teach one the basics of the game.
Gameplay wise, this game has been in the arcade for some time now and has been played in tournaments since 2 years now. Because of that, the game balance is very finely tuned and whenever I lost, it felt like it was due to my own inability or inexperience.
Overall i am very pleased with the game. The lack of game modes are of course a bit saddening but I guess most people would spent most their time in online play anyway. As far as I see it, this is a must have for any fighting game lover.

When I saw "Control both brothers at once” I thought, “this will be a great co-op game” – I was wrong. When I reached what I though was the end I though, this would be a great movie – I was wrong. Don’t get me wrong, the gameplay is great and two-players is quite possible and could be enjoyable. The story is also just beautiful on its own. But the tear jerking moment when you, alone, reach the end and have to guide both brothers at the same time, the realisation that comes with the fact that you are pressing the buttons, the details like there being two stones to climb at the end (sorry if this gives away too much)… You just have to grab the controller with both hands and try it. When you do, you will understand how much sentiment a single button can convey.
Just a further notice, on a more technical side of things, the game warns you it is best played with a controller and while it is playable with keyboard (I played the first levels that way), it is easier with a controller when you have to press several buttons at once. If you can, buy or borrow one and use it. I used a €10 generic one and besides a small documented bug where one of the joysticks had its y-axis switched (something that was correctable if you look it up on google and could probably be from the controller itself) everything went smoothly. Other than that the game is well built, had a few hiccups with animated portions repeating themselves (probably because I kept the triggers pressed during them) it runs smoothly and gives you a short (just the right size) yet powerful story.

You can tell this game was made by a film director: the pacing is spot-on; the characters are few, but well developed; and unlike many games I've played, this game actually managed to impact me emotionally.  It's brief- just a touch longer than most Hollywood movies, but it's so polished and enjoyable to play that it's worth every cent.
I love games that have no problem with being a fun diversion, but this game really succeeds in making an emotional connection between the player and the characters you control, so if that grabs your interest, then I highly recommend "Brothers".

is a 3D, atmospheric, mechanic and story based experience. An a amazing experience in fact. You control two brothers, one brother with the left analog stick and left trigger and the other brother with the right analog stick and right trigger. You solve puzzles, run, swim, rock climb, fly, and various other things. Single player coop at its finest! The mechanic works well throughout most of the game. The story is about two brothers who are looking for a cure for their sick father. There are many emotional moments in this story as well, I won’t go into full detail cause spoilers. There are great characters, fun moments, and breath-taking sections too. You will fly a hang glider across a forest, climbing in a troll mining shaft, swim across lakes, and climb giant towers. You also meet many humans and creatures along your journey. For example, trolls, owls, giants and wolves! Did I mention there is no understandable voice acting? How are there great characters if there is no understandable voice acting? Good question. What makes this game have good characters is good writing, animation and direction. It took me about 3 and a half hours to beat the game. Even though it is so short, it is so good that it makes up for it. Honestly there are movies out there that are shorter than this and are not as up to par to this game.

In short, this is a good game if you want a short, fun, fulfilling experience that will stay with you for the rest of your life. For 15 dollars it is worth it. Just make sure you have a controller (I reccomend logitech, xbox or a playstation controller), it will make a lot of the game easier to pay.

Feels like a classic 90s LucasArts comedy game. That's both a good and a bad thing, really.
The good:
- Great art.
- Rock solid voice acting.
- The puzzles don't quite get as obscure or ridiculous as 90s adventures, which is a good thing since there's nothing like the infamous Monkey Wrench puzzle here.
- Some neat innovations in 90s adventure game playability. Clicking the middle mouse button highlights objects you can interact with, whilst scrolling it brings down your inventory. Feels natural.
- Characters are mostly good. I feel Rufus has a good progression from self-centered idiot to someone who actually wants to do good by the end, and that's a nice progression. Other characters serve the plot well too, except for Goal (see below).
- The setting of Deponia feels very alive, like a lived-in place with backstory, and not just a shoestrung setting for some doofus causing havoc.
The bleh:
- Animation is a mixed bag.
- Humour is also mixed. Some jokes are funny, others not so. I think the visual gags work well, whereas the "witty" puns fall flat eight times out of ten. That's what you get when translating German jokes, I guess.
- Goal's character. Don't know anything about her, since she's barely awake for most of the game. Can't say she's particularly bad, but I'm unconvinced she's a worthwhile heroine at this point.
- The plot is interesting, but largely unremarkable, especially the romance. It's kind of the typical 'save the world and win the girl as a trophy' trope that's all tired out. As far as that goes it's competent, but I'd have liked to have had a better motivator.
The bad:
- The ending is a total bummer, and you feel like you've accomplished nothing.
- Some plot threads I feel should've been addressed in this game, have instead been held off for the sequel.
- Some puzzles feel obscure, and only after accidentally solving them do you "get it". I felt I stumbled into as many solutions on Deponia as I had eureka moments, which felt very unsatisfying.
All told, I think the good outweighs the bad, and none of the bleh moments particularly spoiled the game. If you like 90s LucasArts comedy games (Monkey Island 1-3, Day of the Tentacle, Sam & Max, and the like) then you will probably get your money's worth out of Deponia, and not feel like you've wasted your time.

This one was hard for me to decide on.  Diablo II was one of my all-time favorite and most played games.  Torchlight was good, scratched the itch, but didn't really 'hold' me.  I had a lot of hope for Torchlight II, but like TL1, it just sort of felt.. empty.
What works: The atmosphere is pretty good, I like how the monsters 'exist' before you wake them up in various sets of realistic repose.  Very nice touch.  The game is colorful and generally graphically engaging, although I don't really like any of the character designs.  It /is/ a Diablo clone, so it has that addictive loot-gathering gameplay, but I can't really evaluate it, because I didn't stick with it long enough for that to become relevant.
What doesn't work:
The skill trees feel bland, with a limited number of 'correct' choices.  The class-specific charge bars are terrible - either really boring (wizard and archer) or uninteractively 'see-sawing' power spikes (berserker).  The engineer is the only one that feels like it 'works'.
Melee still feels kind of like a bad choice, with the amount of damage enemies deal at closer range.  As a ranged fighter, much of the combat takes place off-screen, which is terrible game design (albeit, extremely common in the genre).
Having some skills be dropped or bought (for example, most of the summon spells) makes building characters even /more/ dependent on drop luck than is the norm.  It also breaks down some class variety.
Most significantly, the game just felt off, for reasons I struggle to describe.  I never felt fully engaged.  I put a fair amount of effort in, pushing multiple characters through act 1, but every time, I found myself fighting boredom by the halfway point, and had totally lost interest by the time I stumbled blearily into the desert.  (Act II is a desert?  How novel!)
I kind of regret voting 'no' on this one, because it's plainly a labor of love, because I had high hopes for it, and because I still desperately want to like it, but it is what it is.  Not recommended.

So I just beat the campaign to Sniper Elite 3 (played on Sniper Elite difficulty) and it was pretty good! The sniper gameplay is much like Sniper Elite V2 with a fresh coat of paint... and wow is it a lovely coat of paint. The graphics are phenomenal and the game runs so damn good too! They really brought the Afrika Korps to life in this game. You'll see beautifully rendered Panzer III and IV tanks, including the British Matilda... there's also the Tiger I Tank that looks badass.
The sound effects are the next improvement... wow I love the sounds of the guns in this game. The MP 40 especially. The way it sounds when it fires or reloads is fantastic! I also love that creepy sound the game makes when enemy snipers are trying to get a bead on you or when enemies go into combat mode... kinda reminds me of 70's horror movie sound effects when the killer is sneaking up on you... freaks me right out heh.
I guess I can talk about the sniper gunplay next since it's the main part of the game heh... well? It's handled quite nicely and the x-ray mode is improved over the second game in the series... but it's odd, sometimes the bullet cam gets confused and flies at full speed instead of slowing down or fails to recognize a double kill (can happen if enemies are too close together) but the rest of it works great. The controls are just about perfect... I say just about as I wish it had a button to toggle what shoulder you're looking over. it's annoying when trying to come around some corners if you're not hugging said corner to try and force the camera to pan shoulders...
The campaign is actually quite the nice length as it took me 16.2 hours to beat so I feel it's actually a really nice length to it. The environments are varied and they don't feel the same which is nice since of course the gameplay options are a bit limited.. snipe, run away and return and snipe seems to work the best. It does feel like a bit of a gameplay flaw that enemies can't figure out where you are if you quickly run away and return to the same spot while they're in caution mode (yellow compass warning)... because if I ran away and came back in real life? They'd still figure out I'm in the same spot kind-of thing.
Which leads me into AI... they're decent in this game but they give up WAYYY too easily. I mean... I just sniped two of your comrades! They're dead near you!!! What do you mean you're already returning to normal patrol? Aren't you worried that you're probably next? Hahaha.... So sometimes when I feel like a challenge? I'd place anti-personel mines at the bottom of stairs or ladders leading to me and set up... and then they never charge me. Instead they just keep tossing grenades at me... so that sucked. I'd recommend to other players doing the singleplayer to just set up traps in front and below where you want to snipe in positions you figure where the enemies will try and toss grenades from. I've also had AI run off bridges to their deaths and also run into fire from a left over explosion and get themselves killed haha... so yeah, AI isn't the best in this game and if I did a future playthrough I'd definitely do the hardest difficulty.
So? 16.2 hours for the singleplayer campaign and I got it on a weekend sale. I'd definitely recommend it on those sales for the singleplayer. Tbh I don't really see myself doing multiplayer as I'm not the best at sniping haha so I'll keep my multiplayer gameplay to the likes of World of Tanks. So? If you enjoy

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is essentially a very story driven experience with some interesting puzzle elements to break up the gameplay. I don't want to say much more than that as the 'game' is very much the experience rather than the gameplay.

In fairness it's only one of the bold decisions the developers made with Brothers, and for me most (if not all) of them worked.
The use of dual analog sticks; the belief in their storytelling being strong enough to not include subtitles to translate the pseudo-langauge they created within the game; and ultiamtely the story you experience.
It's a short review for a short game that lasted just shy of 3 hours in total, and the only thing I can really end this recommendation is:
If you enjoy indie games and the 'Art' experience they often deliver this for you. If you prefer deeper gameplay than this might not be what you're looking for, but it's still a worthwhile purchase for the narrative and platform-puzzle elements it provides.

Almost equal part survival horror game and shooter, Doom 3 is a departure from the original classics. Blaring MIDI metal and full speed circle strafing gives way to silence and methodically checking every corner for monsters. The story is surprisingly lengthy and involved, taking inspiration from the Alien films with a demonic Starship Troopers B-movie vibe. It was somewhat divisive when it originally released; the slower pace and heavy reliance on light management wasn't helped by the concurrent rise of the vocal, entitled, forum-dwelling “gamer” that was adverse to change of any kind. This backlash quickly led to a popular “flashlight mod” for the game; a cheat that bypassed the need to switch from your weapon to your light source and completely changed the nature of play. Once this “fix” was in circulation and accepted as a superior way to play the game, subsequent releases (the BFG Edition) used it as a new standard with no option to experience the game as originally intended. A decade later, it's pretty clear those people were wrong. The BFG Edition of Doom 3 is a fairly forgettable corridor shooter. This true version of Doom 3 is still fantastic and is much more influential than anyone seems to give it credit for.
Lighting is a central mechanic to Doom 3. While some of the character models and textures are starting to show their age, the lighting effects and art direction are still incredibly impressive. You use the “F” key to switch to your flashlight frequently; much of the game is filled with moody shadows and often complete pitch blackness. It's not uncommon to have to make a choice to either aim for a demon's glowing red eyes or lure it toward a more helpful light source, hoping you don't back into a trap in the process. It's ballsy how willing Doom 3 is to engulf the player in darkness, knowing their choice is to either be able to see or defend themselves. You can't do both. Walking through hostile environments armed with only a flashlight is it's own genre now; Outlast, Slender Man, Alien: Isolation... that disempowerment was a cornerstone of Doom 3.
Most of the weapons and enemies from the previous games return: the possessed soldiers, the standard Imps, floating Cacodemons, dead-raising Revenants, towering Hellknights, and the big bad Cyberdemon. A few new ones make their appearances, notably the weak but swarming spiders and creepy winged baby things. Then there are standard zombies, which aren't much of a threat on their own but have a habit of trapping you in corners if you're not careful. They're also great chainsaw fodder. Weapons include the all-around handy shotgun, the hammering chaingun, plasma gun, a new standard if generic assault rifle, and the legendary BFG. Ammo conservation and choosing the right tool for the right situation seems more vital than ever, as weapons have a pretty clear rock-paper-scissors relationship to most monsters. And the monsters can be right aggressive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, relentlessly chasing you down and teleporting toward or behind you. Some attacks and scripted “jump scares” seem almost impossible to avoid damage from, causing health and ammo rationing to ratchet up to true survival horror levels. Also new (though introduced late in the game) is the Soul Cube, an alien artifact that charges up by killing five enemies, which can then be thrown for massive damage and health regeneration. It's an odd weapon, but it does add an additional layer of strategy as you prioritize low ranking demons for the charge to obliterate the tougher foes.
A gripping narrative and the Doom name doesn't exactly go hand-in-hand, but a surprising amount of care went into building the game's lore and the pacing is actually spot on. You play The Marine, a voiceless guy who shows up on a Mars base in the future. Almost immediately♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan and the base's personnel gets a bad case of the Satans and demons start coming through portals. There's a mad scientist intent on helping the demons (or something), and the demons want to ultimately conquer Earth because they're actually an ancient race that humans have descended from. It's real campy schlock, but it's very self aware and dips into outright comedy at times, then presents truly dark and disturbing imagery in the next beat. I'd describe the tone as The Evil Dead meets Aliens.
You interact with the environments in a number of ways to solve puzzles; many of the computers can be cursored over in order to raise bridges, move machinery, or access camera or communication feeds. It's quite an impressive level of detail, mechanics that predated modern games like SOMA, Dead Space, and Alien: Isolation (again...). In addition to the standard finding of keycards and badges to raise your security clearance and unlock doors, Doom 3 features another form of storytelling collectible that has become prolific enough to become a cliché: audio logs and e-mails. Now, this certainly isn't the first video game to have the player sift through characters' personal files, but the game came out well before the method had overstayed it's welcome and is still some of the best implementation I've come across. Some of the exchanges between staff are genuinely funny, and the Martian Buddy spam is a forgotten classic. Even the video discs have a distinct style and personality, and even if some of this fluff can be criticized for slowing the game down, it's optional and I enjoyed diving into every last one. It can't be understated how great (and often tense) it is to be able to listen to audio logs as you explore and fight; something other games still screw up to this day.
Doom 3 holds up better than just about any other game of it's vintage I can think of. It remains super tense and oppressive, and I found myself leaning toward the screen as I played with baited breath. With a good pair of headphones and a darkened room it's just as effective (if not more so) than most modern horror games. When the bullets and fireballs start flying it's still definitely classic Doom, but the new emphasis on narrative and lore-building allow the masterfully crafted, cramped hellish battlefields to legitimately scare the crap out of you. It plays silky smooth while still feeling brutal and visceral. Doom 3 may be a different breed of Doom, but now when it kicks♥♥♥♥♥you might just♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself in the process.

It kind of goes without saying that the original Doom was a hugely influencial game that basically defined what a first person shooter should be and inspired countless other games to follow in it's footsteps. Doom 3 takes a slightly different approach than the previous entries in the series. The story and atmosphere play more like Half-Life than classic Doom but that's actually a good thing. Instead of just mindlessly running around shooting monsters you'll be carefully checking out every corner and room for precious health, ammo and PDAs so you can figure out what the hell has been going on. It's very cinematic. The flashlight plays a key role in this as you'll need it to see into the shadows. Players that want every first person shooter to be the same will be annoyed by this but it's inclusion kicks the intensity up a few notches.
Speaking of light this is the type of game you'll want to play with all the lights off (or not). Even over a decade later the visuals and dark atmosphere are still impressive and often just downright unnerving. The human characters are a little on the blocky side but the demons, futuristic machinery and realtime lighting do a great job in immersing you in the environment. The sound design is also very well done with very effective and creepy ambiant noises. There is some seriously scary stuff going on in the walls and air vents in this game. Headphone users be advised.
Note: This is the version to buy and not the "BFG Edition" which has brightened graphics and screws up key features (flashlight is no longer selectable). Basically just a misguided cash grab. Avoid.

The Quest might be one of those games that at first glance you feel like you should ignore.  It has a distinct "indie" look to it at first glance and drowns in a sea of lower priced indie games fighting for your attention.  But let me tell you if you have even the tiniest nostalgic bone in your body, you are doing yourself a great favor in picking up this game!  I am quite a fan of the older RPG games, particularly games like the Elder Scrolls Daggerfall, Lands of Lore and the Might and Magic and Wizardy series of games.  The Quest hits those notes with plenty of charm to spare!
There are the standard fare of classes and races to choose from, giving you the opportunity to tailor your own character to the style of play that you enjoy the most.  I personally set out as a mage, and I get all the right feelings from that, including feeling like a wimp at a low level.  Leveling up and purchasing better equipment actually feels to make a difference.  I am able to creep ever farther out into the dangerous wilds as bit by bit I get just a little better and wield better equipment.
The imagery is nicely stylized and consistent throughout from what I've seen.  It does have that "low budget" sort of look which makes for unimpressive screenshots but once you immerse yourself in this world, you are easily lost in it and the funny looking features of the landscape don't bother you much.  It's the large world seemingly filled with exciting adventures that you here for after all!
The controls have taken me a bit to figure out.  Some things aren't as intuative, like clicking on a crack in the floor sometimes opens up my inentory, as if it is a container, sometimes it initiates an attack, sometimes nothign happens at all.  And there doesn't seem to be any visual feedback to let you konw which will happen.   Because of this, it took me several play sessions before I wasn't accidentally attacking small children in town, or firing off a healing spell when I meant to look at my character sheet.  but given a bit of time, you will become familiar with the keyboard shortcuts.
I think the lack of intuitive interface, or maybe I should call it "hand holding" actually lends itself to this game as a benefit.  I'm actually enjoying learning in a more natural way all of the different ways I can interact with the world I'm finding myself in.
The music is nice and fitting for the situations. The sound effects are just fine.  I actually wince each time I'm minding my own business wandering through the forrest only to be ambushed by an amazonian looking archer woman.  The sound of her arrows thudding into me, and the sharp grunt my character makes me cringe every time.
Don't let any doubts about first impressions keep you from picking up this game (as I did at first), you owe it to yourself ot get started on this exciting quest!

The Quest is a beautifully crafted world, with lots of interesting quests, I don't find them repetitive and I actually really enjoy the challenge the game brings, it's not too easy, but if you prepare then it's not too hard. I'd recommend researching the game a little before buying, as this genre is a bit like marmite. you either love it or you hate it.
I'd recommend this game to any of my old school RPG loving friends

If you are looking for a great RPG reminiscent of what this genre was like between, say 1990 - 1995, then look no further because "The Quest" might just be what appeals to you! Personally, I am very happy I found this gem on Steam. Hate to think of what I would have missed if I had passed it up. What first attracted me was the handdrawn art seen in the screenshots. "The Quest" is a beauty and also very fun.
Older titles that come to my mind are Might and Magic 3/4/5. However, "The Quest" formulates its own style in both atmosphere and mood, and it does not feel too much like M&M or really any other title I know. If Redshift has modelled the mechanics of their game after some other title that inspired them, then it's one that I have yet to play. Suffice it to say, I enjoyed "The Quest" immensely and I am very much looking forward to the promised sequel. The stories in both the main game and its expansion captivates with numerous twists that kept me questioning the motives of the more important characters you are forced to interact with. There are plenty of interesting moral choices to be made both during the main questline or during sidequests which might prompt a reload of your save just to see the effects of what happens when you act differently. Atleast that is what I did - often. :) Playing cards at the inns is another addiction.
Also, technically, the interface in this game is simple in a positive way and allows you to focus on gameplay rather than zillions of statistics or needless tabs that serve no practical purpose. Its nice for a change. What I am saying is basically that "The Quest" is easy to get into but hard to put down. Frequent patches has also killed of most bugs reported and I did not runt into as much as a single issue while playing. 100 % stable.
I could go on about everything else I like about this game but other reviews might might say it better or offer other more detailed perspectives on various aspects of gameplay I haven't covered here. It's not a game for everyone but rather a matter of taste (as with everything). Still, if you approved of the older M&M - or similar - then I don't see why you should dislike "The Quest". The island of Freymore awaits.

For the record, this game is REALLY underrated and imo underadvertised. This is one of those games where you play it not so much for the plot, rather if you had a bad day and really want to let off all your anger frustration but don't know how. Boot up this game, jump in your saddle, and swing your sword/axe/polearm to your heart's content. You'll feel better in no time.
Okay, in all seriousness, this game is really amazing. It may not be for people looking for a deep and riveting plot. It definitely falls short compared to other games out there today in terms of graphics. And there will be quite a bit (a lot) of grinding, especially early on. But this game is perfect for anyone looking for a solid first person medieval-era fuedal style war game while still having basic troop control (kind of like in Total War, but far more simplistic and far less troops). You get to recruit, train, and fight alongside each member in your army, and both your character and certain recruitable "companion" characters have a decent range of customizable skills and equipment. A variety of weapon types are avaiable, including swords, spears, bows, crossbows, throwing knives, maces, staffs, and shields. The economic system is pretty important and balanced in terms of troop wages and income from owned property. The game has six factions that occasionally declare war with each other, and everyone who has played the game knows that the troop types of each of these factions aren't exactly "balanced". You can join one of these factions, or start your own. The point of the game is to take over every other faction so you or the faction you are in is the ruler of, well, basically everything.
Overall I really love this game. It can be played as both a pick-up-put-down casual game or marathoned for days on end. There are so many other things to do besides fighting in wars, ranging from tournament games to starting your own business in various cities to courting and marrying someone. I feel like this game does a tremendous job blending action-packed first person combat with the immersive medieval feel of courtship and managing businesses and resources. As it is on sale right now I highly encourage everyone to buy it, but even if there is no sale it is well worth the money. This is the first game that I have written a review for, which goes to tell you just how much I enjoy this game. If you read all the way to the end of this review I'm actually quite surprised. Thank you for taking the time to read my review.
P.S. I have never played multiplayer so everything above is about single player. Also I play mainly offline so I have played WAY more hours than it says I have. I would not write a review for a game if I haven't at least put in 100 hours into it :P.

"It's kind of pathetic: you get all erratic, about dirty dishes congesting the sink.
I'm tired of your bothers; remember our fathers, who dwelled in a world filled with rubbish and stink..."
And so the story begins. Deponia is the tale of Rufus, the son of the man who founded Rufus's hometown of Kuvaq and subsequently disappeared, and his attempts to escape the junk-strewn planet of Deponia. During one of his infamous "perfect" plans, he runs into a girl from the romanticized, junk-free world of Elysium, nearby.
The two become wrapped in each other's quests, for better or for worse. Rufus is stuck with Goal, because she's his only ticket out of this dump, and Goal is stuck with Rufus because, well, she's unconscious, and she doesn't really have any say in the matter. Plus he's the person with the closest thing to her best interests at heart, between the town of Kuvaq, who wish to keep her as a trophy resident, and the Organon who seemingly have their own agenda.
Rufus is not the most selfless hero. In fact, he's rather vain and self-centered. He manages to pull it off and remain endearing, however - at least to the audience. His neighbors in Kuvaq are painfully tired of his absent-minded and often quite dangerous (to Rufus, and everyone else in a several mile radius) plans and experiments. In a way, maybe I find Rufus endearing because he reminds me so much of, well, me. He's lazy, but dreams big, and feels he deserves to be the one to make it simply because he wants it more.
Deponia's a silly game, the kind where great bodily harm is often cartoonishly shrugged off when it's not important to the plot. It made me laugh quite a few times, and most of the characters are well-written and well-voiced. The Organon bug me, with their loud, crackly, sort-of-digitized voices, but most of the others sound alright to downright enjoyable. The music is a perfect fit, evoking the rattling and banging of garbage, while still remaining pleasant to listen to. I'm quite fond of the bar theme in particular, to the point where I would sometimes stop in at the place even after I had no business left there, simply to listen for awhile. The world is beautifully drawn, and most importantly, interesting. There are surprises everywhere, and the world itself is rather unusual, and nicely characterized as you go about your journey.
The puzzles are challenging, without ever seeming unfair. You do have kind of an unusual amount of "gather cleaning supplies and clean this thing off" puzzles, but then this IS a planet covered in discarded scrap and refuse, so it's at least justified. On the whole, Deponia's puzzles and style feel to me like a proper evolution of the classic Lucasarts SCUMM adventures. The sense of humor, however, is unique, and I love it. It really feels like Daedalic had fun writing and designing this game, and I'm glad, because I had fun playing it.
It's not the longest adventure game, but it's long enough (I clocked about 11 hours of quality adventuring on my playthrough), and I absolutely cannot wait to play the next installment in the Deponia trilogy.

Lukewarm experience on the whole. Since Steam forces you to recommend it or not, I gave the thumbs down, but if the story grabs you in a way it didn't grab me (or if you value aesthetics over tight gameplay) you might very well enjoy it. Certainly many others seemed too (and it even inexplicably made it on a number of people's top 10 lists for the year).
Pros:
-nice to look at with inventive environments (in the second half of the game; first half much less exciting).
-a few segments are quite fun to control (particular the section where you're roped together).
Cons:
-Though only 3 hours long, the gameplay gets boring well before this, with no significant ramping up of challenge in the second half versus the first.
-Very linear; always obvious exactly where to go. Hall blocked less by puzzles and more simple obstacles (e.g., use one brother to open a door for the other sorts of things).
-Controls are certainly playable but never particularly fun (my, and I think most people's brains aren't really designed for controlling two things at once--I imagine if you're a drummer or pianist it might be more enjoyable and less a chore). The game is easy enough that any difficulty with the controls will not hamper you completing it.
-Storyline, such as it is, is risibly melodramatic towards the end. Any potential emotional impact is subverted by the annoying SIMS style non-speech. During moments of particular melodrama in the last two chapters I literally laughed out loud at the histrionics on display rather than feel the emotions the producer intended. All this is to say that the game did a poor job, in my case, of making me care about the characters.

A really memorable and well-crafted experience. It's one of the few experiences that actually reminded me of how I remember my childhood: it started with a strong fairy tale feel where something is not quite right, and gradually grew progressively grim as the brothers were thrust into a world where children are not immune to hardship. Before playing it, I was concerned it would be another recycled story about annoying/sad/bratty stock-character kids, but I'm pleased to say that it's one of the more balanced and mature portrayals of children that shows them as human beings with an actual personality.
In terms of gameplay, the way they combined it with the story development makes Brothers one of gaming's gems: all the story is told through the environment and the interactions the player has with the world, and there is no (comprehensible) dialogue.
The best story moments are twists based on how you control both brothers in different situations. One of my favorite examples is an area where you need to avoid detection from a monster by hiding in specific positions behind frozen statues. Another is a battlefield for giants, where navigating the environment becomes a nice twist. All the areas you explore are filled with little contextual interactions that will make you will feel like you "toy"with this unforgiving world and its inhabitants, just like a child would.
Complementing this approach is a truly special and stylized art direction, the kind that makes me stop and take screenshots every minute or so.The amount of soul & care put in the details of this game, from memorable story moments to little interactions in the world, is rare to find in games nowadays. Very short but very sweet.

First, I will admit to beta-testing this for Mac. This does not affect the review.
Second, I see two distinct types of players of The Quest: old-timers who played it in the iPhone (and PPC) days, and newbies who found this game on Steam and maybe wishlisted it.
If you're one of the old-timers, get this game. Period. Even though you don't have the luxury of expansions, mod support should come out soon enough.
If you're a newbie: You should buy this game. For about ten dollars, it's a steal. The graphics are vintage, looking like they date back to about 2005. As a person who cares more about gameplay, this doesn't matter. My point is even though it doesn't have the visual quality of The Witcher 3 or Skyrim, you should still get this.
This is a CRPG, which means it's open world. Some of the quests in this game might be rather generic and basic, but others give you a freedom of choice not seen in many other RPGs. You can choose to live a pious life or be as evil as you want, based on your actions. In addition, there's a good and evil ending. You also get the freedom to teleport (though limited) to whatever location you want through Mark and Recall spells, as well as the ability to enchant your armor, weapons, and jewelry with whatever you want. You want to give your dagger a +2 Personality enchantment? Go ahead!
In terms of length, one could see about 20-50 hours of gameplay in this game. However, I've not played the base game by itself up until now, since I played it on iPhone with expansions, so this is a rough and wildly variable estimate. Redshift updates their game very frequently, so any glitches you find will get patched out within a week at most.
In short: Purchase this game if you like RPGs. Period. It's only $10, but worth so much more. If you've played it before in the past and enjoyed it, I'd be surprised if you didn't get it.

tl;dr Wonerful little RTS with virtually infinite possibilities- would certainly recommend, but only to players who are willing to spend some time learning mechanics.
Wargame: Red Dragon is an awesome little realistic RTS that simulates war on a scale rarely seen in such a genre, spanning miles upon miles of territory. It forces one to use real logic and strategies to outfox and eliminate the enemy. For example, approaching the enemy without combined arms is a disaster waiting to happen- e.g tanks without AA will easily die to helos and planes, infantry without armoured support gets obliterated by tanks, etc.
The game can be split into two parts- building 'decks', in which a player builds a force using 'cards' of various units, and actual combat. The battles, on the other hand, are (quite literally) bloody fantastic. Every small detail from the whistle of the Katyusha as a salvo of death gracefully flies across the map to the empty cartridges ejecting out of an infantryman's rifle is faithfully modeled, as Soviet-backed Warsaw Pact and allied countries engage in a massive showdown of epic proportions against NATO nations and their supporters in the beautifully depicted landscape of East Asia. A huge number of units from both sides feature, compelling the player to make several crucial decisions that could turn the tide of battle- whether it be to risk sending an unsupported force against what you hope is the last thing the enemy has, or to pin your hopes on a small squad of recon infantry to find and take out the enemy's command vehicle before they can call out more reinforcements.
But something one can really appreciate about this game is the diversity of the units, allowing the player to send out more or less any kind of unit fielded during the era of the 80-90s- whether it be surplus WWII-era T-34/85 tanks supporting North Korean reservists armed with Chinese PPSh-41s, all the way to the cream-of-the-crop T-90 tank and elite troops armed with grenade launchers. This could lead to some interesting realistic strategies, such as sending out cheap 'meatshield' tanks to weaken enemy defenses and waste their ammunition, before deploying a proper, competent task force to finish 'em off.
Of course, like any other RTS, the game suffers from a couple of balancing issues, such as a pathetically underpowered North Korean military (even though it's 1980) and a rather controversial DLC pack, but otherwise most nations are similarly competent against eachother. Usual issues such as kiting isn't very common, since ranges are very strictly controlled (e.g all tanks in the same class have the same engagement range) but issues such as the infamous "helo spam" (self-explanatory, some jackass sends a ton of Hinds your way, can (sometimes) be dealt with by spamming your own AA but unrealistic and not very fun nonetheless) remain. Also worthy of note is the extremely shortened engagement distance in this game- the longest ranged tanks in the game have a maximum range of 2.275km.
However, the game really isn't new-player friendly. The community is your best bet for learning this game- the "tutorials" in W:RD are among the worst I've seen, simply being pure text about how to use the menu and introducing the naval units, with nothing actually explaining how to fight! Thankfully, an AI skirmish mode featuring some of the most incompetent AI I've ever seen exists, so that can be used as a stepping stone. Many guides exist on the Steam and Eugen forums about how to actually play, along with many excellent videos one can find on YouTube.
Overall, in conclusion, this game is great albeit slightly flawed, but it's a perfect fit for RTS fans and military enthusiasts of the Cold War. Granted however, it's quite difficult and frustrating- but playing it properly will reward you with hours upon hours of fun. Oh, and one last thing-
Expect most of those hours to be in menus.

I only discovered the Wargame franchise this week due to the sale.  I can't believe this one slipped under my radar.
I'd say of all the RTS games I've played over the last few decades, the one this is closest to is World in Conflict.  However, there are way more units, and the high level campaign is really well done.  It's like a game of chess, even more so than in any Total War game I've played, since you don't have an economy / research you can lean on to stack the odds in your favor.  It's all about how you set up the board.  You can recruit new units, but there are only one of each type in the end that can be used on the map.  The name "Wargame" isn't just a cool sounding title; it's very, very apt.
The simplified rock, paper, scissors approach of traditional RTS (i.e. calvary beat archers who beat infantry who beat calvary) is greatly enhanced by the variety of real-world units.  You'd need a lost more nouns than rock, paper and scissors to make that metaphor apply here.  This game is very well done.
A couple very minor gripes, mostly with lack of documentation on gameplay mechanics:
1) the manual doesn't explain a whole lot.  I can't figure out of there's a way to issue complex movement commands (waypoints) like you can in every other RTS game.  Maybe shift right click works, but there's no clear indicator.
2) What does R&R do?  Does that give you more command units?  I think there was a pop up somewhere that migth have told me, but I can't find that online, and it's not in the manual.
3) How precisely does Line of Sight Work?  How far from the edge of the woods does you scout need to be?  Do you need to zoom into the scout to see what it sees?  Does it matter which direction it faces?  I frequently find my scout units fail to find targets I would think they should see.
Nice wargame!

I'm not a sniper. Anyone who ever had the misfortune of playing a shooter with me will confirm I'm physically incapable of hitting the broad side of a barn at point blank range. I still had fun with Sniper Elite 3.
Here's the thing: the main selling point of its series is its wonderful ballistic model, with which you can set up a sniping experience as close to real as possibly, taking into account distance, muzzle velocity (whatever the hell that's supposed to be), gravity, wind, heartbeat, phase of the moon and the zodiacal sign of the poor sod in your sights. Screw that.
My elite sniper used his sniper rifle about a third of the time in missions. The rest was spent running around the maps at full speed while cackling wildly as he led the obliging Afrika Korps into landmines, carelessly placed munition boxes and lookisthatacorpseoverthereBOOM situations. The maps are pretty large and set up in ways that almost always leave you to pick your approach - and there's plenty of opportunities for guard AI mind♥♥♥♥ery, usually involving explosions. I mean, you can sneak and stab and snipe if you want to, but finally it's just an option.
Oh, and there's a story. Thankfully it's mostly unintrusive, excpet for a couple of laughably hammy cutscenes near the end and incredibly overacted narration by our badass hero. One nice touch though - the rather silly and completely ♥♥♥♥ing useless superweapon we're trying to stop the Germans from building is actually one they were really considering. Historically nice.
To sum it up: the Sniper Elite games were always marketed as this weird ballistic simulator marketed toward WW2 nerds and people willing to wait five hours to take the perfect shot. Nothing wrong with that and it's still there - but this time around  it comes packaged in an actually good game. Wouldn't pay more than ten euros for it, though.
Oh, and if you buy the DLC, you get to shoot Hitler in the balls.

Did you ever enjoy Diablo? This game is for you.
Didn't play Diablo? Well, if you like RPG's with progressive skill trees, different character classes, lots of monsters to kill, and great dungeons to explore, this game is still for you.
In either of those cases, at $20, this game is well worth the money. However, at the $5 sales which happen a few times a year, this game is absolutely a STEAL. Incredible value for the price.
The comparisons to Diablo are well deserved, but the fact of the matter is that this game does play different and in a good way. Anyone who has played Diablo 2 probably remembers that 95% of items you find were useless, and the in game gold was almost worthless. This is absolutely not the case in TL2. The item system is deep and complex, with multiple ways to gear any given character ranging from tankiness to pure glass cannon DPS. And gold is extremely relevant as the shops sell good items, additional spells, and the gambling store rolls uniques frequently enough to spend your actually hard earned gold there. As for item drops, you will often find useful gear and have to make decisions like 'do I want that extra armor, or that little bit more damage?' all the time. Eventually you will be looking for some very specific gear which will be hard to find, but it takes a long time to get to that point and even then you don't often blindly sell all but 1-2 items on a given run.
Also there are personal stashes for each character, as well as a shared stash which mixes the best of both worlds between Diablo 2 and 3's stash systems. You can use characters as mules like in D2, but you can easily transfer items between all your characters through the shared stash. If you like to use one character to provide good equipment, or just pass down such items, to your lower characters it is a piece of cake. This is also helpful because of class-specific uniques which drop.
As far as the skill system goes, it is very diverse which each character having 3 skill branches. Each branch has 7 skills and 3 passives. Skills have tier levels when 5, 10, and 15 points are placed in them to unlock extra bonuses, but the passives do not. Skill points are actually limited though. The maximum amount is 132, but if you play for a while you'll find yourself wishing for a few extra points to throw into skills. This gives the game great build diversity, and often will leave you desiring to have more than 1 character per class to explore all the different options.
The combat system is great as well, and the monster difficulty scales well throughout the levels. Depending on your setup, some areas will be easier, but others will put a lot of stress on you. If you play carelessly, you can die really fast. The multiplayer system is great too, and some characters even have skills which lend themselves assisting your teammates in multiplayer but are useful enough in single player to allow you to boost them and then play either way you wish.
The only downsides to the game to me are in two areas. One is the story is underwhelming, and really didn't interest me. That said, most people don't play Diablo for the story so that probably isn't a big deal. The other thing I dislike a bit, and this is probably just more of a personal issue than anything, is that just like Diablo 2/3, Act 2 is a huge desert act which can be somewhat annoying to navigate. I would have been nice to have a change of pace from the same old desert crap. Although at least the bestiary is substantially different.
I love this game more than Diablo 3. It has a much more fluid style of gameplay, and getting gear doesn't feel like a grind.

This game is insane, but really fun and addictive.
You essentially play as a 2D sprite (which changes every time you die) who shoots green monsters, big and small, and collects crates which change the characters weapon. The aim of the game is to collect as many crates as possible without dying, as 1 crate = 1 point.
You soon realise that some weapons are better than others, and therefore you have to collect crates quickly in order to replace the bad weapon with a better one. However, at the same time you are being bombarded by green creatures and floating white skulls whose touch equals instant death. This game involves multi-tasking, and improves hand-eye coordination at the same time.
I would recommend this to anybody who has a lot of spare time on their hands, or is just looking for a retro-style game which can be played over and over again. :)

For me, the benchmark for that kind of game is M&M X Legacy. The Quest, being indie game, is not nearly as polished. I played other games like that, e.g. Grimrock, but I never could play past 15 min. The story of The Quest looks strange at first, but I learned to enjoy it over time. Skills and items are all quite interesting as well, and excitment from visits shops doesn't wear off fast.
What's fresh here - it's old school progression system. Neither narrative nor regions decide for you when you qualify to go and fight. You do it the old fashion: you run, you train hard on weaker enemies, do quests, have a shopping spree, then you go back to the dungeon and kick♥♥♥♥♥of that spongy litte ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. And you save a lot, how else would you know when to run? There's nothing new in combat system, it's just ok (I find it quite underwhelming being an archer in games like that). Good-evil alignment is real and affects a lot of stuff including gear you can use. And, most importantly, what really keeps me going is exporation I think.
The game has its flaws, needs more graphics settings, could use more polish (UI), but if you are ok with that and if you can lay aside inconveniences like lack of quest tracking and quick bar for iteam/spells or accidental attacking of civilians then you will have a lot of fun with The Quest.

One of the best semi-realistic strategy games out there. One of the things I really like about the game is the fact that it is quite realistic.
Most strategy games focus on massing one or two units (Command and Conquer for example), or hitting special timings (Starcraft for example). In this game this is simply not viable, because of the scale of the maps you are fighting in and the way the game works.
For instance, you just can't move your tanks across the map, because there might be anti-tank infantry hiding in the woods or the houses, which basically kill your tanks with 1 or 2 hits (like in real-life). Next to that, you can't detect enemies easily without using dedicated recon units (like in real-life), which ensures you will have to think about scouting first and being careful moving your units around. On top of all that, you have to take into account things like: fuel, ammunition, armor (front armor is stronger than rear armor for instance), armor penetration (armor penetration is less efficient the further away you are from your enemy), terrain (you can't shoot while your view is blocked by trees/rocks/houses for instance).
This makes the game realistic and for people who really like to play a somewhat authentic war strategy game, this game is the real deal!
Also, there are a lot of different factions and playstyles possible. Normally a typical RTS would have 3 or 4 different factions or types of armies and 10-20 different units per faction/army. In this game, each faction has about 100-200 different unit types. This might sound overwhelming, and to be honest, there is a steep learning curve, but once you understand how the mechanics work and how the different types of units should be used, this game is awesome.
Imo, one of the best strategy games ever built. Can't wait for a followup!

It's a train simulator. You drive trains. There's not really much more to it than that, though there are "scenarios" where you have to drive a route and be on time, or pick up or drop off freight on a siding, some of which are easy and some are challenging.  It's also more complicated to drive a train than you think.  You'll learn how to set your "reverser" correctly, for instance, and a million other details that'll make you scratch your head and ask, "Why won't this blasted train move?"  And it takes a bit of trial and error to become skillful enough to stop right at the platform without inching up to it or overshooting it.  In a nutshell, if you like detailed nit-picky simulators and/or you're a railfan, this is a great game for you!  If you're neither of those things, you'll probably wonder, "What's the point?"  But then again, if you liked to play with electric trains, give it a try!

This is an excellent game without doubt. I have not had it for very long and I've had loads of quality fun and time with it. There are bugs and issues with it however, most notably braking issues on the diesel models, and some scenarios not ending properly which is annoying after 1-2 hours of concentrating play.
You cannot get away from the fact that the game is so well made and the scenery so utterly brilliant, that it draws you in expecting certain programming and quality standards to have been met, only to find they have not been.
This is extremely frustrating after having bonded with the product.
Some of the more minor tracks such as refirgeration storage and container crane tracks although accessible, are bugged with phantom collison detection errors which ends the scenario. That combined with braking issues on the diesels (brakes not resetting) and scenario instability (not ending properly with a tick or stars) is disappointing.
The game has a mixture of utter brilliance combined with an unfinished feel. There is no way I could not recommend this game based on what it already is, and I didn't even buy any expansion packs to arrive at that conclusion. Most of my time was spent on Sherman Hill and some time on the Norfolk Southern coal routes. They are outstandingly good and well modelled.
I would hope that more time is spent on programming errors in the future, and maybe even the additon of a campaign mode, and working cranes and scripting possibilities in user made scenarios.
Very, very good product indeed, and I sincerely hope more fixes and developments are planned for it.

To the point that some items like a yacht that does basicly next to nothing, cost up to $10.000.000 of ingame currency (which is about €75,-. the most expensive sharkcard avaible). And with every update more and more expensive vehicles, homes and businesses keep getting added whilst nerfing the older stuff to entice people to buy the new stuff. And the new businesses that are being added barely make enough money to cover the investments that you made to set it up. All of this is being done just to sell more Sharkcards.
And if that isn't bad enough, there are hackers in nearly every goddamned online session.
Sure some are practicly harmless and give you loads of money, however the vast majority stops at nothing to act like a pain in the neck. I've lost count of how many times i've entered a session only to get blown up along with everybody else in the session. Some people have even had their money taken away by these hackers and had their levels decreased. Any other company would have done their best to get rid of this menace as soon as possible (protecting their investment and all that). Not Rockstar though, The worst thing that can happen is that these hackers get booted from Rockstar Socialclub. Only for them to go on greymarket sites and buy a key for €25,- and do it all over again.
I could go on and on about what is wrong with GTA Online, however that would mean i'd be busy typing this review till next year.
In short; if you're looking for a fun online game to play with your friends, look elsewhere.

Anyone who is in the Tekken community has already purchased this game, simply for the concept of finally being able to play this game on proper hardware.
I feel the community here on PC has the potential to be one of the more competitive, and I hope people can overcome the extreme difficulty of this game and try to understand it.
Because it truly is one of the greatest fighting game experiences, and in my opinion, the most rewarding.
So, for those who are uncertain, I'll explain concisely why this game is worth your time.
--
Tekken is worth it because of depth it contains, and because of that depth, you have the ability to creatively form strategies around any character you like.
Tekken is played on a 3d plane, movement is an essential element of the game that 2d fighters simply cannot do justice. Of course, those who have been playing Tekken for as long as I have, understand that the movement is one of the more complex aspects of the game, so I won't really go into it.
Just understand, that this is not a 2D fighter, and you should not play it like one, and because of this you can further create your playstyle how you want to play,
And finally, Tekken is legacy game that has remained rather similar throughout the entirety of it's existance. And due to this, anything you learn in Tekken 7, or you have learned in previous titles, will carry on forever. It's not a game you learn, and need to "relearn" or "reunderstand" in the next installment. What you learn here aren't the concepts of Tekken 7, they're the concepts of Tekken.
In addition, the cast has also evolved over years and years. What you find here only the most current version of what will continue to evolve and change.
Simply typing a review about it doesn't do it justice, so if you're in the market for a deep, legacy fighting game with a whole lot to learn, and a whole lot to gain from it, give Tekken a go.
This is the first time it's ever been on PC and I really hope it can stay here.
Catch you online fellas, and if you have questions about the game feel free to comment here and I'll be more than happy to help you out.

This review is purely from first time experiance of playing this game and will be updated as time goes along i'd also like to state that the quality of spelling and grammer of this first version of the review will be bad as this was written from 1:30AM BST. now onto the quick little review.
(Method of obtaining this game: won the deluxe editon via a contest however this does not cause bias as i intended on getting the product)
I've always been a Street Fighter and SoulCalibur type of guy and never was a Tekken guy untill i played Tekken tag 2 and found it a enjoyable experiance so when i saw tekken 7 was annouced i was happy as i felt that it will bring a nice light to the japanese fighting game market since Street Fighter V and the mess it caused (Personally i think SFV is a good fighter just lacking content badly). so pretty much i was hype for this game to come out and i can glady say its lived up to it. as it has blown tekken tag 2 out of the water in gameplay and presenation in my opinon.
The biggest diffrence i noticed was that Tekken 7 felt quicker than tag 2 and other games which felt tankish at times this might deter tekken fans as its known for its tanky feel but dont worry they made the game play quicker while keeping its classic feel i also really like the rage mode which is in this game as it reminds me of Street fighter IV's ultra moves however i really like the presenation of this game the most as the camera zooms into the characters during the final hit which really adds hype factor and intensity to the game especially when both characters health is extremly low and could go ether way, this is a great feature and will create many amazing moments in tournments and when playing with friends or strangers online. Character customisation is back in tekken 7 which is great for those who like putting characters in silly outfits or if you was like me and spent hours on soul calibur creating characters building outfits for your faveouite characters to suit your style and tastes.

In conclusion from my first play of the game this is well worth the price as they game comes with alot of content out of the box unlike other fighting games (looking at you killer insinct and street fighter v) and runs smoothly and plays well obviosuly my opinon may change in the future if any cracks start to show however i highly doubt it will.

I've been with the game's community since Fall of 2014, so I know stuff, m'kay?
While I rarely play the steam version (personal preference for the most part, I do like my browser edition!), I've got several hundred hours in-game alone clocked under my belt, and what must be thousands on the forums.
Heroes and Generals is a game that seems to get a lot of hate for reasons that I cannot seem to actually find, in my hours of play.
Some common misconceptions:
"The Game is Pay 2 Win!!!"
No, it's not. If you definition of Pay 2 Win is a game that essentially makes you pay to get the better content, or has a paywall of some sort, then H&G should be fine for you. All content that affects gameplay is available for free users, and while the game has a bit of a grind, it's nothing impossible. One piece of advice though, plan ahead. Know what you want on what soldier, because trying everything out on your first guy will result in one soldier with a lot of stuff who can only use one set of stuff per match - make a new soldier for each playstyle you want to have access to in-game.
"Newbies are underpowered (or some variation)!" At first you have an unmodified Semi-auto rifle, and the boots on your feet.
Your rifle can be one of the most potent weapons in the game, and with skill and the right upgrades, you can turn your lowly M1 Garand/SVT-40/Gewehr 43 into an efficent killing machine. The game has a steep skill curve. You'll be up against 4+ year vets; BUT, not at first. For several hours you'll be up against people who have roughly the same time as you.
Just take heed, as soon as you buy a weapon that has the "gold matchmaking group" tag or you enter the gold matchmaking group via the player ranking system, you WILL run into players who have been playing for months, years, possibly since the game started. And yes, at first you'll get roflstomped. And then you won't. You should learn. Watch people of a higher rank, see how they move, etc. Hell, even ask them questions if they're in the deploy queue, f.e.
The game is hard. No purpose sugarcoating it.
However, it's nowhere as terrible as some of these keyboard warriors with <10 hours make it out to be. Frankly, a lot of them sound like entitled little rats, but whatever. If you like the game, play it. If you don't think it's the game for you, then take your business elsewhere. But give H&G the chance it deserves. It's a damn good game, even if it has its quirks here and there. I strongly encourage anybody who has the time to check it out. It's the least you could do.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

Yay, after many years, I get to play another humor adventure game. So how does Deponia measure up?
To begin with I very much like the art style. It's got 2D fully animated characters with some pretty nice painted backgrounds. Everything's easy to move around and interact with. Thankfully you can double click to instant-move to a location.
Music is serviceable. I like to think of it as elevator music. It's there, and you notice it, but it won't stick, may irritate after a while, and you'd probably rather listen to your own music.
The story is all right. The main character is perhaps a little too genuinely self-centered, but he gets better... somewhat... I think...
The game's humor falls a bit on the flat side, which is a shame. I don't think I had a laugh out loud moment, just some grins here and there. I was willing to ignore it though, in order to find out what happens next. I admit I'm more than curious as to what is going on with Elysian physiology, but that wasn't answered in the first game, so I guess I'll have to play through the next (two?).
Now for the meat and potatoes of the game - the puzzles. This is where I feel the game was lacking. There are several areas where you are just bombarded with random items you pick up, and very poor clues as to where to go or what to do. Ordinarily I do my best to avoid guides, but I ended up using one for this game. It didn't even feel rewarding for the stuff I DID manage to figure out on my own.
I guess I'd rate this game a 7/10. It's no King's Quest, it's certainly no Monkey Island.

For the record, this game is REALLY underrated and imo underadvertised. This is one of those games where you play it not so much for the plot, rather if you had a bad day and really want to let off all your anger frustration but don't know how. Boot up this game, jump in your saddle, and swing your sword/axe/polearm to your heart's content. You'll feel better in no time.
Okay, in all seriousness, this game is really amazing. It may not be for people looking for a deep and riveting plot. It definitely falls short compared to other games out there today in terms of graphics. And there will be quite a bit (a lot) of grinding, especially early on. But this game is perfect for anyone looking for a solid first person medieval-era fuedal style war game while still having basic troop control (kind of like in Total War, but far more simplistic and far less troops). You get to recruit, train, and fight alongside each member in your army, and both your character and certain recruitable "companion" characters have a decent range of customizable skills and equipment. A variety of weapon types are avaiable, including swords, spears, bows, crossbows, throwing knives, maces, staffs, and shields. The economic system is pretty important and balanced in terms of troop wages and income from owned property. The game has six factions that occasionally declare war with each other, and everyone who has played the game knows that the troop types of each of these factions aren't exactly "balanced". You can join one of these factions, or start your own. The point of the game is to take over every other faction so you or the faction you are in is the ruler of, well, basically everything.
Overall I really love this game. It can be played as both a pick-up-put-down casual game or marathoned for days on end. There are so many other things to do besides fighting in wars, ranging from tournament games to starting your own business in various cities to courting and marrying someone. I feel like this game does a tremendous job blending action-packed first person combat with the immersive medieval feel of courtship and managing businesses and resources. As it is on sale right now I highly encourage everyone to buy it, but even if there is no sale it is well worth the money. This is the first game that I have written a review for, which goes to tell you just how much I enjoy this game. If you read all the way to the end of this review I'm actually quite surprised. Thank you for taking the time to read my review.
P.S. I have never played multiplayer so everything above is about single player. Also I play mainly offline so I have played WAY more hours than it says I have. I would not write a review for a game if I haven't at least put in 100 hours into it :P.

Spelunky is an interesting specimen. Initially I didn't find much about it to be interesting, but I did find myself coming back to play it time and again. I should mention that I started off with the freeware version. Such humble beginnings.
The beauty of this game is that the more I played the game, the more I realized why I wanted to keep playing and the more I wanted to experience more of what the game had to offer. This is a game all about learning. Learning about game mechanics, about enemy behavior, about little tidbits about how the world works and about the hidden lore underneath the surface.
Every game is about learning, right? So why is this such a big deal? In Spelunky, it's kind of a very big deal because you will not win the first time you play. Or the second time. Or the third. Or possibly even within the first hundred times you've played. Death will come early and often. But each time you die, you walk away with a little bit more experience. Just a tad more wisdom. "Oh, okay, next time I WON'T throw that rock at the shopkeeper. That's a BAD idea." Over time you start to pick up on the little nuances. Every run you're just a little bit better. But there's always more to learn. To this day, I have played the game for countless hours and still have runs where something completely unexpected happens and I experience something new (like falling to the platform below me only to be met in mid-air with an icy blast that freezes me instantly and upon my arrival on the ground I shatter into a million pieces. Right AFTER using the Ankh to get the Hedjet. I wasn't even mad. I just laughed).
This game has so much to offer and a world that is enriched with a myriad of details and hidden truths, and the only way to truly experience it all is to just keep playing the game. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys adventure and discovery and doesn't mind a bit of suffering to get it.
