Iv played this game for at least a year and a half and i would openly reconmend this game.
First the possitive
If your looking for WW2 FPS similar to Battlefield, this game is for you.
Is this game pay to win? HELL NO!
While its true at first you wont make many credits, as your soldier lvls up he will earn more credits, and the battles are rewarding enough that it doesn't feel grindy. Killing tanks as a soldier is good way of makeing money as a tip. The Benfits of Vet Membership boil down to extra money and the abilty to Equip 2 Combat badges which are "perks" that range from a slight damage reduction to carrying more ammo or exposives. You can also name your Troops, Vehicals and Assult Teams as well.
Weapon customization consists of nameing it and mods that have both PROS and CONS, for example ammo that does less damage but is more accurate or a trigger that gives more RPM for less accurasy.
6 ways to play: there are six classes in HnG, Infantry, Tanker, Pilot, Paratrooper, Recon and General.
Infantry: Has every weapon the game has to offer, excusively has access to Machine Guns's, Assult Rifles and Bazookas. they have access to cars, moter bikes, mobile spawn trucks and Anti Air Trucks for support.
Tanker/Pilot: these classes are restricted to Smg's, pistols nades, ATmines, melee and in the U.S's case, they have the m1a1 carbine.
What they lack in personal armament they make up for in vehicualer firepower, tankers have access to light, medium, heavy tanks and Tank Desteryors. Armed with powerfull cannons and machine guns they are potent weaposn but by no means invincable, its best to stick with friendly forces for protenction form enemy personal.
Pilots are similar, there fighter planes are armed with MG's low caliber cannons and BOMBS! they have 2 roles, clearing the sky of enemy aircraft and devistating ground forces while dodgeing Anti Aircraft fire.
Paratrooper: the best way to decribe paratroops is "light infantry" they have access to semi-auto rifles, smgs, pistols, grandes, ATmines, melee and "special weapons" which consider of MG's for German and U.S, and the U.S also have veriants of the M1 carbine for those that prefer flexabilty to firepower. The best part is you dont pay for the Transport planes you jump out of to get everywhere!
Recon: Weapons consist of Bolt action, Semi-auto Rifles, Smgs, pistols, grandades, and are one of 2 classes to have anti peronel mines(the other being infantry) they have access to moter bikes and Infantry Fighting Vehicals, which are open toped cars with light tank weaponery. What makes a recon special is they have upgrades such as 8X scopes and better berrals that infantry lack for bolt action rifles.
General: Genrals dont play the Action side of Hng, heck they dont even has salaries, Generals let you have More command points which let you have more assult teams for the startgic game. Command points are first unlocked at rank 12, you have a max of 4 at rank 18 which is the highst lvl you can go without converting to a general, these point let you command assult teams which are groups of resorces on the Stratgic map, Generals at max have 13 points when max rank and the war victory ribbion maxed out.
Now the Neative
Bolt actions are arguabley OP: Bolt actions by default are well balanced, they fire around 35 rounds which is SLOW considering most weapons fire over 200-600 rpm and even more so when modded, However a bolt action will 2 hit kill anyone not wereing Heavy Set. it take 4-2 shots to kill anyone by default assumeing all the shots it the torso, vs 1 headshot. The problem comes with modding, its possible to get a One hit kill anywhere from a range of 250m (thats right off the wiki) or a 350m One hit if your not whereing Heavy Set.
Vehical Combat SUCKS!: I will admit that the Vehical combat at the moment IS TERRABLE, tanks are a cat and mouse game, you shoot first, your gonna win most of the time, Planes arnt much better, if you load teh cannons with HE rounds you can easlly kill the pilot without needing to shootdown the plane(you do get more xp if you do shoot it down though)
Statigic map: Whats wrong with teh stratigic map? THE QUEUE TO DEPLOY LET ALONE REINFORCE YOUR ASSULT TEAMS CAN BE OUTRAGOUSLY LONG! I'm talking THOUSANDS of players queued up waiting for there troops to apper or get reinforced.
This problem is partly do to the MILLIONS of players that play HnG these days, but that also shows on the stratgic map as well, a glance at any battle on the map will show THOUSANDS of infantry fighting in one place, small armys worth when only 20 people on both sides (or 3 sides for the RARE 3 way battles.) actully fight. Now these battles come down to those players skill but the equipment they have access to doesnt hurt, a few tanks can tip the scales in favor of one or the other.
In Concuslion, I recomend this game to anyone looking for FTP FPS, can the game be grindy at times? yes it can, but as stated earlyer, you are rewarded well, plus what Free to PLAY game doesnt have some sort of grind involved. while the game does have its problems, id say at least give it a shot and if you dont like it well at least you game it a shot.

It's a really neat idea, but I have a difficult time just navigating the menu (which you control with a simulated surgeon's hand, controlled very meticulously with several keyboard keys and the mouse). The idea is you're a surgeon performing surgeries. You have one simulated hand, which you control with both of your actual hands: one on the mouse and one on the keyboard.
Sounds cool, right? It is. The problem is that a keyboard press is a binary event. You're either pressing a key or your not. So when each virtual finger is bound to a physical key, every finger is either open or closed, with the short intermediary of an "in-between" state.
Very frustrating game, but somehow also really, really fun. I recommend it, but I guarantee you WILL get frustrated by the controls. But that's part of the fun.

TL;DR Good free snowboarding/skiing game. Would buy for ~$10-$20 when finished.
Long Version:
I love free games. I love snowboarding games. I like this game.
Gameplay: 8.5/10
Really nice handling, like the mechanics. As a guy who's never gone snowboarding or skiing, it feels really good, especially with a controller. Only problem with it is that there's too many buttons to press while trying to time your trick, so you end up flopping on the snow like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fish. Also physics glitches. Not much else to mention, it's a skiing/snowboarding game.
Graphics: 7/10
Would give extra point if there were some more weather options. Snow looks nice, ski and snowboard marks are really nice. Props and everything are HD, as far as you can tell, and the trees looks really good. Unfortunately I love clouds. There aren't enough clouds in this game, and weather effects should be added.
Sound: 9.5/10
Great soundtrack, consisiting of 3 in-game indie snowboarding songs, and one relaxing main menu theme. Wind sound builds up as you gain speed, sound of board/ski against snow is crisp, nice. Only problem is that the sound the ragdoll makes when you fall into the snow is somewhat annoying, otherwise, is perfect.
UI: 6/10
Looks nice, but is clunky and unresponsive at times. UI is also less than optimal when navigating, and somewhat confusing.
Multiplayer: 7/10
Pretty good for a free game. Doesn't allow you to ragdoll when falling off, however. Allows you to play with friends, but only on a limited number of servers, and you can only "reserve" by getting an empty one.
Stability: 6/10
Besides somewhat-rare physics glitches, such as falling over when just starting, the game requires you to have a connection to the main levelling server at all times, otherwise it tries to quit. And if you don't have a connection to the server, it doesn't just quit, it stops working, and you have to use task manager to stop it.
Overall: 8/10
Good for a free game, maybe recommend if under $20. If you like snowboarding games, it's nice, and relaxing to play.

Sniper Elite 3 is a fun casual sniper game.  I'm giving it a thumbs up because by itself its an alright game.  However that said, I'd like to point out that in my opinion this game is a step back from Sniper Elite v2.  Here's how the two compare in my opinion:
Improvements:
- less linear maps
- improved graphics
- more customizable weapons
Cons:
- Empty lung ability now shows where to aim to adjust for gravity and wind (even on the hardest difficulty).  Sniper Elite v2 is incredibly fun when you get dialed in to a rifle and pull of numerous long range consecutive headshots.  You'll do that in SE3 as well, but it'll be so easy you won't even notice.
- The new detection mechanics are broken. While SEv2's were admittedly pretty simple SE3's is just to wonky to ignore.  Get caught in your sniping nest?  No worries, walk 50 meters away, then walk back and the Nazis will forget all about where you've been picking them off from for the past 10 minutes.
- Poor clipping on cover.  It's always annoying when you shoot the barrier in front of you when your scope shows a clear shot, but this is especially bad in SE3 where the detection mechanism penalizes you for every shot.
- Poor checkpoint system.  Sometimes it saves after objectives, sometimes it saves when you're sitting in a bush, and sometimes it doesn't save at all.
Kidneys, Hearts, Brains, even testicles. Whatever your body has, you can shoot it.

Ah, The Quest. Years ago, I played this for tens of hours on iOS and loved every minute of it. Now that it's out on Steam, I'm excited to be picking it up again.
The Quest is a perfect blend of single player, open world RPG and grid-based dungeon crawler. It has a lot more in common with, say, the Elder Scrolls series than it does with something like Lands of Lore. You're a lone hero, so there's no party to manage while you travel about the land of Freymore (something I adore about this game!). With a difficulty level that is completely spot-on, you'll be doing plenty of exploring, dungeon diving, character building, alchemy, and fighting as you work your way through the game's many quests.
And the quests are really where the game shines. They are plentiful, well written, and almost never as they first appear. For example, an early quest has you seeking a boy to recruit as an agent of the kingdom...but shortly into the quest, it branches and gives the player multiple options for completion. Will you force him to come with you? Will you recruit someone else in his place? Player choice and twists like this are a common theme throughout the game and allow you to role play and build your character as you please. The depth is a refreshing departure from the "kill 10 rats" trope and really shows the care that went into crafting the world and its stories. It's even fun to tell friends the crazy stuff that happens because it's often hilarious and totally unexpected, and you don't always get that in RPGs.
The game also received an HD facelift when it came to Steam, and the new art really works and looks quite charming. I've been able to run the game on multiple devices with different resolutions and have had no issues at all. On the other hand, the music and sound hasn't been updated. This is a non-issue for me since the music, albeit midi, is quite good, and the sound effects are perfectly serviceable. As a side note - the developer includes the old development version of the game, with the old graphics, for the low price of zero dollars.
The developer also added a lot of convenience options like key rebinds, tool tips, inventory sorting, quick saves, cloud saves, touch mode and I'm sure a ton more I'm missing. It does a lot to bring the game up to date and it feels a lot more modern than it used to. They're continuing to release updates and fixes to the game as well, and it's obvious they are listening to the community. My wishes include getting the expansion content - and mods - in addition to native controller support. This game would work amazingly well in Big Picture with a 360 controller!
Suffice it to say that I'm totally impressed with this new version of The Quest. What I initially thought would be a quick port ended up being a developer's genuine effort to bring an old classic up to date and to a new audience. This does not feel like a mobile port in any way. It's a full-fledged and substantial PC release and I really feel it really has that "special something" that a lot of RPGs lack. I'll soon come back and spend even more time with it than I did on iOS. Here's to hoping the expansion content is released and that the Quest 2 gets made!

Dungeon Crawler: When considering what dungeon crawler games to play on Steam you’re going to find people make mention of a lot of titles before they ever, if they ever, consider The Quest. That’s not an indictment on the game but rather of how few people have discovered it yet. Of course, most Steam players will be familiar with titles such as the Legend of Grimrock franchise and some of the various titles that actually feature the word ‘dungeon’ in their title yet The Quest may be much better than some of them and closely behind the icons in the genre (such as Grimrock). The Quest offers everything that a lover of dungeon crawlers would hope to find in a title. It’s tough as nails and very challenging, the game world is sizeable enough to allow the player to explore to their heart’s content and it’s got enough old school charm that it’s going to remind some of their favorite dungeon crawlers from yesteryear.
Solid hand drawn graphics:  The graphics being entirely hand drawn adds a tremendous amount of character to the game. It’s a nice touch and one that most players will appreciate. The only slight niggle is that some areas have had much more attention to detail paid than others. This inconsistency is very noticeable, almost from the very start of the game, and can become a bugbear. When the attention to detail is at a high level the graphics reach an exquisite level and truly add something special to the game.
More depth than the Mariana Trench: The Quest truly is one of those games that is seemingly easy to learn but difficult to master. There are a ton of skills, abilities and variants that you can and have to learn in order to become a proficient player. However, you do get an opportunity to jump on into the dungeon crawling aspect of the game before you have to learn these types of skills if you already have some prerequisite knowledge of traditional RPG character builds. As you level up you get to put points into character skills and abilities that supposedly make the game easier. This may be at such a small incline that you may not notice very big differences between individual levels but ultimately they do add up.
Stop following me: When you realize that the mob that you are facing is going to overpower you they will seemingly forever chase you all over the map. This is particularly devastating when the difficulty spikes are sudden. This starts from the early game and is relentless throughout the game – or what I have played of it thus far. I died quickly and often when I first started playing to the point where I decided to role what is the game’s variant of a heavy armor clad barbarian. I don’t particularly enjoy playing this class but it was the only one that seemed to give me much of an opportunity to get into the game. The clothies and the ranged attackers seemed to get eaten alive.
It’s a great case study in how to move from mobile to Steam: The final note that I wanted to make on The Quest is that this game was originally a very good mobile game. However, I would argue that it is even better on Steam than what it is on mobile devices. It’s one of those games where I have to imagine that the developers at Redshift believed that their game would ultimately reach the PC format. Had I not been told that this title was on mobile a long time prior to its PC incarnation I would never have guessed that it was a mobile game. I don’t believe it’s fair to call it a ‘port’ but I’m not exactly certain just how reimagined it really is.  However, I can imagine that it was a relatively seamless transition from mobile to Steam. It’s a game that should be considered a great case study for developers looking to make the jump.
The Quest is a fantastic dungeon crawler that deserves increased attention from what it has had to date. The $14.99 asking price maybe a little high but not unrealistically so. I would recommend it to all RPG fans.
Note: Elendil from Redshift has corrected me and advised that although the game first appeared on mobiles that it’s heart was always a PC game. However, Steamified maintains that if you are going to release on both mobile and PC that The Quest is an important case study for other developers to follow.

This is one of the most beautiful games I've ever played.  The atmosphere is just amazing.  The game begins simple enough, two brothers on a quest to save their ailing father.  3/4 through the game it shifts gears and takes a darker tone, and the visuals continue to deliver.  It's one of those games that you have to play to believe it, but it really is something special.

The gameplay of 'Brothers' is simple and relaxed. As a puzzle platformer it is forgiving and laid back, with only sufficient difficulty to make progression through the story immersive and satisfying. Set in a fantasy world being traversed by two boys on a quest to save their father, the mechanics focus on controlling two main characters simultaneously and overcoming obstacles by making them work together. While visibly designed to be played using a controller, the game is fully playable via keyboard. One is hard-pressed to notice the occasional clunkiness from keyboard controls when confronted with such an enchanting world to explore.
That said, 'Brothers' is an absolutely beautiful game whose music, atmosphere, and story are deeply memorable and inspiring, and unlike almost anything you'll find elsewhere. The encounters and experiences of the journey range from everyday to extroardinary, beautiful to grisly, exciting to sorrowful, and from the charming to the truly dark.
'Brothers' has my highest regards, absolutely worth every penny whether it's on sale or not. I also highly recommend the game's soundtrack.

Well, finally I was forced to write this...
Let me start off with a simple statement: GTA V was and is a great game. I have mixed feelings about GTA Online but I'm going to leave that aside for now.
This game (singleplayer) has a great story, amazing freedom and stunning graphics. I played it on PS3 and was satisfied by the PC version. It keeps the traditional GTA setting with the introduction of some fresh ideas. This balance was maintained and was one of the reasons this game is so good. The state of GTA Online upon release was satisfying. The game recieved numerous updates and although it all started with thematic updates with just a few cars and guns it was enough to keep players entertained. Heists released and it was a blast. There is something important about this update though. At that point the game started being more centered on cooperative play so it is strongly recommended that you find a crew to play the game with. Later on we've seen massive additions to GTA Online and recently we've gotten two very controversial DLCs: Import/Export and GTA Online: Gunrunning. The reason behind this controversy is that the more conservative players (longtime fans) tend to believe these updates are ruining the realism of GTA and that it only caters griefers and kids and is all about Microtransactions (Shark cards). There is a whole article worth of explanation here, but I don't have enough time to write it all down. The other part of GTA community (mostly new fans) states that GTA Online is all about fun and does not concern realism. While I agree to some of the parties' opinions I do have to say that the problem isn't entirely in the players (although some of them are the reason I play GTA online in public lobbies less and less). This is where we get to the part where I explain why I don't recommend this game anymore.
It is my belief that making GTA V Rockstar games did an excellent job. It is made in a wonderfull manner and the online segment was initially a great thing. HOWEVER the publishers (Take Two interactive) have done a horrible job of catering the players (+ruining R*'s reputation). Don't get me wrong, T2's mission is to squeeze out the biggest possible amount of money from the game. They are a business, after all. The problem is that Take 2 took it way too seriously. They made GTA online a horrible experience by ruining it with microtransactions. They also do not maintain contact with consumers which isn't what a user-friendly company usually does. They have taken down an alternative Online service because they feared their $w33t $hark card revenue would be hurt. They have taken down a converted RDR map mod. They are constantly taking down any attempts of users to make the game more fun, fearing that modders make better content than them and constantly trying to make people play GTA Online exclusively. Furthermore, they are constantly trying to make people buy shark cards. The amazing greed this company has has lead it's aim to become nothing more than to suck out all of life from the original, true community and turn it into a heaven for the neo-gaming generation. Their final step was nothing but disgrace to the GTA V PC community: They have taken down the biggest modding tool for GTA V. Their actions are completely unacceptable and are harmful to the fanbase. This is the reason I'm giving the game a negative review.
It used to be a glorious gem, but Take2's greed was too heavy, it crashed into a million pieces.

This game makes me, somehow, like dying.
In spelunky, you wander into a strange mine filled with creatures and traps. You wander level after level until, you die and have to restart from the begening. Don't worry, you can unlock shortcuts,
. You won't keep any progress from one game to an other except your skills and knowledge.
This is a 2D platformer. You don't jump very high versus other platformers but you can climb edges and use your ropes to get higher. You also have a short ranged whip to slay the snakes and the bats wandering around and bombs to dig your way through walls when you're too lazy to take the long way. As you gather gold, you can also buy weapons and tools to help you travel. (You can also steal them but I wouldn't recommand it unless you want to be shot in the *ss.)
So why is Spelunky so amazing?
Because 95% of the times you die, you could have done something else. You can totally win the game in a single run without shortcuts, but you got to know what you are doing. I have around 20 hours in the game and it was 20 hours full of dying, learning and practising.
I don't mean that you won't be able to play in the beginning. The controls need to get used to but jumping around, climbing and killing snakes is some easy stuff.
The harder part is knowing what everything does and what is the best to to against each patern of ennemies. A bat in an open space, a bat in a closed space, a bat close to an arrow shooter, a bat on a very low roof... There is, in my opinion a different way to handle each and you get to struggle until you find what's the best in your opinion.
Unforgiving and ridiculously hard platformer with short runs and a very long life time, you'll love it, really!

What starts off as an unforgiving and somewhat brutal platformer, Spelunky blossoms into a richly deep and satisfying game which rewards patience and strategy. It definitely takes quite a number of hours of play before you can get far, but once you do you will be absolutely hooked.
As a rogue-lite platformer, each game is randomised and death is never too far away, as you only start off with 3 health.
Decisions you make in the game are often trading off risk vs reward. Much of the game is optional, as getting to the exit of each level, if done directly, is quite easy. The trick is when to know to venture from the beaten path, and how to take on various enemies to score loots.
Recommended that after a few hours of play to check out the wiki, but even at almost 20 hours I find I'm still discovering subtle mechanics and new strategies.

This title turned out to be quite a pleasant surprise for me. I mean, I already imagined that it had a premise of being a vertical bullet hell shooter, which in a sense it was, but in a very unique way.
So yes, the game offers you a basic story just to illustrate what you're doing, but there's not really much immersion, other than hearing the pilot that you control complaining about this and that. The graphics are nice, the soundtrack and effects are ok, there's nothing to complain about this. As for the gameplay, that's when the surprise factor kicked in.
For starters, something that made me feel uncomfortable right at the beginning, was the fact that you couldn't just sit your finger on the gamepad button, you had to keep on pushing it like crazy in order to shoot. Then, I think I understood the reason behind this: If you keep on shooting like crazy, I mean, without planning on what you're going to hit ahead of you, you might block your path. Because this game also has some "Match 3" characteristics (I believe it's easier to understand that while you're playing it). Either way, I think that it wouldn't be much to ask for the developers to at least allow the players to trigger the "turbo mode" right before the boss battles, because there's not a single reason in the world why you wouldn't be shooting them like there's no tomorrow.
The game also offers you some power-ups that are spread throughout the levels, and at least 10 different ships, each with their own special proprieties. There aren't way too many levels and achievements, so I believe you can get to unlock them all in one or two sittings.
Overall, it's a fun game to kill some time and it has an awesome price, especially during the Steam sales. If you're a fan of the genre, I honestly advise you to give it a try.

Sniper Elite 3 is a third person tactical shooter developed by Rebellion Developments and published by 505 Games. This game was released on PC, PS3, PS4, 360 and Xbox One in June 2014. It is a prequel to Sniper Elite V2 and the third game in the sniper series.
The gameplay in Sniper 3 is based heavily on being slow and steady with your approach to completing objectives, with an also strong focus on sniper gun play much like the previous games. What I really liked about Sniper 3 is that the stealthy approach is pretty much the only viable way to go on most missions otherwise you'll just be pinned down in a firefight and outnumbered. The stealth aspect of the game is done extremely well, you probably will be detected by the enemies whilst taking down the guards, but it is all about cleaning up after yourself by dragging bodies to the long grass, or how you escape and hide away until the enemies give up searching for you. You can use various methods to distract enemies such as throwing rocks and laying traps. Before each level you get to choose your load out, you get the choice of a sniper rifle, a secondary weapon, side arm, and various other items such as grenades, medi-packs and traps. As you level up between stages you also unlock further rewards and items.
Of course, a Sniper game wouldn't be complete without the stunning slow motion graphics of your bullet soaring through the air and them piercing through your foes scrotum, this my friends is the pinnacle of slow motion gaming. Granted after a while you'll be skipping them because they will grow tiresome as they play after every kill with your sniper, but still, this gives you a chance to get some brilliant cinematic screenshots to show off your sniping skills.
Graphically, Sniper Elite 3 is gorgeous, I wasn't able to push out full graphic settings on 4k resolution, but even on the lower resolutions (1080p), it still looks stunning. There is a wide array of setting to choose from which is always good to see. The visuals are amazing though, the night time levels really show of the games truly stunning lighting effects as well. I was a little disappointed to see the lens flare effect being used a bit too much, but everything else is truly stellar.
The game is fully voice acted, with the enemy soldiers speaking in German too, so subtitles are recommended for that. The sound effects really add an extra level of immersion to the gameplay. A nice feature which is added is that you can disguise your bullet shots underneath the sound of loud sounds in game too, which really helps you in your efforts to complete levels as stealthy as possible.
I have to admit, this game is quite difficult, even on the easiest settings; you really do need to take each level with a sense of slow and steady. There is really no point in running in all guns blazing because you will just get gunned down within seconds of being spotted. You will need to backtrack plenty of times in order to escape being detected, you'll be needing to hide in rooms, crawl under buildings, anything which you can imagine you doing in the situation you are in, you can do. The latter levels of the game also ramp up the difficulty significantly as well, as each level slowly introduces more and more enemies for you to deal with.
Each level in Sniper Elite 3 is massive. Each level will have its own main objective, but as you progress and reach new areas of the zone, you'll also unlock optional objectives, which can be things such as destroying some trucks, cutting off communication or something searching for secret plans. These optional objectives reward you with additional experience at the end of the level and also add an extra element of immersion to the game as well. The size of each level really means that you can get stuck in, and explore to your hearts content. There are countless amounts of collectable items for you to find if that is your thing too. Each of the games objectives, whether it be main or optional, will have more than one way of you being able to complete them, which will really add some replay ability to the game on your second run through.
I was a little let down by the fact that I finished the game's single player in about five hours, granted I was playing on the easiest difficulty, but for a big release like this, I was expecting something more to be honest. I can see there being an essence of replay ability due to the nature of the levels being able to be completed in more ways than one, but I would say that there is no real need for playing through the game more than twice at least. There is a multiplayer side to the game, which I tried out, but it seems to be a little on the low side of players, and struggled to actually get into any proper gameplay, because given that it is a sniper based game, most people are camping in well-hidden places just picking people off when they try and complete objectives, for me I didn't really enjoy the multiplayer.
Technically, I had a one major problem with Sniper Elite 3, and that was that the game kept crashing on launching the title, it would reach the title screen, but then just crash to desktop. This actually turned out to be an issue with Malwarebytes closing it, so it would be highly recommended that you add the Sniper Elite 3 folder into the exception settings for Malwarebytes if you run that AV. Granted that it wasn't actually Sniper Elite causing the crash, you would still expect the game to have been tested with various popular AVs like this to see if they caused any compatibility problems.
My conclusion of Sniper Elite 3 would be that I would only recommend the game as a single player title; because the multiplayer just didn't do it for me. Given that the single player side of the game can be completed in almost five hours, the full price tag of £39, 99 is absolutely absurd, and is actually fairly offensive that they can charge that amount of money for such little content. I would only say this game is worth picking up when it is below the £10 mark, yes the gameplay is top class, and the graphics are stunning, but you can pick up any of the other Sniper games for the same experience in both of those departments for cheaper. Actually saying that, it looks like all of the games in this series are expensive. Definitely wait for sale season to start before adding Sniper Elite 3 to your library.

The way the scenery will sometimes block you, such as a thin light pole requiring you to actively move around it.
The useless save functionality where on the few occasions you get immersed in the game and lose track, get killed, and find yourself way back at the beginning because the idiot programmers made seemingly arbitrary decisions about when the game might auto save.

It's just a good idea, and done well would make a great game, but sadly implemented by people whose personal motto might as well be 'meh, that'll do'.

Admittedly, the huge amount of paid dlc put me off at first. And this game really is just about driving trains, performing some tasks and not messing up. I do however like trains, and so far I've enjoyed myself learning to drive them. The dlc is something I choose to see as collecting a model train set. In that sense, comparing it to dlc of an average game where more gives you often a fuller experience, does not work.
If you are considering this game you likely are looking to just experience driving trains, drive through some nice scenery, enjoy controlling something that requires some proper timing. This game offers that properly in my opinion.
Moreso than with other games your purchase will depend on how you regard the pricing scheme. You will likely want some new routes or trains to play with after a while. Do you consider the large offering of paid routes and trains as essentials that should have been (much) cheaper? Then perhaps better stay away. Do you consider this a hobby that will likely require or at least warrent future investments (which you can afford and feel reasonable enough, possibly during sales), then this is indeed a good simulator of what it claims to be in my opinion.

No on-board train announcements on any routes except WCML Trent Valley DLC Add-On.

Some locomotives engines are just taken from any old DLC that Dovetail make, i.e On the class 321 add on the door sounds are from LU 1938 stock. The class 378 sounds are just copypaste from the class 377.
Some trains are missing branding, either because dovetail don't have a licence from the operator, or are just too lazy.
There are a lot of buttons in the cab which are restricted and you can't use which makes it less realisitc.
Trains can tend to not move at all at times.
I know this sound a lot of bad things, but trust me these float in and out at times and I still say that this is a must buy game. "War never changes." Is a quote thrown around often.  While philosophically it may not, strategically it sure as hell does.  Wargame: Red Dragon is a lesson in that. The learning curve is less of a curve, but more of a vertical line, when passed you can hold your own against another experienced player.  This is a target that I am still trying to hit, while I pride myself as a quick learner every map, every game, and every encounter is a mix between luck, recon, and unit composition, which I haven't quite nailed down yet.  A huge variety of units is at your discretion, from the absurd to the very practical, and all of them are worth giving a shot, provided that they are utilized properly.  The controls are simple and endlessly customizable.  The UI is a bit big by default but you can change the size to fit your preference in the options.  The game allows you to make everything just as you like it, which is great for someone who is moving from another game and wants their hot-keys to be the same or someone like me who wants less clutter on the screen.
The AI that you can fight is not a very good opponent, it makes stupid decisions but it's a great way to learn the controls, and test performance (which unless you play on a potato is great).  Take a quick run through a campaign that is intrigues to you and then try the multiplayer.  I also suggest sticking with the default decks, or if you are so inclined building your own, be warned every unit has a ton of info, and some aren't as good as the prices suggest, read each stat and use the compare button as needed, also check out the competition through the armory, it lets you see every vehicle you could ever want to know about or kill, also hover over icons if you don’t know what they mean, sometimes they have multiple definitions that change between units even if they look the same, they can also give hints to the role of the unit.  Alternately if you tire of the provided decks but don't trust your building skills, you can import them, all it requires is a simple copy and paste and there are great resources online.
This game is a wonderfully strategic, if you have the cash pick it up now with the Israel DLC, otherwise wait for a sale.  Any new players would be a great help in revitalizing the player base, and I can promise that this is the best realistic strategy game you can buy.  This game offers hours of endless–admittedly stressful–fun which I personally love, while games can run long, on a weekend it's a great way to break boredom.
A couple of quick tips:
RECON EVERYWHERE- there is no sense in charging blind
CHEAP UNITS FIRST- when advancing it makes no sense to put your valuable units first, let the replaceable stuff take the hit, it can save you from a bad advance
DO NOT FORCE UNFAVORABLE ENGAGMENTS- unless you’ve been forced back to your spawn there is no reason to keep throwing units at a wall, you can always retreat, reorganize, and then soften your enemy with artillery or airstrikes
IF YOU LIKE IT HIDDEN DISABLE ITS GUNS- if you want to keep a unit hidden in a forest or some other type of cover, make sure that their guns aren’t on, they stop being hidden when shooting, this is especially important for forward recon that doesn’t really have a need to fight, if you want it to fire just turn them back on.
COMMUNICATE- if you are doing an air heavy rollout tell your team, so that they don’t waste points on their own aircraft, or if you want to take a specific point, call it out, so that your allies can focus efforts elsewhere.

The Quest is a great game with a vast open world. Combat is turn-based, allowing you to take your time in making you decisions. At the same time, since the enemy moves right after you do, there is some strategy involved (it is very hard to lose an enemy once you have encountered them).
I love the openness and the skill development that The Quest has to offer. You define your class, but you are not bound to it. However, each levelup you get 10 points to distribute amongst your skills. Each class skill only takes 1 point to raise, while each non-class skill takes 2. So it is important to pick the skills you are most likely to use.
My hope is that the developers will release some expansions for the PC edition just like they did for other systems. I am far from finished, but this is definitely the type of game that I can play to the end.

By far one of the best games I have played recently, The Quest is simply addictive.  Be prepared for spending many hours exploring, fighting, playing cards in the Taverns and eventually solving the main quest of the game.  I finished the game in just under 40 hours, however I still have more of the map to explore, and want to play as a full Mage class on my second run of the game.
Difficulty is very well balanced in the beginning and middle game.  At the beginning you feel powerless, as you should, but gain a few levels and things begin to even out.  Still you will be have to use strategy to defeat your foes depending on your build.  My physical fighter had some difficulty with magic based attacks...higher level enemies in particular can destroy you especially with lightning attacks.  Still there are many ways to buff your character to overcome this.
My only criticism is I felt the end game was a little too easy.  In the game you can enchant items buffing your stats considerably which does take away some of the challenge.  Enemies don't scale to your level (which I like), and you get good satisfaction slaughtering enemies that gave you trouble in the early game.  Enemies also respawn after a while (a week?) which helps you to gain more experience and precious gold.  Be wise with your money...I ended up with just over 4000 gold at the end game after amassing over 20000 gold throughout the game.
So yeah this is a pretty special game, that will appeal to those who enjoy turn based combat, grid movement and games like the early Might And Magic series.  I really look forward to the sequel and if possible an expansion to this game would be a great addition.  The Quest is a first class game from beginning to end.

While this game's origins are on mobiles and PDAs, don't let that put you off; it's from a time before microtransactions and wait timers plagued these games. In fact, it's always felt like a game that would be at home on PC. And it is.
The Quest feels like an homage to the dungeon crawlers of the late 80s and early 90s, with player choice firmly leading the way. Nearly every quest will have multiple ways to solve it, and the idea of what's good and bad is constantly foggy due to the fame system. As opposed to a meter telling you if you're a saint or sinner, you get a meter of fame, which decreases when it looks like you've done something bad, and increases when it looks like you've done something good. This may sound like the same thing, but sometimes the person you're sent to "rescue" doesn't want to leave, and was actually forced into a life they hated back home. Sure, getting them back would give you fame - it looks like you're helping - but is it really the right thing to do? This system really changes up how you approach your tasks, as it's not uncommon for what looks like the right thing to do to actually lose you fame - those in power have influence, but often tainted morals.
On top of that, the combat has surprising depth to it as enemies seem to be able to have all the resistances and weaknesses you do, and finding these out can really be the difference between life and death. This really makes scraping through some of the tougher fights - even those fairly early on - really satisfying. Dungeons - while often fairly small - contain traps to disarm and secrets to find. Even potion crafting is fun to play with when you get some levels in alchemy, as some combinations of ingredients will have some unexpected results, and stumbling into one of these when you need it the most is so, so relieving. Everything you'd expect from a first person grid based CRPG is right here, and executed brilliantly. On top of this, the attention to detail is often staggering: even your outfit changes how people interact with you, with fancier clothes letting you get more favour with the posher characters, but also causing the lower class citizens to often be not so friendly. There's even a small card game to play in the inns to earn money, which may seem simple at first, but can be quite involving, and is a very fun distraction when you start to set up massive attacks with your buffs, and some large attack combos. The game is really full of depth, and you shouldn't ever be lacking for something you want to do, as the writing - while sometimes imperfect - does enough to make you actually want to help the characters who need it.
Though not everything is perfect. My main complaint would be that there's really no way to escape a melee enemy that's too strong for you - you have to let them hit you once to figure out they'll destroy you, and from then they'll shadow your movements. They'll even follow you all the way back to a town, and just stay infront of the guards, who will do nothing to help, making you essentially trapped. While this is less of an issue when you get the paralyze spell, it's still quite annoying until then. But quite frankly, this is nitpicking more than anything else, and not enough to dampen my enjoyment of this game at all. Highly recommended to all CRPG fans.

The gameplay consists of having to control two characters at once, and eventhough I heard it is quite difficult to play on a pc, I have played and finished it on my laptop, and I barely had any issues. It's a bit tricky at times but nothing that frustrated me. It was a fun challenge. I love the way you have to make the brothers work together to advance, it's very inventive. Even if you do die, there is no big loss, checkpoints are everywhere, everytime I did die, the game started me off back from where I died.
This game was a great experience and I will probably play it once more. I have played it twice already while screensharing with different friends who really loved watching it and helping me figure out how to solve certain situations. The "puzzles" are not too complicated, yet sometimes it takes some exploring/poking around to figure out what to do, which is good. I love this game, and I recommend it to anyone who likes a good adventure fantasy filled yet realistic story about death and love. I am honestly jealous of anyone yet to play this game, because they get to see everything for the first time, and that is such an exciting thing!

I cannot recommend this game highly enough. It's a brief journey clocking in at only three hours long, but it's well worth the investment.

The main attraction to Brothers, however, is its plot. Don't be turned off by the small amount of game time, because the story is introduced, unfolded, and concluded so perfectly that it needn't be any longer than it is.
If you're in to games that try to move you, you can't do much better than Brothers.

So, I typically avoid Early Access like the plague. Not sure why I broke my rule for this game, but so far I am cautiously optimistic that it was a REALLY good choice.
X-series inspired space combat/economics/empire building, with a really flexible and "occasionally intuitive" ship builder added on top. Lots of procedural generation, but even with the limited "types" of systems that can be randomly generated, they've mostly avoided making it feel too "samey". I can only assume that's only going to get vastly better as the game grows and adds more content. Ship combat is fun and chunky, even salvaging wrecked ships is fun (loot pinatas!), mining is a bit tedious but a good way to get started. Trading is a bit iffy at the moment but I understand that the developers will be focusing on the economy next. Managing your fleet of other ships is possible but quite limited at the moment. Some pretty important minor features like renaming a ship are missing and require dramatic workarounds to accomplish.
The biggest challenge for this game, and the biggest risk to an Early Access buyer, is the background simulation. The major feature of the X-series is that all the systems are simulated continuously. That's a huge contribution to immersion and that feature is what allows much of X's emergent gameplay to develop. Unfortunately, Avorion does NOT simulate systems in the background, at least not for long. Only the system you are currently in is continuously updated. After you leave a system it goes into "stasis" and nothing will happen there until you return. I don't know whether full background simulation is planned, but the developers will have their work cut out for them to accomplish it if so.
It will be a HUGE challenge. X had to make major sacrifices to the complexity of the background (Out-of-Sector or OoS) simulation in order to get it to work with the hundreds of systems in X's universe. Avorion has not just hundreds but probably tens of thousands or even hundreds of thousands of possible systems, since they are all procedurally generated. It will require some clever design to make this vastly larger galaxy work as richly as the X universe.
With that caveat under consideration, it is still a great game as-is, and I'd still recommend it for many hours of fun, but it will never be a proper successor to X as an empire-builder and economic simulator without the background simulation.

These guys created an absolutely perfect 16-bit SNES game. They're maybe 25 years late, but it really feels like something that could be released on a cartridge in early 90s (unlike most pixelated games these days). As of the game itself it's pretty much a shmup, told to be mixed with color match puzzle, however, it feels like you're just pushing through the wall of blocks. Some of them will turn into unbreakable blocks and I guess there are some rules about it, but it's not really necessary to learn. Nice one.

This is a mix of an old school shmup in the vein of the old Aleste or Super Star Soldier and a puzzle game. The old school is no joke: forget of autofire, break modes, double break or hypers, here it's tap and tap the fire button like in the old days until your fingers hurt.
You can pick a multitude of ships with different (and helpful) powers and upgrade them with a twist: your upgrade points are limited to 18 so you have to choose very carefully which ships you'll max out.
The game provides a very decent challenge for shmup fans and will probably murder on sight newbies, especially in Boss Rush Mode where you die in one hit.
Anyway, the goal here is to cut your way through alien waves without blocking yourself from the scrolling screen and dying. You can touch the aliens and objects but if the screen catches up you'll die regardless. Having that pressure and making sure you didn't crystallize an alien in the wrong spot helps.
Unlike Bot Vice, here I thank that there is no scoring system because sometimes you'll see yourself restarting endlessly until you get the stages right. With such a heavy case of restart syndrome, it helps a lot that scoring is off the table and you can focus on solving the "puzzles" present in the stages,
Quite worth a try really but forget about making everything explode, this is on the methodical side of the shmup sphere, usually a tag reserved for horizontal STGs.

+Boss Rush mode is fun as well, Bosses aren't terrible bullet sponges like a lot of shmups
+Procedurally generated levels, but fun and consistent mechanics make for great replayability.
+Worth the $5
Cons-

Spelunky is a fantastic game. It may seem very simple and unforgiving at first, but this game truly is a test of your skills, hand-eye coordination and memory. If you die in Spelunky, odds are it's your fault.  There is emergent gameplay situations happening all the time and more than a few ways to go about any playthrough. The super tight controls make this game what it is, use a Xbox 360 controller!  Obviously, the procedural level design makes the replayibility very high.  There can be some moments where the game is not 100% fair, for example a shopkeeper might be set off when you're still at the start of a level, but even that challenge is not insurmountable and that really happens very rarely. The Daily Challenges are a fun feature and a good way to test your ability against other people.  The only drawback I can think of is that co-op is local only but that's not that bad at all.  Stop reading this and go play Spelunky!

This is actually a remaster (remake?) of a game that came out on Pocket PC and iPhone in 2009.  The art style kinda dips into the uncanny valley at times, especially when you look at peoples' faces.  There's quite a few different play styles with the different skills that you can pick from, so you're liable to find something that suits you.
There's a lot of dialogue that really lends itself to making the world feel more alive.  The writing is sometimes a little bit off and the AI is a little silly (I had a horde of bandits follow me to the town and camp outside waiting for me... guards sat and just had tea with them) but the game keeps pulling me in and makes me want to see how powerful I can get and what lies just beyond what I have currently explored.
If you're looking for an old-school RPG experience that won't break the bank, this is for you.

Before I bought the game, I was a bit disapointed by the animations of the characters. I couldn't really get into it. About the game:
You're playing two characters at the same. An elder and a younger brother. - Awesome detail

I picked this game up during the Steam Summer sale for a couple of dollars and it did not disappoint.  The game intrigued me in the way the controls were set up with you controlling both brothers at the same time with the different joint sticks.   The controls were simple and accurate with only my brain getting in the way when the brothers crossed each other on the screen.
The level design is pretty incredible.  The chapters varied in locales but it didn't feel like the developers used a locale just to do so; they all seemed to fit right in with the story.  Believe me, I would love to go into more detail, but I don't want to ruin the experience for others.  I did love the fact you could sit on the benches and just enjoy the view though.  It was a great time to use Steam’s built in screenshot capture.  I may make a slideshow wallpaper for Windows with them.
The story really got me from the start.  It simply begins with the brothers' father coming down with an unknown illness and needing medicine.  From there the journey starts and it was incredible.  It was very reminiscent of the Prince of Persia games with all of the climbing and moving of objects to complete a goal.  There is no direct hand to hand combat, however, so when an enemy presents itself, you must use the Brothers in tandem along with your wits.  Nothing was too terribly difficult and I clocked just over 3 hours to complete the game.
All in all, just a great little game certainly worthy of the $14.99 price tag.  It was a great getaway from the FPS games I usually play.  Highly recommend you get this game.

I used to be a loyal fan of all things Rockstar. I bought this game three times at full retail price (PS3,PS4,PC). Your parent company's decision to send OpenIV a cease and desist is not only anti consumer but also goes against this series history of supporting mods.

Well, finally I was forced to write this...
Let me start off with a simple statement: GTA V was and is a great game. I have mixed feelings about GTA Online but I'm going to leave that aside for now.
This game (singleplayer) has a great story, amazing freedom and stunning graphics. I played it on PS3 and was satisfied by the PC version. It keeps the traditional GTA setting with the introduction of some fresh ideas. This balance was maintained and was one of the reasons this game is so good. The state of GTA Online upon release was satisfying. The game recieved numerous updates and although it all started with thematic updates with just a few cars and guns it was enough to keep players entertained. Heists released and it was a blast. There is something important about this update though. At that point the game started being more centered on cooperative play so it is strongly recommended that you find a crew to play the game with. Later on we've seen massive additions to GTA Online and recently we've gotten two very controversial DLCs: Import/Export and GTA Online: Gunrunning. The reason behind this controversy is that the more conservative players (longtime fans) tend to believe these updates are ruining the realism of GTA and that it only caters griefers and kids and is all about Microtransactions (Shark cards). There is a whole article worth of explanation here, but I don't have enough time to write it all down. The other part of GTA community (mostly new fans) states that GTA Online is all about fun and does not concern realism. While I agree to some of the parties' opinions I do have to say that the problem isn't entirely in the players (although some of them are the reason I play GTA online in public lobbies less and less). This is where we get to the part where I explain why I don't recommend this game anymore.
It is my belief that making GTA V Rockstar games did an excellent job. It is made in a wonderfull manner and the online segment was initially a great thing. HOWEVER the publishers (Take Two interactive) have done a horrible job of catering the players (+ruining R*'s reputation). Don't get me wrong, T2's mission is to squeeze out the biggest possible amount of money from the game. They are a business, after all. The problem is that Take 2 took it way too seriously. They made GTA online a horrible experience by ruining it with microtransactions. They also do not maintain contact with consumers which isn't what a user-friendly company usually does. They have taken down an alternative Online service because they feared their $w33t $hark card revenue would be hurt. They have taken down a converted RDR map mod. They are constantly taking down any attempts of users to make the game more fun, fearing that modders make better content than them and constantly trying to make people play GTA Online exclusively. Furthermore, they are constantly trying to make people buy shark cards. The amazing greed this company has has lead it's aim to become nothing more than to suck out all of life from the original, true community and turn it into a heaven for the neo-gaming generation. Their final step was nothing but disgrace to the GTA V PC community: They have taken down the biggest modding tool for GTA V. Their actions are completely unacceptable and are harmful to the fanbase. This is the reason I'm giving the game a negative review.
It used to be a glorious gem, but Take2's greed was too heavy, it crashed into a million pieces.

As tempted as I am to call this "X3 Lite" that wouldn't do this game justice, nor would it be very fair, because this game does a lot of things better than the X games have, and it doesn't have nearly the learning curve they require nor the clumsy and overly complex interface. If you want the TL;DR of my review below, I'll just say this: If you like X3, buy this game. If you like Robocraft, Minecraft, or Crossout, buy this game. If you like games, you should buy this game. Simply put, you should probably just buy this game, because it's GOOD.
GAMEPLAY: One of my biggest gripes with the X games has always been the lack of options for ships. This game not only answers that, but puts the power in your hands to build your vessel from the ground up, and instantly tailor it to any specific needs you might have as long as you have the resources, so when you get yourself killed because you fly your poorly handling brick into an asteroid, you only have yourself to blame. Find a lucrative trade mission that requires a large cargo hold? No problem, edit your ship and build a bigger one, then remove it after the mission to regain maneuverability. The concept is exellent, and it's well executed. The ship builder has a slight learning curve, but once you get the hang of it, you'll be cranking out excellent performing and looking ships and it's very satisfying when you get it down.
VISUALS: The NPC ships can look a bit ridiculous and impractical being that they're procedurally generated, but you can make some seriously beautiful and angular crafts. After some tinkering, you'll have no issue making replicas of any of your favorite sci-fi craft, as many in the worshop have already demonstrated. The backgrounds and planets are all gorgeous, as well as the fog effects, and the inclusion of supersampling is an excellent addition that really makes things polished looking and aliasing free. You will always lose a little visual fidelity when you're working with this type of crafting system, especially with the low poly asteroids, but the reflections, lights, weapon effects and everything you'd want as far as visuals in a space game go, are all very nice. Also, the amount of debris within sectors is absolutely astounding, and the amount of stuff flying around never seems to negatively effect the framerate. Impressive to say the least.
PHYSICS: For the most part the physics are good. You don't have to be terribly specific in designing your ship to make it fly well, so the flying physics are definitely what I'd call "arcade." Also, the NPC ships often do some really awkward things, especially if they're one of the extremely long "stick" ships that pop up more often than you want. If you're concerned about spaceflight realism you can opt out of using the inertia dampeners if you'd like a more realistic experience, so you'll have to burn retrograde to slow your ship. The more powerful weapons have a recoil effect as well as an effect on your opponents flight, which I find pretty cool. However, this also can be a bit awkward, and it seems like there are still a few bugs to iron out in how this works, especially with NPC ships.
SOUND: While I won't comment on the music, because I always turn game music off, the sounds are mostly satisfying, and done well. Larger ships make larger explosions, the various weapons sound unique and interesting. It would be nice if the various levels of engines had alternate sounds as well, as the generic exhaust drone can get a little old, but there really isn't much to complain about. Leveling is done well, apart from some explosions being a little over the top, but everything seems blended together well.
NETWORK/MULTIPLAYER: I only spent a little while playing online, as I prefer the single player experience in this game. There also seems to be a few stability issues with servers crashing quite a bit in the current build. After the server I tried out crashed twice, I opted out of the multiplayer for now. However, everything seems to be there from the multiplayer perspective, and once the stability issues are ironed out I can see this being an excellent co-op experience with hours of fun.
OVERALL: Excellent. I'm a bit late to this game as I accidentally stumbled upon it, but I've already gotten my moneys worth out of it and will be playing this a lot. I hope more will buy this game as the developers are clearly talented and seem to be pretty active within the community. If you missed the sale for this game, don't worry about it, it's worth every penny even at full cost. I hope the developers continue adding to this game, as they potentially have a superior rival to X3, which for me, is saying a LOT.

Super Star Path has a bit of a neat gimmick, but overall isn't executed very well. First of all, every level starts off as a puzzle but finishes with a sort of shmup boss of varying degrees of annoyance, if (when) it kills you you have to go through the entire puzzle process over again, which does nothing to warm you up for the shmup ahead. I feel like if DYA wanted to make a puzzle game, they should've just made a puzzle game instead of making such a strange compromise.
The puzzle elements are pretty random, and can vary wildly in difficulty. I suspect some shuffles may even be impossible on the final stage, but I couldn't say for sure. It doesn't ruin the game for me since a given stage is pretty short, but it does seem like more could've been done to make it consistent. It's also pretty easy to get pinched at the bottom of the screen, I probably died about a dozen times being crushed by the gem left from the alien I just killed, again not really a big deal, but it does feel disappointing to miss out on the narrow save. I'm a bit surprised that SSP doesn't include a score attack or endless mode, something along the lines of Mr. Driller, but maybe attempts at that just highlighted issues with how the puzzle sections were being built.
Many of the ships seem designed to trivialize some new aspect of a stage, they each have some passive ability or other, most of which let them ignore a type of damage, but they're also restricted by tier, so basically I wound up just using the highest tier ships I had access to. Obviously whether you use a given ship or not will be up to you, but it would be nice to have the option of fully stating out the basic ship for instance.
I'm a bit let down by this game. It had a fair bit of promise, but I don't feel like enough was done with the puzzle system, and the bosses just kinda felt thrown in from another game. Puzzle games need puzzles bosses. Also our pilot Capt. Obvious was really obnoxious, thankfully you can turn off the voice over.
It's an enjoyable game, but not much to get excited over ultimately.

Neat concept, challenging, terrific art and music. I do have some problems with the gameplay though, and it has to do mostly with the ships.
Each ship is designed to be immune to a certain stage hazard (which only appears in that specific stage), and the ships have stronger base and max stats the harder they are to unlock. This is frankly pretty boring, since there's not much difference in playstyle between them (with the exception of one ship having diagonal shots against bosses and another ship having money gain) and they're basically intended to be discarded once the player has finished the stage they're designed for. This could have been made way more interesting if each ship had more varied base/max stats, such as a ship with high defense but low offense, or a ship that starts out great but can't be upgraded, etc. The way it's set up now, the playing field is tilted and you should just avoid investing into the early ships entirely.
This becomes a problem when you compound it with the limited upgrades, which are not enough to max out all of the ships you purchase. I did not know this starting out, and I invested upgrades into weak ships, leaving me crippled against the later stages. I had to erase my file so I could max out my stronger ships. Bad design.
But I mean, the gameplay other than that is pretty cool. It's fairly short, but the stage gimmicks keep things interesting and there's some intense SHMUP bosses at the end of every level as well as a boss rush. Worth getting on sale. Just don't upgrade the basic ship and you'll have a good time.

Spelunky is a fantastic game. It may seem very simple and unforgiving at first, but this game truly is a test of your skills, hand-eye coordination and memory. If you die in Spelunky, odds are it's your fault.  There is emergent gameplay situations happening all the time and more than a few ways to go about any playthrough. The super tight controls make this game what it is, use a Xbox 360 controller!  Obviously, the procedural level design makes the replayibility very high.  There can be some moments where the game is not 100% fair, for example a shopkeeper might be set off when you're still at the start of a level, but even that challenge is not insurmountable and that really happens very rarely. The Daily Challenges are a fun feature and a good way to test your ability against other people.  The only drawback I can think of is that co-op is local only but that's not that bad at all.  Stop reading this and go play Spelunky!

Wow. Like a lot of people I was turned off by the "was on mobile/pocket PC". But the game had such good reviews, I had to try it out. And I'm really glad I did. The best way to describe it is TES mixed with the mid-generation Might and Magics - World of Xeen era. (I love MM 4-7. I even like 8 too) It really feels like a good turn based/semi realtime game from the mid 90s. And I mean that in the best way possible. Graphics are colorful, bright, and appear hand drawn in a well done mid-90s style- People move about, and clicking on things in the viewscreen allows you to interact. You can pick flowers & herbs, look at signs, examine things, talk to people (or sneak around from behind and steal), and so on and so forth. You can even read books. Some contain short stories, some useful alchemy recepies you can make from the herbs collected out wandering around. Personally, I love that. I'm one of those weirdos who's read literally every single book in TES.
Combat is handled through a turnbased system on the overworld map kind of like M&M. IE - an enemy moves on the same overworld map as you, it doesnt go into a combat screen. They can even snipe at you from a distance with a ranged weapon. I was out screwing around in the wilderness, and all the sudden I started taking damage. I looked around, couldn't see anything. I took a step and got hit again. I saw movement, and realized an f'n archer was sniping at me behind a bush. I ran at her and she actually dodged out of the way so I couldnt hit her. Not bad. Once you get close, the game goes into a turn based mode, noticable by the fact that there appears to be a slight lag as the triggered enemy(s) move or attack. You can move(turning in place is free)/attack, then the enemy(s), then you. You are free to go wherever, so if you dont want to fight, just take off in the opposite direction and hope you're fast enough to get away.
Theres plenty of people to talk to and sidequests so far. My one complaint about that is although there is a journal system for actual quests, there isnt an ingame note system where you can type simple notes to yourself for info that may be related to your quests. So if someone tells you "the mayor's house is in the Northwest" or "I heard the smuggler (name) has a secret tunnel hidden in the SW of (place), you better write it down or remember it, the game wont remember it for you even if its a clue directly related to an in-journal quest.
The class and skill system is pretty cool for a game like this. Its completely customizable. You pick a basic race, and are free to pick a base class. Then you can tweak the skills you start with however you want. Want a necromancer mage that steals and dual wields light weapons? You got that. A ranger that sneaks around and specializes in mind magic and heavy weapons? Yep.
Another cool thing is based on your starting character, you start in a slightly different area of the game with a slightly different intro book. Its a nice touch.
In the inn theres a nice little card game you can bet money with.  There are 3 decks to choose from, each deck has slightly different style cards. The object is to play a card every turn and drop your opponents HP to 0 with attack and DoT cards while keeping yourself alive with defense and healing cards. Its a fun little diversion.
The sound is the one part the game isnt that great in, but thats fine. Not much sound at all, steps on hard surfaces, rustling in the woods and just a thwock-oof (or other appropriate monster noise) when you hit or are hit in combat.
Overall, this game is a surprising little gem. Anyone who loves the mid-90s style RPGs should take a look at it. Its surprisingly complex and nothing like what youd expect from a "mobile game". My one concern with that is I'm wondering how long the game actually is, I mean they did such a good job on such a restrictive platform I'm wondering if they had to sacrifice content?

This game is a fusion of grid based dungeon crawler in the vein of Might&Magic, Dungeon Master and Eye of Beholder with open world RPG akin to TES and Gothic series. The Quest borrows the best of both worlds and is packed with fun features from dungeon puzzles, to non-linear quests, to robust outdoor exploration, to elaborate alchemy system. Never mind the game's mobile origins, this is a full fledged CRPG which rivals in quality some of the top genre representatives.

This is a beautiful game that is a great callback to early RPGs.
The Quest is a turn based, first person, open world game where you have to work your way to clear the island from evil. You will be faced with choices that will either make you famous, or infamous.  The best way I can describe this is if Skyrim was put into an old RPG engine.
If you've played the game on ios or android, it's pretty much the same, only the graphics have been massively inproved as has the framerate.
The only downside to this game I can think of is that if you drop an item that's required for a quest and the item disappears, you cannot finish that quest. A minor complaint, but one I think actually adds to the realism of the game.
If you're a fan of old rpgs, this game definitely won't disappoint.

This game is great for anyone looking to get into the grid based RPG Genre who wants combat that is built solid, same goes to the veterans looking for anything new to return to the grid based RPG Genre without the need of fancy gimmicks or over the top story for immersive gameplay.

「The Quest 」
Originally a Pocket PC game this RPG, whilst simplistic in style, was ported to iOS phones back in 2009 back when I was heavily attached to my iPod Touch back in the day. I bought this back then a little while after its release as the style of gameplay reminded me of older turn / tile based RPGs such as Daggerfall.
The gameplay is addictively fun and simple, you can move quickly over tiles whilst out of combat but when within range of another enemy the speed slows down to help you plan your next move, take a potion or choose a spell to fire. The story is nicely written and interesting to get involved with and the music is very relaxing when exploring towns and forests and equally immersive in dungeons.
There were a number of expansions for The Quest that were released on iOS that all expanded on regular gameplay and were also playable standalone, I'd like to see them make an appearance on the PC port as well.

'Wargame: Red Dragon' created by Eugen Systems for their game series titled 'Wargame' is a real-time strategy game where the player commands a military unit that comprises of everything from logisitic assests to naval assests. The game or more correctly the entire 'Wargame' series has the player either play as a country or coalition from NATO or the Warsaw Pact, as the game takes place during the Cold War era. Specifically for this release of the 'Wargame' series the developers have you be in East Asia, focusing mainly on the relations NATO and the Warsaw Pact through the Korean Peninsula.
In the several months that I had played 'Wargame: Red Dragon', I found that the game has an amazing assortion of different units from both sides and from many countries, inside that assortion were tanks like the Centurion to the M1A2 and infantry equipment ranging the early L1A1 to the modern C7.
Playing the game I also found that it has your brain working and improving overtime, this is the case because the game expecially in multiplayer where you're pitched against expierenced strategists, has you thinking critically on where you would or could be moving your assests you, where could that enemy mortar be, what would the enemy throw at me this time. Like these questions I have just said even if they sound vague to you right now is something that has you seriously thinking and probably in-game could possibly have you panic depending on the situation. This is an even more accurate statement as even though there are a few assortion of maps that people actually play, the maps themselves could even if you have a superior force could have you play yourself, everything from difficult terrain to forests, strange terrain angles and small towns, perfect for an ambush or an artillery bombardment or aerial strike.
However playing the game, I have found that the naval assests no matter how amazing that sounds like, is utterly bland there is variation of naval units strangly from 9-12 different nations on the NATO side and there is also no variation of units from the 6 nations of the Warsaw PACT side. In addition to that I have also found that the ships on the PACt side are utterly overpowered, you would find it impossible to kill their ships compared to those on NATO.
Nonetheless, I find that 'Wargame: Red Dragon' is a highly enjoyable game especially once you actually put yourself into it. It has it's flaws but overall a really good build and on a side note if the developers of the game actually read reviews from the community "FIX THE NAVAL AND ADD MORE NAVAL". Overall I rate the game out of 10 a 7.5.
