This review applies to online mostly, as I haven't played much of the story. The game is lots of fun when it works, but there's too many issues for me to recommend as "good". The experience inevitably gets frustrating after not very much play.
Pros
+Free DLC with lots of content
+Some extremely fun and unique game modes.
+Something for everyone. There's a million different ways to play.
+Tons of vehicles. Collecting, personalizing, and driving around cars is how I have the most fun
+Benny's cars have a ton of personalization options. (I wish every car had that level of customization)
Cons
-You can't get a world record on any race, all the times are hacked to a few seconds.
-Long loading times. Wouldn't be such a big deal on its own but generally annoying.
-You can't try out different color combinations on vehicles before paying. If you try one color combo, switch to see another, and switch back, you'll end paying three times for each color change. This applies to all vehicle upgrades (spoilers, performance upgrades, etc) This bothers me because the MKII weapons added in the Gunrunning update have upgrades and color options as well, but once you buy a paint scheme or a scope, you own it forever. You can switch between any purchased upgrades for free. Cars should work this way as well. Just makes me feel like the game is nickel and diming me.
-Any time the game fails to join session, it boots you right into singleplayer automatically. It wastes my time because I'm typically not in the mood to play singleplayer if I'm online. Give me the option to retry joining online instead of forcing me to load singleplayer than join multiplayer again. This makes zero sense from a user experience perspective. Also, it usually fails to join session because I alt-tab to do something else because the wait times are so long. The game doesnt like losing focus even in Borderless windowed mode.
-In some competetive game modes (gta races, deathmatches) where you can use your owned weapons instead of a predetermined set, there is a 'Buy all ammo' button which is supposed to fill all your owned weapons. It always takes my money but rarely actually fills all my ammo. Also, most of the time when I buy ammo for MKII weapons, it disappears from my inventory next time I log in. I've filed support tickets for both of these issues, but the outsourced support department just runs me through a script of basic troubleshooting items (verifying game cache etc) before just offering to compensate me for the lost money without addressing the root of the problem.
-Daily objectives would be a great way to make money, but many are nearly impossible to complete without friends. There's just so many gamemodes and half of them have no one playing. I appreciate that we have a lot to do but oversaturation has divided the playerbase. For example 'Complete a Capture-Contend'. Barely anyone plays Captures and the fact that they've divided into 4 types doesn't help.
-A lot of useful game functions, like replacing a destroyed vehicle, going off the radar, summoning a vehicle from your garage, are handled through the in-game phone. The problem is that half the time, the phone rings a few time and doesnt pick up (the menu acts like a simulated phone conversation). The whole phone thing is for immersion I guess but I will never understand why I cant just access these options on the first try. Also, there's a second in-game menu (interaction menu) that also has similar features but works differently. The two need to be merged. You also can't climb or shoot while using the phone, which is frustrating,

Never provided any additional content for single player opting instead to exclusively focus on the cash grab that is multiplayer. Now they're going after the modding community. I don't recommend and will steer clear of Rockstar and Take Two's products in the future.

An interesting arcade-style shoot-em-up with an unusual game mechanic where shooting a group of coloured blocks will destroy all attached blocks of the same colour, and turn any blocks of a different colour to the left, right and top of the last block to be cleared into indestructable frozen blocks. Which means that unlike most arcade style shooters you won't want to spam the fire button constantly because this behaviour could quite easily see you stuck behind a dead end made up of frozen blocks.
Collisions with blocks which are about to go off the bottom of the screen can feel a bit harsh at times, just brushing up against such a block can lock your controls and drag you off the bottom of the screen to your death. But collisions with projectiles and the like on the other hand can be a bit generous, there were a few times when I was facing a boss and I was sure I took a hit, but apparently didn't.
There are a few different ships to be unlocked by completing levels, purchased using collected gems and upgraded using collected power-ups. Buying new ships seems to be the only use for gems. All the ships have their own properties, making each one only really usefull for completing the level which has the kind of obstacle that the ship in question is invunerable to. Each level has three power ups to collect, speed, power and armour. But the number of power-ups are far fewer than the number of upgrade slots on all your ships, so you may wish to refrain from upgrading ships until you really need to.  Each level also has three green emeralds to be collected, and collecting these is one of the main objectives of the game. I'm fairly sure you need all 18 of them to beat the final boss.
When you die you get to keep all the gems, power-ups and emeralds you've collected, but when you quit playing via the pause menu you don't. Which is mildly annoying when you find yourself blocked in an unwinnable situation, the player should be able to just select quit and try again instead of waiting patiently to die.
Ultimately there's not a whole lot of game here, I achieved 100% achivements in about four hours. It's not that the game's difficulty is lacking, I spent about 60-90 minutes each on completing the final level and boss rush mode, it's just that there's only six levels and it won't be very long before you've seen all of them. I suppose this could be good if you're looking for a game to easily score 100% achivements and boost your avarage completion rate.
(this game has 15 trading cards, and you'll probably have at least two card drops remaining by the time you've finished it, but I'm not deducting any points for that)
I had to seriously consider if I was going to recommend this game or not, and had to go with recommended, as it is a reasonbly fun and challenging game despite its shortcomings. But you might want to consider picking it up only if it's on sale.

I picked this game up during the Steam Summer sale for a couple of dollars and it did not disappoint.  The game intrigued me in the way the controls were set up with you controlling both brothers at the same time with the different joint sticks.   The controls were simple and accurate with only my brain getting in the way when the brothers crossed each other on the screen.
The level design is pretty incredible.  The chapters varied in locales but it didn't feel like the developers used a locale just to do so; they all seemed to fit right in with the story.  Believe me, I would love to go into more detail, but I don't want to ruin the experience for others.  I did love the fact you could sit on the benches and just enjoy the view though.  It was a great time to use Steam’s built in screenshot capture.  I may make a slideshow wallpaper for Windows with them.
The story really got me from the start.  It simply begins with the brothers' father coming down with an unknown illness and needing medicine.  From there the journey starts and it was incredible.  It was very reminiscent of the Prince of Persia games with all of the climbing and moving of objects to complete a goal.  There is no direct hand to hand combat, however, so when an enemy presents itself, you must use the Brothers in tandem along with your wits.  Nothing was too terribly difficult and I clocked just over 3 hours to complete the game.
All in all, just a great little game certainly worthy of the $14.99 price tag.  It was a great getaway from the FPS games I usually play.  Highly recommend you get this game.

Wow!  What a wonderful game!  Using a single gamepad to control both brothers at the same time is challenging but rewarding when you get it right.  And That Moment...  It's been a long time since a game had such an impact on me.  And to think that Brothers did it with just a simple button press.  Fantastic!

I've heard this game was very well done from other reviews, but nothing can prepare you for how great this game really is. Fairly short, about 3 hours to beat. But the story itself is deep, emotional, and amazing. The two brothers you control (using a controller) each has their own joystick to control and the triggers on each side has an action for them to perform if there is one. Very easy to control, though sometimes my thumbs and brain would get confused and have them running away from what I wanted them to do. Great storytelling. Highly recommended.
This game was so well done! It's a fast play, but definitely worth playing.

I really enjoyed this game. The mechanics are pretty simple but unique. You control the older brother with the left joystick and the younger brother with the right. You can have them interact with things around the world by using the left/right triggers. Often times, you'll have to use one brother do one activity (like whistle to distract a dog) while the other does something else (like run across a field while the dog is distracted).
None of the characters speak English so the story is simple and pretty predictable but what the game lacks in plot, it makes up for with the interesting game mechanics and the absolutely stunning enviroment. Seriously, most of this game just seems like walking through an artists gallery. There are even benches throughout the game where you can sit down and enjoy the view.
My only complaint was that it was difficult to take the screen shots I wanted to take because if you were holding down buttons (for example, to sit on the bench), the screen shot wouldn't take using the controller. And I'm just not dexterous enough to hold the controller and hit the prtsc key on the keyboard.
My final recommendation is to try it out. I think this is a pretty unique game. It's not an action game but it's a cool experience and it won't take up too many hours of your time (I took my time and finished everything in about 4 hours). I would wait for it to go on sale though, because I would have been annoyed if I paid $15 for it (I paid a lot less during summer sale 2014).
Spoiler section. I'm going to talk about the very end of the game here.

I never really cry or get choked up about stuff, and certainly not about games. Sure I get excited some times when I win something cool or beat a hard level, but never that deeply. This game did that for me. The artistic style and design is not limited to level design or the scenery. The entire game, from interface to sound track to landscapes, all of it blends together in a magnificent fusion of a compelling self-driven narrative. There does not appear to be any pre-rendered scenes either, and the immersion never seems to break until the credits roll.
This is the perfect example of a game done magnificently - every aspect of it contributes to the story being told. Buy it now and play it for yourself.
The only negative I could note is that it only took me a little under 3 hours to finish my first play-through. Also, those who may not deal well with a heavily emotionally charged story will want to pace themselves so they don't get overwhelmed. Note: you WILL want a controller for this, and I would say that if you don't have one already it is worth getting one (you can also use it for other games too).
Overall: 11/10 - an exceptional score for an exceptional game. Best game I've ever played in my entire life.

I picked this up in the Steam Summer Sale, thinking nothing of it really. Just another game going cheap to add to my collection. No hurry to install, just leave it there on my list until I'm bored one day.....
Well, one day I was bored, so I installed it and, with not much expectation I loaded it up. Well, to put it simply....
...What a game! You start with two brothers, whom, after a short series of events, find themselves embarking on a quest to save their father from an unknown illness. The story itself is something of a rarity, something truly compelling. Despite being short, I found myself utterly involved with it and couldn't put my controller down. As the quest reaches it's conclusion, you will find yourself shocked, amazed and somewhat shaken. You won't forget this one in a hurry.
Graphically, the game is beautiful. Stunning vistas will come and go, with weather effects that are equally as good. Character animations are brilliant, and really help to enhance the emotional impact and carry the storyline (these characters don't speak English, the game uses it's own made-up language). I lost count of how many screenshots I took, the game looks that good!
Sound wise, the soundtrack is excellent. The music is full of ambience and really gives the game an extra lift. Characters and environments also sound really good.
In terms of gameplay, the game is unique. I would highly recommend a controller to play it. The left stick is then used to control big brother, and the right control for little brother. This is still quite a challenge but, much much easier than trying to use a keyboard, trust me. Some of the puzzles and climbs require a little finesse, I died a few times trying to get both brothers across a few of the jumps and up some of the climbs, but overall, it works well.
In conclusion, a highly recommended game that's well worth your time and the rewards it has won. 9/10

Wonderful grid-based first person RPG that feels like it came straight from the golden age of such games.
Don't be fooled by this game's iOS/mobile background and your (honestly, completely reasonable) preconceptions about games made for such platforms! The Quest is one huge, deep, and exceptionally well-crafted RPG experience.
Large and beautiful open world that truly feels like it was carefully hand-crafted, one that is rich with nostalgic fantasy atmosphere and filled with loads of interesting locales to discover, dungeons to plunder and quests to solve (which often can be done in more than one way, or sometimes in a way that is connected with other seemingly separate quests). Game features a reputation system where your fame/infamy increases or decreases depending on your actions and way in which you complete quests, which in turn can influence your future quests and your interactions with some of the game's NPCs.
Combat is fully turn-based, highly enjoyable and deceptively simple. Game offers deep and open character customization, wide variety of equipment and spells, and sufficiently deep alchemy system. It's definitely a kind of game where trying out a vastly different character build is a good enough reason for a full-fledged replay.
This new re-release comes with a fully redone HD visuals, and I must say that team did a pretty good job there: game looks -gorgeous-, at times almost like a beautiful hand-drawn fantasy illustration, fully retaining its original charm reminiscent of 90s games that influenced it.
Easily my favorite game of all time, not buying it would be doing yourself a disservice. It's beautiful, immersive, and immensely entertaining; a true work of art.
Still as fun as the first time I played all those years ago.

I used to play this game on my Palm PDA and loved it. The graphics overhaul looks great and keeps the original art style. The game has a great story and is incredibly addicting. There is a large world to explore and many things to do. I would recommend this game if you are into turn based games.

First of all, I am a huge fan to these kinds of games! It's very similar to the classic Might and Magic games such as MM3 and World of Xeen but with a little more depth in the skill system. So far the difficulty level seems just right. One difference from the Might and Magic and The Quest is that you play solo in this game. There are no party members, but it's still pretty fun playing solo. You will meet interesting characters, browse through shops with many goodies, and crawl through dangerous dungeons! I'm also liming the art in this game, it fits it well. The Quest is also turn based with grid movement which is a huge perk IMO. So, do yourself the favour and buy this gem! I recommend this game to any CRPG and Might and Magic fan. 10/10!

The Quest is a truly amazing and immersive game, that is a prime example of a better time of Role Playing Games. All games should strive to be this detailed and interesting. If you ever feel the need for a good old role play, dungeon crawl, or just have a love for video games, this game is for you. The story is really good, and each quest has great writing and isn't just some fetch quests. The NPC's really bring the game to life. This game is definetely a must buy, and I would snag it early during the sale. As you can see by my play time, I've been playing it non-stop since I bought it. A drawback to the game however, is that it is sorta hard to start off. It is a little complicated at first with all the character building, and you being thrown in the middle of a town to fend for yourself and find quests. I'd recommend the guides Sylon compiled in the official RedShift Forum. There is a button in the menu screen to get there, but I'd recommend using the steam overlays browser functionality to have the ability to open guides at any time. Keep in mind though that pressing shift within the game is the attack button, so when you open the overlay press tab first so you don't trigger an attack.You wouldn't believe how many times I've accidentally hit someone while opening the overlay and having to pay off the fine. Anyway with all that said, The Quest is a great must-immediately-buy game, and while it's on sale you can't go wrong with buying it! Hope it wins an award!

I like Point & Click Adventures. I love how they tell their stories and create their worlds. But I must make an admission about me and this genre.
I cheat profusely at Adventure games...
To me its the destination thats more crucial to Adventure games than the journey. It takes away from the overall experience if I have to try every item on my inventory on everything in the environment. so apologies to those who object me to using walkthroughs. Moving on....
Deponia's story is an interesting one. Rufus, a do nothing, egotistical and self-involved young man who desperately wants to leave his stinking junkyard homeworld Deponia for the utopian floating city of Elysium. His latest hair brained plan to escape almost succeeded had he gets involved in an incident and rescues a mysterious girl, knocking her into a coma in the process. Its a funny and light hearted story with a touching cast that still delivers some swift plot twists and one liners (all voiced as well). All of which is pleasingly punctuated by the games detailed, cartoon art style that takes you in (with some help from the music....).
Gameplay is as it has always been for Point & Clicks; you study the scene, collect everything and solve esoteric puzzles that put the Gordian Knot to shame. I'm not gonna delve too much into it since I use walkthroughs. But I will say its a fair bit better controls than other adventure games I've played.
Deponia is a fun game, but like all Point & Click adventures its not for everyone. More for the inquisitive type in it for the story than the action. I'm already ready too dive into the sequel.

Doom 3 is a game that is very overlooked. It was Id's flagship title and features a very powerful game engine. It contained enhancements such as dynamic lighting, physics, bump mapping, portal technology among many other things we now take for granted. This was all months prior to Half Life 2 wowing us for the same thing.
Doom 3 is essentially a remake or reboot of the series. It shares virtually the same premise as the original Doom, except set on Mars instead of it's moons. In a way this sort of gives the game it's own style but makes it feel less original. The aesthetic of the game was nailed very well, however the levels do get very samey after a while. For the vast majority of the game you're mostly running through maze-like corridors looking for ways to open doors. This was the first game I remember where I started to notice maze-like level design felt antiquated. I always kind of wished this game was more open and less claustraphobic.
The game is still a horror game so they introduced dark environments with enemies shuffling around them. It also took a very bold risk where the player's flashlight is a separate weapon you equip. I personally like this mechanic but a lot of people, especially at the time hated it. And it was a frequent source of ridicule for the game.
The gunplay in Doom 3 is something I never particularly liked, especially compared to it's successor Quake 4. The pistol is a joke that is never used after you get the shotgun, the shotgun is what you use for 70% of the game, the machine gun's firing sound effect makes it sound like a cap gun, the chaingun is very slow and cumbersome, the rocket launcher is extremely cool but only used on bigger enemies, and the plasma gun feels too slow to be useful. This was all corrected with very fantastic modifications but at the time I can understand why people didn't like it.
In a way that's why I recommend this game. The engine Doom 3 used allowed it to be very heavily modified. There are a great deal of very good total conversion mods for the game, and it allowed Doom 3 to live on in our collective consciousness despite the game being only "okay". I do recommend the game for it's modifications more than anything else since that is what this game is most remembered for.

Amazing. Tekken - finally on PC and done extremely well.
I pre-ordered this game to show my support to Namco expecting it probably wouldn't even start up on my low-end hardware (Intel Compute Stick - Core m3 with 4 GB Ram and Intel HD 515 graphics). Having been a Tekken fan from Tekken 1 onwards - I just had to buy it at full price to show my support and expected to be able to play it in the future at some point.
BUT - IT'S ACTUALLY PLAYABLE ON A CORE M3 COMPUTE STICK! Of course with everything dialed down to minimum settings etc, but still - actually playable. Amazing.
Even Mortal Kombat X dialed down to the lowest of the low doesn't play as well as Tekken on this hardware. Yay Namco - awesome job! (Even online play and local VS matches run smooth!!! The same can NOT be said for MK X on this hardware...not at all...)
As for the game itself? What can I say - it's Tekken. Tekken updated with fantastic graphics, engaging story mode etc.
For those that don't know Tekken very well: In my opinion Tekken is the most intuitive fighting game out there; techniques begin to flow together quite naturally after only a few tries and it even features a 'take-over' mechanic (where a punch or a kick of an opponent can be caught and he / she will either be thrown or forced into a submissive locking technique). Virtua Fighter also features this but it is too complicated by comparison. (Plus there hasn't been a new Virtua Fighter in a long while... especially on PC...)
Unlike Mortal Kombat for exampe where playing quickly becomes "button mashing" trying to remember and execute a large number of moves without any subtle grappling / take-over mechanics whatsoever. In my experience it mainly amounts to who can mash the other to bits the fastest. Tekken is simply way more nuanced. One can play it simple or one can turn it into a "combat chess" game of sorts. Tekken also beats Street Fighter in my opinion as SF is a 2D based fighting mechanic with 3D graphics, whereas Tekken is true 3D and again - Tekken features the beautiful "take-over" mechanic. (Only DOA features this as well (other than the 'dead' Virtua Fighter franchise), but that's a story for another time).
Online play is also great fun and the network code is done really really well. When trying to play with a specific friend there may be lag (but that's not Tekken's fault, simply a reality of long-distance networking) - but when playing random opponents online play is a thing of beauty.
For those with some Tekken background - This episode of Tekken follows suit with Tekken 5 and 6 - no  "ridiculous characters" like in Tekken 3 (Gon, Bosconovitch) and no serious imbalance such as the demi-Gods/Demons in Tekken 5 (Jinpachi) and Tekken 6 (Azazel). Personally I do find Akuma a bit out of balance as he can shoot a variety of Hadoken (Fire balls) too easily compared to the vulnerable states that Devil Kazuya / Jin find themselves in when ramping up to shoot their demon... erm... "eye laser beams?"..
The game features an in-game fight money system to unlock lots of items in the customise character and gallery-sections of the game - but unlike Street Fighter V - fight money is relatively easy to come by (it's balanced and fair in my opinion).
All in all: AMAZING... Namco.... My hat is off to thee, thou art the greatest!!! ^^
Was so blown away with the results that I just had to write this brief review, now back to playing Tekken :))))))
---
(Extra info: I'm running this on a 2nd generation Intel Compute Stick... (STK2m3W64CC).... Who would have thought... Tekken on a stick... awesome...
(Using a Samsung USB3.1 SSD for storage as the onboard storage is of course not big enough)).
(Running @ 720p with everything low, no motion blur, no antialiasing etc: 42FPS in game)
---
Lastly - Dear Namco, I have but two requests -
1. Please release a Linux version of this game... if you can do that I would be eternally grateful :)
2. Please release the traditional clothing for Asuka (hakama, dogi) - because... well it's bad enough to have to play a girl before being able to find a character with Koryu moves... please give her hakama and dogi back... Playing an attractive young girl in hot pants - just to get some nice throws and locking techiques... is well... a bit silly.. I'd prefer another character (reskin of Asuka.. a brother or cousin maybe?) would be even better, but at least return her Hakama and Dogi like she had in Tekken 5 and 6.....

It's a quick little game that is fun to play. It accomplishes a mix between shmup and puzzle game. The first part of each stage is spent calculating a path through enemies which you can actually close off (i.e. make impassible) if you are not careful. The second part of each stage (a boss) is more like a traditional shmup.
There are six stages total, plus a boss run mode, where you fight the six bosses with a single shield (though weapons and speed are maxed), using the ship of your choice. I found that most bosses took no longer than 30 seconds to beat, fewer in boss mode because of the maxed weapon damage.
The game has music that fits with the fast pace style, and the puzzle aspect is interesting enough for the time the game lasts.
To beat the mission mode and boss rush mode, it took a total of 1.5 hours on my first play through, so if you're concerned about length of a game in relationship to the price, I would venture the game would take 1-3 hours depending on your level of familiarity with shmups.

Having said that, there is only one fixed difficulty, and said difficulty feels just right; It's not so easy that you can't pay attention, but too hard as to turn players away in frustration. It should be worth noting, however, that I obtained 100% completion in a mere 93 minutes. The rest of my playtime was spent idling the main menu to obtain the trading card drops.
The game's mechanics may seem tricky at first, but it is very intuitive and easy to get used to. Gameplay consists of choosing one of five levels (you can play them in any order you want), then navigating through a swarm of enemies that
. Props to the devs for that; if contact damage for the standard enemies was a thing, the game would then go from "fair and challenging" to "disproportionately brutal and not worth playing". After clearing the initial 5 levels, the final level is unlocked to play.
Levels consist of two phases, which I'll call the "puzzle" phase, then the "boss" phase. During the puzzle phase, you guide your spaceship and navigate through a swarm of enemies. Of course, the enemies will block your path; if you shoot one, it will explode and subsequently kill all enemies of the same color near it, causing a (potentially large) chain reaction. When an enemy of a different color is hit by the chain reaction, it will freeze and become indestructible, forcing you to navigate around it. These standard enemies
do direct damage; the challenge of the puzzle phase comes from having to navigate through the horde of enemies without getting pushed to the bottom of the screen. Each level has its own gimmick, such as a certain type of enemy appearing, or a certain obstacle. The level-specific enemies
do damage, so be wary of that. Fortunately, each ship (except for the starting ship) has some special ability or perk that can mitigate a certain stage's gimmick, encouraging the player to unlock and use different ships for each level.
The Boss phase is very straightforward; a standard-difficulty bullet-hell boss appears and shoots bullet patterns at you, in which you avoid and shoot back. Shoot it until it dies. It should be worth noting that during the puzzle phase, your ship uses single-fire shots, and during the boss phase, your ship automatically uses automatic fire, a quality-of-life improvement that makes this game more enjoyable to play. For those who want a classic bullet-hell experience, there is an unlockable Boss Rush mode.
Each level has collectibles, such as ship upgrades (to improve a ship's attack, defense and speed) and gems to buy new ships with. If you die, all upgrades and gems you've collected will be retained, and levels can be attempted as many times as you want without penalty. However, each level only provides one of each upgrade, so you can't farm for infinite upgrades; you must use them wisely.
The game has adjustable volume levels and an option to turn the voice acting on or off. You can't remap the controls yourself, but there are different pre-mapped controls (that you can select via the options menu) that cover a decent selection of bullet hell controls. For example, the default setup uses arrow keys for movement with Z and X as your main buttons, but there's an option to use the WASD keys for movement with J and K for your main buttons. The game even has controller support if you want to use a controller.
In conclusion, Super Star Path is a unique shoot-em-up that requires the player to make quick decisions during the puzzle phase, then unleash their proper bullet-hell skills during the boss phase. The soundtrack definitely fits the arcade-theme that the game presents, without the frustrations that come with typical arcade games. The game is (mostly) fairly challenging, and the lack of detrimental penalty upon death mitigates frustration in the event that the RNG decides to screw you over. I'd recommend it as a good bullet hell game for people who like quick strategic thinking and don't have extreme bullet-dodging skills (as required in other bullet hell games).

A very short but nice game that uses an interesting, unique mechanic in comparison to most shoot'em'ups.
In Super Star Path, you'll be controlling a ship and shooting at colored creatures on the way. The mechanic is that once you shoot a creature, it'll destroy all other creatures of the same color that are nearby, but at the end of it, all nearby creatures of different colors will become frozen and impossible to be destroyed, so the player has to manage his way through so that they don't end up locked up.
All levels have three upgrades that can be found, along with three emeralds too, and some levels will have certain traps to be avoided like spikes or proximity mines. At the end of each level, there is also a boss to be fought. After each level, new ships can be purchased, each ship has their own stats (damage, speed and defense) and some of them also have some special abilities like being able to destroy armored blocks or ignore certain traps, making certain ships better at certain levels.
The game presents a decent level of challenge, but sadly it's way too short. It also has one problem - upgrade points are permanent, once you spend an upgrade on a ship, you can't take it back, so you need to administer your upgrades very carefully (or start over). Also, the game can only be actually beaten once you have done something specific and the game doesn't actually tell you that until you've gotten to the very end. Spoilers:
Could be better, but it's a fun game nonetheless.

Super Star Path is an arcade styled space shoot ‘em up, with a puzzle element thrown into the mix. Although the game doesn’t last very long, there’s enough here to justify a hefty bit of entertainment. It’s also one of the few games that doesn’t rely heavily on the ‘bullet hell’ gimmick… well until you reach the boss fights, but even then it’s not too bad. All in all, the game is a solid offering that’s well worth the price tag.
PROS:
-	It’s original.
-	Decent soundtrack and sound effects that complement the game well. The pilot’s voice is also well done.
-	Has that great arcade feel to it – as though you’re playing it on the SNES or on an arcade machine.
-	Has a nice intro and outro.
-	Fifteen cool looking trading cards to collect, if you’re into that sort of thing.
CONS:
-	With only a handful of levels, and each level being rather short, it’s not going to take you too long to finish.
-	Whilst the Pilot’s voice is cool, it can quickly get on your nerves, especially when you keep repeating the same levels. It also distracts you in boss fights. You can turn the voice off, but you still see the text at the bottom of the screen.
-	You can’t destroy those crystallised aliens.
OVERALL SCORE: 74/100

After over 100 hours in this game (including one day where I myself and friends played the first day of 14 hours straight) - I can safely say this game is beyond amazing.
The mechanics are brilliantly executed with thoughtful and inovative design. The game runs super smooth regardless of how many ships are in a sector and how many guns are shooting and how many crashes are happening. It is a joy to play with friends, offering long sections of time where we were not even talking but instead building our ships and fighting our own battles until suddenly we are all together, messing around and exploring the beautiful universe that has been created.
The procedural generation of sectors works exquisitly to offer a unique experience where ever you venture and enables an almost role playing style of game.
The vastness of activities is what has kept us coming back to the game and we are still discovering more and more things that have been implemented. Just recently using the trading systems and finally getting all the xotan artifacts. The sheer detail that has gone into what seems to be a passionately created game is the fundamental example of how a game should be made and an inspiration to me as a game developer, offering a goal to become as good as the creaters and to build something to such a standard.
Of course there are a few bugs but this is the most fleshed out 'early access game' that I have had the joy of playing (mostly the long silly ships that spin around when shot which can be very annoying to fight) with so many wonderful ways to play. I have a few notes of feedback which I would be happy to discuss with the developers and I look forward to watching this game grow. It deserves the attention of all who seek a true space exploration / sandbox / rpg / flying / trading / tactical game (not sure how to describe, it was a case of having to show my friends which quickly convinced them to get the game too)

Everyone knows Spelunky is hard. Hard as nails. -The art is deceptively cute, which contrasts the gameplay well.

-The music is atmospheric, if not a bit repetitive. Thats probably because I die a lot, though.
All-in-all, if you like difficult platformers, you're gonna love this one. Buy it at your own risk, though, because you may not see the light of day for a very, very long time.

What will set the game appart for fans of loot em' ups as I refer to this type of game are the following:
1. weapons and gear can be slotted with gems that can radically alter their parameters
2. The very easy application of mods means that even the least technically savvy can tailour this game to their liking with up to 10 mods of ther choosing which range from more classes to full game overhauls.
I would like to warn against one thing however, the enemy count gets real out of hand real fast and the unprepared or those that like to be more slow and methodical may find themselves overwhelmed and getting frustrated. I would very strongly recomend this game however to fans of RPG's loot based games and those that simply like vibrant and colourful game worlds. The boss fights I have had so far were very fun for me but as I mentioned before watch out for getting zerged by the little anklebitter enemies.
I would give this game a 8.4 out of 10 based on the fact that it is excellent value for money, wildly replayable and easily rivals Diablo III for only €5 at the time of writing, it simply is not balanced very well and this prevents it from getting a 10, which I will only give to a game that I think anyone will like without fail.

I remember the hype for this game being almost impossibly high, understandably so in order to follow in the legacy of the classic DOOM games.  Does it live up?  Almost, but I think its hard to think of a game that can build on the simple yet perfect conceptual chemistry from DOOM/II.  Instead with the new DOOM 3 engine id software designed the game to be more survival horror, where you engage one to a couple of enemies at a time in unexpected areas.  It doesn't go into modern/realism shooter territory either, only adding reloading, crouching and zoom to its gameplay.  It's not the best "action horror" game of its kind, but there are some things that make it a great game.
The amount of production quality put into this game is amazing.  The engine highlights include stencil shadows, high resolution textures, normal bump mapping, some blurring effects, etc, not to mention the detailed sound system.  SFX are scattered all over the levels, so the "music" you hear in the game is similar to a kinect movie set with machines everywhere.  The shadows create an atmosphere that perfectly encompasses you into the scenario that the story has presented for you.
DOOM 3's biggest flaw is perhaps the downside to its lighting engine.  Since this was made before ambient occlusion became standard, light sources make the levels visible only in small fields.  Everywhere else is hard to see, and makes the action part of the game much more annoying than it has to be.  This is because you have to switch between weapons and the flashlight to see what you're doing.
All of the weapons and monsters make up a great roster that mostly builds on the original games, except for the imp which looks out-of-place & is encountered way too many times in the whole game, which leads me to pacing.  My opinion is that the game starts out great, then the first half of the game stretches out the tech base with zombies/imp to the point where you get bored of repetition.  After getting some good weapons and meeting the more tougher monsters it picks up, and then you get to the hell level.  Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥  This level is by far the best in the game and feels like what DOOM 3 should be, buy it just to play this level.  It's probably the best representation of hell in a video game.
Unfortunately it's only one level (I would have liked to have the last third set in hell), you go back to same old tech levels again.  The enemy encounters are much more intense now, but it seems like finally enough, too late in the game.  With the pacing issues in mind, the game's length is definitely satisfactory, it took me about 12+ hours.

Doom 3 is a long-awaited game of Doom franchise, a dark first-person shooter and sequel to icon of FPS games. It was developed and released by id Software in 2004, after few delays and annual showcases at E3, with one of those alpha versions of a game ending up leaked. It differs in that it takes more on slower survival horror side while still remaining an old-school shooter. Even if very slow one.
It also got remade/remastered as part of BFG Edition deal, where it was brightened up, eliminating darkness aspect of gameplay. If you are one of those people who agree with joke that to copy Doom 3 gameplay you just have to turn off monitor screen and then direct flashlight at it, then you better check that version out instead.
It also was ported to Xbox. Sure thing it was cut down and simplicifed, but overall stayed true to the source. Didn't play it myself. One nice feature it had over PC version was 2-player coop, with levels being edited to fit into such gameplay. But since Xbox Live service was shut down it's not actual anymore. Sadly.
And so after launching the game and choosing ultra-quality, while laughing as I remember my old PC back few years ago struggling with low-quality setting and even freezing, I started a new game. And was awed. By how much more ugly it was compared to clean image I had in my memories.
You see, the game fails to recognise memory amount on modern hardware correctly and so it sets the textures quality to the minimum. Tweaking settings in-game will not change it. Instead you have to go to game folder and edit config file. I recommend looking at PCGamingWiki site which has a good example of Autoexec file.
But the small graphical problems still remained. Perhaps it's because I tweaked config files manually, but I had a few glitches. First, corpses of non-demons (and spiders) behaved funnily when gibbed. They would start dissintegrating, then when almost finished they would suddenly go back to look same as before, just without heads, and then they just suddenly dissapear few seconds later.
Another rendering problem would occur after getting to the next level during gameplay, where lights/shadows will start to slowly glitch out slightly here and there. Got tiresome to restart the game after few levels. Some on other hand were complained about objects fully dissapearing, so watch out.
And strangely enough game stutters here and there even on modern hardware. Some blame Steam version.
Nope, no widescreen by default. But people would just tweak config file and I never heard any complaining. Didn't check myself.
Multiplayer community is pretty much dead, I didn't find anybody playing game. Aside from that one time where they were playing on server with some mod, but I failed to join. So I don't have vanilla experience. From what I can tell multiplayer was pretty much tucked on the game, it being a small-scaled deathmatch, with 4 players limit. Things move fast though and even keeps same shadow play as single-player game. Still, I doubt that it was all that hot.
Community made a coop mod, by the way, maybe it's worth checking out with a friend.
Plot follows a lone space marine, who is not same guy as that Doom guy from original. And you are this time on Mars, where UA Corporations is having teleporter experiements, with half of a staff having asian look. After a short introudction levels, hell will break loose.
And so Doom 3, while keeping arsenal fo weapons and monster types recognisable from the original Doom games, albeit with style change, leans onto more of Survival Horror aspect. Now, mind it, it still has you run'n'gunning. Well, walk'n'gunning, as the game became much more slower-paced. You will walk slower and you will encounter far lesser enemies, somewhere like Quake 1. Which means less but a bit tougher. You will also have monsters ambushing you often, pouncing at you as soon as door opens and test your reaction like that, as well as just spawning into room. Spawn takes ages however and by the time that monster will actually teleport in you will be already aiming your shotgun up-close at the main mass.
Yes, it has design hiccups. But it does excells in atmoshpere and one of the main unique things it brings in is light/shadow play. As you know, engine blew everybody mind, at least in 2002 E3 event, with combination of bump-mapping and dynamic shadows, with shadow rendering the same no matter if it's level or model. While being sexily precise. While other games in the end would just put it in for farts, Doom 3 used it to enhance the style and gameplay. And boy, does it look still awesome. Not as pretty as Half-Life 2, mind it, but I really wanted to screenshot occasional room, seeing how all the monsters, bump-shaded sci-fi textures and action is illuminated. Shame that screenshot function on Steam overlay was disabled.
It also bring a thing or two in gameplay. Darkness is often covering parts of a room. You can either hold a flashlight or use a weapon, never both. As a result, you have to decide if you want to see where monster is or just shoot blindly. Actually, I pretty much recommend you to use flashlight as little as possible and never in a firefight. This way you will actually will be more effective, as you will learn to recognise monsters by the little lights they give away, whether fireballs or just their eyes, as well as recognising that monster is there by sounds they make. Most memoriable scene for me was after imp, fireball throwing medium demon, killed the only light in a room and two more arrived soon, as I had to tell away where they were by the light that their fireballs emitted.
No other FPS would combine both old-school shooting and survival horror aspect this way.
Well, if forget that for survival horror it gives way too much ammo. Or even for standard FPS. That, or maybe that's because I opened every closet. You see, game placed a lot of devices around the levels that would show you email and audio log of some person. They are mostly there to improve backstory. And to reward players who read them developers would put closet codes into logs too. But to be honest, while amusing, they weren't exciting and it only putted away players who didn't care about those things.
Was quite easy on Normal too. Should had increased difficulty. Hmmm.
Also, two lockers want you to check easter egg websites that actually was on Internet. If forget that it not redirects you to Doom3BFG site. Just search through some easter eggs website.
And yes, it tries to scare player all the time. And to be honest, it doesn't work. Not even as jumpscares. Or maybe it wasn't intented to be truly scary. In all honesty I just recommend to immerse yourself into atmoshpere and enjoy all the freaky stuff going on, taking it as a just cool special effect. Relax and enjoy.
Game also doesn't use music tracks, instead putting combination of ambient sound into every room. Some of those sounds were quite musical. It was a good experiement idea, but fails in this case, as I don't remember anything good. But I guess it works. Could use proper ambient track though.
It still is clunky at times, gameplay isn't as smooth as in original Doom. For example Shotgun isn't all that reliable, it can shoot in such way that every pellet will be outside of a center. Or focused on one side. Most of encounters don't last long. Melee zombies are just there to be beaten up by flashlight. It also overuses futurustic base setting, only once breaking into Hell level or such. Now, I loved taking slow and being careful in these dark rooms of UAC base, but even I grew tired toward the end. That and final boss sucks.
And well, it's plainly way too long for what it is.
But in the end, Doom 3 still manages to fill the niche. But you gotta love slow-paced actiony gameplay and to appericate some shadow work. Even if it's not 2004 anymore, it still looks nice too. And just have to be in the mood to love it.

I like this game, quite a bit. It's enough there to be an enjoyable game, however there is a lot of areas that could be improvded that would turn this into quite simply a masterpiece. I paid about $14 for this and played 32 hours (as of writing this), that definitely hits the right price point for me and what is better is all of those hours were spent being completely captivated by this game. I love(d) it!
I think I'm starting to get bored of it and I will explain why. Basically, the game is broken up into "tech tiers". To get cooler stuff, you need better materials. Better materials are closer to the center of the galaxy. Natrually, you start on the outside and work your way in.
Tier one: iron. It gets the job done.
Tier two: titanium. Introduces new tech and is lighter and stronger.
Tier three: naonite. Introduces new tech.
Tier four: trinium. Introduces one new tech and is lighter and stronger.
Tier five: xanion. Just stronger.
Tier five: ogonite. Did not explore.
Tier six: avorion. Did not explore.
The problem is, for me, at tier three, naonite, you've beaten the game. At least I felt like I beat the game. Why? Because the most signifigant tech you unlock at this tier (and what I think is the most significant in the game) is shielding. Shields allow you to make your ship VERY tanky, almost immediately upon equipping you are nearly invincible. Some weapons can penetrate but they are rare. Others must wear your shields down until they can even scratch you. The big problem is that by the time you hit tier 4, everything there is useless. Yeah, you unlock one new tech but it is so unneccesary. By that point I have so much naonite that my ship can take on three large fleets of anything at my tier singlehandedly. I barely dug into the xanion tier, hoping that maybe things got a bit more interesting, but alas they did not.
So, here I am. My biggest enemies are asteriods (flying into them often has explosive results!). Yeah I could just B-line to the center of the galaxy to find a challenge but I just felt disconnected at that point. Why is tier 4-6 even here? Why do they exist? They do nothing for me. That said, I do love this game. I think they are looking at making shields less tanky. I also think they are looking at adding more of a story which would really help. At the moment you are kind of just a dude, yourself if you will, and the game is what you make it. Maybe I will play again after a few updates. For now, I think I'll dock my ship and watch how the game grows.

Torchlight II is like a more colourful and lightearted diablo II which is as accurate a synopsis as I can give. In a nutshell this game is about choosing one of several distinct classes whom each have 3 skill trees and going out into the world. This time to stop an evil wizard's rampage instead of a Devil's. What will set the game appart for fans of loot em' ups as I refer to this type of game are the following:
1. weapons and gear can be slotted with gems that can radically alter their parameters
2. The very easy application of mods means that even the least technically savvy can tailour this game to their liking with up to 10 mods of ther choosing which range from more classes to full game overhauls.
I would like to warn against one thing however, the enemy count gets real out of hand real fast and the unprepared or those that like to be more slow and methodical may find themselves overwhelmed and getting frustrated. I would very strongly recomend this game however to fans of RPG's loot based games and those that simply like vibrant and colourful game worlds. The boss fights I have had so far were very fun for me but as I mentioned before watch out for getting zerged by the little anklebitter enemies.
I would give this game a 8.4 out of 10 based on the fact that it is excellent value for money, wildly replayable and easily rivals Diablo III for only €5 at the time of writing, it simply is not balanced very well and this prevents it from getting a 10, which I will only give to a game that I think anyone will like without fail.

TLDR: Spend your well-earned money elsewhere. Infinitesimal Point is a borefest of a Twinstick Shooter/RPG hybrid, with monotonous gameplay that lasts 5 hours.
Where do I start...
Infinitesimal Point plays as a Twinstick Shooter and RPG hybrid, that feebly attempts to combine top-down shooting action with Leveling Mechanics. After the cutscenes that reveal the games premises (your arm is chopped off and you are sent to another world where some mystery entity replaces your arm with a bionic one), you will feel this game's slow pace. This will allow you to notice some admittedly good traits about the game such as:
1. Graphics - Well... it's not THAT good. But it is pleasant to me at least. You'll notice that the protagonist's "shooting arm" points to where you are aiming relative to his body's position (it looks funny at times). The visual effects of your shots and spells do look believable.
2. The Leveling System - this game does uniquely blend stat management with the acquisition of abilities. On the games "ability chart", you will see a four cornered shape that will eventually expand as you increase your stats. Ability icons that have been "covered" by the expanding shape are considered to be obtained and thus usable. The slow pace of the game allows you some time to plan ahead as to what stats you want to level and which skills you want to obtain.
... however...
Past the first hour, you will immediately start to feel as sluggish as the game's pace yourself. You will find yourself utterly bored and willing to quit the game for something else because of the following.
1. Swarming - the game does NOT introduce monsters that are fought in unique ways. Monsters are typically ranged or melee, and will mostly vary in speed and the projectile they shoot. Instead, the game will habitually swarm you with bunches and bunches of enemies that would almost run towards you SINGLE FILE if it weren't for the fact that they spawn in different points. Really, if you use the fire skill (which shoots in a straight line) you will find that the AI will easily be made to behave this way if you slightly adjust the angle you are backpedaling with. This is the same type of gameplay you will encounter from Hour 1 to Hour 5.
2. Monster Spawns - Alright, so they swarm you. Okay. That means we have to move carefully and slowly. You move to an area, alright it's clear. You continue to move forward and you begin to see monsters spawn in front of you. But what's this, you suddenly see monsters spawning from areas that YOU ARE VERY SURE YOU HAVE ALREADY EXPLORED. This immediately throws strategic maneuvering right out of the ♥♥♥♥ing window and making it clear that the only available option is to face the bunches of beasts head on. Oh, did I mention that for as long as monsters are around the objectives that you can normally interact with using the E button are FREAKING DISABLED UNTIL ALL THE MONSTERS ARE DEAD?
3. Missing Skill/Weapon Information - Alright, okay. So, this game wants you to fight head on. Fine, let's build our character for that purpose and optimize our weapon selection (as in setting them on the hotkeys) for this scenario. Since we're facing them head on, let's use the game's "shotgun" equivalent. It says "1" beside the "stopwatch" icon indicated on the weapon description. That must mean it takes one second in between shots, and it does! But what's this? After firing four shots, my weapon just ceases to function for som- *death*.
The game leaves out critical information for the weapons and skills you obtain. For instance, the game doesn't tell you that your "shotgun" has four shots, and afterwards you won't be able to fire until the icon for said weapon reverts to normal color (it turns reddish when on "reload"). Another example is that enemies burned by the "fire blast" ability can burn others by being in physical contact with them. This omission of information makes your weapons unreliable, and when the weapon's disadvantages kick in, it usually ends in death by monster swarm. While you can switch to other weapons and skills using the hotkeys, they won't always be fit for the situation or something you're not accustomed to- *death*
4. Horrendous Hitboxes - But, hey! It should be your responsibility to familiarize yourself with the weapons you have, right? Right, so let's practice by finding these monsters. Let's place our "crosshair" over these monsters and fire. We'll see what these weapons do to our ene- wait. The bullets just pass through. My crosshair is DIRECTLY over the stationary target and it just passes through. Oh wait, maybe we have to place the crosshair behind the targe- that didn't work either. Oh wait, I -*death*
You can find a stationary target, place your "crosshair" over/behind it (along the trajectory), and you'll hit maybe 50% of the time. Geez, what is up with the hitboxes in this game? You can shoot the shotgun point blank and have the "pellets" appear to pass through the target dealing ZERO damage. Urrrggggh. This will sometimes force you to use your "skills" sub-optimally, because they're marginally more reliable than the weapons. I hope you have lots of mana, before the buzzer kicks in signifying that you can't use the skills anymore. Speaking of which...
5. Lack of Feedback - There are sfx that represent levelling up. You'll barely hear them through the rest of the sfx, and there's no visual feedback to complement it. By the time you realize, you'd have about 10 stat points (5 levels worth) unspent. There are sfx for when you can't use a weapon/skill, but yet again no visual feedback. Good luck figuring out why. Am I clicking too fast? Or is the weapon "reloading" (see above)? Am I out of mana? Is the skill on cooldown? Let's check. Aha! I kno- *death*
*Ahem* There are sfx for when you get hit and thankfully, it does come with visual feedback (blood spatters). But you will barely see this because of the camera. Which reminds me...
6. Clunky Camera Controls - The camera starts so impractically zoomed into you, but thankfully you can zoom out with the mousewheel. But what's this, a roof? A lamppost? A bridge? Quick, game! Zoom into the player so he can focus on the character instead of the bunches of monst- *death*
7. Boring Boss Battles - Finally, a Boss! It's been a slog so far, but this is finally a new enemy to fight. I can hardly wait. This is exciting! I wonder what monstrosities we have to- huh? It's small, just like the enemies we've fought up until now. Looks the same too. Behaves the same too. Is that it? Seriously!? What the FUUUUUUUUU- *suicide*
But hey, at least they have more hp, which means it'll take longer to ki- oh... *death*
8. The Story - Well... I suppose we can enjoy the story. What's that? What is this for a place? You can't answer question? Well, then. I don't know what is happen. Smoke and guns. The whole world is explo- *translation error*
9. Nimrod's Navigation - ♥♥♥♥ it. I'm getting tired of this. Let's just make sure to finish the game. Good thing I can press "F" to let me know where to go nex- wait. This is a dead end. Wtf is this? Where am I supposed to go from here? Do I have to explore? Fine. Wait, not fine, i'm stuck in another swarm of- *death*
Alright. Maybe that was an exaggeration. Pressing F does point you in the right direction most of the time. But everynow and then it'll funnily point to a dead end, or that stupid elevator that you know you've already been into, or anything BUT where you really need to go.
After suffering these 9 things for 5.2 hours, I finally finished the game on Normal Difficulty. This allows you to unlock the "massacre" difficulty, but at this point you won't be invested in a new game +, let alone one more minute of the sodding game. The conclusion is simple. I can't recommend it. If you've bought it prior to this review, it's at least a functioning game. However, you can easily do better with other games.

Lots of good things to say about this game, but they've already been covered.  I'm giving this game a thumbs-up, but I'm focusing on the negatives in hope that some of these things can be improved.
1) The targeting cursor is difficult to see - especially in brightly-lit areas, and while the cursor is moving.  This is probably the most important issue.  If the targeting cursor was outlined in black - or customizable in the settings - it would be an improvement.
2) The zoom is problematic.  I like being able to use the mouse-wheel to zoom - but I do NOT like the game automatically adjusting the zoom when I'm close to certain objects. If I'm running from several enemies, I don't want them to suddenly be out of my vision range just because I walked too close to a tree, or behind an obstacle.  Other games manage this by keeping the zoom constant, and making players / enemies visible through the obstruction as an outline or shadow.
Also, the maximum zoom-out needs to be increased.  The player should never have to "blink" to an off-screen location, and hope for the best.
3)  I haven't been playing the game for long, but many of the early upgades border on useless.  The only one of value seems to be the shotgun.  This may change as I play longer, of course.
4) There's no noticable notification when my character reaches a new level.  Even once in a while I'll check, and discover that I've gone up two or three levels without realizing it.
5) The "enemy locator" at the bottom-left of the screen borders on useless.  The red dots indicating enemies are barely noticable.  I've been playing the game for an hour or so, and I just noticed the dots.  Given the limited vision range in the game, a system like this is useful - but it needs to be improved.
==============
Again - this is a good game, and it has a LOT going for it.  I'm just pointing out a few of the negatives in hopes that some of them are addressed in future patches.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Infinitesimal Point is an overhead twin-stick shooter with RPG-like character development in a science-fiction setting.
In the game you play an unnamed man attacked by a creature late at night on Earth, teleported accidentally through a portal to another planet. Losing your arm in the attack, you wake up to find a cybernetic arm, complete with a claw hand capable of firing plasma bolts, grafted to your body. A slightly dysfunctional AI introduces itself as your saviour and asks you to complete an errand for it. And so it begins.
Graphics - The graphics in Infinitesimal point are excellent. There's great lighting and shadows and the main character model is detailed and well animated. The game makes use of a very convincing DoF effect, blurring the tops of tall objects close to the game camera in order to focus on the action.
Explosions are a bit disappointing, though, and water doesn't look that great.
Sound - Sound is good, but mostly not outstanding. Weapons sound a little underpowered, but music and other effects are generally good. The music works up into a more electronic sort of beat that I really like, but which may not be to everyone's tastes.
Gameplay - Infinitesimal Point is a twin-stick shooter, through and through. It's crying out for full controller support, but at the moment it only natively supports keyboard and mouse.
Rather than going down the path of many games in this genre and have you collect new weapons or money to buy new weapons, Infinitesimal Point instead has you gain levels as you progress, unlocking skills from the skill tree. Spending points in different directions in this skill tree unlocks new powers for your cyber arm, improving upon the basic plasma bolt available at the start. Points can also improve in the direction of your 'blink' ability, which you can use to teleport short distances out of trouble, with each stat you increase giving you different 'powers' from your arm. This allows for some variety in play style.
Pros:
+ great graphics
+ character progression similar to a RPG game
+ interesting plot
Cons:
- poor English translation (e.g. "What is this for a place?")
- no native controller support; keyboard and mouse controls can be a little fiddly
Infinitesimal Point is a fun twin-stick shooter with great graphics, character progression, and an interesting story to tell. Recommended.

It's pretty good.
The graphics are cutting-edge, the framerate is consistent and I got over 100 FPS in many cases, dipping down to 50 FPS at the worst of times rarely.  Everything works.  It doesn't even feel much like an indie game, this is a polished product.  I was shocked that a developer actually *finished* a game for once.
So in this case, we have to consider the game is technically perfect and just focus on the gameplay itself.  Well, I sure would have loved controller support.  This is a twin stick shooter and it even has a nice arm movement (animation) where you can run forwards but shoot backwards or in any direction, and I found the mouse control to work fine but I would have really enjoyed it more with a controller.  The whole game is set up perfectly for a controller if it was supported.
I found the viewing angle to be a little bit short.  As in, you really can't see what you're doing.  Thankfully, you can press a button which brings up an arrow pointing towards your goal, so you can't ever be lost.  You don't really need to see what you're doing in this case, but you'll be playing at the maximum zoom level.  Zoom in only to get a closer look at something, but I really wish I could tilt the camera a little bit further back so I could enjoy the closer zoom because everything is so highly detailed.  You have this one dashing ability which is used as a "jump" in an early platform puzzle and it is also really handy in combat since you can get to a safe distance in a flash, but the distance you dash is very far and it is almost the entire length of the camera view.  So again. it would have been better to allow us to zoom the camera out further so we could be more strategic in where we dashed, instead of just blasting in one general direction.
I liked the auto-healing.  If you are super low on health, let's say 2%, it auto-heals to 50% in just a few seconds outside of combat and the 51%-100% healing is also auto-healing but very very slow.  It's a very good mixture.  I never got far enough in my session to experience any abilities or other weapons, but the whole time I found the combat to be fair.  I died a couple of times, but it was not impossible to consistently win.
This game did an EXCELLENT job at in-game cutscenes.  They look very professional.
All in all, I love it.  But I would actually sit down and play it a bit more if I could use my controller!  :)

Whenever a boss is reached it's almost as if the puzzle section never existed because of how much of a reflex-incentive game it suddenly becomes. It's even mentioned on the Steam store page that it's short and that it's "more puzzle than SHMUP".
There's more control over the movement with a controller than there is using a keyboard. Can't rebind the controls but instead they only give you 3 keyboard control schemes and only 2 controller schemes. I've got more problems with the 2 controller schemes because all that they  use and switch around are (A) and (B) which does "Action" and "Cancel" with "Action" being the "Fire" button when in-game. For a game where you can shoot as fast as you press the button I always figured to put that on the left face button (X) but I don't even get a choice on that matter.
There are 5 missions represented by planets to freely choose from and one unlockable final mission after completing the 5. Each one can be completed in a couple of minutes without having to start over upon death. There's a how-to on how the puzzle works and it's a little harder to actually do properly when put into practice since you're constantly dealing with the auto-scrolling  and trying to stay alive so as not to be crushed by enemies that head toward the bottom of the screen. Once this puzzle section is over though and the boss fight comes then it suddenly becomes a bullet-hell-lite of sorts, almost as if the puzzle section just became irrelevant.
All of the bosses hardly vary from one another; their attacks are hardly different from one another aside from some very slight speed, angle, & visual changes and each boss always has one bullet spreading attack that's no different from what the previous boss does.
In the puzzle sections for every mission you're supposed to collect three highly limited ship upgrades that you can apply to whatever ship you have and collect these True-Ending-material Emeralds. Once you collect whatever collectibles you find you can die or finish the mission and they'd stay collected so even if you didn't grab all in one run you can go back to the mission and grab 'em. For each mission there are three Emeralds and three upgrades to grab.
Enemies & such that are destroyed in missions drop currency that's only used for buying new & unlocked ships that have different effects and stats from one another. Ships are unlocked upon completion of already uncompleted missions. The upgrades can boost their stats to a specified max but there are more ships & stats than there are upgrades throughout the entire game so you're strongly encouraged to save them until you unlock the final and higher-in-stats ships.
There's not much replayability since all missions & bosses are practically similar to one another and it's a short game overall. After beating the base game you unlock a Boss Rush mode where you're pitted against all the bosses one at a time. Whatever ship you choose for that mode can only take one hit of damage but is highly buffed out everywhere else for quicker kills. After that there's really not much else to do with the game.

Doom 3 was a hit when it came out and is an absolutely necessary game to play if you are a fan of the original doom series.  There are pros and cons, however, to this game.  It seems that id tried harder to create a horror game than an action game.  The original Doom games were screens filled with enemies to take out with over the top action.  Here the action is still over the top, but you fight against a maximum of 5 creates at a time at the most, and not screens full of enemies.  This changes the pace of the game and lowers the bar for the action a bit.  Also, by trying to make it scary, the levels are very dark.  This is too bad because the graphics are beautiful, but hard to see when the lighting is so low.  I would say though that the graphics compared to Source didn't age as well when compared to today's graphic abilities.
However, this is still Doom.  This is still a game of kill or be killed and you are still a bad♥♥♥♥♥with a gun.  All of the old guns come back from the previous games and they feel great.  The levels are corridor levels, and not open areas, but that helps with making this more of a horror game.  The sounds are good and the music is pretty much the same as quake with a heavy metal focus.
Do I like this game better than I loved the original Doom, no.  But I can't not recommend this game, as the graphics and its brand name set a standard that all other games of the future look to copy or surpass.  id did not make the impact with Doom 3 as they did with the original Doom, but this is still worth your time playing.

I'm not generally a big RTS player, but this game has such depth (and a steep learning curve) that it has sucked me in. Great fun to plan out and build decks around a strategy or style of play you have in mind. I much prefer this style of game, in which you call in and deploy units, to the type of RTS games where you have to build and manage a base.
If you're on the fence about it, there's no question that you should pick it up next time it goes on a $10 sale-- that is an absolute steal. I'm also glad I picked up the DLC nations as they are all fun to play and tinker with.

This is my first RTS purchased on Steam and it's certainly going to be my last because no RTS compares to Wargame: Red Dragon in terms of depth, eye candy, difficulty, realism and entertainment!
I don't even need to entail why. Look gameplay footage of this game. Now compare that to spamming bunch of units of one type in a tight cluster attacking another set of units in a tight cluster with a 5 inch distance between the two groups like you see in other RTS's. Case closed.
If you're a scrub-weakling like me then I hope you have a lot of patience and love for the game element because this game is ABSOLUTELY ruthless and you really have to dig across the internet to get every bit of knowledge needed just to figure out what to do. Then comes execution and I find this game challenges your micromanaging abilities but not so much that it's Starcraft AZN APM or die level. It's just that you need both to do well.
I still recommend this game to beginners because there are valid alternatives via doing comp stomps (You and rl people versus the AI), Single-Player Skirmish Mode or just simply finding a weaker player than you. Just note that you should pursue 1v1's instead because 10v10's diminish your ability to influence games. Plus, all RTS's are a pain to learn so really seeking easier RTS to get gud at will still leave you feeling frustrated, especially since this is the BEST RTS ever in terms of realism, graphics and gameplay YET YOU DON'T OWN IT because you're still playing Battle of Toontow...err I mean RA 3.
Expert RTS'ers should buy this because I'm obviously qualified to tell you so. Really though, I'm not a expert RTS'er so I'm in the dark about everything.
Watching replays is quite a satori though. Especially if you're a beginner and you win you first match and it's well executed.
Also qualifies as a educational game. Good for the children to teach or just those who like learning new things about real life military equipment and outfits.
Community is toxic. Much worse than the World of Tanks community from my experience.
Tl:Dr: Best RTS ever with the same hard af learning curve. Good for beginners because all RTS'es are hard to learn either way and might as well pick up a S tier RTS. Extreme challenge with extreme rewards.

What is cool about it:
-It's Free2Play (so don't expect to have some Battlefield 1 graphics),
-You don't need a gaming beast to run this game,
-You don't have to pay to access everything this game has to 'offer',
-Gameplay is quite good for a Free2Play.
The fails:
-The Premium shop is TOO expensive. The minimum you can spend is 6€, with which you aren't going to be buy yourself much. Even if you spend a lot, it will just go away too fast. I definitely don't recommand you to purchase premium stuff, unless you want to support the developpers...
-The in-game credits go away too quickly, everything is expensive (again), only mods are easily affordable,
-The various upgrades, guns and vehicules, you can have (by farming ribbons--->exp), can be sometimes really though to get.
-Switching from a career to an other is not cheap, plus if you want to switch back to your old one, you gonna have to pay again!
-At the beginning, you need to play a lot to get credits and you will die a lot.
My recommandations for new players:
-The first soldier you have, don't you ever change it's career, unless you are sure you don't want to go back, else it's a waste of time and money.
-Play only one faction to farm faster. Nazis generally have the best guns, Soviet guns are good in average, and they have a super, but hard to get, anti-light vehicule rifle, the PTRD (I kinda love it :3), and American weapons are a bit similar to German ones, but not as good.
-Don't spam grenades, it's expensive,
-Try to play with friends, it's always good to have someone that can help you, and with who you can have fun (right ?).
I'd give an 8/10 to H&G, because its fails aren't too important, compared to other F2P such as WoT, WT and many others, were you need to farm a lot more, for not much...

This epic game is, in my opinion, the best game in the Alien and Predator series by a huge margin.
Its single player storyline is nealy non-existent, but the levels are large and fun to play through, especially compared to modern hand holding "corridor shooters". Once the single player is completed, each species can unlock five bonus missions that enrich the single player experience by allowing that species to play on a level associated with one of the other two.
On top of that, most of the single player missions (and bonus levels) have "side missions" that unlock single player cheat modes upon completion. These cheat modes allow you to alter your single player experience in various ways, such as setting your enemies on fire, turning the level upside down exc'.
The cheat modes and bonus missions add a great deal of replayability to the game.
Multiplayer wise, the game has a bunch of fun gaming options varying from the good old Deathmatch and Species Deathmatch to a Coop mode and even unique game types such as tag games and Last Man Standing.
The multiplayer community for this game is still alive, but remains small and casual, which is a huge achievement in my opinion considering this game is 14 years old and managed to change 3 client softwares in that time.
Most of the veteran players in this game know one another, and are generally open to newcomers, so the best way to get a game going is to join a community group and get to know some of the regulars.
Due to the small amount of players, the scene is no longer competitive. However, the game does provide a high skill ceiling for those who seek a good challenge.
Some of the weapons in this game are frowned upon by the community, such as the Predator Disc and Pistol, as well as the Marine Grenade Launcher and Skeeter Launcher, but they are also easy to disable when hosting games.
To sum up, this game is definitely worth your 5$ (or less, if it is on sale), even if you are not an Alien/Predator fan. You will get your money's worth and more on the single player content alone.
