Super Crate Box is an addiction.
Super Crate Box is all about collecting crates. These crates not only contain weapons that help you defeat the enemies falling your way, but they also count as your score, meaning while you can kill as many gargantuan green monsters as you want, it won't mean anything unless you get more crates. These crates also contain random weapons, with more weapons unlocked as you collect more crates, meaning you don't know what you'll be using when the next crate comes your way.
While the amount of weapons, enemy types and levels are limited, the controls and level design go a long way to making sure that Super Crate Box is infinitely replayable. The controls are precise and responsive, meaning every mistake made is a mistake YOU made, and not a mistake caused by floaty controls or laggy responses. The level design is also wonderful; single-screen arenas make sure that the game isn't unnecessarily complex, and since they never change over time, you grow accustomed to the lay-out.
The only problems that Super Crate Box has are due to the Steam release. The Steam overlay is non-existent, and leaderboards are not supported, meaning that if you've had a particularly good run (like my best score of 602 crates), the score won't be uploaded.
Gameplay-wise, however, everything is perfect. Since the game is very easy to learn, almost anyone can play it, but it takes dedication to build up the skill required to get better scores. That, plus the "just-one-more-try" appeal of the game, makes Super Crate Box a game I'd highly recommend to everyone.

Super Star Path has a cool hook; a puzzle/shooter combo. Unfortunately that hook doesn't really lend itself to being endlessly playable like other puzzle games nor is it an especially challenging shmup. Let me tell you why.
First and foremost, there is a huge missed opportunity here; there is no arcade/score attack mode. There is a story mode and after you beat that, there is a boss rush mode. I 100% the game in a little over an hour. Mileage may vary some, but I can't see most people spending much more than that on this game, which is a shame because the actual gameplay is solid and the music and graphics are appealing. I get that the game itself is somewhat randomly generated. I get that it may have been technically challenging creating an endless arcade score attack mode. But without it the game is over so quickly that it's hard not to feel a bit ripped off, even at the lower price range. Heck, I got it on sale for $1.99 and I still feel a little ripped off, and I feel like a bad person for admitting that.
Also, the game has strong cursing in it for pretty much no reason. The pilot will randomly say a few one liners here and there, and then suddenly he'll drop the f-bomb. It's strange, because he also says "heck" every so often, so tonally it just seems like a strange decision. Anyways, if you were planning on letting a young child play the game because it looks like a harmless retro game (which it otherwise totally is), maybe reconsider, or mute it I guess.
Let's talk more about its good qualities. It has a rockin' soundtrack, emulating that 90's Sega Genesis/Megadrive sound. Likewise, the game visually looks like it would have fit right into an arcade in the 90's. The game has the player shooting different colored aliens on a vertically scrolling plain. Whenever you shoot an alien that is in a group of similar colored aliens, the whole group will explode. However, aliens that are not the same color that are on the edges of a chain will be crystallized. What that means is that you cannot pass through them and they can no longer be destroyed. It makes for an interesting mechanic, occasionally turning the game into more of a maze than a shooter/puzzle game, and it was fun navigating through the levels. I died at least a couple times by getting stuck due to poor planning on my part.
In addition to clearing out a path from the colored aliens, there are also different kinds of obstacles and traps in every stage. It reminded me of Super Puzzle Platformer in that sense. Difficulty ramps slowly, and while you collect gems and power ups (which you keep even if you die), you can plan on buying more powerful ships with better abilities and specs. There is a boss encountered at the end of each stage and would really only give you a hard time if you've never played a shoot em up before. For someone who enjoys bullet hell shooters specifically, these bosses will seem like jokes.
As I mentioned previously, the main issue with this game is its short length. It has minimal replay value aside from earning the true ending, which I did on my first attempt. To get the true ending you are supposed to collect 3 emeralds across all six levels. These emeralds drop from special black colored aliens, and like gems and power ups, are kept even if you die mid-stage. The game could have been slightly (very slightly) longer if the emeralds were only collected upon completion of a stage, but that isn't how it works. Additionally, when levels are replayed, the level bosses are not re-battled. The stage simply ends and you go back to level select.
There is a boss rush mode that is unlocked when the game is completed. It has a leaderboard (seen outside of the game itself, through Steam's interface). I got 23 seconds on my second try. That isn't really bragging; it's more of an indicator of how easy the mode is. You see, the ships are all fully powered up, except that they only have one health point, so you can't take any damage. But when you're fully powered up and just spam the shoot button, most bosses are down within just a few seconds.
Speaking of leaderboards, there are timed leaderboards per stage, which doesn't make sense to me. The level scrolls at a fixed rate, so I don't understand at all why there are speed leaderboards per stage. I don't think the boards are for that though; I think it's for how quickly you beat the bosses encountered on that stage. But since you don't fight the bosses after having beaten them within the stage itself, it seems like a completely pointless feature.
I can't in good conscience recommend this game, despite enjoying it in many ways. It's just too short and simple to satisfy on a long-term level, and even at its low price point, there are other similar games that are better worth your money. That Super Puzzle Platformer game I mentioned earlier, for example; it's great and has lots of replay value. This however was just a somewhat amusing distraction that only lasted for an hour.

Super Star Path caught my eye because of its appealing pixel art, but I really jumped on board because it is a unique blend of puzzle and shmup. Every level is broken into two parts. You start off confronting masses of multicolored, stationary aliens as you push forward. Shooting them makes them explode in connected colored chains, but there's a catch - if a chain explosion hits an alien of a different color, it will be frozen solid and become an indestructible obstacle. In other words, you can't go into every stage shooting all nilly-willy or else you will create an impassable wall and resign yourself to death. Once you pass the aliens you go into a boss confrontation, where the game turns into a true bullet hell shmup. It's an odd combination juxtaposing planning ahead and methodically cutting through walls of enemies with frantic boss fights requiring raction time and good hand-eye coordination.
Each level has unique stage hazards that make things that much harder, and there are 10 ships you unlock gradually with increased stats and unique features (immunity to certain hazards, gem doubler, etc). Hidden in every stage are three aliens holding upgrade points you can use you increase your ships attack power, hit points, and speed. There are also three black aliens per stage holding green emeralds as per the storyline, and collecting them all will get you the true ending when you beat the final boss.
It's a short game. I beat it completely - every stage, every item, all ships unlocked, boss rush - in about 2 hours. Yet I feel satisfied. It's a tight package, with a great soundtrack to boot. Strangely, you can't reassign upgrade points, and there are a finite amount you can get in the game. And some of the later levels feel cheap with an abundance of hazards and chains of aliens you have to hit just right or end up screwing yourself. But I can forgive its faults because the overall package was worth a couple of moments of frustration.
Pros
- Unique blend of gameplay
- Clean and bright pixel art and color palette
- Awesome retraux soundtrack
- Cheap price
Cons
- Short
- Upgrade points can't be reassigned
- Cheap hazards late in the game
- Some of the ships are useless
I'd love to see a sequel expand on this game's concepts!

Super Star Path is a great little game !
Mixing Shoot'em up and Puzzle games doesn't sound like an obvious idea, but it works really well in game. Every level is composed of two parts: one where you have to find your way through a maze of enemies (the Puzzle part) and one where you must kill a dangerous boss (the Shoot'em up part).
The real idea of this game is in the Puzzle part: when shooting an alien, you kill it as well as all the other same-colored aliens near him. However, that also crystalised the aliens near by, turning them into indestructible walls. In order to reach the end of the level, you'll have to cleverly choose which aliens to shoot!
In addition of this, you can also buy new ships with specific caracteristics (more powerful, doesn't get hit by small bullets etc.) which you can upgrade using gems you can find in the puzzle parts. You'll also have to collect 3 emeralds in every level in order to finish the game. Then, you'll have to kill every boss with only one HP. Good luck on that!
Tl;dr: Great idea, well executed, great art style and atmosphere, with the only down point of the game being short.

DOOM 3 flawlessly creates an immersive survival horror fps, which is great fun to play through and explore. The game is genuinely challenging on harder difficulties, including Nightmare mode, and features excellent gunplay.
Sound design is masterful, as well as the game's artistic style. Everything looks and sounds right in every situation. The aesthetic of Hell in particular is particularly unnerving, you can tell that the guys who made this had a good time imaging creepy stuff.
All the guns from DOOM return, from the lowly pistol, all the way up to the devastating BFG 9000. Another of the game's strong points is that every gun, including the aformentioned pistol, feels powerful.
The monsters also return, with a few new ones, and have been given (at the time) modern facelifts. Imps are just as annoying as ever, and Hell Knights are particularly terrifying.
The game is also jam packed with lore and collectable goodies to discover. Read the PDAs of your fallen comrades to reveal personal emails and voice recordings which tell you everything about the situation, as well as other funny situations they may have been in.
All in all, DOOM 3 provides a memorable horror FPS experience which, despite its age, holds up well to this day. If you don't own this, get it, whether it's on sale or not.

This is the most detailed, tactical RTS you've ever played. It is quite well balanced even for multiplayer, with no single team holding advantages that can't be counteracted by other teams. The community is generally pretty good. You do occasionally find people surrendering too early in multiplayer games, especially 10v10, but if you're playing 10v10 you're not taking advantage of how tactical the game can be.
Micro is somewhat important but not to the same degree as in other RTS - tactics is at least as important. The wide variety of nations and coalitions to play and the variety of units within them will see you not get bored.
This game rewards attention to detail, well-planed logistics, knowledge of each army and general tactics, and dedication bordering on study.
The multiplayer community is still active several years after release.
The bad:
There is a steep learning curve to this game. It is likely more complex than other RTS you have played before. There is no build queue so preserving your units, accomplishing actual objectives and getting your logistics right will be unfamiliar to someone coming from other games. However, you can download other people's decks (army composition), watch replays online and there are extensive beginner and advanced guides out there.
Buy this game. You will come to judge all other RTS by it.

Wargame: Red Dragon is the third installment of the Wargame franchise, and is an excellant work of Eugen.
+ Great gameplay experience.
+ Variety of nations: 17 in base game and additional 4 in DLC.
+ Large variety of units with deck building system allowing to customize your play style.
+ Well-designed textures, even able to run on older hardware.
+ Modding capacity available for those interested.
+ Replays
+ Both small-scale and large-scale battles are available.
+ Customizeable match settings
+ Large variety of different sized maps, each well-done.
+ A strong 8/10
- UI is distinguished, yes, but could be more customizeable.
- AI is simplistic and difficulties of AI offer little change.
- More available default decks, such as one for more prominant "coalitions," or pair-ups of nations, would allow for new players to adapt to the deck-building system better than one or two default decks.
- Multiplayer community is uncommitted to the game, as multiple players may leave in the middle of a match for trivial reasons.
- Campaigns are lacking and no additional content is provided for them.
- Naval units are lacking and no additional content is provided for them.
* Not base building RTS
* Multiplayer focused
* Takes time to learn units and how to use them well. Game does provide armory where player can view every units characteristic.
Credit to Sunbeam for original review format.

Lots of reviews complaining about the DLC prices, but no-one is forcing you to buy. There's actually lots to do in the core game. I picked it up years ago for -85% and it's been significantly developed since then. It's very meditative to drive the train. If you see it deeply discounted, give it a chance.

A simulation that exists somewhere between 'game' and 'realistic'.  There is a variety of driving offered, from high-speed modern electrics operating fast passenger routes, diesel shunting in rail yards, to vintage steam locos.  Train driving itself isn't so much of a challenge as operating to a tight timetable without giving your passengers a severe case of whiplash or screeching to a stop about three miles beyond the station platform!  A range of difficulties and lengths of play are offered in both career and non-career missions.
Driving a more modern train included in the base game is easy: start, stop and a few speed settings in between when using basic controls.  You can opt for more advanced controls and difficulty options (like your train being forced into an emergency stop if you run a red signal - it will take you about 900 years to get back to speed again so kiss goodbye to your timetable)!  The difficulty comes in maintaining safety while keeping to a brutally tight real-world timetable.  Steam locos are considerably more difficult, but this is where Train Simulator is really immersive.  The levels and dials are best operated in 3D for a full simulation experience, and you probably won't be able to see clearly where you're going - that's IF you're going, rather than chugging out a lot of black smoke!
Also included in the product are all the tools to make your own routes.  You are rather left to your own devices with what appears to be a very confusing interface at first.  However, quite a few of the DLC routes now sold through Steam started life as fan-made routes using the tools.  There are likely some decent user-created guides out there by now (this game started out as Rail Simulator many years ago so it's been around for a long time now).
The UK, US and Germany are heavily supported (the base game was originally only these countries and players who went on to make DLC routes tended mostly to be from those same countries).  There is (slowly) increasing support for other countries through third-party developers offering coverage of some routes in Canada, China, Netherlands and South Africa for example.  Mostly, this has been left to gamers to provide this content, but much of it is every bit as high quality as the base game assets, if not better - and has started to earn its creators some money.
Mostly, the negativity has been because of the DLC pricing, with some claiming that it will cost you in the region of $5000 to buy it all.  But they miss the point.  You're not meant to 'buy it all' (and if you did, there probably wouldn't be enough years of 'useful life' of your PC, your version of Windows or life-span on Planet Earth to play it all).  No, the idea is that there might be 2-3 routes that interest you in addition to those provided in the game, and a few locos that you like or which suit your routes.  As a guide, since 2009, I've acquired in the region of 7 routes, and perhaps twice that number in locos, and have had literally hundreds of hours of play from them.  Although DLC locos are sold with missions that might depend on a particular DLC route, if you don't have the route you can still place the loco on one of your owned routes.  There are hobby sites such as UKTrainSim as well as Steam Workshop that offer free content, and plenty of third-party sites like JustTrains that sell advanced DLC.  The DLC made by the game's developers is usually half-price during Steam sales, with mega-bundles being an excellent way to grab a lot of content relatively cheaply.
In a highly moddable game such as this, there are also the inevitable bugs.  In the base game, these are fairly minimal, but additional content from third-party creators can be the cause of crashes and failing routes (as usual with any game that supports player content, mods can clash or cause crashes, and not all creators update their creations to keep in line with each iteration of Train Simulator).
Finally, performance is a constant bugbear.  This game has always been a mixed bag on performance, with some heavy city locations with busy rail traffic and overhead catenary slowing even the best of PCs to a crawling framerate.  Mostly though, the game plays very well on a gaming-grade PC.  It is both CPU and GPU heavy, and places similar demands on your system as MS Flight Simulator FSX does, so the majority of players find that they're dialling down a few settings for better performance.
This won't be a game for everyone.  It's a rather niche product with a dizzying array of DLC (much of it expensive - wait for sales) and it needs a beast of a PC if you can't live without using SSAO graphics settings!  However, picking a few favourite locos and a couple of routes in addition to the decent amount of content in the base game will keep you happy (if not your passengers - poor things) for some time to come without breaking the bank.
And if you are the first person ever to have bought ALL that DLC, can I have a new car please?!  One of those swanky sporty things that millionaires have...  I would catch a train instead, only I crashed the last one.

Amazing. Torchlight II is all about skill trees, equipment, looting, equipment, defeating hordes of monsters, making your name known to the world, and equipment. Did I mention equipment? Because you'll be finding tons of that. I love that changing equipment actually changes the appearance of your character (I wish there were vanity items because sometimes I went with the prettiest gear, not the ones with the best stats).
Playing with a friend is, naturally, a lot more fun than on your own though, to be honest, all you need is the pet you choose at the very beginning because SPOILER: it will never die. There are a handful of such pets to choose from and the pet system is one of my favourites out of any I've experienced because, not only do they act as a completely necessary additional inventory (did I mention you'd find a lot of equipment?) but because you can send them off to sell the goodies you no longer need. Mind blown. If you're getting this game, that should be reason enough.
There are also classes with their own customizable skill trees--both of which keep growing in diversity due to mods from other players. There's something for everyone: if you're into blasting everything to pieces with a cannon, do that. Fan of fire? There's a class for you, too. The world is constantly growing for new and old players alike.
Torchlight II is a hack and slash adventure that will have you traipsing through zombie infested bogs, crossing the desert and going to the underworld itself in order to save your world from the evil Alchemist. I invested a solid 20 hours during my first playthrough and I'm ready for a second round with a whole new class.
Buy it.

There is one glaring flaw in this game that prevents me from giving it the full score I originally wanted: the profanity.
Yes. This game uses both s*** and f*** very frequently and it stunned me when I first heard them.
Super Star Path has all of the aesthetics of a great mid-90's shooter: colorful, vibrant graphics; great music reminiscent of a by-gone era; solid vertical shooting; and a unique implementation of Bejewled style puzzle gameplay. Players scroll upwards, shooting everything in their path. But, there's a twist: wisely choosing which enemies to defeat to grant an optimal path is necessary. Essentially, defeating enemies of a common color results in a chain reaction, thus giving you more room to move. But, every enemy adjacent to the last defeated enemy will turn into a crystal, blocking your way. On top of this, each stage has three power-ups and three emeralds to collect. While this may sound tedious, unlimited lives and continues coupled with a great gameplay choice in allowing players to keep everything they've earned (even if they haven't completed the stage yet) make SSP a very balanced game.
There are a variety of ships to choose from, each granting the player different immunities and power specs (which can be upgraded as long as the power-ups are found.) Simply put, the game has great variety.
But. During gameplay your pilot will speak and comment on the action at hand. When I got hit at one point he exclaimed, "What the f*** was that?" Another time he said, "I'm too old for this s***" While this may seem dumb and inconsequential, it's completely unnecessary as he repeats it over and over (especially late game where the challenge increases.) No solid arcade shooter back in the day needed content like that to be good. It's abrasive and it clashes terribly with the colorful 16-bit aesthetic it boasts. I sorely implore the developers to patch those words out. Even if the pilot says the classic, "I'm too old for this" and cuts the word out, it would be fine. As it is though, I can't recommend this to everyone because of that content.
Super Star Path is a fantastic game to play that is limited terribly by the weirdest and most unnecessary inclusion of profanity I've ever seen in a game. Be aware of this when you buy it.

It's a very simple game, with nice graphics and basic gameplay.
It has OK story and good pacing, but most of the gameplay aspects feel too simplistic.
Mainly, you just run forward and kill everything that moves with two mouse buttons.
That's a bit weird from story side: to have an audience with the king and convince him that you're on his side you kill every person you meet in his kingdom. It's OK with offensive monsters, but killing all dwarves, humans and all elves feel plain.
Pros:
+ Simple and dynamic gameplay, which allow you to play short sessions. If you like to play 30 to 60 minutes and then do something else, this game is good for that.
+ Atmospheric graphics, which kind of gives you a vibe of older games. Dim and not flashy but in good sense.
+ The game is pretty short which is good for gameplay it presents. Does not have time to become very boring.
+ Fairly cheap price
Cons:
- Skills. Very small skill tree, which even more limited by level thresholds for unlocking.
Mostly you use 3-4 skills. Only after lvl 10 and lvl 20 you may unlock few more skills.
I'm not a fan of big branched unbalanced skill trees, where half of skills just modified copies of each other or usless weak skills. I prefer to have 15-20 skill set, where every skill is important and where you can combine skills to have additional effects and use combos against certain types of enemies.
Skill tree in this game is too small even for me, no combos available.
- Combat. It's a Diablo-style clicker and I not really mind that.
What really makes it plain is that all kinds of enemies die pretty much the same from any offensive skill or weapon, no immunities/vulnerabilities are involved.
Toxic cloud against skeleton? Sure. Fireball against fire-spitting spider? Why not.
- Weapons, armor, items. Fairly quickly inventory is filled with pretty much the same armor/weapons (only color is different, and names correspondingly "red armor", "blue armor", "black...", etc.), where the stats differ by 1-2 points, and the difference seems to have a non-existent effect on gameplay.
Stats of looted items grow gradually with a level of hero and enemies, so there is no feeling that you actually level up something.
- NPC and dialogues. No optional dialogue lines, no ability to make a choice by the hero.
Aside from kings, there are no notable NPCs to talk to.
- Sound effects. After a while, you start to tire from sound effects, because all enemies of the same class are making the same(or too similar and too short) sounds that sound like mobs are choking or have a hiccup.
- No map. Locations are small, but sometimes they make you run many rounds just because you did not notice a small turn. It's annoying especially later in the game where quests (not skippable) make you run back and forth on previously cleared empty level.
Game saves only when you clear area completely and back to area selection screen. If you decide to exit without clearing level, all progress will be gone. Checkpoints on the level are for inner use only, i.e. hero resurrects on this checkpoint if die. Ability to manual save is absent.
In my case game crashed on alt+tab. All progress in the game was lost, so I needed to start from the beginning.
I'm not saying that my review is strictly negative (even if it have more cons), it's an OK game for its price which could be the great game if it had little more of complexity in every described above point.

It's ok, but not a lot of depth. I played to the end in about 10 hours with a Warrior on Normal mode, using mouse and keyboard, and it's kind of easy. The Warrior does a lot of damage, has good crowd control, and has plenty of defense and heal ability.
There's a nice variety in environments and decoration, and the map layouts get more interesting in later levels, but there isn't a lot of variety in combat. There are really only 4 types of enemies: melee, swarm, missile, and big. There's a little additional tactical variety from the choice of skills when you level up your character, but about halfway through the campaign I'm pretty much unstoppable if I'm careful not to be surrounded. The variety runs out, and it feels like a lot of the same thing over and over.
Possessing enemies is fun for a little while, but there's not really much variety there either. It's not very different from climbing into an armored vehicle and shooting or bashing enemies until the vehicle fails.
I also played a little Wizard and Rogue. The Rogue seems a little easier, and the Wizard seems a little harder, but I didn't play enough to understand their skill tree. Relying on missile attacks makes the game kind of dull, since about 80% of combat is picking off enemies as they move straight toward you.
The mouse control is a little fiddly: it's easy to accidentally move instead of attack. Shift-click will always attack instead of move, but shift also triggers an attack's special mode, which uses MP.
Another problem I ran into: sometimes I'll hold down mouse button 1 and move the mouse, expecting my character to move, but it doesn't move, just kind of swivels in place. This happens because the button press was on an enemy or an object, so my character is in combat mode, not move mode. Annoying when I'm trying to run away from a crowd, but not a big deal once I realized what was happening.
The story is kind of predictable and nothing special. Except I'm a little weirded out by the weak justification for killing all the soldiers of the kingdom I'm trying to save.

I’m surprised the She Wants Me Dead versions on iTunes and Google Play are completely free yet the PC version is leaning towards the overpriced side.
You control the silent protagonist who’s the hapless owner of a lunatic house cat with solid engineering skills. Lula the Cat just as the game’s title implies, wants you dead and will stop at nothing to achieve her goal. Not much of a story here, is it? Most side scrollers are barebones like this, in terms of a coherent plot and a well defined cast of characters.
The one area in which the game truly shines is the visual department. I absolutely dig the near monochromatic style which offers the title a shot at the Noir subgenre. Of course it couldn’t be all Black&White without just a dash of Red. And a couple other colors since you have plenty of player customization options. It may be a fully fledged 2D title yet motion and shadow use offer at least the illusion of 2.5D. From a graphical perspective there’s not much to complain since it runs smoothly and offers sufficient sprite and background variety, even if the traps themselves aren’t that diversified.
This song explains it better than I could.
As for the gameplay and objectives to accomplish, the situation is clear from the start. You must survive any trap layed ahead by Lula and reach the safe house at the end of each of the 10 levels. I hope I don’t have to explain to you how a side-scrolling title works, right? You always move your character to the right side of the screen, if you wish to reach the end of the level at some point. In SWMD, you may have to avoid deadly obstacles but the principles of all its arcade predecessors still apply. Only one way forward and not a lot that you’re leaving behind.
Quick reflexes and patience are still crucial prerequisites in side scrollers now, as they have been for the past 40 years (Wikipedia claims that the first side-scrolling game was released in April 1977) since the genre’s inception. There are unlockables which also function as incentives for you to press on and complete the levels with as few fails as possible. The coins you gather give you access to a wide variety of clothing options, to add a personal touch to your unfortunate digital cat owner. Calling SWMD unforgivingly difficult, is an understatement. You will succumb to your in-game injuries quite frequently and the title even quantifies the number of fatalities in the Main Menu. Talk about shaming.
I enjoyed playing She Wants Me Dead, despite its inflexible difficulty and that one song which kept repeating over and over again. It might force some players to mute the sound and listen to their own playlist. In anycase, I had to rate the game accordingly by its inexplicably high price tag which really doesn’t reflect in either the gameplay or graphical overhaul on PC compared to SWMD’s mobile counterparts. If you can grab the game once its bundled or during a Steam Sale, by all means do it. It’s a quirky 2D platformer that can stand out from an “ocean of mediocrity” as you can refer to the vast majority of  Steam indie side scrollers.
+ Steam Trading Cards.
+ Old school type of difficulty.
+ Character customization options.
+ Pleasant graphics and level design.
- Cool albeit repetitive soundtrack (the variations of a single track).
- Slightly overpriced considering the free mobile versions.
- Only 10 levels and not a lot of replay value.
- No difficulty scaling or slider.
- No Steam Achievements.

Super Chain Crusher Horizon (SCCH) is an unconventional, horizontal scrolling arcade-style mono-shot space ship shooter for one or two local players simultaneous. Its a game about making enemies explode and chaining those explosions into one another for big points and your survival. You're flying against a never ending armada of space ships big and small, hurling themselves in your general direction. Its an accessible easy to play shooter.
What do I mean by mono-shot? You only fire one projectile at a time, but the longer you wait between shots the more your charge meter builds up. You have three tiers to this meter, each will cause a progressively larger explosion with the final tier wiping half the screen with a giant explosion. Each chained explosion is smaller than the last until you get down to the smallest explosion.
Even the smallest explosion can take out a dozen enemies that run into it. Your projectiles aren't any larger, just the explosions, so you need to use aim and timing to explode the most strategic enemy. Even if you miss, there are enough ships coming that you're bound to hit someone else. Having to charge leads to a risk reward game play. Do you let the screen fill with enemies as you're waiting or do you kill them one by one?
These explosions continue to kill enemies off screen that you haven't seen yet and you won't, because they're dead. While they're still exploding, it gives you a chance to recharge your shot. Thankfully the game doesn't have you hold the button down to charge it.
Before I get more into the game, there's a daunting problem that people including myself have when they start it. The game starts far over to the left of your screen. So you'll have to open the program, hover your mouse over the icon in the task bar, wait for the program bubble to show up, right mouse click the bubble and move the game all the way to the right. This is a giant hurdle for people that the developer was kind enough to help me out with. The game only plays windowed and for me the resolution is stuck at 1900 x 560, but scrunched down to fit my 1360w x 768 monitor. Everything appears narrow and scrunched even if screen shots appear perfect. Its still a playable game, but this will impede many people.
Super Chain Crusher Horizon is a game with controls so simple that could have been an Atari 2600 game. I mean that as a compliment. You've got your joystick to move and a single button to shoot. Your space ship can move all over the screen. Its just that easy.
Behind your ship is a giant electrical wall that's there to kill you and collect the trash like flypaper. This wall is the left side of the screen. Any enemies that you miss will pile up behind you making it more challenging as time goes on, because everything you touch will kill you. You're forced to be ahead of the wall giving you less time to react and charge. It causes situations where you need to ponder, do you take out a ship that's about to hit a wall or do you just save your charge for the next array?
There are no landscapes or tight passages, nothing will shoot at you, but the enemies themselves are the obstacles.  Destroyable obstacles of course. There are several different types of enemies, ones that fly in wavy chains. Others that seek you out. Some that act like slow moving fodder, preventing you from using a first tier shot from chaining explosions. Others that fly in brief straight lines, then make a 90 degree turn as they head toward you.
Soon the enemies build up and there are faster moving foes that bounce off the top and bottom of the screen to add pressure to that electrical wall behind you. Larger ships that are just as easy to destroy as the smaller ones, but they're ultimately faster. All the enemies have red jet streams and some rotate so it looks like a beautiful ribbon trailing behind them.
There are carrier vessels that spawn enemies. Some are destroyable, others just drift off after a certain amount of time. The destroyable vessels can double as mini bosses. You can't shoot them, because their hulls are too thick, instead you need to chain an explosion into them. They can't be small first tier explosions, they need to be larger to get to the core. All the bosses are like this no matter what they are. Bigger bosses have thicker hulls with smaller cores.
The bosses don't feel too aggressive except for the biggest one that will fly straight at you with your only safe place being a tiny gap between it and the electrical wall. The further you go in the game, the more enemies these bosses will have to accompany them. Fast bouncers, blockers and so on. Everything to make sure your shot isn't charged.
As a game, its levels go in waves. Each wave takes place outside of a different planet, so you start at Earth and on the second wave you're flying by the moon, then Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and so on. After seven waves you're back at earth again and the challenge has gotten increased. Each wave lasts about 3 minutes. From looking at the achievements there are 100 waves and in 5 hours I made it to wave 30, so you're looking at a real time investment if you're out to complete the game.
The graphics look spot on. The planets and space backgrounds are gorgeous to look at as they scroll by. The sound is spot on for an arcade space shooter, and there's some light techno-trance music in the background.
Super Chain Crusher Horizon is never a difficult game. There are hairy moments when the screen fills with enemies, but it feels almost too easy. I had to get two hours in before I even felt like the game was challenging me. Even the later waves I could still get through without dying. Is that a bad thing? You get a lot of play time for your life. That's what it takes to get you into a game.
After every death, you can restart the wave. Your progress is auto saved and you can replay any wave that you've played. Because SCCH only increases the difficulty by the slightest increment, it doesn't feel like I'm progressing that much. At least on wave 10 faster silver enemies were unlocked, but by wave 30 there wasn't anything new or fresh. Just more ships. When you continue the game all those dead ships on the electrical field are cleared away, so its very possible to complete all 100 waves if you invest the time.
There is a second ship that you can play as, but it doesn't allow you to charge. It allows for multiple projectiles on screen at once. There's a balance to that; for every projectile that you fire with this ship or otherwise, it pushes you back ever so slightly. So if you go crazy shooting, you'll eat the electrical field and die.
Aside from the main game, there are special missions. The first is a suicide mission where you have no bullets, your only hope is to survive enemies by dodging them. Originally I thought the object was to ram a ship, cause a chain reaction exploding the core of a carrier then onto the next level. Nope.  Then there's time attack where you see how high of a score you can get, but I think its flawed because there doesn't seem to be a way to get extra time to prolong the experience. Next up is a high speed attack mode that forces you into the alternate space ship with much faster enemies. Its fun and more challenging than the real game. Finally, there's a fourth mode, but after 5 hours, I haven't unlocked it.
The game could get enhanced with high scores and leader boards. Different waves need to have color changes to enemies so I feel like I'm progressing somewhere other than the change of background. In a game that might be 15+ hours long, it needs unlockable ships even if they play the same.
With everything said, I think the things holding this back are the start up problem and how long it takes before it gets challenging. Perhaps a skip ahead to wave 21 would help alleviate that. I'd also like to thank Micky for giving me the game.

The game promises to kill you in creative ways, and it delivers on half of that. An important game mechanic lets you squeeze a little extra health, giving you a chance at 1 per level, but most of the time you lose your health all at once. Stuff tends to send you flying and leave you stunned, which usually just chains you until all your painstakingly hoarded HP is gone. And certain things will just instantly kill you, or deal more than 1 point of damage (read, 5), for SOME reason. Another time, your hit invincibility (which only certain kinds of damage give, for reasons unknown to me) may get you past most of the level, arrows bouncing off you as reel from the impact of that spider bite. Seriously, the way the game punishes you for mistakes is so out of wack and confusing, and I don't see any rhyme or reason behind it.
There's a time limit that spawns an unkillable monster that chases till you advance. Time pressure doesn't really add anything to the game, honestly. There's also a bunch of things in the game that really shouldn't hurt you. I have killed myself many, many times trying throw an object through a small gap. How? A better question is, "Why?"
That brings me to objects. You pick them up, you throw them. Sometimes they have special uses. It's probably one the most important parts of the game. Which is why it's so frustrating that the game barely supports it. There are NO animations for picking things up, carrying them, etc. Whatever it is just floats over your sprite, which wouldn't be that bad if you didn't spend the WHOLE GAME doing it. The control scheme is bad. You cannot, under any circumstances, throw certain items. The game needs one more button, and I have no idea why it doesn't have it. You can only carry one item, and at any given level there's 2-3 things you'd like to, not KEEP really, just MOVE. I'm sure multiplayer makes this better, but if you play alone you will encounter this inconvenience.
People talk a lot about perfect moments they find in the randomized depths, but it's really all the same, as far as I can tell. The different area types have distinct feels to them, not just skin changes but real differences in level design. That's good. But between two stages of the same type? It's all pretty much the same. I find myself clearing out the same rooms with the same keystrokes, and nothing ever surprises me. Nothing really interacts in any interesting ways, and the only chain effects I've seen involve me being bounced around the level by hit-stun.
Now, theres a lot of content in this game that I haven't seen. You can play the later levels, using "shortcuts" which are a ♥♥♥♥♥ to unlock. This new late-game content sure looks like fun, how do I get the shortcut? Looks like I have to spend a bunch time in the early levels. That could only ever have been the exact opposite of what I wanted. Why was it set up like this?
So yeah, I died. It even got a bunch of laughs out of me, when things got absurdly unfair. To be honest, this game really should have been done up arcade style instead of tacking on perma-death in the wake of the roguelike hype we're seeing. It's got the same problem that all the worst roguelikes have; your sexy late-game content means ♥♥♥♥-all if the second I see it I get shunted back to play level 1 again. And what does perma-death add to the game? It doesn't make "choices matter" or make you plan out your moves. It's a platformer. You jump. When you fail, the first thing you want to do is TRY AGAIN. The game takes too long, and is too monotonous for that format to work. If I'm gonna play them a thousand times, those first levels better be phenomenal. And they aren't. They really, really aren't.

I've only played this game for a few hours but even at this early stage I think that this is what the X series should have become. Avorion seems to be heavily inspired by the X-series (and there is nothing wrong with this) and builds a lot of interesting mechanics on top of it. I especially like how the developers managed to get rid of almost any downtime which usually is intrinsic to space games like this. The sectors are nicely sized to limit fly times, you can check all station's offerings without docking, you can repair in space and your crew even slowly auto-repairs your ship. There are no lenghty docking scenes, no running through stations nonsense, no planetary landings which really wouldn't add anything to the game but a glorified docking sequence. If you don't want to micro-manage there is a auto setting managing things like your crew, insurance etc.
I like how the developers really streamlined the game experience and removed the tediousness while keeping the game fun and engaging and deep at the same time. There is really a lot to explore and many unexpected encounters (e.g. a pirate boss fight, helping out other ships in need, etc.). Helping others has tangible benefits (e.g. you get some monetary reward and increased standing which in turn yields other benefits like lower jump gate fees).
The graphics level is not mind-blowing but totally adequate and I love the atmospheric sound track. The game seems to be very stable, I haven't seen any crash or bug yet.
There are a few things that are not so great, yet but these will surely be addressed at some point (the game is still early access):
- While the soundtrack is great, it only seems to have a handful of titles so it gets a bit repetitive over time.
- The sound effects are more on the weak side, some things like mining lasers seem to have no sound at all and the rest is a bit on the generic side of things. Some nice engine sounds would help a lot and also the weapon sounds and explosions could use a bit more oomph.
- The game has no red-greed-color-blindness setting, so it can be a bit hard to distinguish items in space that are only identifyable by color coding.
- There seems to be no quick way of selecting targets in combat (e.g. next target) or stations/points of interest in the sector (e.g. through a list), so you have to roll your ship around a few times until you find that station or jump gate you are looking for.
- Prepare to have a browser ready when playing. The game gives you a quick tutorial on how to build a ship and fly around but many of the game mechanics (e.g. omicrons,  block area vs block volumes, block types etc.) are not explained very well ingame so you either need to experiment a lot or search the internet for more information.

Unfortunately this is the best train sim out there. I say 'unfortunately' because while there's loads of content (that's why it's the best imo) the developers, Dovetail Games, clearly prioritise quantity over quality and will happily overcharge you for unfinished or even unstable DLC. My advice for anyone interested in trains is buy one of the 'first class edition' collections during steam sales - these are great value for money.
Once you've bought the game you can however make it interesting and challenging as long as you get the right addons - avoid some of the standard DTG routes but look for the "proffessional" locomotives. I only know about UK rail, so here are some examples of addons for the best British experience (there are others I may not know about):
- London to Brighton line: comes with train sim UK edition and is a nice quality, stable(ish) interpretation of the UK's most congested railway, with some flexibility for scenario creation.
- WCML 'Over Shap' route by Krossrails, available from Steam: great quality route which provides a challenge and comes with the European assets pack in case you don't have it (you need it). Buying the class 390, Voyager 221 advanced and a commuter DMU such as the class 170 or 150 would mostly complete this route for modern day operations.
- Western Mainlines route from
: the entire Great Western Mainline as far as Cardiff and Exeter, which is easily the best value for money of any UK route given the sheer length of track to play with, of pretty good quality. The 221 also fits here.
My general outlook on this sim is it's great thanks to its community. The only downside of the rich variety of realistic scenarios on the steam workshop is they often seem to require more DLC than you already have. The real opportunities for gameplay lie in the scenario editor and good third party developers, not just what you get with the game.

Stylistically, this game is a substantial accomplishment.  I enjoyed many aspects of the graphics and sound. Unfortunately, this game has many flaws.   I am not sure if I feel compelled to play it again after about an hour of mild enjoyment (punctuated by frustration - and not the good kind.)
- Each stage is divided into a puzzle portion and a boss (bullet hell) portion.  The controls for the ship for the grid-based puzzle portion, however, are almost identical to the boss portion (normal shmup ship controls) which is not well-suited to action puzzle gameplay.  You constantly have to nudge your ship, and maneuvering into gaps in the automatically-scrolling stage is awkward.  I understand the need to dodge bullets, but I think this problem could have been handled more elegantly.
- The ship is destroyed too easily by being "crushed".  In fact your ship begins to explode well before hitting the bottom of the screen.  There should be some wiggle room!
- The stages are randomly generated, and occasionally, there is absolutely no way forward no matter which monsters you shoot.  This happened at least 10 times in my play session.  There is no escape route; your only option is to take your inevitable death.  I suppose the developers thought that not having an Lives made this a non-issue, but I would beg to differ.
- In the same vein, monsters that shoot at you are sometimes placed in a position where they cannot be destroyed by your pea shooter, which only shoots up.  There are no other weapons in the game as far as I can tell.
- Shooting-enemies don't stand out.  You can't be hurt by normal enemies but you can by the shooting ones.  Avoiding them is a needle-in-haystack affair.
- Because you're so busy shooting and collecting gems, finding a powerup or an emerald is 90% of the time a matter of luck.
- There is very little incentive to get better at spotting these special enemies because of the infinite lives and the fact that you keep everything you pick up even if you die.  But when you really need a powerup to defeat a boss or get through a level, you pretty much have to replay it over and over hoping you stumble upon it.
- I liked the music and voiceover for the most part, but the pilot banter got old fast.  The cursing is totally unnecessary and just comes across as immature.  The worst of the audio's sins, in my opinion, though, is the use of SFXR or BFXR.  Those tinny, instantly recognizable tweets, splutters, and tinkles killed what the sound had going for it and the sense of Playstation/Sega Saturn era sophistication.
If it were a 10 star system I would give it a weak 7, but I cannot recommend this game.  The gameplay is just not very deep at all and doing well is mostly a matter of a roll of the dice due to a noticeable lack of polish in that department.
I encourage the developers to make their next game and improve in that area.

This small-studio Action RPG sticks to its guns and keeps it lean and mean, focusing on hitting the mark in lieu of overaiming for a miss, and hit the mark it does, in what I would consider Wizarbox's swan song.
What could be looked at as a mediocre also-click among giants of the ARPG genre in one light, can also be viewed as a triumphant first outing in another. Sure, innovation goes a long way, but the gaming landscape is littered with a littany of titles whose ambitious and inspired innovation was tarnished by ultimately lopsided execution.
R.A.W attempts to take the opposite route. It never tries to break any ground or make any waves, but what it does do in its roughly 10 hours, it does well. Never once losing sight of what it is trying to accomplish, it keeps things tight and conservative, and the result is a consistency and polish throughout. Admittedly, things can feel a little too much on the light side at times. I don't consider it a critical failing as R.A.W still hooked me in and had me playing "just one more" level in the latter half of my playthrough, and when it ended, I was sad to see it was over.
I've noticed that French studios tend to have an eye for aesthetics, and this is no exception. The game looks good, its art direction and graphics almost stellar when they're at their best, and a little too well done to be bland when they're at their worst. You'd be forgiven for thinking the game was worse in this area than it is, by what you see on first glance. The character designs and loot designs being some of the weaker stuff on display. The real eye candy is in the world itself, with each passing level design showcasing the best R.A.W has to offer graphically. They aren't just nice looking; thoughtful attention to the game's lore is on display often. It comes off much better than the first impression you get from the loot for example.
The loot, however, is certainly a weak point. If that's what you play these games for, you'll probably be disappointed. The loot has a decidedly subdued role for an ARPG. It clearly wasn't a priority. But when a massive loot pool can be a major undertaking itself, you can start to see the reasons behind this somewhat passive approach. There's a lot of reuse of a small art pool and a dearth of different types. You'll never fawn over the items in this game. Even so, don't let that scare you. The developers of this consummately competent title wouldn't neglect such a central part of the genre. This is no Bioware loot system.
You'll get loot along the way, you'll compare stats, you'll upgrade, but you'll see pretty much all you'll need to over the course of one playthrough. As someone who plays these games for the lore and world building and gameplay and not the loot, I found this refreshing. I found more success with merchants than drops, as you'll encounter some who have some nice Legendary sets for purchase. It becomes rewarding to make a point of selling loot you don't want. This is marred a bit by an overly simple UI requiring one too many clicks, but in my case at least, it's nothing more than a minor annoyance. Though even as I was about to finish the campaign, I was delighted to find my first named Legendary weapon, with stats to match such rarity, as a random drop from a chest.
The real fun in this game though, is the combat. The mechanics of movement, attacking, and spellcasting never left me wanting, with one exception. The skills in the lone tree you're given, like the rest of the game don't delve too deep, but work well and are really fun to play. On my chosen Rogue class, there were bow skills to shoot, dagger skills to slash, lay a slowing trap, move and attack faster, one to heal, to summon a minion, and go invisible. As well as Magic Find, Critical hit chance boost, and Gold Find options.
Do note most of this is based on a single Rogue playthrough and build. Based on what others have said, it is possible the skill tree and combat system is uneven. This becomes a bigger deal when you have less options to start with. In my case however, I found the skills a blast. The tactical gameplay of R.A.W is fast-paced and engaging. You don't just spend time building yourself some meat and potatoes skill pattern that you throw at the mobs over and over. Instead, you have to pick a playstyle, and pick skills and a method to match. I chose to forgo the usual ranged fare entirely, and instead doubled down on the daggers.
The gameplay for me was a balancing act of see-sawing my dash and spin cooldowns, while throwing out my summons or heal when needed. The game surrounds you with mobs, and you can be staggered. As a Rogue, you're pretty much a glass cannon; you can deal a ton of burst DPS, but getting surrounded can very quickly kill you. Playing tactically is required, and fun. I chose to invest early in the skill that earns you extra XP, and I'm glad I did. I honestly think that's a must pick for this game. The skills and combat are the best the game has to offer, and having a few extra points allows you to max a few more ability lines. I mysteriously picked up a life-steal towards the end-game, which I believe was probably a balancing mechanic by developers who weren't pulling any punches on this game being lighter fare. No complaints, I was happy to have it there. Even though I felt my build was more than enough to handle the end-game, the little tweak ensures you power through the climax of the story even if your build is bad. Not sure if it didn't come from the item set I was wearing though.
One of the hooks of this game is its "Focus" system. Cheeky. Essentially, most active skills work on a two-tier system. The regular, and a "Focus" version which you activate by holding the Shift key before you fire it. This results in one skill being two variants, each with its own cooldown. Your basic attack is treated this way. In the case of my Rogue's heal, the regular version popped an instant heal. The Focus version once unlocked, could be held to heal indefinitely and when released also popped for an instant heal, essentially giving you two. The Focus version took longer to fire though even without any holding business.
I've seen claims the UI is too simple and clunky but I found it perfect. You get two sets of 6 binds you hot-swap with the TAB key. By default, your melee is on left click and your ranged attack is on right click. I rebound my ranged attack to my second set and replaced it with my dagger AOE. This was graceful and gave me fast options. In most ARPGs, the skills you don't build are often all but useless. Not so here, as I was happy to find shooting stayed useful, and was even necessary at times.
I did mention an exception, and there is a UI/combat flaw. Small update here: After firing a skill, your UI will become unresponsive to a tab press. Rarely noticed on my Rogue, but moreso on my current Warrior, the window of the input deadzone depends on skill duration. Longer-animated skills are more problematic. It can be adjusted to, but it's a problem, that can even merit bind changes to avoid it.
A fun enemy posession mechanic, and a graceful way of handling death and checkpoints round out the systems. The narrative is nothing to write home about, but it's not exactly forgettable, either, and by the end I was thoroughly attached to all the players. The game even finds a moment or two for some tongue-in-cheek levity. When it was over, I wondered what was next.
Alas, the studio that developed R.A.W, Wizarbox, is now gone. Shuttered while developing another Point-n-Click Adventure. A shame, as this is a game and world that in my opinion deserves and could deliver more. Like from the lore, maybe a tear for this game's loneliness will fall and lead to the next. Even if it doesn't happen, this game stands as a legacy any studio can be proud of. gg Wizarbox

My buddy and I had a great time playing this one together... took us about 25 hours to get through the whole thing, and we didn't fret too much over finding every little nook and cranny, but we're probably a little more methodical than most (i.e. slow).   We played a couple areas multiple times to beef up a bit for the next area, but not enough to be annoying.  I detest games that make me do the same stuff over and over.  The game is nothing super-duper regarding story, graphics, sound, gameplay... but it all was perfectly okay IMO, and most importantly, it was fun and kept us playing.  And I'm kinda tired of the "this game sucks unless it has 34 stats to compare on every item and 17 branches in each skill tree of 20 different classes" mentality in all the ARPGs these days... I don't really think that makes a game MORE FUN.  If anything, it kinda turns it into a "job".  Replay value?  Grinding the same thing over and over provides little or no replay value (to me).  Anyway, the combat can be tough at times (usually due to certain mobs catching you off-guard), but in general, the game is rather easy once you get the hang of it.  There are some of the skills that work in tandem between the characters different characters.  There was a "suck all the enemies to me" skill on one of our characters, and a "BOOM goes the neighbors" skill on our other character, and the combo just seemed to never get old when we got the timing right.
If you like games Baldur's Gate Dark Alliance, Grim Dawn, Torchlight, etc., or maybe you're just tired of over-statting and grinding, or you just wanna get a friend and go hack and slash and blow up stuff with magic... then this is likely be a good fit for you.
Use gamepads... everything is laid out to take advantage of an XB-compatible pad.  I appreciate how they made this work.  It reminded me of LotR: War in the North, which I really liked as well (an others hate on because there's not 34 stats to compare and 20 classes and 17 branches... blah blah blah).
This game is definitely worth it for a Diablo-style romp with friends.  Didn't play single-player, so that might be a different story.  I find that ARPGs are generally better co-op anyway, especially if there aren't any NPCs or summoned companions to force the fights away from the "everything on the screen just shoots and chases ME"... BORING!
Anyway, get this puppy on sale, and grab a friend or two, some gamepads and put it up on the big screen...

The plot of this game is that there are Nazis within range of your high-powered rifle. There's probably more to it than that, but I wasn't paying attention. Whether I don't remember anything about the story because I played this game half drunk on a lazy Saturday or because the story was just that boring and/or superfluous, I don't know. I suspect it's a combination of the two. What I do know is that the day I need a reason to shoot video game Nazis in the face is the day I renounce my American citizenship and put down my controller. I do note that the story being set in Africa was a nice change of pace from the rather more common setting of "3/4-exploded European city."
But, obviously, I enjoyed this game or I wouldn't have recommended it, and I'm recommending it for the gameplay. I'm not really a connoisseur of shooters, but I thought it worked well.
For the most part, the maps are pretty open, and you're given substantial leeway as to how you're going to get your mission done. Generally speaking, I appreciated this, though it did lead to a couple rather absurd situations wherein I murdered every Nazi in the postal code before accidentally stumbling upon a checkpoint and being informed that I need to make my way through an extra-special dangerous area to accomplish a plot point. Then, the game plays really intense music and the protagonist (who has a voice like disinterested, chain-smoking batman) growls about being sneaky while I take a leisurely stroll to my objective among the recently deceased sons of the Third Reich.
In addition to the maps being fairly open ended, so is the Nazi murder. Your rifle is of course your work-horse, but you're also given plenty of support weapons: pistols, machine guns, land mines, trip mines, grenades, and rocket launchers. So, while the game emphasizes shooting Nazis from far away, you are more than welcome to shoot them from up close and/or explode them.
Relatedly, it doesn't seem like the game knows that it's giving you all this freedom. It gives you great number of tools, tactics, tutorials and terrain with an eye toward killing all sneaky-like, but most missions can be beat quite easily by finding a high point with a good view and decent cover and then just going nuts. You see, if anyone gets close to you, they can often deal a lot of damage very fast, but threats with a range comparable to your own are few (tanks or enemies with their own rifles or rocket launchers) and fairly far-between. The rest of them are left spraying wildly with pistols or sub-machine guns, gradually moving forward into closer cover or--more often--your bullets. This is about as effective as you would imagine, and a couple dozen Nazis will be doing well to do one bandage-worth of damage to you before they're all dead or rolling around on the ground doubtlessly wondering why no one thought to give even one of them a gun that could reliably hit a target more than 30 yards away.
In sum: this game has its fair share of quirks and shortcomings, but I thought the mechanic were reasonably well-executed, and using them to shoot Nazis was fun enough to earn the game a recommendation from me.

The game promises to kill you in creative ways, and it delivers on half of that. An important game mechanic lets you squeeze a little extra health, giving you a chance at 1 per level, but most of the time you lose your health all at once. Stuff tends to send you flying and leave you stunned, which usually just chains you until all your painstakingly hoarded HP is gone. And certain things will just instantly kill you, or deal more than 1 point of damage (read, 5), for SOME reason. Another time, your hit invincibility (which only certain kinds of damage give, for reasons unknown to me) may get you past most of the level, arrows bouncing off you as reel from the impact of that spider bite. Seriously, the way the game punishes you for mistakes is so out of wack and confusing, and I don't see any rhyme or reason behind it.
There's a time limit that spawns an unkillable monster that chases till you advance. Time pressure doesn't really add anything to the game, honestly. There's also a bunch of things in the game that really shouldn't hurt you. I have killed myself many, many times trying throw an object through a small gap. How? A better question is, "Why?"
That brings me to objects. You pick them up, you throw them. Sometimes they have special uses. It's probably one the most important parts of the game. Which is why it's so frustrating that the game barely supports it. There are NO animations for picking things up, carrying them, etc. Whatever it is just floats over your sprite, which wouldn't be that bad if you didn't spend the WHOLE GAME doing it. The control scheme is bad. You cannot, under any circumstances, throw certain items. The game needs one more button, and I have no idea why it doesn't have it. You can only carry one item, and at any given level there's 2-3 things you'd like to, not KEEP really, just MOVE. I'm sure multiplayer makes this better, but if you play alone you will encounter this inconvenience.
People talk a lot about perfect moments they find in the randomized depths, but it's really all the same, as far as I can tell. The different area types have distinct feels to them, not just skin changes but real differences in level design. That's good. But between two stages of the same type? It's all pretty much the same. I find myself clearing out the same rooms with the same keystrokes, and nothing ever surprises me. Nothing really interacts in any interesting ways, and the only chain effects I've seen involve me being bounced around the level by hit-stun.
Now, theres a lot of content in this game that I haven't seen. You can play the later levels, using "shortcuts" which are a ♥♥♥♥♥ to unlock. This new late-game content sure looks like fun, how do I get the shortcut? Looks like I have to spend a bunch time in the early levels. That could only ever have been the exact opposite of what I wanted. Why was it set up like this?
So yeah, I died. It even got a bunch of laughs out of me, when things got absurdly unfair. To be honest, this game really should have been done up arcade style instead of tacking on perma-death in the wake of the roguelike hype we're seeing. It's got the same problem that all the worst roguelikes have; your sexy late-game content means ♥♥♥♥-all if the second I see it I get shunted back to play level 1 again. And what does perma-death add to the game? It doesn't make "choices matter" or make you plan out your moves. It's a platformer. You jump. When you fail, the first thing you want to do is TRY AGAIN. The game takes too long, and is too monotonous for that format to work. If I'm gonna play them a thousand times, those first levels better be phenomenal. And they aren't. They really, really aren't.

Extremely hard and awesome Indie platformer in which everything, stationary or mobile, is out there to kill you. Every dungeon is randomly generated and every death will only respawn you at the beginning lobby.

But little by little you gain knowledge of everything in the game and with this knowledge you will finally survive through Caves, Jungle, Ice Caves, Temple and Hell.
One of the features is daily challenge in which you may compete with your friends or world-wide for the highest score in the same seed(identical maps).
Game can also be played locally with max 4 players and will usually lead to bloodshed, pain and laughter since you can't turn friendly-fire off. If your friend brutally murdered you for your bombs, don't worry. Even as a ghost you may still push your friend into a set of spikes as a revenge.
So if you love challenge, survival and permanent deaths you should buy this game. It's worth it!

Super Star Path is a brilliant fusion between a shoot 'em up and a color match puzzler. The clever way this marriage is implemented though, is really what elevates it beyond the sum of it parts.
It's not just simply blasting waves of enemies to reach the boss, it's about carefully carving a path for your ship to make it through. When you shoot an enemy of a certain color, it's adajcent color matches will explode in a chain. When the chain finally hits an enemy of different color, it will end and turn that enemy into a crystal which you are not able to destroy.
What does that mean exactly? Careless volleys can leave you with a dead end. This principle mechanic for traversing through levels requires you to take precise shots, and plan ahead for survival. Things get even more interesting when other level specific hazards are introduced as well as more traditional enemies. Once you wrap your head around the flow of the game, it's a sublime experience.
The presentation too is stellar. With colorful, vibrant pixel art evocative of the Super Nintendo era and a top notch chiptune soundtrack ranging from melancholic, hypnotic tones to upbeat, excitement builiding battle music.
The asking price is so reasonable that it should be a no brainer for most. You should pick it up!

Nice retro-style shoot-em-up (shmup) with a twist.
In this game the levels consist of colored monsters that just sit there, and when you shoot them they turn into gems to collect.  But some of them turn light blue and are indestructable.  There are other obstacles like rocks and moving enemies to avoid or kill.  Making your way through the maze is difficult.  There are dead ends and if you choose the wrong path, the screen is slowly scrolling down and you can be trapped.  Each time it is randomly generated, so don't bother trying to memorize.  Collect gems but don't take too much time trying to get them all or you will get trapped!  Some enemies drop special icons that you use to upgrade your ship.  Also one enemy in the bunch will drop the Emerald that you need to get
The thing I love about this game is that even if you die you keep all the stuff you collected!  That's right up my alley because I'm not that good at these games.  Use the gems to buy new ships and upgrade the defense, attack, and speed of your chosen ship.  Some ships come with special benefits that are useful on certain planets.
Each planet has the gem collect level and then a boss section.  The boss is typical bullet hell, though not as bad as some I've seen.  When you finish a boss new ships are unlocked for purchase.  You can do the planets in any order.
Graphics:  Nice pixel graphics.  I like how they have the different colored layers in the tunnel to make it look like 3D.  The sprites are cute.
Sound:  There is a narrator in the beginning intro scene and at the start of each level he says something.  You can turn him off if you don't want to listen to it.  The normal pew-pew sounds and background music that sounds retro.
Controller worked fine for me.  I used an Xbox controller on Windows 7 PC.
Final Thoughts:  Might be a little too easy for a pro shmupper, but nice for us regular folks.  It's cheap!  Nice to see a dev that doesn't over-price their games.

At first, this game is extremely frustrating and difficult. The levels are generated randomly, and they come at you seemingly blazingly fast. In addition to the match/freeze puzzle mechanic that separates this game from other shmups, there are some standard enemies tossed at you at the same time, and they take several hits, which makes for a hectic and somewhat annoying gameplay experience.
HOWEVER... As soon as you lock into the swing of things, you will be collecting gems and upgrades for your ships. If you hang in there long enough to beat a boss, you will unlock more ships with abilities above and beyond those found in the initial two that are available. It is, needless to say, a game-changer, to have the ability to be immune to certain types of enemy bullets, or to have the ability to break the previously-indestructible blocks that impede your path. This opens things up, lets you breathe a little, and have a much better time. I quickly went from my typical 5-minutes-and-I-give-up gamer A.D.D. attitude, to "aww man, my wife is home with the groceries... Guess I'd better quit for now and help her bring them in and put them away."
I am still pretty early on in the game, but I didn't want to wait with sharing my recommendation for this new release. For the asking price, I feel that this is a great little vertical-scrolling shmup, with day-one Linux release and gamepad support out of the box (I am using xboxdrv with a lovely Nexus Gamepad).  The only thing I noticed is that I don't hear sound effects (music is fine), which I will report to the devs and hopefully will be patched.

Early on an Elysian girl falls to Deponia and he sees this as his opportunity.  The game suffers from a slow start, but the story picks up later with some suspense & a satisfying ending.

Where to begin…  As I laid on my couch, eyes glazed over, mindlessly clicking through the Steam Queue I happened upon this gem.  Avorion, didn’t immediately look too interesting aside from the tags.  Scrolled down a little further to the reviews, mostly positive.  Hmm I thought.  Ill add it to my wishlist, maybe buy it on sale. “Required space :500MB”.
“well” I thought. “just got screwed out of 18 bucks.”
Within a few minutes the game had finished download and I booted it up.  Immediately my computer began to shake. Rays of blinding light shot from the screen.  I tried to shut it down, but it was too late. My fingers fused to the keyboard   Energy waves started to radiate from the screen thrusting me back into the couch.  Eyes wide open being bombarded with the most beautiful astronomical sights.  With all my strength I looked to my right, fighting the pull of the game.  I looked at my dog who was forced to the wall.
“what have you done?” he says
“I don’t know!”  I yell back
The game pulled me back and I shot into space.  Weeks turned to days, days to hours, hours to seconds.  Like a drone I mined, traded and looted.  Alien societies showered me with gifts and treated me like a low resolution god.
Then darkness…
My computer had run out of battery and I was thrust back to reality with only my memories of glory to hold on to.

*This is a review from someone who hasn't finished the game. Perhaps I'm wrong about everything I say, but keep in mind that this is just an opinion.*
This game is being heiled as some sort of cinematic masterpiece, but it pales in comparison to many other cinematic puzzle-platformers.
The gameplay essentially consists of all the boring parts of games like Uncharted and the modern PoP games. You will spend most of your time moving down a linear path and climbing up some sort of ledge that leads to another linear path. The only thing that hinders the gameplay is that each of the two brothers are controlled with separate analog sticks. While this is a unique feature, all it really does is make movement clunky.
Repetitive puzzle design is another flaw. Most of the puzzles consist of one brother pulling a lever/squeezing between bars/lowering a rope so that the other brother can access another part of the environment, and keep moving down the game's linear path.
These factors made it hard for me to get emotionally invested into the story, but the story doesn't really try to keep you captivated in the first place. None of the characters speak (legibly), and there's not much exposition that the plot can build off of. The only motivation the brothers have to embark on their quest is to save their dying father. It's a pretty generic setup.
On the positive side, the game is gorgeous. The linear paths are filled with artistic detail, and some areas give you a view of previously visited areas, which is something I really like. Some benches are placed in certain locations, which provide a view of the landscape, but that's practically the game just shouting, "LOOK AT HOW PRETTY I AM" at you.
The sound design is good, but nothing to cry home about.
One thing I should mention is that I have not finished the game to completion. But I really don't see why I should. There's not enough in the game to keep me invested in it. While it looks nice, the gameplay is boring and story is generic. Gameplay and story are the two strongest elements that cinematic puzzle-platformers build off of. This game is lacking in both.
Yet the general opinion of this game is highly positive. Pick it up during a sale and see if the game intrigues you more than it intrigued me. If you want a phenominal cinematic puzzle-platformer, go pick up Ico. It shares the core mechanics of this game, but executes them in a much better fashion.
