I understand the game is currently in early access.  I hope further down the line, kinks will be ironed out and more features will be developed.  However, I can not currently recommend this game unless you solely wish to playtest, as there are still game-breaking bugs and frustrating behaviors that will interfere with your enjoyment of the game otherwise.
The ship-building in this game is promising and very flexible.  By snapping together different components at whatever size you wish, you have the freedom to truly make your ships look however you want.  The game handles this well by adjusting your ship stats accordingly, based off factors like component volume (e.g. engines, generators) and placement (e.g. thrusters).  Having enjoyed the ship-building in Space Engineers, I felt like the Avorion takes building in a unique direction because of these facets.
Gameplay includes the typical space-sim fare: mining asteroids for resources, shooting pirates, and trading.  Avorion has an interesting loot system where turrets and system upgrades are dropped by ships, akin to in RPGs.  However, I feel these systems are not fleshed out enough to be fully enjoyable to me.
Mining is tedious, a problem many space games tend to face.  It doesn't have much "character"--since mineable resources are stored in your character's inventory, you don't need to worry about cargo space.  For that reason, any ship can become a miner if you switch out the turrets and maybe pop in an asteroid detector upgrade.
Combat feels good to a degree, but is ultimately held back by its limitations.  Despite having a ship system where every component has its own HP and can be blown off, the game handles ship destruction based off an arbitrary total HP instead.  It seems that, if you take a high enough percentage of your total HP in damage, you get killed.  In practice, this means that if 90% of your ship HP is armor (armor has a very high HP density), when your armor is destroyed, even if your core systems are still intact, you die.  It feels cheap to lose this way.  I rammed an enemy by accident and my ship was destroyed; when I revisited its wreckage, most of the ship was intact save for a chunk of the front.  Think of it this way: if you knick an asteroid with a wing, would you rather lose just that wing, or have your entire ship insta-killed?
Trading involves fitting your ship with a cargo bay, buying low from stations, and selling high to other stations.  The addition of trading related system upgrades adds a nice quality of life touch, as rarer upgrades will help show trade routes and percentage deviations from market value.  However, I ran into issues when trying to trade as certain cargo items simply didn't show up in trade menus, making it impossible to sell the goods I had bought.  I don't know if this is an atypical issue or not, but for me this was a game breaker, as well as small annoyances like being fined large amounts for dangerous goods that my ship automatically picked up when another ship blew up nearby.

Easy to learn, fun to play, intriguing to master.  Building system is a simplified verson of that you might find in Space Engineers type of game, but this also makes it more powerful. Allows you to build the ship of your dreams, fleet to conqour the galaxy, and soon establish your own empire.
And unlike mentioned Space Engineers, the developers are active in the community. Continually work to fix any bugs you might find or issues you may have, they do not simply try to rush out the next big game breaking 'feature'.
Give the game a go, try building a ship and see how you like it. If it's not for you, you can always get a refund, or you can wait and try it again later. There's always things being worked on and updated.

Train Simulator 2016 is a game with literally unlimited potential, yet seems to be plagued with discrete technical issues that for whatever reason, are slow to be addressed.  I had read previous reviews on this game and decided to throw caution to the wind and download Dovetail Games Flagship Product which includes Electric, Diesel and Steam along with the Sherman Pass and UP contender locomotives.  Upon starting the game my 200 watt per channel 5.1 sound systems filled the room with a rail yard ambience that was truly awesome to behold.  So far so good.  The Main Menu Page opened and I decided to invest the time to undertake the tutorial, so that I at least knew what I was doing.  The first tutorial was to move the train, and I followed the prompts and was rewarded with the thunderous sound of a turbo diesel coming to life and the train moving out on a long straight away track.   I spent some time in the cab familiarizing myself with the myriad of controls and push buttons available.  Everything from windshield wipers to lights.  I could see my future on a long lonely night run up out of Cheyenne Wyoming and was already hooked.  I then went on to the next tutorial determined to learn all I could in my new career as a Union Pacific Engineer.
Sadly, it was not to be.  Upon entering the second tutorial the computer locked up and a data dump occurred which even when bringing up the console, was not intuitively escapable from.  I waited for 15 minutes and finally the game crashed to desk top.  I adjusted settings backing off the graphics and audio in hopes that it was hardware or driver settings that my liquid cooled video cards were unable to handle.  Not so!  At one point the computer locked completely and went to a blue screen of death, processing a data dump of its own.  It was then that I went back and did some web research on the issues in this game.  I was not alone and in fact was among many who had similar problems.  Sadly early this morning I removed the game only after a few minutes of play.  Perhaps in a few years if they ever address these stability issues I may return.  I will be watching the reviews in hope of that eventuality.

I picked up Spelunky on a Steam sale not knowing much about the game other than I would die a lot, and I have to say I can't recommend this game highly enough. The art style is impeccable, the gameplay is addicting and fun, and the game controls wonderfully.
While it is certainly true that I have died a lot (and haven't even made it out of the ice caves yet), the deaths don't bother me because they all feel very fair and never cheap. When you do die, you can always attribute it to not looking ahead (or behind) carefully enough. Every trap or enemy in the game can be dealt with given a little proper planning and careful technique, so the fault for every death falls solely on the player.
The daily challenge is another great addition to the game's adventure mode. While it plays the exact same way, every player gets the same dungeon for the daily challenge as opposed to the procedurally generated dungeons of adventure mode. This makes for great leaderboard competition amongst your friends, and because you only get one chance at the daily challenege, it adds an added sense of urgency and importance to the run.
Spelunky is a beautiful, addictive, and difficult game that can be played in short bursts, which is particularly important for those with limited gaming time or a family. It is easy for me to hop on, play for 20 minutes, and then turn the computer over to my wife while still feeling like I had a quality gaming session. That being said, it takes a long time to master this game, so while it can be played in short bursts, it will also keep you playing for weeks (or months) to come.

I dare to claim that this is the best free WW2 game around even thought it has it's problems, but what kind of game doesn't?
Heroes and Generals is fun for hours and hours to play... and you can do it completely free (I haven't spend even a penny in this game). Some people whine about P2W aspect of the game which isn't really that much of a problem. You can buy ANYTHING with ingame credits or with gold (that is accuired with real money). Of course prices are really high to be bought with credits but you gain easily 3k per match, assuming you are decent player and don't have veteran membership. 10k if it's a long one, so it doesn't take too long to get a new weapon or a tank. Grinding credits and ribbons used to be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥but after they cut grind in half I've been getting new stuff way faster.
As there are plenty of weapons and vehicles to chose from (and they just keep adding more stuff in each update) some are way more powerful than others and I've seen people complaining that they can't do anything with starter rifle which is completely false. There are people who are insanely good with them. Gewehr 43, M1 Grand and SVT-40 are great weapons, if used correctly. So stop whining and learn to play ;)
Matchmaking in this game isn't perfect but it has become better. It used to throw noobs and veterans in same battles but nowadays there are bronze, silver and gold matchmaking. Your player level determines in what matchmaking group you belong to, so if you just started to play you don't need to worry about fighting against those who have played hundreds of hours.
Only thing that has been bugging me since I started playing H&G is those damn camping snipers and tankers oneshotting me from across the map. But that happens if you are stupid or insane enough to run around in a field without cover...
Heroes and Generals is a game worth trying out. It only costs your harddrive space.

This game really took me by surprise. I knew from the reviews I saw on this game that it would be good, but I didn't think it would be this good.
It hit a lot of high notes for me personally, such as real time battle, a loot system, body destruction enabled, and even more. It also got me into things I didn't knew I liked, such as taking the time to salvage asteroids or ships for loot and resoures. It's surprisingly calming to to either work your way through a huge rock or on a ship that you just decimated a minute ago. This game also has a trading system for goods, so any of you who are money fanatics can really take advantage of that.
And that's the thing about this game: I can support so many different playstyles. Hit hard and destroy everything in your way, stay near a settlement and be a vulture to wreckages, or just be a trader looking to make some cash. They are all able to play.
Another thing is that the creation system in this game is phenomenal. It feels like you can really create anything (as long as it doesn't have a smooth surface). I haven't taken advantage of it myself, but the workshop has showed me you can make anything from a tiny fighter that can zip through any adversity to a capital ship that can wage war on entire planets. If you have creativity, this game will beg you to use it.
I can't say much for the multiplayer because I haven't used it yet. But I assume that it would be a great deal of fun. You can either join together to destroy everything in your way or take control of a single ship to challenge yourselves on how fast you can fall apart.
Overall, this little gem of a game is well built and very fun to play with, even though it is only in early access. The pacing is great, you can set the difficulty to your likings, and the combat is engaging. The tutoriel is very informational and not too aggravating, which in itself is an acheivement. I would reccomend this game if you love space, real time battle, exploring, and/or trading. It truly is a game that intends to make a name for itself.
Oh, and P.S.: Do NOT try to ram into the enemy at top speed if all of your weapons are down and your ship wasn't intended to do that. You. Will. Die. Instantly. Then you will have to track, probably from the beggining of the game, back to where you died so you can gather back all of your cool stuff. If you have insurance (which is a thing, for all of your crazy people out there) You can rebuild your ship if you have enough materials, but it is still not a good idea to proceed with. Though, it is both hilarious, and effective if you really want to ruin a guy's day.
This game still needs quite some polishing, but it allready is a lot of fun!

This game? Mixed bag. I'm recommending it because it was indeed fun and had me playing it for some time. Yet there were moments that I genuinely hated this game,
Running is fast and awesome, but a single mistake and lead you to take a hit, fall down, take an arrow to the kidney and fall into spikes. This happened so many times that it was simply not funny anymore when I was playing the game obsessively. Every time I had to go through the easier levels I would lose concentration and get hurt because I was speeding, yet, even when being ultra careful, I would find myself sinking into pointy spikes 50% of the time. Not to mention the hypersensitive shopkeepers! I warn you now, do not even SNEEZE in their presence!
Yet at one moment this stopped happening as much as it did in the beginning and I started to appreciate all the small things that this game has to offer. The items you can get, what they unlock, how they unlock- it's all hidden right below the surface, some are easy to find just by playing, others need previous unlocks to be accessible. Sometimes this makes a specific run impossible simply because you missed an opportunity, but that does not matter as much.
The game can get really really exciting. Trying to fly over a spike pit with a bat on your tail and a snail right on your landing platform without taking damage- it can get very intense when you get further than you usually do, and finding a secret is satisfying and takes you all the way back to the oldschool games.
This is a very good game. I wish it didn't depend so much on being careful and mindful. ( running just feels so good in this game, being careful feels like walking with your legs dragging over the ground ) A definite buy for everyone who enjoys a rogue-like old school game with lots of replayability and secrets. Also great with co-op!

Now you've probably read a lot of reviews about how awful this game is. How the network is buggy/laggy, how there are so many hackers in this game, and how certain factions are nerfed while others are buffed,
As someone who has been playing this game for 2 years, I can disprove all of these claims:
But this isn't about debunking all of these awful reviews this game has gotten. This is about how and why I would recommend this game to the people who might actually find enjoyment in playing Heroes & Generals.
With the official release of this game 8 days ago, I can say for absolute certainty that this is one of the most addicting games I have ever played. Keep in mind that I never said it was one of the best, but given a bit more time, it could be.
The devs of this game are veterans; the founders of this game have been in the industry for over 2 decades, so they know what they're doing moreso than these college graduate indie developers who completely give up on a game once they get bombarded with bug reports/cash-grab ponzi scheming accusations. I have been a follower of HnG from the Patton Build to the current Garman Build, and this game has certainly come a long way. And when the Devs said that they will continue developing the game after its official release, I believe them.
The community of this game, however, can be a bit cancerous. As with any MMO, you have your general clueless players who never go to the forums or the Wiki to have their basic questions answered. You have your Wehraboos people who cosplay religiously as Nazis. You have your whiners who cry about how this game is too hard or is rigged against them, as if they are being personally targeted. This is just one of the many flaws that come with any MMO, but it's not completely cancerous. There are a lot of good players, veteran players who have been here since the Alpha, who actually want to help new players get aquainted. These people aren't hard to find at all, and would probably take great pride in helping you love this game as much as I do.
But you're probably still wondering why I would recommend this game. I am one of the few that actually plays with friends and plays like a team with my team. When you're not one of those random players who doesn't know what he's doing, and you're actually playing with friends who work well with you in-game, then this game is definitely worth looking into. I have put in close to 1000 hours on the Browser version because the Steam version of this game constantly crashes on me, even though I run an 8 core, 16gb RAM, GTX 980 beast of a computer, so don't get skeptical just from looking at the 40+ hours I have clocked in on Steam.
Even after reading my review, many of you reading this will not enjoy this game. If any of these fit your description, you should definitely pass on this title:
Honestly, there are a lot of people that have posted negative reviews based solely on these reasons alone. These people have not taken the time to get to know this game, and frankly have no place leaving any kind of review if they haven't put in the time and energy to give this game a thought-out and detailed review.
All that being said, I hope you at least found this review informative and unbiased. I will edit this in the near future, so don't expect this to be my final review. Anything that you think I should cover, I probably will add in later if it hasn't been covered already. Good Luck!

RAW is a budget game with all pros and cons. I'd recommend it for fans of hack and slash RPGs who have finished all other games from this genre and are desperate to play some more. The others should probably look up for the better games first. Torchlight or The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing are examples of the better games.
There are bugs in this game. The first occurred when I tried to load a save file. The game froze. What's more, the game sometimes doesn't recognize pressed buttons, thanks to which your character won't use his/her special ability or drink health/mana potion. My character couldn't continue his journey to the next room because of a bug, so I had to restart the level. However, the biggest problem I had with the game is that it won't save your position in the level. So when you quit the game and want to come back to it later, you have to start from the beginning of the level. And yes, the enemies respawns. I also don't like that the game saves my progress only on checkpoints instead of anytime I wish(like in Van Helsing or Torchlight).
On the other side, the combat is good. I've chosen warrior class and was happy to see how enemies flew away from me whenever I hit them. I felt like a true hero, an unstoppable force who can slay enemies by dozens. The beginning of the game was a bit hard and boring, but after unlocking some powerful skills which could heal me and kill many enemies at the same time, the game began to be fun. The graphics is also good, in my opinion. As for the soundtrack, it does good job to enhance the grim atmosphere of the game.
Beside the warrior class, there are two other classes that you can play- mage and rogue. There are also a few side quests you can complete. The story isn't bad, but I think it's role is something that will motivate you to go further, not something that you will remember.

So far, I've found RAW to be, overall, pretty darn good and quite fun indeed. It may not be the next Diablo, but so what? It's still very enjoyable! In my opoinion, the experience is much better with a controller (I use an Xbox 360), movement is smooth and combat responsive in a way the keyboard & mouse can't quite match. This is definitely an action-oriented game, not a more literary or strategy-minded RPG - and that's one of the things I like about it. Sometimes you just want to bash hell out of stuff! The graphics are better than many of the other reviews here indicate, but anyway these days the graphical presentation of any one game is such an incredibly subjective thing that as long as a game runs smooth visually, that's what is really important. And RAW does. The environments are detailed, the atmosphere is well-crafted, and the overall look of the world is consistent. Oh, and the lighting is very nicely done as well! I've really enjoyed my time with it thus far, and will continue to do so, I'm sure.  -XT

This is not so much a game as it is an experience to be enjoyed.
Stunning visuals, phenomenal soundtrack, and very, very unique gameplay all go into this incredible game, but it doesn't end there. A well-written, believable story featuring no intelligible dialogue contributes vastly as well. And though the characters are left without names (in the convential sense) you find yourself just wanting to call to them anytime something unfortunate happens.
As counter-intuitive as the controls seem at first, it doesn't take long before your figure out the simplistic style and, despite them being easy to understand, they take practice to master. Whether you play just for the story, or embark on the sidequests along the way, you'll have yourself an incredible adventure as you follow these two brothers on their journey.
The story itself will have you smiling like an idiot, crying like a baby, and curling your toes with anxiety. Its fast-paced, fun exterior is coated heavily in a simple plot brought to life by simple characters that you can't help but fall in love with. It's so simple that you add your own complexity to them. Their personalities are shown through the little things you stop and do along the way and less by the story itself.

This is a fascinating puzzle game that is partially undermined by a middling user interface and missing feature.
The concept is creative - paint blocks to anchor houses and keep them from falling out of the sky.  There are different blocks with different abilities (red ones float, green ones are bendy, etc.), and you have a limited amount of each color.  The puzzles start out fairly easy, but quickly become mind-bending.  I was able to solve all but one on my own; unfortunately I'm not seeing a guide to get me past that one, although it's thankfully a bonus.
The game is strong, but it could be better with one thing: the ability to step back to just before you tested your solution so you don't have to redo every puzzle from scratch every attempt. That probably added an hour to the 5 hours it took me to finish. Without that frustration, the ability to experiment more freely would greatly improve the game.  The ambiance and story are cute, the puzzles creative and always providing new twists. If it were just a little more friendly to the player, it would be perfect, instead of just very good. (also, the physics of the drop seem to be a little random; sometimes doing the exact same thing twice would have completely different results. A little annoying, but not too bad).

Wargame is a gateway drug. It's like weed. You may think it's bad, may think it looks bad from its difficulty, or just don't like it anyways. But all your cool friends say it's great and you should try it. So, you being curious, you decide to try it to fit in more with your friends. Turns out that it's better -
better than you expected it to be, and you want more. You say you'll only do it once a month, but that turns into once a week, which turns into once a day, which develops into an addictive death trap. Even if you're a newbie to it you still do it since it's so damn
You do it more. Do it alone. Do it with friends. Do it with strangers. You can never stop; saying "5 more minutes" soon turns into 5 more hours. Once you get the hang of it, you start experimenting more with other things - things that will make your little gateway drug of a Wargame look like a vitamin gummy. Your friend shows you one such thing. It's some strange pill in an orange bottle called "Israel DLC" that's supposedly way better than the Wargame you've been smoking. Pretty soon you've devolved into some froze vegetative zombie state like someone dependent on Opium. You start taking risks, challenging other people, and, worst of all, you cheat. You troll. The warchat - previously the area where all the other junkies like you gathered, has self-destructed into a hotspot of hatred and vice. Your whole personality has changed  just by taking that one choice - something that'll haunt you for the rest of your life. And even if you quit, it'll still haunt you forever.
Take my word for it. I was a Wargame addict for some time - I quit a while back, and I've limited the toxicity coming into my system. I still do it, even if it's wrong, because it feels so right. Every waking hour on this planet I'm thinking of Wargame. It is my only love, and my only life. Nothing can change that. Even as I write this review, I can still hear the voices of my troops, calling out my name for their next objective. I still see rows and rows of tanks on the roads to certain doom, just so that they can satisfy me. And- oh god.. The artillery. The MRLS... The apaches... All those units, all those points gone in an instant, for what? Fame? Bragging rights? Money?
I'm going to have to leave now. My army calls me. I leave you with this message: Don't be like me. Don't be the guy sitting on his♥♥♥♥♥writing reviews for a video game for humorous effect. Don't overdose so much on Wargame. Go outside and ride a bike or something.
I'm Gucci Gilgamesh, and I approve this message.

Although I had some fun playing this game in campaign mode, I don't really know if I could recommend it due to one BIG concern: the game is not ready.
- Bugs here and there. Fall through walls, opponents getting stuck (either where they walk or in other opponents), strange things and actions in the game can happen when loading a savegame...
- Kind of a stupid AI. Your opponents will oftentimes behave strangely and unrealistic. For example, when someone sees a guy shot to death, he gets suspicious and looks around. Then, when he's not seeing you, he will just keep walking about thinking this is nothing to worry about. Can't say that's very realistic.
- The soundmasking of shots is not very consistent. A broken generator with its noise can act as soundmasking but other things which in real life could mask gun shots will not act as the same in the game.
- The shooting/aiming had some problems too.
- Some "obstacles" which you in real life just could climb over, walk over, or crawl under, is in the game unclimbable/unwalkable/uncrawlable. Instead you need to walk around etc.
In short I would say that this is a game with a lot of potential and great fun, but the fact that it is NOT ready yet spoils it. Really hate it when I buy a game and discover that the developer didn't care of making the game ready before releasing it.

This review is ENTIRELY based on CO-op play only!
The game is Good
- You cannot play it like an action game, take it slow and easy
- The game is edged towards sniper shooting therefore, only the sniper gets all the love for customizations
- Don't look for realism, it's not meant to be so
- Only 8 Missions = Almost 3 hrs or so per mission, DLC's add more
- Play co-op, a lot more fun.
What's not to like:-
- The game is not really well designed for Co-op, if one player dies, the game will start from Last check point, there is no drop in and drop off in the game, also if by chance anyone disconnects, you cannot save the game, but WILL have to play ALL the way from the START. This SUX when you've finished everything but the last objective after a 3 hr mission level.
- It is not Assassin's creed, it is not a close quarters stealth game BUT appears to be. The game actually deviates from previous Sniper Elite games in this regard as more often than not, you'll actually be taking enemies down with your silenced pistol close up.
- Close quarters is clunky, use silenced pistol instead as NOT ALL situations lend to taking silent take-downs, this is by design and incredibly silly as it's not intuitive.
- One shot from the sniper gun and the ENTIRE base is almost on you.
- Far too much emphasis on Sniper gun only, everything and the kitchen sink is thrown into it, other guns' accuracy and damage is purposely kept lower.
- Far too much emphasis on Headshots to take down, seriously! Come on. Give extra XP for it, Don't make a player shoot twice just cause he hit at the torso.
- Every mission becomes tediously long of about 3 hrs if you play it slow and hidden in the game.

Let me assume that you like a rts games, may be with emphasis on tactics, with no base building and resource collecting. Let me also assume that you are intrested in mordern warfare, realistic one, with a full variety of war machines... I think you will be intrested in this game.
This game isn't a simulator, there are no real parameters of vehicles, there is no accurate ballistics, there is no physically based armor penetration. This game utilizes a really impressive, tuned for balance and scales of the game, set of parameters to imitate combat like a real one. And what is more important, it does this quite well. The number of fractions and available vehicles are very impressive, nevertheless some intresting ones are absent. There are two blocks - Nato + Allies (Blue) and Warsaw Pact + Allies (Red). Every fraction has it's pros and cons, but overall Reds a less accurate, but more endurable, while Blues vice versa.
The single missions are not very important and can be considered as a training before you jump in multiplayer games. They are all about hypotetical conflicts and quiet entertainig. Unfortunately your experience in these missions won't help you much in multiplayer games. In latter ones you will suffer, because there are a lot of skilled players. They know tactical tricks, they have a good micro, they know maps. Thus it would be much better to play with a friends.
As a summary, Red Dragon is an intresting realistic-like strategy game with emphasis on a multiplayer game, if you like rts genre, you should probably try this game.

Como é que pode um jogo ser sempre diferente e ser sempre parecido? Os levels de Spelunky são gerados aleatoriamente, mas é possível aprender os macetes e pequenos cuidados que devem ser tomados para ir melhorando e percorrer mais rapidamente/eficientemente as fases. Aí você morre e começa de novo, dessa vez num level totalmente distinto... mas que você vai atravessar melhor, porque aprendeu as manhas nas tentativas anteriores. Mas os levels não eram diferentes?
Spelunky é um gerador de pequenas histórias, um mecanismo de criar experiências de apreensão, tensão, excitação (ui) e diversão (seja lá o que signifique isso). Os monstros, itens e as regras do jogo permanecem os mesmos, mas eles podem variar suas posições, quantidade e formas de funcionar segundo a programação do jogo. Por isso, cada experiência será diferente, mas vai manter similaridades com as anteirores. É difícil de entender como isso é possível, mas dá a sensação de que esse é o tipo de jogo que precisamos pro futuro: essa é a forma essencial de gerar histórias emergentes, e não inteligências artificiais perfeitas e/ou tramas bifurcantes com 500 finais diferentes.

Z is an good old RTS game that has the rock em sock em robots kicking each other in the nuts and bolts with guns and tanks. Really that's the kind of story you could think of for this game cause there really not much story to it. You command an army of red robots and use them to fight blue robots off of different worlds...that's mostly the official story.
Single player is alright, played a few missions on normal and found it challanging...maybe just me sucking at RTS games. Though I noticed when pitting a tank against another tank in battle it'll be a gamble...either the enemy tank wins or your's...all depends on if the AI is able to dodge and shoot well. Each mission will introduce you to either new robot units, vehicles, or defense guns to use; also some info about them. Each mission though is the same, capture more land than the enemy to be able to produce troops and vehicles faster; basically being able to over whelm your enemy before they can get reinforcements out. After a few missions though you'll get introduce to a new planet...but still the objectives is the same on each mission; control land and destroy enemy base.
No multiplayer it appears, seems this version of Z is more focus on single player. Speaking of this version, it's a complete port from the mobile platform; meaning some parts not like the original game.
The only controls I've been using is just the pointy device of pointing rudely at things...meaning the mouse. Mouse control is fine, but getting from one part of the map to another is rather slow; even using the minimap doesn't make much of a difference. AI units can get stuck here and there at times, and at other times I feel as if the enemy has more toys to use against me.
What I find interesting about this game is the robots themselves. When selecting a unit you get an image of them displayed in a box, showing their facial reaction during different kinds of situations. They'll cheer when taking out an enemy, they'll panic when taking damage, they'll urge you to attack the enemy base when you hold more land, and they'll call you out as a loser when you're about to lose the game. They also find enjoyment in shooting up the wild life, either being trigger happy or just dislike mother nature. I wish most RTS games of this day would do that.
Anyway, here's the pros and cons ladies and gents.
+Different planets and maps of single player
+Interesting unit reactions
+Decent controls
-Not the original, a mobile port
-repetitive mission objectives
-Poor cutscene quality
-An RNG like combat system between AIs
-No multiplayer.
Despite this game being a mobile port and missing a few things from the original release of the game, it's still a worth a try when a sale hits.

In Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, we have a perfect example of how games can offer a completely different experience that other mediums simply cannot achieve. Brothers isn’t trying to be cinematic, episodic or like a cartoon. It exists as its own style of storytelling that tells the narrative through your hands.
Gameplay/Story?
Brothers puts you in control of two characters simultaneously creating the first one-player co-op game. One brother is controlled with the left thumbstick for movement and the left trigger for actions; vice versa the younger brother is controlled on the right. There is no reason for one brother being assigned to a certain side of the controller but it can be confusing when the brothers cross paths on screen. In fact, having two characters moving in unison in the same direction is a lot harder to achieve than you’d expect. Even towards the end of the game, I was finding this coordination quite difficult.
Luckily, most of the puzzles don’t require this parallel movement and the brothers can be controlled alternatively or whilst one brother is performing a different type of movement. First game of its type so I’ll give an example; one character had to rotate a lever whilst the other had to grab, hold on and release a cable to reach the other side. Having two different types of movement occurring meant one can be a repetitive action whilst the other can be focussed on for precision. It was such a refreshing gameplay style that felt new but intuitive. The puzzles were always so flowing and enjoyable yet it felt like an accomplishment each time, which is the puzzle game nirvana. Brothers is so cleverly designed that the type of puzzles were inspired by the level design making it always feel fresh even if the puzzles were similar.
As I said earlier, the story is in your hands. Because there is no dialogue of any sort, only spoken gibberish, yet the emotion came through the intonation and the body language of characters. This is Starbreeze highlighting that spoken language is only a small percentage of communication. Starbreeze is an interesting company to take on a project of this size, as they have roots in big, sci-fi shooters including one of my favourite games of all time, The Chronicles of Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay. The setting is more related to the Fable series or more likely an interpretation of Swedish scenery and stories where Starbreeze are based.
Not going to spoil anything but the story is a journey to retrieve a treasure to save a loved one’s life. But, as expected, the journey is not a straight-forward one and many interesting characters are met on the way. That’s about as much detail as needed as it has to be played in order to truly feel the strong bonds between the characters and the hardships they have to overcome. It can get quite dark so this isn’t a game for children and it often surprised me how emotional it became. The mechanics connect so beautifully with the narrative that things such as making one brother hold on to another while swimming carries huge, emotional weight. The way the characters interact differently with the same objects also brings out a lot of personality not only individually but as a brotherly relationship. The music also highlights the bittersweet aspect of the story with a powerful main theme that is truncated into variations reflecting each situation. Starbreeze clearly cared and thought about every aspect of the design.
Saying that the game was too short, at 2-4hrs, seems unfair as it needed no more nor warranted any less. Warm porridge, I guess.
Technical
It’s beautiful in its art design and provides long-distance vistas, which adds to its charm. The sound is lovely with a real sense of comfort to make you feel at ease at the beginning before turning darker and colder. Brothers obviously draws its inspiration from The Lord of the Rings, what doesn’t these days, and it has at least one reference to the fantastic indie game LIMBO, but it still feels new and original.
Verdict
Brothers is a beautiful, gaming experience where the bittersweet narrative is told through the controller. And you will need an Xbox 360 controller for this.

Spelunky is a challenging platformer. I prefer a more casual approach to gaming. I need things like save-points and time to explore. This game is too fast paced and unforgiving for me. Eventually you can skip levels to kind of continue where you left off. The levels are randomly created. There is also a decent number of special events and unique bonuses added in. Your character can pick up and throw or swing just about anything. Skill enhancing items can be purchased (or stolen) to give you an advantage.
Bottom line is if you enjoy a challenging platformer, Spelunky has loads to offer you. If a game without the safety net of save-points makes you shudder, skip this one.

Wargame: Red Dragon is an RTS expandalone, so there is no need to buy the other games. In a genre defined by dogma, this game is a beacon of hope. This game has many western and eastern countries, set between 1970 to 2000. This game attempts to strive for realistic depictions of real life hardware.
There is no base building, you create your army before venturing into the flames of battle. It does this in an addictive deck system, in which you can pick and choose your units. There are a staggering amount of choices, including motorized infantry, mechanized infantry, tanks, helicopters, hq units, supply units, planes, and others. The scope of the maps matches the scope of the deck system, including massive maps built for combined ops. This allows for massive engagements with semi-realistic weapon ranges.
Even though this is the third game in the franchise, it does have obvious flaws. One of such is the infantry. Infantry moves strangely, with speed and animation not synchronizing. The formations of the infantry is often staggered circles, they do not take cover unless you shove them in structures. For some reason, tanks and other vehicles cannot use coaxial machine guns. These another factors contribute to make this game's tactical side to appear shallow. There are no strategic bombers or missile launchers, and the ship combat is grossly scaled down and simplified.
This game features multiple "dynamic" campaigns, which are annoying but pretty well crafted. The skirmish and multiplayer are solid. The multiplayer features a very ecstatic community, if you take it with a grain of salt it can be vary humourous.
In conclusion, this game is a fresh new take on RTS, only one of its kind, however it suffers from a lack of polish and attention to detail. I cannot wait until the next installment.

Realms of Ancient War is an action/role-playing game with a strong affinity for hack ’n’ slash, developed by Wizarbox. At the beginning of the story, you must choose whether you are going to spend the game hurling fireballs and deadly spells at numerous foes as a Wizard, slowly ploughing your way through armies of enemies as a powerful Warrior, or utilise your endless skills of survival striking from the shadows as a Rogue. You are then presented with a quick run-through of recent events of the last few decades or so, and then are thrown head-first right into the action, slowly turning your character into an unstoppable whirlwind of fury, complete with a power pretty unique to Realms of Ancient War that allows you to take control of your enemy’s strongest units and turn them on their own.
In the first impressions, Realms of Ancient War has obviously had a lot of time and energy invested into it for its graphics, which really shine through at points. The loading screens are actually some of the most pleasing to the eye and the scenery in the game tends to be very well-put-together. The magic spells especially, although only visible for a short time, look great and the scenery, again, is overall of a very high standard. The title has also managed to ensure that the dead bodies of your former opponents stay on the battlefield instead of evaporating as they tend to do in most other titles, which allows for an enhanced sense of satisfaction as you look around caves that are now marked with your handiwork. In contrast, the actual character design, which looks stunning in all of the artwork, is disappointing. You will certainly notice the main things about your character as they change throughout the game and you equip them with different coloured armor and weaponry, but on the most part all of the little details have seemingly been quickly brushed over, leading to an overall effect which just isn’t quite satisfactory, especially at higher levels where you look almost identical to how you did at the start.
The combat in Realms of War almost certainly delivers on its promise of being a hack ’n’ slash as you work your way through innumerable enemies of different varieties, depending on where you are along the storyline. You will find yourself being ambushed by large amounts of enemies that don’t tend to have that much life at all. You can breeze through most of the game as long as you are careful as to where you run to so you don’t get blocked in, because once you are blocked in you will almost certainly be cut down by the horde which has beelined straight for you – a design you will very quickly be able to use to your advantage. Throw down a poison trap and walk backwards a few steps and it is guaranteed that whatever is running at you will completely disregard the danger and run straight into it. Running away is your number one and only form of defence, seeing as there is not a control for blocking or dodging at all.
Wizard and Rogue classes allow you to use ranged attacks before you go charging in, and although they tend to look great and give you the upper hand in small skirmishes, more often than not you will find that any distance between you and your target has been closed down before you can manage more than a few shots. Luckily, as you grind through enemies you also grind up the levels and you will be given skill points to assign to different characteristics, such as increased ranged damage or an increased mana pool, which make these ranged moments a little more useful; but in the most part, the skill points you assign tend to actually do very little.
Combat-wise, you will also come to grips with the soul gems. During each level, you are only assigned a certain amount, which are used to revive. Running out of soul gems means you are sent back to the start of the level, and it is not until late in the game where you will be given the opportunity to avoid using one. However, it definitely adds a twist to the game, which notches up the difficulty a little and makes the game a little tenser as your supply begins to dwindle.
In addition, Realms of Ancient War has a less-than-gripping storyline, and you will rarely feel the compulsion to carry on playing like you do with other games of the same genre. The lore is vague, and the opening sequence of events that explains the recent history gives you very little idea into this world of warcraft and wizardry and the relationships between the four different sections of the continent, and you don’t really cover much more of this as you work your way through the game. Furthermore, the levels can be a little confusing to navigate at points, due to a strange choice of deciding not to include a map or mini-map; as well, directional arrows tend to point as the crow flies, but if you have some experience with these types of games then there should not be too much problem with finding your way around. The way the dead bodies remain on the floor will almost certainly signal to you that you have been there before.
Finally, although the game lacks multiplayer, you can engage in a co-op campaign by connecting a few wireless controllers. This makes the game a lot more playable and does reduce the chances of your character getting mobbed by the throngs of creatures out for your heads. However, it is a little bit disheartening to find you cannot team up with somebody over the Internet, which would have made the game a lot more appealing in an era where almost every game has some form of online capability.
In conclusion, Realms of War is a title that is on the lower side of average in the genre it exists in. Although the graphics are great from the menu screens and scenery, the characters just never seem to look that detailed or magnificent as you would want them to, and it contrasts greatly with the artwork displayed throughout. The combat system is very basic as it lacks a mini-map, blocking, and dodging; and you tend to spend your time in the middle of a sea of monsters. But to give credit where credit is due, it is still very enjoyable to hack your way through such a large opposition and come out the other end, and the brief moments of rampage as you take charge of some of the stronger units are definitely great fun. The game looks great, but the input problems and clear microtransactions-laiden design chocies make it difficult to enjoy.  It feels like its menu was designed for a tablet, and the tutorial is broken.
Steam page and the in-game messages seem to promote use of a gamepad, but a lot of the moves are only clearly available for keyboard... and you can't remap the gamepad keys.  There isn't even a way to disable the controller in-game so you can remap the controller buttons to keyboard keys.  This proved to be a major headache from the start of the game.
The tutorial also cannot confirm I've landed a grab trick.  This lies in the same realm of problems as the controller input issue I previously mentioned.  It says to hold a bumper button (LB or RB) to do a grab trick.  I had to consult a user-created guide (through Steam's community guides) that explained it wants you to hold a bumper and the right joystick to do a grab trick.  I did that, and I landed the trick, but the tutorial said I wasn't done.  The "basic grab" controls were not explained in-game at all, so I was left scratching my head - which is an awesome thing you can do by the way - wondering why I could not complete such a simplistic set of tasks in under ten minutes.  This game weighs in at 4GB, so I decided to go ahead and stop right there and save that space for a game that's more polished and enjoyable.  Reading other reviews, I discovered that the game has been handled very poorly since its Kickstarter campaign was funded, so I doubt the game will amount to much in the next few months.
Still, it's free to play.  Try it if you have time.  There's very little competition in the snowboarding genre.

Overall I've found Torchlight 2 a good value and spent many enjoyable hours at it. The drops come fast and furious and you don't go very long without finding a unique. The game play is fast and grinding isn't a requirement. The addition of multiplayer is an upgrade from Torchlight 1 but finding your friends to play with can be an issue.
A couple bad points though. The lack of a full respec makes trying out different skills very difficult. Also the difficulty system makes very little sense. There appears to be no difference in drops for normal/veteran/elite. Additionally, you can't change the difficult once you start a character. The New Game plus feature lets you replay the campaign with the monsters at a higher level and get better drops but unless you are just looking for a challenge there is little point to playing on the higher difficulties.

SIMPLE REVIEW:
One of the best space sandbox games ever.
Easy Builder - Can make very complex structures with simple and intuitive controls! (If you're lazy, there are ship generators)
Procedural World - Sectors are always fresh!
Tons of Factions - Makes the world feel more alive!
Fleet System - Build multiple ships, and give them orders!
Great Controls - Third-Person and RTS controls!
Epic Combat - Destruction feels amazing and weapons feel great!
Great Economy - Mine, Trade, Loot, Mess with Factions, etc.! There are even AI Traders that affect the economy!
And a heck of a lot more features, in a simple game.
It's also CHEAP and it puts some AAA titles to shame ;)
Final Review?
9/10 - Almost Perfect ;)

I've played much more of this game than my hours might indicate, and feel obliged to review it. This will be short and to the point.
The sniping mechanics are great. As you crank the difficulty, it gets wildly difficult to pull off 150m+ shots, and they are vastly rewarding.
People are complaining that it's essentially a stealth game and the sniping is tacked on. Not really the case. It does require a lot of stealth, but there are tons of opportunities for sniping shots if you scan the area and make a gameplan beforehand. Train Simulator. I don't really know where to start on the game. I have owned it since Rail Simulator back in the days and when it realeased, it was a good game! However, over the years, the game has been upgraded and features have been added. The development of the game has been taken over by DTG that released it as Train Simulator 2012 and offered free updates over the years. And that is where the problem arises. The game was upgraded with new features that clogged the main engine.
You might think, "Hey, new features, that's nice!" but think again. Most features means more use of resources which, in this game, are pretty scarse. Since the engine is still from Rail Simulator, it is 32-bit, pretty inefficient and it means when you get over 3,4GB of memory (and trust me, you can hit that limit pretty easy!) it runs out of memory and the game crashes in a tempdump, if it hasn't crashed already in a random crash, which happens quite often.
Having that said, the game looks nice. Most train models are good quality and are well worth driving. The BR155, the recently released TGV Duplex on the LGV from Marseille to Avignon, the Class 395 Javelin are all great trains that are worth a drive. With real and correctly working TVM and PZB / SIFA implementations that'll make you scratch your head every now and then why the train throws itself into emergency again.
But what is a train without a railway? The game luckily includes routes where the trains you buy fit on perfectly. Most of the times. Köln - Koblenz, Sherman Hill (re-release!), Rivera Line in the 60s, and the Norfolk Coal District. The Köln - Koblenz route was released around 1,5 years before the release of Train Simulator 2016, Sherman Hill was included in one of the very first installments of Railworks, Rivera Line in the 60s is a re-release in an older era of an existing route and the Norfolk Coal District... *sigh*
The routes included with Train Simulator 2016 were among the most laziest I've ever seen. The developers didn't include any new routes, just one new locomotive (the BR155) with the Koblenz route, the Gas Turbine locomotive with Sherman Hill, some steam engines with the Rivera route and the Norfolk Coal District included some existing locomotives. Also, if you had Train Simulator 2016 and you wanted the new HUD (which was also updated from Train Sim 2015 to Train Sim 2016) you had to BUY THE GAME AGAIN FOR €29,99 (now 22,99). Basically for a worsened HUD and two locomotives from which one is actually really nice.
Having that said, most of the add-ons in this game are not included in the base game. You'll get three or four routes. Depending on which version you buy (German First Class, US First Class, UK First Class, Steam Edition, Epic Journeys). That's it, the rest of the add-ons you'll have to buy. And boy, the prices of these add-ons are ridiculous. Let me take the LGV: Marseille - Avignon as example. You'll get a 100km long route and ONE SINGLE train, the TGV Duplex. All of that for... Just €29,99! Wait, what?! This single route costs more than the base game which included four routes?! And you get only one train?! Yes. DTG is asking ridiculous prices for their add-ons. This LGV route alone costs more than the entire base game conbined. The recently released Maglev route basically lets you press a button before the train drives itself to its destination where the scenario ends. All of that for just 22,99!
Also, DTG does not support other countries than their base three. These are Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States of America. Do you live in The Netherlands (like me), Belgium, Spain, Italy, Switzerland, Japan, India, or any other outside these three, do not expect DTG to make DLC from your country. The French DLC they released was the first (and probably the last) in THE ENTIRE LIFESPAN THAT Train Simulator EXISTS (wait, Semmeringenbahn from Austria was also released. If you don't count that they reused only German assets from previous routes except SOME assets and included only a repaint of an already existant locomotive. Heck, the passenger coaches didn't even include a luggage and first class car). They simply deny that other countires have rail enthousiasts, I think, while they could expand their userbase explosively by adding more and different countries to their collection.
After complaing about the content of the game, let's move on to the working of the game. The trains you drive are pretty good, as mentionned earlier. They work, they drive, they have accurate safety systems. They drive on routes that look pretty nice, but lag at busy places. Mannheim, Munich, London. All these cities lag like crazy. Its not some 'busy area' lag where the framerate drops to 30 instead of 60, but true lag. 5-15fps depending on your system and on what quality you have set the game to. The standard scenario's that come with the games trains or routes usually lack any AI-traffic (trains you meet on the other track or during your journey). Especially the LGV lacked any AI traffic whilst its one of the busiest LGV's in France. If gives you a feeling you're... Alone. It gives the route a feeling of... Emptiness. If you meet or encounter one or two other trains during your drive you are quite lucky. Happily most routes have integration with Steam Workshop, where users can upload their own scenario's. With dozens of proper scenario's you can find some nice scenario's there. But wait, most users use more trains than included in the route you're trying to drive. Yeah, you'll need to buy those first before the scenario works properly, if it doesn't crash because of the memory limit. But Munich station completely empty looks nice, at least.
Creating your own scenario's is quite hard. You need to get used to it first. The AI trains have the mental capability of a teaspoon (©FringeStalin) and usually the dispatcher that checks every order after you insert it and calculates everything between the orders fails if you work either longer than 20 minutes or insert more than 3 AI trains. This makes the scenario fail itself alltogether making you angry and the scenario unplayable. But hey, if you restart the game entirely everything is magically fixed! Only thing you have to wait for are the loading times, which if you are not on a SSD, are amazingly slow.
Don't even bother building your own routes. The number of workarounds and things that are NOT documented by DTG is so high that making a route yourself is close to impossible if you don't put enough time in it.
There is some nice 3rd party material available for free. Altenburg - Wildau from SAD is one of the best available and I highly reccomend you getting this one straight from the start.
Overall I give this game a 4,5 out of 10. There's much more I'd like to tell, but my tip: Only get this game in Steam Sale for 75% or more and make sure to thouroughly check if any add on you want to buy is in a package that's on discount.

It was really hard for me to recommend this game initially. I had played 5-6 levels and I was getting increasingly frustrated with the game. It felt nothing like Doom, and worse still it didn't feel fun at all. Read on and I'll tell you why you should get this game anyway.
First off: This game is old. It runs by default in 4:3 resolution. You can find several solutions to this in the forums.
Doom 3 tries really hard to be FEAR, Half-Life and Doom all at the same time. It takes a more realistic, dark and gritty approach to the original Doom storyline. It replaces frantic gun-blazing and monsterspamming with dark, gloomy and "scary" corridors with fewer, more powerful enemies. This in itself is not a bad thing. After all, Half-Life was a great game!
The narrative is mostly told through voice overs or found PDAs. I kinda like this approach, it keeps you inside the world.
Where this game suffers really badly is the actual gameplay. It tries really hard to be scary and it shows. It's pretentious at best and ham-fisted at worst when it comes to the so called "scary moments" with color shifts, lights going out and comically overplayed "evil laughs" echoing through the halls.
The guns feel like pellet guns. There is no punch to any of the weapons, the sound assets for them are extremely weak and there is no satisfying feel to any of the weapons when you fire them. Enemies feel bullet-spongy and have a really annoying habit of not being present in the game world until you pass a certain trigger. This leads to excessively annoying moments where enemies keep coming from areas that you have already cleared. It's almost every single time you encounter enemies you'll have some coming from behind you. This can be cool for some panic induced fighting on occasion, but this game does it every single time and it gets old FAST.
Now, with all these problems, why do I recommend it? Because I got fed up and installed Doom 3 XTRA mod. This mod updates graphics, model assets, textures and sounds to a more modern standard, but it also fixes all the problems I have with the gameplay. By giving weapons more punch and over all more satisfying oomph and sounds, it makes the shooting fun again. Sure the game is still overly pretentious with its scary "jack in a box" moments and enemies always coming from behind, but you know what? With Doom 3 XTRA I don't give a ♥♥♥♥. Thar be demons to shoot in the face!
So in short, if you intend to get this game don't even bother with the stock game. Doom 3 XTRA turns this game from a boring yawnfest into a frantic shooter with some ignorable issues.

An extreme disappointment.
Perhaps my expectations were set too high by the vast amounts of praise I saw in reviews for this game, but as someone who loved and would highly recommend Journey, I figured this game would be perfect for me. This was not the case, as though this game only took 2.6 hours for me to complete (with a few side objectives, mind you), I could not wait for it to end.
I expected this game to be an immersive experience, nothing more. However, I was immediately ripped out of that illusion by the horrible controls, or rather the lack of any control whatsoever. The single context-sensitive action button is finicky and annoying. Jump heights are inconsistent, and often puzzles are more a test of endurance than a test of critical thinking and timing.
Without spoiling anything significant, there is a section in the game where you are on a hang glider. Simple enough. However, during this whole ~1 or 2 minute section, you are required to hold down both triggers. If you let go for a split second, one of the brothers will let go and plummet to their deaths, forcing a restart. This is infuriating game design, and can be found throughout the game.
Additionally, the above only applies when you are actually playing the game. There are countless sections where you watch a short cutscene, then walk forward ten meters, only to have another cutscene start playing! Rinse and repeat.
I could go into finer details about my disapointment in story and relative lack of character progression, but I must admit that it is hard to do so without spoiling something. In short, this is a game that is definitely supposed to make you feel emotionally attached to the two characters and tug at your heartstrings as you accompany them on their quest. I felt no such connection to the characters, even during the ending and epilogue. I saw what this game was trying to do, but it resulting in nothing but wasted potential.
The only positive thing I can say about this game is that the environments are absolutely gorgeous. Screenshots and videos don't do them justice.
Regardless, I cannot recommend this game to anyone.  I'm shocked that anyone would pay $15 for this game, I feel ripped off even though I got it on sale. Apparantly lots of people have loved this game, but I simply found it to be a frustrating waste of time.
Two and a half hours of pressing forward and holding the triggers once in a while. Think of this game as Dear Esther, but with mindless little obstacles that take no effort to overcome.

As the tale begins .. "A man, clinging to life. His two sons, desperate to cure their ailing father, are left with but one option..."
.. that's right, to go on an epic bro-tastic quest to save him!
Starbreeze studios have created a fantasy world in Brothers that oozes with vibrance, life & atmosphere that really makes the world come alive. This is complemented by excellently detailed character animations & enviromental/weather effects that give additional impact to every scene (and they look really good!). Camera selection/direction is fluid & enhances each specific scene, drawing attention to a beautiful vista or the next path to take. There are also park benches throughout the game, where the bros can sit to view the gorgeous panoramic scenery. This was a really nice touch!
Each controller stick & trigger controls each brother independantly (Left for big bro, Right for lil bro). Dubbed as 'Single player Co-op', this mode of play makes for some interesting gameplay mechanics & puzzle solving challenges (not to mention the challenge of actually coordinating your brain to control two players at once!). Its not that easy trust me lol! The rest of the game in general is very forgiving & overall isn't too puzzling &/or difficult to complete.
Exploring, you can find some fun Easter Eggs, some relating to achievements, but others that are just there to make you smile and have a fun moment :)
For me, the real stand out feature in Brothers was the story, which is a bit strange to say really, as there is actually no understandable dialog in the entire game! Everyone speaks a
language you cannot understand. This actually works in the game's favor due to the quality animation & scene direction; you just understand what is going on naturally & the details of it all become irrelevant. Interestingly, the emotions become more relevant as you watch the brother's story unfold.
It's impressive storytelling, exploring (among other things) family, sacrifice & loss, helping others & overcoming fears, along with some heartwarming & heartbreaking moments too. All moving you forward to the unforgettable conclusion

Overall, Brothers has smooth & relaxing gameplay, devoid of any of those frustrating gamer moments. Impressive graphics, quality sound effects & a musical score that drives the emotional impact throughout extremely well. It's a short, but memorable 4-5 hour experience with immersive storytelling & plenty of adventurous 'Indiana Jones & Tomb Raider-esque' action sequences to enjoy.

This is one of those titles that you should not play unless you know what to expect going into it. On the surface, R.A.W. is another Diablo-style hack & slash RPG lootfest wherein you slay endless waves of strikingly homogenous minions and swap gear out for marginally better gear. In this respect, R.A.W. succeeds where many others succeed and fails where many others fail; gameplay is satisfying (if repetitive at times), programming is relatively bug-free, and the story is... well.. there's a story at least, some games don't even have that. What R.A.W. provides for Steam, however, is all of this formula that can be enjoyed both with a controller and with a local friend. If you own at least one 360 controller, you and a friend can enjoy quite a few hours of good old mindless RPG baddie slaughter. Overall, I'd give this game a 6.5/10; solid gameplay, proper controller support, and local multiplayer often outshine the game's general lack of ambition.

I've banged my head against it for a while and just can't say that I really like this game.
It's similar to Super Meat Boy, in that you can say that it's a skill based platform where most of your deaths are 'your fault' and you slowly build skills through trial and error to beat the game. But the question I ask, as an adult with limited free time, is this: Why are those skills that one would want to build up? What is it that makes it worth it?
In a game like FTL you've got the overarching narrative of the rebellion to keep you hooked in, with a unique story path each time. This is just a vague 'let's explore a hole in the ground' storyline that isn't exactly compelling. There's no payoff other than a scoreboard and achievements. And that's not really enough for me.
Small frustrations also are quite irritating. On three occasions, I've spawned in a level, heard an environmental explosion go off in the distance and had a shopkeeper or Kali shrine get caught in it and immediately blame me. Annoying.
I certainly got a fair few hours out of it. But I'm just not having fun. So I can't really recommend it.

Spelunky is, well, Spelunky. There's no game quite like it, which is a shame, because it truly is the best, most enjoyable game I've ever played. So you can use the ghost to farm money, but you have to be careful about it. Everything is a two-way street in Spelunky: arrows and rocks can bounce back when thrown, traps also affect creatures, and a shotgun's recoil will blast you back (possibly onto a spike trap). Every game something new and spectacular happens, something you wll always remember. The co-op is chaos, with betrayals and teamwork alike, but even after their adventurers are dead your friends will still have a ghostly impact on the game. After some practice you start to predict and look out for things, but your predictions never fail to be slightly wrong, as some critter thows a spanner in the works. Finally, if all of that wasn't enough to convince you to buy it, it was GAME OF THE YEAR from PC Gamer (in my opinion the greatest gaming mag on the planet). Forgive me lord for I have sinned...I didn't buy this game sooner even though I knew it for years, and worse, I got it pirated the first time I played it in the 11th grade because it was being passed around the school while we had tablets...BUT I NOW REPENT! I sell you my soul to become the greatest warrior throughout all of Calradia, to woo a horribly pixelated wife and to make all the self-proclaimed kings bend the knee!
Okay, so all messing around aside, I've played till day 500/600 something (give or take since I had multiple save files) and if my math checks out, that's around a 1000 hours of real time, so I HAVE played enough to give a review despite it saying I've barely touched the game. And, I admit, that's STILL barely anytime compared to other people. Now that THAT'S out of the way, let me just say it right away: This game is GREAT. However, from a review point, that's not useful information, as a review is supposed to help you try to decide if you truly want this game or not, so I'll do the best I can.
This game has amazing replay value, great immersion, and a unique gameplay style that can really hook you if you're into RPGs. You start off as a nobody and have to build your army, join a faction, recruit useful allies to help cover your weaknesses and conquer the land. Unfortunately, that's about as much story as you get, but there ARE certain NPCs that want your help to reclaim "their" throne, and all of them have a pretty interesting backstory that tie in to the lore. But the real draw of this game is the gameplay; Combat can be a choice of first or third person, with the option to be on horseback or infantry, and on the location you're battling, altering terrain. For example, you could be sieging or defending a castle, and depending on which faction you're helping, it'll put you on the appropriate side; attackers will be trying to force their way in, stepping over a literal corpse pile, while defenders man the towers and try to mow down as many as possible before the enemy storms into the throne room, their last defense. THEN, there's the large arsenal at your disposal as well; throwing weapons like spears, knives and even ROCKS, to the classic swords, shields, bows, axes, lances and the nice addition of crossbows. I believe the combats quite simple but I guess that's cause I only play the campaign. I've heard that in multiplayer it's actually quite a challenge to master. But that's just one part of the game; the part I personally enjoy is the strategical overview of Calradia. While not in combat, you'll be spending most of your time travelling on this map with your sprite. To help get you a picture, imagine Final Fantasy 7: You've got the same Over World look then, when you enter combat, you switch over to first/third person and slaughter those poor, naked bandits. There's also an interesting system in which your army actually has morale and it's based on the variety of food you give them as well as the last time they've been in battle; needless to say, a healthy and battle-ready army is leagues better than an army that's only eaten wheat for months and hasn't seen battle in just as long.
Now, of course with all games, there are problems. The game looks a bit ugly vanilla, with characters horribly pixelated like they were from the PS2 era and your allies can be straight up IDIOTS that♥♥♥♥♥♥you off because they'd rather be at a stupid banquet than help you fight off the entire enemy army, but these problems can easily be fixed with the help of mods, and let's be honest, most of us are gonna use them anyway, and there are a WIDE range of mods that can make your experience enjoyable. There're even Star Wars and Lord of The Rings themed mods!
TLDR; (Sorry for long post, and I've never played the DLC before, so I can't say anything about those)
Pros: Great game with great replay value, interesting game play/mechanics, runs fairly well on even non-gaming PCs and a variety of mods to help the base game.
Cons: Dated graphics, stupid A.I., lack of story

An absolutely beautiful, well-designed space survival/exploration RPG. Note I call it a survival game; in present, early game is very much indeed a battle for survival as you hop from sector to sector, constantly under threat of alien or pirate attacks as you mine out all the iron and titanium in one sector, without the added protection of shields until you make it further into the game and find veins of Naonite.
Anyway, after digressing long enough...
-Pros
-Very fun, immersive style that is a particular rarity among "modern" games...
-Highly customizable ship building, ability to make near-invulnerable battleships and entire fighter fleets from within said battleship, along with many different kinds of materials to construct your dream cruiser (talking about stone, reflectors, glass, etc., not Trinium, Naonite, Iron, etc.)
-A highly thought-out economic system going on behind the scenes that you can take part in to boost your own credit income... INCLUDING ILLEGAL SMUGGLING! HOW COOL IS THAT? LITERALLY BECOME HAN SOLO...
-Beautiful soundtracks...
-Astounding procedural generation.
-After dying, you don't have to build your ship from scratch again. Assuming you gave it time to save, just click "Saved Ships" while in build mode and scroll down...
-You can watch entire wars play out in front of you... kick back, enjoy the show, and salvage thousands of Naonite, Trinium, and even Xanion after the battle ends.
-BEAUTIFUL co-op potential... start your own faction, and even wage war on tens of different factions at once if you can convince enough of your friends to buy this.
-Four ways to progress your standing in the galaxy...
*Fight. Destroy big ships, get bigger guns, destroy bigger ships, repeat. Salvage credits from their corpses and use that to buy the resources you need to progress. Harder, but you can progress quite quickly if you sell the thousands of turrets you may acquire...
*Mine. Sit back, mine resources, sell them, repeat. Buy better mining turrets, run from Xsotan and pirates, salvage their guns after the other faction destroys them. Definitely one of the easier AND faster ways to progress.
*Salvage. Wait for the big battles to happen, or find locations where they have already. Once, I even found a destroyed station in a hidden mass sector with 986954 Xanion worth in the wreckage. Salvage high-value generators and shield generators for the most resources. Don't waste time on hull blocks. Easy and probably the fastest way to progress.
*Economize. Hard, extremely slow, and requires you to do a bit of grinding beforehand, but then just sit back and watch as the trade routes do all the work for you (especially in the new economy update currently live on the beta branch at the time of this review's writing...) Once it gets going, your bank will skyrocket. Use this opportunity to buy resources or turrets to buy the resources, buy fighter fleets, and boom, the bosses will vanish from the galaxy like the then galactic federation did when the Xsotan first arrived.
-Just generally a very innovative experience... one of the games I'd always been hoping became a reality. THANK YOU, Boxelware, for making this gem of a space game.
Cons
-Early access. Bugs... (obviously)
-More complicated looking ships like those seen on steam workshop require hours of fine-tuning specific blocks then building the same blocks over and over again... (just download the Victory Class Star Destroyer and select each block of the exterior hull to see what I mean.)
-Good weapons are extremely rare and/or expensive...
-Slow progress, accidentally crash and BOOM it's all gone. Insurance helps, but you still have to hire all your crew members and the like again. Thankfully you can recover all your turrets and upgrades, and at least salvage some of the resources you used.
-Economy system is very tedious to get into. Thankfully the next update that comes out after the time this review is posted will help with that.
Overall, a very, very good game, even for something in such early access. Love it, will continue to play it for a long time.
TROUBLESOME BUGS TO BE AWARE OF...
If the game crashes while transitioning to a new sector (which is common) you will likely be reverted to a previous point in your save file, and spawn in your mining drone with your ship possibly spawning several km away. Your ship may even have been reverted to a previous version. This bug can even spawn duplicate ships in the sector where the crash occurred...

If you played sandbox/(voxel-)building games before and enjoyed "Elite"-type /open world scenarios you might have a pretty good idea what to expect from Avorion. The player starts with limited resources and access to low-level technology and can work their way up to the good stuff. This can be done by mining, salvaging, combat, trade, piracy, payed missions, building own factories... there are a lot of options. A major part of the fun is in the ship building itself as it allows a huge variety of designs without being either too complex nor too shallow.
===
The good, the neutral & the ugly stuff (TL, DR section)
===
+ great ship editor/build mode
+ good variety of content
+ decent graphics
+ good performance (on a rather mediocre rig)
+ fitting and unobtrusive BGM
+ sorted UI/menus (for the most part)
+ learning the basics is (almost surprisingly) easy
+ ship design and operation seem to be quite balanced so far
+ polished game that's actually playable & enjoyble in it's current state (_especially_ considering its price tag and EA status)
===
> not much of a main storyline to push you to any sorts of goal
> there's mining (it's not too grindy)
===
- not all economical options are viable as of now (e.g. player owned factories are somewhat messy right now in terms of suply chains/automatisation)
- no in-game option to manage multiple saves (can be done manually though without much trouble)
- saving ship desigs is somewhat clunky (no easy way to (re)name and sort blueprints)
- seriously, I can't think of many reasons not to recommend it (except you're no fan of the genre)
===
My thoughts
As a fan of sandbox/building type games (e.g. From the Depths, Scrap Mechanic, Factorio) I highly recommend Avorion. It may not be a perfect game but it already feels like a great one for the most part and still decent for the rest. The ship designer is works really well and has a nice variety of handy tools like multiple, freely placable mirror planes, scaling blocks, adjustable grid size and so on. The gameplay is also up to par; none of it feels tacked on or badly executed. There are a few spots that could do with some polish (e.g. player-owned factories) but nothing major I could find. Maybe my biggest surprise is how well Avorion comes together; the editor, the open-world space setting, the solid gameplay and performance made this an enjoyable game for me. Maybe it's not exactly the right game for players who want lots of RPG elements and direct character interaction (there are better ones in this direction) but for evereyone else looking for a "build your own spaceship and blow stuff up" experience it's certainly worth a look.
