This is a poor mobile port of an old pc game.
Your purpose is to capture territory to build infantry and vehicles so that you can destroy the opposition's fort.  Territories may contain factories, radars, or repair stations.  There are no resources to capture, so units are continuously made after a few minutes.  The more territories you capture, the faster the units are made.
Gameplay depth consists of destroying and repairing bridges, destroying buildings, destroying terrain walls, having infantry cross water, and placing turrets.
Vehicles consists of jeeps (which can shoot out infantry in vehicles and turrets), light/medium/heavy tanks, APCs, and missile launchers.
Infantry consists of grunts, psychos (slightly upgraded grunts), toughs (anti-vehicle), snipers (anti-infantry and anti-turret), pyros (upgraded psychos), and lasers (upgraded snipers).
Turrets consist of gatlings (anti-infantry), guns (anti-vehicles), howitzers (long-range guns), and missiles (double fire power).
You select units, give an action, and the game then deselects the units.  Units do not stay selected after giving orders.  You can not deselect units unless you are giving orders or selecting other units.  This gets troublesome when you try to select a building right after selecting a unit or if you change your mind.
There are no control groups.  Your only other option is to cycle through your units.
Units can get stuck on small dens on the terrain.  In the original pc version, these were destructible, but here they are not.  Units may also sometimes take longer routes around obstacles instead of taking the shortest path.  I think they are prioritizing roads over rough terrain.
The game says that you can destroy buildings and bridges, but it does not say that you had to click on specific parts to do so.  You can destroy the opposition's fort, but you have to click on the tower bit.  It also does not tell you that you can enter the enemy's fort to blow it up.  To destroy bridges, you have to click on the edge, or you will get the wagging finger of denial.  There are no issues for other buildings though.
This might be a result of the game being ported, but you have to click at a certain speed to have the game read it as a click.  Luckily, there is no issue in-game.
The other resolutions are fine.
They are skippable, but they are pointless.  There should at least be an option to disable them.
While the original was a decent game, this steam version suffers from a lot of quality of life issues.  This is a result of both being a mobile port and being an old game.  While the concept is decent, this game really needs to be updated to be able to be played well today.

This game is made hard on purpose, i can live with a game being hard.
What i can't live with are controls that are unresponsive.
Tiny movements are extreamly hard to do. For example, you sit on a chair with the hammer beneath you and you want to raise the hamer extreamly slowly, well nope. If you move too slow with the mouse, there is no reaction.
The hammer does not follow the mouse, but it follows a pointer that follows the mouse. This is the entire reason people find the controls unresponsive as each have a delay.
Another problem is that the mouse and pointer will travel back to the hammerhead which is the reason why tiny movements are anoying to do. When falling your camera will move away from your character so that you can not save yourself since you can not see where you are going. Also the hammer will move up automatically when falling and you need to counteract that without seeing that happening.
The narator just annoys you with random poetry. I found myself getting mad at the narator and not the game, falling from a cliff and restarting wasn't frustrating, but hearing him talk was. And the poetry is really random, it has nothing to do with the game and it contains a lot of pretentious stuff.
This game is not hard because of hard level design, this game is hard because the controls are bad. A lot of people will say "get gud", but that isn't the problem here. You can get used to broken controls and start finding them good, but that doens't make them good. A car can have a stearing deficiency and the driver can be so used to it that he doesn't even notice it anymore, but the first other person will nearly crash into a wall since person 2 was expecting normal behavior. Does that make person 2 a bad driver that needs to "get gud"? No, the car's steering is garbage just like the controls are in this game.
The entire difficulty in this game is artificial, once you get used to the controls you can complete this game in 2 minutes.
If you want to play this game, do so expecting to have a bad time, don't expect a hard game, expect a frustrating game, but not a hard game.
If you do play this game, enable the trackpad even if you don't have one. It will remove the mouse acceleration. If you have a mouse with multiple dpi settings, use the lowest setting for all movements and the biggest setting for "flying" as the distance you fly is rougly dependend on the speed you move your mouse.

This amazing, unique platformer is like none other out there. Even after countless hours of playing, it's still extremelly enjoyable to play. There are many hardships in this game, including many deaths by many things which, at times, can infuriating. It will simply take time, paitence, and skill to get better at this game. However, when you finally accomplish something, the satisfaction that you'll feel makes up for it all. This game is very simple yet complex in its own way, hosting many secrets and many different game mechanics. The level generation in Spelunky is random, so every time you play it, it's a whole new adventure. The Daily Challenge and leaderboard system lets you compete with other players, and adds a whole new social aspect of the game. There's also the Deathmatch mode, which is a very fast-paced minigame which consists of a small arena where 2-4 spelunkers with configured inventories fight to the death. There are crates and monsters that spawn which can be used to your advantage or to someone else's. There are many different maps you can choose from, which you unlock by playing Adventure mode and visiting those areas. There is also a co-op system in the game, which can work to your advantage or to your disadvantage. The camera focuses on one player, and this can be confusing for many people. There's also the danger that you can injure whoever is playing with you almost exactly like a normal monster. As of right now, there is no option for online multiplayer. Regardless of all this, the co-op system can be very enjoyable at times. Overall, Spelunky is a great game and one of my personal favorites, that I would recommend to pretty much anybody.

What can I even say.
This game is a masterpiece. I bought it on sale, on a whim. "Eh, it looks pretty good," I thought to myself. How mistaken I was.
I laughed. I cried. I sobbed. This game is an emotional roller coaster of the highest caliber. It chronicles the journey of two brothers to find the cure for their father's illness, taking you through a magical fantasy landscape that capitalizes on the finest fidelity of the unreal engine. The storytelling is the finest I have ever seen, truly uplifting the medium of video games to that of any other fine art. These are not some one dimensional NPC characters. This is a world alive, filled with emotion and heartbreak and moments of pure joy.
The gameplay almost takes a background role in this game, but it is incredibly strong nonetheless. As the game recommends, it is indeed best played on a controller—the rumble effects alone, carefully used to emphasize the environment, make it worthwhile. As you control the characters, you become so intertwined in their identity that it feels like you practically become them.
I'm not a very emotional person. I cry perhaps once a decade. This game brought me to full-on tears. Do not continue your life without this game.
I cannot recommend anything more highly.

Sniper Elite 3 is a satisfying combination of stealth that's not irritating and sharpshooting that's not impossibly difficult, alongside interesting missions/maps. I'll admit, I passed over this one a few times because of the pedestrian-sounding name. "It does what it says on the tin." It is, however, a gorgeous, well-crafted game on par with Wolfenstein, with added history and realism, and without the monsters.
Only two issues: First, Sniper Elite 3 needs more missions (so did v2). We want to play more, we'd happily pay for more DLC, but there is no more. Second, the co-op system could be more robust. Most nights, we can play through a mission with zero problems. Other nights, we'd get 90% through and boom, our game would end because one of us "disconnected" (not really--we were chatting in Mumble the whole time). What followed was a game that often could not be resumed, and much swearing. That said, co-op mode is still the killer feature for us. Great 2-player fun.
If you have a friend, and you both have similar levels of patience (or impatience), add this one to your wishlist or cart right now. It runs great in both Windows 10 and Windows 7 for us.

Doom 3 was in its time a technical marvel, and it will forever be one of the last "game-changing" technical achievements. I remember when this was released and I was in college. All of my friends and I were sharing benchmark results, upgrading computer systems just to get better performance. I was however too cheap with my purple MX440 but I was happy nonetheless. We competed to progress through the game and it was a fantastic time!
From this point, computer game graphics have never really exceeded to amaze, and as the last major release I dedicated time to as a pre-graduate. The game brings together a fantastic new engine compiled by none other than John Carmack. The game demonstrates no unique story, no real plot.
It's a jump scare action shooter, it feels fantastic to shoot, and the game is quite fun and looks great still today. It shows a unique side than games today seem to show: satanic themes. As you progress through the game, you'll get more powerful weapons to face more powerful enemies which are reminiscent of Doom II's demons including the Imps, Pinkies, Archevilles, Mancubus and the rest of the gang. The game itself is traditional id software and there are still many of who love id software and you won't see me complain. Id were never great at story telling - it was all about fun and innovation which they've exceeded expectations due to Carmack's efforts.
The graphics were compared to the original Far Cry in its time and I could never understand how the two compared. Sure Far cry was innovative in its time, it was one of the first open world attempts and it was generally not recognised as a good game until years later in which I still don't find attractive...
Play this game and love it, but you won't need to play it more than once unless you're a fan such as myself. Great fun, good scares that get you jumping and great feeling shooting.

Well... I guess I found my favourite fighting game! Not only is this an Ivory tower among the other games in this franchise, MKX stands tall and proud in the fighting game genre. I sang great praise for MK9's story mode, MKX however boasts an even better experience. The story itself is what you'd expect from any MK game: trashy, silly fun. But the presentation is what makes the story mode so great. Extremely impressive cutscenes, great voice acting and awesome (and oh so silly) characters make the Story in MKX veeery enjoyable. And I couldn't help but chuckle at all the OBSCURE guest characters from the PS2 era of Mortal Kombat (which we all so desperately wish to forget...). The gameplay speaks for it self, it is absolutely amazing and clearly targetted towards a more high-level and competitive scene.
The thing I was most impressed with however, was the damn krypt. The krypt has become something a a staple in the MK games, here, the Krypt is SO ELABORATE. It is an entire horror game on its own. Zelda-esque exploration, fun little areas and those goddamn monsters...THE KRYPT IS A GOOD TIME FOR ALL. This game has so much kontent it really does shame others in the genre. (Didn't you just love the Story mode in Soul Cal V?) The game would be perfect if it wasn't for some of the minor performance hiccups many (including myself) are experiencing, but I'm sure this is something a simple patch can correct. (ok this, for me, has been resolved. I have not had performance issues since the myriad of patches) All-in-all, MKX is just a huge bundle of fun and salt.

This game clearly takes early access seriously. A solid base game, premise and execution which is entirely playable in it's current state with future developments in the pipeline.
The freedom in designing a ship exactly how you want it is great, and the ability to scale as both your abilities and resources allow keeps you entertained and interested. The game was refreshingly bug-free/light for early access, and it most certainly is worth the current price point.

Don't be mistaken, DOOM 3 is in no way meant to be a successor to the original Doom games. But that doesn't at all mean it's a bad game, persay. Some may lambast it for being different, but it's no DNF for sure.
For one thing, DOOM 3's gameplay takes a slower pace than the last two games in the series and benefits greatly from this change. No longer are you speeding through levels, never taking one look backwards at the scene. Instead, the game builds up it's mood to supplement it's slower action.
Weapons mostly share the same functions as the old set from the originals and mostly feel like the original weapons in terms of gunplay. However, it adds a new variable in late game that rewards players for sustained killstreaks. However, the rocket launcher lose it's secondary utility in the closed-off levels.
Now, the enemy AI seems rather one-note. Basic zombies merely walk at a snail's pace towards the player, making it incredibly easy to pick them off at range. Imps merely run after the player, throwing homing fireballs all the while in combination with melee attacks.
But the Z-Sec and the Commando shows that their AI at least has some competency in it's making, if they're not very advanced. They make use of cover, strafe around and make ample use of manuevers in their combat. If I could make a comparison, they fight like the HECU from the original Half Life.

First off, let me just say that this game has to be one of the most powerful stories I've seen in years, and that's without a single line of actual dialouge.  Second, the puzzles, visuals and and control scheme are some of the most interesting and detailed things i've seen in a while.  The game doesnt hold your hand or shove hints down your face, but the puzzles are done in just the way where you can find what to do through simple observation, but not too easy as to be boring.  The visual style isnt the most unique, there isnt much that looks exactly like it, but it's not totally innovative, and the controls are so tight and make so much sense for the way the game is played, they actually help add to the overall feeling of the game.
It's not without flaws though, first off, the game requires a controller, which i dont mind, i have one, but it does seem a bit lazy, considering how plenty of other games have done this with mouse and keyboard easily, there isnt a really much excuse.  Second, the game has no sense of graphical options, it's not difficult to run, but the ability to optimize to your rig is important, and other types of options to help make the game work best for you would be nice.  Next, the controls are great and they work well, but the way you have to hold the triggers so constantly and without any fail does tend to stress your indexes, especially since you also have to use the sticks at the same time, there's one platforming section that lasts an especially long time where you can not let go of them, and it's more of an endurance test than anything else.
But the pros outweigh the cons so heavily you dont notice them (well, the finger pain a little bit) while you're actually playing the game, it's worth every penny of the price and is the perfect example of the interactive journey, where you're involved as much as you can be, and is an amazing gaming experience and would be even without the great story, but the story is the other part of this game's bread and butter.  It's an interesting story that is deep, heart felt, and suspenseful at each twist and turn.   The enviroments tell the story just as much if not more than many games do with dialogue, and the voice acting has done more with zero words than some can do with a thousand.  It's truly impressive how they can actually build chamraderie betwenn you and these characters with such ease.
I truly believe that this game is to be put up into the ranks of the best games out there.  And I almost feel sorry for anyone that hasnt hade the intense pleasure of experiencing this game.  Please pick this up and give all due support to these very talented developers.

It's great that I can play 'Z' again on Windows 10 but there are some omissions that prevent it from being a faithful re-creation and some new additions which some have not been implemented that great.
So the game itself, which the base formula remains untouched in this re-release- Brilliant RTS with a different formula compared to other RTS's out there especially for when it was released. There's no base building instead however,  you capture territories around the map with each territory containing one of the following: Vehicle Factory, Robot factory, Radar or nothing. There's no currency, instead, units are created by time, when the countdown reaches zero, the unit appears out of the factory, the more territories that you control the less time it takes to create a unit.
As the game advances you gain access to more powerful units but the more powerful ones take more time so it's a case of trying to balance your army, do you wait longer for the more powerful units or build quicker weaker units?
The effects are nice with explosions going off each time a vehicle is destroyed or some of the scenery is destroyed. The vehicles are nicely animated with each unit having its own distinctive look, my favourite is the Heavy Tank.
There is some comedy in the game but the game was originally made by a British company called the Bitmap Brothers (Chaos Engine) so some may not get the jokes or the humour.
Now the re-release. The menu has lost its rustic charm, the original had this metal rust dashboard but now it has been replaced by a bland image and dull plain grey buttons.
There used to be an announcer which would praise you or even taunt you when you were losing, that appears to now have been removed. The minimap has been replaced by a very intrusive map located in the bottom right corner which covers a large portion of the screen, mimising it down presents really really tiny minimap which is too small  to effectively use.
The UI has been changed which looks like something tailored for touchscreen users, a lot of charm has been lost.

On the surface, this looks like a rage game-- and it sort of is. But between the soothing voiceover and the genuine challenge of it, I think this game is a lot more rewarding than, say, "The Impossible Game", which, while fun in its own right, is designed to frustrate and annoy. Failing at it isn't just easy in that game, it's expected.
"Getting Over It" has a completely different atmosphere. It's not hard for the sake of being hard. It's
. It challenges you to win, and it does so in such a nonconfrontational, easygoing way (reminding you that it's okay to take breaks along the way), it actually makes you feel
when you do succeed. Not the spiteful kind of "feeling good" you get with most rage games, but... It's like the game asks you a favor, and when you accomplish what it asked of you, it feels genuinely good. I dunno, maybe that's just me being weird, or maybe it's Bennett Foddy's reassuring voice, but it's a refreshing change of pace from the usual vitriol.
This is just a really nice game.

Never before in my gaming career have I wanted a short campaign so, so badly. Please.
This game is a Soulslike, cause, it opens up pathways as you progress farther into the game. Only, these pathways just lead you right back to Firelink Shrine, if Firelink Shrine was a despicable, mud-covered, bittersweet rocky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ neatly contained at the foot of a mountain that harbors ♥♥♥♥ing floating rocks, juvenile, childish oranges and plastic cups, foaming, snarled, disgusting hills of outdoor poolside furniture and the nasty composure of a 47 year old woman, caked in makeup, elbow bent backwards as she crawls at you, feeding at your soul, "You cannot now believe that you will ever feel better" emanating from her mouth as she breathes viciously, words blowing from a sour-chapped excuse of a disheveled, brackish pair of lips, the horrible, wretched design of stone and assorted pebble that calls itself the "bottom" of Bennett Foddy's grand, opulescent, omnipotent, magnaminous Mountain.
Bennettt Foddy's "Getting Over It" asks you a question, one that resonates as you play, as you scale the first hump, climb over the second obstacle, throw yourself atop the third wall, "Why," you ask yourself, "... why?". But yet, you continue.
You are held in a transcendent peace, between the crushing, agonizing defeat, between the regretful hatred, the reluctant ferocity of your inner self, questioning why you don't put this down, return it for a measly $7.49 that you probably spent during the sale, between these, but also between the burning desire to finish it before your friends do. Before you lose your desire to win.
This game asks one thing of you; to trust in it, to let it narrate you, as you climb this mountain. Bennett certainly has no right to hear me cry about my IRL woes, but now he's heard them. He's no interest in my tales of my passionate, discriminatory disdain for a "fat ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥orange". But alas, he hears them anyhow, for even if Bennett never asked me to tell me everything about myself,
the game asks me to tell it. It asks me to tell myself, about myself. It asks me to question why I climb my mountains, why I scale my heights, what is the limit of my patience, how far will you go to achieve something, why do you push yourself forward, what motivates you? What makes you, you?
And so, to these questions, Bennett, I answer that I push myself forward simply to see the end. I'll beat this game, eventually. I likely won't come back; I don't have that much patience, nor do I love this game, or like it. But I'll see it till it's done.
I hope you do, too. It's a nice view.

An excellent game, though for different reasons than its predecessor. The emphasis here is on extended stealth sequences punctuated by brisk, risky sniping segments rather than the nonstop sniper action of V2. This is a much slower, methodical game with massive open levels (perfect for anyone frustrated by the linearity of V2) and a focus on using the terrain to your advantage. However, the player is given great freedom over how they complete each objective, be it smart and quiet or dumb and loud!
Pros:
- Large open levels, with optional side objectives and hidden areas. Exploration is dangerous but often rewarding!
- Sniping, whilst not entirely realistic, is incredibly satisfying (when a single bullet gets two headshots and blows up a panzer's fuel tank you'll understand...)
- The bullet cam is back and gorier than ever. Muscle and nerve endings are modelled on enemies, giving a greater sense of how damaging a sniper's bullet can be. The camera is now also fully customisable.
- Smart AI, brutal at the higher difficulties (though I do wonder why they don't just sound the alarm as soon as they find a friend's body...)
- Greatly improved loadout menu, where you can use weapon upgrades scavenged from the battlefield to fine tune and tweak your rifle.
- Beautiful North African setting - sort of an Indiana Jones aesthetic (you know, fighting Nazis in ancient ruins).
Cons:
- Story is a little threadbare, often predictable and lacks the intrigue and morally ambiguous edge of V2. However, some may prefer the lighter tone, and the gameplay is so fun that you won't care anyway...
- Enemise sometimes feel too accurate, especially with automatic weapons.
- DLC missions are good, but they are hardly standouts that justify their individual price tags. Only buy if you are hungry for more content.
Ultimately a fantastic addition to the franchise that isn't afraid to change up its gameplay. A must for sniping enthusiasts and people who want something different from their WW2 shooters.

The best way I can describe this is like so. It's a stealth game where you are expected to make lots and lots of noise.
: I played this on "Custom" difficulty with Realistic bullet physics, No Tactical assistance (Tagging, Alert meters, ect) and it was a tense, but fun experience!
However for those who just want to Quckscope Nazis in the crotch, you are more than welcome to turn the bullet physics to simple and have at it! Or if you like the idea but are not confident in your aim/infiltration abilities, turn on tactical assistance and it will help you out with things like a red diamond that shows where your bullet will land, radar (which also marks your last known location), tagging, and a whole slew of assistive UI elements.
: The game actually encourages a rather realistic approach to sniping. It's not about how long of a kill you can make (though long kills are an achievement of itself, with the realistic physics at least), but rather how can you make the best of a position? It encourages you to constantly relocate as rifles are loud and the bad guys will know where you are shooting from, or take advantage and dig in with traps (LOTS OF TRAPS!). However despite the only suppressed weapon you have, quite honestly sucks (except at it's designated role, but we'll get there), you still can muffle your shots with ambient sounds like planes flying overhead, loudspeakers, broken/loud machenery, ect. So you still can, theoretically pull off a "no detection run" it's just very difficult as it's often safe to assume you'll get into a firefight.
: Speaking of, you actually have quite a few of these! Ranging from trip mines that are great for covering narrow passages, S-mines for dealing with infantry clusters, landmines for Tanks, and even dynamite! However, the most effective one I've found was flint and steel, it's a good distraction AND after about twenty seconds, it detonates any explosives in a short radius around it!
: Basically Mortal Kombat 9's X-Ray attack, onlly it happens when you make a good shot (At least on minimal, I find it triggers too much on the normal setting). Also cool is that it works on vehicles!
: Interestingly enough your equipment (Aside from your rifle and it's customizations) are NOT there to help make "mile long shots". Instead it's there to cover your bases, with the aformentioned traps, or your sidearms (SMG's that help you in a pinch, your trusty Welrod that sucks as a combat pistol but is AMAZING at preventing the bad guys from raising the alarm since it is suppressed, or combat pistols which help you fight them off), to things like rocks (distraction), AP Ammo (allows your bullets to easily sail through the armored grills of vehicles), and medkits.
: Not only did Rebellion make North Africa very pretty, they also made the levels reasonably open, allowing you to get into positions and make some incredible shots. It also takes the "Goldeneye" philosophy of level design where you have a clear primary objective, but also several secondary objectives you can complete if you wish.
:
-You can get clues on making the mission easier/future objectives if you observe and listen into enemy converstaions
-The Rifle range I found was a very nice tool for breaking in rifles, it even lets you try the DLC weapons (Though you don't really need them)
-The guys at Rebellion REALLY did their homework here! I want to meet their research team and swap notes.
In fact there are no non-lethal means of disposing of the Nazis/Itallians. Most levels I find I kill around 90% of all the bad guys
: Granted on the highest difficulty they were competent when fighting, but they suffer from "Loss of sight" amnesia when you vacate the area without them seeing you, and they resume their patrols, despite the piles of dead bodies you just created.
: In my experience, only two of them were really bad.
However you can get around it by saving afterwards and the game will pick up from there (unless  you are playing in "sniper elite" mode, which is all the difficulties up/real ballistics/ no tactical assistance AND NO SAVING/CHECKPOINTS!)
: despite them doing pretty solid research into the Wonder Weapon*
*Yes it did exist and it is rumored that only one part was finished and used as a part in Hitler's "Atlantic Wall", or for those who don't know, the northern costal defenses in Europe that the Nazis built to prevent an invasion from Great Britain, we all know the story how that turned out.

If you have had fantasies about being Indiana Jones, then this game just might make your dreams come true.
Spelunky is a merciless 2D platformer that will not hand anything to you. Aside from the short tutorial, which will introduce you to the basic controls, the game of Spelunky is yours to explore.
The game offers four main areas, with an additional bonus level. All of the areas are designed with unique challenges, and are always auto generated. Therefore, each time you play (or replay) an area, it will never resemble the previous one you just played.
The game is very difficult, as anything that can kill you, will kill you. However, the game is also rewarding to play, despite its sadistic tendencies to deprive you of your hopes and dreams. Therefore, trial and error are a significant aspect of the game and Spelunky will more than simply challenge your endurance and wits.
Even though caution is advised, you cannot spend too much time loitering around as there is a 2.30 minute limit before a ghost appears that will attempt to hunt you down and kill you, ending your pitiful life and throwing you back to ground zero.
A worthwhile indie game, 10/10.

Doom 3.
General overview - average.
Graphics - 5/10
Sounds - 7/10
Mechanics - 7/10
Storyline - 6/10
Time to complete - around 12-16 hours.
Prologue of the story - The year is 2145. You are an unknown marine sent to a Mars station to reinforce the troops stationed there. Recently there have been many occupants becoming ill and even dying. On board your flight is a councillor from earth to investigate the recent happenings. You are required to grab your equipment and report for duty. This is where your hellish story begins.
This game was released in 2004 and naturally, the graphics look dated. Some aspects are in HD like interactive computer monitors but most of the decals are very pixelated including your weapons which is a shame. The sound is above average with reasonable voice acting but the guns definately needed to sound like they have a heavier punch.
There is a variety of weapons from chainsaws, chainguns, rocket launchers, granades and everything in between to put to good use against the enemy. If you search out the nooks and crannies you will find enough ammunition to keep you going. The AI are generally stupid and will persue you except for the marines. Sometimes they take cover.
The story is slowly revealed to you through a bunch of PDAs the lab scientists have dropped. Not only do they reveal story plots but some will also have codes to gain access to storage lockers. Another cool aspect was having to go outside the station with a limited oxygen supply. It gives a real sense of dread of suffication. To add to the suspense you must lower your weapon to use a flash light. Some will find this a nuisanse if they just want a plain run and gun game.
Conclusion : Don't expect epic content from this game but if you'd like to take a crack at a classic then this would definately count.
Other notes : I had problems choosing a higher resolution to play the game in. It would always crash when I chose which one I wanted. Please check the guides for a work around to get better resolutions. It involves typing commands into the console. Unfortunately you have to do this everytime you open the game. I have a G15 keyboard so I bound the commands to one of my macro keys. Minimised the annoyance.

OK, let's be honest here. Calling this game '2016' is pretty misleading, given that the technology is certainly not on par with what you'd expect in 2016. It's not very pretty, which is a bad thing for a game where just looking around is actually a big part of what you do. And for being ugly, it's also quite slow.
So, it may at least have a rich world full of things that happen, though at a low polygon count, right? Well, no, it doesn't. Not even information displays on the platform do show anything. They are just empty. All the time. There are some other trains, people on the platform, cars on the roads, and that's about it.
Could it be that the simulation is perfectly realistic and provides a very real experience? Hm. Not really. It's kind of OK if the particular aspect of the simulation was implemented, but there are big gaps. Heavily depends on a particular locomotive, some have more advanced functionality scripted in, many don't. Either way, with nearly every model, you get a lot of stuff left out.
OK, then maybe we got a lot of challenging and interesting scenarios, right? And this is possibly the biggest letdown. No, you get just a few and they are maybe even less eventful than my everyday commute as a passenger. Seriously. And on every step you see how limited the options to create an interesting scenario are. There are people sitting in the carriages left on sidings in a depot. Really. The game cannot even properly script this, you just have to ignore it and not think too much about it. Also, the scenarios are buggy. You can get stuck forever behind another train that is supposed to be there as a challenge, requiring you to slow down, but it simply never moves... Uh.
And in overal, yeah, it's not like you get many other options if you want to play with the trains on a computer, so you have to take this anyway. But calling this 2016... just no.

Z is an old school RTS(RealTimeStrategy Title) which can still be fun, if you're "retro-affine" and have no problem with old graphics and one or two gameplay slip(like a non optimized control-setup).
Con:
+No base building. I see it as a pro because it's not generic in its approach and manages to do something different in a good fashion: You have to build/order units(since here your time is your resource) to occupy more buildings on the map which either can order different or more units or have another positive trait for you. The one who does it faster has an advantage. From my experience some Warhammer games have the same system, so experience its ancestor!
+The Visuals still hold up in my point of few. Sure it got old but its style is coherent and presented in a funny and enjoyable way.
+The mini-skits in between each mission. They range mostly from funny to hilarious and the only downside is the horribly small resolution(since they are rendered) and repetitivity(since there is only a handful of unique situations).
Con:
-Repititivity: Since there are only that many different units and about a handful of different planets it gets stagnant really fast, especially if you want to play through it in a couple of sittings(which is possible).
-Sometimes it's just too easy, although it can be enjoyable for some to annihalate your foe.
-There is always just one different player, so just 1v1.
-The price! I mean sure it can be enjoyable for a couple of hours but that's no reason to charge nearly 10€ for it! Especially since the game is about 20 years old... So in the process you pay more for the achievements/trading cards... -.-
-It's too short, I think I played through it in about 5 or 6 hours. If they charge for it they could atleast add a couple of modes/more levels or units or mechanics.
Ideas/Final statement:
Either charge one € or two if you just add a DOSbox for steam with achievements or add new content. It feels like a ripoff at full price, even if it can be quite enjoyable.
Although I liked it quite a bit I can't give it a thumbs up, since not everyone who likes RTS is going to enjoy this, too.
Thanks for reading!

Another positive point is the variety of missions, each mission is different. The X-Ray cam is one of the best things in the game, and it's very detailed.
But there isn't a game without problems in the campaign: there are very few missions and you can make all of them really fast. If you want more missions you have to buy the DLCs. Another problem is the weapons available, just 3 rifles, 3 submachines, the panzershreck and 3 pistols, if you want more, you need to buy the DLCs.
MULTIPLAYER:
The multiplayer mode is good for sometime, but after some hours of gameplay the multiplayer becames sickening. The problem in particular for me is that most of the servers don't allow you to play with the secundary weapons, with this you have to play onlt with rifles and pistols, which led to the match became boring, because you have to wait someone to move or make a wrong decision, but there are one or two servers that allow you to use secundary weapons (even though it doesn't make the game with more movement), allows you to have a little more fun, like ignore everything and just go firing the panzerchreck until the ammo get over, this is funny, but I think is probably because of the risk of someone make this, that most of the servers don't allow you to use secundary weapons.
V2X3:
If you are wandering what of the two sniper elites you should buy (I am ignoring the first, because that one is terrible!) you have to consider this: even though the 3 have less missions it have more time of gameplay, and is more difficult, but I recommend you to wait a good sale and buy both of them.
CONCLUSION:
I recommend you to buy this game, but only if it's on sale, because if don't, you are going to waste your money, not because the game isn't good, but because it's just a few hours of gameplay.

Note: Before reading, just know I'm basically trying to clear up some of the negative reviews on this game. This is purely an opinion from a person who has played this game. If you feel differently, then that's fine.
--
Reading a lot of the reviews, people say Sinper Elite V2 was better than Sniper Elite 3, Personally, I've never played Sniper Elite V2, and nor do I wanna get a game that is that old, as the multiplayer might be taken off soon (not worth the money spent server side) or other reasons. That's why I went for the more recent game in the franchise, Sniper Elite 3.
Since I've gotten it, I love it. I don't see any issues with it, and since I don't know how "great" Sniper Elite V2 was, I'm really not missing out on anything, if there's anything to even miss.
Another concern people have expressed is that this game is less... sniping? Looking at some gameplay videos from both games, then actually playing Sniper Elite 3, I don't see why this is a concern. Sure you sometimes have to rely on your secondary, or performing stealth kills, but you sure as heck can go around and snipe. What's stopping you from doing that? Personally, I love the mix of stealth kills, sniping kills, and sometimes having to switch to a secondary or pistol when in a rough situation. Isn't that a step in the right direction? I more realistic approach on combat? I see no problems with what the company did, and I support the new approach.
People also have said that Sniper Elite 3 is just Sinper Elite V2 but with bug fixes. If that's the case, then that is a good point. They could have just fixed the old game BUT you have to take into account this is a company, and they need to make money. However they do that isn't your decision to say. They felt it would be better to spend their efforts into a new game as opposed to fixing an old game, which is fair. Sure they could've saved their customers some money by upgrading the old game, but in turn they would lose money. Doesn't make sense in their eyes.
--
Overall, I think this game is a great game if you want to snipe, play stealth and take your time to think out the best plan of attack. If you want to just jump in guns blazing, you might want to reconsider which game franchise you want to play. This game is one of the best, and most realistic, sniper/stealth games out there, and I don't think you'll find much better.
If you find this game on sale, then it's a steal. I can see people justifying a $55 price point, so anything lower is a great deal.
--
Again, this is just MY opinion on the game, and I hope it helps some people out when/if they are deciding to get this game.

LONG REVIEW-YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED
Brothers is an indie title coming from the cold but charming land of Sweden, a country well known for its tasty meatballs with warm gravy sauce (I am not even Swedish but that stuff makes me feel happy inside). This land also happens to be home to some of the most talented game developers in the world, and Brothers is a testament and living proof that their talent and imagination knows no end.
Brothers plays out rather simplisticaly, but ingeniously at that: it is a
, where you control two distinct characters simultaneously. One gamepad stick is assigned to the older brother, able-bodied leader of the adventure, while the other stick gives you command of the cunning little brother, who is the brains to his older sibling's brawn when it comes to puzzles.
The story that sets the journey of our two heroes in motion is really strong and emotional, starting with a thump and ending with a bang, having quite possibly a teary-eyed finale if you are a sensitive person (like me).
Despite the fact that sentimentally charged themes drive the narration forward (which, I might add, is a masterpiece in and of itself, since there is not a single line of spoken word to be heard, yet feelings and thoughts are conveyed without the need to hear any dialog), the game does not stop assaulting your senses with just that. It has a meticulously crafted world and environment, designed to draw you in and immerse you with its watercolour-like art style. The general aesthetic is closer to that of a painting in motion rather than that of a photorealistic 3D experience.
Sound and music are tense when the going gets tough, relaxed when the time is right for a breather and a look at the landscape, and sad when things transpire that stress the heroes.
Best of all, the game won't set you back too much financially (and, to be honest, I feel kind of ashamed even mentioning the price factor while describing this game), and it doesn't require a NASA supercomputer to run.
TL;DR Version: It is a game deserving to be experienced, not just to be played.

Before I begin, bear in mind the game is in early alpha and a lot can change before release, I intend to update when it is released in full.
On the positive side of things:
The game is visually stunning.
It has a character creation system. System is extremely limited, may also have political bias (pitch black skin is possible, pasty white is not, face never gets lighter than dark tan).
It has a house building system. Too early for details.
Skills are customizable. Options are mostly dull though.
It has an open ended classless system, technically, kind of like how F2P is technically free.
It is being actively worked on.
On the negative side of things:
The game is bland. It borrows heavily from PoE, and has some influences from Sacred 2, but there's nothing mechanically in it to set it apart from other ARPG's. The game is extremely generic.
One of my biggest issues with the game is the classless system, which sounds great, but the implementation is terrible. The game is balanced around min-maxing, so any attempts at mixing play-styles are punished severely. Sure, you can try to mix a melee and magic build, but you will end up very anemic, unable to effectively progress at a reasonable pace. The game has numerous passives that further lock out the mixing of playstyles, like a passive skill that will increase magic damage by a whopping 30% at the cost of being unable to deal non-elemental damage, every stat has at least one passive like that, some have several. The game is designed to pigeonhole players into classes which works against the appeal of having a classless system in the first place.
This is further accentuated by gear type. All equipment has base stats without enchantments (basic white gear stats that are the same across the board) by class that will improve one or two things usually at the expense of something else, for instance all heavy armor reduces dex by a percentage. The game is being designed in such a way that players have to min-max or GTFO. This is the design direction the game is taking, so if you were hoping for something flexible and dynamic, look elsewhere.
The skill system has upgrades for each skill, similar to Sacred 2 only less interesting. About half the options are just passive multipliers, like choosing between more damage or cheaper cost, which makes a difference, but it's a boring difference. Few upgrades make interesting changes that alter how the skills themselves work. It's not bad, it's just bland and mostly boring.
Character creation is going the simplistic route, you have a grid with 2 axis, muscular vs puny, fat vs thin, although the puny and thin overlap in a hilariously catastrophic way. Without the option of separate sliders, the options are extremely limited and fine tuning is impossible. At present there is nothing that can be altered about faces. Skin tone goes all the way to pitch black making the character look like they are covered in tar, but only goes as light as a mild tan, so pasty white or alabaster skin is impossible. The heads are dark tan until darker tones are reached, so no celts or norsemen. A lot can change between now and release, but the current direction doesn't look promising. Being an isometric ARPG this won't have too much impact on gameplay, you will only see your character up close when selecting characters on the main menu.
A lot can change between now and release, but my major concerns are with the apparent design philosophy and direction. Balance will improve quite a bit, no doubt, but the min-maxing nature and being pigeonholed into builds is unlikely to change.
Edit: For examples of RPG's that use open classless systems look at the Rune Factory series, the Souls series, or the Dungeon Maker series.

R.A.W. is a hack’n’slash RPG where you choose from the standard characters of warrior, dark sorcerer, or rogue. The four kings met in the North to fight back an ancient evil which is trying to come back. Only three made it out beaten and worn and the North King was frozen in crystal. This is where you come in and find the North King and he speaks to you telepathically asking for your help. He melds with your body and sets you on a task to open the four portals of north, south, east, and west lands.
Playing the game isn’t bad it’s just not great. There isn’t much variety in enemies as you’ll fight mostly the same ones over and over which will become monotonous over time. Your weapons and armor don’t really make much of a difference in what you use. Basically you find a better one and it gives you a higher damage or defense. You can also have elemental damage of fire or poison to your weapons but those didn’t seem to add anything noticeable. Skills get added each level but none of them were that great or make me excited to level them up or unlock them.
The story is pretty weak and didn’t really hold me or make me want to pay attention much. You’ll fight through the same levels or what seems like the same levels many times. Make it halfway through the game and then go back and do it all over again. Not too exciting if you ask me.
Overall R.A.W. is a mediocre game which wasn’t bad to play but not worth playing more than once. Co-op may add a little fun to it but since I played it already by myself I don’t see the real reason to play it again unless you want all the achievements.

I finally got my hands on this wonderful game. I gotta say, it is worth every penny, although I bought this with keys, well, erm...
Anyway, I really like Spelunky overall. It is a rogue-lite game (Roguelikes with key differences) with endless replayability. I'm loving this game. A lot. The difficulty is pretty insane, and I love that. Well, I kinda did learn to deal with rage from BOI and FTL... The graphics are cartoony and somewhat sweet, although there is a darker tone to it (e.g. blood, gore, etc etc) and surprises everywhere. The gameplay, at first, is extremely difficult, because you'll try to whip your damsel here and there and accidently kill them, but hey, we all learn from our mistakes, one damsel at a time. Which brings me to another good reason about this game: Even though in lots of roguelikes and roguelites we learn from our mistakes, Spelunky, to me, seems the most visible when it comes to learning from mistakes, which makes it easier for me to understand what I did wrong. Also, at the end, when you die, it'll show your corpse and how you died. Sometimes moments before you die and moments after, something funny will happen. Once, I got hit by a bat and fell to my death, but an arrow shot me and I flew far away and ended my short life by getting impaled by spikes. Another time, I got impaled by spikes, and when it showed my corpse, I noticed my body suddenly jumped off the spikes and hit a snake and killed it. I found those to be hilarious moments, and I cannot WAIT to discover more. The one downside to this game is the soundtrack for me. It just seemed boring and dull, although the song that plays when you're in a shop is pretty relaxing, the rest are pretty dull. I haven't played this game for long, but overall, I'm loving every bit of it.

Well now, lets see what I can say about Z. A fabulous  and oldskool strategy creation by The Bitmap Brothers.
I first played this when I was about 6, and actually played for ages and got to about lvl 13 without realising how to change what units you create, so had masses of grunts getting blown left right and center constantly lol. It was always a bonus when i captured a building that was producing something else lol.
I think Z is a solid game in several ways. Firstly it is a unique and early example of a solid RTS and although i can't say it set any precedences that became the RTS norm, its blend of quirky human, unit management and its concept of building speed being affected by territory owned made it quite fun.
So i guess to explain what exactly Z is think of a Level based RTS set in a universe dominated by hybrid space cowboy robots, being split into two teams which are red (you) and blue (the enemy). You have the typical angled top down view and the map is divided into capturable sectors with each teams respective fortress on the opposite side of the map.
You command your robots to capture sectors by touching that sectors flag, then you take control of any bases in that sector which allows you to build more units or defensive turrets.
Possibly the most unique thing about Z is that your units are constantly building on a timer from your fortress and any bases you control. Different units have different build times, however the more sectors you control the faster your units produce and in turn the slower the enemies.
Taking the above intro consideration means you are in a constant struggle to control as many sectors as you can, and must keep an eye on the battlefield and watch the enemies movements so you can make strategic decisions about your own. Overall the pace feels a little slow but a big battle can happen very quickly and despite a forces size through army control the results can go either way.
The combat and AI isn't exactly great but i really enjoyed how especially in a tank battle you can outmanouveur your enemy and dodge their shots whilst ensuring yours land true by constantly micro controlling your tank/s.
Overall a fun and unique game which holds a nostalgic place in my heart, lol. Recommended for all lovers of RTS games, unique concepts and the oldskool.

Depression has made it difficult for me to enjoy a lot of the experiences that I used to, videogames being no exception. Winning a tense ranked match or beating a difficult level of a game just don't excite me any more, and I can count the times a game has have gotten my blood pumping in the last year on one hand.
But Getting Over It is an exception. It doesn't hold your hand. The difficulty 'curve' makes a Picasso piece look smooth. It doesn't expect you to win, and because of all this I really care when I
win.
Instead of muted acceptance when I fall, I feel a pit in my stomach, because it took me
to get there. Work that I'll have to put in again to get back up. But it's okay, because I can feel my improvement with every climb. Only one thing beats the satisfaction of breezing through all the parts I used to get stuck on - the elation I feel when I finally conquer the next obstacle for the first time.
Beyond all that, however, the part of the game that's really keeping me going is the narration. I love everything the developer has to say about this game, and it's a wonderful treat every time I reach a new voice line. I probably won't replay Getting Over It once I've been through every line of dialogue, despite my love for its gameplay, because that extra push will be gone. But that's totally fine, because I've been extremely invested in the content that
there.

Doom 3.
DOOM 3.
D00M 3.
What else is there to say about this unbelievablly awesome First Person Shooter/Survival Horror game?
This is possibly the greatest Reboot (Except for Wolfenstein the new order) ever made.
The story is good. Even though it's the same story as before, it is expanded on here: there is a whole deep narrative and sci-fi lore that is both mysterious, and exciting, without really getting in the way of the gameplay.
The voice acting, while ham-fisted, is awesome,
The Writing is great, as it was written the author Matthew J. Costello, and the story feels like something out of a science fiction epic, like Dune and Star Trek.
The ambiet noise & atmousphere?
I know there are a LOT of games with good ambiet noise, but
D00M 3 WINS HANDS DOWN, BEST AMBIET NOISE IN ANY VIDEOGAME MADE OR GOING TO BE MADE EVER.
There are so manny sounds atop of sounds atop of sounds underneith sounds ATOP OF SOUNDS, some you don't even hear; they're just THERE.  This extends to the Music.  Now it may look like there are only a few songs, but what you don't realise is that the ENVIRONMENT tells the music. You can hear the oxygen cycle and refreash the room you are in, and the chiming and grunting of machinery can make for some really interesting and creative music and sound.  It's the kind of stuff that you just don't see in videogames anymore.
The horror? Well, it may be cheezy, unoriginal, & full of jump-scares (Not jump-shocks or slender BS), but it feels VERY original for the time and since Doom was scary back in the day, you can't really critique this game for trying.
The opening is well paced, and it set's the mood for the game quite well. Even though Half-Life did it first, D00M 3 does an EXCELLENT job of it too, and sets you up for the odyssey ahead.
Plus that awesome Super Turbo Turkey Puncher 3 game cabinent is more then enough to get you hooked.
The enemy designs are awesome: All (well, 85%) of the original monsters are back, with a few new original ones (Those Zombie Commandos)
D00M 3 also has a HUUUUUUUUUUGE campaign length. Beating it would take roughly 12-17 hours to complete. What was that Killzone Shadow fall? only a 4 hour campaign??
The Weapons are ALL the same from Doom 1 & 2 (abiet updated ones), but you get a Machine gun to use (A good mid-range weapon), Grenades (Bouncy-Bouncy-Bouncy: hard to control but effective) & a Flashlight (Oh yeah...)
The game is VERY dark. That's one of it's selling points & why you should get D00M 3 & not the BFG edition: It's much more darker, & you can hold EITHER a flashlight or a gun. It might come off as annoying at first, but it sinks in, & it adds to the scare factor.
Keep in mind this is a VERY different DooM game, up to the point where people question if it is a DooM game at ALL.
But whatever you may think about D00M 3, it sold more than 5.3 million copies, making it the most successful game by it's developer id Software to date.
I VERY HIGHLY recommend D00M 3 to anyone who likes FPS, anyone who likes Horror-survival, & pretty much to anyone who loves video games in general.

Squishy the Suicidal Pig attempts to win you over on comedy value of its concept. It doesn't.
If you've ever played any of the Karoshi flash games, the concept of having to find a way to make your character die is nothing new. And if you haven't, go play a Karoshi game- there are like 4 or 5 and they're all better than this game.
The problems with Squishy are numerous, but most notably- in a game about having to die, you have to do an awful lot of surviving. Each of the 4 boss battles are pretty terribly designed (Big Bull-y is the least offensive, but they're all cheap in their own ways, even on normal), the entire game suffers from bad hitboxes (especially in the random shmup level), a movement speed that's too slow (especially when pushing boxes) and being forced to repeat large sections of mastered gameplay because some physics interaction wasn't predicted right, or there was a cheapshot in a surviving level.
Squishy has 40 levels and 4 bosses. Of those 40 levels, about a dozen require you to survive to reach a key, and obviously you have to survive the 4 bosses. There was some real potential here to have an inversion of a standard boss battle, where instead of the boss trying to kill you, the boss could be trying to keep you from killing yourself and you win by working out how to outsmart its AI. You know, a puzzle platforming boss where you try to die in a puzzle platformer where you try to die, instead of an action duel that often introduces new mechanics with lots of waiting for vulnerable times and more new mechanics in the second phase or a cheapshot on PHASE THREE of the final boss that hit me twice before I looked up a video to see how I was dying.
Anyway, the devil is the final boss trying to keep Squishy from reuniting with his parents in animal heaven. So there's a perfect opportunity here for the devil to be interfering with all of the suicide attempts in levels, and be outsmarted with trying to idiotproof arenas. **You** could be the boss in the boss encounters! That would have been cool! Instead, we got boss fights that are worse than the actual puzzle levels.
Don't play this game.
Oh, and the music always loops badly and doesn't loop on the map screen. Movement on the map screen is way slower than it needs to be- think Mario 3 overworld maps where each path takes over a second to traverse, and 5-6 between levels on average. Sound effects often peak too high, especially on... the devil boss, where I had to mute my computer to not be physically hurt by the sound effects.
At this risk of being an untasteful joke, Squishy the Suicidal Pig could make you suicidal. If you experience thoughts of death while playing this game, please call your doctor immediately. (suicide is bad k)

This game is escapism turned up to 11. Use two hands IRL and half your keyboard space, plus your mouse, just to control one hand that doesn't even have a full motion range. Sound ridiculous? It is. Oh so hilariously ridiculous...
This is a game for those with a very broad sense of humour, or a well-hidden sadistic streak. When you tear out Bob's lung with a hammer, you have to either laugh, vomit or smile inwardly with sadistic glee. If you chose option one or three, then Surgeon Simulator is well worth the pricetag. If you chose option 2.... then don't watch the trailers.
The gameplay is really really hard to describe adequately; but it's like the drinking game version of the boardgame "Operation". Basically, you're taking bits out of Bob (all three patients are apparently named Bob), and then you put a couple of bits back in. All on two time limits - an actual clock, and the "hard limit" of how much blood Bob can phyiscally lose before he/it dies.
And Bob will die a lot. Sometimes you'll even get an achievement for killing him. But there are a lot of "oh great the drill is stuck in him, I'd better get the hammer to pull it out... great, now the hammer is stuck too, hand me the circular saw". Eventually you get an understanding of how each tool works and how each body part works; and after a messy time learning all these things you can start performing surgical feats.
This game requires a mix of thought, motor skills, practice and patience. The patients, fortunately, are provided - make no mistake, if you tried performing surgeries in this manner IRL you *would* be going away for a long time. In fact, the thing you can leave at the door is realism - a working knowledge of anatomy may be helpful; but I'm thinking more of the kind of knowledge a butcher has than that of a medical professional. If you are a medical professional, leave all that Hippocratic Oath and "duty of care" stuff behind in Surgeon Simulator; at least to begin with. One day it will come in useful as you make precision moves to complete the surgery, but in the early days it's just a case of beating and stabbing the internal organs around until they fall out.
I do reccomend this game as a casual, light-hearted bit of entertainment. Some people may like to take it further and develop the skills to be a "pro surgeon", but a lot more players will just enjoy stabbing poor Bob with a drill. And that's an entirely valid way to play Surgeon Simulator; you can get all your money's worth and more out of that kind of slapstick "hmm I wonder what happens when I..." messing around.

Light years better than the old MSTS, but there are some undesirable similarities. There's no doubt that this sim is a very hard hitter on FPS, with some routes being less affected than others. The way things are progressing it looks as though we're only a couple of years away from route developers offering us DLC routes that only top end systems will be able to handle. Even so, people with top of the range desktop PCs and graphics cards regularly complain of stuttering and poor framerates, so most of us with lesser systems are on a hiding to nothing, and will need to perform the ancient art of "tweaking" to get the thing to run.
Some of the older available Railworks routes are a bit ropey looking, particularly with winter textures, although I suppose the whole sim is about driving trains with the pretty scenery being a bonus, if your system will handle it. Any graphics card with less than 1Gb dedicated capacity will struggle to cope. The clear summer weather lighting can be a bit too bright (at least on my system), and I wish they would make locos with lights that actually light up the track ahead. Night time passenger scenarios tend to involve a lot of guesswork as to where the platforms are relative to your approaching train.
As with MSTS, most of the German and US rolling stock looks a bit toylike. The UK rolling stock generally tends to look more convincing, especially the weathered units.
I would recommend the game to anybody who likes to get the feeling that they are driving (or at least travelling on) a train through reasonably accurately modelled landscapes. I'm familiar with several of the available UK routes, and have been able to identify various locations from the cab view. You will get quite a few instances of the same buildings appearing with annoying regularity, but I suppose you cannot expect the route builders to scratchbuild every building along the lineside.
Oddly enough, I'm not a train buff and my knowledge of railways is pretty sparse. As such, I find the shunting scenarios a bit tedious, especially in Career mode where you are expected to assemble a train and be on your way in a minute or two.
I've never driven a real train/locomotive, so cannot comment on the authenticity of the driving experience. Suffice to say that each unit requires practice so that credible starting and stopping can be achieved, Some of them seem  to have hardly any usable brakes at all, whilst others appear to be able to stop on the proverbial sixpence.
I would advise any undecided prospective purchasers to maybe consider one of the stand alone packs like "Epic Journeys"  before plunging into the deep with the full sim, as those DLCs will play havoc with your wallet if you start to become an "asset collector". The default routes in the full sim are not the best, and the buyer will almost feel compelled to dabble with other more modern stuff. You then feel the need to buy extra rolling stock to get the best out of your new routes, and it all gets a bit expensive.
To the real rail nuts this sim appears to offer a whole lot more than just driving trains, although the developers could do with updating the game physics so that it can be played on Joe Average's computer.
I would also advise users to avoid third party add ons that are created in languages other than the user's operating system. For example, some locos require use of non English keyboards, otherwise they will not funcion properly. Also foreign language manuals will tend to disable the facility to read all of the manuals via the "Tools" option in the game.
As the only half decent rail simulator available, you have to buy it if you want a train sim.

As someone who loves story-driven game, I had always had my eye on Brothers, just wanted to wait for it to go on sale. Now I've finally played it and I have to say it was everything I had hoped and more.
As you probably know, you play as two brothers, each being controlled with a seperate hand on eithert he controller or (as I played it) a keyboard. Either brother has different tasks they can preform, the older being able to pull heavy levers while the younger can get into small spaces or between bars. All this leads to a very unique experience as your brain tries to tell either hand to do different tasks for ither brother or maybe the same task but in reverse, etc. The game never gets terribly difficult, and in all I beat it 100% (for achievements) in about 3 hours, which includes re-playing a few sections I had missed an achievement in. It's not a game for those who want to grind, or have hours of questing adventures. It's an experience, you play through a story, a tale of two sons, if you will. So in the end, it all comes down to, do you wnat to have a fun and heart-wrenching experiene with a game? Then I say definately play this game. If you're not really into that, then don't bother, this games not for you.
So lets get down to the story - oh wait... spoilers incoming, I recommend playing before reading more, or if you don't intend to play it but wnat to know some critical points about the story, read on.
Okay I've rambled enough, I hope thaat helped some. Love the story, very neat controls, very effective ending.

This game was the most challenging, but also the most rewarding game I've ever played.
In this game, you are tasked with with climbing a mountain with only a hammer.  The game looks simple enough when watching people play, but when you actually try to play yourself, the game becomes way harder than it looked.
I never felt as though the controls were unfair.  Unwieldy, yes, but I never felt like they were trying to be unfair on purpose.  Once I got the controls down I felt like I was always in control of my actions and any mistakes made were my fault.
That's what kept me going.  Every time I fell down, sometimes losing hours worth of progress in a few seconds, I knew it was my fault and had this strong urge to try again, and again until eventually (at the time of writing this no less) I beat it.
Because of how punishingly difficult this game was made getting to the end feel like a rush.
I wholeheartedly recomend this game to anyone willing to give it a shot.

Great for a Early Access Game.
Pro for now:
Build your own ship. No longer are players restrict to certain classes. Want a massive cargo ship with the firepower of a capital ship? Go ahead and build it.
Lost your main ship? No worry, all your money and build resources are safety protected in a tiny drone equipped with a endless interdimensional storage.
Weapons and lots of them. Players can choose from bombarding a enemy from afar or getting up close and personal with powerful laser cutters (salvage turret).
Realistic ship damage. In most space games I played, space-crafts are treated as a single entity. Not in Avorion, players can focus fire to separate a ship from its weapons, engine, or power source.
Dymanic trading means players must deal with reality of supply and demands.
Neutral/Potential:
Massive worlds and lots of factions: There are some good things such as discovering unclaimed asteriods, starting your own faction, and etc. However, there are rooms for additional mechanics such as faction wars (players are really the only ones who can start large-scale battles using their own fleet), population (having aj impact on economy), planets exploration (so far I have seen zero planets or at least able to interact with them), and much more.
Missions: There aren't many interesting missions so far, other than we need this material or transport this material to another place.
Con:
Not a lot of players online.
AI poor ship design: Most of the pirates' ships I have seen are long stick design. Making it very easy for players to focus fire their critical parts. Also, most of the AI ships I encounter lacks firepower. They wielded mainly ballistic weapons and usually 2-3 turrets only. In other words, once players get their hands on shield generator, they can literally side-stomp most AI unless facing a ship build with far superior materials.

This game divides people’s opinions to the point where very few games are this polarising, you have what are called the doom purists who absolutely hate this game because it’s not a carbon copy of the originals and you have people who do like it. So this begs the question of how doom-like this game really is.
Similarities:
There is a lot of satanic and gory imagery.
The weapons are the same with a small handful of new editions being: grenades and a machinegun.
The enemies are the same (though some enemies move quicker than the original counterparts and some move slower than the original counterparts, and some are a little weaker than before.) with a few new editions.
The enemies are very predictable and once you know how they function you can use that to your advantage to take them out with the right weapon for the situation and avoid taking damage just like the originals.
There are monster closets everywhere which open when you pick up a specific item and or walk past a specific point just like the originals.
You move level to level just like in the originals.
There are still key hunts and or the equivalent to key hunts.
There are moments where it’s so dark that you can barely see anything just like in the originals.
The game still has secrets and you can find some of the weapons earlier than you would usually find weapons just like in the originals and every old school shooter ever made.
Differences:
Having said that about darkness, doom 3 is very dark for most of the game, and you have to pull out a torch separately rather than having a torch tapped to a gun, this is one of the major criticisms of the game, I don’t have any issues with it, because it’s actually a lot better than the torch in the BFG edition where you can have a torch with another weapon however it’s too far to the left and it runs out of battery really quickly.
You move a lot slower to a more realistic jog and running with a stamina bar whereas in the originals you move at 60mph all of the time.
The enemy count is much sparser and the maximum amount of enemies you will usually have on screen at once is four to eight, whereas in doom 1 it was around fifth teen to twenty, and doom 2 it was around forty, though a lone enemy in doom 3 can be a lot more dangerous than a lone enemy in the originals.
The levels themselves are a lot narrower than before though there are still some open areas here and there.
Sometimes you might have an actual objective to complete and you sometimes come across NPCs and these sentry drones who fight alongside you.
They have tried to have an actual plot but thankfully it’s pretty avoidable and ignorable, and at the end of the day it’s pretty much the same thing as the original plot, and there’s also an emphasis on finding codes for doors and storage cabinets.
There is a focus on horror and some little scripted sequences but that thing is subjective from person to person.
The weapon viability has also been changed around: The fists are just as a very last resort as before however the berserk power up is so rare you only come across it twice, the chainsaw is exactly the same, the torch is good against the unarmed zombies, the pistol is a last resort however unlike the originals it has perfect accuracy, unlike the first game where the shotgun is the go to gun most of the time since it has ridiculously good range and accuracy for a shotgun, the shotgun in doom 3 is only good to use at short to close range due to the large amount of spread, and it has a lower rate of fire, this gun is good to use against the weaker enemies such as the first game. (People complain that the shotgun is really overpowered in doom 3 however it’s the same as the first game in the sense that all of the enemies that can die in one hit in doom 3 can die in one hit in the originals) The machinegun is good for the medium enemies at for when the enemies are at a longer range. The minigun is a heavy weapon this time around and it is good for the heavy enemies and just any enemies though I find myself using it on the heavy enemies when they are too close for the rocket launcher. The grenades are almost useless since they bounce around too much. The plasma guns role is unchanged from the originals. The rocket launcher is good for the heavier enemies and boss fights, and finally the BFG…sadly I only find myself using it twice which are for two different boss fights, whereas in the doom 2 it is very useful for taking out a group of enemies and enemies you want to kill as quickly as possible.

If there’s one problem with Doom 3 it’s that you can’t switch weapons when you reload, that doesn’t sound like much and it also happens in a few other games as well, but in this it means the difference between life and death because you’ll have three or four enemies rushing at you and there’s nothing you can do about it because you are stuck in a reload animation.
Don't get the bfg edition, because it ruins a lot of things in the game: it's far too bright so it basically turns down the atmosphere, there is a crappy torch that you can now use and have a gun out at the same time but it is too far to the left and runs out of battery too quickly, and it's supposed to be a HD re-mastered version of the game and it doesn't look any different, and it is very dumbed down and made far too easy to the point where the explosive barrels do ♥♥♥♥ all, there are too much health and ammo pickups lying around, the enemies do far less damage, and in the expansion pack there's even one section that was removed from the game! (That being that large room with all of the pillars and enemies in hell) Be sure to get the original version.
I love this game as much as the originals though doom 2 is my favourite, this is really one of those games where you have to try it for yourself because of how polarising it is.

This game from the mid 1996 seem to be altered to work on newer software and hardware.
Therefore you will have rather outdated graphics and resolution to handelt with. There is also some input lag to deal with.
Its a real time strategy game with robots and some humour.
You are playing a campaign (lasts about 3 to 5 hours, depending on your gaming style) in which you gradually get more units.
The units consist of different type of infantry and tanks/vehicules (size as well as function). There are no planes.
Each mission starts of with a handful of units (mostly infantry) and it is your goal to get the flags of each map sector.
Most of the time there is a factory (which can either produce infantry or tanks) or other building (radar, maintenance/repair) which then belongs to you.
The more sectors you control, the faster your factories will produce.
I bought the game for old times sake. Played it hours with my friend in "multiplayer" (which does not exist here) ages ago...and we are talking serial/nullmodem cable here ;)
The AI is not particular challenging, its rather easy to win (or I have missed the difficulty level, which does not exist).
And the game is certainly not a beauty for todays standard (was pretty sweet back then in the mid nineties), especially the whole resolution thing.
There was or maybe even still is an open source remake...any remake would be great to be honest.
If you are not somewhat affiliated with this game and suffer from some sort of nostalgia (like I did), I cannot recommend the game. If they did a remake, that would be certainly another story.

Improves on Sniper Elite 2 in most ways, much more polished game. There's not much innovation in the storytelling of the missions, but the gameplay definitely makes up for it. There are also four DLC missions worth doing (one of them does re-use an area from the full game though, booooo). Last thought... I honestly wish Sniper Elite was a first person series. The over the right shoulder camera works well most of the time, but can annoy you when you're trying to look left around an object if you aren't close enough for the 'auto cover snap'. Enemies will see you before you see them.
NOTE - I did encounter a game breaking bug on mission 3 (Siwa) where my quicksave got corrupted in an auto mission fail loop. Ugh, had to repeat mission. As such I recommend doing a conventional save before you climb the tower on that mission.

A disappointing game.
